stories.title: Remembering Afghanistan’s Operation Medusa, 20 years later
stories.summary: A weekend gathering marks the 20th anniversary of the offensive, which included some of the fiercest gunfights Canadians faced in Afghanistan
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
As the 30-millimetre shells from American warplanes rained down, Jeff Rainey tumbled down the hillside where he and other Canadian soldiers had gathered.

“It felt like somebody hit my leg with a sledgehammer and then I rolled over some more, and then I got hit in the back,” the master corporal remembered.

He saw another soldier, Bruce Moncur, with an open skull injury. Despite his own wounds, Mr. Rainey did his best to bandage Mr. Moncur.

They were in Afghanistan, ON Sept. 4, 2006, during the largest Canadian combat operation since the Korean War. Mr. Rainey’s platoon was preparing to attack a Taliban position but instead was mistakenly strafed by its ally.

Now, two decades later, Mr. Rainey and other soldiers will attend a weekend gathering marking the 20th anniversary of Operation Medusa , an offensive that saw some of the fiercest gunfights Canadians faced in Afghanistan.

This year’s reunion comes amid unprecedented acrimony between Canada and the United States, two countries whose military once fought side by side in Afghanistan.

“I cannot believe that we are seeing this,” Mr. Rainey said, describing the American political stance as “a ridiculous anomaly.”

Mr. Moncur says he holds no grudges against the American pilot who fired on his platoon because it was an accident. His feelings are however different when it comes to present-day American policies.

“It’s harder to forgive a deliberate act of aggression rather than an accident like shooting your own side,” he said.

Another veteran, David Goldenberg, recalled the goodwill between Canadians and Americans deployed in Afghanistan. “We did it because it was the right thing to do. So now you sit here 20 some years later … and you’re scratching your head, going ‘This does not make sense’ and it’s sad.”

The three were among more than 40,000 Canadian military personnel who served in Afghanistan in support of the U.S. after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist strikes.

After 9/11, Canada’s military stepped into the global fight on terror as it headed for war in Afghanistan

In the summer of 2006, the Canadian military deployed to Kandahar region, where coalition forces came under the command of a Canadian general, David Fraser.

Mr. Goldenberg, then a warrant officer, landed in Kandahar in August with a military psychological operations team, doing outreach with the local population.

Mr. Rainey and Mr. Moncur, who was a corporal, arrived around the same time, with 8 Platoon, Charles Company, one of the sub-units of the 1st Battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment.

Within weeks, the regiment was called to spearhead Operation Medusa, to clear the Taliban from the Pashmul area, west of Kandahar City.

Operation Medusa: Objective Rugby

Operation Medusa was a major Canadian-led Nato offensive conducted in Kandahar province, Afghanistan, from Sept. 2 to 17, 2006. During the operation, Charles Company of the 1st Battalion, Royal Canadian Regiment, which consisted of 7 Platoon and 8 Platoon, was tasked with capturing a heavily defended Taliban strongpoint known as the White School, designated Objective Rugby. The battle for Objective Rugby was intense and costly, resulting in the deaths of five Canadian soldiers.

The company takes a hillside called Masum Ghar.

The company crosses the Arghandab River, riding in armoured LAV III and G-Wagon vehicles.

*The Canadian combat engineers brought bulldozers to breach some of the obstacles.

8 Platoon begins clearing buildings nearby.

7 Platoon vehicles approach the White School when the enemy opens fire. Sgt. Shane Stachnik and Warrant Officer Richard Nolan are killed.

As the soldiers retreat, a casualty collection point is set up beside a Zettelmeyer wheel loader, which is struck by a Taliban rocket, killing Private William Cushley and Warrant Officer Frank Mellish.

A coalition plane mistakenly drops a 1,000-pound bomb into the scene but it doesn’t explode.

The company returns to the foot of Masum Ghar.

At dawn as they prepare to attack again, 8 Platoon is mistakenly strafed by two U.S. A-10 Thunderbolt warplanes, killing Private Mark Graham and wounding 30 others.

Murat yükselir / the globe and mail, source: in their own words : canadian stories of valour and bravery from afghanistan, 2001-2007. Canadian defence academy press, 2013.; google earth

Charles Company had to take a Taliban strongpoint known as the White School. Four Canadian soldiers of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry had died there during a firefight on Aug. 3.

Before departing, they were advised to call home but weren’t allowed to reveal anything about the mission. Mr. Moncur phoned his aunt to say he loved her. She replied that she loved him, too. He repeated his words with more emphasis but she didn’t pick up on the insistent tone in his voice.

On Sept. 2, Charles Company occupied a rocky height known as Masum Ghar, across a river from the White School. They had been assured that there would be several days of heavy artillery and air strikes before the infantry would start the assault. However, ON the morning of Sept. 3, the troops were told to get ready to attack.

Both Mr. Rainey and Mr. Moncur recalled that the soldiers were unhappy about the order. The coalition had already dropped pamphlets telling civilians to leave so the enemy was certainly alerted to the impending attack. “Any reasonable person would have known that this was not going to go well,” Mr. Rainey said.

Their general, Mr. Fraser, later justified the earlier start by saying that the Taliban were so deeply dug in that “two or three more days of aerial bombardment would have accomplished little.”

The morning of Sept. 3, Charles company forded the Arghandab River. Most of the men rode on LAV III armoured vehicles and combat engineers brought bulldozers and wheel loaders to breach the berms and ditches.

They made their way through tall fields of marijuana. On the left, 8 Platoon dismounted and started clearing a cluster of buildings. On the right, 7 Platoon approached the White School.

“As soon as we walked in far enough, they shot a green pen flare into the air, and that’s when all hell broke loose,” Mr. Moncur said.

The Taliban opened up with small arms, rocket-propelled grenades and recoilless guns on 7 Platoon’s vehicles, killing Sergeant Shane Stachnik and Warrant Officer Richard Nolan .

The Canadians fired back, retrieved their wounded and set up a casualty collection point.

Mr. Moncur recalled that, as bullets ripped through the marijuana fields, the stalks caught fire and it smelled of burning cannabis. He and Warrant Officer Frank Mellish came over to assist at the casualty collection point.

Mr. Moncur saw Mr. Mellish’s self-assured demeanour amid the fighting and that gave him the confidence to open the rear hatch of his LAV and fire his C9 squad machine gun.

Suddenly a rocket flew by his head, singeing his chin and shoulder. It hit the casualty collection point, killing Private William Cushley and fatally wounding Mr. Mellish.

“There’s bodies sprawled everywhere … I’m standing there and I’m watching these guys writhe and move around in pain and screaming,” Mr. Moncur said.

Adding to the chaos, a coalition plane mistakenly dropped a bomb on them. It bounced on the ground like a spiked football but didn’t explode.

The Canadians started to pull back. Mr. Rainey tried to board a LAV and nearly stepped on a friend, Corporal Derick Lewis, who had been shot in the arm and was lying on the cabin’s floor. Mr. Rainey ended up retreating on foot with his machine gunner.

The shootout lasted five hours and Mr. Moncur went through three boxes of ammunition, about 600 rounds.

The next day, Sept. 4, would bring the American attack as they prepared for another assault on the White School. Mr. Moncur wasn’t hungry but sat down for breakfast to give him energy for combat.

Suddenly he was tossed into the air. “I felt like I was being electrocuted. Like I had touched a socket.” His body bent “like an accordion” when he landed, then he blacked out.

When he regained consciousness, his right arm was thrashing about, like a fish taken out of water.

His arm was flailing because the left side of his brain had been hit. “Then the blood started to just pour like a faucet, and now I’m panicked, and I’m trying to catch the blood … my hands were absolutely overflowing.”

He crawled toward Mr. Rainey, who was also injured. He heard someone yell, “Who threw ammunition in the fire?” because they hadn’t realized yet that they had been shot by their own side.

The accidental strafing by the American A-10 attack plane killed one man, Private Mark Graham, and wounded 30 others, including the company commander, Major Matthew Sprague.

Mr. Moncur believed he was going to die and started thinking of his loved ones. A Chinook helicopter airlifted him to an army base for emergency brain surgery. He and Mr. Rainey were among the wounded flown to the Landstuhl military hospital in Germany.

Across the river, Mr. Goldenberg and the psy-ops team were manning a road checkpoint and they saw the strafing from afar, then heard the radio call “check fire, check fire,” as the pilots realized their mistake.

With Charles Company having lost a third of its personnel, including its commander, the rest of the unit was regrouped into an ad hoc force with various other troops, including American soldiers, a Canadian reconnaissance squadron and the psy-ops team. The new unit, called Task Force Grizzly, was commanded by a U.S. National Guard colonel, Steve Williams.

“We worked with them, we ate with them, we sat with them … we had a common goal," Mr. Goldenberg said about joining force with Americans.

The offensive resumed with a push from the north by another Canadian company before Task Force Grizzly recrossed the river. By Sept. 17 Medusa ended with the remaining enemy fighters having fled the area.

While the Taliban no longer engaged in head-on combat, 12 more Canadian soldiers died that fall from ambushes, improvised explosive devices or suicide bomber attacks.

A month after the start of the offensive, the psy-ops team got permission to return to their base. Riding two G-Wagon vehicles, they joined a resupply convoy heading for Kandahar City. The team’s commander, Lieutenant Jason Demaine, was in a G-Wagon with a driver, Corporal Piotr Burcew.

Mr. Goldenberg was in the second G-Wagon, a few vehicles behind. As they entered Kandahar City, the convoy started slowing down.

Suddenly there was an explosion and Mr. Goldenberg saw a gigantic ball of flames ahead. “You’re stunned for a moment because it’s just like, what, what was that?”

A suicide bomber on a motorcycle had detonated himself next to Mr. Demaine’s G-Wagon. The vehicle crashed into a ditch but its two occupants managed to walk out of the fiery wreck.

The other Canadians cordoned off the area but now had to pry away from the burning vehicle a stash of anti-tank rockets, which risked blowing up amid the civilians who had gathered at the scene.

“A number of us ran back and forth from the vehicle and removed the sensitive equipment, removed the ammunition, removed the hand grenades,” Mr. Goldenberg said.

Later that month, back in Canada, Mr. Rainey had been discharged from hospital and he took over his unit’s casualty management section. He had post-traumatic stress disorder and he was frustrated by the red tape preventing wounded soldiers from getting better care. He also felt guilty being home while his comrades still fought in Afghanistan. “It was like this miasma around me … it ruined me.”

Mr. Moncur, meanwhile, needed months of physical and occupational therapy before he regained the ability to read, write and speak without slurring his words. It took him a decade to get Veterans Affairs Canada to recognize that he qualified for a 100 per cent disability pension.

Mr. Goldenberg joined the Durham Regional Police Service. Mr. Moncur became a teacher and campaigns to get federal officials to recognize Canadian soldiers whose acts of bravery weren’t properly acknowledged.

Mr. Rainey, who is a power engineer in Alberta, still thinks about the way the war ended in 2021 when the U.S. military withdrew, leaving behind their Afghan allies and letting the Taliban return to power: “What were we there for?”

Before departing, they were advised to call home but weren’t allowed to reveal anything about the mission. Mr. Moncur phoned his aunt to say he loved her. She replied that she loved him, too. He repeated his words with more emphasis but she didn’t pick up on the insistent tone in his voice.

On Sept. 2, Charles Company occupied a rocky height known as Masum Ghar, across a river from the White School. They had been assured that there would be several days of heavy artillery and air strikes before the infantry would start the assault. However, ON the morning of Sept. 3, the troops were told to get ready to attack.

Both Mr. Rainey and Mr. Moncur recalled that the soldiers were unhappy about the order. The coalition had already dropped pamphlets telling civilians to leave so the enemy was certainly alerted to the impending attack. “Any reasonable person would have known that this was not going to go well,” Mr. Rainey said.
Their general, Mr. Fraser, later justified the earlier start by saying that the Taliban were so deeply dug in that “two or three more days of aerial bombardment would have accomplished little.”

The morning of Sept. 3, Charles company forded the Arghandab River. Most of the men rode on LAV III armoured vehicles and combat engineers brought bulldozers and wheel loaders to breach the berms and ditches.
They made their way through tall fields of marijuana. On the left, 8 Platoon dismounted and started clearing a cluster of buildings. On the right, 7 Platoon approached the White School.
“As soon as we walked in far enough, they shot a green pen flare into the air, and that’s when all hell broke loose,” Mr. Moncur said.
The Taliban opened up with small arms, rocket-propelled grenades and recoilless guns on 7 Platoon’s vehicles, killing Sergeant Shane Stachnik and Warrant Officer Richard Nolan .
The Canadians fired back, retrieved their wounded and set up a casualty collection point.

Mr. Moncur recalled that, as bullets ripped through the marijuana fields, the stalks caught fire and it smelled of burning cannabis. He and Warrant Officer Frank Mellish came over to assist at the casualty collection point.
Mr. Moncur saw Mr. Mellish’s self-assured demeanour amid the fighting and that gave him the confidence to open the rear hatch of his LAV and fire his C9 squad machine gun.
Suddenly a rocket flew by his head, singeing his chin and shoulder. It hit the casualty collection point, killing Private William Cushley and fatally wounding Mr. Mellish.
“There’s bodies sprawled everywhere … I’m standing there and I’m watching these guys writhe and move around in pain and screaming,” Mr. Moncur said.
Adding to the chaos, a coalition plane mistakenly dropped a bomb on them. It bounced on the ground like a spiked football but didn’t explode.

The Canadians started to pull back. Mr. Rainey tried to board a LAV and nearly stepped on a friend, Corporal Derick Lewis, who had been shot in the arm and was lying on the cabin’s floor. Mr. Rainey ended up retreating on foot with his machine gunner.
The shootout lasted five hours and Mr. Moncur went through three boxes of ammunition, about 600 rounds.
The next day, Sept. 4, would bring the American attack as they prepared for another assault on the White School. Mr. Moncur wasn’t hungry but sat down for breakfast to give him energy for combat.
Suddenly he was tossed into the air. “I felt like I was being electrocuted. Like I had touched a socket.” His body bent “like an accordion” when he landed, then he blacked out.
When he regained consciousness, his right arm was thrashing about, like a fish taken out of water.

His arm was flailing because the left side of his brain had been hit. “Then the blood started to just pour like a faucet, and now I’m panicked, and I’m trying to catch the blood … my hands were absolutely overflowing.”
He crawled toward Mr. Rainey, who was also injured. He heard someone yell, “Who threw ammunition in the fire?” because they hadn’t realized yet that they had been shot by their own side.
The accidental strafing by the American A-10 attack plane killed one man, Private Mark Graham, and wounded 30 others, including the company commander, Major Matthew Sprague.

Mr. Moncur believed he was going to die and started thinking of his loved ones. A Chinook helicopter airlifted him to an army base for emergency brain surgery. He and Mr. Rainey were among the wounded flown to the Landstuhl military hospital in Germany.

Across the river, Mr. Goldenberg and the psy-ops team were manning a road checkpoint and they saw the strafing from afar, then heard the radio call “check fire, check fire,” as the pilots realized their mistake.

With Charles Company having lost a third of its personnel, including its commander, the rest of the unit was regrouped into an ad hoc force with various other troops, including American soldiers, a Canadian reconnaissance squadron and the psy-ops team. The new unit, called Task Force Grizzly, was commanded by a U.S. National Guard colonel, Steve Williams.
“We worked with them, we ate with them, we sat with them … we had a common goal," Mr. Goldenberg said about joining force with Americans.

The offensive resumed with a push from the north by another Canadian company before Task Force Grizzly recrossed the river. By Sept. 17 Medusa ended with the remaining enemy fighters having fled the area.
While the Taliban no longer engaged in head-on combat, 12 more Canadian soldiers died that fall from ambushes, improvised explosive devices or suicide bomber attacks.

A month after the start of the offensive, the psy-ops team got permission to return to their base. Riding two G-Wagon vehicles, they joined a resupply convoy heading for Kandahar City. The team’s commander, Lieutenant Jason Demaine, was in a G-Wagon with a driver, Corporal Piotr Burcew.
Mr. Goldenberg was in the second G-Wagon, a few vehicles behind. As they entered Kandahar City, the convoy started slowing down.
Suddenly there was an explosion and Mr. Goldenberg saw a gigantic ball of flames ahead. “You’re stunned for a moment because it’s just like, what, what was that?”
A suicide bomber on a motorcycle had detonated himself next to Mr. Demaine’s G-Wagon. The vehicle crashed into a ditch but its two occupants managed to walk out of the fiery wreck.
The other Canadians cordoned off the area but now had to pry away from the burning vehicle a stash of anti-tank rockets, which risked blowing up amid the civilians who had gathered at the scene.
“A number of us ran back and forth from the vehicle and removed the sensitive equipment, removed the ammunition, removed the hand grenades,” Mr. Goldenberg said.

Later that month, back in Canada, Mr. Rainey had been discharged from hospital and he took over his unit’s casualty management section. He had post-traumatic stress disorder and he was frustrated by the red tape preventing wounded soldiers from getting better care. He also felt guilty being home while his comrades still fought in Afghanistan. “It was like this miasma around me … it ruined me.”

Mr. Moncur, meanwhile, needed months of physical and occupational therapy before he regained the ability to read, write and speak without slurring his words. It took him a decade to get Veterans Affairs Canada to recognize that he qualified for a 100 per cent disability pension.

Mr. Goldenberg joined the Durham Regional Police Service. Mr. Moncur became a teacher and campaigns to get federal officials to recognize Canadian soldiers whose acts of bravery weren’t properly acknowledged.

Mr. Rainey, who is a power engineer in Alberta, still thinks about the way the war ended in 2021 when the U.S. military withdrew, leaving behind their Afghan allies and letting the Taliban return to power: “What were we there for?”

content_blocks.text: As the 30-millimetre shells from American warplanes rained down, Jeff Rainey tumbled down the hillside where he and other Canadian soldiers had gathered.
“It felt like somebody hit my leg with a sledgehammer and then I rolled over some more, and then I got hit in the back,” the master corporal remembered.
He saw another soldier, Bruce Moncur, with an open skull injury. Despite his own wounds, Mr. Rainey did his best to bandage Mr. Moncur.

They were in Afghanistan, ON Sept. 4, 2006, during the largest Canadian combat operation since the Korean War. Mr. Rainey’s platoon was preparing to attack a Taliban position but instead was mistakenly strafed by its ally.

Now, two decades later, Mr. Rainey and other soldiers will attend a weekend gathering marking the 20th anniversary of Operation Medusa , an offensive that saw some of the fiercest gunfights Canadians faced in Afghanistan.

content_blocks.text: This year’s reunion comes amid unprecedented acrimony between Canada and the United States, two countries whose military once fought side by side in Afghanistan.
“I cannot believe that we are seeing this,” Mr. Rainey said, describing the American political stance as “a ridiculous anomaly.”
Mr. Moncur says he holds no grudges against the American pilot who fired on his platoon because it was an accident. His feelings are however different when it comes to present-day American policies.
“It’s harder to forgive a deliberate act of aggression rather than an accident like shooting your own side,” he said.

Another veteran, David Goldenberg, recalled the goodwill between Canadians and Americans deployed in Afghanistan. “We did it because it was the right thing to do. So now you sit here 20 some years later … and you’re scratching your head, going ‘This does not make sense’ and it’s sad.”
The three were among more than 40,000 Canadian military personnel who served in Afghanistan in support of the U.S. after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist strikes.
After 9/11, Canada’s military stepped into the global fight on terror as it headed for war in Afghanistan
In the summer of 2006, the Canadian military deployed to Kandahar region, where coalition forces came under the command of a Canadian general, David Fraser.
Mr. Goldenberg, then a warrant officer, landed in Kandahar in August with a military psychological operations team, doing outreach with the local population.

Within weeks, the regiment was called to spearhead Operation Medusa, to clear the Taliban from the Pashmul area, west of Kandahar City.

Operation Medusa was a major Canadian-led Nato offensive conducted in Kandahar province, Afghanistan, from Sept. 2 to 17, 2006. During the operation, Charles Company of the 1st Battalion, Royal Canadian Regiment, which consisted of 7 Platoon and 8 Platoon, was tasked with capturing a heavily defended Taliban strongpoint known as the White School, designated Objective Rugby. The battle for Objective Rugby was intense and costly, resulting in the deaths of five Canadian soldiers.

The company returns to the foot of Masum Ghar.
At dawn as they prepare to attack again, 8 Platoon is mistakenly strafed by two U.S. A-10 Thunderbolt warplanes, killing Private Mark Graham and wounding 30 others.

stories.title: As AI conquers math, its human counterparts seek to steer its powers
stories.summary: An apparent breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes problem has mathematicians weighing what the tech’s rapid advances mean for their profession
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Claude-Louis Navier was an engineering professor in Paris in the 1820s, where he was known for his deep analytical knowledge of bridge-building, but also blamed for relying too much on theory when a bridge he designed cracked and had to be dismantled.

George Gabriel Stokes was the child of a church rector from the small Irish village of Skreen, whose talent for doing sums eventually led him, in 1849, to become the Lucasian professor of mathematics at Cambridge University, a position once held by Isaac Newton.

Born 34 years apart in different countries, the two never met. Yet, their names are forever entwined thanks to a set of equations they separately formulated, spawning a notoriously pertinacious math problem.

This week, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, as it is known, made headlines after it was declared cracked (like a puzzle, not a bridge) by artificial intelligence.

If verified, the breakthrough is both spectacular and controversial. Mathematicians witnessing first-hand the transformation of their profession by AI are finding it hard to keep up with the growing capabilities of the technology. For some, this week’s news is another sign that, instead of competing with AI, their skills May be better put toward managing its risks.

“I think a lot of us are constantly recalibrating, almost minute by minute, given the pace we’re going at here,” said Deanna Needell, a Vancover-based professor of mathematics at Ucla and the University of British Columbia.

The Navier-Stokes problem concerns the motion of fluids in three dimensions, and whether or not there are circumstances where the equations used to describe them can fail.

Last Tuesday, OpenAI, the tech company behind ChatGPT, said that its AI agents, after 88 hours of computation, had found a situation where this occurs.

This immediately captured media attention, in part because Navier-Stokes is one of seven “millennium problems” that were listed in 2000 as outstanding challenges by the Colorado-based Clay Institute of Mathematics. Each problem is attached to a US$1-million prize for anyone who can provide a verified solution. Prior to this week, only one had been solved, in 2003.

No sooner had OpenAI made its announcement than Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, revealed that he had been working with a collaborator, Levent Alpöge, at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, and they were closing in on their own AI-assisted solution to the problem.

The situation is complicated by the fact that Dr. Buckmaster used OpenAI’s tools for some his research, though OpenAI has said it’s not possible that its model somehow found and used this work to gain the lead in the discovery. Then there’s the question of whether such advancements should be made public in the traditional way, through publication in a peer-reviewed journal.

It’s too soon to know how credit and prize money (if any) will be apportioned, or how history will view the matter. What is not in doubt is that AI has ascended to the highest levels of mathematics with remarkable speed – and likely changed the field forever.

Opinion: The question isn’t whether AI can teach. It’s whether students will let it

The prospect that it could soon climb higher than the brightest human minds is both fascinating and scary.

“I expect most of our research projects ongoing in the world right now to be solved fairly quickly,” said Jacob Tsimerman, a University of Toronto professor. In July, he became the first Canada-based winner of the prestigious Fields Medal , known unofficially as Nobel Prize of mathematics. He added that machines May also “autonomously go on and do math that we haven’t even thought of yet.”

It’s fair to say that many people think of advanced mathematics as the hardest thing the human brain can do. At the professional level, it requires raw intellectual power and years of training to make a meaningful contribution.

One might therefore conclude that mathematics would be among the domains least susceptible to competition from AI. Sure, ChatGPT can write a greeting card poem, but solve a millennium problem?

In fact, Dr. Tsimerman said, what makes math hard for humans is also what makes it amenable to exploration by AI. Unlike the world of everyday experience, the structure of mathematics is formal and logical. Theorems can be proven true or false, with no grey area in between. And, most importantly, from the days of Pythagoras to the present, math is something we perform in an idealized, abstract environment that AI is well-equipped to operate in.

“Math is a closed loop. You can do it just by thinking,” Dr. Tsimerman said.

It was Dr. Tsimerman who instigated the second big math story of the week. A few months ago, after winning the Fields Medal, he revealed he would be working with OpenAI on safety in the use of artificial intelligence – a topic that has become his primary focus. On Tuesday, Dr. Tsimerman said he was launching a new centre dubbed the Mathematical AI Safety Institute in California’s Bay Area, where OpenAI is based.

“Specifically, we’re going to be developing theories with the intention of building safe superintelligence,” Dr. Tsimerman said. The point, he said, is not simply to program AI to avoid bad behaviour, but to make it think in ways that align with human well-being, and follow instructions “not just to the letter, but also in spirit.”

Opinion: Canada promised to watch its doctors train. AI could make that happen

This is a tricky and nuanced pursuit. Until now, Dr. Needell said, AI safety issues have often been regarded as a “masking” problem, which programmers try to address by building guardrails to prevent AI from revealing dangerous knowledge it May have acquired.

Such a stopgap is problematic, however, because it means the knowledge is still in the machine and discoverable in principle. What May be more effective is adjusting the algorithms so they are unable learn certain things in the first place.

Dr. Tsimerman said he hoped current approaches to AI safety will come to be regarded as clumsy early attempts as efforts progress.

The need for such progress was starkly underscored on Thursday, when Anthropic revealed that it had blocked unnamed actors who were trying to use its large language model Claude for research that could lead to a biological weapon.

“I definitely think the work we’ll be doing will be applicable to that problem,” Dr. Tsimerman said. But he added that while the new institute would be concerned with the mathematical side of AI safety, experts in other fields and society at large need to press policy-makers to make those safeguards a priority.

“This is very much an all-hands-on-deck situation,” he said.

This is why an AI victory over the Navier-Stokes problem May pose other challenges. If young researchers decide there is little point in trying to tackle problems that AI will soon master, there will be fewer experts left who can evaluate whether AI is doing something useful or safe.

Davide Gaiotto, a researcher at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Waterloo, Ont., said he can still recall the feeling he experienced at the age of 25, when he realized he had moved from “learning stuff to creating new knowledge.”

He said a key concern in the field now is whether today’s graduate students in math-driven fields will get to feel the same.

If there is a glimmer of optimism, Dr. Needell said, it May lie with what humans possess that machines still lack: real-life experiences and interactions that help to determine what we pay attention to.

“I think there is a human contribution in deciding what is important, what we should be thinking about,” she said. “And I think that is still true for mathematics.”

If there is a glimmer of optimism, Dr. Needell said, it May lie with what humans possess that machines still lack: real-life experiences and interactions that help to determine what we pay attention to.
“I think there is a human contribution in deciding what is important, what we should be thinking about,” she said. “And I think that is still true for mathematics.”

stories.summary: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role, picking tunes for the show. In any given week, that's about 25 songs. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from last week.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role, picking tunes for the show. In any given week, that's about 25 songs. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from last week.
· Posted: Sep 05, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 34 minutes ago
S-Man Lib, Akintoye and Allison Russell are three artists featured on London Morning(Instagram/Facebook)
_WATCH | I Know It:_Video 8

I Know It by S-Man Lib is a nice, chill song to start this list. Mellow island beats and a smooth flow make I Know It a great song to enjoy the last weeks of summer, and it doubles as a relaxed day-starter. If you'd like to see S-Man Lib perform, you're in luck. Just head to Gibbons Park from 11 am to 9 pm today, September 5th. S-Man Lib is one of the performers on the African Caribbean Mosaic Cultural Festival.
_WATCH | The Farmer Freestyle:_Video 9

Have you ever looked down at your plate of food and wondered, how can I thank the farmer that made this possible? That's what rapper Akintoye just did with a new single: The Farmer Freestyle. This outstanding mid-tempo rap track with a luring beat, laced with sweet clarinet will work well on a variety of playlists.
_WATCH | My Love is a Golden Lion:_Video 10

Allison Russell's latest full-length album In the Hour of Chaos is a wonderful body of work with no two songs quite the same. In fact, the new album is a fantastic listening experience because of its diversity of sound. From the new one, London Morning played Love is a Golden Lion featuring Devon Gilfillian. This upbeat and happy-sounding track will work well on your next party playlist or when you want some motivation.

stories.title: St. Thomas cancels L&PS project, but city will keep pushing to rejoin historic rail route - CBC.CA
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video

The mayor of St. Thomas says a council vote this week formally cancelling the city's London and Port Stanley Railway extension project doesn't mean the Railway City is done pushing CN to reconnect the historic link.
· Posted: Sep 12, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
The Port Stanley Terminal Rail operates a tourist train along the former L&PS tracks between St. Thomas and Port Stanley.(Facebook/Port Stanley Terminal Rail)

The City of St. Thomas isn't done pushing CN Rail to reconnect the historic London and Port Stanley Railway (L&PS) route, despite a recent council vote to cancel a related project, the city's mayor says.

On Tuesday, councillors voted to formally scrap the city's unrealized, decade-old L&PS extension project and return the $285,000 still allocated to it into an infrastructure reserve fund. City staff will report back on potential passive recreational uses for the unused land.
While the city hopes to rejoin the former route, cancelling the project frees the restricted funds for other priorities until an agreement can be reached with CN, Mayor Joe Preston said.

“We continue to work with CN. We’re at a stalemate with them … We’re trying to get this connection reconnected. Port Stanley Terminal Rail (PSTR) is the recipient of the connection, and we’ve been trying to help them with it,” Preston said Thursday.
“The city recognizes that, should we be successful … the city would find the funds it needs to do the connection.”
Petition renews push to rejoin former London and Port Stanley rail route
The leftover money has been on the city’s books for a decade. St. Thomas had approved $500,000 for the project in the 2016 budget, with $166,000 from the federal government.
According to a report from city staff, some of the funding was redirected in 2017 to rail-trail active transportation projects, “when it became apparent that the project would not proceed.”
“Administration can confirm that (CN Rail’s) position regarding reconnection of the L&PS rail line to the CN network has not changed,” the report reads.

“CN continues to refuse authorization for a connection to its rail corridor. While advocacy efforts continue, including ongoing support from Member of Parliament Andrew Lawton, the issue remains unresolved and no approval for reconnection has been secured,” the report adds.

CN purchased the L&PS tracks in 1965 from the City of London, and abandoned the portion south of St. Thomas in the early 1980s. PSTR, a tourist train, began operating along those rails in 1983, and CN maintains freight operations on the tracks north of St. Thomas.

Lawton, the MP for Elgin–St. Thomas–London South, has been pushing the federal government to make CN allow PSTR to connect to its tracks, something it was ordered to do in 1990 by what is now the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA).

CN ripped up rail in 1989 between the Barwick Street Bridge and Wellington Street after the CTA ruled the trackage was a spur and exempt from the lengthy process railroads follow to abandon railway lines. PSTR later restored trackage to the north, ending just before Kains Street.
The CTA's order also required CN to replace, at its own cost, a rail diamond it removed south of Barwick Street in 1988, in contravention of an earlier directive.

City staff say St. Thomas “engaged extensively” with CN from 2016 to 2020 in investigating alternate connections after CN refused to allow the original rail crossing to be reinstated — despite the requirement that it replace the rail diamond. No agreement was reached.
CN Rail did not respond to a request for comment before publication, and previous requests in June also went unanswered. A request for comment from CTA was also not returned before publication.
In June, Lawton presented a petition to the House of Commons calling for the transport minister to enforce the CTA’s order.
The government’s official response, filed on Aug. 19 by Transport Minister Mike Kelloway, said neither PSTR nor CN had advised the CTA of concerns related to non-compliance.
Kelloway added, “should the Agency receive information indicating issues with compliance, it will review the matter and determine whether any action is appropriate.”
“I find it a little bit odd that in 30 years of people talking about this issue and raising it, they’re claiming they haven’t heard about it,” Lawton said Thursday.

“But it also gives us a mechanism that PSTR is able to use to put this issue on the agenda, and actually have enforcement of that order take place.” PSTR alone has the legal standing to file a complaint, he said.
“I know the City of St. Thomas will be there to support them. They could even potentially intervene if it were to go to a tribunal. I’ll be there as a supporter as well.”
People board a London and Port Stanley Railway train next to Bathurst Street in downtown London, Ont. in 1956. (CBC)
Dan Vernackt, PTSR’s president, told CBC News the local railway had never filed a complaint with the CTA and had been unaware they needed to do so.
“That was a surprise to me. No one had ever mentioned that,” Vernackt said, adding he plans to submit a letter to the CTA in the next week or so.
PSTR has had more than three decades of dialogue with CN to try and rectify the issue, but “it’s always been squashed in the 11th hour,” he said.

After the former CASO tracks which ran east and west through the city’s core were removed in 2009, the tourist train and the Elgin County Railway Museum, located in the heart of “Railway City,” remain isolated from the national railway network, for now.
Cross-border coalition lays out vision for passenger rail between Ontario, Michigan
The city has been trying to shame CN into being a good corporate citizen, but “they just have not yet caught that disease,” said Preston.
“I understand they’re a business, and they really don’t want a tourism rail line on their freight tracks. But I think we can negotiate the use of it,” he said.

“St. Thomas has just put in a wholly new rail yard in Yarmouth Yards, and CN gets the benefit of that. We’re trying to point out to them, ‘Look, we’re still doing our part for you. Could you do your part for us?’”
A notice at the train station in London, Ont. alerts passengers to the pending end of passenger service along the London and Port Stanley Railway. (CBC)

City staff say St. Thomas “engaged extensively” with CN from 2016 to 2020 in investigating alternate connections after CN refused to allow the original rail crossing to be reinstated — despite the requirement that it replace the rail diamond. No agreement was reached.

CN Rail did not respond to a request for comment before publication, and previous requests in June also went unanswered. A request for comment from CTA was also not returned before publication.

In June, Lawton presented a petition to the House of Commons calling for the transport minister to enforce the CTA’s order.

The government’s official response, filed on Aug. 19 by Transport Minister Mike Kelloway, said neither PSTR nor CN had advised the CTA of concerns related to non-compliance.

Kelloway added, “should the Agency receive information indicating issues with compliance, it will review the matter and determine whether any action is appropriate.”

“I find it a little bit odd that in 30 years of people talking about this issue and raising it, they’re claiming they haven’t heard about it,” Lawton said Thursday.

“But it also gives us a mechanism that PSTR is able to use to put this issue on the agenda, and actually have enforcement of that order take place.” PSTR alone has the legal standing to file a complaint, he said.

“I know the City of St. Thomas will be there to support them. They could even potentially intervene if it were to go to a tribunal. I’ll be there as a supporter as well.”

People board a London and Port Stanley Railway train next to Bathurst Street in downtown London, Ont. in 1956. (CBC)

Dan Vernackt, PTSR’s president, told CBC News the local railway had never filed a complaint with the CTA and had been unaware they needed to do so.

“That was a surprise to me. No one had ever mentioned that,” Vernackt said, adding he plans to submit a letter to the CTA in the next week or so.

PSTR has had more than three decades of dialogue with CN to try and rectify the issue, but “it’s always been squashed in the 11th hour,” he said.

After the former CASO tracks which ran east and west through the city’s core were removed in 2009, the tourist train and the Elgin County Railway Museum, located in the heart of “Railway City,” remain isolated from the national railway network, for now.

Cross-border coalition lays out vision for passenger rail between Ontario, Michigan

The city has been trying to shame CN into being a good corporate citizen, but “they just have not yet caught that disease,” said Preston.

“I understand they’re a business, and they really don’t want a tourism rail line on their freight tracks. But I think we can negotiate the use of it,” he said.

“St. Thomas has just put in a wholly new rail yard in Yarmouth Yards, and CN gets the benefit of that. We’re trying to point out to them, ‘Look, we’re still doing our part for you. Could you do your part for us?’”

A notice at the train station in London, Ont. alerts passengers to the pending end of passenger service along the London and Port Stanley Railway. (CBC)

stories.title: Proof-of-citizenship applications surge, estimated wait time is almost 3 years
stories.summary: Both the wait times and the number of people waiting for a decision regarding their proof-of-citizenship application has surged exponentially since Bill C-3 came into effect, according to new data from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
stories.content:
Both the wait times and the number of people waiting for a decision regarding their proof-of-citizenship application has surged exponentially since Bill C-3 came into effect, according to new data from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada .

More than 136,000 people are awaiting a decision, with estimated wait times now more than 33 months. They include people eligible for citizenship under the amended rules and those who are first-generation descendants. In the case of applications from outside Canada or the United States, the estimated wait time could take an additional three or four months.

The wait time has increased by eight months from this A ugust , when it was estimated to be 25 months. The number of applications has also increased by 14,000.

Bill C-3 , which came into effect in December 2025, amended the Citizenship Act to end the first-generation limit on citizenship by descent, meaning Canadians born outside the country can also pass their citizenship to their children who are born outside the country. It also expanded eligibility to people born before Dec. 15, 2025, if they can prove they’re directly descended from a Canadian ancestor – even if that ancestor left the country years ago.

Half of applications come from U.S.

According to data provided by the Ircc in August, more than 6,100 people have obtained proof of citizenship under these new rules since late 2025.

As of May 31, 51 per cent of all approved citizenship applications under the new eligibility criteria came from people born in the U.S., according to data provided by the Ircc.

One immigration lawyer says the new numbers are “staggering” and “far beyond the capacity of Ircc” to process in a reasonable timeframe.

Kyle Hyndman, an immigration lawyer from Victoria, B.C., told CTVNews.CA on Thursday, that a “significant” number of applications are coming from the south of the border.

“Both what’s happening in the U.S. politically – and also news coverage of the Canadian citizenship situation in the U.S. – have both spurred a lot of interest,” Hyndman said.

“That’s certainly part of the surge, and that’s put all kinds of pressure on every stage in this process,” he said.

Hyndman, who previously served as chair of the Canadian Bar Association’s National Immigration Law Section, said Bill C-3 is certainly a part of the surge, but so is the pressure on the resources of the Ircc.

The unit that handles proof-of-citizenship applications would usually have a small number to deal with, he said, and had the capacity to handle those. But according to Hyndman, it hasn’t been scaled up “sufficiently” to handle the sharp intake.

“Now we’re hearing that they are staffing up, but it seems to me that’s happening almost a year too late,” Hyndman added. “Many of these problems could have been prevented if they’d heeded the warnings earlier on and really prepared for that.”

Are you dealing with delays on your citizenship application? We want to hear from you. Share your story by emailing us at dotcom@bellmedia.CA with your name, general location and phone number in case we want to follow up. Your comments May be used in a CTV News story.

‘A predictable uptake’

Christine Beltempo, the current chair of the Canadian Bar Association National Immigration Law Section and a lawyer with the national law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CTVNews.CA on Friday that she’s seeing many applications coming in from other countries besides the U.S., like Mexico.

“You’re creating additional bureaucracy for some people who actually are presumably, according to the new law, Canadian citizens,” she said, referring to people from countries like Mexico, who need a visa application to enter Canada, unless they get their citizenship certificate.

Outside of the U.S., the most approved applications are from Mexico, Bolivia, the United Kingdom and its territories, China, India, Bolivia, France, Australia and Italy, according to the Ircc’s data.

Beltempo called the surge in processing times “a predictable uptake,” following the amendment to Bill C-3, which is leading to “frustration” among applicants who were looking forward to this legislative change.

“What we’re seeing is disappointment, frustration, mixed emotions and certainly people finding it very difficult to plan their lives and their futures in Canada, without having a predictable amount of time before which they can actually get their documentation,” she said.

Beltempo added that the Ircc is facing backlogs in other departments as well, which needs to be examined by the federal government. She says it’s concerning for associations like the Canadian Bar Association, in terms of access to justice and other programs.

“I think it’s important to remind the public that this change came as a result of a court finding that the previous law was unconstitutional.”

‘When you’re Canadian, you have the right to be here’

Before Bill C-3 was amended, Canadian citizenship by descent was limited to first-generation individuals, born or adopted outside the country by a Canadian citizen. That restriction was subsequently struck down in a 2023 ruling by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, which found it unconstitutional.

Richard Kurland, an immigration lawyer and policy analyst from Vancouver, told CTVNews.CA Friday, that the sudden uptick in the number of applications and the increase in estimated wait times is a combination of the political tension between Canada and the U.S., in addition to the Bill C-3 amendment.

“They certainly drop the ball in failing to resource the citizenship people to process, resulting in three years and longer processing times,” Richard Kurland said. “When you’re Canadian, you have the right to be here.”

Kurland said despite people having a claim to Canadian citizenship, the province they enter cannot allow them access to health care, public education or employment without the paperwork from the Ircc.

“There’s no way that the (federal) government could not know that the inventories would become bloated (and) processing times would go through the ceiling,” he said.

“They dropped the ball big time.”

Meanwhile, multiple factors are to blame for an increase in the volume of applications outside of Bill C-3, an Ircc spokesperson told CTVNews.CA in a statement on Friday.

“Complex cases often require substantial documentary evidence and additional verification, which can extend timelines,” the spokesperson wrote.

“The current estimate should be understood in that context, rather than as a direct comparison with historical figures that were calculated using different inventories or methodologies.”

With files from CTV News’ Daniel Otis and The Canadian Press

stories.title: AI has changed the calculus for computer-science students, and schools that hope to teach them
stories.summary: Faced with the risk that artificial intelligence will drain the job market, some of Canada’s young coders are changing tack at university
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Just a few years ago, applying to a prestigious university computer science program might have been a no-brainer for a student like Mahimn Patel.

Mr. Patel, 18, built software for fun in high school, including an app that helped his classmates track their volunteer hours, and an artificial intelligence agent for realtors in Texas. During a recent video interview, he had multiple AI agents running in the background debugging his latest hobby horse, an AI-enabled app for stock trading.

Getting into computer science, a notoriously competitive program at top Canadian schools, wouldn’t have been a problem for Mr. Patel. He graduated from Central Peel Secondary School in Brampton, Ont., in June with a 97 average.

But Mr. Patel decided not to apply for a computer science program. He chose to pursue a degree in applied mathematics at the University of Toronto, where he started classes last week.

“It’s mathematics and physics that develop your brain the most after four years of education. With AI, that development is what matters more,” he said. “Because if you can think more creatively and more rigorously on your own, you’re able to actually use the AI better.”

Other Canadian high-school students – and their parents – are looking at how AI is revolutionizing higher education and the workplace and making a similar calculation, though the jury’s still out on how the job market will adapt to that change.

Applications to undergraduate computer and information systems programs have plunged at universities in Ontario, the only province that makes aggregate application data public. In the most recent admissions cycle, the number of applications to computer and information systems fell to 45,260, down 44 per cent from a high of just more than 80,000 applications in 2023, according to the Ontario Universities’ Application Centre. (Information systems degrees generally combine IT and business management.)

The decline in that period was more precipitous than for any other category of undergraduate programs. It happened as the overall number of applications grew in the face of Ottawa’s crackdown on international student visas, which hit colleges harder than universities.

And while there isn’t necessarily a straight line between the number of applications a program receives and the number of students it admits, about 2,500 fewer students have accepted offers to start undergraduate computer science degrees in Ontario this fall compared to two years ago.

“This is true all over the world,” said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

Government funding and university priorities factor into the number of students admitted to computer science, and emerging specializations in AI are becoming more popular. But computer science leaders at universities in other provinces are seeing the same overall drop in applications. This suggests Ontario’s figures aren’t an outlier.

Teenagers raised in the just-learn-to-code era worry that AI can already do much of a junior software engineer’s job, and they’re not sure that making “artisanal bespoke human code, like it’s the sourdough bread from the local bakery, is going to be a great job market,” Prof. Daley said.

Waning interest in computer science degrees is to be expected. Big Tech stalwarts such as Meta, Google, Shopify, Oracle, Amazon and others have laid off tens of thousands of workers in recent years. The internet is awash in stories of young tech workers struggling in a brutal job market. And it’s not the first time a broad technological shift has caused students to feel skittish.

In another sense, it’s a surprise. Artificial intelligence threatens jobs of all kinds. But it was born of computer science, and leaders in the field say students will still be the vanguard; programs are tailoring their offerings as such. Surely young people who understand how generative AI works and know how to build with it have the best shot at a safe future?

Either way, trends in computer science education underscore a dilemma facing many teenagers and twentysomethings, regardless of what they want to be when they grow up. AI is improving so fast that no students know what awaits them on the other side of a degree.

“We don’t know what the labour market is going to look like five or 10 years from now,” said Prof. Daley, who was also vice-chair of the Council of Ontario Universities’ AI Task Force . “I don’t think there’s going to be a complete apocalypse of jobs and there’ll be nothing for humans to do. But I think the nature of what we do is going to change.”

Luigi Benedicenti, a professor and dean in the Faculty of Computer Science at the University of New Brunswick, used to be greeted by big groups of students and their eager parents when he spoke at high-school recruitment fairs or university orientation events a few years ago.

Computer science – where students typically studied coding, computer architecture, advanced algorithms and computational theory, among other subjects – was a hot program. His audience viewed it as a ticket to the good life.

That began to change recently, Prof. Benedicenti said. Although UNB, like many Canadian universities, does not disclose application figures for individual programs, the dean said applications plunged two years ago. That’s when computer science suffered the one-two punch of federal restrictions on international student visas and a growing public recognition of AI’s coding prowess, he explained.

“Before we had a room full of parents when we were working on orientation,” Prof. Benedicenti said. “Last year, we had far fewer parents than we would have liked, and that is because, in my opinion, there is this perception that artificial intelligence is, if not a present, then a future danger to the career of young computer scientists.”

While some university officials, particularly outside Ontario, agree with Prof. Benedicenti that Ottawa’s curbing of international student visas contributed to the decline, federal policy changes don’t seem to be the driving factor behind fewer students applying to university computer programs in Canada’s most populous province.

Ouac reports separately on applications from students coming straight out of an Ontario high school and all other applicants, a category that includes international, out-of-province and mature students. Applications to computer programs fell similarly for both streams between 2023 and 2026.

Fewer applications don’t necessarily translate to fewer students majoring in computer science.

Take the University of Calgary, where the number of applications to computer science peaked for entry in the fall of 2023, and has dropped since, a university spokesman said by e-mail.

Despite the decline, registration in computer science was up to 1,745 students last fall from 1,483 three years earlier. That’s partly because the Alberta government funded an expansion of high-demand programs, including computer science, colleges and universities beginning in the fall of 2022.

At the University of Alberta, registrations rose 32.7 per cent between the autumns of 2020 and 2025 across computer-science related programs at the graduate and undergraduate level, a school spokesman said.

In other words, regardless of softening demand, there are still enough students interested in computer science to fill the seats – even in a province that recently increased the supply.

They might just be able to get in with lower marks.

Richard Zhao, the acting co-head of computer science at the University of Calgary, said the average student starting his program this fall graduated high school with a 79.6 average, down from the high 80s at the peak of computer science’s popularity a couple of years ago.

“We are aware of students coming with slightly lower averages, and we’ve essentially adapted our curriculum to account for them,” he said. “We provide more support.”

There are upsides to some Canadian computer science programs being less selective. It opens the door to talented young people who love the logical problem-solving that defines the work, but who couldn’t at age 17 or 18 pull off the A+ marks to earn a spot.

“If you’re getting fewer applications and you’re accepting the same number of students, then the quality is probably going to go down a bit,” said Joanne Atlee, a computer science professor at the University of Waterloo. “I think it’s also true that a lot of the students who might have applied and are choosing not to probably had less of a passion for the field.”

Still, getting into computer science programs remains a cutthroat game at the country’s most prestigious schools.

Dina Dawoud, the associate dean of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Waterloo, said the school continues to receive 12 applications for every computer science student it admits.

Spokespeople for McGill University and the University of Toronto, where undergraduate computer science enrolments have been stable over the past couple of years, also say their applicant pools remain strong.

Eyal de Lara, chair of the Department of Computer Science at U of T, said the department froze undergraduate enrolment about a decade ago because it had already grown “quite large” for a selective program. Applications skyrocketed nonetheless until the volume started to taper off two years ago, he added.

“We had, effectively, an enormous applicant pool,” Prof. de Lara said. “Some students realize it’s going to be impossible to get to U of T and apply to other universities.”

That’s another possible explanation for the drop in applications. As top Canadian computer science programs developed reputations for turning away academic superstars with intimidating resumes, some high-school seniors might have considered applying futile – or simply not worth it if the degree no longer guaranteed a six-figure salary straight out of school.

The reputed competitiveness of computer science played a part in 17-year-old Ella Poku’s decision to pursue a degree in physics instead. She started first-year classes in the discipline at U of T last week.

Although Ms. Poku had marks in the low 90s, coding experience, and two older brothers studying computer science at McMaster University, she feared she wouldn’t get into computer science.

She and her family had recently moved from Ghana to Ancaster, Ont., near Hamilton. “I only moved to Canada in 2023. I didn’t have as many extracurriculars or connections as other people, so that was, like, a big factor for me since I wasn’t too sure about if I would get in or not,” she said. “And if I didn’t, it would be a big problem.”

The job market for computer science graduates worried her, too, and led her to conclude she’d be better off with a more general hard science degree. “I still wasn’t too sure about going to computer science because I’m not the type of person who wants to always be nervous about my job or my stability.”

Are students like Ms. Poku right to be worried? There’s a fierce debate about whether, in the long run, artificial intelligence, which can already write and debug basic code, will steal jobs from computer scientists or create lucrative new opportunities for them.

In the short run, Statistics Canada reported last January that between the launch of ChatGPT in November, 2022, and December of 2025, coding-intensive jobs such as software engineering and web design grew at the same rate as other jobs. But the gains were concentrated among Canadian coding professionals aged 30 to 49; job opportunities stagnated for their counterparts under 30.

In the U.S., a trio of economists at Stanford University mined payroll data to report a widening employment gap between young workers in AI-exposed professions, such as software engineering, customer service, accounting and secretarial work, and their peers in less-exposed industries. As of last month, they pegged the gap for U.S. workers aged 22-25 at 19 per cent. There wasn’t a comparable gap for older workers.

Leo Tenenbaum, 22, found the Canadian tech job market much tougher to crack than expected when they were applying to computer science programs in the fall of 2020.

Although they graduated from the University of Toronto in June, 2025, with a first-place win in an undergraduate student research contest under their belt, their resumes and cover letters went unanswered for months. They applied for about 50 jobs online before a friend of a friend opened the door at Mozilla, where Tenenbaum started as a software engineer in February.

“It was very discouraging at that time,” Tenenbaum said. “I was feeling like I’d never get anywhere.”

Applications and enrolments dropped in the early 1980s and again in the early 2000s, when personal computers and the early internet’s dot-com crash scared students into believing there would be fewer jobs for computer scientists. paragraphs: Just a few years ago, applying to a prestigious university computer science program might have been a no-brainer for a student like Mahimn Patel.

Mr. Patel, 18, built software for fun in high school, including an app that helped his classmates track their volunteer hours, and an artificial intelligence agent for realtors in Texas. During a recent video interview, he had multiple AI agents running in the background debugging his latest hobby horse, an AI-enabled app for stock trading.

Getting into computer science, a notoriously competitive program at top Canadian schools, wouldn’t have been a problem for Mr. Patel. He graduated from Central Peel Secondary School in Brampton, Ont., in June with a 97 average.
But Mr. Patel decided not to apply for a computer science program. He chose to pursue a degree in applied mathematics at the University of Toronto, where he started classes last week.

“It’s mathematics and physics that develop your brain the most after four years of education. With AI, that development is what matters more,” he said. “Because if you can think more creatively and more rigorously on your own, you’re able to actually use the AI better.”

Other Canadian high-school students – and their parents – are looking at how AI is revolutionizing higher education and the workplace and making a similar calculation, though the jury’s still out on how the job market will adapt to that change.

Applications to undergraduate computer and information systems programs have plunged at universities in Ontario, the only province that makes aggregate application data public. In the most recent admissions cycle, the number of applications to computer and information systems fell to 45,260, down 44 per cent from a high of just more than 80,000 applications in 2023, according to the Ontario Universities’ Application Centre. (Information systems degrees generally combine IT and business management.)

The decline in that period was more precipitous than for any other category of undergraduate programs. It happened as the overall number of applications grew in the face of Ottawa’s crackdown on international student visas, which hit colleges harder than universities.

And while there isn’t necessarily a straight line between the number of applications a program receives and the number of students it admits, about 2,500 fewer students have accepted offers to start undergraduate computer science degrees in Ontario this fall compared to two years ago.
“This is true all over the world,” said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

Government funding and university priorities factor into the number of students admitted to computer science, and emerging specializations in AI are becoming more popular. But computer science leaders at universities in other provinces are seeing the same overall drop in applications. This suggests Ontario’s figures aren’t an outlier.

Teenagers raised in the just-learn-to-code era worry that AI can already do much of a junior software engineer’s job, and they’re not sure that making “artisanal bespoke human code, like it’s the sourdough bread from the local bakery, is going to be a great job market,” Prof. Daley said.

Waning interest in computer science degrees is to be expected. Big Tech stalwarts such as Meta, Google, Shopify, Oracle, Amazon and others have laid off tens of thousands of workers in recent years. The internet is awash in stories of young tech workers struggling in a brutal job market. And it’s not the first time a broad technological shift has caused students to feel skittish.

In another sense, it’s a surprise. Artificial intelligence threatens jobs of all kinds. But it was born of computer science, and leaders in the field say students will still be the vanguard; programs are tailoring their offerings as such. Surely young people who understand how generative AI works and know how to build with it have the best shot at a safe future?

Either way, trends in computer science education underscore a dilemma facing many teenagers and twentysomethings, regardless of what they want to be when they grow up. AI is improving so fast that no students know what awaits them on the other side of a degree.

“We don’t know what the labour market is going to look like five or 10 years from now,” said Prof. Daley, who was also vice-chair of the Council of Ontario Universities’ AI Task Force . “I don’t think there’s going to be a complete apocalypse of jobs and there’ll be nothing for humans to do. But I think the nature of what we do is going to change.”

Luigi Benedicenti, a professor and dean in the Faculty of Computer Science at the University of New Brunswick, used to be greeted by big groups of students and their eager parents when he spoke at high-school recruitment fairs or university orientation events a few years ago.

Computer science – where students typically studied coding, computer architecture, advanced algorithms and computational theory, among other subjects – was a hot program. His audience viewed it as a ticket to the good life.

That began to change recently, Prof. Benedicenti said. Although UNB, like many Canadian universities, does not disclose application figures for individual programs, the dean said applications plunged two years ago. That’s when computer science suffered the one-two punch of federal restrictions on international student visas and a growing public recognition of AI’s coding prowess, he explained.

“Before we had a room full of parents when we were working on orientation,” Prof. Benedicenti said. “Last year, we had far fewer parents than we would have liked, and that is because, in my opinion, there is this perception that artificial intelligence is, if not a present, then a future danger to the career of young computer scientists.”

While some university officials, particularly outside Ontario, agree with Prof. Benedicenti that Ottawa’s curbing of international student visas contributed to the decline, federal policy changes don’t seem to be the driving factor behind fewer students applying to university computer programs in Canada’s most populous province.

Ouac reports separately on applications from students coming straight out of an Ontario high school and all other applicants, a category that includes international, out-of-province and mature students. Applications to computer programs fell similarly for both streams between 2023 and 2026.
Fewer applications don’t necessarily translate to fewer students majoring in computer science.
Take the University of Calgary, where the number of applications to computer science peaked for entry in the fall of 2023, and has dropped since, a university spokesman said by e-mail.

Despite the decline, registration in computer science was up to 1,745 students last fall from 1,483 three years earlier. That’s partly because the Alberta government funded an expansion of high-demand programs, including computer science, colleges and universities beginning in the fall of 2022.

At the University of Alberta, registrations rose 32.7 per cent between the autumns of 2020 and 2025 across computer-science related programs at the graduate and undergraduate level, a school spokesman said.
In other words, regardless of softening demand, there are still enough students interested in computer science to fill the seats – even in a province that recently increased the supply.
They might just be able to get in with lower marks.

Richard Zhao, the acting co-head of computer science at the University of Calgary, said the average student starting his program this fall graduated high school with a 79.6 average, down from the high 80s at the peak of computer science’s popularity a couple of years ago.
“We are aware of students coming with slightly lower averages, and we’ve essentially adapted our curriculum to account for them,” he said. “We provide more support.”

There are upsides to some Canadian computer science programs being less selective. It opens the door to talented young people who love the logical problem-solving that defines the work, but who couldn’t at age 17 or 18 pull off the A+ marks to earn a spot.

“If you’re getting fewer applications and you’re accepting the same number of students, then the quality is probably going to go down a bit,” said Joanne Atlee, a computer science professor at the University of Waterloo. “I think it’s also true that a lot of the students who might have applied and are choosing not to probably had less of a passion for the field.”

Dina Dawoud, the associate dean of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Waterloo, said the school continues to receive 12 applications for every computer science student it admits.

Eyal de Lara, chair of the Department of Computer Science at U of T, said the department froze undergraduate enrolment about a decade ago because it had already grown “quite large” for a selective program. Applications skyrocketed nonetheless until the volume started to taper off two years ago, he added.
“We had, effectively, an enormous applicant pool,” Prof. de Lara said. “Some students realize it’s going to be impossible to get to U of T and apply to other universities.”

That’s another possible explanation for the drop in applications. As top Canadian computer science programs developed reputations for turning away academic superstars with intimidating resumes, some high-school seniors might have considered applying futile – or simply not worth it if the degree no longer guaranteed a six-figure salary straight out of school.
