Her reaction reflected much of what Ontario Court Justice Jason Miller said in his decision Friday to reject Gauthier-Neville’s pitch for a conditional sentence that would have kept him out of jail and allowed him to continue as the single parent to his 10-year-old son with special needs.

“I know this wasn’t the result you were looking for. I do think this is the result the law requires that I impose,” the judge said to Gauthier-Neville.

“I take no pleasure in incarcerating people and separating them from their family. The public, however, has to get the message. These offences must stop.”

Miller reiterated what many judges see in local courtrooms – that too many people are choosing to drive after drinking or consuming intoxicants.

Gauthier-Neville fits the profile of most people charged with impaired driving, described by Miller as “a law-abiding, pro-social member of their community.”

“Regrettably, it seems too many otherwise good people are still not properly considering the potentially lethal consequences” of drinking and driving, he said, despite large-scale education campaigns and increased sentences imposed by the courts.

Miller said Gauthier-Neville made a “tragic” decision on March 24, 2025, at about 7 a.m. when he sped south at 148 km/h in the 40 km/h community safety zone on McNay Street near Blessed Sacrament elementary school in his 2021 Dodge Ram 1500 pickup truck. He ran through the red light at Oxford Street and into the side of Ivany’s pickup truck, which was heading east on a green light.

The impact, all caught on surveillance video, was catastrophic. There was no evidence that he tried to brake. Upon impact, Ivany’s truck rolled onto the passenger side and Ivany, 57, was trapped inside.

When she was finally freed 40 minutes later, Ivany was rushed to hospital with serious injuries. Gauthier-Neville wasn’t injured, but he failed a roadside breath test. Further testing after his arrest showed a reading of 140 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood, nearly double the legal limit of 80 milligrams.

At the sentencing hearing last month, assistant Crown attorney Jeremy Carnegie argued for a three-year prison sentence, while defence lawyer Nick Cake asked Miller to consider a conditional sentence that would have kept Gauthier-Neville at home with his son. Instead, the boy is expected to move out of London and away from his doctors to relocate to Kirkland Lake with Gauthier-Neville’s family.

“But for the collateral consequences to Mr. Gauthier-Neville’s family, particularly his son who will no doubt be harmed by losing his father for any period, I would have imposed the three-year sentence sought by the Crown,”Miller said.

In addition to the 30-month sentence, Miller ordered a DNA sample and imposed a five-year driving prohibition to begin once the sentence is completed, which will keep Gauthier-Neville off the road for 7.5 years.

At the time of the crash, Gauthier-Neville was struggling after his father’s death and his sister’s cancer diagnosis. He lost a brother to lung disease. A sister-in-law and a pet also died.

His inability to deal with his grief led him to become a daily heavy drinker. Since his arrest, he has quit drinking and participated in rehabilitative programming for addiction. He also completed 200 hours of community service.

Ivany continues to recover. She suffered fractures in the neck area of her spine, lower spine, collarbone, sacrum, both sides of her pelvis, both hip sockets, ribs and breastbone. Her internal organs were bruised and she had a laceration to her liver.

She required several surgeries and needs more. During the first few months of her recovery, she needed assistance with her daily needs, plus a wheelchair, then a walker, then a cane. She gets injections for pain management.

Ivany was unable to travel to see her ailing father until shortly before he died. She doesn’t feel safe anymore and is anxious while driving.

Her daughter, Ashley, planned to surprise her on the day of the crash with news of a pregnancy. “It turned what was to be a beautiful moment between mother and daughter … into one of fear that she would never see her mother again,” Miller said.

Ivany hasn’t fully returned to work as a home painter and drew on her retirement funds after a GoFundMe campaign gave her initial financial help.

The judge noted that Gauthier-Neville has been remorseful since the moment of the crash. However, his driving was “frightening and horrendous,” and his breathalyzer readings were very high.

Offenders like Gauthier-Neville “do not intend the harm they cause, but they, in fact, cause harm,” he said through their choice to get behind the wheel after consuming alcohol and without thought of potential tragic consequences.

Miller addressed Ivany and her family directly. “I’m very sorry this happened to you. It’s always regrettable to have people come to this building simply because they were in the wrong place at the wrong time and have suffered significant harm.”

He said the courts must continue to increase sentences in impaired driving cases “until law-abiding, pro-social people in the public get the message.”

People with drinking problems should “get help” and “leave your car at home. If they simply make that decision, so much suffering would be eliminated,” he said.

Miller was clear that the crash should not be called “an accident” because “an accident is an unforeseeable event. Calamity caused by drinking and driving is hardly unforeseeable.”

Outside the courtroom, Ivany agreed. “This was not an accident,” she said. “To me, when I look at that video, it looks like I was preyed upon.”

Shona Ivany, 57, was seriously injured by a speeding impaired driver during the morning commute at Oxford and McNay streets 17 months ago. On Friday, driver Mitchell Gauthier-Neville, 32, lost his bid for a conditional sentence and was sentenced to 30 months in prison. (Jane Sims/The London Free Press)
Shona Ivany had tears in her eyes as she left the London courtroom where the drunk driver who seriously injured her 17 months ago was sent to prison.

“I thought I would be happy with the outcome of him going to jail, but I still don’t feel that,” she said after Mitchell Gauthier-Neville, 32, was dealt a 30-month sentence for impaired driving causing bodily harm.
“You still feel sad for his family, for him and for his son. I do know that he needs to pay the price. He did harm to me. He did a lot of harm to me,” she said.
“But I still feel sorry for him because I know he didn’t do it intentionally. But that does not mean he should walk away free. He still needs to pay for it.”

Her reaction reflected much of what Ontario Court Justice Jason Miller said in his decision Friday to reject Gauthier-Neville’s pitch for a conditional sentence that would have kept him out of jail and allowed him to continue as the single parent to his 10-year-old son with special needs.
“I know this wasn’t the result you were looking for. I do think this is the result the law requires that I impose,” the judge said to Gauthier-Neville.
“I take no pleasure in incarcerating people and separating them from their family. The public, however, has to get the message. These offences must stop.”
Miller reiterated what many judges see in local courtrooms – that too many people are choosing to drive after drinking or consuming intoxicants.
Gauthier-Neville fits the profile of most people charged with impaired driving, described by Miller as “a law-abiding, pro-social member of their community.”

“Regrettably, it seems too many otherwise good people are still not properly considering the potentially lethal consequences” of drinking and driving, he said, despite large-scale education campaigns and increased sentences imposed by the courts.

stories.title: How a Newfoundland town’s 9/11 compassion built a bond lasting 25 years
stories.summary: It’s been a quarter-century since New Yorker Tom McKeon was stranded and whisked off a grounded plane by school bus to a small community in central Newfoundland.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Appelton, N.L. - It’s been a quarter-century since New Yorker Tom McKeon was stranded and whisked off a grounded plane by school bus to a small community in central Newfoundland.

Twenty-five years later, McKeon is crashing in the same basement, with the same family who hosted him for those few emotional and troubled days in Appleton — just as he’s done on his many visits back to the province, at host Derm and Dianne Flynn’s insistence.

“I try to insist to Dianne that I want to get a hotel, I don’t want to impose,” McKeon said. “The first time we did that, I think I might have insulted them.”

McKeon was one of the thousands of “plane people” who were stranded in Gander after American authorities shut down the country’s airspace following the Sept. 11 attacks.

‘We really love each other’

Derm Flynn — the then mayor of Appleton — was one of many in the town and the region that opened their homes to the stranded travellers in the days after they arrived.

“I, as mayor, made the decision because people were asking me,” Flynn recalls. “They were saying, ‘Derm, how come there’s people staying, sleeping on the floor? I’ve got two bedrooms at my house!’”

So, McKeon spent a first sleepless night at Appleton’s small-town hall. For the second, he was invited — by either Derm or Dianne — to stay at the mayor’s house, along with five of the other “plane people” who were stuck in the community.

Among the chaos of that second day, the Flynns found a small moment of respite with their new guests – a moment that sparked a friendship that lasts to this day.

“We got back here to this room,” McKeon said from the Flynns’ basement bar. “Derm said, I think it’s time we had a drink.”

“I think he was sorry about that, because he had probably one, and then all of his guests drank him dry.”

The relationship between the two men only grew — McKeon was so moved by the kindness that he came back to visit the community again in the spring of 2002. The Flynns even travelled to New York to visit and would call to mark milestones, births and deaths in their families.

“We really love each other. We’ve been part of each other’s lives since that day.”

Nearly 7,000 people on 38 planes were diverted to Gander in the morning of 9/11, the first arriving minutes after American officials shut down their airspace.

‘My life was changed’

In response, Gander and surrounding communities launched an ad-hoc hosting campaign — finding places for passengers to sleep, eat and call home. The “plane people,” as they are still called, dwarfed the region’s hotel and restaurant capacity.

“The second question wasn’t asked, ‘can you feed them?’ or ‘how are you going to feed them?’ or that sort of thing,” Mac Moss remembers.

Moss was an administrator at the College of the North Atlantic in Gander when hundreds of “plane people” showed up at his door.

“It was just, ‘will you take care of them?’ and everybody said they would, of course.”

Among them was Kevin Tuerff, who was diverted to Gander while travelling from Paris to New York City.

“My life was changed by the amazing compassion of the people who volunteered to help every single one of us who needed food, clothing, shelter,” Tuerff said.

In response, he started the non-profit organization Pay It Forward 9/11, which encourages further small acts of kindness to “pay forward” the kindness shown in 2001, and to honour those killed in the Sept. 11 attacks.

“I’ve been telling this story to anybody that will listen,” Tuerff said. “This is my second full-time job that I don’t get paid for, but I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else.”

Hundreds stayed at churches, community halls and school gyms across central Newfoundland — in towns like Gander, Lewisporte, Gambo, Appleton and Glenwood. More planes landed in other Atlantic airports.

“Here we were being treated like spa guests, you know, having hot showers, having cruise-ship type meals available to us at all times,” McKeon said. “Having new friends who were willing to be our grief counsellors.”

“So I see the friendship beginning kind of right away on the 12th.”

Alongside Friday’s remembrance ceremony, Gander and other Newfoundland communities are also hosting dozens of small reunions —just like the one between McKeon and Flynn, and Moss and Tuerff.

“The family relationship is growing,” Flynn said “It’s continued on right to this day.”

stories.title: Nova Scotia to expand protections for people affected by AI-generated intimate images
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government says new legislation will expand protections for people affected by intimate images created or altered by AI without their consent.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says new legislation will expand protections for people affected by intimate images created or altered by AI without their consent.

The government introduced the new bill on Thursday.

It amends the provincial Intimate Images and Cyber-protection Act, which provides legal protection for victims of cyberbullying and the sharing of intimate images online.

Provincial Justice Minister Scott Armstrong told The Canadian Press in an interview that the proposed changes expand the definition of an intimate image and ensure that victims do not have to prove intimate images were shared without their consent.

This would reduce the burden on victims, when applying for a court order for an image to be taken down.

“Prior to these changes … if someone uploaded an intimate image of a victim, it was on the victim to actually prove that they did not give consent,” Armstrong said. “That’s not trauma informed. The victim shouldn’t have to do the work here.”

Armstrong says the amendments also make it illegal for someone to threaten to share an intimate image online.

He says the changes align with those made to the Canadian Criminal Code in June, which made it illegal to threaten to share intimate images, including sexual deepfakes, without consent.

The proposed legislation also includes amendments to the Safer Communities and Neighbourhoods Act.

One of the changes would give the provincial government expanded powers to take control of a property that is suspected of hosting serious criminal activity.

“This is another tool we’re using to be able to combat human trafficking, in particular,” Armstrong said.

The legislation includes other amendments to improve public safety in the province, including modernizing 911 services.

stories.title: Toronto’s new country bar pays tribute to the late, great Dolly Parton
stories.summary: Dolly’s channels the icon’s glamour and generous spirit to celebrate her legacy
stories.author: Photography and story by Joel Rodriguez
stories.content:
Inside Toronto’s newest country bar – a tribute to the late, great queen of country

The Dolly Parton cutout was hard to miss.

Life-sized and permanently cheerful, she stood at the entrance to Dolly’s, a new country bar on Toronto’s Esplanade, watching over a steady stream of guests in cowboy hats, blond wigs and varying degrees of rhinestone commitment.

This week, the affection for Dolly Parton, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80, has been visible across Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver . Parton’s estate has also announced Dollyfest, a major celebration planned for 2027. The Globe and Mail spent a night at Dolly’s this week for a special celebration in tribute to the queen of country.

The bar takes its name and inspiration from Parton.

“The idea behind Dolly’s was to create a country bar in the city where women would feel safe,” said Taruna Daya, a staff member who welcomed guests as they arrived.

Among the guests was Ayah Conic, Dolly’s main drag performer and host for the evening.

“Dolly didn’t have a mean bone in her body. She was love,” Conic said. “When she could’ve gone and just become a billionaire, she started a charity. I adore her.”

That generosity was part of the tribute itself. The night was raising funds for Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , the program she founded to provide free books to children.

It was an appropriate way to celebrate someone whose public life has always extended beyond music. Parton built a career as a songwriter and performer, while using her success to give back to the communities around her.

But perhaps that is part of what makes Dolly Dolly. The glamour was never the whole story. There was always something given away, whether it was a song, a joke, a book or simply a reason for people to feel welcome.

Among the guests was Ayah Conic, Dolly’s main drag performer and host for the evening.

content_blocks.caption: Dolly drag performer Ayah Conic also lip-synced during the opening performance.

content_blocks.text: “Dolly didn’t have a mean bone in her body. She was love,” Conic said. “When she could’ve gone and just become a billionaire, she started a charity. I adore her.”
That generosity was part of the tribute itself. The night was raising funds for Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , the program she founded to provide free books to children.

It was an appropriate way to celebrate someone whose public life has always extended beyond music. Parton built a career as a songwriter and performer, while using her success to give back to the communities around her.

But perhaps that is part of what makes Dolly Dolly. The glamour was never the whole story. There was always something given away, whether it was a song, a joke, a book or simply a reason for people to feel welcome.

stories.title: Gas prices are expected to drop soon, but geopolitical risks remain
stories.summary: Consumers in Canada could see some relief at gas pumps starting next week as gas refineries go through regular seasonal changes, but how much prices will drop is unclear.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Consumers in Canada could see some relief at gas pumps starting next week as gas refineries go through regular seasonal changes, but how much gas prices will drop is unclear as geopolitical risks keep analysts guessing about the long-term outlook.

A drop in available oil supplies worldwide typically leads to higher gas prices, unless demand falls significantly, while the opposite effect usually will see lower gas prices.

Gas prices in Canada, and worldwide, have skyrocketed ever since the United States and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran at the end of February. The conflict has been ongoing ever since, with a temporary ceasefire in June unravelling after just a few weeks, and all the while keeping the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping channel virtually closed to most oil and gas shipments.

The Strait of Hormuz normally sees about a fifth of the world’s oil supply pass through on a daily basis.

But a switch to winter gasoline blends in Canada could see prices drop starting Sept. 16, as the new fuel starts arriving at retail pumps. In addition, gas prices typically fall during colder weather months because demand for gasoline decreases as Canadians do less driving compared to warmer months.

“Demand for gasoline declines across North America as Canadians and Americans drive less as temperatures progressively cool off. So that drop in demand usually gives us some drop in price,” says petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan at GasBuddy.

“In addition, next week, we make the switch back to cheaper winter gasoline.”

Winter blends of gasoline, De Haan says, are typically cheaper than what is sold during warmer months because the blending components like butane are relatively low cost, but help improve vehicle performance in colder temperatures. The trade off is that butane contributes to more air pollution when temperatures are warm, and as temperatures cool off, more butane is allowed.

The national average price for regular grade gasoline sits at about $1.77 per litre as of publication, according to CAA, up from around $1.75 last week and $1.42 a year ago.

Without global volatility stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions and other economic factors contributing to gas price changes, De Haan says these seasonal changes can usually result in a five to 20 cent per litre drop in the price of regular grade gasoline.

This means filling a 50-litre gas tank could see savings of about $10.

“It does vary year to year, but typically that would be a noticeable amount of relief. This year though, obviously a part of the traditional downturn could be offset by new action overseas,” says De Haan.

“Where we go, whether it’s higher or lower, it’s tough to know based on the balance of all these geopolitical tensions.”

stories.title: Former PM Chretien to U.S.: ‘We bow to no one’
stories.summary: Former prime minister Jean Chretien, during a speech commemorating the 25-year anniversary of Sept. 11, delivered what he called 'a message for our American friends.'
stories.author: Luca Caruso-Moro
stories.content:
Former prime minister Jean Chretien, during a speech commemorating the 25-year anniversary of Sept. 11, delivered what he called “a message for our American friends.”

“Never mistake our generosity for weakness,” he said.

“We embrace our friends, and we help them in their moment of need. But we bow to no one. And the more we are insulted and threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united,” he later added to applause in the room.

“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another.”

Chretien, who was prime minister in 2001, was one of several speakers participating in a memorial event in Gander, N.L., where locals took in thousands of travellers who were grounded during the terror attacks.

U.S. authorities closed American airspace following the attack, forcing all planes to land. Thirty-eight aircraft touched down in Gander, a town of roughly 10,000. Nearly 7,000 passengers were left stranded. Gander residents stepped up to provide shelter to the new arrivals, putting them in hundreds of hotel rooms.

In a preamble to his remarks to the U.S., he said he was not representing “any government.” Rather, he said he was speaking as a 92-year-old former prime minister and a “very proud Canadian.”

“Friends need to be honest with each other. Just as the people in Gander, and anywhere else in Newfoundland and Labrador, they will give you the shirt off their backs. Like they did 25 years ago.

“But they will always show you the respect of telling you the truth. So, my friends, here is to truth, to respect, to friendship and to good neighbours: Vive les États-Unis, et vive le Canada.”

Canada and the U.S. have been in a protracted trade war since February 2025. Both countries have mounted escalating restrictions on a variety of goods, ranging from booze, dairy, metals, softwood lumber and others, affecting billions of dollars in products.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford told business leaders he stands with the prime minister against Donald Trump's trade moves.

U.S. President Donald Trump has also repeatedly called Prime Minister Mark Carney “governor” – a reference to threats from the U.S. administration to pressure Canada to relinquish its own sovereignty to become a U.S. state.

The two countries appeared close to a deal in late August, but talks fell apart after the U.S. tried to introduce last-minute adjustments , according to Carney. Those changes included restrictions on Canada’s trade deals with other countries and its ability to protect the French language, the prime minister claimed.

stories.title: Stellantis, Unifor break off contract talks as automaker pursues sale of Brampton assembly plant
stories.summary: Stellantis confirmed to union it has signed MOU with defence industry supplier Roshel, which wants to buy the factory near Toronto
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Contract talks between automaker Stellantis NV Stla-N and Unifor have broken off after hitting an impasse over the future of the idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant, the union says.

Stellantis confirmed to the union it has signed a memorandum of understanding with defence industry supplier Roshel, which wants to buy the factory near Toronto, Unifor said in a statement on Friday.

“The persistence of the company’s proposal to close and sell the Brampton plant has hindered the bargaining process,” Unifor said.

The two sides began bargaining on Sept. 1, with the union seeking a three-year deal by Sept. 11 that matched the gains made in recent negotiations with Ford and General Motors. Those agreements provided raises of 3 per cent in each year of the deals.

In the Stellantis talks, Unifor had said its priorities were securing a future for the Brampton assembly plant west of Toronto that was idled in 2023, as well as securing production volumes at factories in Windsor and Toronto.

But on Friday the union walked away from the table and said it is “actively considering next steps.”

“Central to the impasse is the future of Stellantis’ Brampton assembly plant,” Unifor said in a statement. “Additionally, the company has yet to confirm forecasted plans for the Windsor Assembly plant and Etobicoke casting plant.”

Stellantis employs more than 9,000 Unifor workers, most of those at the Windsor assembly plant making Chrysler minivans and Dodge Chargers. The carmaker also runs a castings plant in the west end of Toronto. About 2,200 Brampton workers are on layoff.

The Brampton plant stopped production to retool to make the Jeep Compass, but the work was paused shortly after the U.S. placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars in 2025. Stellantis last year said the Compass would instead be made in the U.S. The company told the union in August it was considering selling the plant.

stories.title: ‘I’d do it in a heartbeat again’: Gander residents say 25 years after opening home to strangers
stories.summary: For 25 years Karen Mills has held the memories of 9/11 in her heart and in a binder full of photos she flips through while speaking with CTV News. Mills says she recalls the time like it was yesterday.
stories.author: Heather Butts
stories.content:
Gander, N.L.- For 25 years Karen Mills has held the memories of 9/11 in her heart and in a binder full of photos she flips through while speaking with CTV News.

When the tragedy occurred 25 years ago, she was the manager at a Comfort Inn hotel in Gander, N.L. that housed thousands of “plane people” who were stranded when the FAA closed American airspace forcing all planes to land.

That sent 38 planes to Gander with more nearly 7,000 passengers. In a town of roughly 10,000, that meant Gander’s population nearly doubled in size overnight.

With no committee or association available to help, the people of Gander and surrounding communities stepped up, for those in need.

Mills says she recalls the time like it was yesterday.

“Our switchboard had 12 lines and it (lit up) just like a Christmas tree, it was just buzzing,” Mills said about the time when passengers landed in Gander and need a place to stay.

Although some hotel rooms were already filled with scheduled tourists, when the town declared a “State of Emergency” hotels in Gander were required to give flight crews first access to rooms.

With 7,000 passengers in need of shelter, the few hundred hotel rooms in the entire town were filled in minutes.

“Do you know how many times we had to say, ‘gosh so sorry,’ we felt so bad, you knew people probably slept on the floor somewhere,” said Mills.

The ‘basement boys’

As the so-called “plane people” kept coming, two young men caught a break.

The former Comfort Inn manager of 33 years recalled two young men who were desperate for a safe place to rest their heads.

“They walked in and once again they were like ‘we know you don’t have anything sorry,’” Mills recounted.

“And it was like a boom moment… and I was like ‘wait I got a box spring mattress and a cot you guys can come sleep down in the basement, downstairs in the gym in the fitness centre.’”

The two men accepted with delight, telling Mills the box spring was better than the pool table they had slept on the night before.

Mills dubbed the two men the “Basement Boys,” and even drove them across town to fulfill one simple request: they needed fresh underwear.

The group developed a fond relationship that has run the course of 25 years.

“Every year on 9/11 flowers show up at the hotel. They call themselves the ‘Liverpool Lads,’ they don’t know they’re the ‘Basement Boys,’” she said.

“I did get an email (from them) once and I told them, ‘Do you know how many times I’ve told your story?’”

25 years later, Mills and the community of Gander remains steadfast in their message.

“My god, if we can just be kind, what a world eh… I mean seriously think about it… I think anyone would do what we did.” Mills said. It’s a message she hopes continues to bloom in uncertain times.

Open heart, open home

Decades-old stories of kindness and empathy are commonly shared around the anniversary of 9/11 in the community of Gander.

“I got a call from the (The Royal Canadian) Legion asking to bring a tray of sandwiches to the Legion. I didn’t ask what (it was) for, they wanted a tray, I brought a tray,” said Beulah Cooper, a Gander resident and executive at the local Legion.

Her efforts extended well beyond a tray of sandwiches. With dozens of people sleeping on the floor of the Legion, in community centres and schools, she offered comfort.

“I took them to make phone calls and I asked them if they wanted to come up to my home and get a good night’s sleep,” Cooper said.

One of the people who accepted Cooper’s invitation was American passenger Monica Burke. She is among the many “plane people” who have returned to Gander for the 25th anniversary of 9/11, marking her fifth visit to the community.

“I was kind of shocked that she invited me into her house but I was also very relieved, because I needed some rest and was emotional and exhausted,” Burke said while sitting in Cooper’s living room 25 years after they first met.

Burke had spent 16 hours on the plane, parked on the tarmac and had no real sense of what happened until she arrived at the Legion.

She called her boss in the U.S. to say she wouldn’t be coming back anytime soon. All she knew was that she was somewhere in Canada.

As the world witnessed extraordinary horror, people in Gander gave those in need remarkable hope.

“It kept happening at the Legion. People would just show up and say, ‘I have two beds. Who wants to come home?’ After a while, it was like, ‘Oh, okay, that’s what they do here.’” said Burke.

The bonds capture a strength that is hard for many to describe, people who would otherwise have never met, with seemingly nothing in common, now like family.

Former Gander mayor Claude Elliott “put it right,” Cooper said.

“He said when they arrived, they were strangers, by the middle of the week they were friends and when they left they were family.”

Well into her 80s now, Cooper is still active with the Legion and welcoming “Plane People” into her home. She says she’s humbled by helping so many in such an uncertain time and shares this advice with others:

“If you see someone who needs help, or you can help them do it. Open your home or your heart to them. It makes you feel good it really does, I’d do it in a heartbeat again.”

stories.title: Supreme Court rejects strict deadlines during criminal sentencing
stories.summary: Friday’s judgment answers specific questions amid broader issue of delays in the justice system
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday clarified how the justice system should handle delays after a person is convicted of a crime but before they are sentenced, ruling that such situations must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Friday’s judgment, called R.B.-C., involved a conviction for sexual assault where it took more than a year to deliver the sentence.

The unanimous court took a relatively narrow approach to answer specific questions in the R.B.-C. appeal.

The case intersected with major legal issues: the protection in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to be tried within a reasonable time when charged with a crime, and what happens when that right is violated.

Such questions are usually focused on the process of a criminal trial. The Supreme Court a decade ago, in the landmark Jordan ruling, set strict deadlines for trials to be completed, from charge to conviction. If there’s an unreasonable delay that violates the Charter, a Supreme Court precedent from 1987 called Rahey means that the only outcome is a stay of proceedings. The accused is freed without a verdict.

Delays plague Canada’s justice system. Parliament and the Supreme Court in recent months have wrestled with the challenge. The Supreme Court earlier this year said it might reconsider its Rahey precedent.

Parliament and Supreme Court eye major shift on trial delays

Friday’s R.B.-C. judgment zeroed in on delays between conviction and sentencing. It was written by Justice Sheilah Martin in her final months of work as she retires this year.

If there is a Charter violation of unreasonable delay after conviction, the top court said the remedy in most cases is a reduction in the sentence levied on the offender. The court noted that it had not previously provided such precise guidance.

The court further said that delays after conviction should not be measured against a strict deadline, the way Jordan is used to consider trial delays. The key difference between the two phases is a person at trial is presumed innocent.

In the R.B.-C. case, a man studying for his PhD at a university in Ontario assaulted his new girlfriend one evening in 2019. The Ontario Court of Justice convicted him in 2021, but it took more than a year to render the punishment: a conditional sentence of two years less a day.

The man asked the Ontario Court of Justice for a stay of the proceedings because of unreasonable delay. The court said no. But the Ontario Court of Appeal in 2024 ruled that there was an unreasonable delay. Both courts were working with a rule applicable only in Ontario, a five-month deadline to deliver a sentence after conviction.

The Ontario appeal court reduced his conditional sentence by four months.

Court delays in sex-assault cases increase despite Supreme Court deadlines, report finds

At the Supreme Court, the man, R.B.-C., once more sought a complete stay of the proceedings – which would wipe out his conviction.

On Friday, the top court said no.

The Supreme Court agreed that there was an unreasonable delay in his sentencing, engaging the Charter of Rights. The top court also agreed with the Ontario appeal court’s move to reduce the conditional sentence by four months.

The Supreme Court, however, rejected the idea of a five-month deadline between conviction and sentencing.

Justice Martin, invoking the central rationale of the Jordan ruling, said trial deadlines were established to address a “proven culture of complacency in bringing accused persons to trial.”

On delays between conviction and sentencing, she said strict deadlines didn’t make sense because “no comparable evidentiary foundation has been established.”

Lawyers for R.B.-C. on Friday said they were disappointed that the Supreme Court will allow sentencing proceedings to continue “even after they have become unconstitutional” because of unreasonable delay.

“Courts, more than any other institution, should respect constitutional rights,” said lawyers Arash Ghiassi and Julia Kirby of Savards LLP in a statement.

They said that allowing cases to drag on beyond the point of unreasonable delay “will not fix the system.” They also said Friday’s ruling means that R.B.-C., an Iranian, May be deported back to Iran because of his conviction and his immigration status.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, an intervener in the case, ON Friday said sentence reductions are not a meaningful remedy for a violation of a Charter right. The advocacy group added that the vagueness of the remedy does not “provide the clarity necessary” to push the justice system to render sentences in a timely manner.

Beyond the R.B.-C. case itself, the broader question of how the Supreme Court May grapple with the issue of cases stayed because of unreasonable trial delays is not yet answered.

In May, in another Jordan-related ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the court might reconsider its Rahey precedent, which dictates that a stay is the only remedy for an unreasonable trial delay.

“It May be that the time is near at hand when Rahey should be revisited,” the Chief Justice wrote.

stories.title: Sovereignty referendum would cost at least $130-million, Parti Québécois leader says
stories.summary: Figures will be included in the financial framework that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon plans to make public on Sept. 15
stories.author: Caroline Plante
stories.content:
The leader of the Parti Québecois says it would cost at least $130-million to pay for the sovereignty referendum he plans to hold in 2029 or 2030 if his party forms a government.

In an interview with The Canadian Press, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon detailed all the costs associated with preparing for and holding the referendum.

These figures will be included in the financial framework he plans to make public on Sept. 15, in the midst of a provincial election campaign that will wrap up when Quebecers go to the polls on Oct. 5.

The referendum budget includes $20-million for studies and consultations in the first years of a PQ government mandate. This would include expenses for a roving commission that would study a new provisional constitution, starting in 2027.

Holding the referendum in 2029-30 would cost $110-million, according to the PQ leader.

But St-Pierre Plamondon admitted the cost could exceed that figure if there are “unforeseen expenses.”

“As for the cost of holding the referendum, people will have their say, but we won’t apologize for living in a democracy and for consulting the people if we’ve reached that point,” he added.

St-Pierre Plamondon stressed his party’s commitment to holding a referendum on Quebec sovereignty after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, regardless of whether it forms a majority or minority government.

If he becomes premier on Oct. 5, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would appoint a minister responsible for the independence process, who would replace the minister of Canadian relations.

“We don’t have any plans regarding the size or number of employees per ministry, but … we can commit to not increasing the size of that particular ministry,” he said.

The PQ leader added that the “intergovernmental relationship with Ottawa is also becoming part of the independence project.”

Since the start of the election campaign, the PQ’s opponents have been demanding details on the cost of a potential referendum.

Journalists had asked St-Pierre Plamondon this question on Aug. 28 in McMasterville, Que., but he did not provide an answer at the time.

When pressed again by The Canadian Press, he decided to open the books.

“Part of my opponents’ strategy is to demonize consulting the people about their future, by saying it’s appalling,” he said. “However, overall, we’re proposing to curb historic waste … so I think people will evaluate our political platform as a whole.”

St-Pierre Plamondon is confident his party’s promises have been properly budgeted for, saying “it’s a more than prudent budgetary approach.”

The PQ leader also said the financial framework he will soon table will be “the budgetary framework for a Quebec in the current context.”

It will not take into account, for example, the promise to create a Quebec army after the referendum, should the “Yes” side win.

“Quebec’s budgetary framework will change after Quebec’s independence,” he said.

stories.title: ‘I like to walk’: Japanese man traverses Canada purely for the joy of it
stories.summary: For Nobuaki Okumura, happiness can be a borrowed Habs jersey, making friends with total strangers, or a well-earned meal after a long day of walking across Canada.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
By Jack Rabb

Posted September 11, 2026 2:44 pm.

For Nobuaki Okumura, happiness can be a borrowed Habs jersey, making friends with total strangers, or a well-earned meal after a long day of walking across Canada.

Okumura, who also goes by “Nobby,” just strolled into Vancouver this week after leaving Halifax — on foot — four and a half months ago.

When asked why he began his journey, he said, “For my happiness; just for fun.”

“I’m not Terry Fox,” he said.

“I like to walk, very much.”

Canada is the fifth country he has traversed just because he felt like it. He even set a Guinness World Record in 2024 for the fastest walk across his native Japan.

“Canada’s nature is very good for me, so anywhere I love, but B.C. is very good,” he said.

Okumura documented his journey thoroughly, taking in incredible natural features and wildlife.

He also made friends everywhere he went, saying his success wouldn’t have been possible without the support he received along the way.

“Many people help me,” he said. “I’m very happy. Without their help and support, I can not walk this long way, I think.”

While his venture was ultimately for his own contentment and well-being, Nobby hopes he is able to inspire others to follow their passions and prioritize their own happiness.

“I walk for my happiness, but if that challenge encourages someone, it’s my pleasure,” he said.

stories.title: Researchers confirm sixth tornado in early September southwestern Ontario storms - CBC.CA
stories.summary: Researchers at Western University have confirmed yet another tornado that happened during a series of significant storms that swept across southwestern Ontario last week.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Researchers at Western University have confirmed yet another tornado that happened during a series of significant storms that swept across southwestern Ontario last week.
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 2:12 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

This drone photo shows what researchers call the worst damage point west of Monkton, which includes a partially destroyed farm building, several destroyed grain bins, and a tornado path through the crops.(Northern Tornadoes Project)
Researchers at Western University have confirmed another tornado from a series of significant storms across southwestern Ontario last week.
The Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP) said it found evidence a tornado touched down in the area of Monkton, Ont., ON Sept. 2, alongside evidence of a downburst in Seaforth, Ont.
This brings the tally of tornadoes that touched down in southwestern Ontario on Sep. 2 and 3 to six, and brings the number of downbursts confirmed to three.
Storm that hammered south, southwestern Ontario leaves 'significant' damage, outages as cleanup continues
EF1 tornado confirmed in Wellesley Township, 2 others confirmed in Tavistock
The tornadoes and downbursts now confirmed include:
An EF0 tornado, an EF1 tornado and an EF0 downburst in the Tavistock area on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado in Wellesley on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado near Monkton and an EF1 downburst in Seaforth on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado in Windsor on Sept. 3.
An EF1 tornado and an EF1 downburst in Wheatley on Sept. 3.
Researchers classify these events on the Enhanced Fujita Scale, which ranks tornadoes and downbursts based on wind speed and damage. The the lowest rating is EF0 and the maximum rating is EF5.
This farm located west of Monkton faced a partially destroyed barn, several destroyed grain bins, and a tornado path through the crops. (Northern Tornadoes Project)
The newly-confirmed tornado near Monkton caused damage to crops, trees and manmade structures, according to a report from the NTP.
"An NTP ground and drone survey was completed on September 8, 2026, documenting the reported damage along with damage to two farm buildings," the report reads.
The tornado began in the west travelling 4.91 kilometres toward Monkton with wind speeds of 150 km/h and a width of roughly 50 metres.
This drone photo shows a farm building that was destroyed near Seaforth, days after much of the debris was cleaned. (Northern Tornadoes Project)
In Seaforth, west of Monkton, the downburst caused damage to several farm buildings, trees and power poles, the report reads.
The downburst is reported to have an estimated maximum wind speed of 165 km/h, with damage found across an area roughly 8.5 kilometres long and up to 3 kilometres wide.
NTP officials said in the latest report that no further surveys looking at damage reported during the storms are planned.

stories.title: Middlesex County Warden’s Statement on the 25th Anniversary of September 11
stories.summary: On September 11, 2026 Warden Sue Clarke issued the following statement regarding the 25th Anniversary of the September 11 attacks.
stories.content:
Middlesex County: On September 11, 2026 Warden Sue Clarke issued the following statement regarding the 25 th Anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

Today, we pause to remember the lives lost on September 11, 2001, and to honour the courage, sacrifice, and resilience shown in the face of tragedy. As we mark this anniversary, we reflect on how that day changed the lives of families, communities, and people around the world. We remember the courage of first responders, the compassion shown by ordinary people, and the resilience that emerged. Twenty-five years later, the events of that day continue to remind us how we can come together and support one another, even in times of profound loss. We will never forget those who lost their lives, or the sacrifices made in the days and years that followed.

stories.title: Gander gathers to commemorate 25th anniversary of 9/11 and town’s rush to help passengers
stories.summary: Thirty-eight planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers were grounded in Newfoundland town during the attacks
stories.author: Sarah Smellie
stories.content:
The flags of Canada, the United States and Newfoundland were carried into an arena in central Newfoundland on Friday to mark the start of a ceremony commemorating those killed in terrorist attacks in the United States 25 years ago.

Thirty-eight planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers were grounded in Gander, Nfld., after hijackers took command of four aircraft and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Washington and a field in Pennsylvania.

Military, first responders and some of the stranded passengers were among the thousands of people who gathered for the ceremony to mark the anniversary of Sept. 11, 2001.

People in Gander dropped everything to fill churches and community halls with cots, food and clothing, and they cared for the passengers for days.

The town became a symbol of the kindness shown across Canada as planes were forced to land in airports across the country.

In depth: On a sombre anniversary, Gander welcomes the ‘plane people’ back to the Rock

Percy Farwell, the mayor of Gander, told the crowd that the day is about remembering those who died and suffered, but also about the humanity that emerged 25 years ago.

“In Gander in 2001, we were witness to a time when humanity was thrown into a pile in a time of great distress and turmoil,” he said. “And we were forced to distil our relationships with others down to what really matters: supporting, caring for, loving each other, that we May all endure the challenges.”

Jean Chrétien, who was the prime minister of Canada on 9/11, and Governor-General Louise Arbour were among the dignitaries at the event. United States Ambassador Pete Hoekstra was also expected to address the crowd.

Hoekstra’s visit comes at a painful time for Canada and the United States’ relationship.

U.S. President Donald Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on Canadian goods last month, prompting Canada to retaliate with levies on American products.

Beverley Bass was piloting an American Airlines plane from Paris to Dallas when she got word that the towers had been hit. She told The Canadian Press that she was expecting to be diverted to Toronto or Montreal, and was surprised to be instructed instead to land at the Gander airport, where every spare space was filled with planes and vehicles.

“I looked out both sides of the windows of the cockpit and there were cars everywhere. I said to the crew, ‘I think everybody from Newfoundland is here,’” she said in Gander.

Bass said she’ll never forget the kindness of the people of Gander, who provided three meals a day, parties for children and comfort to the passengers and crew.

“A lot of people did not want to leave on Sept. 15,” she said. “They were so fearful of what they were going back to in our country, which was complete devastation, but we had spent five days living in the most beautiful community in the world.”

Americans mark 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks

In Banff, Alta., Prime Minister Mark Carney also paid tribute to the victims of 9/11, saying Canadians stand with their American neighbours in mourning, remembrance and solidarity.

“This dark moment also brought forth some of our best nature, firefighters climbing the stairs to rescue those in burning buildings, rescue workers working for weeks to bring closure,” Carney said. “I think the lesson of these events is that the response to darkness is to reach out, is to support, to stand in solidarity, as Canadians did, with our neighbours.”

Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a video that was filmed at the 9/11 memorial in New York City that he remembers the generous families of Gander and other Canadians who welcomed passengers from diverted flights.

Raphael Fusco, who was 17 years old on 9/11, had been flying from Milan to Newark, N.J., with his father when their plane was forced to land in Gander. They were taken by bus to Lewisport, Nfld., where they slept on pews in a church for three nights.

Fusco, a musician, says he feels emotional about the anniversary because of how Canadians and Newfoundlanders invited the passengers into their homes and “gave us the clothes off their back.”

“So while the rest of the world was seeing these horrific images, we saw something very different,” he said Friday in Gander. “We saw extraordinary kindness, and to this day, 25 years later I bring that image of altruism, of kindness, warmth, generosity, of treating strangers like family with me everywhere I go.”

There was also a commemoration held in Ottawa attended by about 100 invited guests, including representatives from the RCMP, Canada Border Services Agency and other first responders.

By Michael Talbot and Silvia Pontecorvi

Posted September 11, 2026 1:58 pm.

Former Member of Parliament Francesco Sorbara stands in front of his Woodbridge home clutching a black backpack covered in soot.

The grey dust that still clings to the material conjures conflicting emotions. On one hand, it reminds him how lucky he was. One the other, it’s a symbol of the cruel fate inflicted on thousands.

The soot is from the carcinogenic storm cloud that covered everything in its path when the World Trade Center’s south tower collapsed after it was struck by a plane commandeered by terrorists on September 11, 2001.

Sorbara, who was living in New York City at the time while working for JPMorgan Chase, stood in horror and watched as it toppled before his eyes. Then he ran for his life.

Twenty-five years later, he’s still shaken by the memories.

“It’s something I’ll never forget,” he said of that ill-fated day. “I don’t think about it all the time of course, but at the same time … it left its mark on many of us in different ways.”

Sorbara says September 11, 2001 started as a “beautiful sunny September day where you wanted to be outside.”

He rode the subway towards the World Trade Center for a training session at a building that was directly across the street from the iconic twin towers.

By the time he emerged from the subway system, both towers had been struck by planes.

“When I exited the subway … there seemed to be a lot of confusion … you could see there was some panic, I remember that.”

“I was watching the firefighters walk down toward the twin towers and all of a sudden, it seemed like maybe after five minutes of standing there … the first (south) tower collapses. I thought we were done, there was no way we would survive that.”

He ran as clouds of debris and soot swept over the area.

“It became dark, very, very dark,” he remembered. “I just threw myself near a big cement flower pot and the screams I heard I still remember from people that were near me, because we all had the same inclination that there was no way we are going to make it.”

Eventually he ran into a burger joint that was offering water “to clear your throat because it was all full of soot.”

He then walked to a nearby church on the lower east side that offered a hose to wash off with, and a change of clothes.

Bewildered by the jarring experience, he started walking back to his apartment on the upper east side — a trek through the frantic and eerie streets of New York City that took him around two hours.

At the time, the full scope of what transpired wasn’t clear. But now, 25 years later, he realizes the magnitude.

“It changed history,” he said of the infamous attacks orchestrated by Osama bin Laden.

“The sounds of the screams when the tower collapsed … I will never forget that.”

By Michael Talbot and Silvia Pontecorvi
Posted September 11, 2026 1:58 pm.
Former Member of Parliament Francesco Sorbara stands in front of his Woodbridge home clutching a black backpack covered in soot.
The grey dust that still clings to the material conjures conflicting emotions. On one hand, it reminds him how lucky he was. One the other, it’s a symbol of the cruel fate inflicted on thousands.

The soot is from the carcinogenic storm cloud that covered everything in its path when the World Trade Center’s south tower collapsed after it was struck by a plane commandeered by terrorists on September 11, 2001.
Sorbara, who was living in New York City at the time while working for JPMorgan Chase, stood in horror and watched as it toppled before his eyes. Then he ran for his life.
Twenty-five years later, he’s still shaken by the memories.
“It’s something I’ll never forget,” he said of that ill-fated day. “I don’t think about it all the time of course, but at the same time … it left its mark on many of us in different ways.”
Sorbara says September 11, 2001 started as a “beautiful sunny September day where you wanted to be outside.”
He rode the subway towards the World Trade Center for a training session at a building that was directly across the street from the iconic twin towers.
By the time he emerged from the subway system, both towers had been struck by planes.
“When I exited the subway … there seemed to be a lot of confusion … you could see there was some panic, I remember that.”

“I was watching the firefighters walk down toward the twin towers and all of a sudden, it seemed like maybe after five minutes of standing there … the first (south) tower collapses. I thought we were done, there was no way we would survive that.”
He ran as clouds of debris and soot swept over the area.

“It became dark, very, very dark,” he remembered. “I just threw myself near a big cement flower pot and the screams I heard I still remember from people that were near me, because we all had the same inclination that there was no way we are going to make it.”
Eventually he ran into a burger joint that was offering water “to clear your throat because it was all full of soot.”
He then walked to a nearby church on the lower east side that offered a hose to wash off with, and a change of clothes.
Bewildered by the jarring experience, he started walking back to his apartment on the upper east side — a trek through the frantic and eerie streets of New York City that took him around two hours.
At the time, the full scope of what transpired wasn’t clear. But now, 25 years later, he realizes the magnitude.
“It changed history,” he said of the infamous attacks orchestrated by Osama bin Laden.
“The sounds of the screams when the tower collapsed … I will never forget that.”
Former MP Francesco Sorbara poses with his backpack covered in soot from Ground Zero. Omni News

stories.title: London Vintage Film Camera Show returns Saturday - CBC.CA
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The bi-annual London Vintage Film Camera Show returns Saturday at Westview Baptist Church, with organizers expecting hundreds to attend. More than 45 vendors will offer film cameras, lenses, accessories, darkroom equipment and studio gear.
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 12:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
The London Vintage Camera Show has grown to welcome hundreds of enthusiasts over the past decade.(Maureen Tucker)
The London Vintage Film Camera Show will come into focus this weekend, with organizers expecting hundreds of photography enthusiasts to attend.
About 300 people are expected to pass through the gymnasium at Westview Baptist Church at 1000 Wonderland Road South on Saturday between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.
The bi-annual event features more than 45 vendors selling and displaying film cameras from different eras, along with lenses, accessories, darkroom equipment, studio gear and other photography items.
Organizers say it is one of the largest shows of its kind in Canada.
Q&A Photographer captures balloons 'after the party' to show impact to Ontario waterways
"Our crowd that comes is getting younger and younger," said show director Maureen Tucker. "I think the average age of a person that comes to our show now is probably 25."
Guests take in gear and equipment on display at the London Vintage Camera Show. (Maureen Tucker)
Tucker, who helped bring the event to London about a decade ago, said the growing interest in film photography comes as people look for a more hands-on alternative to digital photography.

"Film is very human," said Tucker. "When you're shooting a film camera, it's you and the tool in your hand, and that's it. There are no tricks, that's it. If you're not a great photographer, you're not a great photographer. There's no crutch."
That's not a photo. Meet a London artist drawing realistic sports portraits
The event is also taking place as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly common in photography and other forms of image-making.
For this edition of the show, organizers have added a display wall curated by Attic Books on Dundas Street.
A darkroom specialist will also be on hand with equipment for people interested in setting up their own darkrooms, Tucker said.
"We will have a couple of local labs, including All Things Film from Adelaide Street North," she said. "They are one of the busiest labs in Canada, located right here in London."
The show is open to photographers and collectors of all experience levels.
Admission is $5 for the day, and parking is free.
Natalie Lovie

stories.title: Police seek public’s help identifying suspect in two London business arsons
stories.summary: London police are asking for the public’s help to identify a suspect believed to be responsible for two arson incidents targeting a business in the city’s west end last month
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police are asking for the public’s help to identify a suspect believed to be responsible for two arson incidents targeting a business in the city’s west end last month.

Police say the first incident occurred around 4 a.m. on Aug. 23 near Oxford Street West and Westdel Bourne. Investigators allege a man approached the business, ignited a Molotov cocktail and threw it at the front of the building, causing an explosion and property damage.

A second arson was reported in the same area around 3 a.m. on Aug. 29. Police believe the same suspect was involved in both incidents.

Officers responded to each call and searched the area, but the suspect was not located.

Investigators have obtained surveillance video and are releasing images of the suspect in hopes that someone can identify him.

Police say that during the Aug. 23 incident, the suspect was wearing a black tracksuit, black shoes and a red-and-white brimmed hat.

During the Aug. 29 incident, the suspect was described as wearing a grey tracksuit, grey slide sandals and black socks.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the London Police Service or Crime Stoppers anonymously.

stories.title: 10/3 podcast: Quebec election: Can the CAQ survive a resurgent PQ?
stories.summary: Amid an ongoing trade war with the U.S., Quebec voters will head to the polls this fall.
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
Canada

Last updated 40 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/10-3-podcast-quebec-election-can-the-caq-survive-a-resurgent-pq#comments-area)

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette hops on her campaign bus in Quebec City on Thursday, August 27, 2026.Photo by Francis Vachon /Montreal Gazette

Amid an ongoing trade war with the U.S., Quebec voters will head to the polls this fall.

Will new CAQ leader Christine Fréchette manage to repeat what Mark Carney did for the federal Liberals, renewing a long-standing government for a new mandate? Or will the resurgent Parti Québécois unseat the CAQ after eight years in government?

Phil Authier, political correspondent with the Montreal Gazette, joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss how the political landscape in Quebec has changed in the last eight years, how the trade war has factored into this race, and what a PQ win could mean when it comes to the debate around Quebec separatism.

stories.title: LeBlanc says no meetings scheduled with U.S. while Mexico works towards a deal
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are no meetings scheduled in Washington.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

LeBlanc said he has been in touch with his U.S. counterparts

Last updated 30 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/leblanc-says-no-meetings-scheduled-with-u-s-while-mexico-works-towards-a-deal#comments-area)

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc speaks during a press conference at the federal cabinet retreat in Banff on Sept. 11, 2026. Photo by Gavin Young /Postmedia

Ottawa — Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are no meetings scheduled in Washington, even as Mexico and the United States are reportedly working towards a completed bilateral deal by November.

“They’ve been at this for a number of months, and speeding towards a deal two months from now doesn’t feel like speed,” said LeBlanc, during a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., ON Friday. “But they are they are having those conversations as we did, as we May again at some point.”

Reuters reported on Friday that Mexican and American negotiators are working towards a bilateral trade agreement before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3.

LeBlanc said he has been in touch with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick recently. The minister said he had reached out to Lutnick to offer his thoughts for him and his family during the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

LeBlanc said he was encouraged by recent comments made by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum last week that all three countries should be at the negotiating table for the renewal of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma). The U.S. declined to renew the trade pact in July, which means all three parties are now subject to mandatory annual reviews.

The trade conflict between the U.S. and Canada has intensified in recent weeks, following the collapse in trade negotiations between both sides last month. U.S. President Donald Trump then imposed a 50 per-cent tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with Canada matching those tariffs, imposing levies ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports this week.

The U.S. tariffs represent about five per cent of Canadian exports to the U.S.

On Tuesday, Trump announced he would impose import bans on some Canadian alcohol products, dairy products and motorcycles, effective Sept. 29. Trump also removed items from the Section 338 tariff list, like cement, road salt, and added new items.

Economists have said the impact from the bans will be minimal on the Canadian economy.

Carney said Thursday evening that Trump’s import bans and changes to Section 338 tariffs were “relatively modest” compared to the president’s previous trade actions. He added that his government was still studying Trump’s latest trade actions and would not confirm whether he plans to retaliate.

Risks also remain that Trump could escalate further. The president has threatened to ban aerospace company Bombardier from selling in the U.S. and intends to impose a 50 per-cent tariff on Canadian autos and trucks on Jan. 1, 2027.

Carney has said Canada’s red lines in relation to negotiations with the Americans remain, including protections of the French language and its sovereignty.

Lutnick and Greer have disputed that the French language was ever a red line for American negotiators.

LeBlanc was asked if that means Canada can return to the negotiating table given the French language is no longer an issue in trade discussions. The minister reiterated that he would be pleased to set aside the matter, should negotiations resume.

Canadian Politics
LeBlanc said he has been in touch with his U.S. counterparts
Last updated 30 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/leblanc-says-no-meetings-scheduled-with-u-s-while-mexico-works-towards-a-deal#comments-area)
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc speaks during a press conference at the federal cabinet retreat in Banff on Sept. 11, 2026. Photo by Gavin Young /Postmedia

Ottawa — Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are no meetings scheduled in Washington, even as Mexico and the United States are reportedly working towards a completed bilateral deal by November.

“They’ve been at this for a number of months, and speeding towards a deal two months from now doesn’t feel like speed,” said LeBlanc, during a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., ON Friday. “But they are they are having those conversations as we did, as we May again at some point.”
Reuters reported on Friday that Mexican and American negotiators are working towards a bilateral trade agreement before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3.

LeBlanc said he has been in touch with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick recently. The minister said he had reached out to Lutnick to offer his thoughts for him and his family during the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

LeBlanc said he was encouraged by recent comments made by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum last week that all three countries should be at the negotiating table for the renewal of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma). The U.S. declined to renew the trade pact in July, which means all three parties are now subject to mandatory annual reviews.

The trade conflict between the U.S. and Canada has intensified in recent weeks, following the collapse in trade negotiations between both sides last month. U.S. President Donald Trump then imposed a 50 per-cent tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with Canada matching those tariffs, imposing levies ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports this week.
The U.S. tariffs represent about five per cent of Canadian exports to the U.S.

On Tuesday, Trump announced he would impose import bans on some Canadian alcohol products, dairy products and motorcycles, effective Sept. 29. Trump also removed items from the Section 338 tariff list, like cement, road salt, and added new items.
Economists have said the impact from the bans will be minimal on the Canadian economy.

Carney said Thursday evening that Trump’s import bans and changes to Section 338 tariffs were “relatively modest” compared to the president’s previous trade actions. He added that his government was still studying Trump’s latest trade actions and would not confirm whether he plans to retaliate.

Risks also remain that Trump could escalate further. The president has threatened to ban aerospace company Bombardier from selling in the U.S. and intends to impose a 50 per-cent tariff on Canadian autos and trucks on Jan. 1, 2027.
Carney has said Canada’s red lines in relation to negotiations with the Americans remain, including protections of the French language and its sovereignty.
Lutnick and Greer have disputed that the French language was ever a red line for American negotiators.

LeBlanc was asked if that means Canada can return to the negotiating table given the French language is no longer an issue in trade discussions. The minister reiterated that he would be pleased to set aside the matter, should negotiations resume.

stories.title: Photos: London marks firefighters’ memorial and 9/11 anniversary
stories.summary: The annual ceremony honoured 51 London firefighters and remembered those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The annual ceremony honoured 51 London firefighters and remembered those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

London Professional Firefighters Association president Jason Timlick presents the Martin E. Pierce commemorative medal to Niki Perryman, whose father, former London fire captain Douglas Ian Perryman, died in January, during the annual firefighters’ memorial at the Horton Street station on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Dale Carruthers/The London Free Press)

Emergency responders, politicians and community members gathered Friday at the Horton Street fire station for London’s annual firefighters’ memorial, honouring 51 local firefighters who died in the line of duty. The ceremony also marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 343 emergency responders and thousands of civilians in New York. Photos by Lfp’s Dale Carruthers.

London firefighters stand at attention during the national anthem at the annual firefighters’ memorial.

Retired London fire captain Phill King sounds the bell – a firefighting tradition used to signal shifts, alarms and the final return of a fallen firefighter – during the memorial.

London Professional Firefighters Association president Jason Timlick presents the Martin E. Pierce commemorative medal to Helen McCallum, whose husband, former London fire captain Dennis McCallum, died in 2007.

London police Chief Thai Truong and other members of the police force attend the annual firefighters’ memorial.

stories.title: 13-year-old charged after firearm seized at Ajax hotel: Durham police
stories.summary: A 13-year-old boy is facing multiple weapons charges after Durham police say a firearm was seized during an investigation at an Ajax hotel.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
A 13-year-old boy is facing multiple weapons charges after police say a firearm was seized during an investigation at an Ajax hotel.

Officers were called to a hotel near Westney Road South and Bayly Street West on Wednesday for an unknown trouble call, Durham Regional Police said in a news release Friday.

When officers arrived, police allege they encountered a boy armed with a knife and arrested him.

Investigators later received information that the teen May have a firearm, prompting officers and the police K9 unit to search the property.

Police said a firearm was also found and seized.

The Ajax teen is facing several charges, including carrying a concealed weapon, unauthorized possession of a restricted firearm, possession of a loaded restricted firearm and possession of a weapon dangerous to the public peace.

He is also charged with three counts of possessing a firearm while prohibited, two counts of failing to comply with a release order and four counts of failing to comply with a probation order.

Police said the teen was subject to multiple release orders when he was arrested, including a weapons prohibition order. He was held for a bail hearing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact authorities.

stories.title: London police seek suspect in two west-end arsons
stories.summary: Officers searched the area but couldn’t find the suspect.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
Surveillance images show a suspect sought in connection with two arsons at a west London business in August. (London police)

London police are asking for the public’s help identifying a suspect connected to two arsons at a west-end business last month.

At about 4 a.m. on Sunday, Aug. 23, a male suspect lit a Molotov cocktail and threw it at the front of a business near Oxford Street West and Westdel Bourne. The Molotov cocktail exploded and caused damage to the property, police said.

At about 3 a.m. on Saturday, Aug. 29, the male suspect returned to the area and committed a second arson, police said.

After obtaining video surveillance footage, investigators said they believe the same suspect May be responsible for both arsons.

During the first incident, the suspect was wearing a black tracksuit, black shoes and a red-and-white brimmed hat, police said.

During the second incident, the suspect was wearing a grey tracksuit, grey slide sandals and black socks.

Anyone with information about either incident, or who can identify the suspect, is asked to call London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips(8477).

A total of 48 charges have been laid against two youths after Windsor police say they were involved in a series of vehicle thefts and attempted thefts across the city.

Officers responded to 11 incidents between July 26 and Aug. 19 involving attempts to steal vehicles.

Police said suspects tried to get into the vehicles by prying off door handles or punching the locking mechanisms on the driver’s side doors.

Two vehicles were successfully stolen during the series of attempted thefts.

Police said one vehicle was taken Aug. 13 from a parking lot in the 200 block of Tecumseh Road East. Another was stolen the following day from a parking lot in the 900 block of Ottawa Street.

Both vehicles were later recovered, police said.

Investigators with the Windsor Police Service’s Target Base Unit identified two youths as suspects.

A 13-year-old boy was arrested Aug. 19 at a residence on the city’s west side, while a 12-year-old boy was arrested Sept. 1 at a separate west-end residence.

The youths cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Each youth is charged with 11 counts of mischief under $5,000, 11 counts of attempted theft of a motor vehicle and two counts of theft of a motor vehicle.

stories.title: Toronto police make another arrest in 2022 Scarborough shooting death
stories.summary: Toronto police say it has made another arrest in connection to the shooting death of a man in a Scarborough plaza nearly four years ago.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police say it’s made another arrest in connection to the shooting death of a man in Scarborough nearly four years ago.

On Nov. 12, 2022, 31-year-old Toronto resident Ding Pang Wang was shot while he was inside a vehicle in a parking lot near Midland and Passmore avenues.

He was approached by an unknown suspect, who opened fire and fled.

Police announced on Aug. 24 that 39-year-old Toronto resident Justin Longshaw was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.

On Thursday, 30-year-old Christopher Atkins-Price was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.

He was also charged with attempted murder in connection to a shooting on March 10, 2023.

That day, a 40-year-old man was inside a vehicle in the same plaza parking lot when he was approached and shot at several times.

The man, who suffered serious injuries, was able to escape and drive away.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: A Niagara winery makes its New York debut under the looming threat of a U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol
stories.summary: Restocking could prove impossible if the U.S.’s proposed ban takes effect later this month
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
This week, the first shipments of Canadian Leaning Post wines were sent out for delivery from their U.S. distributor to fine dining restaurants and wine bars in New York and New Jersey. Restocking the expressive pinot noirs and chardonnays from the family-owned craft winery in Stoney Creek, Ont., ON the edge of the Niagara region, could prove impossible if the U.S.’s proposed ban on importing Canadian alcohol comes into effect on Sept. 29 .

Steve Remming, sales director at New York distributor Lieber Fine Wines, had approached Leaning Post winery after being impressed by a bottle of their pinot noir about a year and a half ago. At a blind wine tasting where bottles are wrapped to disguise their origin, the group of collectors he was with believed it was an extremely high-quality, expensive red from Burgundy until its label was revealed.

Canadian alcohol producers face a U.S. ban, but some shipments can still cross the border

Lieber’s initial order, a 56-case mix of chardonnay, riesling and pinot noir, as well as the single vineyard Senchuk Pinot Noir that first convinced Remming, arrived at the company’s temperature-controlled warehouse in suburban New Jersey last month. Soon after, U.S. and Canadian negotiators failed to reach a trade agreement, and President Donald Trump’s 50-per-cent tariff on a range of goods, including many types of alcohol, took effect on Aug. 22.

“It’s sad for the wine drinking community in New York, who will love wines with this profile at this quality and price point but won’t be able to buy them or will only be able to buy them at a dramatically increased price,” says Remming.

While there is always risk involved in launching an unknown brand, an outright ban would be the worst-case scenario for establishing Leaning Post in his market. If their wines are available, he anticipates a positive reception and intends to expand his range to include other Leaning Post labels.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Leaning Post Wines (@leaningpostwine)

“The typical pinot noir drinker at a Michelin-star restaurant in Manhattan or a wine bar in Brooklyn isn’t wearing a Maga hat,” he says. “Even with the 50-per-cent tariff, the wines from Leaning Post and other producers of similar quality from Niagara are still worth the money. They are less expensive than their counterparts from Burgundy and California.”

Here are six Canadian wines to drink instead of U.S. labels

For Leaning Post co-owner Nadia Senchuk, exporting the wines her husband, Ilya, makes isn’t strictly about turning a profit, it helps build a strong reputation for Niagara wines and other Canadian producers. “Oregon didn’t only sell its wine in Oregon. Those winemakers sold to other markets right from the start and now Oregon pinot noir is established around the world,” she says.

Leaning Post is participating in an upcoming trade mission to Singapore and has completed industry trips to the United Kingdom to help open markets abroad while increasing sales to the Lcbo. Senchuk says sales through Ontario’s provincial liquor stores went from 300 cases in 2024, to nearly 4,000 cases this year.

“We continue to change people’s minds about the quality of local wines a glass and bottle at a time,” she says. “Building our reputation by selling our wine abroad helps sell our wine at home.”
