stories.title: Supreme Court rules no need to set time limit for sentencing proceedings
stories.summary: It says a man is entitled to a reduction in his sentence for sexual assault because the post-verdict sentencing phase of the case took too long
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada says a man is entitled to a reduction in his sentence for sexual assault because the post-verdict sentencing phase of the case took too long.

But the top court also says there is no need to set a time limit for determining a sentence because there is no persuasive evidence of a culture of complacency in sentencing proceedings in Canada.

The man, an Iranian citizen living in Ontario on a post-graduation work permit, was convicted in October 2021.

Sentencing proceedings were ongoing in October 2022 when the man applied for a stay of his case on the basis that his Charter right to timely justice had been infringed.

The trial judge dismissed the application, saying post-verdict sentencing delay was subject to a five-month limit, and that in the man’s case the delay amounted to just under four months.

In its 9-0 ruling today, the Supreme Court says the appropriate test for assessing a sentencing delay is whether the time taken to impose the sentence was markedly longer than it reasonably should have been in all circumstances.

stories.title: Giant MapQuest directions to Lake Ontario appear on billboards across Canadian and U.S. cities
stories.summary: MapQuest has erected billboards across Canada and the U.S. detailing directions to Lake Ontario, in an act of defiance against Donald Trump.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Navigation app MapQuest has put up billboards across Canada and the U.S. detailing directions to Lake Ontario, in its latest act of defiance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the body of water “Lake America.”

The app collaborated with creative agency Quality Meats to install the billboards, and the company shared in an email with National Post that the six-foot posts have been erected in six cities: Toronto, Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.

The designs recreate details from old-school MapQuest printed directions — the company having launched in 1996 as one of the first mapping services on the web — with old highway icons, a banner advert and a long URL running across the bottom of each page.

Canada’s billboard is located at 43 Lower Jarvis St., in Toronto, and includes just one page of directions, as opposed to the other cities’ three pages, owing to its proximity to the lake.

Meanwhile, Chicago’s board is found at State Street and Hubbard Street; Los Angeles’ is on Main Street in Santa Monica; and New York’s board is on East 38th St.; San Francisco’s board is at 490 Brannan St. and Washington, D.C.’s board is in the northwest quadrant of the District at Dupont Circle.

MapQuest’s new campaign comes after the company previously confirmed it has no intention of using the name “Lake America” in a social media post , after Trump’s Aug. 27 executive order directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name.

Both Google Maps and Apple Maps have adopted the name change for users based in the U.S., but MapQuest’s refusal to do the same resulted in a surge of people downloading the app in support of its stance.

In an email to National Post, MapQuest said it has since reached number one in the U.S. App Store in both the navigation category and overall, surpassing two million downloads as the app’s usage rose to roughly 50 times the normal amount.

In a recent interview with CNN , Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, said he has been “blown away” by the response.

When asked what he would do if Trump were to ask MapQuest to change the lake’s name, he said: “We’re fully committed to our users right now, and the users are showing what they believe in by downloading our app.”

He added that MapQuest’s recent actions were not intended to be a political stance, but to give people the names of lakes that they’re familiar with. “It’s fun that we’re talking about geography,” he said.

The company also expanded a feature allowing users to rename Lake Ontario within the app themselves, building on a tool it launched after Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025. It’s now selling Lake Ontario-themed merch, too, including a sweater with “We’re not changing it” written above a graphic of the lake and a tote bag and T-shirt reading “It’s Lake Ontario on MapQuest.”

Meanwhile, Robert Corradino, a Republican and mayor of Oswego, a city in New York State on the shore of Lake Ontario, has also taken a stance against the name change.

He previously told National Post that his community is taking the renaming of Lake Ontario “very personally” and said Oswego won’t alter any signage, tourism materials or official communications to reflect the new name.

In Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford erected a Lake Ontario sign at a cost of $25,000 in Winona, near Hamilton, shortly after Trump signed the executive order.

Unveiling the sign in a video posted on X, Ford said: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

More recently, B.C. has unveiled plans to install signs at its border crossings informing travellers that they are entering territory that is “Never the 51st state” in a rejection of Trump’s rhetoric around Canada.

The worsening of relations between Canada and the U.S. comes after a breakdown in trade negotiations between the two countries last month, which saw 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods imposed on Aug. 22, followed by Canadian counter-tariffs which came into effect on Tuesday.

Later that day, Trump unveiled a series of executive orders to ban certain Canadian goods, including some dairy products, motorcycles and alcoholic beverages, from being imported to the U.S.

T he U.S. president appeared to suggest renaming New Mexico to “New America” in a post on Truth Social over the weekend, while David Maloney, a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania, plans to put a resolution before the U.S. House of Representatives urging the renaming of Lake Erie to “Lake Pennsylvania.”

content_blocks.html: Navigation app MapQuest has put up billboards across Canada and the U.S. detailing directions to Lake Ontario, in its latest act of defiance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the body of water “Lake America.”

content_blocks.text: The app collaborated with creative agency Quality Meats to install the billboards, and the company shared in an email with National Post that the six-foot posts have been erected in six cities: Toronto, Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.

The designs recreate details from old-school MapQuest printed directions — the company having launched in 1996 as one of the first mapping services on the web — with old highway icons, a banner advert and a long URL running across the bottom of each page.
Canada’s billboard is located at 43 Lower Jarvis St., in Toronto, and includes just one page of directions, as opposed to the other cities’ three pages, owing to its proximity to the lake.

Meanwhile, Chicago’s board is found at State Street and Hubbard Street; Los Angeles’ is on Main Street in Santa Monica; and New York’s board is on East 38th St.; San Francisco’s board is at 490 Brannan St. and Washington, D.C.’s board is in the northwest quadrant of the District at Dupont Circle.

MapQuest’s new campaign comes after the company previously confirmed it has no intention of using the name “Lake America” in a social media post , after Trump’s Aug. 27 executive order directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name.

content_blocks.text: When asked what he would do if Trump were to ask MapQuest to change the lake’s name, he said: “We’re fully committed to our users right now, and the users are showing what they believe in by downloading our app.”

He added that MapQuest’s recent actions were not intended to be a political stance, but to give people the names of lakes that they’re familiar with. “It’s fun that we’re talking about geography,” he said.

The company also expanded a feature allowing users to rename Lake Ontario within the app themselves, building on a tool it launched after Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025. It’s now selling Lake Ontario-themed merch, too, including a sweater with “We’re not changing it” written above a graphic of the lake and a tote bag and T-shirt reading “It’s Lake Ontario on MapQuest.”

stories.title: Why are rising bond yields spurring alarm? And what do they mean for you?
stories.summary: Consumers could be facing higher borrowing costs for longer as bond markets are once again signalling rising economic risk to the finance and investing community.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Consumers could be facing higher borrowing costs for longer as bond markets are once again signalling rising economic risk to the finance and investing community amid the Iran war, rising government debt and an escalating trade war.

A bond is essentially a loan that governments and companies use to borrow money from the general public, and in return for providing funding, those that purchase bonds expect to earn interest.

The yield on the 10-year U.S. government bond increased to about 4.9 per cent as of publication — the highest since 2023, an increase of 0.8 percentage points since the start of September. This also comes after the 30-year bond yield spiked over five per cent in July , the highest since 2007.

Meanwhile, Canada’s 10-year government bond yield was at about 3.9 per cent, the highest in nearly two years, with most of the spike happening at the start of the month. This was at the same time that Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect, and raised inflation risks.

Bond yields tend to fluctuate for a variety of reasons, but a sudden sharp rise in bond yields can signal that investors are concerned about inflation, government debt or economic uncertainty and are choosing to sell their bonds because of the increased perceived risk.

Higher yields can also drive up interest rates on mortgages, corporate loans, consumer credit and other products to protect lenders like banks from a higher risk environment. Although the Bank of Canada’s interest rate policy can affect borrowing costs in the short-term, bond market changes have more of an affect on long-term rates.

“You have these higher oil prices because of the Iran war and that’s stoking inflation fears, you’re seeing treasury yields in the U.S. spike, and that’s because investors are demanding a higher return on lending the government their money because they see so much risk there,” says mortgage and personal finance expert Clay Jarvis at NerdWallet Canada.

“That can be tied to the Iran war and the amount of money that is being spent there and the inflationary impact that it’s having on U.S. consumers.”

Bonds are priced based mostly on supply and demand, but the reasons for those changes can vary.

According to a statement released Wednesday from Kana Norimoto, an allocation of assets researcher at Fidelity Investments, long-term bond investors are trying to guess about what will happen with interest rates, inflation, government debt and spending, and says, “When the future feels unpredictable, investors want a bigger payout to take on the risk of holding onto long-term bonds.”

“People are starting to look a little nervous if they’re holding large amounts of government bonds,” says economics professor Moshe Lander of Concordia University.

“That’s not the type of thing that attracts people then, that could actually make them run away, and it could actually exacerbate the problem.”

There are several risks economies worldwide are exposed to, with the U.S. at the centre of it all because it is the world’s largest economy. This includes the war with Iran, which has led to spiking prices for oil and other commodities, and has led to higher inflation.

“As the ceasefire in the Middle East dissolved, oil prices jumped back above US$90 per barrel—the highest level since early June—stoking inflation concerns,” said Vikram Rai, senior economist at TD Bank, in a report on Thursday.

Rai added: “Since the relative low in yields before the conflict with Iran, 10-year yields have risen by about 80 basis points in the U.S. and 60 basis points in Canada.”

Rising U.S. debt is another area of concern for investors.

“The U.S. government is borrowing more as some traditional buyers step back,” said Rai.

“Private investors must therefore absorb a growing share of government debt and are demanding higher yields to do so. ”

Although higher bond yields can present an investing opportunity for certain investors, it can also present affordability challenges for consumers, especially with long-term loan products.

Higher bond yields can effect the interest rates on certain mortgages, car loans, lines of credit and student debt.

With mortgages, for example, if government bond yields are rising, that could result in higher fixed-term mortgages offered by commercial banks and other lenders.

“When these bond yields increase, you often see banks and other lenders increasing their three and five-year fixed rates.”

Higher borrowing costs as a result of spiking bond yields could also indirectly lead to higher prices for some goods and services in Canada.

If a business is faced with higher costs, they May make changes to maintain profits. This can be through increasing productivity, reducing costs elsewhere, or potentially passing along those higher costs to consumers.

“There should still be lots of concerns here for businesses and consumers. If the yields are higher, then that means when the government has to refinance its debt, it’s going to have to refinance it at a higher rate,” says Lander.

“This all of a sudden becomes more expensive than for businesses to raise cash, to pay for capital expansion, to pay for trying to find new markets or new suppliers or to try and take on more workers or replace existing equipment. So all of those things raise the cost of doing business in Canada .”

Lander also says it’s Canadian businesses that don’t have as much market competition, like with groceries, telecommunications and banking, which May find it easier than other sectors to raise prices for consumers when faced with higher costs.

“Will it spill over to the consumer? Yeah, it’s gonna spill over because firms aren’t afraid to pass along that cost to the consumer because there’s nobody there to come and steal their business by undercutting them.”

stories.title: Report: Clippers face criminal investigation for Kawhi Leonard contracts; Raptors trade still on hold
stories.summary: Federal prosecutors began investigating the matter before the NBA announcement and have issued at least one subpoena, per the Times.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
Posted September 11, 2026 12:15 pm.

The Los Angeles Clippers could be dealing with more than just punishment from the NBA for the Kawhi Leonard salary-cap circumvention scandal.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Brooklyn, N.Y., has opened a criminal investigation into allegations that the Clippers helped organize contracts for Leonard that violated salary-cap rules, the _New York Times_reportedThursday.

A spokesman for the office declined comment to the Times, while the Clippers and NBA did not respond to requests for comment.

Earlier this month, the NBA stripped the Clippers of five first-round picks from 2029 through 2033 and fined the team $30 million, among other punishments, after an independent investigation found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations.

Leonard was fined $700,000.

Federal prosecutors began investigating the matter before the NBA announcement and have issued at least one subpoena, the Times reported. The newspaper added that other specifics about that case, including its scope, targets and possible crimes, were unclear.

The Clippers, according to the Times, are considering a lawsuit against the NBA in the aftermath of the punishment.

Because Leonard did not have his contract voided and wasn’t suspended, the NBA’s ruling was believed to have cleared the path for the Clippers to complete a trade with the Toronto Raptors that they had agreed to earlier this summer.

However, the deal hasn’t been officially announced yet, and training camp is set to open later this month. The Raptors paused the deal while waiting for the NBA to conclude its investigation.

The U.S. attorney’s office has been involved in cases of gambling in professional sports, including former NBA guard Chauncey Billups and MLB closer Emmanuel Clase.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada still talking trade with U.S. officials despite no meetings: LeBlanc
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says that while Canada isn't currently in official trade negotiations with the U.S., officials on both sides are still talking.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says that while Canada isn’t currently in official trade negotiations with the U.S., officials on both sides are still talking.

LeBlanc is in Banff, Alta, for the two-day Liberal cabinet retreat , where the ongoing trade war with the United States is a key topic.

He says he has no meetings in Washington scheduled but he has spoken several times with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and sometimes speaks with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as well.

LeBlanc says it’s important to be ready for a possible deal that respects Canadian sovereignty and is the country’s national interest.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed new orders to ban imports of some Canadian products, including most alcohol, and increase tariffs on some others on Tuesday after Canada imposed retaliatory duties on the United States.

That happened after trade talks reached an impasse in August, which led to Trump imposing 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods ranging from honey and sunscreen to sports equipment and milk.

stories.title: Travel between Canada and U.S. was going up before trade talks collapsed
stories.summary: In August, Canadians made 2.6 million return trips from the United States, up 8.8 per cent from the same month in 2025. This marked the fifth consecutive month of growth.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Travel between Canada and the United States was steadily climbing in August, before trade talks collapsed shortly before the end of the month between the two countries and U.S. President Donald Trump escalated his trade war against Canada.

The number of Canadians travelling south fell sharply last year following the growth of the Buy Canadian movement, but the trend had been reversing this year, data from Statistics Canada shows.

On Aug. 21, Canada walked away from talks after the U.S. demanded “unacceptable” last-minute concessions, Prime Minister Mark Carney said. After Trump imposed fresh, sweeping 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, Ottawa responded with dollar-for-dollar counter-measures.

In August, Canadians made 2.6 million return trips from the United States, up 8.8 per cent from the same month in 2025. This marked the fifth consecutive month of growth.

However, the travel figures were still not back to their 2024 levels for August.

While return trips by automobile rose 9.9 per cent compared to August 2025, the number was 27.4 per cent lower compared to the same month in 2024. Return trips by air rose 3.6 per cent compared to the same month last year but were down 22.7 per cent compared to August 2024.

Travel from abroad in August peaked during the long weekend, with 176,900 returning home on Monday, Aug. 3.

More Americans travelled to Canada in August compared to the same time a year ago. U.S.-resident trips to Canada increased 2.4 per cent in August, reaching 2.4 million. This marked the seventh consecutive month of increase, Statistics Canada said.

In August, Americans made 1.8 million road trips to Canada, up one per cent compared to the same month in 2025. They also took 629,600 trips to Canada by air, an increase of 6.8 per cent.

August also marked the first full month of operation for the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which connects Windsor, Ont., to Detroit, Mich.

The bridge was used for 134,900 return-trips by Canadians from the U.S., although more than half (56.7 per cent) were same-day trips.

During the same period, 101,000 Americans made trips to Canada via the bridge, with 52.2 per cent being same-day trips.

August also saw a significant drop in Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge being used, with 348,000 total trips entering Canada. This was a drop of 35.4 per cent from August 2025.

stories.title: A one-time $150 Canada disability benefit supplement is going out next week
stories.summary: The federal government is about to send out payments of $150 to Canadians who qualify for the Canada Disability Benefit (CDB).
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The federal government is about to send out an additional payment of $150 to Canadians who qualify for Canada Disability Benefit (CDB) payments.

The one-time payment, announced Thursday in a release from Employment and Social Development Canada (Esdc), is in addition to the CDB program’s regular monthly payments, to help those individuals offset the costs associated with obtaining the disability tax credit (DTC), including necessary certificates.

The Canada Disability Benefit is a federal program created to provide financial support to low-income, working-age persons with disabilities through regular monthly benefit payments, including on Sept. 17, when those that qualify for the CDB will receive up to $204.20.

In order to qualify for the CDB, one must first be approved for the disability tax credit.

The disability tax credit is available for Canadians with physical or mental impairments to reduce the amount of income tax they owe, according to the Canada Revenue Agency , which adds the credit aims to offset some of the related costs individuals or their supporting family members May face.

To be approved for this tax credit, individuals must obtain a T2201 certificate, which some practitioners May charge a fee to fill out for patients.

“Since its launch last year, the Canada Disability Benefit has helped support the financial security of hundreds of thousands of working-age Canadians with disabilities.

“This new supplemental payment will help cover the cost of getting the disability tax credit, so more people can access the support they are entitled to,” said Canada’s jobs and families minister, Patty Hajdu, in the release.

The payments will be sent automatically to those who qualify if they received CDB payments all at once for a full payment period, as well as people who have received the benefit in the past and could receive $150 for each approved DTC certificate.

The government says an example is someone who only received one CDB payment and is no longer eligible for the CDB.

The one-time payments will be sent on Sept. 17 with the regular CDB payment for eligible recipients who received a CDB payment from July 2025 to June 2026.

Those that received CDB payments since July 2026 will see the additional one-time payment in winter 2027, but a specific date has not yet been provided, and will include individuals who were approved for new DTC certificates.

To date, the Esdc says 335,650 people have received Canada Disability Benefit payments totalling $813,074,098.

stories.title: No need to set time limit for sentencing proceedings, Supreme Court of Canada rules
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada says a man is entitled to a reduction in his sentence for sexual assault because the post-verdict sentencing phase of the case took too long.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada says a man is entitled to a reduction in his sentence for sexual assault because the post-verdict sentencing phase of the case took too long.

But the top court also says there is no need to set a time limit for determining a sentence because there is no persuasive evidence of a culture of complacency in sentencing proceedings in Canada.

The man, an Iranian citizen living in Ontario on a post-graduation work permit, was convicted in October 2021.

Sentencing proceedings were ongoing in October 2022 when the man applied for a stay of his case on the basis that his Charter right to timely justice had been infringed.

The trial judge dismissed the application, saying post-verdict sentencing delay was subject to a five-month limit, and that in the man’s case the delay amounted to just under four months.

In its 9-0 ruling today, the Supreme Court says the appropriate test for assessing a sentencing delay is whether the time taken to impose the sentence was markedly longer than it reasonably should have been in all circumstances.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Sentencing proceedings were ongoing in October 2022 when the man applied for a stay of his case on the basis that his Charter right to timely justice had been infringed.
The trial judge dismissed the application, saying post-verdict sentencing delay was subject to a five-month limit, and that in the man’s case the delay amounted to just under four months.

In its 9-0 ruling today, the Supreme Court says the appropriate test for assessing a sentencing delay is whether the time taken to impose the sentence was markedly longer than it reasonably should have been in all circumstances.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.
Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hoekstra says U.S. needs ‘our allies on board’ to counter terrorist threats
stories.summary: The U.S. ambassador attended a memorial in Gander, Newfoundland to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks on New York City.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The U.S. ambassador to Canada says his country needs their “allies on board” to counter terrorist threats that target Western democracies’ way of life.

Pete Hoekstra was in Gander, N.L., ON Friday to attend a memorial marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks on New York City. The people of Gander took in stranded passengers diverted to the province after the attacks on the World Trade Centre and the Pentagon disrupted air travel.

“We appreciate Canada’s support, their friendship, and the contributions they made that day and for the years since,” Hoekstra told Global News in an interview.

“(The attacks are) the kind of threat we face today that we need all of our allies on board. Not on board America’s strategy, but on board a strategy that says this is an evil that threatens each of our countries … It is a threat, we need to confront it.”

Hoekstra’s tenure as ambassador has not been particularly known for showing U.S. appreciation for Canadian support and friendship.

Instead, it’s been marked by U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats of annexation, snide comments from his cabinet about the Canadian military, and Trump’s ongoing trade war hitting businesses and workers on both sides of the border.

Hoekstra himself has engaged in the cross-border sniping, recently reposting an image on social media with Lake Ontario “renamed” Lake America. He’s previously shared other social media posts promoting Trump’s threats at making Canada the “51st state.”

As of Friday, more than 269,000 people have signed a House of Commons petition to declare Hoekstra a persona non grata in Canada and expel him.

But Hoekstra told Global News he wasn’t interested in discussing bilateral relations Friday.

“I don’t really want to get into it in any kind of depth today, in that the focus is on 9/11. In terms of respect, both ways, that’s an issue that I think we can talk about in the future, and I’d be willing to,” Hoekstra said.

Nearly 7,000 travellers were stranded in the town of Gander and surrounding areas after planes were diverted on Sept. 11, 2001. The story spawned the hit Broadway musical Come From Away, which highlights the town’s kindness and hospitality in the wake of the 9/11 attacks.

stories.title: ‘You live with this every day’: 25 years after 9/11, World Trade Center survivor recounts escape from South Tower
stories.summary: Dittmar reached the 78th‑floor lobby, where evacuees were choosing elevators. He stayed in the stairwell; a decision he says saved his life.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto; Nick Westoll
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto and Nick Westoll

Posted September 11, 2026 10:43 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 10:54 am.

On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks , a South Tower survivor is sharing his story of escape, loss and resilience with CityNews — a detailed, harrowing account of what unfolded inside the World Trade Center as the deadliest terror attack in modern history began.

Joseph Dittmar, then a commercial underwriting executive from Chicago, says he was on the 105th floor of the South Tower for a morning meeting when the first plane struck the North Tower at 8:46 a.m. He was one of 54 people inside a windowless conference room when the lights flickered — the only sign something catastrophic had happened.

“We couldn’t see anything. We didn’t hear anything. We didn’t feel anything — just that flicker of lights,” Dittmar said in an interview with CityNews.

A volunteer fire marshal entered the room and ordered everyone to evacuate. Dittmar was the last person out.

“Fifty-four of us all said the same thing. ‘We’re fine, it’s New York. Stuff happens, don’t worry about it. Let us have our meeting.’ This gentleman was firm and said, ‘Listen, I am a volunteer fire marshal… I can’t leave until all of you leave, and I want to leave.'”

Dittmar says the group was directed to walk down 105 flights of stairs. Cell phones showed no service — the main tower for southern Manhattan was atop the North Tower, already burning.

As they descended, Dittmar said they had no understanding of the scale of the attack.

“All of you knew way more of what was going on than any of us that were right there. We didn’t have a clue.”

On the 90th floor, the stairwell door was propped open. Against fire‑safety training, Dittmar followed others out — and saw the North Tower for the first time.

“Gaping black holes… flames redder than any red I had ever seen… pieces of the fuselage lodged inside the building,” Dittmar explained, telling CityNews he watched furniture, paper and even people being pulled out of the tower.

“My first thought was, ‘My God, how did the pilot not see this building?’ He didn’t miss. He did exactly what he intended on doing. An unbelievable, gruesome sight.”

Terrified, he returned to the stairwell.

“I got to tell you, the first reaction? I was so afraid, so afraid,” Dittmar said. “I didn’t know what I was looking at, but all I did know was that I wanted to get home. I didn’t want to be there. I wanted to get home.”

Dittmar reached the 78th‑floor sky lobby, where many evacuees were choosing elevators. He stayed in the stairwell — a decision he says saved his life.

He was between floors 74 and 72 when the second plane struck the South Tower at 9:03 a.m.

“Never felt anything like that in my life. The stairwell was shaking violently… handrails breaking… concrete spidering… steps undulating like waves,” he said.

A “heat ball” blew past him. Jet fuel filled the air.

“Ignorance was bliss. We didn’t know a plane had gone through our building.”

Still, evacuees continued downward, helping those with injuries or mobility challenges. When Dittmar reached the lobby, he saw twisted steel, crumbled concrete and red markings on the ground.

Security staff directed evacuees into the underground concourse because debris — and bodies — were falling outside.

“I’ve never seen such an outpouring of caring and love… firefighters, paramedics, cops everywhere,” he shared.

Eight blocks north, they heard the South Tower collapse.

“You hear this unmistakable sound of twisting steel and crumbling concrete, and this would sound like a freight train just coming at us. That was the South Tower coming to the ground,” Dittmar shared. “And even more hauntingly, at that same time, the sound of tens of thousands of people on the streets of New York, all screaming the same blood-curdling scream, all at the same time.”

Hours later, watching TV coverage, Dittmar saw the replay of the plane hitting his tower.

“My God, how did I even get out of there? I almost fell to my knees when I saw that because I couldn’t get over the fact that that’s just where I was.”

Dittmar says one colleague from the same meeting died after briefly stopping at a restroom on the 90th floor.

“I had a friend of mine on [floor] 90 who was in the same meeting as me, who came out of the fire stairwell with me, and he looked at me, and he saw me getting ready to get back into the fire stairwell, and he said, ‘What are you going to do, Joe? And I said, ‘I’m getting out. I said, ‘What are you going to do, Lud? And Lud looked at me, and he said, ‘Yeah, I’m going to go, but before I go, I’m going to go, and he pointed to the nearest restroom,” Dittmar recounted.

“That delay and his exiting cost him his life that day. The margins were razor-thin, razor-thin.”

He credits critical decisions, luck and what he calls “divine providence.”

Dittmar says he remains deeply grateful for Canada’s response — from first responders who travelled to New York to the now‑famous Gander story, where thousands of stranded passengers were sheltered for days.

“Every ounce of help we got from Canada was greatly appreciated. We can’t have greater friends.”

He also expressed gratitude to Canadian soldiers who served — and died — in Afghanistan following the attacks.

“Those who served helped make the world a little bit safer. Their efforts were not in vain.”

“That delay and his exiting cost him his life that day. The margins were razor-thin, razor-thin.”
He credits critical decisions, luck and what he calls “divine providence.”

Dittmar says he remains deeply grateful for Canada’s response — from first responders who travelled to New York to the now‑famous Gander story, where thousands of stranded passengers were sheltered for days.
“Every ounce of help we got from Canada was greatly appreciated. We can’t have greater friends.”

content_blocks.html: On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, a South Tower survivor is sharing his story of escape, loss and resilience with CityNews — a detailed, harrowing account of what unfolded inside the World Trade Center as the deadliest terror attack in modern history began.

content_blocks.text: Joseph Dittmar, then a commercial underwriting executive from Chicago, says he was on the 105th floor of the South Tower for a morning meeting when the first plane struck the North Tower at 8:46 a.m. He was one of 54 people inside a windowless conference room when the lights flickered — the only sign something catastrophic had happened.
“We couldn’t see anything. We didn’t hear anything. We didn’t feel anything — just that flicker of lights,” Dittmar said in an interview with CityNews.
A volunteer fire marshal entered the room and ordered everyone to evacuate. Dittmar was the last person out.

“Fifty-four of us all said the same thing. ‘We’re fine, it’s New York. Stuff happens, don’t worry about it. Let us have our meeting.’ This gentleman was firm and said, ‘Listen, I am a volunteer fire marshal… I can’t leave until all of you leave, and I want to leave.'”
content_blocks.html: “Fifty-four of us all said the same thing. ‘We’re fine, it’s New York. Stuff happens, don’t worry about it. Let us have our meeting.’ This gentleman was firm and said, ‘Listen, I am a volunteer fire marshal… I can’t leave until all of you leave, and I want to leave.'”

content_blocks.caption: Photo courtesy: The Associated Press.

content_blocks.text: ‘We didn’t have a clue’ — the descent begins
Dittmar says the group was directed to walk down 105 flights of stairs. Cell phones showed no service — the main tower for southern Manhattan was atop the North Tower, already burning.
As they descended, Dittmar said they had no understanding of the scale of the attack.
“All of you knew way more of what was going on than any of us that were right there. We didn’t have a clue.”
On the 90th floor, the stairwell door was propped open. Against fire‑safety training, Dittmar followed others out — and saw the North Tower for the first time.

“Gaping black holes… flames redder than any red I had ever seen… pieces of the fuselage lodged inside the building,” Dittmar explained, telling CityNews he watched furniture, paper and even people being pulled out of the tower.
“My first thought was, ‘My God, how did the pilot not see this building?’ He didn’t miss. He did exactly what he intended on doing. An unbelievable, gruesome sight.”
Terrified, he returned to the stairwell.

“I got to tell you, the first reaction? I was so afraid, so afraid,” Dittmar said. “I didn’t know what I was looking at, but all I did know was that I wanted to get home. I didn’t want to be there. I wanted to get home.”

content_blocks.caption: Photo courtesy: The Associated Press.

content_blocks.text: The second plane hits the South Tower
Dittmar reached the 78th‑floor sky lobby, where many evacuees were choosing elevators. He stayed in the stairwell — a decision he says saved his life.
He was between floors 74 and 72 when the second plane struck the South Tower at 9:03 a.m.
“Never felt anything like that in my life. The stairwell was shaking violently… handrails breaking… concrete spidering… steps undulating like waves,” he said.
A “heat ball” blew past him. Jet fuel filled the air.
“Ignorance was bliss. We didn’t know a plane had gone through our building.”
Still, evacuees continued downward, helping those with injuries or mobility challenges. When Dittmar reached the lobby, he saw twisted steel, crumbled concrete and red markings on the ground.
Security staff directed evacuees into the underground concourse because debris — and bodies — were falling outside.
“I’ve never seen such an outpouring of caring and love… firefighters, paramedics, cops everywhere,” he shared.
Eight blocks north, they heard the South Tower collapse.

“You hear this unmistakable sound of twisting steel and crumbling concrete, and this would sound like a freight train just coming at us. That was the South Tower coming to the ground,” Dittmar shared. “And even more hauntingly, at that same time, the sound of tens of thousands of people on the streets of New York, all screaming the same blood-curdling scream, all at the same time.”
Hours later, watching TV coverage, Dittmar saw the replay of the plane hitting his tower.
“My God, how did I even get out of there? I almost fell to my knees when I saw that because I couldn’t get over the fact that that’s just where I was.”
The razor‑thin margins of survival
Dittmar says one colleague from the same meeting died after briefly stopping at a restroom on the 90th floor.

“I had a friend of mine on [floor] 90 who was in the same meeting as me, who came out of the fire stairwell with me, and he looked at me, and he saw me getting ready to get back into the fire stairwell, and he said, ‘What are you going to do, Joe? And I said, ‘I’m getting out. I said, ‘What are you going to do, Lud? And Lud looked at me, and he said, ‘Yeah, I’m going to go, but before I go, I’m going to go, and he pointed to the nearest restroom,” Dittmar recounted.
“That delay and his exiting cost him his life that day. The margins were razor-thin, razor-thin.”
He credits critical decisions, luck and what he calls “divine providence.”

Dittmar says he remains deeply grateful for Canada’s response — from first responders who travelled to New York to the now‑famous Gander story, where thousands of stranded passengers were sheltered for days.
“Every ounce of help we got from Canada was greatly appreciated. We can’t have greater friends.”
He also expressed gratitude to Canadian soldiers who served — and died — in Afghanistan following the attacks.
“Those who served helped make the world a little bit safer. Their efforts were not in vain.”

stories.title: Roots reports second-quarter loss, sets date for take-private vote
stories.summary: Shareholders will vote in October on an offer to be acquired by Marquee Brands
stories.content:
Roots Corp. Root-T reported a loss of $6-million in its latest quarter as it set the date for a shareholder meeting to vote on its deal to be acquired by Marquee Brands.

The retailer says it will hold a virtual shareholder meeting on Oct. 13 to vote on the friendly offer by the New York brand management firm to take the company private at a price of $4.10 per share.

In reporting its latest financial results, Roots says its second-quarter loss amounted to 15 cents per share for the quarter ended Aug. 1 compared with a loss of $4.4-million or 11 cents per share a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, Roots says it lost eight cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted loss of nine cents per share in the same quarter last year.

Total sales for the quarter amounted to $49.5-million, down from $50.8-million a year ago.

Direct-to-consumer sales totalled $40.5-million, down from $41-million in the same quarter last year, while partner and other sales amounted to $9-million, down from $9.7-million.

stories.title: ‘Our grief has not faded,’ Carney says on 25th anniversary of 9/11
stories.summary: Carney remembered the nearly 3,000 people who were killed in the attacks, including 24 Canadians, as well as thousands who were wounded.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada will never forget those who lost their lives in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday as the world marked the 25 th anniversary of that devastating day.

“The truest tribute is to serve – to look after the stranger amongst us simply because help is needed,” Carney said.

Carney remembered the nearly 3,000 people who were killed in the attacks, including 24 Canadians as well as thousands who were wounded.

“Twenty-five years on, our grief has not faded – and neither has our resolve to stand against hatred and terrorism,” he said.

Canada will never forget. pic.twitter.com/zvpzoRmrbs — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) September 11, 2026

In his tribute, Carney also expressed solidarity with Americans.

“Canadians stand with our American neighbours in mourning, remembrance, and solidarity,” he said.

In the hours following the attacks, when American airspace was closed off, Canada accepted 224 planes “without hesitation,” Carney said, making a special mention of the town Gander, N.L.

The town of Gander, N.L., a town of around 10,000 people, and surrounding areas took in nearly 7,000 stranded travellers whose planes were diverted.

Nato, the military alliance of which both Canada and the United States are part, invoked a rare article in its charter for the first time in its history. Article 5, which calls on all members to respond to an attack on any one member, was invoked and Canada followed the U.S. as it invaded Afghanistan.

Carney paid tribute to the more than 40,000 Canadians who served in Afghanistan in the years that followed.

“We will never forget those who never came home, the courage of those who ran toward the danger, and the small acts of kindness that brought light to the darkest of days,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also paid tribute to the victims.

“We remember every life that was tragically lost and honour the courage that Canadians and Americans summoned in its wake,” Poilievre said on Friday.

stories.title: Tornado and downburst confirmed in Huron-Perth
stories.summary: The damage, west of Monkton, from a Sept. 2 storm, has been confirmed as an EF1 tornado, by the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
An EF1 tornado, packing winds of 150 km/h twisted a five-storey high steel grain bin into a pretzel, and ripped the roof off a neighbouring shed.

The damage, west of Monkton, from a Sept. 2 storm, has been confirmed as an EF1 tornado, by the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University.

More damage, including a large farm shed being destroyed, near Seaforth, has been categorized as an EF1 downburst, with winds exceeding 165km/h.

The storm left a path of destruction, stretching from Bayfield to Cambridge, uprooting trees, levelling several barns and sheds, throughout Huron and Perth Counties.

EF1 tornadoes have already been confirmed by the Northern Tornadoes Project, to have touched down near Tavistock, Wellesley, and Shakespeare, during the same storm.

stories.title: Justin Trudeau to launch production company at Tiff with former top aide Katie Telford
stories.summary: Company says Hope & Hard Work will create both scripted and unscripted content, and several projects are already in development
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Justin Trudeau is officially getting into showbiz.

The former prime minister is launching a production company with his longtime chief of staff, Katie Telford, called Hope & Hard Work.

They’re announcing the new venture at the Toronto International Film Festival today.

A press release from the company says Hope & Hard Work will create both scripted and unscripted content, and several projects are already in development.

They include Perry Chafe’s Newfoundland-set coming-of-age novel Closer by Sea , and Uzma Jalaluddin’s cozy mystery Detective Aunty , with Trudeau and Telford set to serve as executive producers.

Trudeau stepped back from politics after announcing his resignation in January, 2025 and has been on the speaking circuit, including at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

There, he spoke about the importance of “soft power,” an umbrella that includes popular culture.

He was joined at Davos by his girlfriend, the American pop star Katy Perry.

With the production company, Trudeau follows in the footsteps of former U.S. president Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama, who in 2018 founded Higher Ground Productions.

Their projects include the 2023 biopic Rustin and documentary American Symphony .

stories.title: Tiff 2026: Opening night delivers odd dose of America for this era of Canadian cultural sovereignty
stories.summary: There was a cognitive dissonance in the geopolitical air that the festival could not help but uneasily brush against
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
How does Canada’s biggest film festival kick off an 11-day celebration of all things global cinema – including and especially Hollywood – in the midst of a trade war with the United States? In the case of the Toronto International Film Festival: very, very carefully.

With the festival long past the days when it would open with a Canadian film, the first night of the 51st edition of Tiff on Thursday delivered the world premiere of Being Heumann , a disability-rights drama that was shot in and around Toronto but is funded by Apple, the epitome of Big U.S. Tech.

Although direct or Siân Heder’s seventies-set film hit most of the sweet spots when it comes to a typical Tiff opener – it’s a well-intentioned but stubbornly middle-of-the-road crowd-pleaser, featuring just enough familiar faces to keep corporate sponsors and well-heeled patrons happy – there was a cognitive dissonance in the geopolitical air that the festival could not help but uneasily brush against.

For starters, the film – chronicling an historic sit-in protest coordinated by activist Judy Heumann (played by Ruth Madeley) – is a resolutely American story of revolution and struggle. As Heumann storms a federal building in San Francisco (really, downtown Toronto) with her self-described cohort of “radical crips” in a bid to change the direction of U.S. politics for the better, you can practically hear Heder hum The Star-Spangled Banner in the background. Heck, the film ends with a scene set on the steps of the U.S. Capitol. That’s all well and good for the narrative that Heder wants to tell, but the movie’s themes clashed with the festival sentiments that preceded it.

“Welcome to Tiff, and welcome to the beautiful shores of – say it with me – Lake Ontario!” Tiff chief executive Cameron Bailey said while greeting the crowd inside Roy Thomson Hall, taking obvious aim at U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent attempt at changing universally accepted hydronyms.

That introduction was followed by a similar rallying cry from Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, who noted that Canadian artists are so impactful they “can move mountains, even against the might of the U.S. government,” before also going on to name-check Lake Ontario.

The sentiments are certainly understandable and justified, and the crowd predictably ate it up – even if it felt like Tiff was having its patriotic McCain Deep’n Delicious Cake and eating it, too.

With four premieres, Canadian actor Joe Cobden might be Tiff’s stealth MVP

Given that the cultural tensions between this country and our neighbour to the south are not exactly new, a mildly cynical festival-goer (guilty as charged) might wonder if organizers could have foreseen the uneasiness that might arrive from opening a Canadian arts festival with a distinctly American production.

It’s not as if worthy Canadian films are in short supply this year.

Just down the street from the Being Heumann premiere Thursday night, Canadian director Nyla Innuksuk’s wonderful comedic thriller In the Heart of the South was having its world premiere. Friday, meanwhile, brings the world premiere of Michael Dowse’s action-comedy The Stunt Driver , another worthy contender for opening night. Or if Tiff is dead-set on the inspirational true-story route for its big kick-off slot, there’s the Canadian doc Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story , also debuting Friday, and as a gala title in Roy Thomson Hall, no less.

The last Canadian film to open Tiff was Daniel Roher’s 2019 doc about Robbie Robertson and The Band, which turned out well enough for Toronto (the film was well-received and delivered celebrity sizzle) and Roher (who went on to win the Best Documentary Oscar for his subsequent film Navalny ).

Perhaps in this renewed era of cultural sovereignty, Tiff should plant a flag from Day One of the fest. It’s not like they’d be such an outlier, either. Cannes historically books a French film as its opening-night selection, even if those titles never travel outside of the country, and most international critics visiting the festival tend to skip them. Tiff is our festival – we can have it for one night.

What the festival is surely hoping won’t last longer than one day or night, though, are the hiccups inside its inaugural edition of Tiff: The Market.

Glitz, glam and geopolitical anxiety as Tiff gets under way amid trade war

A seven-day event running parallel to the festival that gathers buyers and sellers of film and television inside the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, the Market revealed some growing pains on its first day, with many delegates reporting surprisingly long lines to pick up their accreditation badges, if the passes had been printed by staff at all. Combine that technical snafu with the sparse level of activity on the convention floor – a space that is taken up by a conspicuously large food-court area, whereas you’d expect more company pavilions – and it wasn’t the best first impression for the Market, which is Tiff’s biggest initiative since opening its Lightbox headquarters 16 years ago.

But every first day of any festival will deliver some snags. And the festival did close off the night with one killer feature – the Midnight Madness premiere of Joshua Giuliano’s woodsy slasher River . Sure, it’s an American production, too, like Heder’s film. But between its masked psychopath and cottage-country setting, it’s not hard to see the flick as a stand-in for the dark, violent forces that are besieging peaceful, wilderness-heavy Canada.

As for the title body of water, it’s never named on-screen. But I have a few ideas.

But between its masked psychopath and cottage-country setting, it’s not hard to see the flick as a stand-in for the dark, violent forces that are besieging peaceful, wilderness-heavy Canada.
As for the title body of water, it’s never named on-screen. But I have a few ideas.

stories.title: What the advice about not making work the centre of your identity gets wrong
stories.summary: It’s time to take guilt out of the identity equation to recognize that work identities help shape and stabilize how we see ourselves, writes Scott Schieman
stories.author: Scott Schieman
stories.content:
Scott Schieman is a professor of sociology at the University of Toronto and author of the new book I Want M.O.R.E.: Why Your Job Still Matters .

Don’t make work the centerpiece of your identity.

That was one of the rules about work that gained momentum in 2021 as the anti-work movement rode the wave of the Great Resignation. Popular advice to “decentre work” is often paired with the transactional vision that work should simply be a means to an end.

It’s like the idea of work to live versus live to work.

As a sociologist who’s spent decades listening to what people think and feel about work, the decentre work advice never really sat well with me. From my read of the data, the narrative surrounding this Identity Rule exaggerates the scope of the problem – that too many make work the centre of their life and that this work-centricity is more virulent now than in the past, partly because of the broader conversations about life priorities during the pandemic.

But is it true that too many people centre work? For a historical benchmark, I went back to the 1977 Quality of Employment Survey, which asked: “How much do you agree or disagree that the most important things that happen to you involve your job?” About half of American workers agreed.

To find out if sentiments had changed, I partnered with Angus Reid Global to field my own surveys in the aftermath of the Great Resignation – just when the anti-work narrative was most intense.

In 2023, the Identity Rule’s grip should have been easy to spot. It wasn’t: Fewer than one in four Americans and one in five Canadians said the most important things that happen to them involve their job. Most of that shift happened not from work centrality to rejection, but to ambivalence.

By 2023, one third of Canadians and Americans neither agreed nor disagreed. So, claims about heightened work-centricity aren’t accurate. If anything, the trend is in the opposite direction and – as my open-ended follow-up questions unearthed – we’re more conflicted about work’s role in our lives. I fielded the same question three years later and found similar results.

A small share of workers continue to place work at the centre of their identity. “Teaching is my calling and the foundation of my existence,” a 52-year-old elementary school teacher told me. “I am always looking for new ways to improve my teaching.”

“My job is part of me as an artist,” said a 31-year-old business owner in e-commerce and publishing. “When I excel in my career, I excel in my life.”

“The process of going to law school, passing the bar exam and becoming a licensed lawyer were some of the biggest accomplishments in my life,” said a 29-year-old lawyer. “There are more accomplishments tied to my profession down the road.”

However, not everyone is so unequivocal. A 29-year-old senior research manager expressed the internal tension: “My job is the biggest part of my life, for better or worse – probably worse. What happens to me during my work will inevitably impact the other areas of my life.”

For a larger segment of the workforce, the experiences are mixed. “Some of the most important things that happen to me involve my job,” said a 48-year-old senior translator and language advisor. “It’s where I spend one-third of my time. But ‘importance’ is relative.”

A 50-year-old senior network engineer elaborated: “My definition of ‘most important things’ changes. When I am doing my job and focus on that, it’s important, and I know my job is how I get paid and that’s important. When I am watching TV or doing other leisure activities, my job is not as important. It averages out to ‘neither agree nor disagree.’”

As a 33-year-old asset manager told me: “I wouldn’t phrase it that way, but I think the idea is correct. I would say ‘the most important things that happen to me’ involve my way of life. However, my way of life is, in a way, my job.”

The largest share of respondents (a similar share as in 1977) openly rejected the idea of centring work, often in moral tones. “Your job is not your life, and it shouldn’t be made to be,” said a 47-year-old payroll administrator.

“I would hope that the most important things to happen to me are personal, not professional,” said a 27-year-old economist.

And a 30-year-old corporate accountant elaborated: “I like to think that while a job is vital to one’s sense of self, unless you are solely self-employed or running your own business, the key elements of your life should be outside of work.”

“Work hard, play harder,” advised a 52-year-old estimator. “I enjoy my family time and my social life. I work to live as opposed to living to work.”

And a 44-year-old policy analyst observed: “It would be a sad world in which job-related events seemed more important than the birth of a child or the death of a loved one.”

This mindset sometimes even pathologizes those who want to make work more central to the core self. “All the saddest, most depressed people I know make their job their life,” a 34-year-old IT educational technician told me. “I have worked very hard to avoid such a sadness.”

In my view, the anti-work pendulum went too far. That’s even more ominous in an era of headlines about artificial intelligence-related job displacement.

To be sure, embracing your work identity doesn’t mean being passive about exploitative employers or being so obsessed with work so that nothing else matters

But it’s time to take guilt out of the identity equation to recognize – perhaps celebrate – that work identities are highly salient for many of us, shaping and stabilizing how we see ourselves.

Work usually isn’t one’s only source of identity. But based on my surveys and interviews, it is high on the list of elements that define how we see ourselves – and how others see us too. Identities ground us and give us concrete markers for understanding who we are and what we aspire to become.

It such turbulent and uncertain times, this anchoring effect is invaluable.

stories.title: StatCan says debt-to-income ratio declined in Q2 as income growth outpaced debt
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the amount households owe relative to income edged lower in the second quarter as income gains outpaced the growth in debt.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A magnifying glass enlarges the holographic image of Parliament Hill's Peace Tower on a 20 dollar bill issued by the Bank of Canada, shown in a display case at the Bank of Canada Museum in Ottawa, ON Wednesday, Sept. 4, 2024. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 11, 2026 8:58 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 9:58 am.

Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the amount households owe relative to income edged lower in the second quarter as income gains outpaced the growth in debt.

The agency says household credit market debt as a proportion of household disposable income fell to 176.4 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis, compared with 178.6 per cent in the first quarter.

It says this means households held about $1.76 in credit market debt for every dollar of household disposable income.

The household debt service ratio — obligated principal and interest payments on credit market debt as a proportion of household disposable income — was 14.52 per cent, down from 14.68 per cent.

The decline came as seasonally adjusted household credit market borrowing, which includes consumer credit as well as mortgage and non-mortgage loans, slowed to $29.4 billion for the quarter, compared with $34.4 billion in the first quarter of the year.

Mortgage borrowing dropped to $19.4 billion in the quarter, the slowest pace of borrowing since the first quarter of 2024, while non-mortgage borrowing, including consumer credit, slowed to $10.0 billion.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sep. 11, 2026.

stories.title: Carney’s cabinet huddles for 2nd day in Banff as trade war intensifies
stories.summary: The two-day retreat comes as U.S. President Donald Trump ratchets up an ongoing trade war by moving to ban some Canadian imports, including alcohol and some dairy products.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s cabinet is set to meet for a second and final day of meetings in the Alberta Rocky Mountain resort town of Banff as ministers prepare for the fall sitting of Parliament.

The meetings are taking place as the province gets set to hold a referendum on leaving Canada in October.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas attended one of the private meetings and says Ottawa is taking a smart approach to the question by being consistently present in the province.

Farkas says separating would put Alberta on track to become the 51st state — and that an “overbearing” Washington would be more difficult to deal with than Ottawa.

The two-day retreat also comes as U.S. President Donald Trump ratchets up an ongoing trade war by moving to ban some Canadian imports, including alcohol and some dairy products.

Carney says that compared to other trade actions Washington has taken against Canada, Trump’s latest move is “relatively modest.”

stories.title: London beverage maker loses $24M in opportunities, plans $45M expansion
stories.summary: Black Fly says strong Canadian demand and new U.S. production are helping fuel its growth despite the trade dispute.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
Black Fly says strong Canadian demand and new U.S. production are helping fuel its growth despite the trade dispute.

Last updated 1 hour ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/London-beverage-maker-loses-24m-in-opportunities-plans-45m-expansion#comments-area)

Cathy Siskind-Kelly and Rob Kelly, co-founders of London’s Black Fly Beverage Co. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press)

The trade dispute between Canada and the U.S. has cost a London business more than $24 million in future sales as customers south of the border anticipate a ban on alcohol from Canada.

But in a twist that underscores the chaos of cross-border trade, Black Fly Beverage Co. has also seen a 25 per cent spike in sales and is making a $45-million investment to double its business in the new year, as Canadians are drinking and it is “onshoring” production from the U.S., company executives said.

“We have not lost business, but there were opportunities that are no longer available that could have been about 12 per cent of our volume,” said Martin Kamil, vice-president of co-manufacturing, as well as chief operating officer and chief financial officer for Black Fly.

For buyers, sellers, renters and dreamers — London's complex, fascinating real estate market is brought into focus and into context with this newsletter.

U.S. President Donald Trump, in retaliation for counter-tariffs Canada is charging on $27.6 billion in goods sold in Canada from the U.S., said it will ban a host of Canadian goods, including alcoholic beverages, starting Sept. 29. That includes beer, wine, cider, vodka, rum and various other spirits and alcoholic beverages.

Tariffs have also increased the price of aluminum cans for drink makers.

Still, despite the challenges and uncertainty in the trade sector, construction is underway on an expansion of the Highbury Avenue business from about 200,000 sq. ft. to more than 400,000 sq. ft. early in the new year, said Cathy Siskind-Kelly, co-founder.

It will also grow its staff to about 400 in 2027 from the 320 it has now.

“The Canadian market is strong and Americans are onshoring here,” Kamil said.

Onshoring means the business has begun production in Canada. It May have happened to avoid tariffs, but Kamil believes it May have occurred regardless, as demand is strong in the sector and Black Fly is established in the industry.

“It makes sense to manufacture where you sell. But trade friction is not a good thing,” Kamil said.

As strong as business is, Kamil is frustrated by lost sales. Tariffs are “preventing us from growing our business. It is disrupting the supply chain and people cannot make business decisions,” he said.

Black Fly makes ready-to-drink “spirit beverages” of vodka, whiskey, rum and tequila mixed drinks. But it also manufactures drinks for other businesses, including many in the U.S. that want a Canadian manufacturing site to avoid tariffs.

It makes drinks for about 40 other brands, called co-manufacturing or co-packing, and that accounts for about 90 per cent of its production, while Black Fly accounts for about 10 per cent, Kamil said.

It makes about 20 million cases of 24 bottles a year for all of its brands, or about 500 million bottles a year.

It is not a distillery or brewer, but buys alcohol and other ingredients and blends them together on site.

It does not sell into the U.S. It used to sell in 11 U.S. states but about seven years ago decided to pull back and focus on Canadian growth, Siskind-Kelly said.

“We decided to focus the business in Canada, growing our market share here and it was a phenomenal decision.”

While she would not state who they manufacture for, anywhere from 25 to 40 per cent of all ready-to-drink labels in liquor or grocery stores are made here in London.

“Our customers are also our competitors,” she added.

That makes Black Fly the second-largest maker of ready-to-drink alcoholic beverages in Canada.

Labatt Breweries, in an email, downplayed the impact of tariffs or a U.S. alcohol ban on its London plant, stating it does not sell beer from here to the U.S.

Equals Brewing Co., ON Sovereign Road in London, is also a beverage maker that manufactures beer for other brewers, and tariffs have had little impact as it sells in Ontario. But the rising cost of oil has increased shipping costs, owner Brian Semkowski said.

“Oil prices, distribution costs, have caused havoc in our industry,” Semkowski said. “We sell across Canada but it is expensive to sell into B.C. and Alberta.”

Tariffs have also stung, increasing the cost of aluminum from about 17 cents a can to 27 cents, he added.

But the greater concern is the impact of the trade dispute on growth. Semkowski wants to expand the business in 2027, but tariff disputes have created market uncertainty, he added.

“We want to grow next year but there are so many question marks. We do not know what it will cost,” he said.

“You just do not know how to plant now.”

stories.title: Gohl preview: New-look London Nationals embrace growing pains
stories.summary: A revamped roster and new GM Sean Ryan are focused on player development while aiming to contend by the new year.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
A revamped roster and new GM Sean Ryan are focused on player development while aiming to contend by the new year.

Last updated 54 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/sports/local-sports/gohl-preview-new-look-London-nationals-embrace-growing-pains-for-success#comments-area)

Chatham Maroons forward Dylan Richter is stopped by London Nationals goaltender Dante Bertolin (30) during their Gohl game at Chatham Memorial Arena in Chatham on Sunday, Jan. 11, 2026. (Mark Malone/Postmedia Network)

The London Nationals want to build back up the right way.

The local Greater Ontario Hockey League mainstay has a new general manager tasked with replacing seven of its top nine forwards and six of its best defencemen as it opens the season against Chatham Saturday (2 p.m.) at Western Fair Sports Centre.

“We want people to be aware of our winning culture and love our style of play,” GM Sean Ryan, a Lucan native and Oshawa Generals scout, said. “We want them to think the Nationals are fun to watch and a tight-knit group with high-character guys. London should be the premium destination in the league and we’re trying to develop players and pattern after the Ontario Hockey League so it shouldn’t be a shock to them when they get there.”

The Gohl has now formally modelled itself as a trusted path to top-tier junior, though the Hunters have already used it that way for years. There are new rules in place allowing OHL teams to send their players, particularly 16-year-old rookies, to Junior B affiliates with fewer restrictions than in the past.

OHL news and expert analysis from Postmedia reporters across the province.

By signing up you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc.

A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.

The next issue of On the OHL will soon be in your inbox.

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

The Nats graduated blue-liners Cooper McAslan, Cody Wood and centre Alex Campeau to the Knights and got more blue-chippers in return. Rookie centre Jack Samek (37th overall) and rearguard Konstantinos Housseas (75th overall), both London prospects, will help immediately, as will local returning d-man William Janicek.

“Samek and Housseas were teammates and we scouted their Markham (Majors) team a lot,” Ryan said. “We’re going to try to insulate the younger guys with five 20-year-olds. Jack McGurn and Nicholas Kiss are 19 so we have enough veterans to guide the way.

“We have to be patient. It’s a whole new group and a lot of new faces. It’ll take time to develop that chemistry, but come the new year, we hope we’ll be one of the top teams.”

London has shown a knack for that, even in its more unstable moments, over the past five years.

Veteran stopper Dante Bertolin should provide some stability in net while 17-year-old Alex Kerr, an Oshawa pick, learns the ropes. The Nationals have some local flavour on board, as well as some true imports in giant Latvian forwards Roberts Jansons and Toms Vavilos.

Keli Corpse, the former GM, took over as head coach after the club parted ways with Brandon Prust last season. Rumun Ndur resigned and Corpse’s son Colt will join his dad on the bench.

“The whole organizational focus is player development,” Ryan said. “We have lots of ingredients here and if we do the development correctly, where we start is nowhere near where we’ll be (at the end). The more guys we move up (to the OHL and Ncaa), there will be more guys who want to come here and do the same thing.

“It’s the same model as the Knights. They’re like an NHL pipeline and we’re trying to be an OHL pipeline.”

Ryan was part of two Oshawa rosters that faced the Knights in back-to-back OHL finals in 2024 and ’25. The Nats’blueprint will be similar to what he has learned working with Generals GM Roger Hunt.

“You’ll notice it in roster construction,” he said. “We want big, fast and physical players and that’s how I’m trying to build this team. If we do it right every year, we’re going to turn over 10-15 guys because they’re getting promoted and going somewhere else.”

The key is to do it while playing an exciting and winning brand.

For the opener, the Nationals are offering a $20 ticket that includes admission to the Western Fair. Fans 65 and older and 10 and younger are free of charge.

OHL Trade:London moved hard-working forward Brody Cook Thursday to Kingston for Brantford’s fifth-round pick in 2028. The 19-year-old Michigander had six goals and 18 points in 57 games last season.

St. Marys Lincolns.Last year: Third, 75 points. Outlook: Another run at a crown.

The London Nationals want to build back up the right way.

The local Greater Ontario Hockey League mainstay has a new general manager tasked with replacing seven of its top nine forwards and six of its best defencemen as it opens the season against Chatham Saturday (2 p.m.) at Western Fair Sports Centre.

“We want people to be aware of our winning culture and love our style of play,” GM Sean Ryan, a Lucan native and Oshawa Generals scout, said. “We want them to think the Nationals are fun to watch and a tight-knit group with high-character guys. London should be the premium destination in the league and we’re trying to develop players and pattern after the Ontario Hockey League so it shouldn’t be a shock to them when they get there.”

The Gohl has now formally modelled itself as a trusted path to top-tier junior, though the Hunters have already used it that way for years. The Nats graduated blue-liners Cooper McAslan, Cody Wood and centre Alex Campeau to the Knights and got more blue-chippers in return. Rookie centre Jack Samek (37th overall) and rearguard Konstantinos Housseas (75th overall), both London prospects, will help immediately, as will local returning d-man William Janicek.

“Samek and Housseas were teammates and we scouted their Markham (Majors) team a lot,” Ryan said. “We’re going to try to insulate the younger guys with five 20-year-olds. Jack McGurn and Nicholas Kiss are 19 so we have enough veterans to guide the way.
“We have to be patient. It’s a whole new group and a lot of new faces. It’ll take time to develop that chemistry, but come the new year, we hope we’ll be one of the top teams.”
London has shown a knack for that, even in its more unstable moments, over the past five years.

Veteran stopper Dante Bertolin should provide some stability in net while 17-year-old Alex Kerr, an Oshawa pick, learns the ropes. The Nationals have some local flavour on board, as well as some true imports in giant Latvian forwards Roberts Jansons and Toms Vavilos.
Keli Corpse, the former GM, took over as head coach after the club parted ways with Brandon Prust last season. Rumun Ndur resigned and Corpse’s son Colt will join his dad on the bench.
