stories.title: 'Total exhaustion': How a Gander college campus jumped in to help plane passengers on 9/11
stories.summary: Mac Moss, then principal at the Gander Campus of the College of the North Atlantic, suddenly had 438 bewildered travellers to look after.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Gander is a tiny dot on the map of northeastern Newfoundland, some 335 kilometres from the provincial capital of St. John’s. But Canadians know it for its citizens’ famous acts of kindness and hospitality, caring for 6,700+ stranded airline strangers in the days after the 9/11 attacks.

Twenty-five years ago, Mac Moss was one of those citizens. Now retired as principal at the Gander Campus of the College of the North Atlantic, he and his team at the school helped 438 people who suddenly found themselves grounded in Canada after U.S. airspace was closed.

“Our college year just started … And it was a normal morning. Everybody was in class, or wherever they were supposed to be,” he recalled in an interview.

Moss learned about the attack in a phone call from one of his staff. “She said: ‘We’re listening to the radio up here. And a plane just flew into one of the World Trade Center Towers.’ ”

The effect on campus, at first, was paralyzing, Moss said. “Everybody started crowding around the television, some radio. And the campus virtually came to a standstill.”

At 1 p.m., the Town of Gander’s emergency services called Moss, asking if the campus could accommodate incoming planeloads of passengers by providing shelter, first aid and food.

“I knew the size of the campus, the space we had available, and I said yes,” Moss said.

At 7 p.m., town manager Jake Turner told him he’d be getting a jumbo jet-load of people. That plane, carrying 234 passengers according to Moss’ recollection, was the first of two whose passengers the college hosted.

It was a stroke of luck that the college had commercial cooking and electronics classes running that day; it allowed students and staff to prepare hot food, set up additional television feeds with microphones in the cafeteria, and gather supplies.

Many people in Gander, including Moss’s wife, the college’s employees and their spouses, volunteered everything from bedding to food for their “guests,” as Ganderites endearingly call the plane people.

Gander provided free medical treatment, such as free prescription renewals, for the passengers as needed. Gander Campus also had a few student nurses available to assist. “We had them set up serving a little triage area,” Moss recalled.

As the “guests” trickled in, many did not even know where they were; they needed to see the news, make calls, or send emails.

The passengers had tight living conditions: “20 or 30 people to a room, and … they were lying on a tile floor, with just a blanket or a sheet underneath them,” Moss recalled. “If they didn’t have a pillow, we give them an extra sheet to put over the shoes for pillows.”

In the morning, though, the guests were in for a welcome surprise: a buffet.

“When the passengers came down to their breakfast, it was like walking into a first-class hotel. I mean, everything in the world that you wanted for breakfast was available,” said Moss.

“The big problem our cooks had, after the first day, was the stores were running out of food,” he said. But “Our cooks had managed to secure, you know, 250 or 300 chicken breasts in their raid of the stores the night before.”

To meet the needs of guests, everyone pitched in. “The Salvation Army took control of the local hockey rink, and … turned that into a walk-in cooler,” Moss recalled. Nearby towns also volunteered supplies.

He felt exhausted after the passengers left, having slept only two hours in the three days his campus hosted the passengers.

Moss would go on to write and publish a book, Flown into the Arms of Angels: Newfoundland and Labrador’s Unsung Heroes of 9/11 , in 2021.

“I did over 300 interviews, and I always asked them the same question: ‘How did you feel after the passengers left?’”

“What they remembered most was the total exhaustion.”

The former principal had trouble sleeping too. “After the passengers left, I don’t think I had a good night’s sleep for two or three months,” he said. He relived every detail of those few days in his mind.

Moss continues to stay connected with some of the guests, such as Kevin Tuerff, a passenger who is portrayed in the musical Come From Away. “Kevin has been a frequent visitor to our house,” said Moss.

Moss has also visited the 9/11 site in New York City.

Twenty-five years after the plane people’s arrival, he says the big takeaway for him is “how well our towns — plural, our towns — were prepared to handle such an event, and they didn’t know it, because they had never experienced (this) before.”

The Town of Gander itself has planned commemorative events for today’s 25th anniversary of the landing of the plane people in Newfoundland. There will be a “Parade of First Responders” and a special remembrance of lives lost on 9/11.

Expected to speak at the commemoration are U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, and former prime minister Jean Chrétien, who held office on the day of the attack and whose government quickly moved to welcome between 225 and 240 flights diverted from U.S. airspace to Canadian airports in what was termed Operation Yellow Ribbon .

The former principal had trouble sleeping too. “After the passengers left, I don’t think I had a good night’s sleep for two or three months,” he said. He relived every detail of those few days in his mind.

content_blocks.text: Moss continues to stay connected with some of the guests, such as Kevin Tuerff, a passenger who is portrayed in the musical Come From Away. “Kevin has been a frequent visitor to our house,” said Moss.
Moss has also visited the 9/11 site in New York City.

Twenty-five years after the plane people’s arrival, he says the big takeaway for him is “how well our towns — plural, our towns — were prepared to handle such an event, and they didn’t know it, because they had never experienced (this) before.”

The Town of Gander itself has planned commemorative events for today’s 25th anniversary of the landing of the plane people in Newfoundland. There will be a “Parade of First Responders” and a special remembrance of lives lost on 9/11.

Expected to speak at the commemoration are U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, and former prime minister Jean Chrétien, who held office on the day of the attack and whose government quickly moved to welcome between 225 and 240 flights diverted from U.S. airspace to Canadian airports in what was termed Operation Yellow Ribbon .

stories.title: 25 years after 9/11, Gander’s message of kindness still resonates
stories.summary: That connection is so strong that many of the people, known affectionately as the "come from aways," have returned to Gander, NL, to mark the 25th anniversary.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Heidi Petracek
stories.content:
Out of the tragedy of the 9/11 attacks in America 25 years ago, a ray of hope emerged on the Canadian side of the border.

The town of Gander, N.L., and surrounding areas took on nearly 7,000 stranded travellers whose planes were diverted after the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

The crisis forged a lifelong bond between some passengers and the locals. Today, that connection is so strong that many of the people, known affectionately as the “come from aways,” have returned to Gander to mark the 25th anniversary.

A special service is planned for Friday and will include Governor General Louise Arbour and U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

“Sometimes it feels like yesterday, because there’s so many memories,” said Derm Flynn, the former mayor of Appleton, N.L.

The small community, located near Gander, scrambled to house the stranded passengers who found their flights abruptly diverted in 2001.

“They were desperately needing help, and needing friendship, and needing comfort,” he said.

Space was scarce, and Flynn recalls people sleeping in the council chambers at the town hall, in schools, churches and private homes.

He and his wife, Dianne, opened the doors to their home, as so many others did, and took in six people.

“I didn’t know he had invited three people to the house, and he didn’t know that I had invited three people to the house,” she recalled.

For those stranded passengers and crew, however, the experience began long before they ever stepped off their planes.

Beverley Bass, a retired American Airlines captain, was at the helm of American Airlines Flight 777, one of the 38 planes that landed in Gander that day.

She recalls being “very surprised” to hear the diverted flight would be landing in Newfoundland.

“We learned, when we were right over the middle of the North Atlantic, that all of the U.S. airspace was closed. So we knew we would divert somewhere in Canada. But the logical cities for us, with a big airplane like that, would be Toronto or Montreal,” she said.

She notes that while pilots who fly to Europe will know of Gander because its airport is considered an emergency diversion airport, most pilots will retire without ever landing there.

In the air, she says she and fellow crew members weren’t aware initially of how significant the Twin Towers attacks were. When she heard about the airspace closure, she realized the magnitude of the situation.

“I think as pilots, we are trained to remain calm, take care of our passengers and crew, and basically just get the airplane on the ground safely. So I don’t think I ever thought about being scared. And in that moment, I didn’t even think about possibly having (a) nefarious person in the back of the airplane,” she said, adding she wasn’t aware hijackers had been involved in the attacks.

“I don’t know they’ve been flown into buildings … I don’t any of these details. So all I knew is I was told to land in Gander and I started preparing for that.”

Once the liner landed, she says Canadian officials boarded and told them they wouldn’t be able to disembark until the next morning. In total, Bass, her crew, and the passengers were on the plane for 28 hours.

By the time they walked off the plane at 7:30 a.m. on Sept. 12, they were met with “tables of food” that had been prepared overnight.

“Every stove in Gander must have been on because they prepared enough food for 7,000 passengers and crew. That was my first realization that we had landed in a very unique place. And from there, the stories continue,” she said.

Bass eventually found her way to the Comfort Inn in town, which was scrambling to find room for all the additional guests flowing into the community.

Karen Mills was the general manager of the inn at the time, and recalls that people were lining up out the door trying to find space, while the inn’s phone lines were ringing off the hook.

“We had these two gentlemen come in from England, and once again I was on the desk and they’re looking for a room, and I was at that point, a broken record. ‘No, I have nothing, no we’re sold out, we’re sold out.'” she said.

She says she told them she was sorry but she had no room. Until she remembered she had a box spring mattress and a cot in the basement, which she could place in the gym.

“I’ll never forget it, as long as I live. They looked at each other, and they looked at me and said, ‘Hm, better than the pool table the night before.’ So I figured, ‘OK, we got a winner,'” she said.

The two men slept in the gym between the treadmill and dumbbells for four days.

She laughs as she tells the tale of how the two men only asked for clean underwear during their stay, which she was happy to help with by driving them to the local Walmart.

A year later, the men — who Mills lovingly calls “the basement boys” — sent a letter and some photographs to her. The photos documented their stay in the basement.

“All these pictures of them on the box spring mattress and the cot with all the dumbbells in their drawers,” she said.

Each year on 9/11, Mills says “the basement boys” send flowers to the inn.

That kind of connection and appreciation for Gander is what brought Bass back this year. It’s the retired airline captain’s seventh trip to Gander.

“We love coming here. It’s almost like coming back home. We have so many friends here. We know so many people,” she said.

“We’re so familiar with the town. We know how to drive around. We don’t even have to use our iPhones for directions. So it’s great. It’s hard for me to believe that it’s been 25 years.”

For former Appleton Mayor Derm Flynn, the anniversary offers a reminder about the importance of friendship during a divisive time in modern Canada-U.S. relations.

“The story is being told over and over again by people all over the world,” he said.

“As we remember the tragic events of 9/11, people are now definitely ready for more good news … or any kind of good news at all.”

One of the people who stayed in his home in 2001 is returning to commemorate the anniversary — and will once again, stay with his family.

He says what Newfoundlanders did 25 years ago was offer more than just a place to sleep or a sandwich to eat. They offered kindness and support.

“We didn’t want anything other than a pat on the back or a handshake when they (went) out the door. But it has brought us back even more than that,” he said, referring to the lasting connections over the years.

“There is still a place in the world where people are still decent to each other, and respect each other.”

Claude Elliott, Gander’s mayor during the crisis, says his community’s sense of generosity hasn’t wavered in the quarter century since 9/11.

“If 38 planes land here tonight, our community would be out to take care of them,” he said.

That kindness is now known around the world thanks to the award-winning Broadway musical Come From Away, which is based on what happened in the small town after the attacks.

It’s a story that has made Gander a destination for visitors who want to experience it for themselves.

“One of the questions that I get asked a lot (is,) ‘How much is it real?’ A lot of people in the world don’t think that there’s good, kind, generous people in our world anymore,” said Elliott.

“That kindness and generosity is still here.”

The recent rhetoric about Canada from the U.S. and the ensuing trade war have left Elliott feeling hurt, he says.

“It hurts us because we’ve always had a good relationship with the United States … I tell people we got to keep politics out of this,” he said.

“We’re going to have to let the powers that be work this out. But to the average person, we got no problems. We’re still friends with the U.S. and I don’t think that will ever change.”

stories.title: Sunshine and warm temperatures set for southern Ontario Friday
stories.summary: A beautiful, sunny day is in store for southern Ontario Friday after some early morning fog clears, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Warm temperatures and plenty of sunshine are expected across southwestern Ontario this weekend, with only a slight chance of showers late Saturday into Sunday, says meteorologist Gary Archibald.

A ridge of high pressure is keeping conditions clear and calm across the region, with temperatures expected to remain above the seasonal average.

“Our average high for this time of year is 22 degrees,” Archibald said. “We’re looking at 25 this afternoon.”

Overnight lows are expected to fall to around 11 C to 13 C, reflecting the gradual seasonal cooldown as summer winds down.

Clouds are forecast to increase Saturday as moisture moves in from the southwest, bringing a chance of light, scattered showers Saturday night.

“It’s very sporadic and very light at this juncture,” Archibald said.

Looking ahead, temperatures next week are expected to fluctuate between 20 C and 25 C, with periods of cloud cover and showers, particularly from Tuesday onward. For now, Archibald said the weather should remain favourable for outdoor activities through much of the weekend.

stories.title: Doctor at centre of Atlantic Canada licensing controversy accused of falsifying evidence about patient in Quebec
stories.summary: Sanjeev Sirpal allegedly conspired to forge a diary entry that falsely portrayed the patient as racist after she complained he sexually assaulted her
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Sanjeev Sirpal, the doctor at the heart of a controversy about Atlantic Canada’s physician licensing program, allegedly conspired to forge a diary entry that falsely portrayed a patient as racist after she complained he sexually assaulted her, a trial in Quebec heard this spring.

Dr. Sirpal is also facing sexual-assault charges in two Atlantic provinces, allegations that have spurred criticisms of the region’s screening process for physicians.

New Brunswick granted Dr. Sirpal the right to practise there in February, 2022. The province’s College of Physicians and Surgeons knew that regulators in Quebec were in the process of revoking Dr. Sirpal’s licence for failing to disclose that he had been dismissed from a Florida medical school before eventually obtaining his degree in St. Lucia. The New Brunswick college wasn’t aware that the Quebec investigation was launched after a complaint of sexual assault.

This spring, Dr. Sirpal was on trial in Laval, Que., for obstruction of justice and counselling someone to commit an offence. The charges stemmed from allegations that he tried to discredit the Quebec sexual-assault complainant by concocting damaging evidence about her.

Details about the trial in Laval in April have not been reported until now. The Globe and Mail reviewed audio recordings of the court proceedings and the trial exhibits.

Quebec Court Justice Frédéric Bénard will render a decision Monday.

Testifying in court, a nurse named Mélina Harrisson described how Dr. Sirpal, who was her boyfriend in early 2021, told her that the Quebec College of Physicians was investigating him for sexual misconduct, and asked her to write a false personal diary entry that depicted the complainant as a Nazi sympathizer.

The Quebec college began investigating after the female patient reported that Dr. Sirpal examined her vagina and breasts when she consulted him for a concussion.

Once Dr. Sirpal was licensed in New Brunswick, an interprovincial licensing program enabled him to work elsewhere in Atlantic Canada even after his permit was revoked in Quebec. He was initially charged with six counts of sexual assault on patients in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Two of the charges have since been dropped. He pleaded not guilty to the other counts.

Physician licensing program in Atlantic Canada undergoing changes after sex-assault charges against doctor

The trial in Laval also addressed two counts of assault that the 39-year-old physician is accused of having perpetrated on Ms. Harrisson.

Dr. Sirpal denied that he had been violent with Ms. Harrisson or had asked her to create a bogus diary. Testifying in his own defence, he described her as a needy former girlfriend who was trying to mislead the court.

He said he had never talked to her about forging a document. “I have no idea what she’s referring to. I’ve never bought her a journal,” he testified.

He also denied that he had acted inappropriately with the complainant. During the college’s probe, he told investigators that, as a member of a visible minority, he had been a victim of racist abuse before, and said that the complainant wore a bandana with a swastika.

Dr. Sirpal was born in the United States and started his residency in Quebec in 2016. Ms. Harrisson testified that she met him in 2019 while they worked at Hôpital Fleury in Montreal, and they began a relationship.

She testified that Dr. Sirpal informed her about the sexual-misconduct complaint early in 2021. “He told me that since I am a very sensitive person who likes to write, I could pen a diary mentioning that on the day of the complaint I was present at the clinic and saw the patient.”

Ms. Harrisson said she went along with his request. “I felt a lot of pressure on his part.”

She testified that Dr. Sirpal asked to see a draft of the diary entry and suggested some changes.

The six-page handwritten diary entry, which was entered in evidence, was full of details – Ms. Harrisson had a manicure and a facial, ate a cheese-steak sandwich and hated Montreal traffic; she dropped by his clinic and saw a patient who wore Nazi insignia; the patient uttered a racial slur and said, “Black lives don’t matter.”

The prosecutor, Nicolas Désilets-Laforge, asked Ms. Harrisson which part of the diary was false. “Absolutely none of it was true,” she replied.

She said she sent Dr. Sirpal screenshots of the final entry but didn’t hear back from him. She reported him to police in June, 2023.

Ms. Harrisson also testified about the alleged assaults. The first incident took place at his house on Aug. 19, 2020. She said he became very angry after she revealed that a co-worker had tried to kiss her, and then Dr. Sirpal grabbed her by the shoulders and shoved her with great force. “He said he wanted to kill me.”

She said that on Dec. 20, 2020, as she drove him to work, he lost his temper and punched her, bent one of her fingers backward and squeezed her right arm so hard it bruised.

In his testimony, Dr. Sirpal denied that he had threatened or assaulted Ms. Harrisson. He said they had arguments because she was disrespectful to his mother, and because he wouldn’t have sex with her unless she got tested for sexually transmitted infections.

Mr. Désilets-Laforge filed into evidence screenshots of an exchange on the Snapchat app between Ms. Harrisson and Dr. Sirpal, whose username was “Superman_snapz.”

In a lengthy message, Ms. Harrisson referred to the two alleged assaults. Dr. Sirpal wrote back that he had never intended to hurt anyone. “I was upset but I absolutely didn’t want to harm you,” his message said.

Dr. Sirpal told the court the Snapchat exchange was misleading: “There are huge intervening chunks of text that are missing here.” However, he said he couldn’t remember what had been removed.

stories.title: Mark Carney’s pursuit of the Gulf
stories.summary: The Prime Minister’s investment summit will test strategic partnerships in the Mideast, a region Canada has long overlooked
stories.author: Campbell Clark
stories.content:
There was a mood to get a deal in record time. Canada and the United Arab Emirates agreed in November, 2025, to strike a trade agreement, and as they prepared to open negotiations, the Emirati President, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, mentioned his country had worked out a deal with India in record time. The Canadians told the Emir they’d beat it.

Prime Minister Mark Carney gave trade negotiators a deadline: from the start of negotiations to the finish line in 47 days. Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu hosted his Emirati counterpart, Dr. Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, in Toronto during the last days of the talks. When they signed the deal on July 24, they both boasted the negotiation was their fastest ever.

The timeline wasn’t really crucial. The Canada-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement was not the biggest or most complicated deal for either country. The speed was a statement of intent.

The UAE, and the wider Persian Gulf region, is now a major Canadian foreign-policy priority.

There will soon be a show-me-the-money test. Gulf investors will be among the biggest players at the Canada Investment Summit taking place in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15, where Mr. Carney will lead a pitch to draw massive sums into Canadian infrastructure, resources and industry.

Everything we know about Carney’s investment summit

Already, the UAE has committed to investing US$50-billion in Canada. XRG, the foreign-investment arm of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, has been kicking the tires on an investment in LNG Canada Phase 2, the expansion of the liquid-natural gas export facility in Kitimat, B.C. The Uae’s US$1.2-trillion Abu Dhabi Investment Authority will be at the summit, as will Investment Corporation of Dubai, ADQ and Mubadala Investment Co. – each with hundreds of billions in holdings.

Together, the Gulf’s sovereign wealth funds hold $5.6-trillion in assets, according to Diego López, managing director of fund-tracker Global SWF. But the flow of deals to Canada, $6.2-billion over five years, is “still very insignificant when it comes to the size of the Canadian economy and potential,” he said.

In Toronto, executives of those funds will look for returns. But the deal-making of Gulf funds is also linked to their nations’ economic strategies. And Mr. Carney hopes to link them to Canada’s.

Europe has been Mr. Carney’s high-profile priority in his campaign to diversify trade and relationships – an effort to reduce dependence on the United States sparked by the domineering trade tactics of President Donald Trump.

But the Gulf has ranked a close second, as Mr. Carney’s government wooed the region with a quiet intensity. The message is that Canada wants investment, but also broad relationships in a region it has long treated as a troubled money pot.

Prospectus for Carney’s summit highlights more than 160 projects open for investment

“I think it’s long overdue that the Canadian government gives the Gulf region this level of priority,” said Arif Lalani, a former Canadian ambassador to the UAE and now a senior adviser with government relations firm StrategyCorp. “All of our European and other allies have made the Gulf a priority for decades.”

The catch-up has been an 18-month pursuit, according to government and business sources from Canada and Gulf countries whom The Globe and Mail is not identifying because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

It wasn’t just that Mr. Carney made trips to the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, a triangle of wealth that hadn’t hosted a Canadian prime minister in decades. Cabinet ministers went, too. There were diligent, repeated visits by a senior prime ministerial aide – and Mr. Carney’s own personal relationships.

Before he took office, Mr. Carney was already well-known in circles of finance and power in the Gulf. He’d visited often, including meeting the Saudi finance minister and central bank governor as governor of the Bank of England in 2015, and attending the COP28 climate conference in Dubai as the UN’s envoy for climate action and finance in 2023. And he did deals with Gulf sovereign wealth funds as vice-chair, then chair, of Brookfield Asset Management.

In office, Mr. Carney texted directly with Sultan Al Jaber, the chief executive officer of Adnoc and chairman of XRG and Masdar, the Uae’s state renewable-energy company, and also the Uae’s Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology. The two had worked together unofficially when Dr. Al Jaber chaired COP28 – where the UAE launched an energy-transition fund, Alterra, that committed US$1-billion in Brookfield Asset Management’s Catalytic Transition Fund.

Canada and UAE sign free trade deal, signal investment deals in energy sector ‘very soon’

Soon after taking power, Mr. Carney and his advisers put together an internal national-security strategy for achieving greater strategic autonomy, according to a government source, revolving around now-familiar themes: diversifying trade, strengthening the domestic economy and attracting investment. Relationships outside of North America were reordered, with the Gulf a priority second only to Europe.

Beyond money, the rethink saw the Gulf as a “hinge region” in geopolitics, a hub for international business, trade, travel and, increasingly, technology – as well as key diplomatic players.

The courtship also epitomized Mr. Carney’s harder-headed foreign policy approach, where disagreements are compartmentalized from interests and dealt with behind closed doors.

In 2018, then-foreign affairs minister Chrystia Freeland’s call for Saudi Arabia to release women’s rights activists sparked a five-year chill. In July, after meeting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, Mr. Carney insisted that “lecturing countries from afar is an ineffective strategy.”

Some critics accused Mr. Carney of silencing values for economic gain, but the Prime Minister nonetheless zealously pursued Gulf partners. The courting of the UAE is a prime example.

Carney focuses on attracting investment and economic growth as U.S. conflict deepens

Weeks after winning the 2025 election, Mr. Carney invited the Emir to attend the G7 summit in Kananaskis, Alta., that June, eliciting a phone call of regrets from Sheikh Mohamed. But the Uae’s foreign minister, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, did come to Canada that June, along with four other Emirati ministers who met their Canadian counterparts and delivered Mr. Carney an invitation to Abu Dhabi.

In the meantime, Mr. Carney’s government kickstarted talks on a Foreign Investment Protection Agreement with the UAE that had languished, with stops and starts, since 2014 – and signed the deal in July.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon visited. Mr. Sidhu and Defence Minister David McGuinty followed.

The Prime Minister’s then-foreign policy adviser and now principal secretary, Scott Gilmore, acted as Mr. Carney’s envoy, shuttling regularly to the Gulf. He was photographed by the state media of Gulf countries meeting senior figures in Doha in August, October and December, 2025; in the UAE in October, 2025, and April, 2026; and in Oman in April. In Gulf countries, where relationships can matter more than titles, he had access high-level government figures.

The agreements that Mr. Carney and his ministers signed with Gulf nations went beyond investment. Canada posted a defence attaché to Qatar and signed a public safety co-operation agreement. Qatari paramilitary forces brought armoured vehicles to Vancouver before a Qatar-Canada World Cup game ahead of training with the RCMP. In Saudi Arabia, there was a memorandum of understanding on AI collaboration and a promise to lead a delegation of Canada pension funds to explore investing there. It was intended to send a message that Canada wanted a broad, multi-faceted relationship.

Canada ranks highly on trust among global investors but must prove it can deliver the projects, survey says

“The Saudis, in particular, don’t want to be seen as an ATM machine,” said Jeffrey Steiner, the chair of the Canada-Saudi Arabia Business Council.

Among some, there was a welcoming response to Mr. Carney’s pitch that Canada wanted to diversify economically and find new partners in its quest for strategic autonomy – a concept well-understood in the Gulf.

Qatar’s Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, discussed that as a historical lesson his country had learned. During a Goldman Sachs forum in January, he noted the Gulf’s pearl-diving economy crashed around 1930 with the advent of cultured pearls, before oil and gas became key to its economy. The Qatar Investment Authority is insurance against another collapse, he said, but also a tool to create global companies so that Qatar’s economy is not “capped” by the country’s small size. “Different crises that we have been through have taught us how to become resilient,” he said.

Gulf nations have pursued different investment agendas abroad. The Uae’s state funds and enterprises, the Gulf’s early movers, already have investments in Canadian real estate and financial services, and a controlling stake in Calgary-based Nova Chemicals. DP World, a UAE-based logistics company that handles 10 per cent of the world’s cargo, operates facilities in five Canadian ports.

Saudi Arabia’s investment strategy, however, is aligned to the domestic economy and the country’s Vision 2030 blueprint, with goals that include developing the country’s mineral wealth, and establishing auto and aerospace industries. It is looking for two-way investment that develops Saudi expertise, especially in mining, Mr. Steiner said.

“Canada is number one in the Saudis’ mind when it comes to minerals,” he said.

The Saudis have already indirectly invested in Canadian mining in a deal that highlights their national investment strategy: Its Manara Minerals Investment Company paid US$2.5-billion to Brazil’s Vale S.A. for a 10-per-cent stake in subsidiary Vale Base Metals, which produces nickel, copper and cobalt key to auto and aerospace manufacturing at operations in Sudbury, Voisey’s Bay, Nfld., and Thompson, Man.

Now, there is an effort to build a path for direct two-way investment, though it won’t be completed in two days in Toronto. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will lead a delegation of Canada’s “Maple 8″ pension funds to Saudi Arabia in November.

There is no doubt about the short-term goal of Mr. Carney’s Gulf initiative, and one day soon, warmer relationships will be judged in the cold terms of investment dollars.

stories.title: Cringe Canadiana is the worst response to Trump’s economic aggression
stories.summary: Rather than cheesy, easy gestures, let’s get down to the hard work of policy change
stories.author: Robyn Urback
stories.content:
At a border crossing in B.C. on Tuesday, Premier David Eby showcased one of the more embarrassing side effects of the ongoing trade war with the United States. After a performance by a rapper named OGR-Scintilla, who performs parodies of pop songs using Canadian-themed lyrics, the B.C. Premier took to the podium wearing a red-and-black plaid jacket, which he dubbed “the single most Canadian piece of clothing” he owns.

Mr. Eby then unveiled new welcome signs that would be erected at U.S.-Canada border crossings, signs that read: “Welcome to British Columbia, Canada. Strong, proud and will Never be the 51st state. Sorry!”

“This is a uniquely Canadian message,” Mr. Eby declared, to cheers from the flag-waving crowd. “It’s confident, good humour and unmistakably clear.”

The stated message might indeed be clear, but the message tacitly conveyed by all of this – the cheesy rapping, the Salmo dinner jacket, the superfluous “sorry!” on our border signs – is far less dignified. It’s cringe Canadiana, an embarrassing parade of the most superficial Canadian tropes, which we might think projects confidence, but actually conveys the opposite.

The appropriate response to U.S. President Donald Trump renaming Lake Ontario is to laugh in his face, and then to continue on with the important work of governing a serious country that is not making enemies of all of its former allies. It is not to spend $25,000 of taxpayers’ money on a giant Lake Ontario sign, as Ontario Premier Doug Ford did, which essentially functions as a massive billboard showcasing how Mr. Trump has gotten under our skin. It is a reaction – not a response. And bullies love a reaction.

Stop taking Trump’s ‘Lake America’ bait. Focus on what really matters

Premiers Ford and Eby have adopted this type of cringe Canadiana because it’s easy: it signals loyalty, costs relatively little, and provides that instant dopamine hit that, for example, sitting around a table for a week and standardizing safety codes and licensing requirements across all provinces does not (that’s a hint, premiers). Regular Canadians have also demonstrated their willingness to make relatively painless sacrifices by buying Canadian when possible, and by making pilgrimages to Costa Rica instead of Florida for the winter. But recent data reveal that Canadians are far less interested in fighting if and when the financial effects are more personally significant.

This week, policy organization Build Canada released the results of a survey asking Canadians how they feel about Ottawa’s response to U.S. economic aggression. It found that Canadians overwhelmingly supported (75 per cent) holding firm against the U.S. and not making concessions, but it also found that that support weakens dramatically when Canadians are asked about specific personal costs. For example, just 15 per cent supported holding firm if it meant higher taxes, and only 6 per cent supported holding firm if it risks household job loss.

These results are not particularly surprising; standing up to Mr. Trump is fun and easy when it means wearing checkered coats and buying local strawberries. It is less fun when it affects retirement savings or amounts to thousands more owed in annual taxes.

Opinion: The whole world is watching as Canada stands up to Trump

The good news is that some of the most important work of responding to U.S. economic coercion is happening quietly, behind the scenes. On Wednesday, Ottawa published a regulatory change in the Gazette that removed certain energy projects from federal Impact Assessment Act (IAA) oversight. What that means is that projects that are already subject to the Canadian Energy Regulator Act (Cera) or provincial environmental assessments will no longer be subject to the IAA, which streamlines regulatory approval, meaning things will get built faster. This is exactly the type of response Canada should have to Mr. Trump’s escalating tactics: continue to forge new trade relationships, lure the best and brightest to Canada, create incentives for businesses to grow and stay in Canada, and remove regulatory red tape. For an economy like Canada’s, which will never match that of the U.S. in size, lashing out will never be as effective as building up from within.

Canada must obviously defend against American economic attacks where appropriate. We should correct the lies. But we should also ignore the ridiculous. If Mr. Trump wants to post his AI-generated fantasies and scribble all over his map with a magic marker, we should let him. Maybe he’ll get distracted by his colouring, or perhaps we can preoccupy him by letting him know that there’s a tributary in the U.S. called the Canadian River. But there’s no reason for us to stoop to his level, or to turn ourselves into a cheap caricature of what it means to be Canadian. It’s ineffective, and also, kind of embarrassing. We can let the U.S. have a monopoly on that.

The catch-up has been an 18-month pursuit, according to government and business sources from Canada and Gulf countries whom The Globe and Mail is not identifying because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

It wasn’t just that Mr. Carney made trips to the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, a triangle of wealth that hadn’t hosted a Canadian prime minister in decades. Cabinet ministers went, too. There were diligent, repeated visits by a senior prime ministerial aide – and Mr. Carney’s own personal relationships.

Before he took office, Mr. Carney was already well-known in circles of finance and power in the Gulf. He’d visited often, including meeting the Saudi finance minister and central bank governor as governor of the Bank of England in 2015, and attending the COP28 climate conference in Dubai as the UN’s envoy for climate action and finance in 2023. And he did deals with Gulf sovereign wealth funds as vice-chair, then chair, of Brookfield Asset Management.

In office, Mr. Carney texted directly with Sultan Al Jaber, the chief executive officer of Adnoc and chairman of XRG and Masdar, the Uae’s state renewable-energy company, and also the Uae’s Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology. The two had worked together unofficially when Dr. Al Jaber chaired COP28 – where the UAE launched an energy-transition fund, Alterra, that committed US$1-billion in Brookfield Asset Management’s Catalytic Transition Fund.

Canada and UAE sign free trade deal, signal investment deals in energy sector ‘very soon’

Soon after taking power, Mr. Carney and his advisers put together an internal national-security strategy for achieving greater strategic autonomy, according to a government source, revolving around now-familiar themes: diversifying trade, strengthening the domestic economy and attracting investment. Relationships outside of North America were reordered, with the Gulf a priority second only to Europe.

Beyond money, the rethink saw the Gulf as a “hinge region” in geopolitics, a hub for international business, trade, travel and, increasingly, technology – as well as key diplomatic players.

The courtship also epitomized Mr. Carney’s harder-headed foreign policy approach, where disagreements are compartmentalized from interests and dealt with behind closed doors.

In 2018, then-foreign affairs minister Chrystia Freeland’s call for Saudi Arabia to release women’s rights activists sparked a five-year chill. In July, after meeting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, Mr. Carney insisted that “lecturing countries from afar is an ineffective strategy.”

Some critics accused Mr. Carney of silencing values for economic gain, but the Prime Minister nonetheless zealously pursued Gulf partners. The courting of the UAE is a prime example.

Carney focuses on attracting investment and economic growth as U.S. conflict deepens

Weeks after winning the 2025 election, Mr. Carney invited the Emir to attend the G7 summit in Kananaskis, Alta., that June, eliciting a phone call of regrets from Sheikh Mohamed. But the Uae’s foreign minister, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, did come to Canada that June, along with four other Emirati ministers who met their Canadian counterparts and delivered Mr. Carney an invitation to Abu Dhabi.

In the meantime, Mr. Carney’s government kickstarted talks on a Foreign Investment Protection Agreement with the UAE that had languished, with stops and starts, since 2014 – and signed the deal in July.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon visited. Mr. Sidhu and Defence Minister David McGuinty followed.

The Prime Minister’s then-foreign policy adviser and now principal secretary, Scott Gilmore, acted as Mr. Carney’s envoy, shuttling regularly to the Gulf. He was photographed by the state media of Gulf countries meeting senior figures in Doha in August, October and December, 2025; in the UAE in October, 2025, and April, 2026; and in Oman in April. In Gulf countries, where relationships can matter more than titles, he had access to high-level government figures.

The agreements that Mr. Carney and his ministers signed with Gulf nations went beyond investment. Canada posted a defence attaché to Qatar and signed a public safety co-operation agreement. Qatari paramilitary forces brought armoured vehicles to Vancouver before a Qatar-Canada World Cup game ahead of training with the RCMP. In Saudi Arabia, there was a memorandum of understanding on AI collaboration and a promise to lead a delegation of Canada pension funds to explore investing there. It was intended to send a message that Canada wanted a broad, multi-faceted relationship.

Canada ranks highly on trust among global investors but must prove it can deliver the projects, survey says

“The Saudis, in particular, don’t want to be seen as an ATM machine,” said Jeffrey Steiner, the chair of the Canada-Saudi Arabia Business Council.

Among some, there was a welcoming response to Mr. Carney’s pitch that Canada wanted to diversify economically and find new partners in its quest for strategic autonomy – a concept well-understood in the Gulf.

Qatar’s Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, discussed that as a historical lesson his country had learned. During a Goldman Sachs forum in January, he noted the Gulf’s pearl-diving economy crashed around 1930 with the advent of cultured pearls, before oil and gas became key to its economy. The Qatar Investment Authority is insurance against another collapse, he said, but also a tool to create global companies so that Qatar’s economy is not “capped” by the country’s small size. “Different crises that we have been through have taught us how to become resilient,” he said.

Gulf nations have pursued different investment agendas abroad. The Uae’s state funds and enterprises, the Gulf’s early movers, already have investments in Canadian real estate and financial services, and a controlling stake in Calgary-based Nova Chemicals. DP World, a UAE-based logistics company that handles 10 per cent of the world’s cargo, operates facilities in five Canadian ports.

Saudi Arabia’s investment strategy, however, is aligned to the domestic economy and the country’s Vision 2030 blueprint, with goals that include developing the country’s mineral wealth, and establishing auto and aerospace industries. It is looking for two-way investment that develops Saudi expertise, especially in mining, Mr. Steiner said.

“Canada is number one in the Saudis’ mind when it comes to minerals,” he said.

The Saudis have already indirectly invested in Canadian mining in a deal that highlights their national investment strategy: Its Manara Minerals Investment Company paid US$2.5-billion to Brazil’s Vale S.A. for a 10-per-cent stake in subsidiary Vale Base Metals, which produces nickel, copper and cobalt key to auto and aerospace manufacturing at operations in Sudbury, Voisey’s Bay, Nfld., and Thompson, Man.

Now, there is an effort to build a path for direct two-way investment, though it won’t be completed in two days in Toronto. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will lead a delegation of Canada’s “Maple 8″ pension funds to Saudi Arabia in November.

There is no doubt about the short-term goal of Mr. Carney’s Gulf initiative, and one day soon, warmer relationships will be judged in the cold terms of investment dollars.

stories.title: ‘There’s been a fundamental change’: How the Canada-U.S. relationship has evolved in the last 25 years
stories.summary: Canada has supported the United States as its closest ally on numerous occasions over the decades. But since 9/11, the relationship has also faced its fair share of challenges.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello
stories.content:
Ottawa – Reflecting on the solemn anniversary ahead of a day of cabinet meetings, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 25 years ago, an ordinary day became one of history’s darkest.

“Nearly 3,000 people, amongst them 24 Canadians lost their lives, killed in the worst terrorist attack in American history. Thousands more injured, countless more forever affected by what happened,” he said.

Citing the immediate response of first responders to ground zero, but also the Canadian government without hesitation welcoming 224 planes at 17 airports, including in Gander, N.L. where strangers were welcomed in and were asked for nothing in return, the prime minister said the tragedy also showed what this country is made of.

“This dark moment also brought forth some of our best nature,” Carney said. “The lesson I think of these events… is that the response to darkness is to reach out, is to support, to stand in solidarity – as Canadians did – with our neighbours, in this case our American neighbours.”

Here’s a look back at a few of the pivotal moments over the last 25 years, how the cross-border friendship has evolved, and whether prominent players from these inflection points think this country would respond differently if a 9/11-type event were to happen again.

Canadian sacrifices, red lines in war on terror

In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, Canada deployed troops to help fight the U.S.-led war on terror in Afghanistan.

“I can still remember the day of 9/11. I was presenting information to create new capabilities in the event of a terrorist attack,” said Maj.-Gen. (Ret’d) David Fraser, a senior Canadian military official at the time, who during the war, led Nato forces in Afghanistan.

The war stretched between 2001 and 2014, making it both the longest war this country participated in its largest military contingent ever deployed – more than 40,000 served – since the Second World War.

And while then-U.S. president George W. Bush balked when Canada refused to help invade Iraq in 2003, a decision taken by then-prime minister Jean Chretien, Americans still recognize and honour the sacrifices Canadians made in the decades since.

“We are so grateful for their selfless service … so that we May continue to enjoy our freedoms, and so the Afghan people can retain the hope of having theirs,” said James A. Winnefeld Jr., then-vice chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, at a 2014 event at the Canadian Embassy in Washington, D.C. featuring Canada’s Afghanistan Memorial Vigil.

“Together we have fought in a noble cause. Together we’ve sacrificed.”

In total, 165 Canadians were killed in Afghanistan, including 158 soldiers and seven civilians.

“Americans understand if we’re prepared to spill blood with them, it means an awful lot, not just to the military, but to the citizens of the United States of America,” Fraser said.

“And that means something. We’re good partners. You know, we have our differences at times, and that’s what democracies are about. But fundamentally, we still like each other.”

Speaking in Gander, N.L. on Friday, U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said the anniversary is an opportunity to remember the “shared sacrifices” and instances where Canadians and Americans have stood side by side in the years since, including in Afghanistan.

“To the nation of Canada, thank you. Thank you for being a partner. Thank you for the shared sacrifices that you have made with us,” Hoekstra said.

Friendly, but not frictionless Obama years

After Democrat Barack Obama became U.S. president in 2009, he chose Canada for his first foreign trip, which set the relationship off on strong footing, coming off what former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne described as an existing “close working relationship” with the previous administration.

Obama and prime ministers Stephen Harper and Justin Trudeau collaborated on a series of border, security and conservation initiatives. Though his time in office was not without friction. That included when in 2015 he rejected the Keystone XL pipeline.

Yet, ON his way out, in a speech to Canadian Parliament a year later, he emphasized how in his view, “the world needs more Canada.”

“In the Obama years, it was about building on a foundation … but it was all in the normal course of business,” Wynne said, speaking of the efforts she undertook to strengthen trade and business ties during her time in office. “There was no panic in it, there was no pressure in those years to do something because we were under threat.

Former Canadian ambassador to the U.S. David MacNaughton presented his credentials to Obama and expressed similar sentiments, noting that under the Democratic president, trade issues existed, but they weren’t insurmountable.

But as Wynne said, “that changed in 2016, and obviously it has it has changed again for the worse now.”

The ongoing acrimonious Trump era

Wynne citing 2016 was of course in reference to the election of Donald Trump, whose time in the Oval Office has brought intense acrimony and strained economic relations.

From triggering of North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta) renegotiation in 2017, to touting its successor, the Canada-United States-Mexico-Agreement (Cusma) reached in 2018, as “the largest, fairest, and most balanced trade agreement ever,” the first round of trade talks with the Americans brought no shortage of drama but ultimately ended in a deal.

In his second term though, Trump has upped the ante, both with his targeting of made-in-Canada goods, and his on-again, off-again musings about making this country the 51st state. Having now imposed a series of sectoral and broad-based tariffs on Canada and declared his intent not to renew Cusma, the U.S. administration is actively taunting Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government in American media and online.

Yet amid all of this, Canadian fire crews have repeatedly travelled to the U.S. to assist in wildfire fights, particularly amid the raging 2020 and 2025 blazes in California.

Citing Trump’s recent renaming of Lake Ontario, his barrage of disparaging social media posts, senior U.S. officials’ insults directed at this country, and the absence of substantive resistance from Americans, MacNaughton said while individual relationships May continue to endure, diplomatic relations face a prolonged recovery.

“It’s going to take quite a while for us to put the relationship back onto a solid footing … It’s more than just ‘oh well, don’t worry about it, there’s only two more years of Trump.’ I think that this is a generational problem,” he said.

Would we respond the same way now?

It’s examples like these, that those CTV News spoke with said make them believe if a similar attack were to ever happen again, Canadians would likely show their support the way they did 25 years ago, despite the current tensions.

“We are people that have strong values, and if this happened again, certainly we would open up our arms and put politics aside because it’s for the better good,” Fraser said. “I think Canada would be probably first to help out.”

Wynne said that while “there’s been a fundamental change” in the relationship, she believes that Canadians wouldn’t be able to stand by and not react.

“Because this is not about the people. It’s not about American people … Maybe I’m being unrealistic, but I really believe that’s who we are. That we would continue to step up,” she said.

“That’s who we are, and that’s not saying that we’re better than anybody else. I just think that we want that relationship to be strong. We want people to be OK, and I just cannot believe that our hearts would not go out to people in the United States, and that we would not take action.”

Though, as MacNaughton noted, that doesn’t mean Canadians consider the friendship to be anything like what it once was.

“Obviously it has deteriorated substantially in the last little while … I do think something fundamental has happened,” he said.

“We’re in for a long, long haul before it gets back to any semblance of what we’ve seen before.”

In a moment of great impact at the Gander, N.L. ceremony, Chretien received a standing ovation and a barrage of cheers when he – after reflecting on the horrors of 9/11, the aftermath, and the state of the relationship— shared a “message for our American friends.”

“Yes, Canada is a generous, open country, and Canadians are tolerant and kind. But never mistake our generosity for weakness. Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never, never mistake our kindness for softness,” he said. “We know who we are, and we are proud of it.”

“We embrace our friends and we help them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one.”

“This dark moment also brought forth some of our best nature,” Carney said. “The lesson I think of these events… is that the response to darkness is to reach out, is to support, to stand in solidarity – as Canadians did – with our neighbours, in this case our American neighbours.”

“I can still remember the day of 9/11. I was presenting information to create new capabilities in the event of a terrorist attack,” said Maj.-Gen. (Ret’d) David Fraser, a senior Canadian military official at the time, who during the war, led Nato forces in Afghanistan.

“We are so grateful for their selfless service … so that we May continue to enjoy our freedoms, and so the Afghan people can retain the hope of having theirs,” said James A. Winnefeld Jr., then-vice chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, at a 2014 event at the Canadian Embassy in Washington, D.C. featuring Canada’s Afghanistan Memorial Vigil.

stories.title: Que. party leaders criticize PQ’s $130 million sovereignty referendum plan
stories.summary: Montreal — Parti Québecois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon came under fire from his rivals on Friday after revealing that his planned sovereignty referendum would cost at least $130 million.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Posted September 11, 2026 5:00 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 4:42 pm.

Montreal — Parti Québecois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon came under fire from his rivals on Friday after revealing that his planned sovereignty referendum would cost at least $130 million.

While three of the five leaders in the campaign argued that there were better ways to spend this money, sovereigntist left-wing party Québec solidaire defended the proposed expense.

In an interview with The Canadian Press, St-Pierre Plamondon had detailed the costs of preparing for and holding the referendum in 2029 or 2030 if his party forms a government.

The referendum budget includes $20 million for studies and consultations in the first years of a Parti Québecois government mandate. Holding the referendum in 2029-30 would cost $110 million, according to the party leader.

St-Pierre Plamondon admitted the cost could exceed that amount if there are “unforeseen expenses.”

“People will have their say, but we won’t apologize for living in a democracy and for consulting the people if we’ve reached that point,” he added.

His party’s figures on a referendum will be included in the financial framework he plans to make public on Sept. 15, the day of the first party leaders’ debate of a provincial election campaign that will wrap up when Quebecers go to the polls on Oct. 5.

Christine Fréchette, leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, said there were still numbers missing from St-Pierre Plamondon’s plan. She said he had failed to disclose the costs that could be triggered after a referendum.

“The Parti Québécois tell us that they evaluate the cost of organizing a referendum at $130 million. What about the cost of year one of a sovereign Quebec? They’re completely mute on that,” she said.

Fréchette, who has declined to say how she would vote in a sovereignty referendum, called herself an “autonomist” on Friday, promising to defend Quebec’s interests within Canada.

“It’s $130 million that frankly, could be invested elsewhere,” she said.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard called the planned expense a misuse of funds in a separate news conference.

“I can tell you what we would do with $130 million. We could offer close to one million hours of home care. We could build probably three elementary schools and 1300 non-market housing units,” he said.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime was also quick to criticize St-Pierre Plamondon’s plan. He said it was “unacceptable” to plan these expenses at a time when the cost of living remains high.

“Unfortunately, the Parti Québecois lives on another planet,” said Duhaime.

“He told us he didn’t want a referendum in the first three years. Now, today, we’re learning that in those three years, they plan to spend money to try to convince us to vote ‘Yes’ in the fourth year when he imposes his referendum,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon has said his party would hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, regardless of whether it forms a majority or minority government.

Asked about this criticism, St-Pierre Plamondon defended his referendum budget and said general elections in the province cost about $110 million.

He also said Quebec independence would lead to savings in the long run.

“The goal is to end federal waste that duplicates everything we do and loses money like nowhere else, costing us billions of dollars,” he said.

Also on the campaign trail, Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal defended the need for an extensive consultation on Quebec sovereignty.

“For us as an (sovereigntist) party, it’s important to have a big consultation — with First Nations, with the people who are afraid maybe to be an independent country, with the anglophones, with the whole social society,” she said.

She said her party has budgeted $220 million for an assembly in charge of writing a new Quebec constitution that would be at the heart of a sovereignty referendum.

If he becomes premier on Oct. 5, St-Pierre Plamondon told The Canadian Press he would appoint a minister responsible for the independence process, who would replace the minister of Canadian relations.

“We don’t have any plans regarding the size or number of employees per ministry, but … we can commit to not increasing the size of that particular ministry,” he said.

The PQ leader added that the “intergovernmental relationship with Ottawa is also becoming part of the independence project.”

Since the start of the election campaign, the PQ’s opponents have been demanding details on the cost of a potential referendum. When pressed by The Canadian Press, he decided to open the books.

“Part of my opponents’ strategy is to demonize consulting the people about their future, by saying it’s appalling,” he said. “However, overall, we’re proposing to curb historic waste … so I think people will evaluate our political platform as a whole.”

St-Pierre Plamondon is confident his party’s promises have been properly budgeted for, saying “it’s a more than prudent budgetary approach.”

The PQ leader also said the financial framework he will soon table will be “the budgetary framework for a Quebec in the current context.”

It will not take into account, for example, the promise to create a Quebec army after the referendum, should the “Yes” side win.

“Quebec’s budgetary framework will change after Quebec’s independence,” he said.

With files from Caroline Plante.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tiff film ‘In the Heart of the South’ explores trauma and Indigenous identity
stories.summary: Toronto — Nyla Innuksuk's longtime love of horror — along with her own feelings of fear and doubt — serves as inspiration for her latest project exploring the uncomfortable subjects people often avoid and the complicated ways they shape friendships.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Diana Mussina, The Canadian Press

Posted September 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 5:22 am.

Toronto — Nyla Innuksuk’s longtime love of horror — along with her own feelings of fear and doubt — serves as inspiration for her latest project exploring the uncomfortable subjects people often avoid and the complicated ways they shape friendships.

A psychological thriller co-written with Ryan Cavan, “In the Heart of the South” premièred Thursday at the Toronto International Film Festival. It is the Nunavut-born filmmaker’s second feature after her 2022 debut “Slash/Back.”

Innuksuk’s past work mainly involves short films and documentaries, so the transition to feature filmmaking in 2022, she said, was like jumping into ice-cold water and learning to swim.

The filmmaker said “Slash/Back,” which follows a group of teen girls fighting an alien invasion in Nunavut, was “ambitious” — at a time when there was a need for more resources and Inuit actors.

She felt better prepared to take on “In the Heart of the South” — but first, she had to confront feelings of fear and doubt, as she didn’t want to seem as though she was exploiting the traumas of Indigenous people, she said.

“Those conversations that we’re just afraid of having because they’re too difficult and uncomfortable,” she said in an interview. “That became the discomfort that I gravitated toward in the film.”

Innuksuk said horror and comedy build anticipation and tension in similar ways and thought it might be interesting to blend darkness with humour.

“That’s something that’s very true of at least for Inuit and for Indigenous people that I’ve met,” she said. “There’s just like this ability to laugh at the darkness of life.”

The film follows Yura Ivalu, a young multimedia artist played by Anna Lambe, who gains recognition after creating an augmented reality piece about the residential school system and struggles to find her place as an Indigenous woman in Toronto’s art scene.

Innuksuk, who grew up in Iqaluit and moved to southern Ontario, said the character’s struggle draws on her own personal identity struggles, including how other Inuit people might perceive her.

“When I go back to Nunavut … they’re like, ‘Oh, you look like an Inuk, but who was raised down in the south,'” she said.

“And I think that there’s just so much that can be caught up in this idea of identity and, for Indigenous people, what our indigeneity means and how Indigenous are we.”

In the film, chaos arrives in the form of Yura’s estranged childhood best friend, played by Zorga Qaunaq. Qaunaq, known for playing gentle and funny characters, takes on an unsettling, enigmatic role as Sesi.

Lambe and Qaunaq previously appeared together in the CBC/Netflix Arctic comedy “North of North.”

“I really, really wanted to play (Sesi),” Qaunaq said on the Tiff red carpet ahead of the film’s première.

“She has parts of me that I’ve been avoiding, like exploring my anger and confrontation and not being afraid to face conflict, to call people out.”

Speaking at the première, the 25-year-old Lambe said playing Yura helped her embrace vulnerability in ways that felt emotionally stressful.

She said she felt strongly about the film’s messages because of how it made her feel called out.

Inuit throat singing, a traditional vocal art typically performed between two people, plays a significant role in conveying the mood of certain scenes as well as characters’ emotions.

Innuksuk said she wanted to evoke a nostalgic atmosphere when, while throat singing, Sesi asked Yura to perform a “love song.”

“It puts the character of Yura in this position of discomfort because it’s all of a sudden. She’s being asked to perform her indigeneity or even it’s being put on the spot.”

The director also asked the sister duo, Piqsiq, to produce and record their own throat singing, which is featured throughout the film.

Innuksuk said she was conscious of how the film might be received by viewers as well as fellow Inuit and Indigenous people.

“We’re aware that we’re saying something that might make people uncomfortable,” she said.

“It’s not a movie that is soft and fuzzy.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

Diana Mussina, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sept. 11 first responders tell of Canada-U.S. bonds at B.C. border ceremony
stories.summary: Surrey — New York first responders on Sept. 11, 2001, have spoken of the enduring bonds between Canada and the United States at a ceremony along the border between British Columbia and Washington state to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canadian and U.S. flags fly atop the Peace Arch monument at the Douglas-Peace Arch border crossing in Surrey, B.C., Monday, Nov. 8, 2021. THE Canadian Press/Darryl Dyck

By Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

Posted September 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 3:15 pm.

Surrey — New York first responders on Sept. 11, 2001, have spoken of the enduring bonds between Canada and the United States at a ceremony along the border between British Columbia and Washington state to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

They were among hundreds of first responders, military and border officers and dignitaries from both countries at the annual Northwest 9/11 Memorial ceremony at the Peach Arch monument between Surrey, B.C., and Blaine, Wash.

Retired New York firefighter Cody Stamberger says he wasn’t scheduled to work that morning, but left a doctor’s appointment to head in as soon as he saw what was happening.

While he believes his roster that day May have saved his life, Stamberger says he was “extraordinarily angry” not to have been with his fellow firefighters the whole time.

The third-generation firefighter says “shoulder to shoulder” solidarity is on display between the two countries at the memorial, decorated with rows of Canadian and U.S. flags.

Stamberger says the event shows the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the United States “doesn’t matter” when it comes to honouring those killed that day.

“This is about society. This is about togetherness, unity, and honour,” he says, describing how Canadian teams had joined Sept. 11 rescue efforts, and the Canadian military fought in Afghanistan.

“We play the game together, and we always have. We’ve done it through everything. D-Day? We stormed the beaches together.”

Retired New York fire department paramedic Roberto Abril was also at the Peace Arch memorial.

His paramedic partner Carlos Lillo died in the attacks.

Abril says the scale of the tragedy had humbled him and given him a reason to “love everybody.”

The retired paramedic has now attended four services at the arch, and says he’s been surprised how Canadians and Americans alike “opened their hearts to us, as if we are a family.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Canada is everyone, for everyone’: Carney signs Forever Canadian campaign van
stories.summary: Banff — The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation says Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the media at a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh THE Canadian Press

By Kyle Duggan and Bill Graveland, The Canadian Press

Posted September 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 11, 2026 4:32 pm.

Banff — The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a “calm” and “reassuring” presence for Albertans.

Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Friday Carney is showing “there is someone at the helm” by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.

Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.

The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canada campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.

The prime minister wrote “Canada is everyone and for everyone” on the campaign’s bright pink recreational vehicle with a black marker.

The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada.

Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.

Lukaszuk said he expects there will be “a stage in the campaign” when the prime minister will become “much more personally engaged.”

“At a time where people go to sleep worried about what tomorrow May bring because of geopolitics, this is a very positive campaign. We’re not voting against anything,” Lukaszuk said.

“We’re just saying, ‘We’re Canadians.’ We don’t care whether you’re Conservatives, or NDP, or Liberal or anything else. This is about the Canadian family.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

Kyle Duggan and Bill Graveland, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Thousands expected in Gander, N.L., for ceremony marking 9/11 attacks 25 years ago
stories.summary: Gander - Thousands are expected to fill an arena in central Newfoundland today for a solemn ceremony remembering those killed in terrorist attacks in the United States 25 years ago.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Gander - Former prime minister Jean Chrétien drew a standing ovation inside a Gander, N.L., hockey arena on Friday as he delivered a pointed message to American leaders during a ceremony marking the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the United States, 25 years ago.

The 92-year-old warned Americans never to mistake Canadian generosity for weakness, nor its kindness for softness.

U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra looked on as Chrétien insisted his pointed words were a sign of friendship. Friends tell each other the truth, he said.

“We embraced our friends and we helped them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one,” Chretien said, as the crowd erupted again.

“The more we are threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves, and stand united.”

“Vive les États-Unis, et vive le Canada!” he boomed, as the crowd stood up, some taking off their hats to wave them in the air.

Thirty-eight planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers were grounded in Gander, N.L., ON Sept. 11, 2001, after hijackers took command of four aircraft and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Washington and a field in Pennsylvania. People in Gander dropped everything to fill churches and community halls with cots, food and clothing, and they cared for the passengers for days.

Their response became a symbol of Canada’s embrace of the United States after a horrific attack that killed nearly 3,000 people and changed the world forever.

Guests at Friday’s ceremony included some of the passengers who were cared for in Gander and its surrounding communities for days, and several speakers said the event was partly to welcome them home.

Government representatives including Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour and federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson spoke of the long-standing partnership between Canada and the United States, but only Chrétien spoke directly to the countries’ deteriorating relationship.

“Yes, Canada is a generous, open country, and Canadians are tolerant and kind,” said Chrétien. “But never mistake our generosity for weakness. Never, never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never, never, mistake our kindness for softness.”

The crowd applauded generously for speakers’ polite mentions of unity and compassion across boundaries, but it was Chrétien’s fiery missive that had them springing out of their seats. His was the last speech of the two-hour-long service.

Hoekstra did not directly mention the strained relations between Canada and his country and the ongoing dispute over tariffs, trade and sovereignty. He opened his speech saying he was in his office, talking to asparagus farmers when he first learned about the planes that had struck the World Trade Center in New York City.

Gander’s care for Americans on 9/11 proved to the world that “good will win” even on days of tragedy, Hoekstra said.

“Once more, we say thank you,” the ambassador said. “As a representative of the United States government, thank you to the people of Gander. Thank you for your friendship.… To the nation of Canada: thank you. Thank you for being a partner.”

When Chrétien finished his speech, Hoekstra walked over and gave him a hug. A spokesperson said the ambassador was not available to speak to reporters and respond to Chrétien’s remarks.

Reporters question U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra about a speech by former prime minister Jean Chrétien at a 9/11 commemoration event in Gander, N.L. (Sept. 11, 2026)

“It was a wonderful program,” said Becca Archer-Knepper in an email. “We refer you to his remarks from the program and his interaction with the former (prime minister) after the program.”

Later Friday, Hoekstra took in a production at a local arts centre of “Come From Away,” the Broadway hit musical that chronicles how the town hosted the stranded travellers.

He would not respond to questions about Chretien’s speech as he arrived, but said the day’s event was a “wonderful ceremony for 9/11.”

But Michael Rubinoff, the originating producer of the show who also attended the local performance, said Chrétien “really met the moment” during the ceremony.

“It really moved the audience. I know it really moved me,” said Rubinoff.

In Banff, Alta., Prime Minister Mark Carney also paid tribute to the victims of 9/11, saying Canadians stand with their American neighbours in mourning, remembrance and solidarity.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre pay tribute to the victims of 9/11. Carney, speaking from Banff and Poilievre speaking during a trip to New York City, both remembered those who died that day, and during the Afghanistan war. (Sept. 11, 2026)

“This dark moment also brought forth some of our best nature — firefighters climbing the stairs to rescue those in burning buildings, rescue workers working for weeks to bring closure,” Carney said.

Percy Farwell, the mayor of Gander, told the crowd that the day was about remembering those who died and suffered, but also about the humanity that emerged 25 years ago.

“Let’s not forget our obligations to each other and the power we each have to truly make a difference in a sometimes broken world,” he said.

Ceremonies were also held across the country, from the International Peace Garden on a remote stretch of the prairies to the nation’s capital.

Erika Olson, U.S. deputy chief of mission in Canada, said at a ceremony at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa that Sept. 11, 2001, was her second day working in the U.S. diplomatic service. She said it’s the responsibility of the people who were alive during the attacks to continue to tell future generations the story of that day and those that followed, to emphasize the importance of public service.

Erika Olson, U.S. deputy chief of mission in Canada, delivers remarks on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks and discusses how the event reflected the friendship between the U.S. and Canada. (Sept. 11, 2026)

“There’s no higher calling than what you all do here in serving your nation, our nations, our communities and our people,” Olson said.

Roberto Abril, a former New York fire department paramedic, was among Sept. 11 first responders who were at a commemorative event at the Peace Arch memorial on the border between Surrey, B.C., and Blaine, Wash.

Abril, whose paramedic partner died in the attack, said he had now attended four services at the arch, and he was surprised how Canadians and Americans alike in the region “opened their hearts to us, as if we are a family.”

At the International Peace Garden, a park straddling the Canada-U.S. border at Manitoba and North Dakota, firefighters from across southern Manitoba marched to the skirl of a bagpipe.

Hundreds gathered at the International Peace Garden to remember the terrorist attacks in the United States on Sept. 11, 2001. The park straddling the Canada-U.S. border at Manitoba and North Dakota includes a memorial with salvaged beams from the destroyed World Trade Center in New York City. (Sept. 11, 2026)

Salvaged beams from the World Trade Center sit in the garden as part of a permanent memorial to the attacks.

“Lord, as we stand along this quiet border, where two nations meet not in division, but in shared purpose, we thank you for that unbreakable bond,” said 1st Lt. J. Nathan Haugen with the U.S. air force.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

—With files from Ian Bickis in Boissevain, Man., Darryl Greer in Surrey, B.C., David Baxter in Ottawa, and Kyle Duggan in Banff, Alta.

stories.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney pays tribute to 9/11 victims
stories.summary: Gander — Prime Minister Mark Carney is paying tribute to the victims of 9/11.
stories.author: News Staff

On the 25th anniversary of the devastating 9/11 attacks, Prime Minister Carney honoured the victims lost that day and called for solidarity with Canada's U.S. neighbours.
