stories.title: Army reorganization formally takes effect with ceremony in Edmonton
stories.summary: New Manoeuvre Division will oversee all of the Army’s combat resources
stories.author: Gavin John
stories.content:
The long-planned overhaul of the Canadian Army took effect Thursday as a ceremony in Edmonton formally brought its combat role under the purview of a single division for the first time since the Second World War.

The event officially retired the 3rd Canadian Division and reintroduced it as the 1st Canadian Division, also known as Manoeuvre Division, which will oversee all of the Army’s combat resources.

Previously, those resources were split between four divisions located across the country.

The commander of the new division, Major-General Wade Rutland, who previously commanded the 3rd Canadian Division, said the change will put the Army in a league with its allies, though the full transformation will take years.

“What’s actually in the 1st Canadian Division, and you compare it with a lot of our allies, it’s a viable force,” he said in an interview earlier this week. “We think in a couple years we’re going to be much more capable.”

The creation of Manoeuvre Division is part of an overhaul that will also see the Montreal-based 2nd Canadian Division, now also known as the Defence of Canada Division, focus on national emergencies and domestic defence . And Support Division, based in Kingston, will provide infrastructure and other resources to the rest of the Army.

The restructuring is a long-term effort by the Canadian Armed Forces to expand its ranks and prepare for the possibility of major conflict.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the Manoeuvre Division is the “expeditionary warfighting division” that will be prepared to fight in the event of a major conflict − overseas or at home.

“We’ll have the highest level of readiness,” he said. “Sometimes defending at home means defending forward. Sometimes it means defending here.”

Dozens of Army personnel dressed in dark green and navy-blue uniforms watched at the Edmonton event as the commander of the Army spoke about past battle honours before offering a blunt assessment of the state of the institution today.

“The Army that we have is not the Army we need,” Lieutenant-General Michael Wright said.

The flag of the 3rd Canadian Division was lowered and replaced with a bright red patch − the new symbol of the Manoeuvre Division − to signal the transition.

Manoeuvre Division will oversee the Army’s three mechanized brigade groups in Edmonton, Petawawa, Ont., and Valcartier, Que. The restructured division also includes four formations: the 3rd Light Infantry Regiment, the 1st Canadian Artillery Brigade, the 1st Canadian Sustainment Brigade and the 10th Signal Regiment.

The federal government has made building up the military a priority, especially as it seeks to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States for trade and defence in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Ottawa is also ramping up its defence spending to meet Nato investment targets.

“The division headquarters has to learn to fight as a division headquarters,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said Thursday, adding that Army personnel will begin conducting combat simulations against a major adversary.

“We need to change now to a division headquarters that has tents, gets its rucksack on, has communications and fights,” he said.

In the meantime, he said, the Army’s work continues uninterrupted. For example, it is preparing to deploy troops to Latvia, as well as to Ukraine for training.

Lt.-Gen. Wright cautioned that the work of transforming the Army won’t be quick.

“Just because it’s the 10th of September doesn’t mean the 1st Canadian Division is completely full of people, necessary people, necessary capability, and able to be that warfighting division,” he said.

“The path toward that starts today.”

He said the new formations are at varying levels of maturity, and the Army’s chief concern is the ability to provide command and control and combat service support.

Much of the equipment the Army says it needs, including ground-based air-defence systems, armoured reconnaissance vehicles and mobile artillery, has yet to be deployed.

Lt.-Gen. Wright said the Himars rocket artillery system the government has purchased will fall under 1st Canadian Division command and that by September, 2027, two of Maj.-Gen. Rutland’s units will each have a sub-unit based on uncrewed systems.

David Perry, the president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, says the modernization of the military will take years and some of the decisions to ensure that happens − such as supplying equipment − rest with the federal government.

“Realistically, we can’t expect the Army to have much more operational capability than it does today for another three to five years,” Mr. Perry said.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said a shortage of equipment is not his concern.

“You’ve got to be ready to fight tonight with what you have,” he said. “If we had to bring [older equipment] to World War III, we’d bring it, we’d dig in and we would shoot it.

“I’ve got what I’ve got.”

stories.title: Carney to headline Liberal fundraiser on eve of investment summit
stories.summary: The Liberal Party would not release the list of its invitees to the event
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting a fundraiser for the Liberal Party on the eve of a marquee summit where he’ll be courting billions of dollars in investment for Canada.

The invite-only fundraising event will take place in Toronto on Sunday night. Beginning on Monday evening, hundreds of senior executives from around the world are gathering in the city at Mr. Carney’s invitation for the Canada Investment Summit, an attempt to get billions in new capital flowing into the country.

The Globe and Mail obtained a copy of the invitation to the fundraiser, billed as “An Evening with Mark Carney.”

The get-together is described as a “unique in-person event as we look at the next steps in our Liberal government’s work to build a better and stronger Canada.”

The location is only provided to those who register and tickets are $1,775 – the maximum annual donation to a political party allowed under election law.

Prospectus for Carney’s summit highlights more than 160 projects open for investment

It’s the latest closed-door fundraiser headlined by the Prime Minister since he became Liberal Leader last year and began rolling back the measures instituted by his predecessor to make political fundraising more transparent.

Mr. Carney held a fundraiser last fall on the sidelines of a Liberal caucus meeting in Edmonton and barred media from attending; under former-prime minister Justin Trudeau, reporters were routinely allowed into fundraisers for the prime minister’s opening remarks.

After the Edmonton event, the Liberal Party said it would instead adopt a case-by-case approach to opening up events to the media.

Then earlier this year, the Liberals introduced legislation that removed the requirement for political parties to proactively publish notice of fundraisers with ticket prices of more than $200, as well as report where the event was being held.

Those requirements were put in place after reporting by The Globe in 2016 about wealthy business leaders using fundraisers to effectively buy and sell access to the prime minister and other cabinet ministers to sway government decisions.

Carney focuses on attracting investment and economic growth as U.S. conflict deepens

NDP Leader Avi Lewis criticized the timing and secrecy surrounding Mr. Carney’s Sunday event.

“Are any of the donors enjoying access to the Prime Minister at this fundraiser the same executives bidding on Canada’s resources and infrastructure at the investment summit?” he said in a written statement to The Globe.

“We don’t know and it’s harder than ever to find out, thanks to rule changes for fundraisers the Liberals made (and we opposed).”

The changes to the notifications for fundraisers and related details were billed by the government as a privacy measure and an effort to protect those who host or attend events from protests or threats.

Now, parties must notify Elections Canada within 30 days of a fundraiser taking place. A report on the event will still be made public after the fact, including the list of who attended, but the address of the event will be redacted from the report posted online.

The Globe asked the Liberal Party if it would disclose who was invited to Sunday’s event for transparency, but it did not.

“As with all of our fundraising events, local Liberal teams work hard to engage supporters in their communities, and the full list of attendees is made publicly available on the Elections Canada website after the events, in accordance with our reporting requirements,” party spokesperson Maggie Morris said in an e-mail.

Since the new fundraising disclosure rules came into effect on June 18, the Liberals have so far reported holding 13 fundraising events, with Mr. Carney in attendance at one of them – a top-donor event on the margins of the Calgary Stampede in July that also featured cabinet ministers.

The regulated fundraising events registry maintained by Elections Canada shows April, 2026, as the last time the Conservatives held a fundraising event.

The Conservative Party did not return a request for comment from The Globe as to whether it has held any fundraisers since April, or if there were events it has not yet reported publicly.

It’s the latest closed-door fundraiser headlined by the Prime Minister since he became Liberal Leader last year and began rolling back the measures instituted by his predecessor to make political fundraising more transparent.

Mr. Carney held a fundraiser last fall on the sidelines of a Liberal caucus meeting in Edmonton and barred media from attending; under former-prime minister Justin Trudeau, reporters were routinely allowed into fundraisers for the prime minister’s opening remarks.
After the Edmonton event, the Liberal Party said it would instead adopt a case-by-case approach to opening up events to the media.

Then earlier this year, the Liberals introduced legislation that removed the requirement for political parties to proactively publish notice of fundraisers with ticket prices of more than $200, as well as report where the event was being held.

Those requirements were put in place after reporting by The Globe in 2016 about wealthy business leaders using fundraisers to effectively buy and sell access to the prime minister and other cabinet ministers to sway government decisions.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis criticized the timing and secrecy surrounding Mr. Carney’s Sunday event.

“Are any of the donors enjoying access to the Prime Minister at this fundraiser the same executives bidding on Canada’s resources and infrastructure at the investment summit?” he said in a written statement to The Globe.
“We don’t know and it’s harder than ever to find out, thanks to rule changes for fundraisers the Liberals made (and we opposed).”

The changes to the notifications for fundraisers and related details were billed by the government as a privacy measure and an effort to protect those who host or attend events from protests or threats.

Now, parties must notify Elections Canada within 30 days of a fundraiser taking place. A report on the event will still be made public after the fact, including the list of who attended, but the address of the event will be redacted from the report posted online.
The Globe asked the Liberal Party if it would disclose who was invited to Sunday’s event for transparency, but it did not.

“As with all of our fundraising events, local Liberal teams work hard to engage supporters in their communities, and the full list of attendees is made publicly available on the Elections Canada website after the events, in accordance with our reporting requirements,” party spokesperson Maggie Morris said in an e-mail.

Since the new fundraising disclosure rules came into effect on June 18, the Liberals have so far reported holding 13 fundraising events, with Mr. Carney in attendance at one of them – a top-donor event on the margins of the Calgary Stampede in July that also featured cabinet ministers.
The regulated fundraising events registry maintained by Elections Canada shows April, 2026, as the last time the Conservatives held a fundraising event.
The Conservative Party did not return a request for comment from The Globe as to whether it has held any fundraisers since April, or if there were events it has not yet reported publicly.

stories.title: 25 years later, who was the 9/11 victim with a Global News reporter’s name?
stories.summary: A Global News reporter uncovers the life and family of Michael J. Armstrong, the man killed on Sept. 11, 2001, who shares his name — right down to the middle initial.
stories.author: Michael J. Armstrong
stories.content:
It’s an awkward thing to say.

But every Sept. 11 , when the names of the 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks are read aloud at the World Trade Center site … I hear my name.

Michael J. Armstrong.

It’s a name I share, right down to the middle initial.

For more than two decades, I wondered about the other Michael Armstrong. Who was he? What was his life like? Who had he left behind?

Years ago, I came across something written by one of his sisters about the family’s efforts to keep Michael’s memory alive. They had created a foundation in his name. So, as I began putting together stories to mark 25 years since the attacks, I decided I wanted to help his family tell his story.

Even reaching out felt uncomfortable.

I knew the email would arrive in his sister’s inbox with one name attached to it: Michael Armstrong. I wondered what it would be like for her to see that name suddenly appear on her screen. And whether I had any right to ask her to open that door.

The ensuing back and forth turned into a visit to her home in Tappan, N.Y., last month.

The walls of Laura’s home are filled with family photos. Michael appears in many of them: Christmas mornings, Thanksgivings, St. Patrick’s Day celebrations, and one where he jumped on their father’s lap. He was goofing around after he as his sister Marian had bought Laura her first digital camera.

“He just had such a hearty laugh,” Laura said. “He laughed a lot.”

“He was just a warm kind of guy and he was great with kids,” Marian recalled.

Dozens of photos have been added to the walls in the 25 years since 9/11. Important events where Michael’s absence is impossible for the family to ignore.

“There are a lot of instances where we think that,” Laura said. “Where he should have been.”

Michael Armstrong was 34 years old and worked in electronic trading on Wall Street with the brokerage company Cantor Fitzgerald.

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Michael was at work on the 104th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center, above the floors struck by American Airlines Flight 11.

After the building was hit, Michael tried to reach members of his family by telephone.

His sister Marion remembers that his final cellphone call was to their mother. The family’s copy of his phone statement showed the call lasted two minutes.

But his mother couldn’t make out his words.

All she heard was static.

The family has always hoped that while Michael couldn’t be heard, he could hear his mother’s voice.

For hours that morning, his sisters clung to possibilities.

Maybe he had been late for work. Maybe what they were hearing about the Twin Towers wasn’t as bad as it sounded. They didn’t turn on the television.

“I really thought he was going to be OK,” Laura recalled. “As crazy as it is.”

The next few weeks in Michael’s life were supposed to be special. He and his fiancée, Catherine Nolan, were set to be married on Oct. 6, 2001.

Instead, Michael’s wake was held on Sept. 23, 2001.

He almost wasn’t in the office on 9/11. He’d been at a funeral the day before and missed work. And later in the week, he was scheduled to be off again for his bachelor party.

“We often said, like, oh, you know, so many things,” Catherine recalled. “If he had only left a few days earlier, if he had a dentist appointment the next day.”

“So many days that week he would not have been there,” Marian said.

Those are the what-ifs that can follow a family for decades.

Catherine eventually married and had children. Her youngest son’s middle name is Michael. She also never really left the Armstrong family.

“I always joke that I’ve got the in-laws without the husband,” she said.

Michael’s brother is godfather to one of her children. His sisters remain part of her life. Twenty-five years later, Catherine is still Aunt Catherine to the next generation of Armstrongs.

There is a gravity to grieving — a force that focuses on the pain. The Armstrongs chose instead to help others in Michael’s name.

Within days of the attacks, they established a scholarship fund at Loyola School, where Michael had been a student and remained an active alumnus. In the months that followed, the family established the Michael J. Armstrong Memorial Foundation.

For nearly 25 years, they have held fundraising events and supported causes connected to Michael’s life, including scholarships at Loyola and athletics at Fordham University, where Michael was an enthusiastic basketball fan.

His sister describes it as a place to channel all the emotions that followed his death. It’s also ensured his story didn’t stop on Sept. 11, 2001.

The family’s effort to remember Michael now extends to people who never had the chance to meet him.

His niece, Keeley, says Michael is a normal household name in the family. He died when she was young, but it has never felt that way.

“It’s amazing how much you can know someone through stories,” Keeley said.

Those stories have given another generation a picture of an uncle they never knew: his enormous laugh, his sense of humour, his bear hugs and his habit of teasing his siblings.

But there is still sadness. The next generation of Armstrongs is now approaching the age that Michael was when he was killed.

“We’re now in that stage of life of people getting married,” Keeley said, with tears welling up. “I can’t imagine that you’re supposed to be going to a bachelor party on Thursday, and then this happens.”

But the Armstrongs also remember something else about those days: how people responded to their pain.

Catherine found herself part of a group no one would ever choose to join — women who, like her, lost their fiancées on 9/11.

They found each other in the aftermath. Twenty-five years later, they still get together every Sept. 11 for lunch.

The support came from all directions. There were countless acts of kindness the family remembers from those first days: people reaching out, showing up and trying to help.

It’s something they’ve carried forward through the foundation, the scholarships and the years spent helping others in Michael’s name.

“I can’t look back at that day without thinking about the kindness, the care everyone took with me,” Marian says. “People are so beautiful.”

stories.title: How torrential rain is pushing this year’s harvest far behind average
stories.summary: Torrential rains late in the season are adding stress at a time that is already taxing for farmers. The recent moisture has prevented producers from getting into fields and further delayed harvest in many parts of Saskatchewan.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Davidson, Sask. - Torrential rains late in the season are adding stress at a time that is already taxing for farmers.

The recent moisture has prevented producers from getting into fields and further delayed harvest in many parts of Saskatchewan.

The most recent government-issued crop report shows only 27 per cent of Saskatchewan crops have been harvested, which puts producers far behind the five-year average of 58 per cent.

Rob Stone, who farms an hour south of Saskatoon, is usually ahead of the provincial average.

But right now, he only has 18 per cent of his crops in the bin.

“Bluntly, it has been a bit brutal,” Stone said.

Stone’s area received about 150 millimetres of rain over the course of a week.

He was forced to wait for fields to dry up before he could get equipment running again.

“Everything is in good shape and we need to go, but the weather needs to co-operate,” he said.

Further south, near Montmartre, Sask., the Kotylaks are still waiting for their crops to dry after torrential rains flattened some of their fields.

“In 37 years, this is the worst canola I have ever seen,” farmer Peter Kotylak told CTV News while standing in one of his waterlogged crops.

“The rain came at the wrong time this year.”

Farmers in certain areas have struggled with the weather all year long.

A late snow dump and spring flooding pushed seeding back. Now rain is prolonging harvest.

“The year got off to a slow start and it has just gotten further and further behind,” said Bill Prybylski, president of the Agricultural Producers Association of Saskatchewan.

“It’s been very stressful.”

The recent rain is not only burning time but also hurting yields and potential profits, Prybylski said.

“Some crops are definitely going to be hurt more than others,” he said.

“There will definitely be some downgrading in the quality of the grain.”

Stone expects his wheat and lentils to decrease in grade and yields due to the rain delays.

The potential losses come at a time when farmers are facing record high input costs.

Tariffs and trade uncertainty drove up the costs of fuel, fertilizer, machinery and repairs.

“This is the most expensive crop we have ever grown,” Stone said.

“If the yields are not there, people will be on the wrong side of profit.”

stories.title: Family mourns death of loved one killed fighting in Ukraine
stories.summary: "He paid the ultimate price for Canada and Ukraine,” said an emotional James Bourgeois, Jessy Bourgeois’ father, in an interview with Global News.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The family of a B.C man killed in Ukraine is mourning his death.

“He paid the ultimate price for Canada and Ukraine,” said an emotional James Bourgeois, Jessy Bourgeois’ father.

The 46-year-old man was killed on Aug. 18 in the Donetsk region near the Russian border.

“They got hit by a drone attack, and Jesse was killed instantly,” said Bourgeois. “Another comrade was critically injured and died several days later.”

Bourgeois lived in Nanaimo, where he was introduced to the Ukrainian church.

His family says he quickly fell in love with the people and culture and eventually felt compelled to help defend the country.

“That’s where his heart laid,” said stepmom Dawn Bourgeois. “We didn’t understand it. We didn’t support it.”

Despite having no military experience, Jessy volunteered in November to fight alongside the Ukrainian Army.

He was working as a drone mechanic when he was killed.

“It’s one day at a time, and we try to find happiness every day. That’s all we can do,” Dawn said.

The Okanagan Falls couple says Jessy believed deeply in Ukraine and its efforts to fight for the country,

“He believed in what Ukraine was fighting for — for their freedom — and there was no talking him out of it,” James said.

Bourgeois leaves behind two children.

His family says they will grow up knowing their father was a hero.

“He was brave. He was brave for what he did,” James added.

The family’s grief comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits Canada, seeking continued support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia.

James says Canada’s support remains important to him, particularly after his son’s death.

“My son lost his life for them,” he said. “I think as Canadians we got to keep backing them.”

Global Affairs Canada says it is aware of the death of a Canadian in Ukraine. The department says it does not keep a registry of Canadians who voluntarily travel to Ukraine to serve, or those who are injured or killed in the conflict.

However, the organization says it is aware of 35 Canadians who have died in Ukraine of all causes since the war began.

Jessy’s body is expected to be repatriated in the coming weeks with the help of the Ukrainian government.

For his family, the grief remains raw, but they find some comfort in knowing Bourgeois believed he was following his heart.

“I’m proud of what he did,” James said. “This was his calling. You look at his pictures, I sure don’t see any fear.”

Instead, he says, he sees determination to help a country in need.

stories.title: Infrastructure investment needed to ‘supercharge’ Canadian mining, BMO analyst says
stories.summary: BMO analyst Matthew Murphy expects mining sector to play central role in discussions at Canada Investment Summit
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
More investments are needed in vital infrastructure such as roads and power lines to “supercharge” Canadian mining, said BMO analyst Matthew Murphy, a few days ahead of a historic Canadian investment event.

Next week, the inaugural Canada Investment Summit will be held in Toronto to attract hundreds of billions of dollars in international investment into Canada to help cushion the blow of the continuing trade war with the United States. The event is being led by Prime Minister Mark Carney and co-hosted by big Canadian pension funds.

In a note to clients earlier this week, Mr. Murphy, mining analyst with BMO Capital Markets, said he expects the sector to play a central role in discussions at the summit, and he addressed the key question of where capital is needed the most.

In a web panel discussion on Thursday, Mr. Murphy said significantly more investment in mining infrastructure could be enormously beneficial for the industry and reward multiple companies.

“There’s a big multiplier effect on infrastructure spending,” he said. “And that’s what you need for a productive economy.”

Mr. Murphy outlined several parts of the country where infrastructure spending is needed, including Northern B.C., home to major copper and gold discoveries; the Yukon; northern Ontario’s Ring of Fire region; and Quebec’s James Bay region, which has promising lithium projects.

He pointed to past infrastructure investments that spurred new development, including British Columbia installing the 344-kilometre-long Northwest Transmission Line along Highway 37. The additional electricity supply facilitated the Red Chris block cave mine development, the Brucejack gold mine, and exploration projects in B.C.’s Golden Triangle.

Several infrastructure projects that would benefit the mining sector have already been referred to the government’s Major Projects Office , which was created last year by Mr. Carney to both reduce red tape and potentially facilitate funding.

Those projects include the North Coast Transmission Line in northwestern British Columbia, the Taltson Hydro Expansion in the Great Slave Lake region of the Northwest Territories, and the Arctic Economic and Security Corridor in the NWT, a 400-kilometre all-season road through the Slave Geological Province to the Nunavut border.

In his report, Mr. Murphy said that infrastructure investment is one of the ways “to truly supercharge growth” of the Canadian mining sector.

He said that while Canadian mining companies can draw on an educated work force, and have strong engineering capabilities, it’s a major challenge to raise the hundreds of millions in capital needed for such projects.

“Mining investors want 15- to 25-per-cent returns on new projects and that’s hard if you have to carry a big infrastructure load as well,” he said.

Large infrastructure funds, such as those run by Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. BAM-T , or BlackRock’s BLK-N Global Infrastructure Partners, could potentially fill in the gap, Mr. Murphy said. These funds tend to have lower costs of capital than mining companies, and their investors can be satisfied with returns of 7 per cent to 10 per cent, he added.

Some mining companies have already successfully off-loaded the risk of building some mining infrastructure to third parties. paragraphs: More investments are needed in vital infrastructure such as roads and power lines to “supercharge” Canadian mining, said BMO analyst Matthew Murphy, a few days ahead of a historic Canadian investment event.

Next week, the inaugural Canada Investment Summit will be held in Toronto to attract hundreds of billions of dollars in international investment into Canada to help cushion the blow of the continuing trade war with the United States. The event is being led by Prime Minister Mark Carney and co-hosted by big Canadian pension funds.

In a note to clients earlier this week, Mr. Murphy, mining analyst with BMO Capital Markets, said he expects the sector to play a central role in discussions at the summit, and he addressed the key question of where capital is needed the most.
In a web panel discussion on Thursday, Mr. Murphy said significantly more investment in mining infrastructure could be enormously beneficial for the industry and reward multiple companies.
“There’s a big multiplier effect on infrastructure spending,” he said. “And that’s what you need for a productive economy.”

Mr. Murphy outlined several parts of the country where infrastructure spending is needed, including Northern B.C., home to major copper and gold discoveries; the Yukon; northern Ontario’s Ring of Fire region; and Quebec’s James Bay region, which has promising lithium projects.

He pointed to past infrastructure investments that spurred new development, including British Columbia installing the 344-kilometre-long Northwest Transmission Line along Highway 37. The additional electricity supply facilitated the Red Chris block cave mine development, the Brucejack gold mine, and exploration projects in B.C.’s Golden Triangle.

Several infrastructure projects that would benefit the mining sector have already been referred to the government’s Major Projects Office , which was created last year by Mr. Carney to both reduce red tape and potentially facilitate funding.

Those projects include the North Coast Transmission Line in northwestern British Columbia, the Taltson Hydro Expansion in the Great Slave Lake region of the Northwest Territories, and the Arctic Economic and Security Corridor in the NWT, a 400-kilometre all-season road through the Slave Geological Province to the Nunavut border.
In his report, Mr. Murphy said that infrastructure investment is one of the ways “to truly supercharge growth” of the Canadian mining sector.

He said that while Canadian mining companies can draw on an educated work force, and have strong engineering capabilities, it’s a major challenge to raise the hundreds of millions in capital needed for such projects.
“Mining investors want 15- to 25-per-cent returns on new projects and that’s hard if you have to carry a big infrastructure load as well,” he said.

Large infrastructure funds, such as those run by Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. BAM-T , or BlackRock’s BLK-N Global Infrastructure Partners, could potentially fill in the gap, Mr. Murphy said. One of the earliest sessions will feature a critical minerals discussion with the CEOs of Canadian miners Teck Resources Ltd., Cameco Corp. and Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd., who will discuss how to transform the domestic sector into a world-beater.

stories.title: Calgary judge sets aside discharge in sexual assault case involving permanent resident
stories.summary: The man’s lawyer argued unsuccessfully that “a discharge is in the public interest” to keep him from being expelled from Canada.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Calgary judge has set aside an absolute discharge in a sexual assault case where a permanent Canadian resident argued he could face immigration consequences for a conviction.

Haagen Sagli pleaded guilty to the May 12, 2024, sexual assault of a woman he met at a bar. The Norwegian citizen has been living here since he was 16, and his lawyer argued a conviction could lead to his deportation.

The Crown successfully appealed Sagli’s discharge, which meant he would not have a criminal record. Instead, Justice Lisa Silver of Alberta’s Court of King’s Bench gave him a 30-day conditional sentence.

“I find that Mr. Sagli’s circumstances present several mitigating features, including his previously unblemished record, positive personal background, guilty plea, substantial rehabilitative efforts, and the serious immigration consequences that could flow from a conviction,” Silver wrote in a recent decision.

“Considered cumulatively, those factors significantly reduce the need for specific deterrence and (support) a rehabilitative sentencing response. However, they do not alter the gravity of the offence or Mr. Sagli’s degree of responsibility for it. Nor do these circumstances change the governing principles for sexual assault that include denunciation, deterrence, and proportionality.”

Sagli, who was 32 at the time of the sexual assault, holds a master’s degree in finance from McGill University and has worked in the oil business.

“Because Mr. Sagli was a permanent resident only, a criminal conviction would likely result in immigration proceedings that could lead to his removal from Canada,” Silver said.

“Any removal decision, however, would be subject to further review processes in which his personal circumstances would be considered.”

No parallel justice system for immigrants, says Quebec judge in criminal harassment case

Indian man avoids ‘immigration consequences’ after spying on women using bathroom at his Ontario home

The Crown refused to answer questions about whether Sagli could face deportation due to his new sentence. Sagli’s lawyer did not respond by press time.

In the appeal, the Crown recommended Sagli get a conditional sentence of six months less a day, considering “the severe effect a six-month conditional sentence would have on Mr. Sagli’s immigration status.”

A permanent resident “is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality” if they get sentenced to more than six months, according to Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

They can also be deemed inadmissible if convicted of an offence “punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years,” according to the Act.

In Canada, the maximum sentence for sexual assault is a decade when it’s an indictable offence. But when it’s a summary conviction such as Sagli’s, the maximum sentence drops to 18 months.

Sagli’s lawyer argued unsuccessfully that “a discharge is in the public interest to keep Mr. Sagli, a productive member of the community, from expulsion from Canada and it enhances the public interest by recognizing Mr. Sagli’s voluntary rehabilitative efforts and guilty plea.”

The court heard that Sagli and the victim met at a bar as part of a larger group.

“After spending several hours together, Mr. Sagli accompanied the victim to her home. She allowed Mr. Sagli to sleep with her in bed. There was no discussion or agreement to have sexual relations,” said the Sept. 2 decision.

“The victim awoke with her pants around her ankles and Mr. Sagli touching her bare buttocks. When the victim asked Mr. Sagli what he was doing, he immediately stopped, explaining he ‘thought she was into it.’ The victim responded that she was asleep, she did not want him to touch her and told him to leave. Mr. Sagli did so.”

Before his guilty plea, Sagli “attended counselling for substance abuse and cognitive behaviour therapy with an emphasis on his sexual conduct,” said the decision.

“Mr. Sagli admitted that at the time of the offence, he was in an unhealthy cycle of drinking to excess. Significantly, since committing the offence he maintained sobriety.”

Sagli “showed insight into his actions and an understanding of the wrongfulness of his conduct,” according to his pre-sentence report written by a forensic psychiatrist.

“Moreover, his risk of recidivism was labelled as very low.”

The woman he sexually assaulted “described the profound and lasting psychological and emotional harm experienced by the incident,” said the decision.

Silver found that the sentencing judge “minimized the seriousness of the offence when he failed to understand the significance of a sexual assault committed against a sleeping victim.”

The woman “had no ability to respond to Mr. Sagli’s actions when he initiated sexual contact, which consisted of pulling down her pants and fondling her buttocks,” said the judge.

“Rather, the sexual assault ended only after the victim awoke and confronted Mr. Sagli’s conduct. In this way, the victim was ‘extremely vulnerable’ and ‘deprived’ of any ability to express her lack of consent or resist when Mr. Sagli started to interfere with her sexual integrity.”

Any removal decision ... would be subject to further review processes in which his personal circumstances would be considered

According to Silver, the sentencing judge “minimized the gravity of the offence …. Sexual offences violate a person’s sexual and bodily integrity. It is a crime of violence that causes harm no matter what the force used in committing it.”

The sentencing judge “erred when he considered irrelevant factors,” Silver said.

“For example, the sentencing judge improperly relied on the victim’s conduct when he referred to her having ‘invited’ Mr. Sagli into ‘her own bed,’ when he was ‘stark naked.’ In this case, the victim did not consent to sexual activity and an ‘invitation’ to share her bed did not change the non-consensual nature of the incident.”

The sentencing judge “failed to outline the basis for imposing an absolute discharge,” Silver said.

“The reasons do not meaningfully engage with the governing sentencing principles, including denunciation and deterrence in the context of sexual offences nor do they address … whether a discharge would be contrary to the public interest.”

Silver concluded that “a short conditional sentence order was the fit and appropriate sentence.”

Sagli’s “actions caused long-lasting harm to the victim and to societal values,” she said.

“The conduct violated the victim’s sexual integrity, dignity, and her right to control her own sexual autonomy. The offence caused meaningful psychological harm to the victim.”

stories.title: No shuttle service for Regina Foo Fighters concert ‘due to timing,’ mayor says
stories.summary: Shuttle service will not be available for people attending the Foo Fighters concert next Tuesday, due to timing issues, the city's mayor said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
One of Mosaic Stadium’s biggest shows will not have its typical, game-day shuttle service, the City of Regina said.

While regular transit will run as normal in Saskatchewan’s capital, shuttle service will not be available for Tuesday’s concert because of the timing, Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski said.

“Just due to the timing of the concert, it wouldn’t be possible for us to have that dedicated chartered service,” Bachynski continued.

He said 4 p.m., when the venue’s doors open, is too close to the end of the workday for the city to offer shuttles, adding that Regina decided against it to ensure regular transit riders’ trips home aren’t interrupted.

“It wouldn’t be possible for us to actually take buses offline for the concert,” the mayor said.

Dave Grohl and company will headline the first concert at the stadium in seven years, and the band’s show is almost sold out, Kyle Russell, vice president of operations and experience with Real District, told Global News. A few last-minute tickets are still available.

The Real District is not providing transportation services and is advising concertgoers to plan ahead.

“This is really going to be an exercise in planning for coming to and from the concert,” Russell said.

He pointed people to the Real District website , where information on getting to and from the venue is available.

“Parking’s on sale for the Foo Fighters concert,” Russell said.

Passes can be purchased online.

“We do encourage fans to prepay for parking in advance because we do anticipate a sellout, but the campus is a big parking lot,” Russell said.

“It’s just going to be a really fun night, and we’re looking forward to people coming out here for a full night of great music.”

The Foo Fighters will be joined by Queens of the Stone Age and Mannequin Pussy. The first opening act is expected to hit the stage at Mosaic Stadium at 5:30 p.m. Tuesday.

stories.title: Man gets four-year sentence in fatal London encampment clash
stories.summary: The judge cited provocation and weaknesses in the Crown’s case in accepting a joint four-year sentence.
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
Seven hours after he had shown up armed with a loaded sawed-off shotgun to rob a homeless encampment, Matthew Harp’s lifeless body was found face-down in a pool of blood in an east London park.

He was found a couple of metres into some tall grass at the north end of Mildred Barons Park at 444 Kathleen St. on Sept. 20, 2024. He was cold to the touch and it was clear before the paramedics arrived that attempts to resuscitate him would be fruitless.

The next day, Broady Salmon, who lived at the tent city with then-girlfriend Ashley Taylor, called police from an east-end McDonald’s restaurant to report that some of Harp’s friends were chasing and threatening them.

Police would learn that Salmon had hit Harp in the head several times with a metal pipe during the robbery attempt. He was arrested and ultimately charged with second-degree murder and possession of fentanyl for the purpose of trafficking.

On Thursday, the 31-year-old homeless man pleaded guilty to the lesser charges of manslaughter and simple possession of the powerful opioid.

“I’m sorry. I’m very, very sorry,” he said before Superior Court Justice Alissa Mitchell agreed to the joint sentencing submission from the Crown and defence of four years. With his time served factored in, Salmon has 21 months left on his sentence.

Harp’s violent death was a snapshot of the unstable, chaotic lives lived by the city’s homeless population, where many, like Salmon, live in constant fear.

Harp was a 39-year-old Indigenous man who was no stranger to the criminal justice system and had an extensive criminal record. At the time of his death, he had fentanyl, cocaine and methamphetamine in his system.

Salmon is a man scarred by a chaotic and violent childhood who has been homeless and addicted to drugs since he was in high school. He was on bail at the time of Harp’s death, but he didn’t have any brushes with the law until 2022.

However, while he has been waiting to resolve his case, he has been under threat and assaulted in custody by Harp’s friends and subjected to the frequent, lengthy lockdowns at the understaffed detention centres where he is housed.

“These are two men whose lives intersect at a spot where society and Canadian institutions have failed,” Salmon’s defence lawyer Geoff Snow said.

But Harp’s provocation loomed large and was a primary reason Mitchell accepted the joint submission.

“I am satisfied that violence is not part of Mr. Salmon’s general character,” she said.

“I do find that Mr. Salmon’s conduct leading to the death of Mr. Harp was provoked … Mr. Salmon did not set out intending to cause harm to Mr. Harp that day. A more lenient sentence, such as the one proposed here, is warranted in the circumstances of provocation.”

Assistant Crown attorney John Lee conceded that the length of the sentence appeared to be “very lenient.” However, the Crown’s case had frailties if it had gone to trial, particularly the testimony from the tent city witnesses.

Seated in the public gallery were some members of Harp’s family, including his mother, Darlene, who wrote a victim impact statement that Lee read into the record.

“I ask the court to recognize that Matthew was a human being who was loved, valued and needed. He was more than the circumstances of his death. He was a son, a father, a twin, a brother, an uncle. He had a life, family, a future and that future was taken away,” she wrote.

“Matthew mattered, his life mattered, his family matters and he will never be forgotten.”

The agreed statement of facts presented to Mitchell pointed to Harp as the instigator of the attempted robbery that led to his death.

Lee told Mitchell that at about 7 a.m. on the day of Harp’s death, an unidentified caller reported a robbery in progress. Another call later said that someone was hurt in the park.

Police checked at 4 p.m. and found Harp’s body. An autopsy showed he had died from brain trauma caused by multiple impacts to his head that led to a cardiorespiratory arrest. The drugs in his system may or may not have contributed to his death.

Several witnesses in the tent city told police Harp came to the park to rob Salmon of fentanyl and money. Harp had the shotgun, while the two associates with him had a black CO2 air pistol that looked like a handgun and a knife.

They went into Salmon’s tent demanding the loot. At one point, Harp pointed his gun at Taylor, while one of the men threatened to slash her with the knife when she asked them why they were robbing homeless people.

Another tent city resident came into the tent and attacked the robbers. Salmon joined the fight. “During the fight, the accused swung a metal pole, which resembled a trailer hitch, and hit all three males who were robbing them, including the victim,” Lee said.

Harp fell to the ground and the two other men fled. Salmon and the other tent city resident chased them. One man dropped his handgun, but they got away with some property, including Taylor’s cellphone. They were last seen getting into a waiting vehicle.

Salmon returned to his camp and found Harp “crawling away from his tent.” He believed Harp may have hurt Taylor and he struck Harp in the head several times with the metal pole “in the heat of the moment,” Lee said.

Police found the loaded sawed-off shotgun with a 44-magnum live cartridge and the black airsoft gun.

When he was arrested, Salmon had two packages containing a composite of fentanyl and caffeine weighing 31 grams. Federal drug prosecutor Laura Tripp said there was no trafficking evidence uncovered, and “the amount found could be an amount that a chronic user of fentanyl could have held for their personal use for a two-week supply.”

Taylor, who is no longer in a relationship with Salmon, was arrested but her charges have since been withdrawn by the Crown.

Snow said Salmon came from a highly unstable home life where he experienced emotional, psychological and physical abuse from addicted parents. He ended up on the street and spent his days trying “just to survive.” By 2022, drugs and instability brought him before the criminal justice system for the first time.

But “this is a scenario where Mr. Salmon is in a tent in a homeless encampment minding his own business. This violence was brought to him. It was put in his face and the face of his loved one,” Snow said.

Since his arrest, Salmon has started a methadone program and taken courses in custody to better himself.

In her decision to accept the joint submission, Mitchell noted Salmon’s guilty plea at an early stage and his remorse. She also pointed to the “chronic state of fear he lives in” while in custody with Harp’s associates.

She acknowledged Harp’s family’s loss but said she was hopeful for Salmon’s rehabilitation.

“I am satisfied that there is very little chance Mr. Salmon will be repeating this type of behaviour,” she said.

“However, this sentence does reinforce the message that Canadian law holds individuals to account for their criminal acts, notwithstanding, in this case, circumstances of provocation.”

stories.title: Czech émigré Otto Jelinek represented Canada as a skater, MP and ambassador
stories.summary: Winning the pairs event with his sister at the World Figure Skating Championships in Prague during the Cold War was the highlight of their skating careers, he said
stories.author: Alan Freeman
stories.content:
It was the depth of the Cold War and the government of Czechoslovakia had scored a coup, securing the World Figure Skating Championships for Prague, an opportunity for the Communist regime to show off.

But there was a problem. Canada’s pairs champions, the brother and sister duo of Otto and Maria Jelinek, were Czech citizens. They had escaped Czechoslovakia with their family in 1948 and sought refuge in Canada, settling in Oakville, Ont. The last thing the Czechoslovak regime wanted was to highlight the success of Czechs in the capitalist West. They refused the Jelineks their visas.

But after the International Skating Union threatened to pull the event from Prague, the Czechoslovak government agreed to allow the Jelineks to relinquish their citizenship and perform at the 1962 event as Canadians. “We were granted visas reluctantly and came to Prague not knowing what to expect,” Mr. Jelinek said in a 2015 interview.

Mr. Jelinek, who was 21 at the time, shouldn’t have been worried. The Czechoslovak public embraced the Jelineks, cheering them on the street and in the arena, where they won the world championship’s pairs event, skating to music from Dvořák and Smetana, both Czech composers. “They stood there for hours, just to see us, to touch us.”

“Winning in Prague was the highlight of our careers,” Mr. Jelinek told another interviewer. “I felt very strongly that I wanted to stick it to the Communist regime and this was an effort that paid off.”

Mr. Jelinek, who died on Sept. 5 in Mississauga, Ont., at 86, went on from his skating career to become a businessman, member of Parliament and federal cabinet minister, eventually returning to the Czech Republic where he spent almost 20 years as a consultant and as Canada’s ambassador to the Central European state.

Throughout these varied careers, Mr. Jelinek was hard-working and single-minded, never afraid to express his views, which in politics sometimes got him the wrong kind of attention.

“He was an ambitious guy,” recalled his younger brother, Henry. “We were brought up with self-discipline and to be competitive. And he [Otto] was very competitive. A go-getter.”

“I’m not a really smart guy,” Otto once told another interviewer. “I am a persistent guy. There are smarter guys in the world than I am.”

Otto Jelinek was born in Prague on May 20, 1940, the middle of five children of Henry Jelinek and his wife, the former Jarmila Zizka. His father was a wealthy industrialist, whose family-owned company manufactured cork stoppers and metal bottle caps for the brewing industry.

When the Communist government nationalized the company in 1948, Otto’s father decided it was time to leave. Through an arrangement with a South American diplomat, whom Henry Jr. said was “paid heavily,” Mrs. Jelinek and four of her children piled into the diplomat’s car and drove to the Austrian border, claiming they were on an overnight trip to the mountains.

The children were told to pretend that the diplomat, who drove the car, was their father and that they only spoke Spanish and to forget their Czech. Despite a few tense moments, the ruse worked, and the family drove all the way to Switzerland, where their father was waiting, along with their oldest brother.

They eventually got to Canada, where the initial welcome wasn’t always warm. “Canada at that time didn’t seem so tolerant of immigrants. And because we spoke Czech among us in Toronto, we were sometimes spat upon in streetcars,” Otto said later. The Jelineks settled in Bronte, a village along Lake Ontario that became part of Oakville and their father re-established the family cork business.

Otto attended Appleby College and a local high school before continuing his studies in Davos, Switzerland but, he never attended university. After winning the world pairs championship, Mr. Jelinek and Ms. Jelinek went professional, performing for several years with the Ice Capades. Mr. Jelinek also became a colour commentator on figure skating for CTV.

In 1970, at the age of 30, he launched his business career, founding Canadian Skate Industries, which manufactured hockey and figure skates. Two years later, he made his debut in federal politics, winning election as Progressive Conservative MP for the Toronto riding of High Park-Humber Valley. He later moved to the riding of Halton, winning six consecutive elections and serving 21 years in Ottawa.

Mr. Jelinek became an outspoken member of the Tories’ right wing. He defended free enterprise, supported capital punishment and opposed the metric system. He also alleged that Pierre Trudeau, prime minister at the time, was a Communist with links to China and the Soviet Union.

“Under the Trudeau administration, we have lost all opportunity and freedom of enterprise,” Mr. Jelinek said in 1978. “And we all know of his background. He was once barred from entering in the U.S. … He’s bringing this belief, this philosophy of his, to the rest of society.”

Mr. Jelinek finally entered the federal cabinet in 1984 as minister of fitness and amateur sport, appointed by Brian Mulroney, whom Mr. Jelinek had supported for leadership of the Tory party. He later held the portfolios of multiculturalism, national revenue and supply and services.

“I have a view on everything,” he told reporters in 1993, saying that when it came to multicultural policy, he resented being called a hyphenated Canadian. “I believe we have to get rid of hyphenated Canadians.”

When sprinter Ben Johnson was stripped of his gold medal at the 1988 Seoul Olympics because of doping, Mr. Jelinek came to his defence. “Ben Johnson has said he didn’t know. And I believe him … I believe him as I would believe my own mother.”

He also once complained that Ottawa was forced to spend so much on health care “just because every time a little kid has a runny nose, the mother takes him to a doctor.”

Later, as minister of national revenue, Mr. Jelinek defended border seizures by Customs officers of gay literature and attacked the Canada Council. “Some of these ridiculous grants are enough to make me bring up,” he told a business audience in 1990, referring to funding for a gay theatre group. “Whether the arm’s-length funding policy is sacrosanct or not, we’re going to tamper with it.”

Mr. Jelinek was revenue minister in the fractious period before the 1991 imposition of the GST, forcing him to defend the new tax before angry groups of small-business people. He noted to a journalist that the revenue job was a lot less interesting than the sports portfolio and that “the fun had gone out of it but the challenge is there.”

After the departure of Mr. Mulroney, Mr. Jelinek briefly mulled a run for the Progressive Conservative leadership, but in the end left politics and didn’t run in the 1993 federal election.

A year later, Mr. Jelinek decided to take a two-year sabbatical in Prague, his hometown, which turned into a stay of almost two decades. It was in the heady years just after the fall of Communism when business was opening up through privatization and foreign investment.

Mr. Jelinek became a prominent member of the business community as chair for Central Europe of Deloitte, the accounting and management consulting firm. He ran his own consulting firm. For a time he was chair of the Czech subsidiary of the Canadian mining company TVX Gold, which was trying to build a gold mine in Bohemia. But the project had to be shelved in the wake of strong opposition from local residents.

Margaret Huber, who was Canada’s ambassador in Prague from 2000 to 2003, said that Mr. Jelinek was “well-connected in Czech circles, whether political, economic or social” and was very helpful to visiting Canadian officials and businesspeople in helping them navigate the country. “He would always make himself available,” she said.

The Czech government appointed Mr. Jelinek as tourism and international business development co-ordinator, reporting directly to the prime minister. But there was controversy as well. After the Czech Republic joined Nato, the government agreed to lease a fleet of Gripen fighter jets from the Swedish firm Saab and BAE Systems of the U.K.

In 2007, Swedish TV alleged that secret payments had been made to three Czech intermediaries, including Mr. Jelinek, to help secure the contracts. Asked about the allegations by The Guardian, Mr. Jelinek said that he had been paid by BAE as a private citizen, adding that “it is personal, like my sex life.”

BAE later admitted to charges of false accounting and was fined US$450-million in the U.S. and the U.K. related to several contracts, including the Gripen deal in Czech Republic. But no charges were ever laid against Mr. Jelinek.

In 2010, Mr. Jelinek retired and returned with his family to Oakville but in 2013, he was asked by prime minister Stephen Harper to return to Prague, this time as Canada’s ambassador.

When the Jelineks fled their home in 1948, they left behind their villa in the centre of Prague, which later became the Austrian ambassador’s residence. In 2014, 80 members of the extended family came from Canada and elsewhere to celebrate Christmas in the house, lent to them by the Austrians.

“It was very emotional,” Henry Jelinek said. “There were lots of tears and lots of smiles.”

Mr. Jelinek’s stay as ambassador was brief. In 2016, shortly after the Liberals returned to power, Mr. Jelinek was one of several Harper-era appointees who were removed from their positions.

Shortly before leaving Prague, Mr. Jelinek was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, which “got progressively worse” after he returned to Canada, according to his brother Henry. The last few years, which included several back operations, were tougher still.

Mr. Jelinek was inducted into Canada’s Sports Hall of Fame in 1962 and Skate Canada’s Hall of Fame in 1994. He was honoured by the Czech government with the Medal of Merit for Diplomacy in 2024.

Mr. Jelinek leaves his wife, Leata; sons, Jamie and Misha; sister, Maria; and brothers, Richard and Henry.

stories.title: Generic over-the-counter pain reliever recalled due to ‘foreign material’
stories.summary: A generic over-the-counter pain reliever sold in pharmacies across Canada is being recalled due to what the manufacturer says is the presence of “foreign material.” Teva Canada Limited says one lot of Novo-Gesic Forte 500 mg acetaminophen tablets May contain the potential presence of phenolic resin or epoxy which, if ingested, May cause injury to […]
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Posted September 10, 2026 5:49 pm.

A generic over-the-counter pain reliever sold in pharmacies across Canada is being recalled due to what the manufacturer says is the presence of “foreign material.”

Teva Canada Limited says one lot of Novo-Gesic Forte 500 mg acetaminophen tablets May contain the potential presence of phenolic resin or epoxy which, if ingested, May cause injury to the digestive system.

The affected product, bearing the Lot #100083040 and an expiry date of January 31, 2029, was supplied to pharmacies in 1,000-count bottles and was dispensed to patients in smaller quantities, according to the drug maker.

“Immediately stop using the affected product. Return it to the pharmacy where it was purchased for a replacement and for proper disposal,” Teva Canada said in a release distributed by Health Canada.

While there have been no reports of anyone being negatively affected by taking the product, officials say you should consult your healthcare practitioner if you have used the affected product and have concerns about your health.

stories.title: Community pushback fails to halt Sarnia Road development at city committee - CBC.CA
stories.summary: Despite heavy pushback from neighbours, an eight-storey, 204-unit development on Sarnia Road has been approved by a City of London committee. It now heads to council for a final vote.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Despite heavy pushback from neighbours, an eight-storey, 204-unit development on Sarnia Road has been approved by a City of London committee. It now heads to council for a final vote.
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 5:34 PM EDT | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
A concept drawing of the proposed eight-storey development on Sarnia Road approved by the Planning and Environment Committee on Wednesday.(Zelinka Priamo)
Despite heavy pushback from neighbours, an eight-storey, 204-unit development on Sarnia Road has been approved by a City of London committee.

The planning application by Kimko Inc. and a numbered company, both located in the Greater Toronto Area, sought to add an additional two storeys to a previously approved plan for a six-storey, 150-unit development at 299-307 Sarnia Road.

Eleven community members spoke against the development at Wednesday's meeting of the Planning and Environment Committee and 13 submitted letters opposing it, but they were unable to sway the committee.
"I don't think their concerns are being taken seriously," said the area's councillor, Sam Trosow, who spoke at the committee meeting but did not get a vote. "It bothers me a lot"
Residents have been "acting in good faith" to work with the developer to find a compromise, he added, but "no sooner do they compromise at six (storeys), the developer is back for eight."
8 storeys a 'bridge too far' for some neighbours of Sarnia Road development
CBC News was unable to reach the owner of the property, which property records list as owned by an Ontario corporation with a mailing address in Markham headed up by David Ho.
In the end, four out of five committee members voted to accept a city staff recommendation to approve the development. Council will now get the final say on September 22.
Trosow said he will be voting against the project and encouraging his colleagues to do the same.

City staff did flag concerns with the development, including local sewer capacity and the building's "institutional appearance," which they recommended be modified to blend with the "residential character" of the area. The project would be placed on hold until necessary upgrades are made.
But community concerns also focused on increased traffic, lack of parking, noise impacts and removal of trees.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who voted in favour of the project, said while he appreciates those concerns, staff's recommendation for approval was clear, and the project follows all zoning and height rules.

"As councillors, we don't get to say 'well, the neighborhood doesn't like it even though it fits the zoning, so we're going to say no,'" he said. "We have to follow the zoning regulations and we have to follow the provincial Planning Act regulations."
The area is in an urban corridor, close to Western University, he added, which is exactly where London can expect to see changes like this.

stories.title: Outlaw biker loses appeal to keep horse-racing licence
stories.summary: The tribunal cited Stewart McQueen’s Outlaws membership and the club’s rules against co-operating with police in upholding the decision.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
A tribunal has upheld a decision to not renew a horse-racing licence for a Southwestern Ontario man because of his membership in the Outlaws Motorcycle Club and his involvement in a violent clash in Sarnia last summer.

Stewart McQueen filed an appeal with Tribunals Ontario after the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, the provincial regulator of the horse-racing industry, denied his application to renew his horseperson licence.

Adjudicator Bruce Stanton cited McQueen’s membership in what he found to be a one-per cent motorcycle club – a term used to distinguish outlaw biker clubs from law-abiding motorcycle enthusiasts – and the Outlaws’ rule barring members from co-operating with police in his decision to deny the appeal.

“I accept that the appellant has no interest in involving himself with criminal activities but his association with an organization that literally wears its ‘not law abiding’ identity on its sleeve, whose members have been involved in serious crimes, and which forbids co-operation with law enforcement, is incompatible with holding a licence for which the holder must be depended on to uphold the law and act with integrity, honesty and in the public interest,” Stanton wrote in his decision released last month.

“Permitting a person affiliated with the OMC (outlaw motorcycle club) to have a horseperson licence would undermine confidence in the integrity of the horse racing industry, an industry that . . . is already vulnerable to the influence of criminal organizations.”

Neither the Outlaws nor Gerald Hodgins, a paralegal who represented McQueen, immediately responded to a request for comment.

Advertisement 1Story continues below

The commission requires anyone involved in standardbred, thoroughbred or quarter horse racing to obtain a horseperson licence and a secondary licence in a category such as driver, owner or exercise person.

McQueen, who has no criminal record, testified he has been involved in the racing industry from a young age and has brought family members back into the sport. He said he spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to support the industry.

He also admitted to being full-patch member of the Sarnia chapter of the Outlaws, the second-largest outlaw motorcycle club in the world, but said he joined for the brotherhood, drinking and events. McQueen claimed the Outlaws do not condone criminal behaviour and do not receive the proceeds of crime.

The commission contacted McQueen on Aug. 26, 2025, after learning Sarnia police had recently charged him. McQueen confirmed the charges were laid, but didn’t provide any additional details, saying he was presumed innocent and was in good standing with the regulator.

McQueen, 44, and a 66-year-old man were charged with assault, causing a disturbance and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence following a fight outside a grocery story that injured a 54-year-old man on Aug. 8, 2025, Sarnia police said at the time.

OPP Det. Steve Gray of the equine drug unit, which works with the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, drew on a Sarnia police officer’s synopsis of the fight to testify about the clash.

A full-patch member of the Outlaws, identified only as A.S., confronted a man wearing a Hells Angels support shirt while he was walking on Exmouth Street, the officer testified. A.S. reached out to McQueen, a probationary member of the club at the time, who arrived on his motorcycle, the officer said.

Outlaw motorcycle clubs have strict rules that only allow members to wear clothing featuring the club’s names or logos, but anyone can buy the clubs’ support gear that typically uses an acronym or numbers representing a club’s initials.

McQueen punched the man wearing the support shirt multiple times and put him in a headlock, while A.S. also struck the man as several people watched, the officer testified. The men left before police officers arrived, the officer said.

But McQueen said he acted in self-defence after he stopped to speak with a man who was yelling obscenities at him. When asked why he didn’t provide police with his version of events, he responded: “I was not asked to provide a statement.”

Court records show all of the charges against McQueen and the 66-year-old man were later withdrawn at the request of the Crown.

Stanton noted the charges didn’t result in a conviction and the police account was based on witness testimony, but he said “the incident supports the reasonable grounds to believe that the appellant will not act in accordance with the law and in the public interest.”

The “melee is indicative of the character and culture” of outlaw motorcycle clubs and shows how rivalries can lead to violence, and probationary members are compelled to act when called upon by full patch members,” Stanton said.

The longtime rivalry between the Outlaws and the Hells Angels – the dominant club in Southwestern Ontario, with chapters in London and Windsor – has led to bloody clashes in the past and the OPP-led biker enforcement unit has warned the public not to buy or wear biker support gear.

Stanton also cited a landmark 2014 decision by the Ontario Court of Appeal involving London strip club owner Robert Barletta, who told the Alcohol and Gaming Commission at a hearing he was a Hells Angels member and a past president of the club’s London chapter.

While the court noted Barletta had no a hearing criminal record, it rejected his appeal of a Tribunals Ontario decision to revoke his liquor licence for Famous Flesh Gordon’s, a strip club on Dundas Street, because of his ties to outlaw motorcycle clubs.

stories.title: Charges not laid against RCMP officer who broke woman’s arm in Saskatchewan
stories.summary: Despite finding that a Melfort RCMP officer used excessive force when they broke a woman's arm during her arrest, Saskatchewan's police watchdog opted not to lay charges.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s police watchdog will not lay charges against an RCMP officer who broke a woman’s arm during her arrest.

On July 2, 2025, a 38-year-old woman was leaving Melfort Hospital against the advice of her medical team after a mental health stay. She was said to be wandering through the facility’s parking lot in a hospital gown, which prompted staff to call the police that afternoon, according to the Saskatchewan Serious Incident Response Team (Sirt).

One of the two responding Melfort RCMP officers informed her she was being taken into custody in accordance with the Mental Health Services Act. At that point, Sirt said an altercation began between the two , which escalated after she knocked the officer’s hat off while running away.

“A confrontation occurred between the subject officer and the affected person (the woman), which culminated in a struggle on the ground. During that struggle, force was used on the affected person, which resulted in a fractured right humerus,” according to the team’s investigative summary.

Sirt members interviewed two police officers, including the arresting officer. They also spoke with the hospital staff member that called police, the person who took the woman to the hospital and a patient who witnessed the incident in the hospital parking lot, as well as the women herself.

The police watchdog said it consensually reviewed her medical records.

“Those records revealed that during the incident, the affected person (the woman) sustained a spiral distal fracture of the right humeral shaft and, upon admission to hospital, screened positive for various substances, including cocaine and methamphetamine,” Sirt’s report reads.

While the officer was within their rights to arrest her, the police watchdog concluded that excessive levels of force were used.

“When considering both the observable decrease in the affected person’s level of resistance, as evidenced by twice offering her hand, and the level of anger displayed by the subject officer through his words and demeanour, both the level of force and the motivation underlying the application of force appear to fall outside the legal protections provided to police,” Sirt said.

In a statement to Global News, Saskatchewan’s justice ministry said charges were not authorized because Public Prosecutions felt the officer’s charges could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt in court.

“Before proceeding with a case, Public Prosecutions must measure it against a higher standard than ‘reasonable ground to believe.’ There must be a reasonable likelihood of conviction and a criminal prosecution must be in the public interest,” the statement reads.

It said after the prosecution did not believe the charges could be proven to that extent, meaning there was no reasonable chance of conviction.

“A confrontation occurred between the subject officer and the affected person (the woman), which culminated in a struggle on the ground. During that struggle, force was used on the affected person, which resulted in a fractured right humerus,” according to the team’s investigative summary.

Sirt members interviewed two police officers, including the arresting officer. They also spoke with the hospital staff member that called police, the person who took the woman to the hospital and a patient who witnessed the incident in the hospital parking lot, as well as the women herself.
The police watchdog said it consensually reviewed her medical records.

“Those records revealed that during the incident, the affected person (the woman) sustained a spiral distal fracture of the right humeral shaft and, upon admission to hospital, screened positive for various substances, including cocaine and methamphetamine,” Sirt’s report reads.
While the officer was within their rights to arrest her, the police watchdog concluded that excessive levels of force were used.

“When considering both the observable decrease in the affected person’s level of resistance, as evidenced by twice offering her hand, and the level of anger displayed by the subject officer through his words and demeanour, both the level of force and the motivation underlying the application of force appear to fall outside the legal protections provided to police,” Sirt said.

In a statement to Global News, Saskatchewan’s justice ministry said charges were not authorized because Public Prosecutions felt the officer’s charges could not be proven beyond a reasonable doubt in court.

“Before proceeding with a case, Public Prosecutions must measure it against a higher standard than ‘reasonable ground to believe.’ There must be a reasonable likelihood of conviction and a criminal prosecution must be in the public interest,” the statement reads.
It said after the prosecution did not believe the charges could be proven to that extent, meaning there was no reasonable chance of conviction.

stories.title: From concept to reality: Monument to the fallen emerges in London’s Springbank Park
stories.summary: A new monument to the fallen and those who served is taking shape in Springbank Park.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A new monument to the fallen and those who served is taking shape in Springbank Park.

The first sections of the Byron Springbank Veterans Memorial were carefully placed on Thursday.

The London senior is overwhelmed to see it take shape.

“Never let your dreams die,” he told a CTV News camera proudly.

Mantz, a long-serving padre to surviving Korean War veterans in London, worked with a local South Korean-born designer on the project.

For her, the concept is simple.

“About life and death and the sacrifices for other people,” said Kyung (Kay) Jang.

The sacrifice made by members of the armed forces in conflict and in peace is represented by what will eventually become 14 separate figures of men and women. Each will be presented alongside a QR code offering passersby insight into the monument’s meaning.

“And when you understand what is behind the sacrifice of our veterans, it’s their love for this country. Their love for us, love for the people that weren’t even born yet,” explained Mantz.

It’s hoped the monument’s prominent pathway location encourages engagement, according to Barry Murphy, a project consultant.

“The pedestrian traffic that comes through Springbank Park in this location, it’s huge pedestrian counts, that makes it paramount in its location from an educational standpoint and a view standpoint.”

The monument, which will be officially dedicated on Oct. 3, will also serve as the new home for the Byron Legion Remembrance Day ceremony.

Branch 553 is among the many groups, organizations and businesses that contributed to its creation.

The fundraising campaign set at well over $400,000 was exceeded.

The additional funds will go towards new features and ongoing maintenance of a site that more than a decade ago was just a concept.
