stories.title: Ontario announces 40,000 new seats at universities and colleges, with focus on practical job training
stories.summary: Enhancement of Stem, health care, teaching and trades programs comes at critical moment for local businesses and the higher-education sector
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The Ontario government has reinforced its preference for practical job training over the liberal arts by announcing that 40,000 new seats at the province’s universities and colleges will go to Stem, health care, teaching and trades programs.

Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, said Thursday that new funding for postsecondary education – first announced in February – would be geared toward meeting the labour needs of local businesses, many of which are fighting to survive the Canada-U.S. trade war.

The province set aside $1.7-billion to add more than 70,000 spaces at publicly funded colleges and universities, 40,000 of which were allocated through a new process. Schools had to confer with local industries to identify in-demand careers, then make proposals to the ministry over the summer explaining why particular fields of study deserved more seats.

“We know what Hamilton needs is different than what Thunder Bay needs, or what Belleville needs, or what Sarnia needs,” Mr. Quinn said at a news conference at Hamilton’s McMaster University. “This investment is not growth for the sake of growth. It is a targeted, strategic investment in our workers, our businesses and our economies.”

Mr. Quinn made this latest announcement at a critical moment for the higher-education sector. Many Canadian postsecondary institutions are still trying to recover from Ottawa’s decision in 2024 to cut the number of visas for international students. Their high tuition fees had become critical sources of funding, especially for public and private colleges.

The Ontario government responded in February by lifting a long-standing tuition freeze, promising $6.4-billion in new funding for the sector over four years and shifting the Ontario Student Assistance Program away from non-repayable grants toward more repayable loans. The $1.7-billion for 70,000 new seats is part of that $6.4-billion commitment.

At the same time, universities and colleges are grappling with how to prepare the next generation for a job market that could be fundamentally changed by artificial intelligence. Premier Doug Ford acknowledged the game-changing potential of the technology by adding an associate minister of AI adoption to his cabinet in a shuffle unveiled Thursday.

Some observers argue the economy could be better served by more graduates with degrees in the humanities, social sciences and other liberal-arts disciplines, because they learn critical-thinking skills that set them apart from bots and machines.

“University graduates often don’t even work in jobs that seem to resemble the programs they graduate from,” said Rob Kristofferson, a labour market historian at Wilfrid Laurier University and president of the Ontario Confederation of University Faculty Associations.

“It’s because they learn all sorts of transferable skills in those programs,” Prof. Kristofferson said, adding that this applies to humanities and social sciences as well as science, technology, engineering and math (or Stem) programs. That kind of adaptability will be especially important in the face of AI, he said.

Mr. Quinn and the ministry released only high-level information Thursday on the new seat allocations. Of the more than 70,000 newly funded spaces, 40,200 are in Stem programs, 16,100 are in health care programs, 7,900 are in education, 3,800 are in trades and 3,000 are in other “labour market-driven” programs.

Details were otherwise thin. The minister didn’t identify any specific schools or programs that garnered new seats other than McMaster, where the announcement was held. The Hamilton university is receiving $90-million to fund 2,769 new seats starting this academic year.

Seat allocations for other colleges and universities will be released in the coming weeks. The allocation for the initial 30,000 seats was announced back in May.

McMaster president and vice-chancellor Susan Tighe said in an interview after the news conference that her school expects details from the ministry very soon about which programs garnered the more than 2,700 new spots.

She said she thinks most will be in health care and Stem, and she singled out nuclear medicine, nuclear energy and training for physician assistants as McMaster programs that could be on the list.

“We’re not in the business of being everything to everyone, but what we do, we want to be world-class and do it well,” Prof. Tighe said.

The Council of Ontario Universities and Colleges Ontario, each speaking on behalf of their sectors, welcomed news of the new seats.

stories.title: Canada’s army overhaul aims to be ‘more agile, lethal’ amid threats
stories.summary: CFB Edmonton will now be home to the 1st Canadian Division — the main force responsible for deploying large-scale combat operations and responding to crises at home and abroad.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
The Canadian Army is making one of the biggest structure changes in its history, shifting from four divisions based on geography to three that are built around specific purposes.

“Our structure, our equipment and the way we do business had to change,” said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the new 1st Canadian Division, in an interview with Global News.

“This is not an exercise in restructuring the deck chairs,” he added in comments to The Canadian Press.

“We’re doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada."

CFB Edmonton held a signing ceremony and parade on Thursday to stand up the 1st Canadian Division , which will be headquartered in Edmonton and will serve as the main force responsible for deploying on large-scale combat operations and responding to crises.

“We’re designed to be the expeditionary war-fighting division — whether that’s overseas or in Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're designed to be the expeditionary war-fighting division — whether that's overseas or in Canada."

Before Thursday’s reorganization, the army had a structure where every type of unit in the west, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic regions were in geographical division, responsible for everything that happened within its area.

Rutland said that system worked during Canada’s peacekeeping years, the war in Afghanistan and the earlier years of Canada sending battalions of 500 to 1,000 troops to Latvia as part of Nato deterrence and defence measures across the Euro-Atlantic region.

But, the global threat environment has changed and he said the military recognized the army it had is not the army it needs.

Rutland said the world is returning to large-scale combat operations like Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, involving the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers.

“You need to be able to put up what we called a fighting division — which means you can sense and shoot out to 100 kilometres, you can control multiple brigades in close combat, and you can sustain all that over hundreds of kilometres of lines communication,” Rutland said. “You also have to be able to integrate capabilities like cyber, space, air.”

At the same time, Canada faces perils both within and abroad.

Rutland gave examples like threats to Canada’s critical infrastructure and climate change — the latter which experts have said is fuelling more natural disasters like fires and floods, leading to more requests for military aid within provinces.

The military is also mindful of air and ballistic missile threats, he said, and of protecting Arctic sovereignty.

“We’re moving to a more functional, efficient structure in order to face the threats that are more prevalent today.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're moving to a more functional, efficient structure in order to face the threats that are more prevalent today."

The three new function-based divisions with their own specific mandates are now: 1st Canadian Division (the Manoeuvre Division, based in Edmonton), 2nd Canadian Division (the Defence of Canada Division, based in Montreal), and the Canadian Army Support Division, based in Kingston.

Headquartered at the Edmonton Garrison , the 1st Canadian Division will bring many capabilities together under one roof, such as tanks and other armour, artillery, light infantry, paratroopers and engineers.

“There’s going to be more people moving into Edmonton, more infrastructure,” Rutland said, explaining over the next few years, about 1,000 more soldiers will be based at CFB Edmonton.

“That also means 1,000 — sometimes — families, places to live, et cetera.

“It has a really high economic impact.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It has a really high economic impact."

Rutland said says it’s a big administrative change that required a lot of work over the past year.

“It’ll be phased over the coming years, but certainly Edmonton is a place that, for the Canadian Army, is going to grow.”

The base in Edmonton has a long history of leading the charge, the major general said.

“CFB Edmonton has been the launching pad for operations for decades, quite frankly, from Cold War units into launching troops into places like Bosnia, former Yugoslavia. First army troops that went into Afghanistan came from this base. First troops that were into Latvia came from this space.

“We like to think that we’re first out the door.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We like to think that we're first out the door."

Western Canada — Alberta in particular — has extensive training areas and established infrastructure that Rutland said is almost unmatched in the rest of Nato. More troops will also be headed to the province’s three other military bases.

“CFB Edmonton, CFB Wainwright, Cold Lake, Suffield — huge amount of land and infrastructure that the Canadian Armed Forces relies on right here in Alberta. So it’s not just Edmonton that’s gonna feel the effects of all this.”

The division is assuming command of the three regular Canadian Mechanized Brigade Groups in Edmonton, Petawawa, Ont., and Valcartier, Que.

The incoming brigades will remain in their current locations across Canada, but will now report to the Edmonton division headquarters.

Four new formations are now part of the 1st Canadian Division:

3rd Canadian Light Infantry Regiment : A reassignment of existing units, staffed with high‑readiness forces for rapid crisis and Arctic responses.

1st Canadian Artillery Brigade : Tasked with centralizing and coordinating the Division’s artillery in support in the deep fight, shaping the battlefield and setting the conditions for manoeuvre formations to fight and win

1st Canadian Sustainment Brigade : manage logistics depth in prolonged, high‑intensity operations

10th Signal Regiment : brings modern situational awareness and communications across all formations together under the 1st Canadian Division, connecting the headquarters, manoeuvre brigades, and supporting units into a single, coordinated fight

The military said the new arrangement retains the army’s coast‑to‑coast footprint while streamlining the chain of command structure. There will be new patch colours as part of the reorganization.

“For the 1st Division, we’re going back to what we call the ‘old red patch’ which we used in World War I and World War II,” Rutland said.

The 1st Canadian Division dates to 1915 and the First World War battles, including Vimy Ridge. For the past 16 years, the 1st Canadian Division was headquartered in Kingston, Ont.

The standing up of the 1st Canadian Division means the 3rd Canadian Division — which also traces its history to the First World War — is being retired to the supplementary Order of Battle, which happens when a regiment is powered down but continues to exist on paper in case it needs to be returned to duty.

“Our structure, our equipment and the way we do business had to change,” said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the new 1st Canadian Division, in an interview with Global News.
“This is not an exercise in restructuring the deck chairs,” he added in comments to The Canadian Press.

“We’re doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada."

CFB Edmonton held a signing ceremony and parade on Thursday to stand up the 1st Canadian Division , which will be headquartered in Edmonton and will serve as the main force responsible for deploying on large-scale combat operations and responding to crises.

“We’re designed to be the expeditionary war-fighting division — whether that’s overseas or in Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're designed to be the expeditionary war-fighting division — whether that's overseas or in Canada."

Before Thursday’s reorganization, the army had a structure where every type of unit in the west, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic regions were in geographical division, responsible for everything that happened within its area.

Rutland said that system worked during Canada’s peacekeeping years, the war in Afghanistan and the earlier years of Canada sending battalions of 500 to 1,000 troops to Latvia as part of Nato deterrence and defence measures across the Euro-Atlantic region.
But, the global threat environment has changed and he said the military recognized the army it had is not the army it needs.
Rutland said the world is returning to large-scale combat operations like Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, involving the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers.

“You need to be able to put up what we called a fighting division — which means you can sense and shoot out to 100 kilometres, you can control multiple brigades in close combat, and you can sustain all that over hundreds of kilometres of lines communication,” Rutland said. “You also have to be able to integrate capabilities like cyber, space, air.”
At the same time, Canada faces perils both within and abroad.

Rutland gave examples like threats to Canada’s critical infrastructure and climate change — the latter which experts have said is fuelling more natural disasters like fires and floods, leading to more requests for military aid within provinces.
The military is also mindful of air and ballistic missile threats, he said, and of protecting Arctic sovereignty.

“We’re moving to a more functional, efficient structure in order to face the threats that are more prevalent today.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're moving to a more functional, efficient structure in order to face the threats that are more prevalent today."

“That also means 1,000 — sometimes — families, places to live, et cetera.

stories.title: Canada, U.S. continue to work together despite trade war, Carney says
stories.summary: Two leaders spoke about war in Iran and ‘other global developments,’ Prime Minister says
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government is still studying whether to retaliate against the latest countermeasures from the United States in its trade war with Canada, but played down the severity of the most recent salvo from Washington.

“We’re looking closely at the measures that the Americans have just recently announced,” he told reporters in Banff, where his cabinet is holding a two-day retreat that wraps up on Friday.

Mr. Carney said he realized that for affected companies and sectors the reprisals are significant, but he added that in the context of previous retaliation taken by the U.S., “these are relatively modest measures and so we take that into context.”

Earlier this week, Canada’s former ambassador to the U.S. Kirsten Hillman told The Globe and Mail in an interview that she expected it would be months before Ottawa and Washington resume formal talks. Canada walked away from negotiations in August and Mr. Carney has said the U.S. trade proposals would “destroy” large Canadian industries, including automobiles, steel and aluminum.

Mr. Carney, during a separate press conference Thursday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said he maintains regular contact with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the trade conflict. He said recent talks have focused on matters related to Ukraine and Iran.

“We continue to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize,” he said.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump issued a sweeping ban on imports of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products as Washington ratcheted up pressure in response to Ottawa’s latest countertariffs, heightening a trade war that has been ramping up since Canada walked away from the negotiating table last month.

In addition, Washington adjusted a number of the levies it imposed last month using Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 – adding 110 new items to the list, while removing a handful of others.

Mr. Trump also said he would order the U.S. General Services Administration to remove Canadian products from its Multiple Award Schedule program, which government agencies use to purchase things such as information technology and office supplies – a blow to companies selling from Canada.

These measures are expected to come into effect in the coming weeks.

Asked if the fact there is a delay before these new import bans take effect means the U.S. is leaving an option for talks to resume, the Prime Minister said it’s up to Washington to say. “It’s really for the Americans to answer the question, but I wouldn’t overinterpret a delay, if you will, or a lag,” he said.

“We’re always ready to sit down in a professional way to negotiate. We think there is a mutually beneficial deal possible that respects our sovereignty and is in the interest of both countries.”

Separately, in New York, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre spoke out in support of tariff-free trade with the U.S. but declined to criticize Mr. Carney’s handling of the trade dispute when asked by Cnbc. “Look, I’m not going to attack my Prime Minister on foreign soil,” he told the network Thursday. “It’s just not something I am going to do.”

He said the U.S. started this war.

“The administration hit us with tariffs first, and everything escalated thereafter.”

Mr. Poilievre told Cnbc that Canadians are feeling wounded over how their country ended up as a major target for Mr. Trump.

“We’re kind of confused as to how it is suddenly that Canada ended up in the crosshairs.”

He said removing tariffs will help Americans. “We can save money and jobs for both our people if we get back to two-way tariff-free trade. That will bring down the cost of living for Americans. It will grow pay cheques on both sides of the border.”

Ian Bremmer, president of the research and consulting firm Eurasia Group, was among the people briefing Mr. Carney’s cabinet retreat. Ahead of those meetings, Mr. Bremmer told reporters that the federal government needs to prepare for tariffs to be a permanent part of the trade relationship with the U.S. – no matter who is in the White House.

“There’s almost no one in Washington that wants to stop taking in income from tariffs,” he said. “The United States is not going to be the architect or the proponent of a global free trading system, but rather we’re going to see more industrial policies, more subsidies, more tariffs.”

Mr. Bremmer said Ottawa needs to separate out the permanent changes in U.S. policy that Mr. Trump has spearheaded and the President’s “unpredictability and unreliability.”

“I do not believe it will ever come back to what it was, but I also think there’s a great deal of repair that can and will be done.”

Mr. Bremmer has many ties to Mr. Carney and his advisers, and the Prime Minister’s wife, Diana Fox Carney, works for the Eurasia Group. Mr. Bremmer said he was not paid to attend the retreat and does not do any lobbying work.

stories.title: Impresario Craig Martin mounted tribute shows for a generation raised on LPS
stories.summary: Champion of the electric sounds of his youth founded Classic Albums Live, in which musicians lovingly replicate records such as Dark Side of the Moon, cut by cut and note for note
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Rip this joint, going to save your soul

’Round and ‘round and ‘round we go

Craig Martin would tell the story about an aha moment that happened while he was fronting the Midnight Ramblers, his Rolling Stones cover band. While driving back to Toronto from a gig in Montreal, the Stones’ Rocks Off , the first song on the 1972 album Exile on Main St ., came on the radio. When it was over, the album surprisingly continued to play on uninterrupted to the second track, Rip This Joint. Was the disc jockey on a smoke break?

Mr. Martin was a child of the Seventies, an era when music fans listened to full album sides, whether on vinyl or cassette. He suggested to his bandmates that they play a complete side of Exile for their next show.

That was just the start. In 2003, Mr. Martin founded Classic Albums Live, a Toronto-based Canadian success story that now employs approximately 100 musicians to perform entire classic-rock albums, cut by cut and note for note, in venues across North America (particularly Florida) and some in Britain.

On any given night, Classic Albums Live might present Supertramp’s Breakfast in America at the Confederation Centre of the Arts in Charlottetown, Led Zeppelin II at Ruth Eckerd Hall in Clearwater, Fla., and a Stones album somewhere else.

Mr. Martin conceived the concerts as rock ’n’ roll recitals, not theatrical tribute presentations. “No cheesy costumes, no bad impersonations,” as he explained it. “Just the purity of the music. That’s all you need.”

Mr. Martin, a musician, an entrepreneur and a dogged champion of the electric sounds of his youth, died of cancer on Aug. 23, in Toronto. He was 64.

The achievement of his concept can be attributed to the widespread fandom of a rock music canon that originated in a time when kids grew up with largely the same pop culture references. The generation who listened to “LPS” on “hi-fi” stereos now purchase tickets for concerts to revisit their melodic past in the cushy seats of theatres and music halls.

“No matter how good or bad the music was when we were 16 years old, we’re connected to it,” said music historian Bob Wegner, a former member of the Classic Live Albums rotating roster of musicians. “But in the case of classic rock music, it’s objectively good.”

While much of the Classic Albums Live repertoire comes from the 1960s and 70s, albums such as Madonna: The Immaculate Collection , Van Halen’s 1984 and U2’s Achtung Baby from 1991 are presented as well.

“I sell nostalgia, and I am not ashamed of it,” Mr. Martin told the Financial Post in 2023. “Music takes us back to the prime of our lives and, for a lot of us, those memories can be pretty golden.”

Mr. Martin was a stickler for recreating memories meticulously, right down to the cash register effects from Pink Floyd’s The Dark Side of the Moon and the stage banter of the Beatles when presenting the semi-live Let It Be .

“It’s based on a love and respect of the music, and Craig demanded a great deal from his musicians,” said musicologist Mike Daley, part of the Classic Albums Live stable of performers from 2003 to 2009. “The workload could be crushing if you were a core member of his troupe.”

Classic Albums Live began at Toronto’s Phoenix Concert Theatre, a general admission club with no seats, where Mr. Martin presented a monthly series. The first concert was The Dark Side of the Moon .

Guitarist Des Leahy was part of that first show. He remembered the experience as nerve-racking: “I wondered if people would show up. But Craig told me, ‘You gotta play a card.’ And the club filled up. He was on to something.”

Though the concert series at the Phoenix was quickly successful, eventually the presentations were shifted to seated venues.

“We realized the people who were coming out to the shows were an older crowd who didn’t want to stand,” said Mr. Martin’s sister, Tracy Martin, referring to baby boomers and Gen-Xers. “When we moved to the soft-seaters, things really took off.”

Toronto’s Massey Hall regularly hosts Classic Albums Live. Typically, the venue, which welcomed Enrico Caruso, Joni Mitchell, Miles Davis and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, does not book what some might call a cover band. Classic Albums Live is an exception.

“Their attention to detail and level of musicianship is impressive, and a big part of what distinguishes them,” said Jesse Kumagai, president and CEO of Massey Hall and Roy Thomson Hall. “If the recording had three guitars all playing the same part, you’ll see three guitarists on stage. No shortcuts are taken.”

Mr. Martin had a deep reverence for the music he presented. He believed in the Beatles as others might admire Beethoven and Bach and he saw his operation as comparable to the TSO. “They play cover music, we play cover music,” he reasoned.

Many of the albums covered were originally recorded by artists who are no longer active. And while legacy acts such as the Eagles still perform live, the prices charged to see them are prohibitively high for many fans. Where rock legends AC/DC fill stadiums, Classic Albums Live offers the group’s iconic Back in Black record in intimate, affordable settings.

“Craig turned our collective passion for the music into something that brings us closer together,” Mr. Kumagai said, “which is something very special and desperately needed in today’s world.”

Craig Ray Martin was born Sept. 2, 1961, in Toronto. He was one of two children born to Maureen Martin (née Flower) and Ray Rade Martin. They both worked in advertising promotion.

He attended Wexford Collegiate Institute (now known as Wexford Collegiate School for the Arts) in Scarborough. Like many teenaged boys in the 1970s, he was a fan of Mad magazine and loud guitars.

“It was wood-paneled basements and all that, and if you didn’t have a Rush record or Kiss or Led Zeppelin, they’d throw you right out of Scarborough,” said Classic Albums Live drummer Rick Vatour, who met Mr. Martin in Grade 9.

Mr. Vatour first saw Mr. Martin’s Rolling Stones cover band at a motor inn in Richmond Hill, Ont. “He was a leader even back then. He could convince an audience they were having the greatest night of their life.”

Mr. Martin spent time with a celebrity tribute-act company, imitating Mick Jagger and others in glossy productions. He saw a future in presenting albums live, but without the Vegas-style glam and shenanigans. His vision was specific and unyielding.

“The idea was to present the albums as whole works, and not to pander to the audience members who just wanted to hear the hits,” Mr. Daley said. “After the intermission we would play what were called ‘outros,’ which were songs not on the featured album. Sometimes they were hits, sometimes obscurities. Craig pleased himself first and didn’t try to guess what the audience wanted. I think that was the right decision artistically.”

He was involved in every area of the organization he ran as a family business, whether handling the sound checks and hiring musicians or playing rhythm guitar for the Creedence Clearwater Revival shows and singing Bruce Springsteen’s Born to Run album.

Mr. Martin was complicated and could be challenging to interact with. “When you worked for him, you had to have a bit of a thick skin,” said Ronnie Littlejohn, a Toronto singer and Jazz.FM91 radio host. “He was going to tell you how it is. But it made you a better musician.”

Mr. Littlejohn credits Mr. Martin for giving him his career highlight. He was hired to sing Van Morrison’s part in the presentation of the Band’s star-studded live album The Last Waltz .

“Other than my honeymoon, singing Van’s Caravan at Massey Hall was the greatest four minutes of my life,” Mr. Littlejohn recalled. “It was magical.”

In 2016, Mr. Martin wrote, directed and produced GIG , a musical about the music industry’s grittier side. It was mounted at Toronto’s Panasonic Theatre (now the CAA Theatre) for a seven-show run. Though it was a fictional rock ’n’ roll tale, Mr. Martin explained that it was, in a sense, autobiographical.

“I’ve played the Hells Angels’ clubhouse in Sherbrooke, Que.,” he told the Toronto Star. “I’ve played maximum security prisons. I’ve talked my way out of some very difficult border situations. I’ve walked offstage mid-show. I’ve blown record deals. I’ve turned down a reality TV show. I’ve loaded pinball machines into the van in lieu of payment.”

And now he had a musical that wasn’t particularly successful. “It’s misshapen and cringe-worthy,” Samantha Wu wrote for Mooney on Theatre.

Heartbreak struck his family when Lucas Martin, one of two sons, died of cancer four days after Christmas in 2016. He was 18 years old. Mr. Martin took up painting after his boy was diagnosed with an aggressive form of the disease. His first canvas was a box for a bulletin board he purchased to keep track of all the required medications.

He often gave away the paintings, with a request that a donation be made to Canadian Cancer Society.

“I don’t know where I’d be without painting,” he told the Financial Post. “With Lucas’s passing, you kind of get to the point where nothing can get you now. It is like a gift he left behind − you’ve been to the abyss, you have looked in − and so if a flight gets cancelled, or there is a problem with the road venue, who gives a crap.”

Mr. Martin leaves his mother, Maureen Martin; sister, Tracy Martin; son, Jackson Martin; and ex-wife, Susan Hanley.

On Aug. 28, Classic Albums Live presented Led Zeppelin IV in Houston’s Miller Outdoor Theatre. Mr. Vatour was on drums; Nick Hildyard sang. Both were part of the ensemble which performed the album at the Phoenix Concert Theatre in July, 2003 − one of the first Classic Albums Live concerts.

The Houston show was dedicated to Mr. Martin. One of the extra songs was The Rain Song , an epic, affecting ballad − “Upon us all, a little rain must fall” − performed with a string section. The orchestral numbers were Mr. Martin’s favourites: There could never be too many musicians on stage for him.

“It was an emotional night, but the crowd was very respectful of our feelings,” Mr. Vatour said. “They understood. I believe they got it.”

Following the Classic Albums Live presentation of The Dark Side of the Moon at Massey Hall on Sept. 11, musicians will pay tribute to Mr. Martin by performing some of his favourite songs.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

Guitarist Des Leahy was part of that first show. He remembered the experience as nerve-racking: “I wondered if people would show up. But Craig told me, ‘You gotta play a card.’ And the club filled up. He was on to something.”
Though the concert series at the Phoenix was quickly successful, eventually the presentations were shifted to seated venues.

“We realized the people who were coming out to the shows were an older crowd who didn’t want to stand,” said Mr. Martin’s sister, Tracy Martin, referring to baby boomers and Gen-Xers. “When we moved to the soft-seaters, things really took off.”

Toronto’s Massey Hall regularly hosts Classic Albums Live. Typically, the venue, which welcomed Enrico Caruso, Joni Mitchell, Miles Davis and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, does not book what some might call a cover band. Classic Albums Live is an exception.

“Their attention to detail and level of musicianship is impressive, and a big part of what distinguishes them,” said Jesse Kumagai, president and CEO of Massey Hall and Roy Thomson Hall. “If the recording had three guitars all playing the same part, you’ll see three guitarists on stage. No shortcuts are taken.”

Mr. Martin had a deep reverence for the music he presented. He believed in the Beatles as others might admire Beethoven and Bach and he saw his operation as comparable to the TSO. “They play cover music, we play cover music,” he reasoned.

Many of the albums covered were originally recorded by artists who are no longer active. And while legacy acts such as the Eagles still perform live, the prices charged to see them are prohibitively high for many fans. Where rock legends AC/DC fill stadiums, Classic Albums Live offers the group’s iconic Back in Black record in intimate, affordable settings.
“Craig turned our collective passion for the music into something that brings us closer together,” Mr. Kumagai said, “which is something very special and desperately needed in today’s world.”
Craig Ray Martin was born Sept. 2, 1961, in Toronto. He was one of two children born to Maureen Martin (née Flower) and Ray Rade Martin. They both worked in advertising promotion.
He attended Wexford Collegiate Institute (now known as Wexford Collegiate School for the Arts) in Scarborough. Like many teenaged boys in the 1970s, he was a fan of Mad magazine and loud guitars.

“It was wood-paneled basements and all that, and if you didn’t have a Rush record or Kiss or Led Zeppelin, they’d throw you right out of Scarborough,” said Classic Albums Live drummer Rick Vatour, who met Mr. Martin in Grade 9.

Mr. Vatour first saw Mr. Martin’s Rolling Stones cover band at a motor inn in Richmond Hill, Ont. “He was a leader even back then. He could convince an audience they were having the greatest night of their life.”

Mr. Martin spent time with a celebrity tribute-act company, imitating Mick Jagger and others in glossy productions. He saw a future in presenting albums live, but without the Vegas-style glam and shenanigans. His vision was specific and unyielding.

“The idea was to present the albums as whole works, and not to pander to the audience members who just wanted to hear the hits,” Mr. Daley said. “After the intermission we would play what were called ‘outros,’ which were songs not on the featured album. Sometimes they were hits, sometimes obscurities. Craig pleased himself first and didn’t try to guess what the audience wanted. I think that was the right decision artistically.”

He was involved in every area of the organization he ran as a family business, whether handling the sound checks and hiring musicians or playing rhythm guitar for the Creedence Clearwater Revival shows and singing Bruce Springsteen’s Born to Run album.

Mr. Martin was complicated and could be challenging to interact with. “When you worked for him, you had to have a bit of a thick skin,” said Ronnie Littlejohn, a Toronto singer and Jazz.FM91 radio host. “He was going to tell you how it is. But it made you a better musician.”
Mr. Littlejohn credits Mr. Martin for giving him his career highlight. He was hired to sing Van Morrison’s part in the presentation of the Band’s star-studded live album The Last Waltz .
“Other than my honeymoon, singing Van’s Caravan at Massey Hall was the greatest four minutes of my life,” Mr. Littlejohn recalled. “It was magical.”

In 2016, Mr. Martin wrote, directed and produced GIG , a musical about the music industry’s grittier side. It was mounted at Toronto’s Panasonic Theatre (now the CAA Theatre) for a seven-show run. Though it was a fictional rock ’n’ roll tale, Mr. Martin explained that it was, in a sense, autobiographical.

“I’ve played the Hells Angels’ clubhouse in Sherbrooke, Que.,” he told the Toronto Star. “I’ve played maximum security prisons. I’ve talked my way out of some very difficult border situations. I’ve walked offstage mid-show. I’ve blown record deals. I’ve turned down a reality TV show. I’ve loaded pinball machines into the van in lieu of payment.”
And now he had a musical that wasn’t particularly successful. “It’s misshapen and cringe-worthy,” Samantha Wu wrote for Mooney on Theatre.

Heartbreak struck his family when Lucas Martin, one of two sons, died of cancer four days after Christmas in 2016. He was 18 years old. Mr. Martin took up painting after his boy was diagnosed with an aggressive form of the disease. His first canvas was a box for a bulletin board he purchased to keep track of all the required medications.
He often gave away the paintings, with a request that a donation be made to Canadian Cancer Society.

“I don’t know where I’d be without painting,” he told the Financial Post. “With Lucas’s passing, you kind of get to the point where nothing can get you now. It is like a gift he left behind − you’ve been to the abyss, you have looked in − and so if a flight gets cancelled, or there is a problem with the road venue, who gives a crap.”
Mr. Martin leaves his mother, Maureen Martin; sister, Tracy Martin; son, Jackson Martin; and ex-wife, Susan Hanley.

On Aug. 28, Classic Albums Live presented Led Zeppelin IV in Houston’s Miller Outdoor Theatre. Mr. Vatour was on drums; Nick Hildyard sang. Both were part of the ensemble which performed the album at the Phoenix Concert Theatre in July, 2003 − one of the first Classic Albums Live concerts.

The Houston show was dedicated to Mr. Martin. One of the extra songs was The Rain Song , an epic, affecting ballad − “Upon us all, a little rain must fall” − performed with a string section. The orchestral numbers were Mr. Martin’s favourites: There could never be too many musicians on stage for him.
“It was an emotional night, but the crowd was very respectful of our feelings,” Mr. Vatour said. “They understood. I believe they got it.”
Following the Classic Albums Live presentation of The Dark Side of the Moon at Massey Hall on Sept. 11, musicians will pay tribute to Mr. Martin by performing some of his favourite songs.

stories.title: What could greater cooperation between Canada and the EU look like?
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to address the European Parliament next week as Canada looks to strengthen ties with the continent amid America’s trade war.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney was tight-lipped Thursday when asked whether Canada could seek future membership in the European Union, but reiterated his desire that the country “deepen” ties with the economic and political bloc.

While Canada officially joining the EU has been recently raised in the context of worsening relations with the United States and U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, experts suggest that formal membership is unlikely.

Still, with Carney set to address the European Parliament next week, the prime minister has made it no secret that he wants to see closer economic, security and political ties with European nations.

“We will be looking to use the coming months to explore a deepening of that partnership across a broad range of areas and we’ll have more to say to that (next week) in Strasbourg,” Carney told reporters in Banff, Alta., Thursday, where his cabinet is gathering for a planning session.

Both the Canadian and European sides have been talking up the idea of “deepening” ties for more than a year, largely driven by their shared most important ally — the U.S. — pursuing sharply protectionist trade policies including trade wars and tariffs on broad swathes of the globe, as well as a broader retreat from diplomatic and strategic partnerships with allies.

In June 2025, Canada and the EU laid out a framework for greater cooperation, identifying fostering increased trade and economic security, cooperation on supply chains, and regulatory alignment.

The document also outlined a desire for stronger defence partnerships, collaboration on the “digital transition” and educational exchanges, and shared action on both climate change and other geopolitical crises.

Christian Leuprecht, a professor with the Royal Military College in Montreal, said the EU is the “most obvious partner” if Carney wants to make good on his push to diversify Canada’s trading relationships.

stories.title: United Way Perth-Huron launching lofty 2026 fundraising goal
stories.summary: The United Way of Perth-Huron is raising the bar for fundraising this year, attempting to reach $2,682,720 to help fund the work they do, along with 15 other social agencies in the two counties.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The United Way of Perth-Huron is raising the bar for fundraising this year, attempting to reach $2,682,720 to help fund the work they do, along with 15 other social agencies in the two counties.

“This community is incredibly generous. And every year that I have been a part of this organization, we have either hit or exceeded our goal. And we’re going to do it again,” said United Way Perth-Huron CEO Ryan Erb.

At it’s public launch in Listowel Thursday, United Way supporters not only talked about fundraising, they got their hands dirty, packing kits to be distributed to vulnerable members of the community.

“We’re calling them the First Step kits. They’ll be delivered to vulnerable folks in our community, and they have a range of tools and comfort items in them to assist those folks. Give them a little leg up when they’re feeling a little down or in trouble,” said Todd Kasenberg, Mayor of the Municipality of North Perth, as well as Community Development Manager for the United Way in North Perth.

As mayor, Kasenberg says he’s seen both the need for expanded social services in the Listowel area, and that void being filled by organizations, like the United Way, and others funded by the United Way.

“It is honestly hard as mayor and as a United Way guy to go to bed at night, sometimes realizing there are people out there in -20 temperatures. It is the burden, I think, of an elected official to be thinking about their community, and the needs and the challenges that are faced. And certainly that is a challenge. But we’re trying to turn the story, and we need help from everybody in the community to help us do that,” said Kasenberg.

One of the ways they’re doing that is through United Housing, a new agency within the United Way of Perth-Huron that is actually building affordable housing. 10 units are nearing completion in downtown Listowel, right now.

“Every United Way is local, and we are addressing local needs in ways that government is either choosing not to, or unable to fully do. And so the United Way is a significant supporter of health and social services and services across the age span in our communities, and that’s important to people,” said Kasenberg.

“The needs are growing in our community all the time. Sadly, people are lining up for services and they still can’t get the help they need. So we’ve got to raise more money to operate services in this community,” said Erb.

Last year, the United Way of Perth-Huron raised $2.56 million, exceeding their goal of $2.53 million.

stories.title: Edmonton police charge suspect in Sikh temple screwdriver stabbings
stories.summary: A 27-year-old man faces multiple offences as police investigate whether it was a hate crime
stories.author: Daniela Germano
stories.content:
A man faces multiple offences in a stabbing last month at a Sikh temple in Alberta’s capital, but police said Thursday there’s so far no evidence that the attack was motivated by hate.

Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart of the Edmonton police announced that 27-year-old Austin Sim-Pelletier was charged Friday with assault causing bodily harm, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose and mischief.

“We are still collecting evidence, and we’re still working through it,” Stewart said at a news conference. “But currently, at this time, there wasn’t the evidence to support those (hate crime) charges.”

Sim-Pelletier was arrested Aug. 21, after two worshippers at the Nanaksar Gurdwara Gursikh Temple in northeast Edmonton were stabbed by an intruder with a screwdriver.

The victims, who are 75 and 51, were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries and are still recovering, Stewart said.

A day before the attack, Sim-Pelletier was released from prison for aggravated assault and assault on a peace officer, said police.

Stewart said Sim-Pelletier was supposed to meet with his parole officer, but that didn’t happen and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

Police are still investigating how he got to the gurdwara from where he was dropped off by corrections officers in Edmonton, said Stewart.

“Some of the reasons of how he got there, why he went in, his actions inside, are still part of the ongoing part of our investigation,” Stewart said.

“Right now, there’s nothing to say that he has been up there before.”

Edmonton police have laid charges after two worshippers were stabbed last month with a screwdriver at a Sikh temple.

The Canadian Press

Asked about the delay between the arrest and charges being announced, Stewart said there was less urgency because Sim-Pelletier was quickly returned to prison and there wasn’t a further threat to the public.

“We first want to work with the community and want to work with our victims to ensure that we are providing them the support they need,” Stewart said.

“We also wanted to make sure that we conducted a thorough investigation to get to where we are today.”

On the day of the stabbing, the World Sikh Organization of Canada said there were reports that the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, a sacred scripture, was also attacked.

Stewart said there was no damage to the scripture.

stories.title: 'My life is effectively destroyed': Allison Inquiry exposes twin faces of fight against COVID vaccine policies
stories.summary: Patricia Leidl arrived in Ottawa this week eager to tell a painful story about her reaction to the COVID-19 vaccine.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Despite her experience with the COVID vaccine, Patricia Leidl says she isn't anti-vax

Patricia Leidl testifies at the Allison Inquiry in Ottawa on Sept. 10, 2026. Photo by Blair Gable /Postmedia

Ottawa — Patricia Leidl arrived in Ottawa this week eager to tell a painful story about her reaction to the COVID-19 vaccine that even some of her own friends have questioned.

After an uneventful first shot against the COVID virus, Leidl received a second dose of vaccine on June 10, 2021, just days before she was planning to head off to Vienna for a new job she couldn’t wait to start.

But seven days after that second vaccine, the Salt Spring Island, B.C. resident woke up in pain. Leidl got up and then collapsed. In the ensuing five years, Leidl told the Allison Inquiry into the effects of the COVID vaccines on Thursday, she hasn’t stopped suffering. Her list of conditions and symptoms is lengthy, many of which she says suggest neurological damage and chronic inflammation.

” she told National Post during an interview.

Despite her experience with the COVID vaccine, the former World Health Organization communications employee says she isn’t anti-vax.

Before offering her testimony to the MPs and senators, however, Leidl and dozens of others keen to share their stories of suffering and lost loved ones had to make their way past a lively protest assembled outside Ottawa’s Wellington Building.

The old downtown edifice, normally a site for parliamentary committee meetings and other staid events, became a second home this week for a few dozen protesters. Many believe that the COVID vaccines were part of a government plan to limit individual rights and gain further control and, in contrast to most of those providing testimonials inside, represent a different side of the dissent against the shots and the government’s pandemic policies.

Sporting a red ball cap that reads “Save Canada” with a giant, homemade hypodermic needle strapped across his shoulder, Howard Kwan says Canadians have bought into a massive coverup.

As he protested this week, Kwan said that the federal government worked with the pharmaceutical industry and others to convince Canadians that everybody needed to get the shot.

And since the pandemic faded, the Ottawa resident says, they’ve been trying to justify that effort and to hide the negative effects ever since.

The bigger picture government goal, Kwan says, is to rebuild society “in their own way.”

Kwan and a cohort of about 25 protesters who braved the rain Wednesday are among the thousands of Canadians who believe that the vaccination effort during the pandemic went too far, that the vaccine wasn’t safe, or that it was part of a full-blown government conspiracy.

While some have been galvanized by heated online chat, the Freedom Convoy trucker protests of 2022, and their shared concern about government overreach, these protesters are part of the very visible face of the fight against the government’s pandemic policies.

By contrast, Leidl, a former World Health Organization employee, is still not anti-vax.

A visual artist, writer and international development professional, she was in good health when she got her COVID shots, a non-smoker, light drinker and physically fit.

But in the days following her second shot, everything changed. Her symptoms include central nervous system pain, migraines, bi-lateral tendinopathy, arteriosclerosis, light sensitivity, tinnitus, chronic gastritis, and a heart rhythm problem called tachycardia. She has also lost the use of one of her ears, is in pain if she tries to sit or stand in one place for too long, and worries that she has deteriorating cognitive abilities.

Leidl, 64, said she hasn’t been able to work much during that period — including forfeiting the job in Austria — and has been put in “social exile” by some friends who have questioned her symptoms. She’s also spent about $250,000 over the last five years trying to get well.

For Leidl, unlike Kwan and most of the protesters in downtown Ottawa, her fight isn’t overtly political.She says she resents being labelled a “right-wing wingnut” because she’s suffering from vaccine injuries.

These twin faces of the battle against the government’s pandemic policies, or at least the effects of those policies, May have their differences. But they agree that Ottawa and the provinces should take responsibility for a vaccine that was rushed into millions of arms during a crisis and, to a degree, was mandated.

The vaccines were widely seen at the time as a medical miracle and the key to restoring normalcy after months of lockdowns and other restrictions. Canadians were immunized at record levels and in record time.

But that doesn’t change the fact that thousands of vaccine recipients were hurt — some in very serious ways.

Governments haven’t denied that the vaccines caused health problems, but have been tepid in deciding what to do.

Beyond the fact that a parliamentary committee is listening to experts and victims, Ottawa has also established the Vaccine Impact Assistance Program (Viap), which provides financial support to Canadians who have suffered serious or long-term damage from a vaccine that was approved by Health Canada. The program, which began accepting applications in 2021 and is administered by the Public Health Agency of Canada, doesn’t assess blame, just whether it was likely that somebody was harmed by a vaccine.

Deanna McLeod, a medical researcher and founder of Toronto-based Kaleidoscope Strategies Inc., told this week’s inquiry that doctors’ rules changed during the pandemic so that patients’ health care was guided by the collective good, not that of the individual needs.

“Public health became the (companies’) marketing arm.”

The inquiry, scheduled to hear from its final witnesses on Friday, is largely in listening mode. It has no mandate to issue findings or rule on whether certain vaccines caused harm, but could refer questions to Parliament.

stories.title: Ontario Science Centre lays off entire science department as part of restructuring
stories.summary: Government is building a new $1-billion science centre at Ontario Place
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
The Ontario Science Centre has laid off 30 workers including the entire science department, The Canadian Press has learned.

Science centre CEO Paul Kortenaar told employees at a meeting Thursday that the organization is being restructured.

“As part of the changes, some departments will no longer form part of the new organizational structure,” Kortenaar told staff in a video conference call, a recording of which was obtained by The Canadian Press.

“In some cases, this means entire full teams are impacted, including business development, science, security and live exhibits.”

The province abruptly closed the science centre in east Toronto in the summer of 2024, citing an engineering report that found deficiencies with the roof. Critics have questioned that reasoning given the roof has survived record snowfall and rainfall in the past two years.

The government is currently building a new $1-billion science centre at Ontario Place with the goal to open by 2029.

The province said the science centre is making changes to “effectively and successfully deliver science learning experiences and new programming” at its interim and future locations, a project it said will create 1,000 new jobs.

“To be clear, science programming, expertise and exhibits remain embedded across the entire organization,” said the office of Tourism, Culture and Gaming Minister Zee Hamid, who was appointed to the role in a cabinet shuffle earlier on Thursday.

“There will be no change to the science programming and other learning experiences delivered by the Ontario Science Centre,” it said.

New roles will be available for some of the impacted workers at the interim and permanent locations, Hamid’s office said.

The province was working to relocate the science centre to Ontario Place before it closed the old facility, and a business case for the relocation suggested moving the centre could help temper criticism of the other main part of the Ontario Place revitalization, a spa and waterpark from European company Therme.

Kortenaar said the restructuring will help the science centre move forward as it prepares to open the new building.

“As part of this restructuring, several departments and functions will be streamlined, consolidated or reconfigured and new positions will be created requiring different skill sets and expertise,” he told employees.

The science centre is also creating new teams, he said, including a research and impact team.

The centre currently runs an interim location in downtown Toronto and periodic pop-up locations while staff continue to deliver programming in schools.

“While our organizational structure is changing, our mission is not,” it said in a statement.

“Science remains central to the organization’s mandate and is embedded across many departments that deliver science learning, engagement, programming, exhibitions and public outreach.”

The union representing science centre workers was livid about the layoffs.

“How can you have an Ontario Science Centre with no science unit?” said Raluca Ellis, president of the Local 549 branch of the Ontario Public Service Employees Union.

“With these job cuts, over 540 years of combined service would be eliminated.”

Kortenaar tried to explain the rationale behind the cuts to staff.

“Our organizational reality has changed significantly and changes are needed to prepare us for the future,” he said. “It is critical that we adjust our structure and plan for future operational and programming needs.”

Adil Shamji, the Liberal provincial legislator who represents the area where the old science centre was located, urged the province to reconsider plans for the new science centre and return programming to the old building.

He called the move to eliminate the science department a “real head scratcher.”

“What is a science centre without its science staff? It’s like a hospital without doctors and nurses or a fire department without firefighters,” he said.

stories.title: Popular farmers' market vows fixes after fire department orders closure
stories.summary: The market says it is working with fire officials and its legal team to address the safety concerns.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
Trails End Farmers’ Market management says it’s working with officials to correct safety concerns after the site was ordered closed by the local fire department earlier this week.

In a Wednesday statement issued to vendors, families, employees and loyal customers and posted to social media and its website, management of Trails End Farmers’ Market – located about 1.5 kilometres east of London at 4370 Dundas St. – said it was working to address safety concerns the Thames Centre Fire Department deemed hazardous enough to order the site closed earlier this week.

“We would like to inform you that we are working diligently with the fire department and our legal team to remedy the issue and rectify any outstanding concerns with respect to the closure notice we received from the fire department this week,” the statement said.

“Please bear with us. We should have some answers for you within the next 24 to 48 hours,” the statement said. “We thank you for your continued support.”

When The Free Press contacted Trails End Farmers’ Market on Thursday, a person who answered the phone said the owners weren’t available for comment at the time.

The order to close the market was approved by the Ontario fire marshal’s office, the Thames Centre Fire Department said in a statement earlier this week, noting “serious and life safety deficiencies (were) identified on the premises.”

Inspection orders were issued under the Fire Protection and Prevention Act and copies of the order to close will be posted at the market, the statement added.

“Under the terms of the order to close, the building is to remain closed until the corrective actions set out in (two inspection orders) have been satisfied,” the department said. “The department will require a follow-up inspection before authorizing the premises to be reoccupied.”

The Thames Centre Fire Department said it recognized that closing the building is a serious measure, but because of the conditions observed during the inspection process, Trails End Farmers’ Market required an intense response due to the fire and life safety concerns identified.

“The life safety of the public, the vendors and the regular occupants of the building remains the fire department’s highest priority,” the department said.

In 1993, a building known as the London Sales Arena, which was previously located on the property, was destroyed by a blaze, the fire department said, noting the structures at the property now exhibit “many of the same issues” identified with the previous building.

Trails End Farmers’ Market is family-owned and has operated since 1983, according to its website, which lists 56 vendors. The market operates Saturdays from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

stories.title: Republican lawmaker wants to rename Lake Erie: 'Let's call it Lake Pennsylvania'
stories.summary: The lake's "modern economy and identity" is tied to Pennsylvania boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it, Maloney said.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Canada

Congressman David Maloney says he will put a resolution forward calling on President Donald Trump to rename the lake shared with Canada and three other states

Last updated 3 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/republican-lawmaker-wants-to-rename-lake-erie-lets-call-it-lake-pennsylvania#comments-area)

People ride a personal watercraft in Lake Erie at Rondeau Provincial Park in Morpeth, Ont. on August 27, 2026.Photo by Geoff Robins /Geoff Robins/The London Free Pre

A Republican congressman from Pennsylvania is planning to put a resolution before the U.S. House of Representatives urging President Donald Trump, Congress and the United States Secretary of the Interior to rename Lake Erie as “Lake Pennsylvania.”

The reasoning behind the name change derives from the lake’s modern identity, David Maloney said in a press release issued by his office on Sept. 8.

“Every summer, Pennsylvanians head toward the lake … with boats, fishing gear and families in tow,” Maloney said. They spend the weekend on Pennsylvania’s Great Lake shoreline, he added, noting that the area attracts millions of visitors annually.

The release states that about 74 per cent of surveyed anglers reside in Pennsylvania, travelling an average of 103 miles to reach the water, along with out-of-state visitors coming from New York and Ohio to access Erie County’s “Steelhead Alley.”

Despite having a small share of the lake’s shoreline, according to the release, Pennsylvania stocked nearly 500,000 yearling steelhead in 2025 — approximately 40 per cent of all steelhead stocked and more than any other state or Canadian province. It also noted that Pennsylvania supplied all the brown trout stocked in the lake in 2025.

“This is Pennsylvania’s only Great Lake. Its modern economy and identity are increasingly tied to the boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it,” Maloney said. “Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others.”

But Pennsylvania only has one, said Maloney, advocating: “Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania!”

Of the four states that border the lake, Pennsylvania’s shoreline is the second smallest behind Ohio and New York. Only Michigan’s is shorter.

Lake Erie first appeared on French colonial maps in the mid-1600s, according to the PBS station in Erie, Pennsylvania. Erie is a shortened form of “Erielhonan,” named after the Erielhonan Indigenous peoplewho inhabited the lake’s southern shores.

The proposal comes in the wake of Trump’s changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in August.

Prior to that, in January 2025, Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. He also ordered that Mount Denali in Alaska revert to its previous name, Mount McKinley (named for William McKinley, a previous president who favoured the use of tariffs). Former President Barack Obama changed the name to Denali in 2015 to reflect Alaskan Indigenous traditions and the preference of many Alaska residents.

As with Lake Ontario, U.S. government approval of a name change would only apply within the U.S. Canada has its own geographical naming authorities and would not have to recognize the name change.

By Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

Posted September 10, 2026 3:03 pm.

Last Updated September 10, 2026 3:54 pm.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday he has spoken to U.S. President Donald Trump “a couple of times” in recent days as the trade war between the two countries continues to escalate.

At a news conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Carney said he speaks to Trump regularly.

“We continue to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize across this,” Carney said in response to a question about Canada’s role in pursuing peace in Ukraine.

The prime minister said part of the leaders’ responsibilities is to work together to resolve global issues like the war in Ukraine. Carney said he and Trump also spoke about the war in Iran and “other global developments.”

The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed the two leaders have spoken in the last few days but would not provide any details about when exactly the conversation took place, including whether it was before or after the latest escalation in trade actions.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, of 15 to 50 per cent, ON dozens of American imports took effect on Tuesday. That was followed almost 24 hours later by Trump signing new orders to ban imports of some products, including most alcohol, and increase tariffs on some others.

All of that came after an impasse in trade talks in August, which led to Trump imposing 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian goods, ranging from honey and sunscreen to sports equipment and milk.

The two sides have blamed each other for the trade hostilities, with Canada accusing the U.S. of trying to impose last-minute demands that would have restricted Canada’s protections for language and culture and its ability to negotiate trade deals with other countries.

Carney said Thursday any deal with the U.S. must not undermine Canada’s sovereignty or its ability to protect and promote official languages and Canadian culture.

“Canada is always ready to strike a fair deal,” he said. “We believe there’s a mutually beneficial deal for Canada and the United States and our team, myself, are ready.”

Canadian politicians are pushing back on Trump’s executive orders limiting Canadian businesses’ access to procurement contracts and deploying a new set of tariffs.

The five new orders, which will take effect Sept. 29, will completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products and alcoholic beverages.

They also remove some items from the tariff list completely, such as toilet paper and cement, while adding new products to be tariffed, including additional dairy products.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Thursday that businesses affected by tariffs and bans will be eligible for the province’s support programs.

In a speech to the Toronto Region Board of Trade, Ford said Ontario will expand eligibility for its tariff support programs to the affected industries so they can keep the lights on.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt has ordered the province’s public sector to stop buying American products when Canadian substitutes are available. She said the move is a response to the latest round of U.S. tariffs.

Holt said her government is also looking to see if it has the authority to prevent Americans from obtaining fishing and hunting licences, as well as mining claims.

Her government will also ban the purchase of U.S. goods and services for contracts valued at more than $5 million starting Oct. 1.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Glitz, glam and geopolitical anxiety as Tiff begins amid U.S. trade war
stories.summary: More than 200 feature-length and short films are screening at Tiff from dozens of countries across six continents
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Two factions of the film world converged at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday.

Fans filed into star-studded screenings at what’s long been known as the “people’s festival” for its publicly available tickets, and a larger-than-ever contingent of industry delegates gathered at a nearby convention centre for the inaugural edition of Tiff: The Market, a trade event that connects creatives with film financiers.

It comes as U.S. President Donald Trump pushes for Hollywood films to be shot in the United States, rather than outsourced to other countries as has been increasingly common in recent years.

“There’s definitely a lot of attention on what’s going to happen south of the border right now but what we have to do is really take pride in what Tiff has been able to build, which is a world-class marketplace that is going to bring everyone together,” said Damon D’Oliveira, a producer who sits on the boards of both Tiff and the Canadian Media Producers Association.

“This is where we have a real edge. We’ve got countries from around the world that are here at the market right now for the first time.”

More than 200 feature-length and short films from dozens of countries across six continents are due to screen over 10 days. Their countries of origin range from Iran to Ireland and Rwanda to Romania – and, of course, the United States.

Tiff CEO Cameron Bailey said he understands the protectionist impulse, though he argued that Hollywood is richer for Canada’s contributions.

“Hollywood is obviously the leading film industry in the world, but it makes for a stronger industry when it’s able to work with talent from every corner of the planet,” he said on a recent video call.

Ahead of this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, Tiff CEO Cameron Bailey discusses how the festival’s downtown hub, anchored by Tiff Bell Lightbox and surrounded by historic venues, has helped create a natural centre for the event.

The Associated Press

But as tensions with the United States remain, Canada’s film industry is looking to partner with other so-called “middle powers.”

Julie Roy, executive director and CEO of Telefilm Canada, noted that she was just in France for the Lumiere Summit focused on international cinema, hosted by France and South Korea.

“I feel very energized about that because more and more with this context, international co-operation and collaboration is a necessity,” she said by phone. “And Canada is the leader in that field. I mean, we are having treaties of co-production with 57 different countries.”

Telefilm has the largest pavilion at Tiff: The Market, where they’ll facilitate meetings between Canadian creators and international financiers.

She likens it to Team Canada at the Olympic Village – but in the audiovisual sector.

By early afternoon, the Metro Toronto Convention Centre was filling out with market delegates.

Paul Spurrier, who is representing the Thailand Pavilion, said he’d met a number of filmmakers in the first few hours of the market who were interested in filming in Thailand.

In addition to selling the country as a potential destination for international filmmakers, Spurrier is also hoping to drum up interest in Thai films. “I think that a lot of producers are being pressured to maintain the quality of their productions but to cut costs. And so Thailand is actually in a very good position to be part of that, where you can still get great crews and a great look to your shoot but at a much lower cost,” he said.

As the businesspeople geared up for a week of wheeling and dealing, crews were literally rolling out the red carpet for the public-facing festival.

Guilherme Bonamigo was walking along King Street, taking in the first-day atmosphere. Originally from Brazil, he has lived in Toronto for the last 10 years and said he looks forward to this event every year.

“It’s a fact that anyone can come,” he said. “Of course, there’s some very buzzy sessions, but anyone can buy a ticket. Even today there’s still tickets for some of the screenings … I don’t think in any other festival, I would have the chance to watch so many movies.”

He’s planning to attend about 30 films at this year’s fest.

The opening night film is Being Heumann , a biopic about American disability rights activist Judy Heumann, from Oscar-winning filmmaker Sian Heder.

Another hot ticket is Fjord , this year’s Palme d’Or winner that dissects what religious tolerance looks like in secular Norway, starring Sebastian Stan as a devoutly Christian father of five.

Stan is among the celebrities expected on Thursday, as is Jodie Comer, who plays a mortician-turned-taxidermist in the musical rom-com Stuffed , and Naomi Watts, who stars in historical drama The Housewife from Canadian director Ben Shirinian.

Film fans from near and far were out on a blocked-out portion of King Street, also known as Festival Street, to soak in the atmosphere ahead of opening night of Tiff.

The Canadian Press

Waiting in line for rush tickets Thursday was Rachel Helzerman, 22, a visitor from Ann Arbor, Mich., where she studies film.

Helzerman, who hopes to one day be a film critic, said she was here as part of a study abroad program.

She was aware of the recent tensions between the neighbouring nations but hoped that Canadians realized they “are just solely the fault of the current administration and that doesn’t actually reflect a general American view of Canada.”

“More now than ever it’s really important as an American to continue going out into the world and trying to put our best foot forward, showing that no, we’re not the administration, we’re not like what you see in the news and I personally love learning about other cultures,” she said.

Meanwhile, 29-year-old Julia Wigdor, of Toronto, said she specifically sought out Canadian-made productions when she was purchasing tickets.

“With the rise of Heated Rivalry and Yaga coming and more and more Crave originals as well…it’s just a really, really cool time to support Canadian art,” said Wigdor.

“Hollywood is obviously the leading film industry in the world, but it makes for a stronger industry when it’s able to work with talent from every corner of the planet,” he said on a recent video call.

Ahead of this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, Tiff CEO Cameron Bailey discusses how the festival’s downtown hub, anchored by Tiff Bell Lightbox and surrounded by historic venues, has helped create a natural centre for the event.
The Associated Press
But as tensions with the United States remain, Canada’s film industry is looking to partner with other so-called “middle powers.”
Julie Roy, executive director and CEO of Telefilm Canada, noted that she was just in France for the Lumiere Summit focused on international cinema, hosted by France and South Korea.

“I feel very energized about that because more and more with this context, international co-operation and collaboration is a necessity,” she said by phone. “And Canada is the leader in that field. I mean, we are having treaties of co-production with 57 different countries.”
Telefilm has the largest pavilion at Tiff: The Market, where they’ll facilitate meetings between Canadian creators and international financiers.
She likens it to Team Canada at the Olympic Village – but in the audiovisual sector.
By early afternoon, the Metro Toronto Convention Centre was filling out with market delegates.
Paul Spurrier, who is representing the Thailand Pavilion, said he’d met a number of filmmakers in the first few hours of the market who were interested in filming in Thailand.

In addition to selling the country as a potential destination for international filmmakers, Spurrier is also hoping to drum up interest in Thai films. “I think that a lot of producers are being pressured to maintain the quality of their productions but to cut costs. And so Thailand is actually in a very good position to be part of that, where you can still get great crews and a great look to your shoot but at a much lower cost,” he said.
As the businesspeople geared up for a week of wheeling and dealing, crews were literally rolling out the red carpet for the public-facing festival.

Guilherme Bonamigo was walking along King Street, taking in the first-day atmosphere. Originally from Brazil, he has lived in Toronto for the last 10 years and said he looks forward to this event every year.

“It’s a fact that anyone can come,” he said. “Of course, there’s some very buzzy sessions, but anyone can buy a ticket. Even today there’s still tickets for some of the screenings … I don’t think in any other festival, I would have the chance to watch so many movies.”
He’s planning to attend about 30 films at this year’s fest.
The opening night film is Being Heumann , a biopic about American disability rights activist Judy Heumann, from Oscar-winning filmmaker Sian Heder.
Another hot ticket is Fjord , this year’s Palme d’Or winner that dissects what religious tolerance looks like in secular Norway, starring Sebastian Stan as a devoutly Christian father of five.

Stan is among the celebrities expected on Thursday, as is Jodie Comer, who plays a mortician-turned-taxidermist in the musical rom-com Stuffed , and Naomi Watts, who stars in historical drama The Housewife from Canadian director Ben Shirinian.
Film fans from near and far were out on a blocked-out portion of King Street, also known as Festival Street, to soak in the atmosphere ahead of opening night of Tiff.
The Canadian Press
Waiting in line for rush tickets Thursday was Rachel Helzerman, 22, a visitor from Ann Arbor, Mich., where she studies film.
Helzerman, who hopes to one day be a film critic, said she was here as part of a study abroad program.

She was aware of the recent tensions between the neighbouring nations but hoped that Canadians realized they “are just solely the fault of the current administration and that doesn’t actually reflect a general American view of Canada.”

“More now than ever it’s really important as an American to continue going out into the world and trying to put our best foot forward, showing that no, we’re not the administration, we’re not like what you see in the news and I personally love learning about other cultures,” she said.
Meanwhile, 29-year-old Julia Wigdor, of Toronto, said she specifically sought out Canadian-made productions when she was purchasing tickets.
“With the rise of Heated Rivalry and Yaga coming and more and more Crave originals as well…it’s just a really, really cool time to support Canadian art,” said Wigdor.
