stories.title: Canada needs up to 4.69 million new homes by 2036, but construction could slow: Cmhc
stories.summary: The federal housing agency says Canada narrowly chipped away at its supply gap over the past year, but the country still needs up to nearly 4.7 million new homes over the next decade to restore pre-pandemic affordability by 2036.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

Posted September 10, 2026 11:15 am.

Last Updated September 10, 2026 12:07 pm.

The federal housing agency says Canada narrowly chipped away at its supply gap over the past year, but the country still needs up to nearly 4.7 million new homes over the next decade to restore pre-pandemic affordability by 2036.

Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. released its latest supply gap estimate report, which said between 417,000 and 469,000 new housing units are needed per year across the ownership and rental markets over the next decade to reach affordability targets.

That’s down slightly from its last estimate in July 2025, when Cmhc said the pace of home construction would need to roughly double to between 430,000 and 480,000 new units annually over the coming decade.

But the agency warned recent affordability gains are at risk as new home construction is instead expected to slow, especially in the home ownership market.

“Although slower population growth has brought some improvements in affordability, new construction is slowing faster than demand,” Cmhc deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

“The key risk now is Canada underbuilds during this softer market and finds itself further short of housing when demand strengthens again.”

A total of 131,851 housing starts have been recorded so far this year through July, down four per cent from the same seven-month period in 2025.

At the current pace of housing construction, Canada is on track to add around 231,000 housing units per year over the next decade, according to the report, around half the annual pace needed to reach the 2019 affordability levels by 2036.

The agency defines affordability as the share of income that goes toward housing. In general, it aims to return to levels of affordability at which adjusted house prices are no higher than 30 per cent of average gross household income.

The report said meeting future housing demand will depend on the pace of new construction. But the sector is facing pressure from high construction costs, while presale financing conditions remain difficult for some projects. Weak condominium market conditions are also making developers cautious about launching new projects.

“Housing supply needs will increase over the long term. Population growth is expected to recover across most major cities, and rising incomes will support housing demand,” the report said.

“As a result, there will be a need for more homes. Some households May have delayed forming because of affordability challenges. As conditions improve further, some of this suppressed demand will re-emerge.”

While Cmhc said the national supply gap is broadly unchanged from the assessment last year, there are key differences across regional markets.

Since the agency’s previous estimates, it said the housing supply gap has narrowed in Toronto, as lower home prices have improved affordability. However, new construction activity has weakened “sharply,” particularly in the condo market, limiting ownership housing supply.

The gap has remained stable in Vancouver, where improved affordability and stronger construction levels have been offset by slower future supply growth and population pressures.

Record housing construction in Calgary has narrowed that city’s housing supply gap by almost half, the report said, however affordability challenges remain, especially for lower-income households and prospective homeowners. Elsewhere in the province, Edmonton remains the only large market in Canada without a housing supply gap “because housing construction has generally kept pace with population growth.”

But the gap has grown larger in both Montreal and Ottawa compared with a year ago. In Montreal, housing construction levels remain high, the report said, but new supply is concentrated in rental housing, while weak condo supply is limiting ownership options.

Similar challenges persist in the country’s capital city, where affordability has deteriorated, Cmhc said.

“We expect housing demand to grow faster than the housing supply despite strong construction activity,” it said of Ottawa.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Windsor council candidate calls Zionists 'terrorists' and 'serial killers'
stories.summary: Windsor city council candidate is facing fallout over remarks calling Zionists "terrorists" and "serial killers" who should be locked up.
stories.author: Derek Spalding
stories.content:
Canada

Rasha Zaid said her opposition to Zionism should not be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people

Rasha Zaid, an organizer with the Windsor4Palestine organization is shown on Thursday, January 23, 2025.Photo by Dan Janisse /Windsor Star

A Windsor city council candidate is facing fallout over public remarks referring to Zionists as “terrorists” and “serial killers” who should be locked up, comments that have drawn attention well beyond the city as the municipal election campaign gets underway.

Rasha Zaid, one of five candidates seeking the Ward 4 council seat in the Oct. 26 election, made the statements during a protest in Windsor. Video of the speech has since circulated online and the controversy has attracted international attention, including coverage by the Jerusalem Post.

“Every person that announced that they’re Zionists must be locked up,” Zaid says in one video clip. “They should all be locked up. They’re terrorists.”

In a second clip Zaid goes on to say, “t hey are nothing but serial killers on the loose, and they must be held accountable.”

The Windsor Jewish Federation and Community Centre said broad comments like these risk leaving people feeling targeted because of their beliefs or identity. Officials issued a statement saying Zionism broadly refers to the belief that Jewish people have a right to self-determination in their ancestral homeland and does not necessarily mean support for any particular Israeli government, policy or military action.

“Because many Jewish people consider Zionism part of their identity or connection to Israel, comments directed broadly at ‘Zionists’ can have a significant impact on members of the Jewish community,” the federation said in a statement. “Members of our community have expressed concern that rhetoric of this nature contributes to an increasingly difficult environment and makes some people more cautious about openly expressing their Jewish identity.”

In an interview, Zaid said her opposition to Zionism should not be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people.

“Zionism and Judaism are not the same thing, and the constant conflation of the two must truly be put to an end,” she said. “One is a faith, and one is a political ideology.”

Zaid said she does not object to Jewish self-determination but opposes actions she believes have been carried out under the banner of Zionism.

“I’m vocally anti-Zionist for many reasons, for what has been done and what has been carried out under the political ideology of Zionism,” she said.

Asked whether she believes merely identifying as a Zionist should be grounds for imprisonment, Zaid said that was not her position.

“I didn’t say if you have a political ideology of Zionism, you should be locked up,” she said, adding that her comments were directed at people responsible for war crimes.

Online criticism, though, points to how her words captured on video were broader: “Every person that announced that they’re Zionists must be locked up.”

But Zaid said the circulating video was a short excerpt taken from a much longer speech at a Windsor protest and did not provide the context surrounding her remarks.

“When somebody takes bits and pieces of an entire speech to only fit a certain narrative, that is not honest journalism,” she said. “It completely changes it around. It’s not fair.”

Zaid also rejected equating anti-Zionism with antisemitism, saying many Jewish people are anti-Zionist and, “criticizing political ideology does not mean you’re antisemitic.”

She wants to put the latest discussions about her protests behind her and instead focus on her campaign and municipal issues, such as building affordable housing, boosting the local economy and ethical spending, and creating safe spaces and an active community.

“I honestly will no longer be answering any questions regarding this matter (about Zionism comments) because I think I’ve made my point very clear, many, many, many times,” she said.

Zaid is running against Mike Burton, Catherine Gariepy-Schulze, Chris Holt and Xsander Moisenko for the Ward 4 council seat.

Officials issued a statement saying Zionism broadly refers to the belief that Jewish people have a right to self-determination in their ancestral homeland and does not necessarily mean support for any particular Israeli government, policy or military action.

“Because many Jewish people consider Zionism part of their identity or connection to Israel, comments directed broadly at ‘Zionists’ can have a significant impact on members of the Jewish community,” the federation said in a statement. “Members of our community have expressed concern that rhetoric of this nature contributes to an increasingly difficult environment and makes some people more cautious about openly expressing their Jewish identity.”
In an interview, Zaid said her opposition to Zionism should not be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people.
“Zionism and Judaism are not the same thing, and the constant conflation of the two must truly be put to an end,” she said. “One is a faith, and one is a political ideology.”
Zaid said she does not object to Jewish self-determination but opposes actions she believes have been carried out under the banner of Zionism.
“I’m vocally anti-Zionist for many reasons, for what has been done and what has been carried out under the political ideology of Zionism,” she said.
Asked whether she believes merely identifying as a Zionist should be grounds for imprisonment, Zaid said that was not her position.
“I didn’t say if you have a political ideology of Zionism, you should be locked up,” she said, adding that her comments were directed at people responsible for war crimes.
Online criticism, though, points to how her words captured on video were broader: “Every person that announced that they’re Zionists must be locked up.”
But Zaid said the circulating video was a short excerpt taken from a much longer speech at a Windsor protest and did not provide the context surrounding her remarks.
“When somebody takes bits and pieces of an entire speech to only fit a certain narrative, that is not honest journalism,” she said. “It completely changes it around. It’s not fair.”
Zaid also rejected equating anti-Zionism with antisemitism, saying many Jewish people are anti-Zionist and, “criticizing political ideology does not mean you’re antisemitic.”

She wants to put the latest discussions about her protests behind her and instead focus on her campaign and municipal issues, such as building affordable housing, boosting the local economy and ethical spending, and creating safe spaces and an active community.
“I honestly will no longer be answering any questions regarding this matter (about Zionism comments) because I think I’ve made my point very clear, many, many, many times,” she said.
Zaid is running against Mike Burton, Catherine Gariepy-Schulze, Chris Holt and Xsander Moisenko for the Ward 4 council seat.

stories.title: Buffalo Bills recruit Barenaked Ladies to play O Canada at home opener
stories.summary: The Nfl's Buffalo Bills have enlisted Canadian rock band Barenaked Ladies to perform O Canada at the team's home opener this month.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Canada

The NFL club is owned by Terry and Kim Pegula, proprietors of the NHL's Buffalo Sabres, a club that's played the Canadian anthem at every home game since 1970

Last updated 13 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/buffalo-bills-barenaked-ladies-o-Canada-home-opener#comments-area)

The Nfl's Buffalo Bills have enlisted Canadian rock band Barenaked Ladies to perform O Canada at the team's home opener this month.Photo by Contributed/Barenaked Ladies

When the Buffalo Bills christen their new US$2.2 billion football stadium later this month, they’ll pay tribute to the city’s long-standing affinity for its Canadian neighbours on the other side of the Peace Bridge by performing O Canada along with the U.S. national anthem.

“For the first time in Highmark Stadium history, we will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame,” the Buffalo Bills shared on X Wednesday, highlighting Canada’s Barenaked Ladies as performers for the latter.

Auliʻi Cravalho, who voices Moana in the Disney movies of the same name, will sing the Star-Spangled Banner at the Sept. 17 game against the Detroit Lions.

National Post has inquired whether the organization intends to play the anthem at every regular-season game or just the home opener.

The Bills are owned by Terry and Kim Pegula, also proprietors of the NHL’s Buffalo Sabres, a club that has performed O Canada at every home game — even those that didn’t feature a Canadian team. The practice began upon the team’s founding in 1970, as a nod to the many fans co-owner Seymour Knox III knew they would attract from the nearby lower Niagara and St. Catharines area in Ontario.

When anthem singer Cami Clune’s microphone failed during a playoff game earlier this year, the Sabres faithful were quick to pick up the anthem and sing it to completion.

Fun fact: the Sabres were named by a Canadian — Toronto filmmaker Harry Cole, who entered and won a 1969 contest to name the team — and Knox said he specifically chose the Canadian English spelling of the word to honour the Canadian fans, according toThe Hockey Writers. (The swords are sabers in the U.S.)

Minor league baseball team the Buffalo Bisons, the AAA affiliate of the Toronto Blue Jays, and the National Lacrosse League’s Buffalo Bandits also perform O Canada before home games.

stories.title: London man killed Thursday morning in Oxford County crash - CBC.CA
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Oxford County say a 50-year-old London man is dead, and another driver is in hospital with life-threatening injuries, after a serious crash Thursday morning in East Zorra-Tavistock.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Oxford County say a 50-year-old London man is dead, and another driver is in hospital with life-threatening injuries, after a serious crash Thursday morning in East Zorra-Tavistock.
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 10:54 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Police say a section of Highway 59 northeast of London will be closed for several hours Thursday as they investigate a fatal crash.(Ontario Provincial Police)
Emergency crews were called to the intersection of Cassel Sideroad and Highway 59 at around 5:10 a.m., police said. The crash involved a pickup truck and an SUV.
The man driving the SUV was taken to hospital where he was later pronounced deceased. The driver of the pickup truck remains in hospital with life-threatening injuries.
Highway 59 will be closed for several hours between Cassel Sideroad and Maplewood Sideroad as police investigate the cause of the crash.
Anyone with information or video footage that could help with the investigation is asked to contact the OPP.

stories.title: Ottawa announces $5 million for HIV self-test kits, more support staffers
stories.summary: Winnipeg — The federal government is dispatching 80,000 HIV self-test kits across Canada to expand access to HIV prevention.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer, speaks during a news conference following the release of opioid data, in Ottawa, Monday, June 15, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld

By Brittany Hobson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 10, 2026 10:52 am.

Last Updated September 10, 2026 2:24 pm.

Winnipeg — The federal government is dispatching 80,000 HIV self-test kits across Canada to expand access to HIV prevention.

“HIV is a manageable condition, and people living with HIV deserve to live healthy, full lives without stigma or discrimination,” Manitoba Liberal MP Doug Eyolfson announced Thursday.

“This funding is about making it easier for people to get tested, know their status, and access the care and support they need.”

Ottawa will provide $5 million to increase access to the kits and to hire peer-based support workers for communities facing the highest burdens of HIV. There is $2 million for the tests and $3 million for peer support networks.

The federal government says 2,300 new HIV diagnoses were reported in 2024, and an estimated 7,000 people live unaware they have HIV.

HIV, short for human immunodeficiency virus, attacks the immune system. Without treatment, it can weaken the body’s defences and progress to Aids, which can be life-threatening.

Advocates say self-tests can be a way to overcome barriers — including racism and geography – that could prevent people from seeking help.

A breakdown of where the tests will be distributed is being finalized. Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s chief public health officer, said underserved communities are the priority.

“That would include community organizations working with Indigenous populations, men who have sex with men, Black communities and other racialized communities, and people who inject drugs,” Reimer said.

The Manitoba Harm Reduction Network, an advocacy group that works to reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections, said the self-tests are just the start and there needs to be followup help.

“Being able to access dignified care is also part of the plan,” said Shohan Illsley, the network’s executive director.

The issue is comparatively acute in Manitoba. In May, the province declared a public health emergency over HIV rates that it estimates are three times higher than the rest of Canada.

In 2024, the province reported a rate of 19.5 cases per 100,000. The national rate was about a quarter of that. The province said new cases have been increasing over the last six years, with 328 detected last year compared with 90 in 2019.

It called for more help from Ottawa to address the sharp rise in cases.

Uzoma Asagwara, Manitoba’s health minister, said Thursday’s announcement was a “big step” in addressing the issue but promised to continue to advocate for more investments.

The funding was welcomed by Catie, an advocacy group that provides information on HIV and hepatitis C. It said it will help get Canada closer to its commitment to eliminate HIV as a public health concern by 2030.

“With Canada reporting a 23 per cent increase in estimated HIV infections, community-based workers have their work cut out for them,” said Jody Jollimore, executive director of Catie.

“To keep the epidemic under control, we need long-term commitment.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Brittany Hobson, The Canadian Press

paragraphs: Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer, speaks during a news conference following the release of opioid data, in Ottawa, Monday, June 15, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld
By Brittany Hobson, The Canadian Press
Posted September 10, 2026 10:52 am.
Last Updated September 10, 2026 2:24 pm.
Winnipeg — The federal government is dispatching 80,000 HIV self-test kits across Canada to expand access to HIV prevention.
“HIV is a manageable condition, and people living with HIV deserve to live healthy, full lives without stigma or discrimination,” Manitoba Liberal MP Doug Eyolfson announced Thursday.
“This funding is about making it easier for people to get tested, know their status, and access the care and support they need.”

Ottawa will provide $5 million to increase access to the kits and to hire peer-based support workers for communities facing the highest burdens of HIV. There is $2 million for the tests and $3 million for peer support networks.
The federal government says 2,300 new HIV diagnoses were reported in 2024, and an estimated 7,000 people live unaware they have HIV.
HIV, short for human immunodeficiency virus, attacks the immune system. Without treatment, it can weaken the body’s defences and progress to Aids, which can be life-threatening.
Advocates say self-tests can be a way to overcome barriers — including racism and geography – that could prevent people from seeking help.
A breakdown of where the tests will be distributed is being finalized. Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s chief public health officer, said underserved communities are the priority.

“That would include community organizations working with Indigenous populations, men who have sex with men, Black communities and other racialized communities, and people who inject drugs,” Reimer said.

The Manitoba Harm Reduction Network, an advocacy group that works to reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections, said the self-tests are just the start and there needs to be followup help.
“Being able to access dignified care is also part of the plan,” said Shohan Illsley, the network’s executive director.
The issue is comparatively acute in Manitoba. In May, the province declared a public health emergency over HIV rates that it estimates are three times higher than the rest of Canada.

In 2024, the province reported a rate of 19.5 cases per 100,000. The national rate was about a quarter of that. The province said new cases have been increasing over the last six years, with 328 detected last year compared with 90 in 2019.
It called for more help from Ottawa to address the sharp rise in cases.
Uzoma Asagwara, Manitoba’s health minister, said Thursday’s announcement was a “big step” in addressing the issue but promised to continue to advocate for more investments.

The funding was welcomed by Catie, an advocacy group that provides information on HIV and hepatitis C. It said it will help get Canada closer to its commitment to eliminate HIV as a public health concern by 2030.
“With Canada reporting a 23 per cent increase in estimated HIV infections, community-based workers have their work cut out for them,” said Jody Jollimore, executive director of Catie.
“To keep the epidemic under control, we need long-term commitment.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.
Brittany Hobson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Are you willing to pay more to stand up to the U.S.? What readers told us
stories.summary: Global News asked its readers, 'Are you willing to pay higher prices or change brands in order to support the country's response to Trump's trade war?'
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
The United States escalated its trade war with Canada on Tuesday, announcing an upcoming ban on some Canadian dairy products and motorcycles as well as most alcoholic beverages after retaliatory Canadian counter-tariffs took effect on about $28 billion in U.S. goods.

Those counter-tariffs followed the U.S. imposing 50 per cent tariffs on Canada in August.

U.S. President Donald Trump also moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term U.S. government contracts.

The latest U.S. bans are set to take effect Sept. 29 and cover various Canadian wines and spirits, some motorcycles and mopeds, dairy products including whey and some types of molasses .

Canada’s tariffs on U.S. goods took effect at 10:01 a.m. Tuesday and hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, with rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent or 50 per cent.

Eight of 10 Canadian provinces have already continued to restrict or ban sales of U.S. alcohol.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada’s response is about reducing its dependence on the United States rather than simply weathering the latest tariffs.

“It’s about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live,” he said.

As Canada’s counter-tariffs kick in, Global News asked its readers, “are you more or less determined to Buy Canadian? Are you willing to pay higher prices or change brands in order to support the country’s response to Trump’s trade war?”

These are some of your responses.

The vast majority of respondents said they would not be buying American products and will continue to Buy Canadian.

“Of course I am willing to pay more and continue to Buy Canadian. Although it will hit my pocket book harder, I believe that we have no other choice. Elbows up,” said one reader, Sallie.

Reader Denny said that they are “willing to support my country by paying higher prices to Buy Canadian.”

“As a retired Canadian, I am all in. I think it is time for Canada to make changes that have been required for decades to protect our nation from facing future trade wars as we are seeing in these current times. Our children and grandchildren are counting on it. Canada Strong,” said Bob M.

Reader Kim W. said she is “willing to do whatever it takes, including paying more for Canadian goods, to counter” Trump’s tariffs.

“My household is determined to avoid purchasing any U.S. product even if it means paying a little more for a Canadian product,” said Chris D.

Maureen H. said that the “retaliatory tariffs won’t hurt you if you don’t buy American.”

“Anything I haven’t found a substitute for, I do without. Hasn’t hurt me in the slightest,” she added.

“I will buy Canadian, so I hope more and more merchandise is made in Canada, from Canadian materials. I Refuse TO BUY ‘Made IN THE USA’. If this means paying a bit more for things, I will, gladly,” said reader Mary S.

James W. said he started “avoiding U.S. products during Trump’s first term and will most likely continue the rest of our lives.”

We’ll continue to buy Canadian first before buying products from countries that strongly support democracy,” he added.

Many readers also said they would be boycotting all things American, including travel.

“We have not and will not travel to the USA until a new leader who reverses all the tariffs is elected south of us. Where possible we have changed brands that are not American. Where possible we buy Canadian and then revert to Mexican Italian English. USA products are our last choice. Keep up the good work Mr Carney,” said Glenda C.

Reader Eric E. said that he is willing to do “whatever it takes to eliminate trade with the United States” and he has “ no interest in ever going back to the United States even for a visit.”

Sonja K. said that they have “bought Canadian products wherever possible” and has not “travelled to the U.S.” since Trump took office.

“Definitely will never buy any American products or travel to States, we support our country and government,” said reader Annie S.

“My husband and I are both determined to buy more Canadian! Even though we are seniors, we are willing to pay higher prices or change brands in order to support the country’s response to Trump’s trade war. And that includes no longer crossing the border and spending our Canadian dollars on American goods,” said Leni V.

For some readers, they say they would be willing to Buy Canadian but worry Canadian consumers will likely face higher prices as a result of new counter-tariffs.

“I would be, but only if Canadian companies and food stores do not put higher prices on Canadian goods made here and say because of tariffs the cost is higher. If Carney was to gives Canadians the item that Trump is placing tariffs on, so that Canadians know what products not to buy. On the energy liquid gas and hydro front stop sending it the states and use it to keep gas prices and hydro cost lower for Canadians,” said Brad N.

Darrell B. suggested that the counter tariffs are “only going to destroy the economy even more” and “make life even more unaffordable.”

“Counter tariffs are really the Canadian government telling its citizens that they will bear the brunt of the tariffs in order for Canada to stand up to the US. Both tariffs are counterproductive….smaller Canadian firms will suffer and probably close if this continues,” said reader Tom A.

Reader Rod C. pointed out that the U.S. “is Canada’s single most valuable trading partner” and said the country should “never jeopardize this relationship.”

“I would not be willing to pay more for necessary items. Groceries and clothing are on that list,” he added.

There was, however, a minority of respondents who said they would not be interested in paying a higher price and are less determined to Buy Canadian.

“No I will not buy Canadian unless it is the lowest priced item on the shelf. With the rising costs, we as Canadians have to support our selves and having to pay more for items is not what I voted for,” said Dale C.

“I definitely do not agree with Carneys position. He is making things worse with the U.S.,” said Winnie D.

The Government of Canada launched the Buy Canadian policy in December 2025, to protect and prioritize Canadian workers and industries while strengthening Canada’s domestic economy.

The changes were created to help create a strong Canadian supply chain by prioritizing Canadian suppliers and Canadian-made goods and services wherever possible.

They also aim to help Canadian industries become more self-sufficient and resilient to changes in the global economy.

That came after the movement gained traction across the country in early 2025 shortly after Trump was inaugurated and imposed the first rounds of his tariffs on multiple sectors of the Canadian economy.

—With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Harry Styles to play two shows in Toronto’s Rogers Stadium next year
stories.summary: British pop star will perform on May 7 and May 8, marking his first tour stop in Toronto since 2022
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Harry Styles fans, get ready to dance some more.

The British pop star will play two shows in Toronto next year as part of his expanded “Together, Together” tour.

The Watermelon Sugar singer will perform at Rogers Stadium on May 7 and May 8, marking his first tour stop in Toronto since 2022.

It’s the only Canadian stop listed among the 25 new dates across 12 cities.

Styles is currently in the midst of a 30-night residency at New York City’s Madison Square Garden, which is set to wrap in October.

Rogers Stadium has been in the news recently after the north Toronto outdoor concert venue sustained extensive damage caused by a major thunderstorm last week.

Live Nation, the operator of the stadium, says engineers determined that sections affected by the severe weather event will need to be removed and rebuilt, leading to the cancellation of an AC/DC concert that was scheduled for Sept. 16.

The show was set to be the last of the season for the 50,000-capacity venue.

The news release says tickets for Styles’ North American shows will go on sale Sept. 16.

stories.title: Ontario Premier Doug Ford to shuffle cabinet Thursday
stories.summary: Office positions the move as a response to Canada’s trade war with the U.S.
stories.author: Laura Stone, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
will shuffle his cabinet on Thursday, a move his office is positioning as a response to the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump.

The cabinet shuffle is likely to address vacancies on Mr. Ford’s front bench, including Treasury Board President, which was previously held by Caroline Mulroney. Ms. Mulroney resigned as both a minister and MPP in June, and her cabinet post was temporarily taken up by Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy.

Mr. Ford’s office confirmed the shuffle will happen Thursday, and the Premier is expected to take questions from the media midday.

There are also questions about the fate of some of Mr. Ford’s top cabinet ministers, including Labour Minister David Piccini. Late last year, Ontario’s Integrity Commissioner Cathryn Motherwell launched an investigation into whether Mr. Piccini contravened any laws in his handling of a controversial $2.5-billion skills training fund.

Mr. Ford spoke at Toronto Regional Board of Trade event Thursday morning but did not mention the shuffle and did not take questions from reporters. He reannounced plans to make businesses in more sectors eligible for the government’s existing $1-billion fund for loans meant to assist companies affected by U.S. tariffs.

stories.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet with Carney and cabinet in Banff
stories.summary: is set to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney and his cabinet Thursday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada’s military needs “millions” of drones for the modern battlefield but only has 2,000, as he signed a new deal with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to boost the country’s production and share them with Ukraine.

Zelenskyy met Carney and his cabinet Thursday in Alberta during a previously unannounced two-day visit to Canada.

During a joint announcement with Zelenskyy, Carney announced a new Defence Drone Initiative Marketplace (Ddim) that he said would give Canadian government agencies and their allies “privileged access” to roughly 400 Canadian drone suppliers.

The prime minister said the new deal aims to increase Canada’s drone production tenfold in coming years.

“This is a key part of our plan to build industrial capacity here in Canada to produce millions of drones within the next two years, and today’s contracts will increase the number of drones available to the cap tenfold,” Carney said.

“Importantly, one third of all the drones we manufacture will go to support Ukraine’s defence of its homeland,” he added.

Carney and Zelenskyy also signed a declaration committing to a future 100-year partnership in fields such as energy, security, defence and critical minerals. Carney also promised Ukraine over $400 million in loan guarantees to help the Eastern European country purchase energy for the coming winter.

Zelenskyy also said this signature was the first step to another “big drone deal” coming between Canada and Ukraine.

“Thirty per cent of these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to battle. Immediately to our people, our soldiers, to save our children, our families,” he said.

Trump's latest trade actions are not 'an escalation,' economist says

Diana Fox Carney says she realizes the personal 'opportunity' offered by her husband's position

The Ukrainian president landed in Calgary with his wife Olena Zelenska on Wednesday evening, where he was greeted by Canadian and European dignitaries as well as Foreign Minister Anita Anand.

He will meet with Carney in Calgary and then travel to Banff, Alta., where he is expected to speak to cabinet during its two-day retreat beginning Thursday. The Ukrainian president then plans to travel to Toronto and North Bay before leaving Canada on Friday.

As is usual for Zelenskyy’s travel during his country’s ongoing war against Russia’s invasion in 2022, his visit was kept under wraps until his arrival.

“Canada has been and remains one of our closest partners. We value all the support from Canadians and the decisions that help Ukraine stand strong and protect our people,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media while announcing his visit.

“The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter. We will discuss how to strengthen our resilience, support our people, and ensure that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs to defend itself,”

In a separate statement, Carney said the focus of the visit was “deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation.”

“It will also address the human cost of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries,” Carney said in a statement.

stories.title: Carney to hold joint press conference with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the meeting will focus on the countries' shared priorities, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Canada is pledging more support for Ukraine as it grapples with Russia’s ongoing invasion by deepening cooperation in key areas such as defence, critical minerals and intelligence sharing, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a joint statement.

Zelenskyy is seeking military support from allies as Russia’s attacks from the air target Ukraine’s energy grid.

“Meeting at a moment of global rupture, the leaders reaffirmed their intention to build a new order founded on trust, rooted in shared values, and underpinned by the strength and determination to uphold them,” a joint statement from the two read.

Both countries agreed to establish “a long-term defence industrial partnership,” including the joint production of counter-drone capabilities.

“Canada will always stand in solidarity with Ukraine,” Carney said.

Canada and Ukraine also agreed to ensure “safe and secure navigation in the Black Sea,” a key shipping route for food grains for markets across the world.

Carney and Zelenskyy signed a “Declaration for a Hundred Year Partnership” between Canada and Ukraine.

Ottawa and Kyiv “will codify a long-term framework for cooperation across defence and security, trade and investment, reconstruction, energy, critical minerals, and technology,” Carney said.

“We are already strong, but we have to be stronger to have a real dialogue with Putin,” Zelenskyy said that the “best way” to defend Ukraine is to find a way to end the war.

The federal government will also ramp up its defence drone production, with a plan to “produce millions of drones within the next two years,” he added.

Based on a model employed by the Ukrainian government, Canada will set up a “national drone market place,” which will give access to the Canadian Armed Forces to around 400 Canadian drone suppliers.

“One-third of all the drones we manufacture will go to support Ukraine’s defence of its homeland,” Carney said.

4:46 Trump says Putin wants peace deal for Ukraine amid continued strikes

Canada still working with U.S.

Canada can “continue to work with the United States” when it comes to supporting Ukraine despite ongoing trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington, he added.

“We can compartmentalize,” Carney said, adding that a “mutually beneficial deal” was still possible on trade.

“Canada is always ready to strike a fair deal. We believe there’s a mutually beneficial deal for Canada and the United States, and our team (and) myself are ready. I speak regularly to President Trump,” he said.

5:06 Carney says he remains in regular contact with Trump despite trade war

In addition to a broader cooperation agreement, Canada and Ukraine also signed an energy cooperation agreement.

Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson and his Ukrainian counterpart Denys Shmyhal signed an agreement that would see deeper cooperation on LNG and energy security.

The agreement also included commitments on nuclear energy, as well as hydroelectric power and other forms of renewable energy.

Zelenskyy last visited Canada in December, stopping in Halifax, amid efforts to end the war that Russia started in 2014 and escalated with a full-scale invasion in February 2022.

1:26 Carney says he’d tell Putin to ‘get out of Ukraine’ if the latter attends upcoming G20 summit

Kyiv has suffered a barrage of Russian airstrikes in recent months, and Ukraine has pleaded for more air defence support from its allies.

Since 2022, Canada has pledged $6.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine running through to 2029.

“Canada remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine’s defence, recovery, and reconstruction,” Carney said in a statement Wednesday.

–with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario to expand tariff support program eligibility to businesses affected by new U.S. tariffs
stories.summary: The Protect Ontario Financing Program gives loans for businesses to use for payroll, lease and utility payments
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Businesses affected by a new round of American tariffs and bans set to take effect later this month will be eligible for Ontario’s support programs, Premier Doug Ford announced Thursday.

U.S. President Donald Trump has announced that in response to Canadian counter tariffs, he would ban imports of certain Canadian goods, including alcohol, motorcycles, some dairy products like whey and cheese, and molasses.

Additional 50 per cent tariffs on other goods including certain steel and aluminum products, some dairy and specialty cheese products, mattresses, furniture and paper products are set to take effect on Tuesday.

In a speech to the Toronto Region Board of Trade, Ford said Ontario will expand eligibility for its tariff support programs to the affected industries so they can keep the lights on.

“I’ll be clear: Our government is going to do whatever it takes to protect workers and businesses from President Trump,” he said.

The Protect Ontario Financing Program gives loans for businesses to use for payroll, lease and utility payments, and the Ontario Together Trade Fund gives grants or loans to small- and medium-sized businesses to help reduce reliance on American supply chains.

Ford said in his speech that Prime Minister Mark Carney was right to respond with dollar-for-dollar tariffs, “to show President Trump that Canada will stand up for itself.”

The Toronto Region Board of Trade also backed Ottawa’s approach in the trade war, saying Thursday that Canada is in a uniquely difficult position due to its long-standing trade relationship with the United States and the resulting cross-border product supply chain.

“Make no mistake, Ontario is the country’s economic flywheel and it’s in the crosshairs. Businesses are getting hit hard, particularly industrial sectors core to the Toronto region,” the board’s president and CEO, Giles Gherson, said in a speech at the event.

“Businesses need new tools to find new markets, pivot to different products, innovate more aggressively and become more agile, critically become lower-cost suppliers,” he said.

Economic upheaval requires policy intervention and while some steps have been taken, “we’re going to need more and in short order,” he said.

stories.title: 3 candidates vying to become next mayor of St. Thomas - CBC.CA
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The race to become St. Thomas's next mayor is taking shape, with three candidates seeking to replace Mayor Joe Preston in the Oct. 26 municipal election.
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 9:29 AM EDT | Last Updated: 9 hours ago
The three St. Thomas mayoral candidates (left to right) are Aidan Frederick, Jeff Kohler and Corey Janzen.(Aidan Frederick/Jeff Kohler/Corey Janzen)
The mayoral race is well underway in the Railroad City, with three candidates looking to take over when Mayor Joe Preston vacates the role.
Preston has served as mayor since 2018, winning two terms after previously representing Elgin-Middlesex-London as a Conservative MP from 2004 to 2015.
He announced earlier this year that he would not seek re-election.
St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston announces he won't seek re-election
The next mayor will take office as St. Thomas continues to grow, with several major industrial projects expected to bring new jobs and investment to the city.

The city was chosen as the site of themassive PowerCo battery plant, a division of Volkswagen that has hired nearly 400 employees as construction continues. Norway's Vianode has also announcedit will build a battery materialsfacility in St. Thomas.
Aidan Frederick, Corey Janzen and current city councillor and former mayor Jeff Kohler are seeking the mayor's chair.
Aidan Frederick, 27, is the youngest St. Thomas mayoral candidate in this election. (Aidan Frederick)
At 27, Aidan Frederick is the youngest of the three mayoral candidates.
A St. Thomas native, he studied software engineering at Western University before working in the technology sector and later moving into accounting.
Frederick says his work on municipal audits has given him some familiarity with municipal finances and operations.
He's running because he believes the future of St. Thomas is exciting.
"We're at this turning point almost with the growth of our city," he said. "I think we need some new faces in City Hall, some new ideas."
Some of his biggest priorities over the next four years are building more housing and improving transportation.
On transportation, Frederick says the city needs to consider how people move within St. Thomas as well as how they travel to surrounding communities.
Frederick also believes his age is an advantage in the race.
"I think being a younger person running for this position is helping the younger folks realize that our problems matter," he said. "The things we're facing do matter and that we can make a change."
Jeff Kohler was Mayor of St. Thomas from 2003-2006, and currently serves as a city counsellor. (Submitted by Jeff Kohler)
Raised in St. Thomas from the age of five, Kohler is a familiar face at City Hall.
He served as mayor from 2003 to 2006 and currently serves as a city councillor.
Kohler says he is running because he can offer what he describes as "capable, local, proven leadership."

"The conditions have been set in St. Thomas and the future is looking bright regardless of the national and provincial trends," he said. "And effective leadership and capacity is what St. Thomas needs and what the residents are looking for."
The next four years will require fiscal responsibility, he said, adding that the city needs to ensure money is spent wisely and within its municipal mandate.
Kohler is also pointing to his experience in local politics, his involvement in decisions that he says helped bring the city to where it is today, and his relationships with city staff.
He says the city's strategic plans would continue under his leadership, rather than "just go on a shelf and get dusty."
That includes the city's goal of eliminating homelessness by 2027.
"We're one of the only municipalities that's actually been able to reduce it...we're proud of that, and we're hopefully going to be able to achieve that goal and continue that."
Corey Janzen filed his nomination papers on the last day with the goal of raising awareness of a 20-year-old City Hall scandal. (Submitted by Corey Janzen)
Corey Janzen is a lifelong St. Thomas resident who has spent the past 20 years working as a truck driver. (Submitted by Corey Janzen)
Corey Janzen, a lifelong St. Thomas resident of Mennonite heritage, has spent the past 20 years working as a truck driver.
He says he decided to run to offer voters an alternative to the other candidates.

When Janzen saw Kohler was entering the race, he says he also wanted to draw attention to a controversy involving the city's corporate credit-card system during Kohler's previous term as mayor in the early 2000s.

St. Thomas city council records show councillors raised concerns about the use of corporate purchase cards in 2005 and 2006. In February 2006, council considered a proposal for a forensic audit of purchase-card accounts from 2003 to 2005, including the mayor's account.

Council later established a Corporate Credit Card Committee to examine the issue. By July 2006, the city's treasurer told council there were no outstanding matters requiring reimbursement to the city.
Kohler told CBC News that his use of a city-issued purchase card involved an honest mistake and that he repaid the money immediately.
"After 20 years, I think a lot of people are unfamiliar with this scandal and why this all happened," Janzen said. "So I finally put my name in on the last day."
Janzen said his campaign is about more than the issue involving the credit-card system.
He doesn't want job creation to rely too heavily on the battery plant, and wants the city to continue working to attract other employers.
Janzen also believes greater transparency is needed at City Hall, including simpler ways for residents to stay informed about municipal decisions.
He's hoping his working-class background will resonate with voters.

"I'm like most people in St. Thomas," he said. "When I think of my work ... it's not white-collar, it's not photo opportunities. I know that's part of the job of mayor, but I think that what it brings to the table is just a very normal experience for most people that live in St. Thomas."
In addition to the three mayoral hopefuls, the list of certified candidates running for city councillor and school trustee can be found on the city's website.
Voters will head to the polls on Oct. 26.

Frederick also believes his age is an advantage in the race.
"I think being a younger person running for this position is helping the younger folks realize that our problems matter," he said. "The things we're facing do matter and that we can make a change."
Jeff Kohler
Jeff Kohler was Mayor of St. Thomas from 2003-2006, and currently serves as a city counsellor. (Submitted by Jeff Kohler)
Raised in St. Thomas from the age of five, Kohler is a familiar face at City Hall.
He served as mayor from 2003 to 2006 and currently serves as a city councillor.
Kohler says he is running because he can offer what he describes as "capable, local, proven leadership."

"The conditions have been set in St. Thomas and the future is looking bright regardless of the national and provincial trends," he said. "And effective leadership and capacity is what St. Thomas needs and what the residents are looking for."
The next four years will require fiscal responsibility, he said, adding that the city needs to ensure money is spent wisely and within its municipal mandate.
Kohler is also pointing to his experience in local politics, his involvement in decisions that he says helped bring the city to where it is today, and his relationships with city staff.
He says the city's strategic plans would continue under his leadership, rather than "just go on a shelf and get dusty."
That includes the city's goal of eliminating homelessness by 2027.
"We're one of the only municipalities that's actually been able to reduce it...we're proud of that, and we're hopefully going to be able to achieve that goal and continue that."
Corey Janzen
Corey Janzen filed his nomination papers on the last day with the goal of raising awareness of a 20-year-old City Hall scandal. (Submitted by Corey Janzen)
Corey Janzen is a lifelong St. Thomas resident who has spent the past 20 years working as a truck driver. (Submitted by Corey Janzen)
Corey Janzen, a lifelong St. Thomas resident of Mennonite heritage, has spent the past 20 years working as a truck driver.
He says he decided to run to offer voters an alternative to the other candidates.

When Janzen saw Kohler was entering the race, he says he also wanted to draw attention to a controversy involving the city's corporate credit-card system during Kohler's previous term as mayor in the early 2000s.

St. Thomas city council records show councillors raised concerns about the use of corporate purchase cards in 2005 and 2006. In February 2006, council considered a proposal for a forensic audit of purchase-card accounts from 2003 to 2005, including the mayor's account.

Council later established a Corporate Credit Card Committee to examine the issue. By July 2006, the city's treasurer told council there were no outstanding matters requiring reimbursement to the city.
Kohler told CBC News that his use of a city-issued purchase card involved an honest mistake and that he repaid the money immediately.
"After 20 years, I think a lot of people are unfamiliar with this scandal and why this all happened," Janzen said. "So I finally put my name in on the last day."
Janzen said his campaign is about more than the issue involving the credit-card system.
He doesn't want job creation to rely too heavily on the battery plant, and wants the city to continue working to attract other employers.
Janzen also believes greater transparency is needed at City Hall, including simpler ways for residents to stay informed about municipal decisions.
He's hoping his working-class background will resonate with voters.

"I'm like most people in St. Thomas," he said. "When I think of my work ... it's not white-collar, it's not photo opportunities. I know that's part of the job of mayor, but I think that what it brings to the table is just a very normal experience for most people that live in St. Thomas."
In addition to the three mayoral hopefuls, the list of certified candidates running for city councillor and school trustee can be found on the city's website.
Voters will head to the polls on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Toronto couple say Trump birthright citizenship law cost them their surrogate pregnancy
stories.summary: It could be the "collapse" of the U.S. surrogacy industry because a lot of agencies are primarily helping international would-be parents.
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
Renee and her husband had endured a decade of exhausting efforts to start a family, including multiple fruitless treatments and medical issues that seemed to make pregnancy impossible.

Then this April the Toronto couple’s ordeal seemed finally to be heading for a happy ending. An American agency had found a surrogate mother in the States to carry their longed-for baby, and the surrogate even visited the would-be parents in Toronto.

Four months later, Donald Trump in effect put an end to the arrangement.

The president was actually pursuing his goal of limiting so-called birthright citizenship. He issued an executive order that included a section barring American officials from issuing passports to babies carried by U.S. surrogates for international clients.

Such documents are crucial to foreign “intended parents” taking their newborns home and without them travel would be more complicated and time-consuming, experts in the field say. There are also fears the parents themselves could be refused entry to the U.S. under another executive order. As a result, some of the American surrogacy agencies suspended their international business altogether.

The company Renee and her husband used refunded the hefty fee they had paid – even though the firm was “very out of pocket” – and left them to start all over again.

“It’s certainly been a setback,” said the 44-year-old lawyer, who asked that her full name be withheld for privacy reasons. ”While it’s disappointing, we have quite a bit of practice in accepting bad news.”

The couple are not alone. The head of one prominent Canadian surrogacy agency says over 100 intended parents from Canada and other countries have contacted her in the last few weeks after the White House edict indirectly quashed their U.S. arrangements.

Trump's latest trade actions are not 'an escalation,' economist says

Diana Fox Carney says she realizes the personal 'opportunity' offered by her husband's position

The agencies in many cases refunded fees that typically run over $200,000, said Sally Rhoads-Heinrich of Surrogacy in Canada Online. A judge recently issued an injunction halting the White House measures, but an appeal seems likely. Coupled with some states banning international surrogacy in part or entirely, the development could deliver a sharp blow to the U.S. business – and the foreigners who use it, said Rhoads-Heinrich.

“If you look on any of the U.S. (online surrogacy) professionals groups, they’re scared,” Rhoads-Heinrich said. “They’re saying it could be the collapse of the U.S. surrogacy industry because there are a lot of agencies that are primarily helping internationals.”

Close to a third of surrogate arrangements in the States involve out-of-country parents, according to a 2024 study from Georgia’s Emory University.

Many such clients are now pivoting to Canada – where surrogates can’t charge commercial fees and the costs for parents are much lower – but the pool of “gestational carriers” here is way too small to meet the demand, said Rhoads-Heinrich.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis did not respond to questions about the surrogacy situation, but repeated an earlier criticism of the recent judgment halting the executive order.

“This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda,” she said.

American surrogacy agencies contacted by the National Post did not respond to requests for comment.

Most U.S. states allow commercial surrogacy, meaning more women become surrogates there and the wait time for parents who can afford to “match” with one is in the months, not years as in Canada.

The recent trouble essentially began in January 2025 when Trump tried to curb the right of any baby born in the U.S. to citizenship. The country’s Supreme Court overturned the policy this June, noting that the right is enshrined in the 14th amendment of the U.S. constitution.

That decision prompted the administration to issue the new orders on Aug. 6. One said that several categories of babies – including those born to surrogates for international clients – would be denied passports and other citizenship documents. Another said parents who were engaging in “birth tourism” by having a baby in the States just to win the child citizenship could be refused entry.

Tifany Markee, a lawyer who advises U.S. surrogacy agencies, said she has yet to hear of any newborn being refused a passport. But if that were to happen, the orders would make getting out of the U.S. much more difficult, likely forcing the parents to obtain a passport from their own nation for a child born in the States, and requiring American agencies to engage with unfamiliar foreign laws, said Markee, of Kansas City-based Foster and Bloom Family Formation Law Group.

As a result, several have proactively chosen to at least temporarily halt their international surrogacies, she confirmed.

“It makes travel more complicated,” said Markee of the orders’ potential impact. “Fundamentally, that’s what these families care about more than anything. It’s not really about the citizenship. It’s about their ability to then travel out of the U.S. and come home.”

That 2024 study suggested that 32 per cent of surrogacy clients in the States are from out of the country, about 41 per cent of those from China, followed by France and Spain at nine per cent each, with Canada also a significant source of intended parents.

Meanwhile, Renee’s hopes have recently been raised again. Another American agency told the couple it is willing to take them on and match them with a surrogate, despite the upheaval around Trump’s policy.

They turned to the U.S. in the first place after years of fertility treatments and medical complications in Toronto, then being told by Canadian surrogacy agencies that the average wait time was more than three years and could be as long as six. With both husband and wife now middle-aged and their parents aging, they decided time was of the essence and were fortunate enough to be able to go the more expensive American route.

But even if the episode does end happily for the couple, Renee has a beef with Canadian law in the area. Surrogates here can only ask for their receipted expenses to be repaid, a requirement of legislation that seeks to keep “assisted human reproduction” non-commercial.

Renee said surrogates should be paid commercial fees, not only to increase the pool of gestational carriers as fertility rates in Canada decline, but to properly compensate the women for an arduous task.

“If you asked 100 men ‘Would you ever consider carrying a pregnancy for someone and not be compensated for that?’ – I don’t think you’d find even one,” she said. “Our government has what I think is a very archaic and antiquated way of viewing this issue. There is a way to do this that makes sense where people aren’t being exploited … You can have a win, win, win.”

stories.title: Concerns over growth, traffic shaping the race in Ward 3 - CBC.CA
stories.summary: Peter Cuddy is running for re-election in Ward 3, an east London ward where residents are dealing with higher rental costs and growing traffic concerns.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Peter Cuddy is running for re-election in Ward 3, an east London ward where residents are dealing with higher rental costs and growing traffic concerns.
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 10
For Coun. Peter Cuddy, the calls from Ward 3 residents over the past four years, and now on the campaign trail, have run the full gamut.
There are frequent questions about the obstacle course of construction projects spread across a suburban ward that's tucked into London's northeast end, and includes the airport and Fanshawe College.
There were calls about the state of downtown and questions about why there is no London Transit bus service to many of the ward's neighbourhoods, such as Cedar Hollow.
Got a minute? Tell us what changes you want to see in London, Ont., and area this election
Cuddy, who is running for re-election in a field of six candidates, says despite the challenges he's comfortable defending his record ahead of the Oct. 26 vote.
"I'm grateful to see so many candidates in the race," said Cuddy. "I work hard for my constituents and that's what I've done for four years."
Cuddy points to his work on London's renoviction bylaw, which makes it more difficult for landlords to use renovations as a way to remove long-term tenants.
He attended a 2023 protest by residents facing eviction from a group of apartments on Webster Street.

In one incident captured by CBC News cameras, Cuddy intervened during a confrontation between a tenant and a security staffer working for the landlord. The confrontation threatened to become physical and police were eventually called.
"I think it's an excellent bylaw," said Cuddy. "These people, many of them are on Odsp and can't handle a rent increase."

Cuddy is also touting his vote to expand the urban growth boundary, which opens up some areas of the ward to development. While the London Plan calls for "inward and upward growth," Cuddy says the boundary had to be expanded.

"We would have people in Ilderton or Strathroy or Komoka and driving into the city, using services here and then going back home and paying taxes in their communities," he said. "We have to have responsible, sustainable development."
While Cuddy points to his record, his opponents say they can do better.
Among them is videographer Ben Durham, 32, who says expanding the growth boundary will lead to a loss of farmland and add to the city's servicing costs. He's made a detailed YouTube video about it.

"It's the most fertile land in most of world and we're paving it over when we have land banking going on in the city," he said. Land banking happens when developers intentionally don't build on land parcels with the intention of building later when land values are higher.
"We need to continue growing, but we have so much land within the boundary we don't need to expand it further," said Durham
Durham, who is using a cargo e-bike to do his canvassing, wants better separation on streets between vehicles and bikes.
Another challenger in Ward 3 is 27-year-old Zak Rahim, who says a key issue is slowing down traffic in residential areas and near schools.
Rahim met with CBC News on Oakville Avenue, a residential street north of Huron Street where traffic has been a problem. It's on an LTC bus route and also serves Chippewa Public School.
"There's street parking on both sides of the road, and often there is congestion and safety issues," said Rahim, who said the congestion is worst during school drop-off times.

"Because of the lack of traffic calming on this street, parents don't feel safe letting their kids walk to school, so we have an increase in traffic," he said. Rahim has been working on a traffic-calming petition for the street, but said the city hall process for getting traffic-calming measures approved is too slow. It's a complaint CBC News has reported about before.
Speed bump approval process too slow for Aldersbrook resident
"When the local councillor understands the complaints of the neighbourhood, we should speed up this process," said Rahim.
This is Rahim's first run for elected office after helping on many other political campaigns, including Cuddy's last election. Asked if that's awkward, Rahim said he'd rather focus on the issues.
A trustee with the Thames Valley District School Board, Leroy Osbourne is also making traffic management a key part of his campaign as he looks to switch over to city council.
Osbourne said he witnessed a T-bone collision on Fanshawe Park Road while canvassing a month ago.
"Making a left turn onto Fanshawe Park Road, it's unsafe," said Osbourne, who works in student affairs at Yorkville University, an online school for graduate students.
Osbourne said many of the voters he's speaking with are worried about housing stability and affordability.

The last council approved a residential property tax increase of about six per cent averaged over the four years. Josh Morgan has vowed to hold tax increases in the three per cent range if he's re-elected as mayor.

On housing, Osbourne wants the city to take a closer look at miniature homes for people priced out of the market for starter homes. Under this model, the city would own the land while the buyer can get a starter home in the $200,000 range.
Other candidates in the race who weren't available include Harkirat Kaur, whose campaign website is here and Riya Philip, whose campaign information is here.
Voters in Ward 3 head to the polls on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Carney’s cabinet meets in Banff as Trump escalates trade war
stories.summary: Trump lashed out again Tuesday by signing executive orders to ban certain Canadian imports later this month, including alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is gathering his cabinet today and Friday in the mountain resort town of Banff, Alta., for closed-door meetings as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war intensifies.

Trump lashed out again Tuesday by signing executive orders to ban certain Canadian imports later this month, including alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products.

The latest tit-for-tat comes after Ottawa levied tens of billions of dollars in counter-tariffs on the United States.

That came after bilateral trade talks broke down at the eleventh hour and Trump pushed ahead with new duties on Canadian products.

The cabinet retreat comes as the Liberal government plans its agenda for the fall sitting of Parliament in less than two weeks.

Carney’s office says ministers at the retreat will hear from guest speakers on the economy, Indigenous partnerships and international affairs in closed-door sessions.

stories.title: Police to share update on probe into stabbing at Edmonton Sikh temple
stories.summary: Police in Edmonton will hold a news conference Thursday afternoon on their probe into the stabbing of two worshippers at a Sikh temple in the city’s northeast.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police have laid charges against a 27-year-old man after two worshippers were stabbed last month at a Sikh temple on the northeastern outskirts of Edmonton.

The attack on Friday, Aug. 21 happened during early morning prayers at the Nanaksar gurdwara — a large, white, ornate Sikh temple along Manning Drive between Edmonton and Fort Saskatchewan.

Police responded just after 5 a.m. to the stabbings at the gurdwara near 14 Street and Horsehill Road, where officers arrested a man.

Police said the man had been let out of prison elsewhere in Alberta the day prior.

Nanaksar Gurdwara Gursikh Temple staff said both victims, men ages 75 and 51, would recover.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the attack.

Police said the accused had been in prison for aggravated assault and assault on a peace officer, and has a history of violence .

2:06 Man with history of violence arrested after 2 worshippers stabbed at Edmonton Sikh temple

Court documents show the accused was sentenced to 28 months behind bars for aggravated assault in December 2024, and a few days later in a different court case was sentenced to six months for assaulting a peace officer.

On the day of the attack, Edmonton Police Service Chief Warren Driechel said the accused was released after serving about 20 months of a 31-month sentence. He was supposed to report to a halfway house in Edmonton, but did not.

2:29 Immigrant groups say racism increasing in Alberta, is linked to independence referendum

While charges were announced Thursday, police said the matter of if the it was a terror attack or hate crime continues to be investigated.

“This investigation is complex and involves numerous investigative steps that we are still diligently working to complete,” said Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart with the EPS Investigations Branch.

Police said the EPS Investigative Response Team and the Hate Crimes Unit continue its ongoing assessment of any evidence relevant to the application of hate-related criminal provisions.

“We want to thank everyone for their cooperation and patience and on behalf of the Gurdwara, kindly ask the media and public to give their community space and privacy at this time.”

Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, is charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm, possession of a weapon and mischief.

Sim-Pelletier is next set to appear at the Edmonton law courts on Sept. 18.

stories.title: With hundreds of planes in the air on 9/11, Canada had minutes to respond
stories.summary: Officials had to tell about 270 planes to turn around and go back across the Atlantic to Europe. The remaining planes had to land somewhere fast
stories.author: Sarah Smellie
stories.content:
As hijackers slammed two planes into the World Trade Center in New York City 25 years ago, there were hundreds of other aircraft in the sky. The usual round of early flights had taken off from Europe, carrying thousands of passengers over the Western half of the North Atlantic region, off the Canadian coast.

David Collenette was speaking to a crowd at an international conference of airport executives in Montreal when a staff member slipped him a note saying there’d been a tragedy and he had to wrap up his speech. Then Canada’s transportation minister, he raced back to Ottawa as hijackers slammed a third plane into the Pentagon in Washington. A fourth crashed in a Pennsylvania field.

When the United States shut down its airspace that morning, there were about 500 planes in the air over the Western North Atlantic, with an estimated 85,000 people on board, Collenette said in a recent interview. A plane was entering Canadian airspace every 90 seconds, he said.

“We had to make a decision on the spot,” Collenette said. “We had no hours. This was minutes.”

On Thursday, Collenette will be in Gander, N.L., where 38 planes landed on Sept. 11, 2001, and the town of about 9,000 people dropped everything to care for some 6,500 passengers stranded there for days. He’ll be sharing his story at an event called “Untold Stories” at the Gander International Airport, ahead of a 9/11 commemoration ceremony on Friday.

The event is among many planned across Canada to remember the nearly 3,000 people who were killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks, and to honour the unquestioning support Canadians offered to their American allies.

“We’re there for a solemn reason, but we’re also there to celebrate the goodwill of Canadians,” Collenette said. “It just showed that Canadians could all come together.”

Back in Ottawa on Sept. 11, 2001, it was immediately clear that Canada had to shut down its airspace, too, the former minister said. Officials had to tell about 270 planes to turn around and go back across the Atlantic to Europe. The remaining planes – more than 230 – had to land somewhere fast, Collenette said. Many were directed to Atlantic Canada, where there are several Second World War-era airports with large runways, he said. Others were sent to large, central cities such as Montreal and Vancouver.

Collenette said he is still struck by how quickly people across the aviation community and the country worked together to land all the planes and keep all their passengers safe.

“Nobody disputed the orders given by our air traffic controllers to return to Europe or to land in Gander, N.L., or Stephenville, N.L., or Moncton, N.B., or Halifax,” he said.

“And nobody at the time said, ’Look, we got all these people, it’s gonna cost a lot of money,’” he added. “That’s what the remarkable thing was. People … opened their homes. They opened their fridges. They cooked. They donated.”

Gander’s story stands out because of its size, he said: the town’s population almost doubled when all those planes landed, and every person was taken care of. But people across Canada took care of stranded passengers, just as people in Gander did, he said.

In Toronto, the U.S. Consulate is hosting an exhibition of pen-and-ink drawings by Canadian artist John Coburn, which he created at Ground Zero and throughout New York City following the 9/11 attacks. The show is called “25 Years of Healing Hearts: A Tribute to 9/11 in Drawings.”

In British Columbia, a cross-border memorial ceremony is planned on Friday at the Peace Arch border park in Surrey. Expected guests include New York police officers, a firefighter and paramedic who served on 9/11. U.S. Homeland Security helicopters are scheduled to do a flypast.

Organizers say they expect hundreds of Canadian and American first responders, and military and border officers to attend.

The International Peace Garden in Manitoba is also holding a memorial event with officials from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol and the Canada Border Services Agency. North Dakota Parks and Recreation representatives are also expected, alongside members of the United Fire Fighters of Winnipeg.

stories.title: From Haiti to Canada, a Quebec debut novel reaches for France’s top literary prizes
stories.summary: For a Quebec writer — especially a debut novelist — the recognition is highly unusual, said Michel Lacroix, a professor of literary studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
When Thélyson Orélien learned that his first novel had made it on a shortlist for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt, he thought about two places: Haiti, where he was born, and Quebec, where he says his life as a writer truly began.

“It’s difficult to take in, to be honest,” Orélien told The Canadian Press from Paris, where he was on a press tour following the announcement. “Humanly, it’s dizzying.”

His fiction novel, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying,” is among 16 books on the initial shortlist for the Goncourt, one of the most important prizes in French-language literature.

The novel follows a Haitian man named Jonas Dorléon, who is forced to leave his country and undertake a perilous journey through the Americas.

For a Quebec writer — especially a debut novelist — the recognition is highly unusual, said Michel Lacroix, a professor of literary studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal.

The book has also recently been shortlisted for two other prestigious French literature prizes: the Femina and the Renaudot.

“It’s extremely rare, almost unheard of in the history of Quebec literature,” Lacroix said.

Orélien, who left Haiti for Quebec after the devastating 2010 earthquake, said the recognition he is getting is also providing an opportunity to put a human face on migrants at a time when they find themselves at the centre of intense political debates.

Born in Gonaïves in 1988, Orélien was already writing poetry before arriving in Quebec.

He said his experience of leaving Haiti and the stories of other migrants helped shape the novel, although he noted that Jonas Dorléon’s story was a fictional account.

The book’s main character is a history and geography teacher and a poet living in Port-au-Prince. He does not begin the novel as a migrant. But he becomes one when he is forced to flee his home due to escalating civil unrest and violence.

“Before being a migrant, he is a person,” Orélien said of his protagonist. “You become a migrant in the eyes of others,” he said. “You become a migrant on paper. You become a migrant at the borders you cross.”

The protagonist’s journey takes him from the Dominican Republic and South and Central America, including the dangerous Darién Gap, before he eventually reaches the United States to make his way to Quebec.

Along the way, the professor takes on identities imposed by circumstances and by the people around him, in what Orélien describes as a “slow erosion of the self.”

But the book’s main character remains the man he was before he left — with memories, desires, and a history.

“That doesn’t disappear because you’ve crossed a border,” Orélien said.

That distinction resonated with a Haitian mother who arrived in Quebec in the winter of 2026 after fleeing her country with her young daughter.

The woman said becoming a migrant can mean being seen differently by those around you. The Canadian Press interviewed the Haitian mother several times before and after she arrived in Quebec and agreed not to name her because she was afraid going public could affect her daughter’s life in Canada.

“You’re almost no longer considered a person in your own right. You’re more of a statistic,” she said.

Her journey was different from Orélien’s character. She first fled Haiti for the United States before eventually crossing the Canadian border on foot with her daughter during a chilly winter night.

In the book, the protagonist was able to cross into Canada through the Roxham Road, which closed in 2023.

But ”changes to the migration trajectory of migrants won’t prevent people from coming,” believes Frantz André, a retired businessman who founded a Montreal-based migrant advocacy group.

”When people don’t have a choice, they will find a way to cross borders, whether it’s done legally or irregularly,” said André.

These issues, featured in the book, are now on one of the biggest stages in French literature after making it onto the Goncourt shortlist.

Orélien said he was trying not to think about whether it will advance further. The 16-book list will be narrowed twice before the prize is awarded in early November.

For Orélien, what matters most is whether it changes the way readers see the people whose experiences it depicts.

“Literature isn’t there to replace political debate or to say what public policies should be adopted. That’s not its role,” he said. “But I think it can put a human being back where public debate sometimes ends up seeing only a category.”

Twenty-six countries have acquired the rights to the book, which is currently being translated into 22 languages, including English.
