stories.title: Can Tiff navigate a global film industry facing a ‘turning point’?
stories.summary: The pressure is rising for Toronto to deliver a festival that has real impact
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
If it feels as if the Toronto International Film Festival is on the precipice of existential change, that’s partly because the entire industry is.

This past Monday, smack in the middle of the Venice and Telluride film festivals and three days before Tiff opens its 51st edition, more than 200 film-sector heavyweights from around the world – Tiff chief executive Cameron Bailey among them – gathered in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, for the inaugural Lumière Summit.

The confab organized by the French government was formed to address how, as France’s national film board chief Gaëtan Bruel put it, “our entire image-based civilization is at a turning point. How we create, produce, distribute, watch and pass on stories is changing profoundly, with consequences for individuals and societies alike.”

While the one-day conference opened with a serious rainfall of cash (France and South Korea pledged to jointly fund a €1-billion initiative to support the global screen sector, a pact that is open to any other country), there wasn’t much in the way of concrete answers to the most vexing issues of our moment: consolidation, artificial intelligence, cultural sovereignty. And it is just as unlikely that 11 days of Tiff will provide any tidy solutions.

But if festival organizers want Tiff to continue to have a seat at the global table, then the success of this year’s edition feels more weighted with consequence than ever before.

It all starts, fairly or not, with Tiff’s programming – and fortunately, this year already feels like a marked improvement over the last .

With the caveat that even a festival of Toronto’s massive size and scale – 294 titles this edition, including shorts and series – cannot possibly program every buzzy title out there, Tiff’s lineup has just about everything that a demanding audience could possibly desire.

The experimental Wavelengths program has been restored to proper size after 2025’s regrettable reduction . The Canadian lineup is promising, including new work from both fresh faces and such mainstays as Michael Dowse and Sophie Deraspe. And then there are all the hotly anticipated Oscar-tipped films, including new work from Martin McDonagh ( Wild Horse Nine ), Jesse Eisenberg ( The Debut ), Danny Boyle ( Ink ), Chris Rock ( Misty Green ), Mike Leigh ( Tender Loving Care ), Lee Chang-dong ( Possible Love ), plus almost every notable title from this past spring’s edition of Cannes – the gang’s all here, minus a Nathan Fielder movie or two.

Yet what about the films that are not only skipping Toronto, but also bypassing every other festival? A sizable wave of ostensibly fest-flavoured titles – Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning , Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Tom Cruise vehicle Digger , Taika Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun , David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Robert Eggers’s Werwulf , Georgia Oakley’s new version of Sense and Sensibility – are sitting out the entire circuit, from Venice through London.

We can blame increasingly cost-conscious Hollywood executives who don’t see the value in spending dump trucks’ worth of money to send celebrities to festivals when they can instead pay influencers a pittance to spread the good word. Just as studios are increasingly skittish about debuting their high-profile titles in front of unpredictable critics months before they have the chance to control the marketing narrative.

Either way, following the dearth of U.S. films from this past spring’s edition of Cannes and Warner Bros. holding its eventual Best Picture winner One Battle After Another from any festival run last fall, the festival landscape is undoubtedly shifting .

The big question is whether Tiff – which has spent the past decade building its brand around the red-carpet allure of celebrity, and not always in tandem with the quality of the films they’re presenting – will try to grasp onto something that is slipping away, or embrace an altogether new model.

Part of that answer might be found in this year’s launch of Tiff: The Market , a seven-day event running parallel to the festival that gathers buyers, sellers and creators under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre.

Designed to fill a presumed gap in the global industry calendar between Berlin’s European Film Market in February, the Marché du Film in Cannes every May, and L.A.’s American Film Market in November, Tiff’s new initiative marks the organization’s single biggest undertaking since the opening of its Lightbox headquarters 16 years ago.

This includes $23-million in federal support, which will expire March 31, 2027, requiring the Market to be self-sufficient going forward. (Although few in Toronto or Ottawa expect that Prime Minister Mark Carney will not provide some level of renewed funding, given this timely moment for cultural sovereignty.)

Talk to enough industry players about the market, and you’ll get the sense that most desperately want the event to succeed – they just aren’t sure how Toronto can pull it off.

For starters, the original purpose of a physical market feels rooted in the past. The era of the overnight festival bidding war, for instance, and the hot-house environment that it spawned for all levels of deal-making, is now gone, largely owing to the rise of deep-pocketed streaming giants, which come in with fat cheques for worldwide rights and quash any sense of genuine competition.

Meanwhile, the lower-scale, multiterritory negotiations that still take place between producers and distributors now stretch into months-long discussions, the dragged-out timeline making it difficult to pin success to any one single market. The back-to-school timing of Tiff also doesn’t help, given that many European and U.S. players take the summers off, and will come into Toronto without having had much time to regroup.

Finally, the industry’s biggest buyers have been flying into Tiff to conduct business on the festival’s sidelines for ages – no official convention floor or costly delegate badges or pavilions required. What incentivizes them to play into that game now, especially in this moment of belt-tightening?

In an interview with The Globe a few weeks before opening night, Bailey said the market’s success will be measured in terms of “how many people are showing up to do business, how many delegate badges we sell, how many stands are on the floor of the convention centre, how many market screenings we’ve sold – we have about 230 market-only screenings available, and they’re nearly all gone.”

Ultimately, though, the real test for the market will be not just gauging the energy on the floor, but whether delegates leave it feeling that they received a solid return on their investment.

This includes the many emerging or mid-level Canadian producers and creators who, not having much experience with how Cannes or Berlin operate, have been sold a certain air of expectation by Tiff. And though Tiff has invited hundreds of international buyers who either haven’t been to Toronto before or stopped coming years ago – with the festival subsidizing travel and accommodation for some – will the newbies find it a useful enough experience to pay their own way going forward? The festival needs plenty of repeat customers if it hopes to grow delegate attendance from 6,000 in this first year to 12,000 by 2030.

Already, the market has claimed its first aggrieved party: the press.

With Tiff now requiring more screens to run private market showings for buyers, the number of press screenings for most of the titles in the festival itself has been limited to just one per film, whereas in the past it was typically two, allowing a certain level of flexibility for harried members of the media. Understandably, there are only so many screens available around Tiff’s King West stomping grounds. But if you want critics and reporters on your side, perhaps don’t alienate them before the festival even begins, let alone compel them to treat each screening like its own individual edition of the Hunger Games.

Outside of the market, meanwhile, there are myriad other challenges.

Does Tiff’s marketing department genuinely want the organization’s brand to be associated with a chintzy 50/50 raffle that’s hawked throughout the festival? How about TikTok, whose short-form video platform feels anathema to the “transformative” art that the festival presumes to be championing? And by hosting AI-focused panels at the market, including one event from the leading generative-video platform Kling AI, is Tiff tacitly endorsing the slop-ified technology, which is rightly loathed by the organization’s base?

Then there are the increasingly tense geopolitics that surround international cinema, an issue that no festival has been able to swerve around. After last year’s back-and-forth debacle over the Oct. 7 documentary The Road Between Us , how will Tiff leadership approach the inevitable discourse over the politics nestled inside this year’s lineup, which includes the Israeli film Our Loves (which dramatizes the Oct. 7 attacks) alongside a handful of Palestinian films such as Thirteen in Gaza (which follows life inside a refugee camp)?

On that front, Bailey told The Globe that “the lesson I’ve learned is that it is more important than ever to keep a space open to find films and select them based on quality and relevance to our audience, and to keep a space open for those films to be seen for their quality and their relevance – to be talked about and discussed as we’ve done for five decades.”

In terms of year-round finances, Tiff seems to be building on momentum coming out of the strike-plagued 2023 edition, when it faced a $6.6-million deficit. After ending its 2024 fiscal year with an excess of $3.1-million in revenue over expenses, the organization closed out 2025 with a surplus of $4.4-million – although a sizable portion of that was due to a 158-per-cent jump in federal funding, from $3.6-million in 2024 to $9.3-million the following year. (At the same time, Tiff saw its salary expenses rise 17 per cent, due to the launch of the Market.)

There are hopeful long-term signs, though, found in the Lightbox’s year-round box-office receipts, which are seemingly benefitting from the larger postpandemic rebound in moviegoing, especially among younger audiences.

According to data obtained by The Globe, the Lightbox’s 2025 year-round box office, outside of the festival, came in at just more than $1.6-million, the theatre’s highest annual gross since 2018. And theatrical revenue for 2026 appears to be keeping pace so far, with top performers including Park Chan-wook’s thriller No Other Choice and Jane Schoenbrun’s meta-slasher Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , the latter of which Tiff wisely programmed alongside a mini-retrospective of the director’s work.

“Our current strategy plan, which we’re smack in the middle of, has three pillars: relevance, reach and performance,” Bailey said. “Relevance is the market piece. The reach pillar is continuing to engage a young audience and expanding things we do like the Next Wave Festival. And performance is making sure we’re working as effectively as possible within our staff, our systems, to deliver the other two pillars. And we’ve seen results.”

It is of course easy to criticize and fret about Tiff before the latest edition of the festival has opened. Just as the larger industry faces one battle after another, so, too, can everyone involved in the Tiff ecosystem come together to offer one, two, or a thousand victories.

As always, the film world is watching – here’s hoping Toronto will put on a show they’ll remember.

Either way, following the dearth of U.S. films from this past spring’s edition of Cannes and Warner Bros. holding its eventual Best Picture winner One Battle After Another from any festival run last fall, the festival landscape is undoubtedly shifting .

The big question is whether Tiff – which has spent the past decade building its brand around the red-carpet allure of celebrity, and not always in tandem with the quality of the films they’re presenting – will try to grasp onto something that is slipping away, or embrace an altogether new model.

Part of that answer might be found in this year’s launch of Tiff: The Market , a seven-day event running parallel to the festival that gathers buyers, sellers and creators under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre.

Designed to fill a presumed gap in the global industry calendar between Berlin’s European Film Market in February, the Marché du Film in Cannes every May, and L.A.’s American Film Market in November, Tiff’s new initiative marks the organization’s single biggest undertaking since the opening of its Lightbox headquarters 16 years ago.

This includes $23-million in federal support, which will expire March 31, 2027, requiring the Market to be self-sufficient going forward. (Although few in Toronto or Ottawa expect that Prime Minister Mark Carney will not provide some level of renewed funding, given this timely moment for cultural sovereignty.)
Talk to enough industry players about the market, and you’ll get the sense that most desperately want the event to succeed – they just aren’t sure how Toronto can pull it off.

For starters, the original purpose of a physical market feels rooted in the past. The era of the overnight festival bidding war, for instance, and the hot-house environment that it spawned for all levels of deal-making, is now gone, largely owing to the rise of deep-pocketed streaming giants, which come in with fat cheques for worldwide rights and quash any sense of genuine competition.

Meanwhile, the lower-scale, multiterritory negotiations that still take place between producers and distributors now stretch into months-long discussions, the dragged-out timeline making it difficult to pin success to any one single market. The back-to-school timing of Tiff also doesn’t help, given that many European and U.S. players take the summers off, and will come into Toronto without having had much time to regroup.

Finally, the industry’s biggest buyers have been flying into Tiff to conduct business on the festival’s sidelines for ages – no official convention floor or costly delegate badges or pavilions required. What incentivizes them to play into that game now, especially in this moment of belt-tightening?

In an interview with The Globe a few weeks before opening night, Bailey said the market’s success will be measured in terms of “how many people are showing up to do business, how many delegate badges we sell, how many stands are on the floor of the convention centre, how many market screenings we’ve sold – we have about 230 market-only screenings available, and they’re nearly all gone.”
Ultimately, though, the real test for the market will be not just gauging the energy on the floor, but whether delegates leave it feeling that they received a solid return on their investment.

This includes the many emerging or mid-level Canadian producers and creators who, not having much experience with how Cannes or Berlin operate, have been sold a certain air of expectation by Tiff. And though Tiff has invited hundreds of international buyers who either haven’t been to Toronto before or stopped coming years ago – with the festival subsidizing travel and accommodation for some – will the newbies find it a useful enough experience to pay their own way going forward? The festival needs plenty of repeat customers if it hopes to grow delegate attendance from 6,000 in this first year to 12,000 by 2030.
Already, the market has claimed its first aggrieved party: the press.

With Tiff now requiring more screens to run private market showings for buyers, the number of press screenings for most of the titles in the festival itself has been limited to just one per film, whereas in the past it was typically two, allowing a certain level of flexibility for harried members of the media. Understandably, there are only so many screens available around Tiff’s King West stomping grounds. But if you want critics and reporters on your side, perhaps don’t alienate them before the festival even begins, let alone compel them to treat each screening like its own individual edition of the Hunger Games.
Outside of the market, meanwhile, there are myriad other challenges.

Does Tiff’s marketing department genuinely want the organization’s brand to be associated with a chintzy 50/50 raffle that’s hawked throughout the festival? How about TikTok, whose short-form video platform feels anathema to the “transformative” art that the festival presumes to be championing? And by hosting AI-focused panels at the market, including one event from the leading generative-video platform Kling AI, is Tiff tacitly endorsing the slop-ified technology, which is rightly loathed by the organization’s base?

Then there are the increasingly tense geopolitics that surround international cinema, an issue that no festival has been able to swerve around. After last year’s back-and-forth debacle over the Oct. 7 documentary The Road Between Us , how will Tiff leadership approach the inevitable discourse over the politics nestled inside this year’s lineup, which includes the Israeli film Our Loves (which dramatizes the Oct. 7 attacks) alongside a handful of Palestinian films such as Thirteen in Gaza (which follows life inside a refugee camp)?

On that front, Bailey told The Globe that “the lesson I’ve learned is that it is more important than ever to keep a space open to find films and select them based on quality and relevance to our audience, and to keep a space open for those films to be seen for their quality and their relevance – to be talked about and discussed as we’ve done for five decades.”

In terms of year-round finances, Tiff seems to be building on momentum coming out of the strike-plagued 2023 edition, when it faced a $6.6-million deficit. After ending its 2024 fiscal year with an excess of $3.1-million in revenue over expenses, the organization closed out 2025 with a surplus of $4.4-million – although a sizable portion of that was due to a 158-per-cent jump in federal funding, from $3.6-million in 2024 to $9.3-million the following year. (At the same time, Tiff saw its salary expenses rise 17 per cent, due to the launch of the Market.)

There are hopeful long-term signs, though, found in the Lightbox’s year-round box-office receipts, which are seemingly benefitting from the larger postpandemic rebound in moviegoing, especially among younger audiences.

According to data obtained by The Globe, the Lightbox’s 2025 year-round box office, outside of the festival, came in at just more than $1.6-million, the theatre’s highest annual gross since 2018. And theatrical revenue for 2026 appears to be keeping pace so far, with top performers including Park Chan-wook’s thriller No Other Choice and Jane Schoenbrun’s meta-slasher Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , the latter of which Tiff wisely programmed alongside a mini-retrospective of the director’s work.

“Our current strategy plan, which we’re smack in the middle of, has three pillars: relevance, reach and performance,” Bailey said. “Relevance is the market piece. The reach pillar is continuing to engage a young audience and expanding things we do like the Next Wave Festival. And performance is making sure we’re working as effectively as possible within our staff, our systems, to deliver the other two pillars. And we’ve seen results.”

It is of course easy to criticize and fret about Tiff before the latest edition of the festival has opened. Just as the larger industry faces one battle after another, so, too, can everyone involved in the Tiff ecosystem come together to offer one, two, or a thousand victories.
As always, the film world is watching – here’s hoping Toronto will put on a show they’ll remember.

stories.title: Toronto-born Miku Martineau steps into her latest starring role on Netflix’s Crew Girl
stories.summary: Martineau plays a star rower forced to start over at an elite prep school
stories.author: Max Gao
stories.content:
Miku Martineau has quietly become one of Netflix’s most bankable leads. After making her feature film debut opposite Mary Elizabeth Winstead in 2021’s Kate , the Japanese-Canadian actor broke out as high-stakes gambler Yumeko in the international hit series Bet .

Now, Martineau steps into her latest starring role for the mega-streamer in Crew Girl (premiering Sept. 10), playing Teagan Tao – a star rower forced to start over at an elite prep school, where she becomes the coxswain of a dysfunctional all-boys team.

While set in the U.S., Crew Girl was shot in Victoria and Vancouver, with a predominantly Canadian cast and writing team. The series is part of a growing push for more Canadian-made productions designed for international audiences, giving Martineau plenty of reason to champion her home industry.

“The Canadian film industry deserves its flowers too, so I’m so happy and proud that it’s blooming, and I can’t wait to see it continue to grow,” Martineau said. Beyond celebrating local roots, however, she remains fiercely focused on helping to shift the landscape for Asian representation. “We live in such a diverse world, and we deserve media and entertainment to portray that in the correct way,” she said.

Born and raised in Toronto, Martineau still maintains strong ties to the city, where her father, Peter, owns the Beacher Cafe and her mother works alongside him as a waitress. On a recent video call from her home in the city, Martineau talked to The Globe and Mail about the surprisingly meta experience of learning to row for Crew Girl and how an abridged school production of The Wizard of Oz first planted the acting seed.

A lot of your past work fits into the sci-fi and fantasy genres, but Crew Girl feels much more grounded in the real world of classic teen dramas. What intrigued you the most about Teagan’s journey in this first season?

She’s a 16-year-old girl whose life just got completely turned upside down, so she’s kind of facing life as it comes at her. She’s navigating who she is, who her friends and romantic interests are, and her family dynamic, which is huge in the show. I think that’s something we all feel as teenagers when we’re trying to figure out who we are as individuals.

I also grew up playing so many sports – mainly gymnastics, hockey and volleyball, but also basketball, soccer, figure skating and dance. You learn really great qualities of resilience; you’re understanding how powerful your mind is and how strong you are. So I was like, “Oh, it would be really freeing to play a young woman who’s pursuing something she’s passionate about while also learning who she’ll be in this world.”

All of that sporting experience probably helped with your strength and conditioning, but you and your cast had actually never rowed prior to being cast on this show.

I have so much respect for rowers. It’s a sport that takes not just physical strength, but a lot of mental strength and coordination. During rowing training, all of us were becoming a crew. We’re all making this together, and it takes teamwork, patience and kindness, and those are all things that Teagan and her team are also learning in the show. That mirrored the real-life dynamic between me and my cast on a purely friendship level.

Crew Girl is surely going to be the next YA drama to ignite a fiery debate over a central love triangle, so I have to ask: Between arrogant team captain Josh (Sam Braun) and quiet underdog Cam (Kyle Clark), which team are you on?

I’m Team Teagan! I love the dynamics between Josh and Cam. Josh and Teagan are fiery, intense, passionate. She and Cam have more common ground of being the underdog, of wanting to prove themselves. She tries to get Cam to stand his ground a little bit more in the most positive way. So there’s great things about both of those guys – and they’re both studs. Come on! People are going to love them.

You grew up in the Beaches neighbourhood in Toronto without any connection to the entertainment industry. Did you always know that you were destined to be a performer?

When I was younger, I didn’t really watch that much TV or American cult classics. My dad is a very outdoorsy person. My mom immigrated from Japan, so we would watch a lot of [Hayao] Miyazaki movies. But I never really watched something and was like, “Oh wow, I want to do that.” It happened very naturally. I was a very imaginative kid.

I went to a very small elementary school, and we did this one play called Oz-some – our rendition of The Wizard of Oz . I was in Grade 3. Later in elementary school, I did something called show choir, which is the Canadian version of Pitch Perfect . I got a scholarship to go to this arts camp in New York City, and I also got a scholarship to go to Randolph [College for the Performing Arts in Toronto]. I did both of those two-to-three-week camps the summer right before high school, and I was like, “I love doing this.” I started taking workshops, and then through those workshops, I found my agent and booked Kate . Ever since then, I’ve been lucky enough to pursue this passion and also live a very normal life.

I’d imagine that part of that normalcy has to do with the fact that you could always go back and work at your family’s restaurant if acting doesn’t work out.

My brother’s a year and a half older than me, and he definitely worked there a lot more. I grew up with the restaurant being so embedded in my family. It’s not easy to own one restaurant – it’s a lot of work, labour, energy. I did not, respectfully, want to work there. I wanted to explore and try new things.

As one of the few Asian leads on Western television, do you feel a unique sense of responsibility in the roles you take on? How has your Japanese-Canadian heritage shaped that perspective and the stories you want to tell?

I’m just so proud to be a Japanese-Canadian actor. A common thing with younger people is that you just want to fit in, and growing up in a predominantly Caucasian neighbourhood, I definitely felt a little bit like an outlier, and I had insecurity surrounding my identity. But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized it is a huge part of who I am. It’s a huge part of why I have the work ethic that I do, why I have my positivity that I do. I love that I get to represent as an Asian actor in this industry because there was a time where we wouldn’t be getting the opportunities to be playing such a variety of characters.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: For First Nations, Trump’s lake renaming is much ado about Niiganii-gichigami
stories.summary: An American President can’t take away the name of a lake that was never his in the first place. Water can’t be owned. Water is alive
stories.author: Tanya Talaga
stories.content:
Lake Ontario is Niiganii-gichigami in the Anishinaabemowin language. Elders tell me the lake was always known as this.

But what, exactly, is in a name?

For First Nations people, I know that regardless of which community you are from, names have meaning. They can provide information, and signify respect. So when an American President renames a body of water on an angry whim by writing “Lake America” over “Lake Ontario” on a map with a marker, it means nothing to us – those who have lived here since before all these lines were drawn and borders created.

Mr. Trump loves to recolonize. He did it to the Gulf of Mexico in January, 2025, when he renamed it the Gulf of America. He also changed the name of the Alaskan mountain Denali, which had been reverted to that traditional Koyukon Athabascan name under Barack Obama, to Mount McKinley. But the Anishinaabeg have lived in and around the Great Lakes since well before Canada or America was a country. In Anishinaabemowin, the “Great Lakes” are Nayaano-nibiimaang gichigamiin : the five freshwater seas. Niiganii-gichigami, our name for Lake Ontario, translates to “the leading lake.” “Ontario,” meanwhile, comes from either Wendat or the Haudenosaunee word “kanadario,” referring to beautiful or sparkling water; the Haudenosaunee, the people of the long house, also live here, and the Wendat were an Iroquoian speaking nation.

My friend, Dehaeho:węhs Amos Key Jr., is a Faith Keeper from Six Nations of the Grand River in Ohsweken. When I asked him what Ontario means, he said: “When you study the etymology of our Haudenosaunee languages, and you add the suffix ‘ri:io to a word or phrase, it gives it the meaning of something being very precious, coveted and gifted from Shögwayadisöh, our Creator.” The French picked it up and the name has been in use since 1641, noted Prime Minister Mark Carney, who schooled the U.S. leader about the origins of the name on X. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he said. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

The Prime Minister was right to brush off Mr. Trump’s silly stunt – especially during an escalating trade war. The fact that Mr. Trump was focused on such colonizing tactics shows you where his head is at and what his ambitions are.

But this is what we know: An American President can never take away the name of a lake that was never his in the first place. Water can’t be owned. Water is alive. It has spirit. It ebbs and flows and it fills our bodies. Water gives us life and it can take it away. Renaming our beautiful, glimmering and wide Niiganii-gichigami “Lake America” means nothing to any of us living here in Canada.

Mr. Trump’s childlike act has only mobilized Canadians, and brought us closer together. Suddenly, those who live here are getting a taste of the threat of colonization. Indigenous people have experienced this before, more than 150 years ago. We know how this playbook goes. But this time, those who colonized our ancestors are being threatened alongside us.

This is a tiresome fight, and Indigenous peoples have seen it all before. We are so done with those that come from foreign lands to take our water, our critical minerals, our sense of self. They will not tell us who we are. It makes sense that it was Manitoba’s Anishinaabe Premier, Wab Kinew, who pushed back when the Prime Minister asked the provinces to return American alcohol to liquor-store shelves ahead of the since-scuttled deal. “Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person,” the Premier said . We still have agency, Mr. Kinew said, so we don’t have to give in to a bully and make a deal that leads us down the wrong path, even if it hurts: “I think we should fight.”

Canadians now have a choice. They can look inward. Buy food grown on this land. Change habits. Learn and embrace true history, not deny it. Be proud of the Indigenous peoples who have taken care of the waters, the Earth, the animals. Recognize our collective history by, among other things, supporting Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30. And we can act like we say we are: Canadians who say “Ontario” and “Niiganii-gichigami,” because the whims of an American politician mean nothing to those of us with long memories.

When I asked him what Ontario means, he said: “When you study the etymology of our Haudenosaunee languages, and you add the suffix ‘ri:io to a word or phrase, it gives it the meaning of something being very precious, coveted and gifted from Shögwayadisöh, our Creator.” The French picked it up and the name has been in use since 1641, noted Prime Minister Mark Carney, who schooled the U.S. leader about the origins of the name on X. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he said. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

The Prime Minister was right to brush off Mr. Trump’s silly stunt – especially during an escalating trade war. The fact that Mr. Trump was focused on such colonizing tactics shows you where his head is at and what his ambitions are.

But this is what we know: An American President can never take away the name of a lake that was never his in the first place. Water can’t be owned. Water is alive. It has spirit. It ebbs and flows and it fills our bodies. Water gives us life and it can take it away. Renaming our beautiful, glimmering and wide Niiganii-gichigami “Lake America” means nothing to any of us living here in Canada.

Mr. Trump’s childlike act has only mobilized Canadians, and brought us closer together. Suddenly, those who live here are getting a taste of the threat of colonization. Indigenous people have experienced this before, more than 150 years ago. We know how this playbook goes. But this time, those who colonized our ancestors are being threatened alongside us.

This is a tiresome fight, and Indigenous peoples have seen it all before. We are so done with those that come from foreign lands to take our water, our critical minerals, our sense of self. They will not tell us who we are. It makes sense that it was Manitoba’s Anishinaabe Premier, Wab Kinew, who pushed back when the Prime Minister asked the provinces to return American alcohol to liquor-store shelves ahead of the since-scuttled deal. “Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person,” the Premier said . We still have agency, Mr. Kinew said, so we don’t have to give in to a bully and make a deal that leads us down the wrong path, even if it hurts: “I think we should fight.”

Canadians now have a choice. They can look inward. Buy food grown on this land. Change habits. Learn and embrace true history, not deny it. Be proud of the Indigenous peoples who have taken care of the waters, the Earth, the animals. Recognize our collective history by, among other things, supporting Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30. And we can act like we say we are: Canadians who say “Ontario” and “Niiganii-gichigami,” because the whims of an American politician mean nothing to those of us with long memories.

stories.title: East Lions pool to reopen ahead of schedule
stories.summary: The pool has been closed since July while repairs were carried out to replace damaged windows and improve the facility’s resilience to future damage.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The pool at East Lions Community Centre will reopen to the public Sept. 12, two weeks ahead of schedule.

The pool has been closed since July while repairs were carried out to replace damaged windows and improve the facility’s resilience to future damage.

To mark the reopening, the city will offer a series of free drop-in aquatic programs on Sept. 12, including lane swims, an aquafit class, a parent-and-tot swim and a recreational swim.

City officials said the project included replacing damaged windows, modifying the window design to better withstand future impacts and making components easier to replace if repairs are needed again.

While the pool was closed, the community centre also underwent maintenance work, including painting at the front desk, cleaning and other minor upgrades following a busy summer camp season.

Registration for fall aquatic programs is open through the city’s recreation registration website.

The city thanked residents for their patience during the closure and said it looks forward to welcoming swimmers back to the facility this weekend.

stories.title: Stevenson launches mayoral campaign promising sweeping changes at London city hall
stories.summary: London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson welcomed supporters inside her new campaign office on Wednesday evening.
stories.content:
London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson welcomed supporters inside her new campaign office on Wednesday evening.

During her speech, the crowd cheered several commitments about greater accountability at city hall and changing London’s approach to homelessness.

“I’ve asked questions and I’ve pushed for answers. I know how much is at stake here. Londoners are doing their part, and it’s time that city hall did its part,” she said from a podium. “To change the future we have to change the present, and that is why I’m running for mayor.”

Stevenson has served as Ward 4 councillor since being elected in 2022.

She outlined her campaign platform’s six priorities, promising to provide greater details at a series of events over the coming weeks.

Restore a sense of safety and pride in our city

Help small businesses thrive

Bring accountability back to city hall

Transportation that works

Strengthen practical partnerships

Leadership that shows up

As part of restoring a sense of safety and pride in the city, Stevenson promised significant changes to the response to the homelessness crisis.

“Londoners are done with all the garbage, open drug use, and problem properties. My platform will explore weekly garbage options for summer, impose good neighbour agreements for homelessness and housing contracts, with restrictions on handing out drug equipment.”

Her long list of commitments included a nod to affordability, but she declined to making a specific pledge about property tax increases until an event next week.

“As mayor, I will put taxpayers first. That means controlling spending, protecting the services people rely on, and opening the books to meaningful scrutiny,” Stevenson said.

She also alluded to addressing neighbourhood concerns about infill developments, “[I’ll] ensure neighborhoods have a better voice in local developments and empower their ward councillor. Every neighborhood matters.”

After her speech, she provided details about her intent to move London from a “harm reduction model” to a “recovery model” for addressing street level drug use.

Asked how a recovery model would work in a city with insufficient treatment beds, she told CTV News, “We need recovery pathways for these people to walk a very long-term recovery journey. We can have all the mental health hospitals and treatment centers we want, but if people don’t have a safe place to live after, we’re not setting people up for success. We’ll have people relapsing and coming back onto our streets again.”

Stevenson worked as a professional accountant for 25 years and in leadership development for five years before being elected to council.

She grew up and raised her family in London.

In February, London’s integrity commissioner ruled Stevenson did not violate the council code of conduct following three complaints related to her decision to move a citizen’s camera during a ward meeting.

In December 2024, council docked Stevenson 30 days’ pay after an investigation by the previous integrity commissioner found she bullied and harassed a senior city staff member.

In 2023, council formally reprimanded her for posting photos on social media of identifiable homeless individuals while implying criminality.

Stevenson has maintained the investigations by the previous integrity commissioner were unfair and improperly conducted.

Stevenson ended her speech with a call to action, “Tonight we open these doors. On Oct. 26, let’s open a new chapter for London. Let’s put taxpayers first. Let’s restore safety and pride. And let’s bring new leadership to City Hall!”

stories.title: 'Consequences we live with': How 9/11 changed Canada's approach to national security
stories.summary: Before the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Steven Backman could usually cross the Canada-U.S. border with a simple wave.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Before the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Steven Backman could usually cross the Canada-U.S. border with a simple wave. Backman, like many residents of St. Stephen, N.B., would travel frequently to neighbouring Calais, Maine.

“When locals would go through the border, often the U.S. customs or the Canadian customs would just poke their head out, see it was a local person crossing, and just wave you through,” he said. Going through the border would become less simple in the years after al Qaeda operatives crashed passenger planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on Sept.

11, 2001. Starting on June 1, 2009, U.S. law required Canadians to present a valid passport or another approved, secure document when entering the United States by land or sea. Stricter requirements for arriving by air had already kicked in.

Canada recommends that U.S. citizens entering Canada carry a valid passport to prove identity and citizenship, regardless of age. Backman, now mayor of St. Stephen, said things have become more relaxed at the border since the tense period immediately following the attacks.

But he routinely pulls out his passport when crossing. “That’s never gone away.” It’s just one of the many ways the fear of international terrorism helped shape modern life after 9/11. ‘This was already a problem’ Twenty-four Canadians were among the nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks.

Three days later, about 80,000 people attended a solemn memorial on Parliament Hill. Minutes of a Sept. 13 meeting of key Liberal cabinet members say John Manley, the foreign minister at the time, suggested the gathering be held outdoors as “a ceremony of the people.” The collective mood of shock and grief rapidly shifted to one of intense focus and activity as Canada grappled with the implications of 9/11.

Manley would soon head up the ad hoc cabinet committee on public security and anti-terrorism. That committee reviewed proposals from departments to keep terrorists out of Canada, protect Canadians from attacks, devise tools to identify, prosecute, convict, and punish extremists, keep the Canada-United States border secure and open to trade, and work with the international community to bring terrorists to justice.

Manley worked closely with Tom Ridge, who stepped down as Pennsylvania governor to become the first director of the U.S. Office of Homeland Security. Manley noted Canada already faced American pressure over border security following the dramatic arrest of Algerian al Qaeda extremist Ahmed Ressam, who was caught in December 1999 trying to drive a carload of explosives into Washington state from British Columbia.

His ultimate goal was to blow up Los Angeles International Airport. “He was on our watch list and we had lost him,” Manley said in a recent interview with The Canadian Press. “This was already a problem, that there was a perception that somehow we were a bit sloppy and that we were the soft underbelly.” Manley recalls seeing a sign of the enduring nature of the Canada-U.S. friendship while visiting Ridge at the White House — all of the photos on the wall outside the Oval Office were of the recent vigil in Ottawa.

“That was pretty remarkable.” Ridge was raised in Erie, Pa., not far from the Canadian border, and told Manley about spending time in Toronto. “He said he visited places on Yonge Street that he didn’t want his mother ever to know about,” Manley said.

“And he said to me, the president’s instructions to him were to keep the United States safe, but not interfere with trade. He had the right direction from the top, and he and I built a relationship which continues to this day.” Civil liberties On Dec.

10, 2001, the Chrétien government’s budget allocated $7.7 billion over five years to enhance security. More than $1.2 billion of that sum was aimed at strengthening the border by stopping individuals and shipments that pose a security risk while speeding up legitimate traffic.

On Dec. 18, Canada’s new Anti-Terrorism Act received royal assent. The legislation allowed the federal government to brand individuals and organizations as terrorists, and to impose stiff penalties on anyone who participates in their activities or assists members of terrorist groups.

The law also gave police the power to make “preventive arrests” of those suspected of planning a terrorist attack, and required anyone with information relevant to the investigation of a terrorist act to appear before a judge.

Many of the measures drew cries of outrage from civil libertarians. The government created the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority to carry out airport screening previously performed by airlines, an approach the government said would ensure consistency and accountability.

Ottawa also reorganized agencies to create the Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness Department, poured billions of new dollars into security intelligence organizations and assembled a no-fly list. Under a 2011 continental security pact, Canada and the United States agreed to set up co-ordinated systems to track the entry and exit information of travellers.

The effort involves exchanging entry information collected from people at the land border, so that data on entry to one country serves as a record of exit from the other. The data includes the traveller’s name, nationality, date of birth and gender, the country that issued their travel document and the time, date and location of their crossing.

Despite the investment of energy, money and time in remaking the security landscape, Canadian officials often found themselves trying to dispel misconceptions. Manley said one of his assignments was to inform U.S. legislators — including Hillary Clinton — that none of the 9/11 hijackers entered the United States from Canada.

“And when corrected, her reaction was, ‘Well, if they didn’t, they could have, and security trumps trade,’” he said. ‘Succeeded beyond their wildest imaginations’ A quarter century after 9/11, Canadians are reminded of how their world changed every time they’re asked to remove their belt or discard liquids while going through airport security.

Many routinely encounter airport-style scrutiny when attending sporting events, or even visiting city hall. If the 9/11 perpetrators hoped to cost the developed world a lot of money and time, “they succeeded beyond their wildest imaginations,” Manley said.

The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group, a national coalition formed after the adoption of the Anti-Terrorism Act, argued in early 2003 that the association of terrorism with Islam had led to the racial profiling of an entire community.

Manley said the government tried to emphasize publicly that 9/11 “was not motivated so much by religion as it was by a twisted ideology that May have been religiously rooted, but was not characteristic of most Muslims.” The legacy of 9/11 lives on in the choices made by governments in the immediate aftermath, “and those are also consequences that we continue to live with to this day,” said Steve Hewitt, an associate professor of North American history at the University of Birmingham in England.

Scores of Canadians lost their lives and many more were wounded in the war in Afghanistan that followed the attacks. Maher Arar Canada’s embrace of the fight against terrorism led to other tragic consequences. Maher Arar, a Syrian-born Canadian, was detained in New York in September 2002.

Deported by U.S. authorities, he wound up in a grave-like cell in Damascus. Under torture, Arar gave false confessions to Syrian military intelligence officers about his supposed collaboration with the al Qaeda network. A federal commission of inquiry led by Justice Dennis O’Connor concluded that faulty information the RCMP passed to the United States very likely led to Arar’s yearlong ordeal.

In October 2008, an inquiry led by former Supreme Court justice Frank Iacobucci found Canadian officials contributed to the torture of three other Arab Canadians — Abdullah Almalki, Ahmad El Maati and Muayyed Nureddin — by sharing information with foreign agencies.

Iacobucci concluded the men were abused in Syrian custody and, in the case of El Maati, in Egypt as well. The former judge said the RCMP, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the Department of Foreign Affairs all made mistakes in the cases.

In 2006, authorities foiled a terrorism plot by the so-called “Toronto 18.” Eight years later, a man killed an honour guard at the National War Memorial before storming Parliament Hill. He said his actions were spurred by Canada’s military involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Hewitt, author of the forthcoming book “A History of Terrorism in Canada,” acknowledges these episodes. But he points out that some of the most appalling assaults in Canada since 9/11 — including a mass shooting at a Quebec mosque and a vehicle attack on a family in London, Ont. — have been driven by hatred of Muslims.

Manley said while the recent rise of neo-Nazism and white supremacy is a generation removed from the Sept. 11 attacks, they are “direct results of some of the antagonism and hatred that emerged post-9/11.” “It began pitting citizens against one another,” he said.

“I think it’s one of the things that we have to regret in the modern world.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026. Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

“That was pretty remarkable.” Ridge was raised in Erie, Pa., not far from the Canadian border, and told Manley about spending time in Toronto. “He said he visited places on Yonge Street that he didn’t want his mother ever to know about,” Manley said.

“And he said to me, the president’s instructions to him were to keep the United States safe, but not interfere with trade. He had the right direction from the top, and he and I built a relationship which continues to this day.” Civil liberties On Dec.

10, 2001, the Chrétien government’s budget allocated $7.7 billion over five years to enhance security. More than $1.2 billion of that sum was aimed at strengthening the border by stopping individuals and shipments that pose a security risk while speeding up legitimate traffic.

On Dec. 18, Canada’s new Anti-Terrorism Act received royal assent. The legislation allowed the federal government to brand individuals and organizations as terrorists, and to impose stiff penalties on anyone who participates in their activities or assists members of terrorist groups.

The law also gave police the power to make “preventive arrests” of those suspected of planning a terrorist attack, and required anyone with information relevant to the investigation of a terrorist act to appear before a judge.

Many of the measures drew cries of outrage from civil libertarians. The government created the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority to carry out airport screening previously performed by airlines, an approach the government said would ensure consistency and accountability.

Ottawa also reorganized agencies to create the Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness Department, poured billions of new dollars into security intelligence organizations and assembled a no-fly list. Under a 2011 continental security pact, Canada and the United States agreed to set up co-ordinated systems to track the entry and exit information of travellers.

The effort involves exchanging entry information collected from people at the land border, so that data on entry to one country serves as a record of exit from the other. The data includes the traveller’s name, nationality, date of birth and gender, the country that issued their travel document and the time, date and location of their crossing.

Many routinely encounter airport-style scrutiny when attending sporting events, or even visiting city hall. If the 9/11 perpetrators hoped to cost the developed world a lot of money and time, “they succeeded beyond their wildest imaginations,” Manley said.

The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group, a national coalition formed after the adoption of the Anti-Terrorism Act, argued in early 2003 that the association of terrorism with Islam had led to the racial profiling of an entire community.

Scores of Canadians lost their lives and many more were wounded in the war in Afghanistan that followed the attacks. Maher Arar Canada’s embrace of the fight against terrorism led to other tragic consequences. Maher Arar, a Syrian-born Canadian, was detained in New York in September 2002.

Deported by U.S. authorities, he wound up in a grave-like cell in Damascus. Under torture, Arar gave false confessions to Syrian military intelligence officers about his supposed collaboration with the al Qaeda network. A federal commission of inquiry led by Justice Dennis O’Connor concluded that faulty information the RCMP passed to the United States very likely led to Arar’s yearlong ordeal.

In October 2008, an inquiry led by former Supreme Court justice Frank Iacobucci found Canadian officials contributed to the torture of three other Arab Canadians — Abdullah Almalki, Ahmad El Maati and Muayyed Nureddin — by sharing information with foreign agencies.

Iacobucci concluded the men were abused in Syrian custody and, in the case of El Maati, in Egypt as well. The former judge said the RCMP, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the Department of Foreign Affairs all made mistakes in the cases.

In 2006, authorities foiled a terrorism plot by the so-called “Toronto 18.” Eight years later, a man killed an honour guard at the National War Memorial before storming Parliament Hill. He said his actions were spurred by Canada’s military involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq.

But he points out that some of the most appalling assaults in Canada since 9/11 — including a mass shooting at a Quebec mosque and a vehicle attack on a family in London, Ont. — have been driven by hatred of Muslims.

Manley said while the recent rise of neo-Nazism and white supremacy is a generation removed from the Sept. 11 attacks, they are “direct results of some of the antagonism and hatred that emerged post-9/11.” “It began pitting citizens against one another,” he said.

stories.title: 25 years since 9/11, Canada is not further ahead on tackling Islamophobia: advocates
stories.summary: Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center spurred widespread surveillance and hostility against Muslims around the world, the work of countering Islamophobia in Canada still rests largely on those it targets, a major Islamic organization said in the lead-up to the anniversary.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center spurred widespread surveillance and hostility against Muslims around the world, the work of countering Islamophobia in Canada still rests largely on those it targets, a major Islamic organization said in the lead-up to the anniversary.

As Muslims suddenly found their faith wrongly linked with extremist acts in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, many Islamic institutions in Canada responded to the growing fear and suspicion by trying to build bridges with their communities, opening their doors to neighbours and joining vigils for the nearly 3,000 people killed.

Those efforts were fuelled partly by a feeling of “collective responsibility to push back at somebody trying to hijack our faith,” and partly by the need to ensure ordinary Canadians and policymakers had a real perspective of Islam outside of what they heard on the news, said Safwan Choudhry, spokesperson for the Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama’at Canada, an Islamic organization with dozens of mosques throughout the country.

“There wasn’t any other platform or narrative available, so you had no choice but to open your homes and open your mosques and send your youth out to blood banks and talk to people and be available wherever the public dialogue was,” Choudhry said, adding that some of those initiatives continue today.

While there are now far more avenues for outreach and public education, in many ways, “it feels as though nothing has changed and we’re not further ahead,” he said.

Much like after 9/11, Choudhry said, “(we) recognize that that responsibility lies with us, that we have to do more. ... We have to do much more to try and stop this acceleration towards a much, much more dangerous and a much more destructive condition around the world.”

The anniversary comes as the annual number of hate crimes against Muslims remains higher than it was five years ago — 204 were reported to police forces across Canada in 2025, compared with 142 in 2021 — with some experts and advocates pointing to rising tensions amid the Israel-Hamas war as a key contributor, as well as social media’s role as a powerful vector for harmful rhetoric.

At the same time, some experts say, hard-won progress in addressing anti-Muslim discrimination is being rolled back with the elimination earlier this year of the office of the special representative on combating Islamophobia, a position advocates hailed as historic when it was created three years ago.

The decision to replace the office with a broader advisory council on equality and inclusion signals Islamophobia is no longer on policy agenda for the federal government – a “slap in the face” for Muslims who have consistently been sharing their experiences with discrimination over the last 25 years, said Fahad Ahmad, an assistant professor of criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University.

“There was this hope that ... we were turning the corner in terms of addressing Islamophobia, but I do think the (Mark) Carney government has shown that actually we don’t really care about that,” said Ahmad, who co-wrote an op-ed denouncing the office’s elimination with his colleague Asmaa Malik, a journalism professor at the university.

Several new laws quickly enacted by the current Liberal administration, including a hate-crime law that creates new offences for intimidating or obstructing someone outside a religious or cultural institution, suggest a “strengthening of the national security state” and a sidelining of any scrutiny toward these government institutions and their role in perpetuating Islamophobic practices and policies, he said.

A spokesperson for Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture Marc Miller said the new advisory council has a clear mandate to help guide the government’s efforts to combat racism and hate “in all their forms,” including the “distinct and persistent challenges posed by Islamophobia in our communities and institutions.”

As well, Hermine Landry wrote in an email, the Combating Hate Act passed this year “directly addresses hate-motivated violence and the targeting of communities” while significantly strengthening the Criminal Code through the creation of new offences. The work is part of a plan launched two years ago to empower communities and prevent hate including Islamophobia, she said.

“We will remain steadfast in our commitment to combat all forms of hatred and racism and to build a Canada where everyone can thrive and feel a sense of belonging,” Landry wrote.

As the United States’ war on terror gripped global politics in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, Canada brought in new security measures at airports and borders and passed controversial anti-terrorism legislation that created several new offences and for years allowed police to detain people they believed were about to commit an act of terror without first obtaining a warrant.

The government’s security certificate system also allowed it to detain and deport non-Canadians considered a risk to the country based on classified evidence not shared with the accused. The system sparked lengthy legal battles and was struck down by Canada’s top court in 2008 before the government amended the law.

Meanwhile, hate crimes against Muslims spiked, with the Canadian Islamic Congress reporting 173 incidents in the year that followed 9/11, up nearly 1,600 per cent over the 11 incidents the organization recorded the previous year.

“That period, like 2001-2006, was a really heightened dark period where, you know, I think this balance between rights and security was trying to find footing,” Ahmad said, recalling an atmosphere of anxiety that dominated the era.

Later, as prosecutions under the new terror laws began, “essentially, terrorism became analogous with Muslims and Islam,” Ahmad said. The vast majority of terror trials have involved ideology related to international groups such as al-Qaida or the Islamic State, even as security officials increasingly recognize the threat of right-wing extremism and white supremacy.

For years, Muslim community leaders sought to engage with Ottawa but were met with resistance, Ahmad said. The 2015 federal election that propelled Justin Trudeau to power brought “a bit of a shift,” more of an openness to engage on Islamophobia, he said.

Then, two mass killings of Canadian Muslims sent shock waves through the country and set many on edge amid renewed fears for their safety.

A gunman opened fire at a mosque in a Quebec City suburb in January 2017, killing six men and critically injuring five others in a matter of minutes. Though Trudeau denounced the killings as a terrorist attack, the gunman wasn’t charged with terrorism offences and pleaded guilty to six counts of first-degree murder and six counts of attempted murder.

More than four years later, a self-described white nationalist mowed down a Muslim family in London, Ont., with his truck, killing four of them and injuring another. The murder of the Afzaal family as they were on an evening stroll in June 2021 scarred the southwestern Ontario community and left some Muslims afraid to go outside in traditional clothes.

A judge later deemed the attack terrorism -- the first case to recognize terrorism on grounds of white supremacist ideology. Nathaniel Veltman, the man convicted of first-degree murder in the family’s deaths, was a “voracious consumer of extremist right wing internet content” who wanted to intimidate the Muslim community, the judge found.

At the time, Amira Elghawaby, then Canada’s special representative on combating Islamophobia, said the terrorism finding would have “profound reverberations across Canada” as she called for urgent efforts to tackle the proliferation of online hate.

“It wasn’t until this massacre at a place of worship (in 2017), the first and hopefully last massacre at a place of worship in our country, happened that Canadians really, finally, I think, began to understand the degree in which the hatred of Muslims was proliferating online, as well as in public discourse,” she said in a recent interview.

“And then it actually took the attack on the Afzaal family ... for there to be fuller consensus across political lines that Islamophobia needed to be addressed in our country,” said Elghawaby, a former journalist and human rights advocate.

More recently, more than 21 violent incidents against Muslims have been documented over four months, including one in which a mosque in Winnipeg was shot with a pellet gun while worshippers and children were inside, she said.

“I often think to myself, thank goodness that we didn’t have the same online climate (in 2001) that we have today because there was an ability to actually create sort of local connection and reconnection and allyship in our communities after 9/11, which was so valuable and helped to stem the hate,” she said.

“We were hoping that 25 years on ... our kids wouldn’t have to deal with the stigma, with the suspicion, with all that we had to do at that time,” said Elghawaby, who was working at the CBC when the twin towers fell.

In the last few years, and particularly since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on Israel that marked the beginning of the Israel-Hamas war, “we have seen this re-emergence of scapegoating entire communities, of looking at our communities within a framework of supporting terrorism simply for speaking up for Palestinian human rights and international law,” she said.

During her tenure as Canada’s first and only special representative on combating Islamophobia, Elghawaby’s office accomplished “historic” work, including the publication of a comprehensive guide on understanding and fighting Islamophobia, she said. Canada, which led the G7 in terms of hate-motivated killings of Muslims, was seen as having taken a leadership role in addressing the issue, she said.

Another report commissioned by her office examined how Muslim charities continued to face disproportionate scrutiny under anti-terrorism and anti-money laundering frameworks, she said.

Asked about the government’s decision to scrap the office in favour of an advisory council, Elghawaby said there were “valuable efforts” to promote inclusion and combat hate within the federal government, including the anti-racism strategy and the anti-hate action plan.

For Asmaa Malik, the TMU journalism professor, getting rid of the office marks “a really huge step towards even dismantling the concept of Islamophobia,” she said.

Malik, who is researching media coverage of hate crimes against Muslims with Ahmad, said it contributes to what sociologist Jasmin Zine has dubbed Canada’s “national amnesia” regarding Islamophobia.

“As long as there’s no one to actually help account for this and you don’t name these patterns, then the work of white supremacy is happening,” she said in a recent interview.

Choudhry, the spokesperson for Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama’at Canada, said that while offices and institutions play an important role in tackling hate, they will never be enough to solve the issue altogether.

“We understood early on that combating Islamophobia could not be left to the government or even policymakers, the ultimate responsibility rests with Muslims,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

“We were hoping that 25 years on ... our kids wouldn’t have to deal with the stigma, with the suspicion, with all that we had to do at that time,” said Elghawaby, who was working at the CBC when the twin towers fell.

In the last few years, and particularly since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on Israel that marked the beginning of the Israel-Hamas war, “we have seen this re-emergence of scapegoating entire communities, of looking at our communities within a framework of supporting terrorism simply for speaking up for Palestinian human rights and international law,” she said.

During her tenure as Canada’s first and only special representative on combating Islamophobia, Elghawaby’s office accomplished “historic” work, including the publication of a comprehensive guide on understanding and fighting Islamophobia, she said. Canada, which led the G7 in terms of hate-motivated killings of Muslims, was seen as having taken a leadership role in addressing the issue, she said.
Another report commissioned by her office examined how Muslim charities continued to face disproportionate scrutiny under anti-terrorism and anti-money laundering frameworks, she said.

Asked about the government’s decision to scrap the office in favour of an advisory council, Elghawaby said there were “valuable efforts” to promote inclusion and combat hate within the federal government, including the anti-racism strategy and the anti-hate action plan.
For Asmaa Malik, the TMU journalism professor, getting rid of the office marks “a really huge step towards even dismantling the concept of Islamophobia,” she said.
Malik, who is researching media coverage of hate crimes against Muslims with Ahmad, said it contributes to what sociologist Jasmin Zine has dubbed Canada’s “national amnesia” regarding Islamophobia.
“As long as there’s no one to actually help account for this and you don’t name these patterns, then the work of white supremacy is happening,” she said in a recent interview.

Choudhry, the spokesperson for Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama’at Canada, said that while offices and institutions play an important role in tackling hate, they will never be enough to solve the issue altogether.
“We understood early on that combating Islamophobia could not be left to the government or even policymakers, the ultimate responsibility rests with Muslims,” he said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.
Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Investigation needed into how Iranian VP’s son got government contracts, groups say
stories.summary: A Global News investigation found an Edmonton resident won millions in federal contracts while under investigation for allegedly helping Iran's missile program.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
The Prime Minister is facing calls to investigate how the son of Iran’s former vice president won millions in government contracts while security agencies were probing his suspected role in the Islamic Republic’s missile program.

In a letter to Mark Carney , four Iranian-Canadian organizations said the case of Mohammad Reza Ghafouri Fard , who has been living in Alberta, suggested government agencies were not sharing information.

Ghafouri is the son of a conservative Iranian politician and allegedly worked on military projects for the Iranian military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps before arriving in Canada in 2013.

Although government records show Ghafouri was flagged by Canadian national security agencies in 2017, the RCMP, Department of National Defence and other agencies later awarded him contracts.

“The facts reported in this case raise concerns that go far beyond immigration enforcement,” the groups, as well as Iranian-Canadian academics and a former Ontario MPP, wrote in the letter to Carney on Wednesday.

“They point to a potentially serious disconnect between Canada’s national security, immigration, law enforcement and government procurement systems.”

The letter was signed by the Iranian Canadian Legal Professionals, Canadians for Democracy in Iran, Iran Justice Collective and Iranian Women Organization of Ontario, as well as seven individuals.

It asked Carney to launch an independent probe into how Ghafouri “was able to obtain the necessary security clearances, approvals, contracts or access despite the reported concerns regarding his alleged connections to the Islamic Republic regime and its missile program.”

“The investigation should examine whether information was properly shared among government agencies, whether existing screening and security protocols were followed, and whether any deficiencies, omissions or breaches occurred.”

Global News revealed last week that the Iranian citizen was living in Edmonton, where he runs businesses under the name “Sal Ghafouri” that have worked for federal, provincial and local governments.

2:46 Canada gave contracts to Iran VP’s son while investigating role in regime missile program

Through his lawyer, Ghafouri denied the government’s claim he is a security threat, disputed the allegations against him and said he intended to pursue “all available legal avenues” to resolve the matter.

But according to government records, prior to coming to Canada under the government’s skilled worker program, he allegedly worked as an engineer at a Tehran company that developed weapons for the Iranian regime.

The weapons went to Iran’s military and Revolutionary Guard , which control’s the country’s ballistic missiles and drones, conducts overseas operations, and sponsors regional terror groups such as Hamas .

A Canadian Security Intelligence Service report alleged that Ghafouri also helped Iran dodge sanctions by using a front company in Malaysia to illicitly procure materials for military projects.

Upon arriving in Canada, he incorporated two Alberta companies, Melanite Group Ltd. and Radian Group Ltd, which bid on government procurement contracts.

The RCMP confirmed it had awarded a contract to Melanite Group in 2019 to purchase a borescope device and provide training but said “no security requirements were associated with the contract.”

“Prior to contract award, the RCMP completed the required integrity verification. The contract has since been completed and closed. Since its award in 2019, the RCMP has not entered into any other procurement transactions with Melanite Group.”

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada also confirmed it awarded a 2021 contract to Melanite Group “for scientific equipment used for type approval testing of measuring devices and services rendered,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

“Ised can also confirm that $15,000 was awarded to Melanite Group in the form of a grant under the Canadian Digital Adoption Program Boost your Business Technology Stream in 2024.”

The Canadian military has not responded to questions about several contracts it awarded Ghafouri’s companies. Global Affairs Canada also did not answer questions about why it invited him on official Canadian trade missions.

But the Toronto-based Abraham Global Peace Initiative called for an investigation, saying it was “appalled” by the “apparent failure of government agencies to share security information.”

“Canada cannot condemn the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps while allowing individuals allegedly connected to its military infrastructure access to sensitive government procurement.”

“We demand an immediate independent investigation, full public accountability, and reform of Canada’s security-screening and contracting systems,” said the group, headed by activist Avi Benlolo.

In May, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada told Ghafouri it had initiated proceedings to refuse him citizenship on the grounds he was a security threat to the country.

The agency declined to comment, citing privacy.

Canada launched a crackdown on Iranian regime officials living in the country in 2022, and has been attempting to deport them along with others who have aided Tehran as it has repressed its citizens and sponsored terrorist groups.

But the Ghafouri case stands out for the seriousness of the allegations about his suspected role in Iranian weapons proliferation, the length of time it has taken the government to act and his extensive contract work for Canadian agencies.

Opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also raised concerns about the case, writing on social media, “Why is he still in Canada? Get active Irgc regime operatives out of our country.”

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA
