stories.title: Cannabis-smoking Ontario stabber gets day passes despite 'significant threat'
stories.summary: The man, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia and cannabis use disorder, was found not criminally responsible in his latest stabbing attack.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Ontario man found not criminally responsible twice for stabbing two people in the back multiple times in the span of a decade has been granted a series of day passes even though he’s still deemed a “significant threat to the safety of the public.”

Muneeb Ali Ghawar — who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and cannabis use disorder “in remission in a controlled environment” — was found not criminally responsible (NCR) in February 2024 for aggravated assault and wearing a disguise in his latest stabbing attack one year previous at a cannabis store in Hamilton.

The Ontario Review Board (ORB) heard Ghawar walked into Sweet Releaf Cannabis around midday on Feb. 3, 2023, wearing a mask and a trapper hat pulled down low. When a female clerk moved to ring up the weed he asked for, Ghawar got behind her.

“He pulled out a knife and began stabbing her with it in the back. She was stabbed upwards of seven times and suffered a severed bicep and collapsed lung amongst other injuries,” said a recent decision from the independent tribunal that regularly reviews the status of individuals found not criminally responsible due to mental disorder.

When another employee screamed and went to call 911, Ghawar ran from the store. Detectives later identified Ghawar using surveillance video from his previous visit to the cannabis operation when he wasn’t wearing a mask. He was arrested six days after the stabbing.

Ghawar has been experiencing mental health symptoms for many years, and he is now under the jurisdiction of the review board for a second time, said the Aug. 28 ORB decision.

The first time he was declared NCR was for a 2014 attack in which he stabbed an acquaintance five times in the back and torso. He remained in hospital until March 2016, when he was discharged to live with his family.

“Mr. Ghawar was compliant with his medication, met consistently with the outpatient team, and maintained stable mental health. He was granted an absolute discharge on February 11, 2019,” the ORB ruling said.

Schizophrenic man who killed his mom has cannabis ban removed to see how he handles it

Drug ban lifted for Ontario man who stabbed 83-year-old stranger while on drugs

He lived with his parents until the February 2023 stabbing.

Ghawar reported that he started using cannabis at the age of 15, stopped for a time, then started again in August 2019.

“He resumed using cannabis during the time he was living with his parents,” said the ORB decision.

Ghawar was ordered detained last year at St. Joseph’s Healthcare, with privileges allowing him to enter the community of Hamilton under indirect supervision.

Indirect supervision means the patient agrees to periodically check in with the hospital and a designated person on the clinical team knows the patient’s whereabouts at all times.

At his most recent ORB hearing, the panel “concluded that Mr. Ghawar remained a significant threat to the safety of the public and that a detention order was necessary and appropriate. With respect to the additional privileges suggested by the hospital, the panel determined that it was appropriate to include in the disposition seven day passes accompanied by an approved person, and seven day passes indirectly supervised with a pre-approved itinerary.”

Ghawar had been treated by a psychiatrist for anxiety and depression since 2012, according to his hospital report.

“In April 2014, Mr. Ghawar stopped taking his antipsychotic medication, and his mental health symptoms intensified almost immediately. According to his family, Mr. Ghawar became very anxious and irritable, and would refuse to leave the house alone. The parents advised that they did not see anything in his behaviour to suggest he was capable of assaulting anyone on the day of the index offence in May 2014.”

Ghawar has a criminal record that includes assault, mischief, break and enter and assault with a weapon.

A September 2023 psychological assessment indicated Ghawar “expressed delusional thought content, such as the victim of the index offence was ‘selling bad cannabis to kids in order to draw them into sex trafficking,” said the ORB decision.

“The conclusions from the assessment were that Mr. Ghawar has limited intellectual abilities and experiences significant impairment in neurocognitive functioning which is likely the result of his mental illness and substance use.”

Mr. Ghawar stopped taking his antipsychotic medication, and his mental health symptoms intensified almost immediately

When he was examined after his latest stabbing, Ghawar “acknowledged longstanding auditory hallucinations, and displayed indicia of paranoia and grandiose delusions. Mr. Ghawar also acknowledged that he had stopped taking his medication prior to the index offence and was smoking marijuana.”

Ghawar “has remained mentally stable the past couple of years,” said the ORB decision.

“There has been no evidence of mood disorders or psychotic breakthrough. He engages appropriately with co-patients and staff and is always pleasant and polite during interactions.”

Ghawar’s urine tested positive for pot on April 12, 2025. He denied it, suggesting a cigarette had been laced with cannabis.

He tested positive again for cannabis use twice last December.

“He again denied using cannabis, and suggested that the positive result was from others smoking cannabis around him,” said the decision, which notes staff detected “a strong odor of cannabis coming from his jacket” this past February and found what appeared to be pot in his pocket.

Ghawar suggested someone must have placed it there, said the decision.

“Mr. Ghawar used cannabis as recently as July 6, 2026.”

His “persistent use of cannabis is a significant risk factor,” said the ORB decision.

“He was using cannabis at the time of the first index offence in 2014, and at the time of the current index offence in 2023. He became extremely psychotic and committed very violent offences that could have resulted in the death of either victim.”

Ghawar visits his family regularly, but that doesn’t mean he’s ready to move back in with them, said the decision, which notes he was living with them at the time of both stabbings.

According to his psychiatrist, Ghawar’s “insight into his psychotic symptoms, the need for treatment, the effects of cannabis use, and his risk for violence is limited.”

Meanwhile, Ghawar’s parents want to take him to Pakistan to get married.

“This would be an arranged marriage to a woman he has not met,” said the ORB decision, which notes his psychiatrist “expressed concern that bringing another person into the family home would increase the stress at a time when Mr. Ghawar is struggling with cannabis use.”

Ghawar had been treated by a psychiatrist for anxiety and depression since 2012, according to his hospital report.

“In April 2014, Mr. Ghawar stopped taking his antipsychotic medication, and his mental health symptoms intensified almost immediately. According to his family, Mr. Ghawar became very anxious and irritable, and would refuse to leave the house alone. The parents advised that they did not see anything in his behaviour to suggest he was capable of assaulting anyone on the day of the index offence in May 2014.”
Ghawar has a criminal record that includes assault, mischief, break and enter and assault with a weapon.

A September 2023 psychological assessment indicated Ghawar “expressed delusional thought content, such as the victim of the index offence was ‘selling bad cannabis to kids in order to draw them into sex trafficking,” said the ORB decision.

“The conclusions from the assessment were that Mr. Ghawar has limited intellectual abilities and experiences significant impairment in neurocognitive functioning which is likely the result of his mental illness and substance use.”
Mr. Ghawar stopped taking his antipsychotic medication, and his mental health symptoms intensified almost immediately

When he was examined after his latest stabbing, Ghawar “acknowledged longstanding auditory hallucinations, and displayed indicia of paranoia and grandiose delusions. Mr. Ghawar also acknowledged that he had stopped taking his medication prior to the index offence and was smoking marijuana.”
Ghawar “has remained mentally stable the past couple of years,” said the ORB decision.
“There has been no evidence of mood disorders or psychotic breakthrough. He engages appropriately with co-patients and staff and is always pleasant and polite during interactions.”
Ghawar’s urine tested positive for pot on April 12, 2025. He denied it, suggesting a cigarette had been laced with cannabis.
He tested positive again for cannabis use twice last December.

“He again denied using cannabis, and suggested that the positive result was from others smoking cannabis around him,” said the decision, which notes staff detected “a strong odor of cannabis coming from his jacket” this past February and found what appeared to be pot in his pocket.
Ghawar suggested someone must have placed it there, said the decision.
“Mr. Ghawar used cannabis as recently as July 6, 2026.”
His “persistent use of cannabis is a significant risk factor,” said the ORB decision.

“He was using cannabis at the time of the first index offence in 2014, and at the time of the current index offence in 2023. He became extremely psychotic and committed very violent offences that could have resulted in the death of either victim.”
Ghawar visits his family regularly, but that doesn’t mean he’s ready to move back in with them, said the decision, which notes he was living with them at the time of both stabbings.
According to his psychiatrist, Ghawar’s “insight into his psychotic symptoms, the need for treatment, the effects of cannabis use, and his risk for violence is limited.”
Meanwhile, Ghawar’s parents want to take him to Pakistan to get married.

“This would be an arranged marriage to a woman he has not met,” said the ORB decision, which notes his psychiatrist “expressed concern that bringing another person into the family home would increase the stress at a time when Mr. Ghawar is struggling with cannabis use.”

stories.title: London economic leaders discuss tariff impacts, job protection
stories.summary: London’s economic leaders are looking for ways to protect local jobs and help businesses navigate ongoing uncertainty in the trade relationship with the United States.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
London’s economic leaders are looking for ways to protect local jobs and help businesses navigate ongoing uncertainty in the trade relationship with the United States.

The group discussed recent tariff changes, the potential impact on local industries and workers, and ways to strengthen London’s economy through diversification and government support programs.

“We have a rapidly changing environment that is impacting jobs in this community, potentially a significant impact across multiple sectors as well as potentially consumer prices,” Morgan said.

He said the city is also looking at ways to help small and medium-sized businesses access federal and provincial funding programs.

Morgan said larger companies often have the resources to navigate government applications, while smaller businesses May not have the same capacity.

“We recognize that there are small and medium businesses, sometimes with a handful of people or a few dozen people working for them, that don’t have the capacity to navigate government programs,” he said.

The city has also adjusted its procurement strategy to include domestic supply chain considerations, Morgan said.

Kapil Lakhotia, President & CEO at the London Economic Development Corporation said the city is continuing to invest in infrastructure and attract businesses from markets outside the United States.

“We’ve been successful in attracting new plants despite all this economic chaos. This year, we’ve had several expansions that focus on other parts of the world as well,” Lakhotia said.

He pointed to the expansion of Innovation Park and new food-processing initiatives as examples of efforts to diversify the local economy.

Cristina Fox, CEO of Tech Alliance, said businesses need to consider the potential impact of tariffs throughout their supply chains, including customers and suppliers connected to other markets.

“Making sure that we have a critical mass of strong supply chain in this region and beyond Canada,” explained Fox. “Companies are thinking about their vendors vendor, and how are they actually entering new markets outside of Canada.”

Jason Bates, general manager of the London Region Manufacturing Council, said some manufacturers are exploring opportunities to expand their customer base in Canada and other parts of the world.

“In lieu of working strictly and solely with the US as their export market, we’re seeing a lot of exploration of doing business in Canada, Canadian supply chains as opposed to American supply chains,” Bates said.

Morgan said the goal is to protect jobs, support businesses and ensure London is prepared for further changes in the international trade environment.

Morgan noted that a national event that will be held in London next week, where intel will be presented on the impact of the trade war and how municipalities are responding.

stories.title: Globe reporter Rudy Platiel gave Indigenous people a stronger voice
stories.summary: A friendly fixture on the national news landscape, he witnessed half a century of progress that advanced ‘light years beyond anything I actually thought possible’
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Rudy Platiel was hopeful for reconciliation between Indigenous peoples and the rest of Canadian society decades before it became a buzzword.

The Globe and Mail reporter and photographer, who died on July 27 in Burlington, Ont., worked in journalism for more than three decades, during which he often wrote about Indigenous people.

Rudy Emil Platiel was born during the Great Depression, ON Oct. 2, 1934, in Owen Sound, Ont., to Louisa and Emil Platiel. Mr. Platiel considered himself lucky to work first as a teenage factory worker, a bookkeeper and then finally a reporter for the Brampton Times and Conservator before being hired as a freelance writer and photographer for The Globe and Mail. He soon joined the staff and remained at the newspaper until his retirement in 1997.

As a teen, he developed a friendship with the Johnston family from Neyaashiinigmiing, part of the Chippewas of Nawash (formerly known as Cape Croker). His family says this friendship planted a seed in him that led him “to give First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples a stronger voice in the Canadian media.”

In the 2020 book Seen but Not Seen: Influential Canadians and the First Nations from the 1840s to Today , author Donald B. Smith refers frequently to Mr. Platiel’s work.

In the prologue, Mr. Smith lays out an incident in 1969 in which the Liberal government of the day tabled a white paper in the House of Commons that aimed to upend the status rights of Indigenous peoples and eliminate treaties, reserves and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

Opposition among Indigenous groups was strong and Indigenous groups mounted vigorous protest and presented the government with their response, known as the Red Paper. The federal government eventually withdrew its policy proposal.

Mr. Platiel witnessed the Red Paper’s submission and 50 years later, recalled the experience in Mr. Smith’s book: “In 1970, I was assigned by The Globe and Mail to travel for a year across Canada to write about the situation of Indigenous people – then called Indians.

“Despite the now continued existence of systemic racism, the March of Indigenous rights and their reality, today is light years beyond anything I actually thought possible back then. This progress gives hope that despite our human flaws and occasional cruelty, as a nation we May one day yet reach a new dawn of acceptance and cooperation between two societies that at times seems so tantalizingly far beyond us today. There is indeed hope.”

Over the next two decades, Mr. Platiel was a friendly fixture on the national landscape of Indigenous news, contextualizing stories and going beyond basic reporting that often stereotyped Indigenous people as troubled, plagued and contentious.

In the newsroom, Mr. Platiel was known as a kind and gentle soul, virtues “worth a lot” says Sean Fine, who sat across from him in the Globe and Mail newsroom at the beginning of his career, circa 1989. “He seemed to have covered everything. Reliably and fairly,” Mr. Fine said.

However, one day in 1966, when Mr. Platiel was covering two simultaneous trials at the Halton County Courthouse, he inadvertently caused a mistrial in one of the cases and received a $100 fine for contempt.

The episode has since become a cautionary tale known to journalism students at Carleton University taking the mandatory media law course.

The story, as told in part by Wilf Kesterton in his book The Law and the Press in Canada , goes that while a judge was deciding in voir dire (a trial within a trial) whether certain evidence would be permitted in the trial of four men charged with criminal negligence, Mr. Platiel was in another courtroom reporting on the second trial.

Upon his return, Mr. Platiel asked a reporter from another media outlet what he missed and was briefed on the evidence considered by the judge. But the other reporter failed to tell Mr. Platiel that the judge had deemed the evidence inadmissible – so it was therefore not publishable.

The headline that appeared with Mr. Platiel’s byline in the paper the following day contained the exact evidentiary detail that the judge had ruled out.

His fine was appealed and later withdrawn before a judge scolded The Globe and Mail (which was also fined) for assigning the reporter to do double-duty.

True to his humility, Mr. Platiel would later explain to Mr. Fine the circumstances of the voir dire mishap, without taking any offence at the subject.

“I’m pretty sure we laughed about it,” Mr. Fine recalled.

Mr. Platiel’s creative force of storytelling didn’t end with retirement. Staying forever curious, he continued to capture the stories of his family and friends’ lives through writing and photography. He also wrote a work of fiction for young adults, In The Land Of Ebyam: The Dangers of the Shadow World are Real , as well as having the occasional byline in the Globe.

A “gentle giant” to his grandchildren and nieces and nephews, Mr. Platiel was 91 years old. He leaves his wife of 63 years, Agatha Platiel, their three daughters Tina, Louise and Vicki; and four grandchildren.

stories.title: Ottawa will not recognize ‘southern Inuit’ as holding Indigenous rights
stories.summary: Inuit governments dispute the Nunatukavut Community Council's (NCC), a group representing roughly 6,000 people in southern Labrador, claims to Indigeneity.
stories.author: Melissa Ridgen, Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The federal government has halted the process to recognize a controversial Labrador group which self-describes as “southern Inuit” as holding Indigenous rights.

The Nunatukavut Community Council (NCC) represents roughly 6,000 people in central and southern Labrador, and has been fighting for years for land, hunting and fishing rights despite not being recognized by other Indigenous organizations and communities.

The question of which communities Ottawa recognizes as Indigenous has implications not only for First Nations, Inuit and Métis people, but also affects billions of dollars worth of federal funding and access to other government programs.

The NCC style themselves as “southern Inuit,” and have referred to their organization as Métis in the past. Under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, the group had entered into the process to gain treaty rights under section 35 of the Constitution Act.

A spokesperson for the department of Crown and Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada (Cirnac) confirmed Wednesday the government has halted that process. The department said their rejection of Ncc’s claim to section 35 rights included “updated submissions, internal historical and legal analysis, expert reviews” and discussions with the group.

“Canada has determined that the evidence submitted does not satisfy the court-established tests for Indigenous rights and title,” wrote Jennifer Cooper, a spokesperson with Cirnac, in statement to Global News.

“This decision specifically concerns the assessment of section 35 rights. It does not affect Nunatukavut’s ability to apply for federal programs, services and partnerships that do not depend on section 35 recognition.

Rebecca Alty, the minister responsible for Cirnac, was travelling Wednesday and unavailable to comment, her office said. NCC President Todd Russell, a former Liberal MP who has long campaigned for his group’s recognition, was also unavailable to comment, his office said.

Inuit groups and the Innu Nation — which comprises the Innu of Labrador — have long pressured the federal government not to acknowledge the Ncc’s claims, suggesting they’re a settler group posing as Indigenous.

In a statement Wednesday, Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK), a national group representing Inuit communities, called the NCC a “fraudulent collective” that “undermines” and diverts funding away from Inuit people and communities.

“We urge the federal government to proactively prevent Inuit identity fraud by enacting a recognition policy that is consistent with the definition of Inuit provided in the federal Inuit Nunangat Policy,” the ITK statement read, referring to an umbrella policy that governs federal policies toward Inuit communities.

“This would help ensure that federal funds, programs and supports intended for Inuit or Indigenous peoples broadly are not misappropriated by NCC or other fraudulent collectives in the future.”

The federal government’s decision was also welcomed by the Nunatsiavut Government, a group representing Inuit peoples living in Labrador.

Johannes Lampe, the group’s president, the federal government’s concluding talks with the NCC brought “long-needed clarity” to the discussion.

“Inuit identity is not something that can be self-declared — it is affirmed by Inuit, grounded in our culture and history. Concluding this table (discussion) is an important step toward ensuring our rights, as Inuit, are protected, respected and upheld,” Lampe said in a statement.

A years-long investigation by Global News has revealed significant problems with how the federal government identifies Indigenous communities and recognizes rights, particularly in the federal Indigenous Procurement Program.

The program was designed to set aside tens of billions worth of federal government contracts for businesses majority-owned and -operated by First Nations, Inuit and Métis people.

But the Global News investigation found Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) failed to properly vet businesses to ensure they were actually Indigenous-owned.

An independent federal procurement watchdog’s report earlier this year found ISC repeatedly ignored safeguards meant to ensure the multi-billion dollar annual program benefited legitimate Indigenous businesses.

stories.title: Feds drop plans to skirt species at risk act for major projects
stories.summary: The federal government is abandoning plans to exempt certain projects from laws designed to protect species at risk.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Orcas play in Chatham Sound near Prince Rupert, B.C., Friday, June, 22, 2018. THE Canadian Press Jonathan Hayward

By Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

Posted September 9, 2026 4:30 pm.

Last Updated September 9, 2026 4:51 pm.

Ottawa — The federal government is abandoning plans to exempt certain projects from laws designed to protect species at risk.

But environmental groups say Ottawa can still bypass the Species At Risk Act through other means.

Ottawa is planning to introduce legislation in the fall to speed up approvals for major projects.

Part of the initial proposal was to give cabinet ministers “limited” power to exempt projects from what’s known as the “jeopardy test” for species at risk.

As first reported by The Toronto Star, the federal government is dropping those plans.

A senior government source confirmed to The Canadian Press that feedback received from more than 26,000 submissions overwhelmingly raised concerns about species at risk protections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

stories.title: N.S. government tables bill to review new regulation system for Nova Scotia Power
stories.summary: The government says the regulation could create incentives for the company to meet targets and trigger penalties for poor performance.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 9, 2026 4:24 pm

Updated September 9, 2026 5:34 pm

The premier of Nova Scotia Premier says his government is triggering a review into how the province’s major power utility earns its income in order to see whether this leads to better service and accountability.

Houston, who is also minister of energy, tabled a bill that would require the Nova Scotia Energy Board to begin the review of Nova Scotia Power.

The review would examine a performance-based regulation for the utility.

Houston says many Nova Scotians feel they aren’t getting good value for what they pay in electricity costs.

He adds he wants to examine whether changing how the utility earns its income could improve services and accountability.

The legislation says a performance-based regulation would link a portion of a utility’s revenues, earnings, incentives or penalties to measurable outcomes such as reliability, emissions reduction and customer service.

The government says the regulation could create incentives for the company to meet targets and trigger penalties for poor performance.

The government also proposes to begin the review 30 days after the law comes into effect, and to publish the final report.

stories.title: Unions, employers split on government intervention in labour disputes
stories.summary: The federal government says employers and unions are divided over how much power Ottawa should have to intervene in labour disputes.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government says employers and unions are divided over how much power Ottawa should have to intervene in labour disputes.

Employment and Social Development Canada released a report Wednesday documenting what it heard from stakeholders over the spring and summer about the state of labour relations in the country.

That review will inform future legislative changes to the Canada Labour Code with the fall session of Parliament just around the corner.

The report said employers and labour groups both felt the existing system for collective bargaining functions well in the vast majority of situations and any reforms should be targeted, not sweeping.

But participants in the review said that framework is not well suited to handling highly complex disputes that can result in sprawling economic disruptions beyond a particular industry.

The department said most employers asked for stronger government powers to intervene when labour disputes in federally regulated industries threaten the national interest.

They argued work stoppages at major railways and ports can affect Canada’s reliability as a trading partner at a time when U.S. trade restrictions are escalating and Prime Minster Mark Carney is looking to reorient Canadian exports to overseas markets.

Unions, meanwhile, opposed any measures that would curtail workers’ right to strike in pursuit of a deal.

“While generally supportive of measures that strengthen bargaining relationships and help parties reach negotiated agreements, they expressed significant concerns regarding proposals that could prolong the bargaining process, infringe on workers’ right to strike, or increase government intervention in labour disputes,” the report said of unions’ feedback.

Both sides were in favour of measures that increase certainty in the collective bargaining process.

Employers and unions diverged strongly on the use of Section 107 of the labour code. This contentious measure has been used increasingly often to curb work stoppages in key industries by referring disputes to the Canada Industrial Relations Board.

The federal government has leaned on Section 107 in recent years to get workers off the picket lines at Canada Post, the CN and Cpkc rail companies, and at the B.C. and Montreal ports. Air Canada flight attendants defied an attempt to use the measure to end their strike in 2025.

While employers were broadly supportive in the review of having a tool like Section 107 available to the government, labour groups strongly opposed it as overreach. Some unions felt the section should be repealed entirely or restricted to apply to only narrow circumstances.

There was some mixed reaction to the idea of introducing a new special mediator role to the collective bargaining process that could provide a neutral party’s opinion to the government, employers and workers before a dispute escalates.

Employers were broadly in favour of such a role, while some unions endorsed the idea with reservations. There were fears on the labour side that the mediator’s report could create the basis of a collective agreement that would hold employers’ back from negotiating in good faith.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Employers were broadly in favour of such a role, while some unions endorsed the idea with reservations. There were fears on the labour side that the mediator’s report could create the basis of a collective agreement that would hold employers’ back from negotiating in good faith.

Employment and Social Development Canada released a report Wednesday documenting what it heard from stakeholders over the spring and summer about the state of labour relations in the country.
That review will inform future legislative changes to the Canada Labour Code with the fall session of Parliament just around the corner.
The report said employers and labour groups both felt the existing system for collective bargaining functions well in the vast majority of situations and any reforms should be targeted, not sweeping.
But participants in the review said that framework is not well suited to handling highly complex disputes that can result in sprawling economic disruptions beyond a particular industry.
The department said most employers asked for stronger government powers to intervene when labour disputes in federally regulated industries threaten the national interest.

They argued work stoppages at major railways and ports can affect Canada’s reliability as a trading partner at a time when U.S. trade restrictions are escalating and Prime Minster Mark Carney is looking to reorient Canadian exports to overseas markets.
Unions, meanwhile, opposed any measures that would curtail workers’ right to strike in pursuit of a deal.

stories.title: N.S. mother vows to finish late son’s fight for improved income support for tent residents
stories.summary: A Nova Scotia woman is calling on the province to reverse a decision that has cut off people who live in tents from accessing enhanced income assistance.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia woman is calling on the provincial government to reverse a decision that has cut off people who live in tents from accessing enhanced income assistance.

Jackie Lowe said she’s determined to see her son’s work through.

“As Bradley’s mom, I wanted to carry on his fight and finish what he started,” she told reporters Wednesday at Province House.

Bradley Lowe died at a Halifax encampment site in 2023, amid his legal fight for improved income assistance for people living in tents.

The 30-year-old was receiving $380, the standard payment for someone without a home, to pay for “essentials” such as food and other necessities. But he had argued he was eligible for $950, the standard rate for people with disabilities who live in a household.

“He was fighting for change because he saw others around him experiencing the same things he was,” said Jackie.

On Aug. 5, the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal ruled a tent qualifies as “accommodation,” meaning people sleeping rough should be able to access enhanced income assistance support. However, the province updated its legislation weeks later to exclude tents, effectively cancelling out the ruling.

The province made additional changes to the income assistance disability supplement in early September to exclude people living with a disability, who are also living in tents, from accessing extra funds.

Jackie said she hopes the province will reconsider its actions.

“I just think it’s really sad to give people hope and then to take it away so quickly,” she said.

The NDP introduced a bill Wednesday called Bradley’s Law, in honour of Jackie’s son. The bill would ensure financial support is given regardless of a person’s housing status.

“The bill does what I think the court decision intended, (and that) was to codify that any kind of dwelling is eligible for the income assistance amount and the disability supplement,” said NDP Leader Claudia Chender.

Human rights lawyer Vince Calderhead, who represented Bradley in the case, said he’s asked the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission to investigate what’s transpired.

“From a legal point of view, in my view, it’s a clear human rights violation,” he told Global News.

“When you think about how deep a poverty level people in that situation are living in, this is just inexcusable.”

In response to the criticism, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said his government is making investments to support people sleeping rough, and that these particular supports weren’t necessarily applicable to people living in tents.

“We have the income assistance program, we’re indexing that for the first time ever,” Houston said.

“I think the specific program was the enhancements to income assistance, that enhancement is for people who have additional expenses like rent, like the cost of an apartment, so it’s not really appropriate in all situations.”

But advocates say taking money away from people who are struggling won’t help them get ahead.

“Limiting someone’s income when they have found themselves, in what is often the most difficult and desperate times of their life, to then also reduce their income just sets them so much further back from being able to ultimately, eventually, not be on income assistance,” said Emma Halpern, executive director of the Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia.

For Jackie, she says more help is needed for people experiencing circumstances similar to those her son faced before he died.

“We need to look at them as people,” she said.

— with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘I just keep going’: Bedford man takes 46-km walk in honour of Terry Fox, late mother-in-law
stories.summary: A Nova Scotia man who was inspired by Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope when he was going through his own health struggles, embarked on a 46 km walk to inspire others.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Residents of Bedford, N.S., outside Halifax have grown accustomed to seeing Patrick Doyle on his walks and strolls through the community.

For about five years now, the 61-year-old has been lacing up his shoes to raise awareness for various causes, becoming a well-known figure in the neighbourhood.

On Wednesday, he embarked on his biggest mission yet: an approximately 46-kilometre trek from Bedford to Hubbards in honour of Terry Fox and in memory of his late mother-in-law.

“I hope that some money is raised for research because it really pays off. And me, I’m an awareness person. I want to bring awareness,” he said.

Fox embarked on his Marathon of Hope in 1980 to raise money for cancer research after having had one of his legs amputated during his own treatment for the disease.

His cross-country tour began in St. John’s, where he dipped his foot into the Atlantic Ocean but was forced to end his journey five months later in Ontario when the cancer returned.

Since then, his Marathon of Hope has continued, with events in communities and schools across the country.

Doyle first became inspired by Fox when he was going through his own personal health struggles from 2011 to 2017 when he underwent 11 brain surgeries due to epilepsy.

“I started YouTubing and Googling and then I seen this guy Terry Fox hobbling with one leg,” he said. “And then I said, ‘Well gosh this guy’s got cancer but he’s not laying down taking it. There’s no reason me to lay in this bed and just take it.'”

He decided to take on walking as a way to stay active and healthy, and to support groups and causes in his community.

“I found walking, and … I fell in love with it. It just made me happy. I just had the drive and I would just think, ‘He didn’t stop. So people have it a lot worse off. I’m here. I can do it.’ So I just keep going,” he said.

Doyle’s connection to Fox would turn even more personal when his mother-in-law, Jean Pinkerton, passed away in 2018 from the same type of cancer that Fox had.

“She had her leg removed right through to the hip,” he said. “Her and I were so close, she was just … no slowing her down.”

Area councillor Jean St-Amand was on hand at DeWolfe Park on Wednesday morning as Doyle began his latest mission.

“He’s really thrown himself into a level of service and awareness for a number of causes and today is just another example of that. He’s been talking about his commitment to the Terry Fox run for a very long time and so I’m just here to demonstrate my support for his effort,” said St-Amand.

The Terry Fox Foundation called this one of Doyle’s “most important walks yet.”

“Doyle spoke very highly of Terry Fox and how Terry was a personal idol for him, and how his determination and his run many years ago was an example for (him) when he was recovering from his many brain surgeries,” said Krista O’Connor, community development director for the foundation.

“So it was really touching for him to tell us that and to share his story with us. And that’s part of the reason why he’s doing his walk today.”

In a Facebook post Wednesday afternoon, Doyle posted photos of himself after completing his journey in Hubbards. He had completed the trek in eight hours and 13 minutes.

Meanwhile, the 46th annual Terry Fox Run takes place across the country later this month. In Nova Scotia, some 50 communities and schools will take part on Sept. 20.

— with files from David Murdock

stories.title: Trump's latest trade actions are 'not an escalation,' economist says
stories.summary: The economic impact of presidential proclamations targeting trade with Canada will not have significant impact on the Canadian economy.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – The economic impact from U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest series of presidential proclamations targeting trade with Canada will not have significant impact on the Canadian economy, according to economists.

“I think the overall effect might be limited,” said Trevor Tombe, economist and professor at the University of Calgary. “Adjusting what products are covered by the tariffs isn’t something that should be, in my view, interpreted as escalation.”

The orders from Trump also ban some dairy products and motorcycles, while adding more products to the list of Canadian exports subject to 50 per cent tariffs that came into effect last month.

Trump also removed 50 per cent tariffs from several products, including toilet paper, cement, bedsheets and salt. The bans will come into effect at the end of this month, and the modification of tariffs under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 will take effect on Sept. 15.

“They realized they had hit things that they shouldn’t have, and so they took about $1.7 billion dollars off their list, added different products, almost as a one-for-one swap,” said William Pellerin, international trade partner at McMillan LLP, noting that the newly added items on the tariff list amount to about $1.8 billion.

Pellerin, like Tombe, said Trump’s latest announcement should not be interpreted as a major escalation in the trade conflict between Canada and the U.S.

However, one industry that is set to be hit the hardest is the Canadian alcohol industry, with outright bans on Canadian alcohol products.

Even this U.S. tariff advocate is urging Canada and the U.S. to drop retaliatory duties

How will counter-tariffs impact Canadians? Here's the potential cost

Tombe said the ban will impact 90 per cent of Canadian alcohol exports to the U.S., adding that roughly 13 per cent of Canadian alcohol production is exported to our southern neighbour.

It is the first time Trump has used import bans, which Capital Economics economist Stephen Brown interprets as bad news for the possibility of resolving the trade dispute and renewing the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma).

“Nonetheless, Trump’s willingness to impose an import ban is further evidence, if it were needed, that these latest measures are about inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue,” said Brown, in a note to clients.

“That calls into question our assumption that the sides will eventually resolve their broader differences around the Usmca, leaving the agreement in limbo and at risk of breaking down entirely,” he added.

Brown estimates the bans will impact just 0.25 per cent of Canadian exports to the U.S.

Pellerin said the import ban sounds like tough language, but he noted that much of the products that are subject to the ban, were previously hit by the 50 per cent Section 338 tariffs.

“In many cases, that 50 percent tariff effectively worked as an import ban already, right?” he said.

Tombe said the U.S. action is mimicking the alcohol bans carried out by provincial liquor boards in Canada.

Pellerin said while the macroeconomic impact might be limited, new products added to the Section 338 list of tariffs could be devastating for some companies.

“That’s catastrophic,” he said. “That business will see its sales potentially go to zero in the United States,”

Pellerin said that will be mean layoffs.

Tombe said trade uncertainty with the U.S. will continue to have a lasting negative impact on the Canadian economy.

“We’re about two per cent smaller as an economy than what was projected to be at this point,” he said. “That’s because of the uncertainty.”

Tombe said that uncertainty contributes to a drag on investment and hiring decisions.

The federal government has promised $7.5 billion in aid to help businesses and workers deal with the impacts of tariffs.

Brown said the 50 per-cent tariffs imposed by the U.S. will lead to a 0.4 per-cent hit to Canada’s GDP, with the federal government’s fiscal cushion only partially offsetting the drop in economic activity.

“While this should be partly offset by the Canadian government’s increased fiscal support for the affected firms and workers, there would also likely be a negative effect from delayed investment and hiring among other firms worried about the prospect of future U.S. tariffs,” he said, in a note. “As a result, Canadian GDP is likely to stagnate or even contract in the fourth quarter if the tariffs remain in place. ”

stories.title: How much will Trump’s ban on alcohol, dairy hurt Canada?
stories.summary: Canada's economy could be facing a bigger dent from U.S. tariffs after President Donald Trump escalated his administration's trade war to include full bans on certain products.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada’s economy could be facing a bigger dent from U.S. tariffs after U.S. President Donald Trump escalated his administration’s trade war to include full bans on most Canadian dairy and alcohol products.

Trump signed five executive orders late Tuesday which adjusted some of the previous tariffs to exclude items like cement and road salt, while also imposing full import bans on Canadian-made cheese and other dairy products, as well as alcoholic beverages. Trump justified the move as retaliation for Canada’s counter-tariff measures , which went into effect earlier on Tuesday.

Although the U.S. launched a trade war with Canada and the world in early 2025, Canada and the U.S. have been engaged in particularly tense negotiations and back-and-forth tariffs and counter-tariff threats since the U.S. threatened 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products in July , which went into effect in August.

Canada pulled out of trade negotiations last month , with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying his team “walked away from a bad deal,” and then imposed retaliatory counter-tariff measures this week.

“There are a number of industries and entrepreneurs and workers who will feel the brunt of this, specifically in alcohol, wine, Canadian-made beer, rye whiskey, products like that are clearly on the list,” says Matthew Holmes, executive vice president and chief of public policy with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce .

“They’re being directly targeted and the U.S. is viewing that as retaliation for the alcohol bans that provinces have put in place .”

Export Development Canada (EDC) estimates the value of Canada’s exports that could be subject to these import bans is roughly $778 million, which is somewhat modest compared to Canada’s total exports, which was $779 billion in 2025, according to Global Affairs Canada.

However, EDC says the impacts will still be severe for some businesses.

“Canadian exporters in these industries will find it harder to diversify, with the U.S. market accounting for anywhere between 70-95 per cent of total export sales. That makes firm-level impacts potentially quite severe, even if the aggregate Canadian GDP effect is fairly modest,” said Edc’s chief economist Stuart Bergman in a statement.

Here’s how much the full import bans could cost the Canadian economy.

Canadian wine, beer and spirits producers sell the vast majority of their products within Canada, but the overwhelming majority of the small amount that is exported internationally is sent to the United States.

If the U.S. imposes a full import ban on all Canadian alcohol, nearly all of that export figure could be erased.

According to the Government of Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, Canada exported $1.36 billion in alcoholic beverages in 2023 and 90 per cent of those exports were sent to the U.S., with two-thirds being for spirits alone, including rye whisky, gin and vodka.

Wine Growers of Canada tells Global News that approximately $8.3 million of wine was exported to the U.S. in 2025, and although it’s a relatively modest amount, the impact is concentrated regionally in Ontario, which makes up 90 per cent of that value.

Wine Growers of Canada also says that of the $8.3 million of wine exported to the U.S., more than half (57 per cent) was for icewine alone.

“Canadian wineries have also invested many years in building relationships with U.S. importers, distributors, retailers and consumers,” Wine Growers of Canada says.

“While we cannot control decisions taken by the White House, federal and provincial governments in Canada can control the measures we take here at home to strengthen and grow the Canadian wine industry.”

When it comes to beer, Canada exported about $28 million dollars in beer products outside of Canada in 2025, according to Beer Canada, which makes up close to 10 per cent of all the beer Canadian breweries produce. That means about 90 per cent of Canadian-made beer is sold and potentially being consumed within Canada.

“Our number one partner for beer exports is certainly the United States. The overwhelming majority of that $28 million in exports would be headed south to the U.S. market with a very, very small share going overseas,” says Luke Chapman, vice president of federal affairs for Beer Canada .

“The broader conflict is creating uncertainty though across the industry and adding costs at a time that is already challenging for Canadian brewers.”

Banning Canadian dairy imports adds to an already complex system, where dairy trade between Canada and the U.S. has long been governed by agreements on import and export quotas , including relevant tariffs.

For example, Canadian dairy processors, including those producing cheese, generally prioritize Canadian dairy farmers when sourcing ingredients.

That’s one of the issues Trump has taken exception to when he threatened a full ban on Canadian dairy products, and less than a month after imposing 50 per cent tariffs on the same sector.

Canada sent just over $700 million in dairy exports to the U.S. in 2024, according to Statistics Canada, although it’s unclear how much of those dairy imports would have been impacted otherwise by a full out ban, as Trump has threatened.

“The continued escalation of trade actions including a ban on certain Canadian dairy exports and additional tariffs on others is deeply concerning for Canada’s dairy sector,” said Dairy Farmers of Canada in a statement.”

“As determined by the most recent Cusma dispute settlement panel, Canada is currently respecting its dairy trade commitments with the U.S. unwarranted tariff measures and import bans only serve to create further uncertainty for farmers, processors and businesses on both sides of the border.”

Dairy Farmers of Canada would not confirm to Global News the annual value of dairy exports to the U.S. or how much would be impacted by a potential ban.

“Some of those dairy companies are going to feel it directly in terms of how big and how much of the U.S. market represents for them,” says Holmes.

“That action is very precision targeted at an industry that they feel is part of the trade irritant and grievance between the U.S. and Canada this time in terms of what they have access to in terms our market.”

The U.S. ban is set to take effect on Sept. 29.

content_blocks.text: Canada pulled out of trade negotiations last month , with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying his team “walked away from a bad deal,” and then imposed retaliatory counter-tariff measures this week.
content_blocks.html: Canada pulled out of trade negotiations last month, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying his team “walked away from a bad deal,” and then imposed retaliatory counter-tariff measures this week.

content_blocks.text: “There are a number of industries and entrepreneurs and workers who will feel the brunt of this, specifically in alcohol, wine, Canadian-made beer, rye whiskey, products like that are clearly on the list,” says Matthew Holmes, executive vice president and chief of public policy with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce .

content_blocks.text: “They’re being directly targeted and the U.S. is viewing that as retaliation for the alcohol bans that provinces have put in place .”
content_blocks.html: “They’re being directly targeted and the U.S. is viewing that as retaliation for the alcohol bans that provinces have put in place.”

content_blocks.text: Export Development Canada (EDC) estimates the value of Canada’s exports that could be subject to these import bans is roughly $778 million, which is somewhat modest compared to Canada’s total exports, which was $779 billion in 2025, according to Global Affairs Canada.

content_blocks.text: Alcohol
content_blocks.html: Alcohol

content_blocks.text: Canadian wine, beer and spirits producers sell the vast majority of their products within Canada, but the overwhelming majority of the small amount that is exported internationally is sent to the United States.
content_blocks.html: Canadian wine, beer and spirits producers sell the vast majority of their products within Canada, but the overwhelming majority of the small amount that is exported internationally is sent to the United States.

content_blocks.text: If the U.S. imposes a full import ban on all Canadian alcohol, nearly all of that export figure could be erased.
content_blocks.html: If the U.S. imposes a full import ban on all Canadian alcohol, nearly all of that export figure could be erased.

content_blocks.text: According to the Government of Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, Canada exported $1.36 billion in alcoholic beverages in 2023 and 90 per cent of those exports were sent to the U.S., with two-thirds being for spirits alone, including rye whisky, gin and vodka.

content_blocks.text: Wine Growers of Canada tells Global News that approximately $8.3 million of wine was exported to the U.S. in 2025, and although it’s a relatively modest amount, the impact is concentrated regionally in Ontario, which makes up 90 per cent of that value.

content_blocks.text: Banning Canadian dairy imports adds to an already complex system, where dairy trade between Canada and the U.S. has long been governed by agreements on import and export quotas , including relevant tariffs.

stories.title: B.C. unveils new border signs: ‘We will never be the 51st state’
stories.summary: B.C. Premier David Eby held his press conference hours after counter-tariffs on nearly 28 billion dollars of U.S. goods went into effect.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
B.C. Premier David Eby unveiled some new border signs at a press conference on Tuesday.

Eby said the signs will be posted at the B.C. border with Washington State.

One of the signs welcomes people to B.C. and says: “Strong, proud and will Never be the 51st state. Sorry!”

A second sign welcomes people to B.C. and says, don’t litter, 60 mph equals 100 km/h, respect fire bans, kindness does not equal weakness, watch for moose and Canada will never be the 51st state.

In August, U.S. President Donald Trump appeared to revive his “51st state” rhetoric as he made his first comments on the collapse of trade talks between Canada and the United States.

“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!” Trump wrote in a post on his social platform Truth Social. “They have charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!! President DJT.”

In early 2025, several Canadian provinces, including B.C., removed U.S. alcohol from their shelves in response to Trump’s trade war and his 51st state comments.

On Tuesday, Eby said the province is once again encouraging people to buy local.

He held his press conference hours after counter-tariffs on nearly $28 billion of U.S. goods went into effect.

He said the province is looking to strengthen the established Buy BC program to include products beyond produce and beverages.

Eby added that, like other Canadian premiers, he anticipates the trade war could drag on, impacting numerous businesses and industries.

“I don’t expect this to end quickly,” he said.

“Neither Canada nor the United States are at the table together. We’re not talking right now. The only hope that we have is ultimately that the American people understand our relationship and support candidates that promote a strong, unified relationship between Canada and the U.S.

“And currently, that is not this administration.”

-with files from Sean Previl

stories.title: ‘Dynacare sucks,’ Kinew says, as company orders striking employees back to work
stories.summary: Manitoba Premier says he May de-privatize lab testing after his NDP government intervened to end the strike
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, a day after his government intervened to end a medical workers strike, called out their employer and suggested he may de-privatize lab testing.

“Dynacare sucks. Dynacare sucks,” Kinew repeated numerous times Wednesday when asked by reporters about the one-day walkout by 350 Dynacare lab technicians and technologists.

“The workers are frustrated. Absolutely they’re frustrated (and) rightfully so,” the premier added.

“Dynacare, get back to the (bargaining) table and give these people a raise.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, a day after his NDP government intervened to end a strike by medical workers, questioned their employer and suggested he may de-privatize lab testing.

The Canadian Press

The workers walked off the job Tuesday morning, shuttering 22 Dynacare lab locations across the province and stopping the collection of thousands of tests, including blood work, urinalysis and prenatal checks.

Hours later, Kinew’s government successfully argued to the Manitoba Labour Board that Dynacare work is vital to the health system. By day’s end, the board ordered the workers back.

The union, the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals, complied and the employees were back on the job Wednesday morning.

The union and Dynacare didn’t have an essential workers agreement in place in case of a strike.

Kinew lambasted Dynacare for “making a mess of the situation” and said his government had no choice but to intervene, because it has a higher responsibility to keep the health system running.

“Nobody should be using the results of a cancer test as leverage in a negotiation. Nobody,” the premier said.

The strike centred around wages. The union said its workers earn as much as 20 to 50 per cent less than counterparts in the public system.

Dynacare said in a statement that it shares Kinew’s commitment to maintaining reliable lab services and that’s why it’s pushing for a “sustainable” collective agreement.

“We acknowledge that this has been a difficult situation for patients and for the province, and we share the premier’s desire for a resolution,” the company said.

It said it has offered a substantial pay increase and has proposed arbitration as the fastest path to a fair resolution.

Union president Jason Linklater said workers are determined to close the wage gap and aren’t prepared to risk that in arbitration.

He said the premier has the power to fix the problem, including by adding a wage agreement to the existing contract, and making more of the contract public.

Linklater said he wants to know why Kinew renewed the contract last year without better wage supports for workers and has now cut off the union’s ability to strike.

“Government intervened; they totally took away the single piece of leverage,” he said.

“There’s a whole bunch of anger right now, and people who feel betrayed. But I have to remain hopeful that there’s still a solution.”

He pushed back on the province’s perspective that critical testing would be lost, noting that Shared Health had said essential services would be maintained through government labs.

Kinew said fault also lies with the former Progressive Conservative government for contracting out all non-hospital testing to Dynacare – a private operator.

He said his NDP government is considering de-privatizing the testing but acknowledged it’s a tall, very expensive decision.

“The PCs privatized this system,” Kinew said. “Once you privatize something and it goes to the private sector, it becomes extraordinarily costly to bring it back into public hands.”

Asked for a response to Kinew, Progressive Conservative labour critic Josh Guenter, in a statement, said, “Under the NDP, we have seen wait times continue to go up across all sectors of our health-care system.

Guenter added, “We saw, once again, this premier – who ran on fixing health care – choosing conflict over care.”

stories.title: Ryan Brown’s bagpipe talent strikes a chord with London Knights
stories.summary: The Dallas Stars prospect showed off an unexpected skill during the Knights’ trip to Victoria, B.C.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Every hockey team with a lot of new faces needs something fun to break the ice.

The London Knights used their trip to Victoria, B.C., for that purpose. Little did they know they would share a moment over bagpipes.

“We were walking to dinner and there was a guy on the street just playing,” veteran forward Ryan Brown said. “I went up to him and asked if I could play a song and do the notes for him.

“He let me.”

As the whole team watched, the Dallas Stars prospect displayed a hidden skill he had honed since Grade 7 at St. Andrew’s College in Aurora. The bagpipes are notorious for requiring patience and discipline to learn properly.

“They have a world-renowned piping class and program there,” the 18-year-old Newmarket native said, “so I thought it was pretty unique to start and learn it. I loved the sound of it and kept it going.”

Brown hasn’t performed much in public, but he did play at a funeral once and occasionally piped his lacrosse team onto the field at school – right before taking part in the game.

Would he play the national anthem at Canada Life Place in uniform before a Knights game if GM Mark Hunter asked?

“If he wants me to, I would,” Brown quipped. “I’ve got my own (set) just to keep it up and practice, to have the music in shape and my memorization of everything.”

Every once in a while, he plays for his billet family.

“They think it’s pretty cool,” the 2023 Sarnia Sting first-rounder said. “They’re loud, though. I think if I played them every day, they would get tired of it sometimes.”

Brown went to SAC with Senators first-rounder Jaxon Cover, one of the Knights stars this season, for a couple of years. Did his teammate from the Cayman Islands join him in the woodwind section?

“I don’t think he played any instrument,” Brown said. “He was pretty good at soccer, though.”

STING ON DECK: The Knights’ older players are scattering for NHL rookie and training camps this week. So it will be a younger crew that dresses in the final pre-season tune-ups Thursday (7 p.m. at Canada Life Place) and Friday in Sarnia (7:05 p.m.) against the Sting.

The Knights don’t expect to see new import signee Marcus Nordmark, the Ducks first-rounder, until he is done trying out for Anaheim. For many, this week is the last chance to crack an increasingly competitive roster.

“The pre-season has been a good test to see our team together,” Brown said. “Victoria is a good team and it was cool to play against a full group of new faces. It’ll be good for the younger guys to get some time in against Sarnia and we’ll be ready when everyone comes back.”

Brown didn’t communicate much with Dallas ahead of the NHL draft and was pleasantly surprised to hear his name called while he watched from home. The 6-foot, 192-pounder exploded offensively after being acquired from Sarnia for fellow forward Logan Hawery – with 16 goals and 40 points in 33 games, then three goals and five points in five playoff tilts against Sault Ste. Marie.

“Being a late (birth date), guys my age got to go to camps and play rookie tournaments last year,” he said, “so being able to experience it will be super cool and a good learning experience to play with older players.

“I’m happy with how my year went and I think this one will be even better. In London, we need to make a little bit of a deeper run in the playoffs this year, which is the goal.”

There will be some challenges along the way, of course.

But it probably won’t be as difficult as trying to master the bagpipes.

stories.title: Trump’s latest trade threat weighs on Canadian firms with U.S. contracts
stories.summary: Shares of Canadian companies doing business with the U.S. fell following Trump’s threat to products being sold to federal contractors.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Shares of Canadian companies that do business with the U.S. government fell following President Donald Trump’s threat to bar Canadian-origin products from being sold to federal contractors.

“From now on, NO Reciprocity – NO Access!” Trump said in a social media post Tuesday afternoon, saying Canadian and provincial governments ban U.S. firms from winning contracts in the country.

He directed the U.S. General Services Administration to work with the U.S. Trade Representative to “take all necessary steps to Remove Canadian-origin products from Gsa’s Multiple Award Schedules unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies.”

Share prices for IT consulting company CGI Inc., engineering firms WSP Global Inc., AtkinsRealis Group Inc. and Stantec Inc., and construction firm Aecon Group Inc. had all dropped by more than 2 per cent in Toronto as of Wednesday afternoon.

It’s not yet clear how “Canadian-origin products” are defined, and whether the directive includes services or parent companies of U.S. subsidiaries.

CGI has “relatively material exposure” to U.S. government contracts, National Bank of Canada analyst Doug Taylor wrote in a client note. “We estimate U.S. government revenue could represent between 15 per cent to 20 per cent of Cgi’s total revenue.”

But the company primarily sells services, not goods, in the U.S., which means CGI May be “potentially more insulated than the current scope of the language implies,” Taylor said. “Risk would become more meaningful if restrictions instead apply based on Canadian (parent) ownership, e.g., if U.S.-based subsidiaries of Canadian companies are also included.”

CGI said in an emailed statement that CGI Federal, which serves U.S. federal agencies, is a “U.S.-based, wholly-owned operating subsidiary,” and that it employs over 8,000 people “who live and work across 60 U.S. locations.”

Trump strikes back with executive orders banning Canadian goods, including alcohol and dairy

Trump targets Bombardier, Canadian dollar in Truth Social blitz ahead of tariff deadline

“CGI Federal is proud to provide U.S.-originated technology services and core business platforms under a wide range of contract vehicles to support the federal government’s mission-critical objectives,” it added.

Following the first round of U.S. tariffs in 2025, the Canadian government introduced a policy that favours local businesses in federal procurement and prioritizes Canadian materials in major construction and defence projects. The move came alongside a push to make Canada more self-sufficient and sovereign in digital capabilities.

Provinces have also announced limits to U.S. procurement. For example, the Quebec government said this week that it will reserve certain calls for tenders for Canadian firms, and Ontario has a policy that greatly restricts procurement from U.S. businesses while preferring local firms.

stories.title: AI minister says solutions exist after Anthropic researcher quits over safety fears
stories.summary: Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says the government is following the situation at Anthropic after a researcher who quit the firm said people in the industry fear AI could 'kill us all.'
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal artificial intelligence minister said the government is closely following the situation at Anthropic after a researcher who resigned from the company Tuesday said people in the industry fear AI could “kill us all.”

Evan Solomon also told reporters Wednesday such warnings aren’t new and that there are both regulatory and technical solutions to the dangers posed by AI.

He pointed to the Liberal government’s efforts to introduce privacy legislation. “We’re establishing a new regulator that will have the power to hold these big companies to account,” he said.

Solomon also said the government is investing in AI safety and noted ongoing work by Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio on safe AI. Solomon added the government is also working with other countries on ways to protect citizens.

He said there are “real concerns” about the negative consequences of AI.

On Tuesday, researcher Jacob Coxon, who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said in a post on X that neither “company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below. — Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

He said those who are building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Adding that this is “not a marketing stunt,” Coxon said that many in the industry will use more measured phrasing when speaking publicly, even as they express fear in private.

Solomon made the comments in Edmonton, where he announced the launch of a new initiative to boost AI literacy among Canadians.

That initiative includes “AI essentials” courses for students, educators and Canadians in general. The government is partnering with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, one of Canada’s three national AI institutes.

“We’ll invest $13 million to launch this course, to expand AI literacy for every single Canadian,” Solomon said.

Last week, he announced new voluntary principles for building data centres in Canada in response to growing backlash against data centres across the country.

The federal government won’t be enforcing the guidelines. Solomon told reporters last week decisions on data centres fall under provincial and municipal jurisdiction.

In response to a question about whether the government will monitor compliance, Solomon said the agreement will provide reliable and verifiable information on the standards that were set.

“Those are going to be enforced by the municipalities or the provinces,” he said.

The framework says data centres must “create lasting local benefits,” can’t shift electricity costs to Canadians, and must minimize water use and their impact on the environment. It also calls for transparency on local impacts and says data centres have to “bring strategic value to Canada.”

The list of signatories includes Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Bell, Telus and Anthropic.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: New Toronto condo will feature porcelain tile handpicked in Italy
stories.summary: Summerhill-Rosedale project possesses the same DNA as many other Woodcliffe developments
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
Joseph Notarfonzo has been cutting the hair of investment bankers, real estate moguls, creative types (such as this columnist), fellow Yonge Street retailers and office stiffs since 1961. If you were to ask, he’d likely be able to tell you how many times the floor tiles have been replaced at his little barbershop at 1204 Yonge St., or give you an accurate estimate how long a pair of shoes lasts for someone who spends all day on his feet. A good storyteller and a sharp wit, the octogenarian might also tell you he’s ready to retire.

But it’s not true, said Eve Lewis, CEO of Woodcliffe Landmark Properties: “Paul [Oberman] bought the building, and we’d always worked together, but I had never worked with the tenants, so I introduced myself to Joe and he said, ‘Well, you know, I am thinking of retiring’. That was 15 years ago,” she says with a laugh.

Like barbers or architects or artists, real estate developers never really retire. Had it not been for the 2011 plane crash that took his life, Mr. Oberman would be standing beside his wife, Ms. Lewis, at Yonge Street and Birch Avenue, admiring the enormous poster promoting “The Summerhill,” a boutique condominium that, once construction begins, might be the only thing to part Mr. Notarfonzo from his scissors.

For the company that gifted the city, in the first decade of this century, the restoration of Canadian-Pacific’s North Toronto Station (1915, now home to an Lcbo) and the beloved shops known as “The Five Thieves” (1892) – both across the street and both sold in 2016 – it’s a fitting location for Woodcliffe to build again.

But, unlike the slapdash condominium towers that dot the city, this one will be special, even on the outside, thanks to a shipload of Italian porcelain and architect Peter Clewes, who has “designed every single inch of this building,” said Ms. Lewis.

“We went to Modena, in Italy, with Peter in June,” said Woodcliffe VP of investments and corporate strategy Stratton Townley. “That’s where 90 per cent of Italian porcelain comes from. You go to these factories, and they show you not only the materials and how they manufacture it … but they also show you the mounting systems that they recommend.”

Mr. Clewes, principal/owner at architectsAlliance, could, at this stage of his career, pull a Frank Gehry and scribble a few things onto a cocktail napkin and let a gang of underlings decipher his chicken-scratches. But that, he said, would just add to the commodification that has plagued residential high-rise design for the past decade.

“It’s less about beautiful buildings and well-proportioned living spaces, and more about the number of investment units that can be packed into buildings with massing and program dictated by tall building guidelines,” said Mr. Clewes. “This project represents an opportunity to return to my roots as a designer, to create something compelling, beautiful, contextual … to think deeply about how the building meets grade, about materiality; above all else, about creating a beautiful place to live.”

Clad in that scrumptious imported porcelain intersected by bits of champagne-coloured metal and featuring acres and acres of glass, it will be beautiful indeed. Plus, with the heritage restoration of the stores along the Yonge Street sidewalk, the project possesses the same DNA as so many other Woodcliffe developments: “Paul loved retail restoration, office, more than he liked residential,” said Ms. Lewis.

“We’ve shifted our focus to mixed-use,” said Mr. Townley. “We still love doing office and retail, but we’ve added the residential component.”

At the sales office down the road, Brodie Townley of Market Vision fires up a full-wall video screen. With the push of a button, he can place potential owners on any of the building’s 33 storeys. On floors with only two units, he can demonstrate how one can, literally, trace the path of the sun.

“Do you love morning or evening light?” he asks as he dials up 6:50 a.m. in June. “This is on the 28th floor, and you can just feel the expansiveness of where our views in this building are protected.” Lower down, and North Toronto Station’s clock tower – inspired by the Campanile in St. Mark’s Square in Venice – seems so close one could reach out and touch it.

Mr. Clewes’s sashless corner windows and staggered balconies, which eliminate that annoying roof overhead, means each unit enjoys a feast of sky, clouds, the trees of north Rosedale, and the mighty asphalt river of Yonge Street, which effortlessly divides the city into east and west.

“It was a real challenge to design that building because it has such a small floor plate,” said Ms. Lewis. “But the opportunities it created is that for 1,800 square feet, you can still have three sides of glass, which is unheard of.”

Interiors come courtesy of Brian Gluckstein, and, while minimal, landscaping is from the imaginative minds at Claude Cormier’s CCxA (the firm that gave Toronto the dog fountain and Berczy Park) and will feature a horse: “So, at [the grocery store] Harvest Wagon, there’s a wagon outside that Paul and I put there,” Ms. Lewis said with a smile. “So, this is the horse that got away from the wagon.”

And speaking of horses, the one Toronto rode during the condo boom has left the barn: the market has crashed and most developers have switched to building rental buildings. But Summerhill-Rosedale is a horse of a different colour and snack bracket, said Ms. Lewis: “The upper end of the market is a market that has the opportunity to be able to make choices for themselves, so our plan is that we could probably be under construction in 12 to 18 months.”

As to where all those movers and shakers are going to get a haircut, well, that’s another story.

stories.title: SIU charges London police officer after man injured at hospital
stories.summary: The constable faces an assault causing bodily harm charge stemming from a March incident.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The constable faces an assault causing bodily harm charge stemming from a March incident.

Last updated 28 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/SIU-charges-London-police-officer-after-man-injured-at-hospital#comments-area)

Special Investigations Unit. (File photo/Postmedia Network)

Ontario’s police watchdog has charged a London police constable after a man was injured during an interaction with an officer at Victoria Hospital.

Police arrested and apprehended a man under the Mental Health Act – legislation allowing a person to be apprehended and taken for psychiatric examination – on March 18, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said on Wednesday.

The man, whose name and age weren’t released, was taken to Victoria Hospital, where he was seriously injured during an interaction with an officer, the SIU said.

Const. Stephen Farrand is charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm. He is scheduled to appear in court on Sept. 22.

“As the matter is before the courts, and in consideration of the fair trial interests of the accused, the SIU will not provide further comment on the investigation,” the agency said in a statement.

London police issued a media release one day after the incident, saying the SIU had invoked its mandate and providing additional details.

Police responded around 11 a.m. to a report of a man who refused to stop at an east-end intersection that was closed for a traffic investigation, police said at the time.

Officers located the man in his vehicle. He was in distress and officers broke a window to remove him, police said.

The man was apprehended and taken to hospital. He suffered an injury requiring medical attention, police said.

The SIU investigates cases involving serious injury, death, gunshots and allegations of sexual assault involving police officers.
