stories.title: Born on 9/11: Canadians turning 25 mark a day of both happiness and mourning
stories.summary: 'I never realized the gravity of my birthday until the first time my dad took me to New York when I was 10 years old.'
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
When Monica Spoletini tells people she was born on Sept. 11, 2001, “Nine times out of 10 I get a look and … nine times out of 10 the second question is ‘on the year? On 2001?’

“And I just smile and (say) yep,” she says.

2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the hijacked airplane strikes on the Twin Towers, the Pentagon, and the crash of a fourth plane in Pennsylvania. All told, the attacks claimed the lives of 2,977 people , including 24 Canadians .

On that same day, as many as 13,238 people were born in the United States. It’s not known exactly how many Canadians also took their first breath Sept. 11, 2011, but Statistics Canada says average daily births in September in that period numbered 1,067 .

Among those Canadians were Monica and her twin brother, born in Chestermere, Alta. Both will turn 25 on Sept. 11. Spoletini now works as a hairdresser in Edmonton, where her family moved when she was 12. (Her brother declined an interview.)

Neither twin has yet visited the 9/11 memorial in New York City; however, they were acquainted with the events of 9/11 from a young age, because their father read them articles about it, says Monica Spoletini.

“(He) wanted to educate us a little bit (about) why everyone knows our birthday so much and why it’s so recognized,” Spoletini says.

One of her most vivid memories is of an old article that her parents framed on the wall, featuring her family. “I would say maybe (we were) eight or nine years old, and we could really understand why” it was so significant.

Christopher Rutkowski was born in Oshawa, Ont. on Sept. 11, 2001.

He says some of his friends believe he is a reincarnated 9/11 victim. “I was born about six hours before the first plane hit. And I have a birthmark on the right side of my face.” His friends theorize that he was initially a financier working in the towers. “I didn’t make it (out alive) — and then, ‘real Christopher’ was born.”

Rutkowski has visited the memorial at the site of the World Trade Centre three times, the most recent visit in August.

“I never realized the gravity of my birthday until the first time my dad took me to New York when I was 10 years old,” he says. He also visited on his 15th birthday.

With his father, he went to the Ground Zero museum, which he recalls displayed “steel columns and pillars and escalators (from the site)… and people’s stories and phone recordings.”

Rutkowski, who calls himself a “big reader,” says he has spent years expanding his home library dedicated to 9/11 to properly commemorate the event.

The Spoletini twins, who had planned to visit the site some years ago, were delayed when COVID struck. Now that they lead independent lives, coordination is a bit of challenge, Monica Spoletini admits, adding that “it definitely is something that the two of us want to do together.”

The challenge of being born on 9/11 has been difficult for some.

For instance, “My family pretends it isn’t a thing. My birthday, I mean,” one person wrote on Reddit. “I was born in NYC, actually between the time the first and second towers were hit. My parents were pretty scarred (sic) by it so we just pretend I don’t have a birthday.”

Another posted: “My best friend was born on the date. She gets a lot of sympathy aww’s and, “Oh, honey” comments. She does joke that our high school has an assembly for her birthday every year though so … ”

“My daughter was born on 9/11/2001 a few hours before the 1st plane hit. First few birthdays were rough for the family and we didn’t celebrate day of but by now we do. I think it makes her feel kind of special being born that day. But she shows respect and knows the significance of the tragedy,” wrote one mom.

For his part, Rutkowski believes in balancing both aspects of the date — taking joy at being born, yet honouring the victims of the tragedy: “It’s a double-edged sword in a sense.”

Spoletini feels the sadness too. But she also believes in a purpose: “I was raised religious, so normally… my parents would say: ‘there was a reason God brought you into the world on that day.’ I also believe in God, but I also do believe in the universe as well.

“I do think, you know, the universe or God, or whoever’s outside of us, brought us here on that day too. To… teach us.”

Both have major plans for their birthdays.

For the Spoletinis, it is the time for a family reunion, and, says Monica, “I’m planning … to realize that I’m actually 25 years old and that my brain is fully developed and that I’m grown up.”

Rutkowski, ON his third visit to the site last month, stopped in at Fire Engine Company No. 65, which was among the first to respond to the disaster. Rutkowski met New York firefighters at the station during one of his earlier visits too.

He is also training to run a 5K obstacle course to honour the victims of 9/11 and demonstrate resilience: “(T)his will be my first year doing it.”

And he concludes: “If things are going bad or I’m having a bad day, you know, people have had a lot worse days or the bad doesn’t last forever or there’s always going to be some sort of good in something bad that happens.

“And so, it’s taught me to be patient and full of gratitude.”

stories.title: Jay Baruchel’s fast and furious dream to rocket Canadian film into the stratosphere
stories.summary: Ahead of The Stunt Driver’s Tiff world premiere, the star talks with Barry Hertz about the film he’s been working his entire career toward
stories.author: Barry Hertz, Photography by David Kerr
stories.content:
The plan was simple. Construct a 430-metre ramp on a patch of farmland near Morrisburg, Ont. Then use that ramp to launch a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental across a 1.6-kilometre stretch of the St. Lawrence River, where the vehicle would land safe and snug on the other side of the Canada-U.S. border, a bed of freshly planted roses cushioning its fall. The only challenge: There had to be a person behind the wheel of that Lincoln. And that person would need to survive the ramp, the jump, and, of course, the landing.

In 1976, Ken “The Mad Canadian” Carter planned just such a feat, as much a bid to cement his daredevil legacy as it was to prove to the world that Canadians had just as much heart, courage, and never-say-die tenacity (to say nothing of unhinged audacity) as our neighbours to the south. And now, a half-century and a few cultural-sovereignty crises later, actor Jay Baruchel is immortalizing Carter’s 400-km-an-hour journey in director Michael Dowse’s The Stunt Driver , a wild, hilarious, heartbreaking, and surprisingly timely new movie that only a fellow Mad Canadian such as himself could headline.

“First and foremost, this is just a great entertaining old-school movie. But it is also very much a meditation on the condition of being Canadian. It works on a bunch of different levels and scratches a bunch of different itches. But any Canadian who sees themselves in it, that’s not an accident,” says the Ottawa-born, Montreal-raised, and now Toronto-based actor.

“That’s something we talked about throughout the entire movie, and everything you’re feeling connected to as a Canadian is all deliberate. That is all a bunch of Dowse and I and a bunch of crabby Canadian men of a certain time period getting a lot of stuff out of their system.”

It is a few weeks before The Stunt Driver makes its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, and Baruchel is interrupting his last-gasp-of-summer vacation at his cottage about an hour outside Kingston – a wood-panelled hideaway with mosquitos and spotty Wi-Fi, or about as Canadian a retreat as it gets – to trace the development of what might be the movie that he’s been working his entire career toward .

In the business for more than a quarter-century, starting with roles on such tween-flavoured series as Are You Afraid of the Dark? and Popular Mechanics for Kids , Baruchel spent much of his 20s and 30s keeping one foot in Hollywood, the other at home in Canada.

At a certain point, it might have simply been easier for the actor to migrate south completely like fellow Canadian Seth Rogen, the two actors becoming key players in that now-distant, bygone era when any Judd Apatow-associated comedy ( Knocked Up , This Is the End ) could dominate the box office and discourse for weeks. Instead, Baruchel kept evolving his roster of collaborators – Clint Eastwood to Ben Stiller to David Cronenberg to a pre- Heated Rivalry Jacob Tierney – while increasingly focusing on what he could do within, and for, the Canadian industry.

“I grew up in Montreal and I also grew up in Oshawa at the arse end of the eighties, and it was a pretty bleak time in Canada. I was a TV and movie addict, but I’d go outside in Oshawa and be like, well, I might as well be on Mars because how do you get into that? From here to there?” Baruchel recalls. “The one thing that would tell me I could do it here was the existence of the National Film Board and the CBC. They have been many things to me, but one of them is a beacon. So if we can play even a tiny role in that, that’s a pretty big source of pride.”

Just as Carter himself needed to endure countless bone-crunching stunts in Ontario and Quebec before he could convince foreign broadcasters to broadcast his St. Lawrence jump – the show-off always keeping one eye trained at outdoing his American rival, Evel Knievel – Baruchel’s performance in The Stunt Driver is built atop years and years of getting battered and bruised within the Canadian system. And if there is one knock-down, drag-out, homegrown rumble that would eventually lead Baruchel to this new movie, it was his work co-writing and co-starring in the 2011 hockey comedy Goon , where he first connected with Dowse.

“When you go to war alongside someone, which was what it was like making Goon , you grow strong as you’re in the trenches with them, and it just galvanizes the relationship,” recalls Dowse who, like Baruchel, has found a way to work both in Hollywood ( Stuber , last year’s Trap House ) and at home ( Fubar , The F Word ). “We worked again for a few episodes of the show Man Seeking Woman , but it wasn’t until I saw BlackBerry that I thought, maybe Jay can play Ken. He’s older now, he intimately knows that lower Notre-Dame-de-Grâce world where Ken was from. And Jay just put this film on his back. He knew the responsibility this was, and he rose to the challenge.”

For Baruchel, Carter offered a juicy role, certainly – a dreamer who loves the thrill of the road despite not having a driver’s license, a husband who adores his wife (played by Laurence Leboeuf) yet can’t find it in himself to stop giving her nightmares every time he steps behind the wheel. And in his performance, Baruchel nails all those knotty contradictions with tragedy and electricity. But the character of Carter is also emblematic of a sliver of the Canadian psyche, in direct dialogue with Baruchel’s work in BlackBerry as the stymied engineer Mike Lazaridis.

“As different as the Lazaridis and Carter characters are, they’re both patriots with small-man chips on their shoulders. They have windmills in common, and they’re mine as well,” says Baruchel. “The fact that Ken is as direct and on his sleeve with his patriotism, that’s me, man. Look, you don’t have to wave a flag, but to pretend and aspire to do that somewhere else for another flag – to replace your flag – I have contempt, I’ll be honest, for those people. And I have a great deal of respect for people who are proud to be here, and long before it was financially or culturally or politically expedient or convenient. It’s got a currency to it now, but what about when that wasn’t sexy?”

While Carter perhaps wasn’t as sexy a figure back in 1976 as his rival Knievel (who is played in Dowse’s film with a sly blend of charm and smarm by the American actor Ben Foster), the showman was savvy enough to garner the attention of a National Film Board crew led by documentarian Robert Fortier, who trailed Carter around for years. And it was Fortier’s resulting 1981 documentary, The Devil at Your Heels , that years ago turned Dowse onto Carter’s somewhat forgotten role in Canadian history. So much so that The Stunt Driver ’s narrative is built around the struggle of making the NFB doc itself, with Fortier played by veteran Canadian character actor Joe Cobden.

“It’s funny when you think about it, because life imitated art in a lot of ways on this,” says Dowse. “And it’s a similar sort of quixotic relationship a director has with a film that Ken has with his big jump. It’s for all the glory, just like a film lives on past you. You want to have an impact, you want to have a name. All that stuff that Ken is trying to do drives a lot of filmmakers, as well.”

Depending on the success of The Stunt Driver , Dowse and Baruchel might be able to get another collective shot or two at seeing their work live past them. Currently, they’re developing a reboot of Dowse’s 2009 Showcase sitcom The Foundation , as well as a feature-length comedy about, in Dowse’s words, “a doomsday cult that is actually right.” (Tentative title: Cult De Sac. )

But for now, Baruchel feels as if The Stunt Driver – and so many other projects being produced within the Canadian system – is offering him an answer to those cultural frustrations he wrestled with as a kid in Southern Ontario, when he felt as if he were light years away from anything exciting.

“I’m encouraged every year by the kind of vitality of the movies and TV shows that we’re creating,” the actor says.

“Does that kid in Oshawa now see himself more reflected onscreen? I think that he does. The biggest TV show on the planet last year was a Canadian show that actually took place in Canada ! We live in a country where we have agreed that it’s important for all of us as a country to make these things and to provide resources to make them. What a special, crazy, cool thing.”

The Stunt Driver screens at Tiff Sept. 11 and 12 ( tiff.net ), before opening across the country Sept. 25.

stories.title: Okamoto, Smith hit home runs to help Blue Jays down Athletics
stories.summary: Toronto (73-73) sits one game back of the Cleveland Guardians (74-72) for the third and final American League wild-card spot.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Posted September 9, 2026 5:21 am.

Kazuma Okamoto and Josh Smith hit home runs, José Soriano worked seven innings of two-run ball, and the Toronto Blue Jays beat the Athletics 4-2 on Tuesday night.

Toronto (73-73) sits one game back of the Cleveland Guardians (74-72) for the third and final American League wild-card spot. The Guardians beat the Baltimore Orioles 9-5 earlier in the day.

The Texas Rangers, who beat the Mariners 10-5 in Seattle on Tuesday, are a half-game behind the Blue Jays.

Smith, who was traded from the Texas Rangers on Aug. 3, opened the scoring in the second inning with a 360-foot shot to give Toronto a 1-0 lead. In his 20 games with the Blue Jays, he has five homers.

Okamoto followed in the next at-bat with the 30th home run of his rookie season. He joins Shohei Ohtani, Hideki Matsui, Seiya Suzuki and Munetaka Murakami as the only Japanese players to complete the feat.

The milestone also marked the first time in major league history that three rookies have hit 30 or more home runs in the same season. Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart is the other.

Okamoto already set the Blue Jays record for most home runs by a rookie in a season when he belted his 25th of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays in August.

Alejandro Kirk hit an RBI single, and Smith capped the scoring by grounding into a one-run double play.

Soriano (12-7), who was traded from the Los Angeles Angels on Aug. 3 as well, struck out three and gave up six hits. Spencer Miles worked two hitless innings for his second save of the season.

Carlos Cortes and Donovan Walton each had home runs for the Athletics.

Athletics starting pitcher Jack Perkins (3-11) allowed all four runs on seven hits while fanning three.

Athletics’ LHP Brady Basso(1-2, 4.32 ERA) takes the mound on Wednesday. The Blue Jays will turn to reliever Braydon Fisher, expected to serve as the opener.

stories.title: 25 years ago, Canada faced a 'dramatic change' as it headed for war in Afghanistan
stories.summary: A quarter of a century ago, the terror attacks of Sept. 9, 2001 forced Canadians to quickly wake up to a world that had changed overnight — and to confront a new war which would change everything for Canada’s military.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A quarter of a century ago, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 forced Canadians to quickly wake up to a world that had changed overnight — and to confront a new war which would change everything for Canada’s military.

The Afghanistan war, Canada’s longest armed conflict, taught harsh lessons — some that Canada learned, others it did not.

Soon after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Canada stepped out of the quiet decade after the Cold War into the global fight on terror, and soon found itself at war with a Taliban insurgency halfway around the world.

“Who would have dreamt the day prior to that, Canadian troops in their thousands would be serving in Afghanistan — Afghanistan, for God’s sake, of all places. It was a dramatic change,” said retired general Rick Hillier, who led a multinational force of Nato nations in Kabul and would become Canada’s best-known chief of defence staff.

“It was a shift in our understanding of how the world functioned. We no longer operated, if you will, as a country isolated from all that upheaval and turmoil and hatred and violence.”

Canada’s ambassador to Nato moved for the alliance to, for the first time ever, invoke Article Five — the clause in the Nato treaty that says an attack on one member country constitutes an attack on all.

Canada went to war with its allies to support the United States and overthrow the Taliban regime which was harbouring the terror group led by Osama bin Laden that was behind the 9-11 attacks.

That alliance spirit is harder to detect today, with Canada’s relationship with the U.S. tanking over a trade war and President Donald Trump threatening to tear up the Nato alliance and pull more troops out of Europe.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, no one knew that more than 40,000 Canadians would serve in the 12-year Afghanistan war and 159 Canadian military members would lose their lives there.

Eugene Lang, a former chief of staff to two defence ministers, said Ottawa thought at the time it was entering a short-term conflict.

“Nobody was really anticipating what we got into, and we weren’t really prepared for it, in terms of the severity of the situation, the complexity of the situation and the duration,” he said.

Military doctrine had to change on the fly as Canadians learned to fight an insurgency and the Canadian Forces scrambled to find Pashto speakers to help soldiers talk to locals.

The operational tempo was fast and the military entered the war short of necessary equipment and personnel after its budget had been slashed over the 1990s.

“We had a Canadian Forces that was under-strength, under-budget, under-equipped and not ready for operations quite literally anywhere in the world,” Hillier said. “While we were trying to rebuild the basis for an armed forces, we were also getting ready to go to war, and those two things were demanding in a way that was quite incredible.”

Hillier said while Canadians rose to the challenge, the lesson of Afghanistan is that countries can’t afford to take a decade to prepare their armed forces for the next war.

When Canadian troops arrived in Afghanistan, they were the only ones to show up in green uniforms. The military also had wound down its tank fleets and would need to acquire new ones to deal with the proliferation of roadside bombs.

While Canada went into Afghanistan believing Nato allies would cover any equipment shortfalls, Canadian troops often ended up last in line to use any equipment that could be spared — and often did without.

Canada didn’t have helicopters suitable to deploy at the outset, making operations more risky. That’s when Ottawa bought the air force’s Chinook transport helicopters.

Another key lesson from Afghanistan, Hillier said, is that fighting a modern war takes an enormous number of people. The size of the regular force contracted by tens of thousands after the end of the Cold War, and numbered around 60,000 by the time the Afghan war began.

Even now, he said, Canada does not have a large enough military.

“The numbers are so far down as to be sort of frightening and we’ve got to rebuild those numbers,” Hillier said. “I hope that we have learned that lesson and that we’re getting back to it.”

Justin Massie, professor of political science at the Université du Québec à Montréal, said he teaches his students the same lesson about Canada post-9-11 as he does when discussing the Korean War — that Canada entered the conflict with allies, was caught unprepared, scrambled to mobilize, then demobilized after the shooting stopped.

“The Canadian Armed Forces weren’t equipped to wage a combat mission abroad to the likes of what we faced against the Taliban, and so the first victims were Canadian soldiers from improvised explosive devices because they didn’t have armoured vehicles, didn’t have helicopters to move from one village to another, didn’t have the right camouflage gear,” he said.

“There are consequences when you start a war unprepared, and I’m not convinced that we are now prepared to face an adversary such as Russia in eastern Europe.”

He said the current government tends to talk about defence policy more as a way to create jobs than to build a capable military.

Lang said the government has learned that getting into such conflicts can happen very quickly and it can be “very difficult to get out once you’re in.”

He also said the Canadian Armed Forces seems to be on a better footing now than when it entered Afghanistan, thanks to rising defence spending, improving recruitment numbers and aircraft fleets being recapitalized.

“I’m not sure you’re ever really prepared for (war) because you don’t know exactly what it’s going to be and how you’re going to be implicated in it,” he said.

Retired Canadian Armed Forces corporal Bruce Moncur still remembers being told to pack his kit and being given 72 hours notice to move after the 2001 terror attacks.

Moncur, who grew up in the U.S., signed up for the military just months before the event that would change the course of his life.

“I wanted to deploy after those attacks. I was immensely affected,” he said. “I had family, I had friends, I lived there.”

Moncur never knew a peacetime military. He missed the “decade of darkness” after the Cold War — when the defence budget was slashed — and joined up just as the Canadian Forces were getting bigger budgets, better exercises and bigger missions.

He would deploy five years later and take part with about a thousand other Canadian troops in Nato’s largest-ever land battle, known as Operation Medusa. Canadians saw some of the most vicious fighting there against the Taliban at the height of the conflict in September 2006.

Canada’s complex legacy from that war snapped into focus for many this year, but not because of 20- or 25-year anniversaries. In January, President Trump publicly cast doubt on Nato’s contributions and claimed allied troops “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines.”

That offhand comment deeply hurt people who fought in Afghanistan — including Moncur, who was shot three times by an American A-10 Warthog that mistakenly strafed his position.

“When Mr. Trump said the Nato forces weren’t on the front lines, that cut deep because I had friends that lost limbs and died and killed themselves over what they saw on the front line,” he said. “That was really hard on me mentally because I almost died for that — going to the defence of my neighbours to the south and to hear that was very, very distressing.”

Since the war, Moncur has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian Afghanistan veterans. He’s led the charge to get the government to reconsider awarding veterans Canada’s top military honour, the Victoria Cross — something Ottawa recently promised to review.

Lang said that as Canadians look back on the war, they must not let it become something like Canada’s Vietnam — a war that everyone avoids talking about.

“We don’t really want to talk about it much as a country because it wasn’t successful in the end. We sacrificed a lot,” he said. “The main thing for me is that we don’t forget about it. We owe that to the people that served there, if nothing else.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

When Canadian troops arrived in Afghanistan, they were the only ones to show up in green uniforms. The military also had wound down its tank fleets and would need to acquire new ones to deal with the proliferation of roadside bombs.

While Canada went into Afghanistan believing Nato allies would cover any equipment shortfalls, Canadian troops often ended up last in line to use any equipment that could be spared — and often did without.
Canada didn’t have helicopters suitable to deploy at the outset, making operations more risky. That’s when Ottawa bought the air force’s Chinook transport helicopters.

Another key lesson from Afghanistan, Hillier said, is that fighting a modern war takes an enormous number of people. The size of the regular force contracted by tens of thousands after the end of the Cold War, and numbered around 60,000 by the time the Afghan war began.
Even now, he said, Canada does not have a large enough military.
“The numbers are so far down as to be sort of frightening and we’ve got to rebuild those numbers,” Hillier said. “I hope that we have learned that lesson and that we’re getting back to it.”

Justin Massie, professor of political science at the Université du Québec à Montréal, said he teaches his students the same lesson about Canada post-9-11 as he does when discussing the Korean War — that Canada entered the conflict with allies, was caught unprepared, scrambled to mobilize, then demobilized after the shooting stopped.

“The Canadian Armed Forces weren’t equipped to wage a combat mission abroad to the likes of what we faced against the Taliban, and so the first victims were Canadian soldiers from improvised explosive devices because they didn’t have armoured vehicles, didn’t have helicopters to move from one village to another, didn’t have the right camouflage gear,” he said.
“There are consequences when you start a war unprepared, and I’m not convinced that we are now prepared to face an adversary such as Russia in eastern Europe.”
He said the current government tends to talk about defence policy more as a way to create jobs than to build a capable military.
Lang said the government has learned that getting into such conflicts can happen very quickly and it can be “very difficult to get out once you’re in.”

He also said the Canadian Armed Forces seems to be on a better footing now than when it entered Afghanistan, thanks to rising defence spending, improving recruitment numbers and aircraft fleets being recapitalized.
“I’m not sure you’re ever really prepared for (war) because you don’t know exactly what it’s going to be and how you’re going to be implicated in it,” he said.
Retired Canadian Armed Forces corporal Bruce Moncur still remembers being told to pack his kit and being given 72 hours notice to move after the 2001 terror attacks.
Moncur, who grew up in the U.S., signed up for the military just months before the event that would change the course of his life.
“I wanted to deploy after those attacks. I was immensely affected,” he said. “I had family, I had friends, I lived there.”

Moncur never knew a peacetime military. He missed the “decade of darkness” after the Cold War — when the defence budget was slashed — and joined up just as the Canadian Forces were getting bigger budgets, better exercises and bigger missions.

He would deploy five years later and take part with about a thousand other Canadian troops in Nato’s largest-ever land battle, known as Operation Medusa. Canadians saw some of the most vicious fighting there against the Taliban at the height of the conflict in September 2006.

Canada’s complex legacy from that war snapped into focus for many this year, but not because of 20- or 25-year anniversaries. In January, President Trump publicly cast doubt on Nato’s contributions and claimed allied troops “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines.”
That offhand comment deeply hurt people who fought in Afghanistan — including Moncur, who was shot three times by an American A-10 Warthog that mistakenly strafed his position.

“When Mr. Trump said the Nato forces weren’t on the front lines, that cut deep because I had friends that lost limbs and died and killed themselves over what they saw on the front line,” he said. “That was really hard on me mentally because I almost died for that — going to the defence of my neighbours to the south and to hear that was very, very distressing.”

Lang said that as Canadians look back on the war, they must not let it become something like Canada’s Vietnam — a war that everyone avoids talking about.

“We don’t really want to talk about it much as a country because it wasn’t successful in the end. We sacrificed a lot,” he said. “The main thing for me is that we don’t forget about it. We owe that to the people that served there, if nothing else.”

The Afghanistan war, Canada’s longest armed conflict, taught harsh lessons — some that Canada learned, others it did not.

Soon after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Canada stepped out of the quiet decade after the Cold War into the global fight on terror, and soon found itself at war with a Taliban insurgency halfway around the world.

“Who would have dreamt the day prior to that, Canadian troops in their thousands would be serving in Afghanistan — Afghanistan, for God’s sake, of all places. Canada’s ambassador to Nato moved for the alliance to, for the first time ever, invoke Article Five — the clause in the Nato treaty that says an attack on one member country constitutes an attack on all.

That alliance spirit is harder to detect today, with Canada’s relationship with the U.S. tanking over a trade war and President Donald Trump threatening to tear up the Nato alliance and pull more troops out of Europe.

stories.title: Building Imnaryuaq: Canada’s biggest icebreaker begins to take shape
stories.summary: From new military investments to Arctic security and sovereignty, Canada is pouring billions into asserting its presence in the North. In the first instalment of a CTV News series, we go inside the shipyard where the country’s future polar Arctic icebreaker is taking shape.
stories.author: Graham Richardson
stories.content:
From new military investments to Arctic security and sovereignty, Canada is pouring billions into asserting its presence in the North. In the first instalment of a CTV News series, we go inside a Vancouver shipyard where the country’s future polar Arctic icebreaker is slowly coming together.

Vancouver – More than 15 years after Ottawa launched its National Shipbuilding Strategy, Canada’s effort to rebuild the industry is taking shape on the West Coast.

Seaspan’s Vancouver shipyard operates around the clock, with much of the work centred on a massive steel structure that will eventually become Canada’s largest-ever polar icebreaker, the Canadian Coast Guard’s 158-metre, 26,000-tonne Imnaryuaq.

Years of design work and planning are now emerging in steel as workers assemble what will become the future flagship of the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.

“It’s a first-in-class vessel. I’m really proud to be a part of this project,” said welder John Searle. “There’s a sense of pride in what you’re building because it is for Canada.”

The contract for the ship alone is worth more than $4 billion.

When it enters service in the early 2030s, the vessel will provide capabilities Canada does not currently have, allowing the coast guard to operate farther north, break through thicker ice and maintain a greater presence in the High Arctic.

“This is huge,” said Jessica Fetterman, Seaspan’s chief engineer for the polar icebreaker project.

“We only build icebreakers in North America once every 40, 50 or 60 years, so this is groundbreaking.”

Fetterman said the ship will be capable of breaking through 2.5 metres of ice and 30 centimetres of compacted snow, nearly three metres in total, while maintaining a speed of three knots for up to 1,800 kilometres without stopping.

Decades of decline in Canada’s shipbuilding industry, combined with aging fleets in the Royal Canadian Navy and Canadian Coast Guard, prompted Ottawa to launch the National Shipbuilding Strategy in 2010.

The strategy’s first major vessel was delivered in 2020. Since then, 11 large ships have been designed in Canada, with most building taking place in Canada.

“The strategic question was whether you buy these ships from another country or try to build them here,” said Dave Hargreaves, Seaspan’s vice-president of strategy and business development.

“The decision was made to build them here, and that has enabled Canada to develop the capability not only to build ships, but to design them as well.”

Seaspan has delivered four vessels under the strategy so far. Two more are under construction, along with the company’s largest and most ambitious project to date, the Imnaryuaq. Seaspan is partnering with a Finnish company on the construction of the Imnaryuaq.

The vessel remains years from completion, but at 158 metres long and 26,000 tonnes, it is expected to become the largest ship in the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.

For workers such as Searle, the polar project, and the other ships, that have been ordered represents long-term employment.

“There’s a lot of longevity here,” he said. “With the contracts we already have and the ones that are coming, there’s an immense amount of work ahead.”

Seaspan is not the only company involved in Canada’s shipbuilding strategy. Chantier Davie Canada Inc., located in Lévis, Que., has been awarded a separate contract valued at more than $3 billion to build another polar icebreaker that will be named the Ccgs Arpatuuq.

The federal government also announced last month that Chantier Davie will lead the construction of six program icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard, which will help maintain year-round trade in Eastern Canada.

That contract is valued at $11.3 billion and is expected to create nearly 5,000 jobs during the construction phase that is set to begin in 2027.

stories.title: Identity politics fade to the background in Quebec ahead of October’s provincial election
stories.summary: Divisive subject could return to the fore when Supreme Court issues landmark decision on Bill 21 in the coming months
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
On the eve of the 2018 Quebec election campaign, François Legault made a promise that would help define his nearly eight years as premier.

A Coalition Avenir Québec government would table a bill on secularism within a year, he declared. Judges, police officers and teachers would no longer be allowed to wear religious symbols on the job.

Bill 21 was the first in a series of controversial and broadly popular laws, intended to defend Quebec values, which became a cornerstone of Mr. Legault’s brand of nationalism. But in this fall’s election campaign, overshadowed by an escalating trade war with the United States, no one wants to talk much about identity politics.

The subject could return to the fore with the country’s top court expected to issue a landmark decision on Bill 21 in the coming months. But ahead of the Oct. 5 election, the province’s political leaders seem to have little desire to reignite a debate over secularism and language rules that now seem like a fait accompli.

Late last month, in the first days of the campaign, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon stood in front of a Quebec City high school and declared that the province’s schools are overflowing because of too many immigrant children. He used the modular classrooms recently added to the school as a backdrop to reiterate his promise to slash immigration to Quebec.

The stunt earned him considerable pushback. Quebec newspaper Le Devoir revealed the numbers he’d cited didn’t differentiate between newcomers and the Quebec-born children of immigrants. Ruba Ghazal, a co-leader of the left-leaning Québec solidaire, demanded to know who Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon considers to be true Quebeckers.

Journalist and author Francine Pelletier said the move blew up in his face. “Suddenly he was being negative and anti-immigrant.”

It was a rare moment in a campaign that has largely steered clear of such thorny subjects. Christine Fréchette, who succeeded Mr. Legault as premier in April, has shown little interest in pursuing her predecessor’s nationalist agenda.

“It’s something that’s uncomfortable and doesn’t come to her naturally, so it’s mysteriously disappeared,” Ms. Pelletier, who recently published a book on Quebec nationalism, said.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump has emerged as the bogeyman of the campaign, and there are “much bigger fish to fry,” she added. “As long as we’re dealing with the monster … I don’t think we’ll be dabbling in quaint provincial policies.”

Montreal-based Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said it’s “actually a breath of fresh air to not see minorities front and centre” in this campaign. The CAQ government has long used identity issues “to play wedge politics” and shore up the nationalist vote, he said, including after its support collapsed in recent years. In the last year alone, the CAQ passed two new laws strengthening the province’s secularism rules, including by expanding the ban on religious symbols and limiting prayer in public places.

But right now, Mr. Brown said, nobody’s interested. “As long as Quebeckers are much more concerned with pocketbook issues, that’s what politicians are going to talk about.”

Still, that silence cuts both ways. If no one is proposing major new identity policies, they’re also not complaining about the ones that already exist. The CAQ government’s laws on secularism and protection of the French language were generally popular in Quebec, and political parties don’t have anything to gain by attacking them, Ms. Pelletier said.

“I think people would like to move on.”

This was on full display last week, when Élections Québec announced it would be mailing out voter information in French only for the first time, to comply with the CAQ government’s 2022 overhaul of the province’s French-language charter, known as Bill 96.

Despite backlash, Ms. Fréchette said the decision would stand, and insisted the rights of English-speaking Quebeckers were being respected.

Eva Ludvig, president of Talq, a group representing Quebec anglophones, said the decision “has created a lot of anger in the English-speaking community.” But she said there is currently no champion of Quebec’s English speakers among the province’s main political parties. And there will be no English-language debate during the election campaign.

“We’ve always had much greater access,” she said. “This is the first time where we are totally excluded from this election.”

Ms. Ludvig said that even the opposition Liberals, traditionally the defenders of minority language rights, have not wanted to rock the boat. The Liberals are lagging far behind the PQ and the CAQ among francophone voters, as Leader Charles Milliard tries to build momentum after a lacklustre start to his campaign.

“He has been really avoiding much of anything that would be perhaps controversial in terms of support for the English-speaking community,” Ms. Ludvig said.

The debate over how Mr. Legault reshaped Quebec nationalism May be on hold, but it’s certainly not over. The Supreme Court of Canada’s coming ruling on Bill 21 could set limits on the use of the notwithstanding clause, which the CAQ government invoked repeatedly to protect its secularism and language laws from constitutional challenges.

Ms. Pelletier said the court’s decision could bring identity politics back to centre stage. “Nothing riles us more here … than having someone outside Quebec tell us what we should do, or tell us who we are.”

A Coalition Avenir Québec government would table a bill on secularism within a year, he declared. Judges, police officers and teachers would no longer be allowed to wear religious symbols on the job.

But in this fall’s election campaign, overshadowed by an escalating trade war with the United States, no one wants to talk much about identity politics.

The subject could return to the fore with the country’s top court expected to issue a landmark decision on Bill 21 in the coming months. But ahead of the Oct. 5 election, the province’s political leaders seem to have little desire to reignite a debate over secularism and language rules that now seem like a fait accompli.

Late last month, in the first days of the campaign, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon stood in front of a Quebec City high school and declared that the province’s schools are overflowing because of too many immigrant children. He used the modular classrooms recently added to the school as a backdrop to reiterate his promise to slash immigration to Quebec.

The stunt earned him considerable pushback. Quebec newspaper Le Devoir revealed the numbers he’d cited didn’t differentiate between newcomers and the Quebec-born children of immigrants. Ruba Ghazal, a co-leader of the left-leaning Québec solidaire, demanded to know who Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon considers to be true Quebeckers.

“It’s something that’s uncomfortable and doesn’t come to her naturally, so it’s mysteriously disappeared,” Ms. Pelletier, who recently published a book on Quebec nationalism, said.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump has emerged as the bogeyman of the campaign, and there are “much bigger fish to fry,” she added. “As long as we’re dealing with the monster … I don’t think we’ll be dabbling in quaint provincial policies.”

But right now, Mr. Brown said, nobody’s interested. “As long as Quebeckers are much more concerned with pocketbook issues, that’s what politicians are going to talk about.”

stories.title: Emac Recording Studios closes after 46 years of 'immeasurable' impact on London, Ont.
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 9, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 9
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 9, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 9
The studio worked with artists including Dolores O'Riordan and Christopher Plummer

After operating nearly out of sight for 46 years in an unmarked brick building in east London, Ont., a prolific recording studio has shut its doors for good—but it's leaving behind a lasting legacy in Canada's first and only UNESCO City of Music.

EMAC Recording Studios was started in 1979 by Robert Nation and Joe Vaughan out of an old Salvation Army building on Rectory Street. It went on to become the largest professional recording studio between Toronto and Detroit.
"We became a great place, with a lot of bands that came in, whether it's local, regional, from out of town or wherever," Nation said.
"I think we created a very creative space, a comfortable space, and got to work with some great artists."
PHOTOS | Artists at EMAC Recording Studios over the years:

Since opening, they have worked with with countless local, national and even international artists, including the late Dolores O'Riordan— former lead singer of The Cranberries—and London 90s metal band Kittie.
They also did work in the film and television industry, including mixing the audio for Michael Moore's documentary Sicko, and Christopher Plummer's dialogue for Pixar's Up.
But after more than four decades, Nation said he and Vaughan knew they would eventually need to move on. After receiving an offer they "couldn't refuse," he said "the time was right."
The impact that EMAC made on the city in those 46 years is "immeasurable," according to Mario Circelli, founder and chair of the Forest City London Music Awards.

London's designation as a UNESCO City of Music was "built on the back" of the musicians who recorded there, and the audio engineers who "tirelessly worked for hours getting great sounds for local, regional and national bands," he added.
Circelli believes the studio will be remembered as a place where "great tracks were laid down from top to finish."

"The legacy will live on," he said. "And those two names, Joe Vaughan and Rob Nation, will live on forever as the individuals who brought EMAC to the city, curated it for 46 years and opened the door to so many bands and musicians."
Circelli would have liked to see someone step up to fill the void left by EMAC, but Nation said finding someone to take over the studio wasn't something he and Vaughan pursued actively.
"I would have liked the studio to carry on, and utilize the beautiful space," he said. "It is actually a beautiful place to work."
"However, I never really thought that was going to be a possibility."
The cost of purchasing the building and setting up a major studio was something Nation could only see a large organization affording, he said.

But at least for Nation, this won't be the end of his career as an audio engineer and producer. He will continue doing mixing, recording and mastering work, he said, and there are some artists he will continue to work with.
"'I'll just have to go to another studio to record it," he said. "I've got some plans—just not fully developed yet."

stories.title: Canada to blame for Washington's escalation of trade war, says Trump trade czar
stories.summary: Washington - U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says Canada is to blame for Washington's decision to escalate the trade war with its northern neighbour.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - U.S. President Donald Trump plans to ban a range of Canadian exports and shuffle tariffs on others as Ottawa and Washington trade accusations over which side is responsible for the escalating trade war.

Most imports of Canadian-made liquor and a handful of dairy products will be banned from the United States at the end of September, but dozens of other products are getting a tariff reprieve.

Trump on Tuesday signed new executive orders ramping up retaliation after Canada imposed its latest set of counter tariffs on the United States.

Article continues below

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

The five new orders, which take effect later this month, will completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products like whey and cheese, and molasses.

Alcoholic products from Canada, including beer, wine, rye and vodka, are also facing a ban.

But the orders also exempt from tariffs some Canadian products, including toilet paper, road salt, cement and fishing rods. Canadian whiskey and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres will also be exempt.

With these exports set for exemptions, new products with a similar dollar value have been substituted on the U.S. tariff list.

The product bans will go into place Sept. 29, while the additions and removals of other tariffs take effect Sept. 15.

Much like Canada was pressured by domestic companies and provincial leaders to back off of seafood tariffs, there has been pressure on the White House from state representatives and American companies about the economic impacts of certain tariffs.

In a statement posted on X Tuesday, Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she appreciated the Trump administration’s flexibility as she continued to press for a trade resolution with Canada.

“I mentioned in a letter to the Administration that Frenchville, a small Maine town on the Canadian border, would incur $10,000 in extra costs for road salt, threatening the town’s ability to provide municipal services,” wrote Collins, a Republican.

“These additional exemptions follow Canada’s announcement that it will carve out American seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariff list, which would have caused significant harm to Maine’s lobstermen.”

Collins said tariffs on forest products were still in place and would lead to higher costs in Maine.

“I urge the Administration to continue to work to de-escalate this conflict,” she said.

U.S. Republican Senator Jerry Moran said on social media that the Trump administration’s decision to exempt salt from tariffs on Canadian imports is “welcome news” for Kansas businesses and taxpayers.

He said salt is a critical commodity in his state, with local governments utilizing it to remove ice and keep Kansans “safe on the roads.”

“When these tariffs were proposed, I urged the U.S. Trade Representative to consider the impact on Kansas taxpayers and local businesses, including Morton Salt and Compass Minerals, both headquartered in Overland Park, which own and operate Canadian mines and bring salt into the United States for distribution,” he said.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said the “reshuffling” of U.S. tariffs will have no new net effect on Canada’s economy. New import bans, while potentially consequential to the industries themselves, are also expected to have a marginal impact on the wider economy.

Porter said by swapping out tariffs on key inputs such as cement, the Trump administration could be trying to avoid further inflaming the inflationary pressures dogging the U.S. economy.

In a statement issued Tuesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for Washington’s decision to escalate the trade war.

Greer said the escalation was a “natural consequence” of Canada discriminating against American exports and choosing “senseless retaliation” over an almost final trade deal.

“President Trump will continue to leverage the tools at his disposal to defend the interests of American workers and exporters, and restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships,” Greer said in a statement.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Ottawa is not ramping up the trade war when he spoke to reporters in Edmonton on Wednesday.

“This is not a trade conflict that we chose. We certainly did not escalate,” Champagne said. “The counter-measures that we have announced were proportionate, were strategic and were targeted.”

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs targeted the same value of goods hit by the U.S. on Aug. 22, and the products affected were drawn from those the U.S. targeted as well.

Most imports of Canadian-made liquor and a handful of dairy products will be banned from the United States at the end of September, but dozens of other products are getting a tariff reprieve.
Trump on Tuesday signed new executive orders ramping up retaliation after Canada imposed its latest set of counter tariffs on the United States.
Article continues below

The five new orders, which take effect later this month, will completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products like whey and cheese, and molasses.
Alcoholic products from Canada, including beer, wine, rye and vodka, are also facing a ban.

But the orders also exempt from tariffs some Canadian products, including toilet paper, road salt, cement and fishing rods. Canadian whiskey and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres will also be exempt.
With these exports set for exemptions, new products with a similar dollar value have been substituted on the U.S. tariff list.
The product bans will go into place Sept. 29, while the additions and removals of other tariffs take effect Sept. 15.

Much like Canada was pressured by domestic companies and provincial leaders to back off of seafood tariffs, there has been pressure on the White House from state representatives and American companies about the economic impacts of certain tariffs.
In a statement posted on X Tuesday, Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she appreciated the Trump administration’s flexibility as she continued to press for a trade resolution with Canada.

“I mentioned in a letter to the Administration that Frenchville, a small Maine town on the Canadian border, would incur $10,000 in extra costs for road salt, threatening the town’s ability to provide municipal services,” wrote Collins, a Republican.

“These additional exemptions follow Canada’s announcement that it will carve out American seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariff list, which would have caused significant harm to Maine’s lobstermen.”
Collins said tariffs on forest products were still in place and would lead to higher costs in Maine.
“I urge the Administration to continue to work to de-escalate this conflict,” she said.

U.S. Republican Senator Jerry Moran said on social media that the Trump administration’s decision to exempt salt from tariffs on Canadian imports is “welcome news” for Kansas businesses and taxpayers.

stories.title: Mountain trail runners describe appeal and peril of sport as Canadian still missing
stories.summary: It's been just over a year since mountain runner Margaux Cohen suffered a life-changing injury while hiking a mountain in Squamish, B.C., after her dog Zion lost his footing, sending them both tumbling down a rocky slope nearly 20 metres.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
It’s been just over a year since mountain runner Margaux Cohen suffered a life-changing injury while hiking a mountain in Squamish, B.C., after her dog Zion lost his footing, sending them both tumbling nearly 20 metres down a rocky slope.

Cohen said she’s still recovering from a fracture of her tibial plateau, but Zion is “doing great,” and she visited the spot where the fall occurred just last week.

“Seeing the cliff a year later was pretty insane because I don’t think I remembered how high I fell from,” she said. “The last week I’ve been feeling even more grateful to be alive because it’s pretty crazy.”

For so-called “skyrunners” or ultra-runners like Cohen, the adrenalin rush of tackling dangerous mountain terrain is worth the risk, which is ever-present on local mountains and famous peaks including the Matterhorn, where famed Canadian skyrunner Kalie McCrystal has been missing for more than a week.

Both frequent mountains around Squamish, about 60 kilometres north of Vancouver, although Cohen said she doesn’t know McCrystal personally.

Cohen said she would still tackle the Matterhorn despite its apparent risks.

“I’m from Europe, so it has the reputation back home. It’s not the biggest mountain but it’s a dangerous mountain,” she said in an interview on Wednesday.

Cohen said she got sober from drugs and alcohol and the solitude offered by running in the mountains helped alleviate her anxiety and depression.

“It’s really something that’s been helping me in a weird way,” she said. “You are in the moment. You’re not thinking about the past or the future. You’re just thinking of what you’re doing right now to not fall to your death.”

Mountain runner Hillary Gerardi, a close friend of McCrystal’s, said traversing perilous terrain as an elite skyrunner is where she and those dedicated to the sport feel most alive, but some routes have little to no margin of error.

The American-born athlete, who has been living in France for the last 15 years, said McCrystal remained missing on the Italian side of the Matterhorn, where she was last seen on Sept. 1.

Gerardi and another friend were set to help McCrystal attempt to break a running record last week, but when they realized no one had heard from her, they alerted authorities. No trace of McCrystal had yet been found.

Gerardi recalled meeting McCrystal a few years ago while competing at the Skyrunner World Series and the two women hit it off, both members of a record-breaking group of athletes pushing the boundaries of the sport.

She said skyrunning for her is like “mindfulness meditation,” requiring full concentration and presence in the moment, unlike a treadmill or a paved path, where the mind can wander free of danger.

Gerardi said the mountainous terrain can involve narrow routes less than a metre wide with a “no-fall zone” on either side, and even the most advanced runners could slip or trip and fall.

“I think I would describe the terrain as entirely unforgiving. There isn’t room for being able to make mistakes, and to be clear, Kalie had gone up and down this route making no mistakes multiple times,” Gerardi said.

“She had been there before and she knew what she was doing and had done it with zero mistakes in the past.”

Gerardi said her best guess in McCrystal’s case was “just some kind slip, some kind of trip, something that happened.”

The area where McCrystal is believed to have gone missing is inaccessible and search efforts have been suspended unless new information comes to light that would allow searchers to narrow their scope, she said.

Athletics Canada said search efforts involved helicopters and drones.

“The Canadian government has also been engaged, and they have been providing support through the consulate in Milan,” it said in an email on Wednesday.

Joel Desgreniers, co-owner of outdoor outfitter SkiUphill — RunUphill in Squamish and Canmore, said McCrystal’s disappearance has been a “a big blow for the community.”

“She was at the forefront of the sport, I’d say, and also she was just a really big name, and she was representing our local community internationally,” he said on Wednesday. “She was really putting the community here on the map.”

Desgreniers said mountain trail running, ultra running and skyrunning fall on a spectrum depending on the environment and terrain, comparing high-altitude skyrunning to downhill mountain biking with the high-level of skills needed.

“The terrain becomes extremely difficult. Most people can’t do it. Extremely involved, the risk of injury is higher,” he said.

He said people are drawn to communities like Squamish for the beauty of the outdoor environment, while accepting its dangers.

“There’s something really special about just like playing in the mountains and using those kind of hostile places as your playground,” he said. “Outdoor pursuits that involve something that’s not done often, that’s considered cutting edge, is dangerous.”

For Cohen, who works at a bar in Vancouver, the fast pace of city life carries stress that melts away in the mountains, and although she’s not back to 100 per cent after her injury, the reward still outweighs the risk.

“As soon as I’m hiking or running or as soon as I am in the mountains, I’m on the trail. I don’t think about anything else. I just feel so good.

“Trust me, if I could live on the peak of a mountain, I would because this is where I feel, I don’t know, my best version.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada Infrastructure Bank closes loan for Nunavut wind project serving gold mine
stories.summary: Hope BAY, NVT. - The Canada Infrastructure Bank has closed a $20-million loan for an Inuit-led wind project serving a gold mine in Nunavut.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Three wind turbine blades, each almost as long as four standard semi-trucks lined up end-to-end, have completed their long, painstaking journey to the site of one of Canada’s northernmost gold mines.

The 4.2-megawatt turbine and a four-megawatt battery energy storage system will help power Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd.‘s operations in Hope Bay, Nvt., helping cut its diesel use by up to three million litres and emissions by some 13,000 tonnes per year.

“To the extent that we can acquire clean energy rather than burning diesel, we’ll do that every single day of the week,” Ammar Al-Joundi, the mining company’s chief executive, said in an interview.

“It’s just the right thing to do, and it’s part of our long-term commitment to sustainability.”

The owners of the wind turbine are the Kitikmeot Inuit Association and Tugliq Energy. They’ve signed a 20-year agreement to sell the power to Agnico Eagle.

The partnership is “not only about transitioning energy use from conventional diesel to alternative wind energy,” said David Omilgoitok, head of the Kitikmeot economic development corporation.

“It is also a partnership intended to grow the Inuit labour market with new skills along with increased investment in Hope Bay and the Kitikmeot Region.”

The partnership has received a $20-million Canada Infrastructure Bank loan as well as a $25-million contribution from Natural Resources Canada’s Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways program.

Pulling off such a project isn’t an easy sell for the private sector to take on by itself, given the harsh climate, painstaking logistics and need for Indigenous buy-in. The infrastructure bank, a Crown corporation, was set up to invest in projects that deliver on some of the federal government’s desired outcomes, but would struggle to attract traditional corporate financing.

The Hope Bay project supports clean energy by displacing diesel and generates economic development in the North, said Ehren Cory, head of the infrastructure bank.

“It really delivers across multiple of those outcomes. We sometimes call these double and triple word scores,” he said in an interview.

“We think it’s a model for a lot of the development to come in the North.”

In May, Agnico Eagle gave the official go-ahead to proceed with its Hope Bay project, an underground mine almost 700 kilometres northeast of Yellowknife, which aims to produce up to 435,000 ounces of gold over 11 years.

The company doesn’t have the option to connect to the grid, as it does in its more southerly operations, Al-Joundi said.

“That’s why this windmill is quite an exciting first,” he said.

In a part of the world where the sun disappears for much of the year, solar was not ideal. One day, small nuclear reactors might fill the North’s energy needs. But in the meantime, wind is the best option to complement diesel, Al-Joundi said.

It hasn’t been easy. The turbine parts, including its 80-metre long blades, had to make their way from Europe to Canada and then slowly travel inland by barge, which is only possible during a tight window of a few weeks. From there, it was pulled at a snail’s pace by tractor to the site, where it’s being stored. The plan is to assemble it and get it up and running in the spring.

If all goes well, Al-Joundi said it’s possible to build four more wind turbines at Hope Bay. With five, he said the mine could eventually offset an average of a third of its annual diesel power use with wind.

Agnico Eagle previously attempted to build a wind farm near another of its mines elsewhere in the territory called Meliadine, which it had been planning to expand. The proposal garnered community opposition. The Nunavut Impact Review Board recommended the extension be rejected and the company withdrew its proposal.

“It was never really a question of technical capability. It’s always a question of ‘what is it that the community wants?’ While we wanted windmills, that wasn’t on their agenda,” Al-Joundi said.

But he thinks the door isn’t shut to having wind power at Meliadine one day.

“They probably will come up and take a look at what we’re doing at Hope Bay and they May change their minds.”

At Hope Bay, the infrastructure bank said the wind project is expected to employ 15 people during peak construction and provide long-term benefits to local communities through profit-sharing.

It’s the second project in Nunavut for the federal agency, following its $6.7-million loan for a wind project in Sanikiluaq, a community on an island in Hudson Bay.

Cory said the infrastructure bank sees big potential for wind power in the North. Some opportunities will be for industrial developments, as is the case for the Hope Bay mine. Some will serve communities that currently rely on polluting and expensive diesel, like Sanikiluaq did. And some May have the ability to blend multiple uses, where industrial operations are close enough to communities.

“There is a real trend happening and it’s very much a place the (infrastructure bank) thinks we can be helpful,” Cory said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Five books shortlisted for the Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction
stories.summary: The $75,000 annual award celebrates particularly literary forms of essays, histories, biographies, memoirs, commentaries and criticism
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Humanity’s relationship with nature is the dominant theme among the five books shortlisted for this year’s Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction.

The $75,000 annual award celebrates particularly literary forms of essays, histories, biographies, memoirs, commentaries and criticism. Each finalist is awarded $5,000, for a total of $95,000 in prizes.

The five authors on the short list announced Wednesday are Toronto’s Dan Werb; Whitehorse’s Trina Moyles; Vancouver’s Julian Brave NoiseCat; Calgary’s Richard Kelly Kemick; and Robert Moor of Halfmoon Bay, B.C.

Werb’s Our Wild Familiars: How Animals Are Adapting to Cities and Reshaping the Natural World , published by Knopf Canada , looks at the lives of synanthropes, those wily, undomesticated animals that thrive in human communities. Should we be worried when the wild encroaches upon the civilized? Werb, an epidemiologist, policy analyst and musician, doesn’t think so.

“I wanted to make sure that this book was about connection rather than stoking fear or anxiety,” he told The Globe and Mail last month. “It’s really about how we can feel more intimate and connected with the places we live.”

Werb previously won the Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction for 2022’s The Invisible Siege: The Rise of Coronaviruses and the Search for a Cure. This year’s jury described him in its citation as an “eloquent storyteller with an international reach, an impeccable scientific communicator, and a lyrical celebrator of animals from bees to a giant Pacific octopus.”

The jury members are Toronto’s Katherine Ashenburg, a two-time nominee for the prize; McGill University professor Debra Thompson, shortlisted in 2022 for The Long Road Home: On Blackness and Belonging ; and Calgary poet and novelist Joshua Whitehead, also a finalist in 2022, for Making Love with the Land .

They cited Moyles’s shortlisted Black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival , published by Knopf Canada , as a “masterclass in prosaically weaving together the personal with the political.” The book by the Whitehorse author and environmental journalist is both a memoir about one woman’s co-existence with bears in the boreal forest and a meditation on sibling loss.

Earlier this summer, Moyles wrote an opinion piece for The Globe in reaction to a viral TikTok video of a grizzly bear charging and lunging repeatedly at a cellphone-wielding woman’s leashed dog in Kananaskis, Alta. Moyles had advice for people in a similar situation: “If you see a bear, even if it isn’t showing aggression, put down your phone and take out your bear spray.”

The Albertan Kemick describes his shortlisted Decadence , published by Biblioasis, as an “accidental memoir of a sort.” The jury cited his whimsical collection of autobiographical essays on such things as love, self-worth, his dogs and the morality of aquariums as “funny, curious, self-deprecating and occasionally and gloriously ridiculous.”

British Columbia-based Moor’s previous book was 2016’s On Trails: An Exploration , inspired by a hike through the Appalachian Trail. For his shortlisted In Trees: An Exploration , published by Simon & Schuster Canada, he branched out to scale a giant sequoia with Sir David Attenborough, trudged through Indonesian swamps to reach a treehouse-dwelling tribe of hunter-gatherers, and travelled to a remote research camp in Tanzania to spend one very uncomfortable night sleeping in a chimpanzee nest – all in pursuit of the hidden wisdom of trees.

“Drawing on an astonishing breadth of research across science, history, and philosophy,” the jury wrote, “Moor writes with the sensibility of a poet and the relentless curiosity of a philosopher.”

The fifth finalist, NoiseCat, is shortlisted for his debut book We Survived the Night: An Indigenous Reckoning , published by Random House Canada. The memoir from the Oscar-nominated filmmaker and former competitive powwow dancer combines journalism, colonial history and Sécwepemc coyote stories to detail a father-son journey and paint a portrait of contemporary Indigenous life.

The Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction was first sponsored in 2011 by the Irish-Canadian businesswoman, philanthropist and writer who served as lieutenant-governor of Ontario. She died last year at 83.

The prize is now funded by the Hilary and Galen Weston Foundation. Recent recipients include Tomson Highway for Permanent Astonishment , Christina Sharpe for Ordinary Notes , Martha Baillie for There Is No Blue , and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson for Theory of Water .

This year’s winner will be revealed at the Writers’ Trust Awards in Toronto on Nov. 10.

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: September 9, 2026
stories.summary: Where are our provincial politicians with these inhumane conditions of homelessness and addiction in cities across the province?
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Where are our provincial politicians with these inhumane conditions of homelessness and addiction in cities across the province?

Closing psychiatric hospitals has had the worst effects on our communities and province. Did it ever occur to our provincial politicians they have a responsibility to resolve homelessness, addiction and mental health crises for cities across the province?

If you wouldn’t live under a tarp or crap on the streets, why is it OK for the most vulnerable in our communities?

A. Hutchison, St. Thomas

Regarding the article CRA wrong to deny jab exemption, board finds (Aug. 20).

Did it ever occur to anyone of religion that God, out of his extreme love for humankind, gave us smart people with the know-how to defeat diseases that have caused suffering and death to millions of people?

Doug Payne, London

I am a Canadian. I write to apologize to our American neighbours and tell them how embarrassed I, and so many other Canadians are, at the actions of our prime minister.

I pray, with elections, whenever they are, we can put an end to this administration and rebuild our friendship with the United States and our allies around the world.

Geoffrey Corfield, London

stories.title: Updated visiting guideline helps patients, care partners, and visitors know what to expect
stories.summary: September 9, 2026
stories.content:
With feedback collected from patients, families, and team members, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has updated its guideline on care partners and visiting hours to create a more consistent experience across its hospital sites.

A care partner is a family member, friend, or other support person chosen by the patient to be involved in their care, provide comfort and support, and help during transitions in care.

Visiting hours are generally 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. , although some units May have different hours or requirements based on patient needs, safety, space, infection prevention measures, or other clinical considerations.

“When a patient is in hospital, the people who know them best can make a real difference,” says Tania Testa, Vice President of People, Communications and External Affairs. “This updated guideline helps make space for that support while giving patients, care partners, visitors, and care teams a clearer, more consistent understanding of what to expect.”

The updated guideline was developed by a working group that included LHSC staff members and patient and family partners – people with lived experience as patients or caregivers of patients at LHSC. Involving patient and family partners helped ensure the guideline is informed by the people it is meant to support and reflects the realities patients and care partners experience when coming to the hospital.

“Being part of this work was an opportunity to bring forward the patient and family perspective in a practical way,” says Elaine Harrison, a Patient and Family Partner who participated in the working group. “Clear information matters when people are coming to the hospital, especially during stressful moments. This guideline helps patients and care partners better understand their role and feel more included in the care experience.”

Care partners are people identified by the patient who provide important support during their hospital stay or appointment. They May help with comfort, communication, decision-making, care planning, or transitions home. A care partner is different from a general visitor, who May be visiting socially but does not provide the same level of support in the patient’s care experience.

With the patient’s or substitute decision maker’s consent, care partners are encouraged to be actively involved in the patient’s hospital experience. LHSC recognizes that care partner presence can support comfort, safety, and well-being.

Standard visiting hours are 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Some units May have different visiting hours to support patient care, treatment plans, safety, space, or infection prevention requirements. If visiting hours are different in a specific clinical area, that unit will communicate the information clearly to patients and care partners. A list of unit-specific exceptions can be found on our website .

In some situations, such as outbreaks or periods of higher infectious illness risk, visiting procedures May be adjusted. General visitors May be restricted, and patients May be asked to identify designated care partners. Care partners and visitors May also be required to follow additional Infection Prevention and Control measures.

Everyone coming to LHSC is expected to help maintain a safe and respectful environment. Care partners and visitors are asked to follow hospital and unit instructions, stay home if they are feeling unwell, perform hand hygiene, and follow any infection prevention requirements in place.

The updated guideline is intended to help patients feel supported, care partners feel included, and everyone know what to expect when coming to LHSC.

Public Service Announcement

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/east-lions-community-centre-pool-reopens)

Wednesday, September 9, 2026

Two weeks ahead of schedule, the City of London is excited to announce that the East Lions Community Centre pool is reopening to the public on Saturday, September 12, 2026!

To celebrate the reopening of this popular community hub, the following drop-in programs will be offered for free on September 12:

Lane swim: 7 a.m. to 8:30 a.m.

Aquafit: 11:30 a.m. to 12:15 p.m.

Lane swim: 12:45 p.m. to 2:15 p.m.

Parent and tot swim: 2:15 p.m. to 3:15 p.m.

Recreation swim: 3:30 p.m. to 5 p.m.

Looking to get back in the pool this fall? Registration for fall aquatics programming is now open at london.ca/PlayYourWay.

The pool was closed in July to protect the safety of lifeguards, swimmers, and construction workers while necessary repairs were made. Damaged windows were replaced, and the design of the windows was altered to be more resilient to any future damage. Changes were also made to make the windows simpler to replace if needed in the future.

While closed for construction, East Lions Community Centre also received a refresh after a busy camp season, including fresh paint for the front desk, a thorough cleaning, and minor maintenance.

We would like to thank Londoners for their patience and understanding while these repairs were made and are looking forward to welcoming you back to the pool!

Wednesday, September 9, 2026
Two weeks ahead of schedule, the City of London is excited to announce that the East Lions Community Centre pool is reopening to the public on Saturday, September 12, 2026!
To celebrate the reopening of this popular community hub, the following drop-in programs will be offered for free on September 12:
Lane swim: 7 a.m. to 8:30 a.m.
Aquafit: 11:30 a.m. to 12:15 p.m.
Lane swim: 12:45 p.m. to 2:15 p.m.
Parent and tot swim: 2:15 p.m. to 3:15 p.m.
Recreation swim: 3:30 p.m. to 5 p.m.
Looking to get back in the pool this fall? Registration for fall aquatics programming is now open at london.ca/PlayYourWay.

The pool was closed in July to protect the safety of lifeguards, swimmers, and construction workers while necessary repairs were made. Damaged windows were replaced, and the design of the windows was altered to be more resilient to any future damage. Changes were also made to make the windows simpler to replace if needed in the future.
While closed for construction, East Lions Community Centre also received a refresh after a busy camp season, including fresh paint for the front desk, a thorough cleaning, and minor maintenance.
We would like to thank Londoners for their patience and understanding while these repairs were made and are looking forward to welcoming you back to the pool!

stories.title: Missing Person – Joan Depeiza
stories.summary: London, ON (September 9, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 75-year-old Joan Depeiza, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 9, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 75-year-old Joan Depeiza, of London.

The missing person is described as a female, White, approximately 5’6”, 150 lbs., slim build, light brown hair with grey roots, and brown eyes. The missing person was last seen in the area of Highbury Avenue and Huron Street on August 28, 2026.

She May be operating a 2012 Dodge Caravan, Grey in colour, with Ontario plates Caem 358.

The missing person was reported missing on September 2, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.
