stories.title: Alberta landowners challenge ‘chronic underfunding’ for orphan well cleanup
stories.summary: Landowners are going to court over what they allege is the Alberta Energy Regulator's failure to fund the cleanup of oil and gas sites with no company responsible for them.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Alberta landowners are going to court over what they allege is the provincial energy regulator’s failure to properly fund the cleanup of oil and gas sites that have no company legally responsible for them.

Lawyers at environmental law charity Ecojustice are representing landowners Dwight Popowich and Teresa Patry, as well as the Polluter Pay Federation and the Alberta Surface Rights Federation.

Their judicial review application in the Court of King’s Bench challenges what they call the Alberta Energy Regulator’s “chronic underfunding” of the Orphan Well Levy.

The regulator deems oil and gas wells “orphans” when an energy company becomes insolvent, defunct or unable to meet its obligations to safely and responsibly close its sites.

Cleanup is managed through the non-profit Orphan Well Association and is funded through an industry fee, the amount of which the AER recommends to the Alberta government every year.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion.

Such wells can come with “significant risks,” the applicants argue in their lawsuit.

“Orphan wells can leak contaminants into the soil, the air and the water, putting Albertans’ health at risk and causing irreversible damage to the environment,” they said in the court document, adding orphan wells can also affect property values and land use and also come with big unpaid bills to municipalities and landowners.

“Oil and gas corporations with closure liabilities that exceed the value of their remaining assets often do not pay their bills, causing economic damage — and taxpayer funds are used to cover these shortfalls.”

The application alleges the AER is in violation of part of the Oil and Gas Conservation Act that says it alone is responsible for determining the amount of the levy, which must be “sufficient to cover, among other things, a number of costs associated with orphan oil and gas wells in the current fiscal year, as well as deficiencies arising from the previous fiscal year.”

The claim also alleges that the regulator has improperly delegated its legal responsibility to set the levy rates to Alberta’s political executive and allows for too much industry influence.

It further accuses the regulator of improperly taking into account factors like commodity prices and the health of the industry when setting the levy.

Among other things, the applicants are asking the court to declare the 2026-27 levy “unreasonable” and order it to be recalculated.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association include an inventory of 7,370 wells in need of decommissioning, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe.

Another 9,151 are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.

In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700.

An inactive well on Popowich’s property in Two Hills, Alta., was designated an orphan in 2025 after eight years of effort on his part, the claim stated.

He was then informed by the Orphan Well Association that it would take 10 to 12 years to reclaim it.

He told a news conference Tuesday that he’s tried to work through the proper channels, but his concerns have been dismissed while the problem keeps getting worse.

“This isn’t complicated. Even my grandkids know that if you make a mess, you clean it up,” Popowich said.

“Landowners have held up their end of the bargain. As Albertans, we understand the importance of resource development to our province, and we welcome that development in exchange for the promise that, when companies were finished producing, they would clean up after themselves.

“That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again."

Patry, who lives near Vermilion, Alta., told the news conference the issue goes beyond finances.

“For years my family has lived with uncertainty about what these sites mean for our home, our land, our health and our future. We’ve experienced unexplained health concerns in our family, worry about our animals and repeatedly tried to get answers from the Alberta Energy Regulator,” she said.

“Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll."

The complainants’ claims have not been tested in court.

The AER declined to comment on the legal challenge Tuesday. But a statement from the regulator noted that the most recent annual levy has increased by seven per cent from a year earlier.

“The increase provides additional funding to help the Orphan Well Association address the growing number of orphaned oil and gas sites across the province.”

Ecojustice lawyer Susanne Calabrese said she’s heard some compare steady increases to the levy to gradually paying down a mortgage.

“That does not make any sense when the amount of wells are just astronomically increasing at the Orphan Well Association,” she told reporters.

“It’s like you’re paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you’re buying 10 more houses.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's like you're paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you're buying 10 more houses."

stories.title: London Majors, Welland Jackfish trading blows in one-run playoff series
stories.summary: London Majors manager Roop Chanderdat expects more drama as his team leads Welland 2-1.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
It’s been captivating so far.

The London Majors and Welland Jackfish are providing great theatre through three games of their Canadian Baseball League semifinal. Each game has been decided by one run, with the opener lasting 11 innings, the Jackfish scoring three times late in a failed comeback bid in Game 2 and London’s five-run ninth inning falling just short of a miracle turnaround Sunday at Labatt Park.

“It’s been a battle,” London co-owner and manager Roop Chanderdat said. “Welland is the defending champion and they’re not going away quietly. Every game is going to be tight.

“It’s exciting.”

That’s nothing less than you would expect from two teams that finished with identical 31-17 regular-season records. The Majors used their three left-handed starters – Victor Payano, Travis Keys and Cesilio Pimentel – in the opening three games and are expected to turn to right-hander Luis Perez to try to grab a stranglehold on the series.

The 31-year-old Dominican pitched the 11th inning in the Game 1 win and surrendered two runs in two innings in London’s Game 2 victory.

“I used Perez out of the bullpen,” Chanderdat said, “but he has been a starter all year and with a long break for him, he needed some work. We knew that it would be a long series going in and I need all four starters. That will leave Payano for Game 5 in London (then Keys and Pimentel in the final two games, if necessary).”

Welland’s probable Wednesday starter Ben Abram, a left-hander, threw five innings of two-hit, one-run ball in the back half of Game 1, but was tagged with the loss.

There hasn’t been much offence generated against either team’s starters. Most of the bigger blows have come against bullpen arms.

“It’s been hard to get hits and string them together,” Chanderdat said. “We had some opportunities we wasted with first and third, less than two outs. We had a runner at second, one out, and couldn’t cash. You get a few and have to capitalize.”

London right-fielder Tucker Zdunich, a 26-year-old Albertan, is leading the charge with six hits in 12 at-bats through three games. Centre-fielder Jarrett Burney chipped in with the walk-off single in the opener.

“You need some guys to be consistent and some guys to be heroes,” Chanderdat said. “You need someone to step up. There’s no quit in these guys. Last game, we fought back in the ninth and knew we had a push in us. After it, everyone was upbeat. Welland has a great bullpen and closer. We wanted our guys to see them and they got some runs off them to get back in it.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint.”

On Sunday, the Majors stranded Jaden Babiuk at third to end the stirring rally. Welland saved the game when second baseman Jonah Weisner snared Burney’s ground ball up the middle with two runners on and recorded a force out at second.

“Otherwise, the game is tied,” Chanderdat said. “They made a couple of great plays defensively. We came up one short. In the playoffs, the next game is always the biggest one. Welland isn’t an easy place to win, but we’ve had some success there.”

They’re going to need the best of Perez and more timely hits to stay ahead in the series.

content_blocks.text: The 31-year-old Dominican pitched the 11th inning in the Game 1 win and surrendered two runs in two innings in London’s Game 2 victory.

“I used Perez out of the bullpen,” Chanderdat said, “but he has been a starter all year and with a long break for him, he needed some work. We knew that it would be a long series going in and I need all four starters. That will leave Payano for Game 5 in London (then Keys and Pimentel in the final two games, if necessary).”
Welland’s probable Wednesday starter Ben Abram, a left-hander, threw five innings of two-hit, one-run ball in the back half of Game 1, but was tagged with the loss.
There hasn’t been much offence generated against either team’s starters. Most of the bigger blows have come against bullpen arms.

“It’s been hard to get hits and string them together,” Chanderdat said. “We had some opportunities we wasted with first and third, less than two outs. We had a runner at second, one out, and couldn’t cash. You get a few and have to capitalize.”

London right-fielder Tucker Zdunich, a 26-year-old Albertan, is leading the charge with six hits in 12 at-bats through three games. Centre-fielder Jarrett Burney chipped in with the walk-off single in the opener.

“You need some guys to be consistent and some guys to be heroes,” Chanderdat said. “You need someone to step up. There’s no quit in these guys. Last game, we fought back in the ninth and knew we had a push in us. After it, everyone was upbeat. Welland has a great bullpen and closer. We wanted our guys to see them and they got some runs off them to get back in it.
“It’s a marathon, not a sprint.”

On Sunday, the Majors stranded Jaden Babiuk at third to end the stirring rally. Welland saved the game when second baseman Jonah Weisner snared Burney’s ground ball up the middle with two runners on and recorded a force out at second.

“Otherwise, the game is tied,” Chanderdat said. “They made a couple of great plays defensively. We came up one short. In the playoffs, the next game is always the biggest one. Welland isn’t an easy place to win, but we’ve had some success there.”
They’re going to need the best of Perez and more timely hits to stay ahead in the series.

stories.title: Online harms now top threat to Canadian children, new report says
stories.summary: Ottawa - A new report says online harms now constitute the top threat facing children in Canada, ahead of bullying, poverty and child abuse.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Online harms now constitute the top threat facing children in Canada, ahead of bullying, poverty and child abuse, Children First Canada said Tuesday in a new report.

It is the first time online harms have been in the top 10 list of threats, the report said.

“We’ve seen how now it’s permeating the lives of every kid in Canada, from birth all the way through adolescence. This is no longer a conversation just about teens on social media,” said Sara Austin, CEO of Children First Canada.

“In the past year alone, we’ve seen particularly the rise of AI-amplified harms,” she added.

The report says kids are coming into contact with AI toys and algorithmic-driven content before they even learn to read. It cites multiple risks related to the online environment, including cyberbullying, child luring, sexual extortion, AI-facilitated abuse and mental health impacts.

Last year’s shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. — which has led to dozens of lawsuits focused on the shooter’s use of ChatGPT — was a defining moment for the debate around online safety in Canada, the report says.

It notes that over the past decade, police-reported incidents of online child sexual abuse have increased by more than 300 per cent, while the Canadian Centre for Child Protection processes more than 100,000 reports of online child sexual abuse and exploitation each month.

“Meanwhile, the emergence of violent online networks such as 764 has prompted law enforcement agencies to warn that Canadian children are being actively targeted through gaming platforms, social media, and messaging apps,” the report says.

The federal government added 764 to its list of terror entities in December 2025. It described the group as a “decentralized transnational network of online nihilistic violent extremists.”

It said members of the group use social media and gaming platforms “to lure, groom, and extort youth to commit violent and sexual acts, including self-harm.”

The report argues Canada has regulations and safety standards in place for other children’s products, including food, medicine, pyjamas and toys — and that tech companies should not enjoy an exception.

Children First Canada is calling on the federal government to strengthen and pass the digital safety bill it introduced earlier this year. Bill C-34 would force social media platforms to at least temporarily block access for kids under 16 and regulate the companies behind social media platforms and AI chatbots by imposing on them a duty to act responsibly, among other measures.

“We’re very glad to see that it goes beyond social media to include AI chatbots, but we know that kids don’t just exist in these two platforms,” Austin said.

The group also would like to see the bill address gaming and live streaming platforms, as well as messaging apps.

Austin said the onus needs to be on tech companies to design safer products in the first place.

The group received financial support and subject matter expertise from the non-profit PolicyWise for Children & Families, the Hospital for Sick Children, and the Canadian Medical Association.

The report argues that online harms aren’t a stand-alone issue.

“They are amplifying many of the other threats facing children, contributing to declining physical activity and play, bullying, violence and child abuse, racism and discrimination through online hate, and even climate change through the growing environmental impacts of digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence,” it says.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Under Stephan Jost, the AGO became more popular – and more polarizing
stories.summary: The director and CEO will depart ahead of the 2027 opening of a large addition to the gallery that he championed
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
If you can discount tariff talk for a minute, the surprise news in the cultural community is that Stephan Jost is leaving the Art Gallery of Ontario in December, before the opening of a big addition to the Dundas Street building that he had initiated. Jost has led the Toronto institution as director and CEO for a decade, a standard run for gallery executives, but his signature project, the 40,000-square-foot Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, is only set to open next year.

Jost May be present at the ribbon cutting but he won’t be leading the AGO anymore, the gallery announced last week. He figures it is better for a new leader to assume the role before the opening to carry the new space forward with momentum, and he wants a break from what he called in an interview “no-win conversations.” Belatedly, the difficult politics of the museum sector, which is increasingly divided between social activists and traditionalists, seem to have caught up with him.

Perhaps somebody had to pay for the Nan Goldin fiasco that in 2025 saw the AGO back away from a proposed acquisition by the artist and pro-Palestinian activist under pressure from donor Judy Schulich . The overreach by the acquisition committee on which Schulich sat led to the resignation of John Zeppetelli, the curator who had championed the purchase of a Goldin video work (unrelated to her politics) – and a lot of public embarrassment when the story got out early this year. Jost’s number two, chief curator Julian Cox, already left the gallery in April.

This was the second time Jost had lost a prized curator to what appears to be politically motivated interference: Indigenous curator Wanda Nanibush , also vocally pro-Palestinian, left in November, 2024. The gallery, apparently unable to square her institutional status with her social media posts, suggested to staff in a memo that her departure was a mutual decision and praised her honesty. However, that departure has been devastating to the Ago’s reconciliation ambitions, splitting up the Canadian-Indigenous curatorial partnership that Nanibush had established with curator Georgiana Uhlyarik. Currently, the gallery has neither an Indigenous curator nor an Inuit one.

Jost has been a popularizer at the AGO, and often successfully so. Perhaps his best legacy is the free pass for anyone under 25, instituted in 2019. The gallery is full of younger visitors from all backgrounds. Some of the programming that draws people is both crowd-pleasing and intelligent. For example, the 2018 Yayoi Kusama show, for which crowds literally lined up around the block, wasn’t just a chance to step inside one of the Japanese artist’s mirrored infinity rooms. It was also an in-depth look at her pioneering art of the 1960s and 1970s, and the relationship between her work and her mental health.

On the other hand, some programming only looks like an attempt to keep the turnstiles spinning. The 2022-23 Leonard Cohen show used the famous name to front an unlikely archival exercise that didn’t have much to say about his actual music. However, it was certainly a step up from this summer’s Eyes of the Storm, merely a visual tribute to the Beatles’ early years featuring enlargements of Paul McCartney’s photographs.

It was not easy keeping a public art gallery going during the pandemic – AGO donors and the federal wage subsidy helped to cover payroll while staff took a 25-per-cent pay cut during the 2020-21 closures – nor recovering from the loss of visitors once it reopened. But Jost’s popular programming has not always sat well with his curators and in recent years the curatorial department seems to have installed a revolving door. Taqralik Partridge, an associate curator focusing on Inuit art, lasted about 14 months from 2022-2024; Xiaoyu Weng, a high-profile Chinese curator appointed from the United States in 2021, served about two years as a contemporary curator.

Of course, the role of the director is not just to attract more people but also different people. In that regard, Jost’s tenure does have one big curatorial win: the creation of the Global Africa and the Diaspora department where curator Julie Crooks has mounted several compelling exhibitions about Black culture as well as overseeing the acquisition of a major collection of historic Caribbean photography. If shows such as the multidisciplinary Leonard Cohen exhibit seemed an awkward move beyond pure visual art, her social documentary approach to her material has worked well – next up is Sunday Best: The Power and Glory of Black Style.

The photography department under Sophie Hackett has also programmed strongly, including the 2020 Diane Arbus retrospective and a clever daisy-chain show that celebrated the department’s 25th anniversary by asking local figures to pick works from the photography collection, each enthusiast’s choice inspired by the one of the person before. Meanwhile ambitious survey exhibitions with inventive themes – Making Her Mark, a show of historic female creativity in 2024, and 2022’s I am Here, a photography and home movie exhibition that juxtaposed professional and amateur work – prove the curators who have stayed are still at the top of their game.

If Jost has been a popularizer, he has also been an expansionist. The collection has grown by 18,000 items during his tenure and the Reiss Gallery – named for a $35-million gift from the Canada Goose CEO – will add 13 new galleries in a five-storey tower squeezed in to the south-east corner of the existing building, above the loading docks. The space will cost at least $100-million and some museum planners May have advocated a satellite instead: A basic building in an under-served new neighbourhood such as the West Don Lands might have got the AGO more bang for the buck.

Meanwhile, the architectural community is not convinced by the mishmash on Dundas Street: This is the third major addition to the site since the 1990s. The Reiss Gallery is connected to the existing building in four locations and the 2027 opening will reveal how people will flow through a building that already suffers from a confusing layout with the back wing added by architect Frank Gehry served by separate elevators from the front. Judgement as to whether the new space is logical or necessary will have to wait until it launches … after Jost departs.

The overreach by the acquisition committee on which Schulich sat led to the resignation of John Zeppetelli, the curator who had championed the purchase of a Goldin video work (unrelated to her politics) – and a lot of public embarrassment when the story got out early this year. Jost’s number two, chief curator Julian Cox, already left the gallery in April.

content_blocks.text: This was the second time Jost had lost a prized curator to what appears to be politically motivated interference: Indigenous curator Wanda Nanibush , also vocally pro-Palestinian, left in November, 2024. The gallery, apparently unable to square her institutional status with her social media posts, suggested to staff in a memo that her departure was a mutual decision and praised her honesty. However, that departure has been devastating to the Ago’s reconciliation ambitions, splitting up the Canadian-Indigenous curatorial partnership that Nanibush had established with curator Georgiana Uhlyarik. Currently, the gallery has neither an Indigenous curator nor an Inuit one.

content_blocks.text: Jost has been a popularizer at the AGO, and often successfully so. Perhaps his best legacy is the free pass for anyone under 25, instituted in 2019. The gallery is full of younger visitors from all backgrounds. Some of the programming that draws people is both crowd-pleasing and intelligent. For example, the 2018 Yayoi Kusama show, for which crowds literally lined up around the block, wasn’t just a chance to step inside one of the Japanese artist’s mirrored infinity rooms. It was also an in-depth look at her pioneering art of the 1960s and 1970s, and the relationship between her work and her mental health.

However, it was certainly a step up from this summer’s Eyes of the Storm, merely a visual tribute to the Beatles’ early years featuring enlargements of Paul McCartney’s photographs.

content_blocks.text: It was not easy keeping a public art gallery going during the pandemic – AGO donors and the federal wage subsidy helped to cover payroll while staff took a 25-per-cent pay cut during the 2020-21 closures – nor recovering from the loss of visitors once it reopened. But Jost’s popular programming has not always sat well with his curators and in recent years the curatorial department seems to have installed a revolving door. Taqralik Partridge, an associate curator focusing on Inuit art, lasted about 14 months from 2022-2024; Xiaoyu Weng, a high-profile Chinese curator appointed from the United States in 2021, served about two years as a contemporary curator.

content_blocks.text: The photography department under Sophie Hackett has also programmed strongly, including the 2020 Diane Arbus retrospective and a clever daisy-chain show that celebrated the department’s 25th anniversary by asking local figures to pick works from the photography collection, each enthusiast’s choice inspired by the one of the person before. Meanwhile ambitious survey exhibitions with inventive themes – Making Her Mark, a show of historic female creativity in 2024, and 2022’s I am Here, a photography and home movie exhibition that juxtaposed professional and amateur work – prove the curators who have stayed are still at the top of their game.

content_blocks.text: If Jost has been a popularizer, he has also been an expansionist. The collection has grown by 18,000 items during his tenure and the Reiss Gallery – named for a $35-million gift from the Canada Goose CEO – will add 13 new galleries in a five-storey tower squeezed in to the south-east corner of the existing building, above the loading docks. The space will cost at least $100-million and some museum planners May have advocated a satellite instead: A basic building in an under-served new neighbourhood such as the West Don Lands might have got the AGO more bang for the buck.

The Reiss Gallery is connected to the existing building in four locations and the 2027 opening will reveal how people will flow through a building that already suffers from a confusing layout with the back wing added by architect Frank Gehry served by separate elevators from the front. stories.title: How much would renaming Lake Ontario cost the U.S.? CBO points to the 'closest precedent'
stories.summary: Renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" will come at a cost to federal agencies in the U.S. responsible for updating maps and databases.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” will come at a cost to federal agencies in the U.S. that are responsible for updating maps and databases, and a previous report by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) offers insight into how expensive this could be.

It’s not the first time Trump has sought to rename a major body of water. In January 2025, he signed an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

In an email to National Post, a spokesperson for CBO said: “CBO hasn’t published an estimate for H.R. 10196, the Lake America Act. The closest precedent is the estimate for H.R. 276, the Gulf of America Act. While that estimate can’t automatically be applied to Lake Ontario, it can provide a sense of how CBO has previously treated similar legislation.”

The 2025 report said the estimate was based on the cost of similar activities that involved updating documents and maps. It added that the Gulf of America Act “could affect direct spending by some agencies that are allowed to use fees, receipts from the sale of goods, and other collections to cover operating costs.”

However, CBO estimated that any changes in spending by those agencies would be negligible because “most of them can adjust amounts collected to reflect changes in operating costs.”

If the cost of renaming Lake Ontario does come in at a similar figure to the estimate for the Gulf of Mexico, it would mean U.S. federal agencies May have spent as much as US$1 million on renaming the two bodies of water.

J.D. Tuccille: Trump shouldn't have the authority to rename Lake Ontario

Republican mayor from Lake Ontario city rejects Trump's 'Lake America'

Elsewhere, the CBO issued another report earlier this year estimating the cost of introducing “Department of War” as a secondary title for the U.S. Department of Defense, after Trump signed an executive order authorizing the use of the new name in September 2025.

It said a “modest implementation” of the name could cost US$10 million, or as much as US$125 million if the name change was implemented “broadly and rapidly.” A statutory renaming, the CBO said, could cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

Another post that showed a map of New Mexico with “Mexico” crossed out and replaced by “America” was reminiscent of posts he made before renaming Lake Ontario.

Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario came after a breakdown in trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S. last month, which saw Prime Minister Mark Carney announce dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs that come into effect on Tuesday.

Politicians on both sides of the border have condemned the name change, with Ontario Premier Doug Ford erecting a new Lake Ontario sign at a cost of $25,000 in Winona, Ont., shortly after Trump signed the executive order.

Unveiling the sign in a video posted on X, Ford said: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

And Robert Corradino, a Republican and mayor of Oswego, a city in New York State on the shore of Lake Ontario, previously told National Post that his community is taking the renaming of Lake Ontario “very personally.”

“Lake Ontario is in the DNA of Osweganians,” he said, adding, “Everything that we are emanates from the lake.”

Elsewhere, polling has revealed that most Americans are against the name change , with Economist/YouGov research finding 68 per cent of Americans strongly or somewhat disapproved of the move. A separate poll conducted by Ipsos published a similar result, with 63 per cent opposing Trump’s executive order.

stories.title: Canadian dollar hits nearly three-week high as investors shake off trade angst
stories.summary: Investors focus on higher oil prices
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar strengthened to nearly ​a three-week high against ‌its U.S. counterpart on Tuesday as investors focused on higher oil prices rather than an escalating trade war between the ⁠U.S. and ​Canada.

The loonie was trading 0.2 per cent higher at 1.3790 per U.S. dollar, or 72.52 U.S. cents, after touching its strongest intraday level since August 21 at 1.3760.

​Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. ‌goods took effect after midnight, intensifying an 18-month-old trade war and spurring Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from the country’s biggest trading partner.

On Monday, ‌U.S. President ​Donald Trump said ‌Canadian private jet maker Bombardier would no longer be allowed ​to sell its planes in the ⁠U.S. unless it started manufacturing in the country.

“Markets ⁠are increasingly tuning out tariffs and threats,” said Adam Button, ​chief currency analyst at investingLive. “For all the angst, the economic impacts are still limited and the Canadian dollar is trading off oil.”

Data on Friday showed Canada’s economy lost 41,700 jobs in August. ⁠The unemployment rate, however, held steady at 6.4 per cent.

Last week, the Bank of Canada said it does not expect new U.S. tariffs to have a large direct impact on the economy, adding that the ongoing ⁠Middle East conflict had raised ​upside risks to the inflation outlook.

U.S. crude oil futures ⁠touched a three-month high at $94.73 a barrel on Tuesday after Iran-backed Houthis ‌in Yemen attacked Saudi energy facilities. Oil is one of Canada’s ​major exports.

Canadian bond yields moved higher across the curve. The 10-year was up 2.3 basis points at 3.802 per cent but held below a two-year high ​it touched during Friday’s session at 3.834 per cent.

stories.title: Record 984 reptile nests incubated in southern Ontario recovery effort
stories.summary: The record year included 458 spiny softshell nests, with up to 7,000 hatchlings expected to be released.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The record year included 458 spiny softshell nests, with up to 7,000 hatchlings expected to be released.

Last updated 5 hours ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/record-984-reptile-nests-incubated-in-southern-Ontario-recovery-effort#comments-area)

A spiny softshell turtle, less than a day old, is pictured at the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority in this Free Press file photo.

It was a record year for endangered reptile recovery in southern Ontario, with 984 reptile nests incubated this year, a local conservation authority says.

In a news release Tuesday, the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority announced its most successful year to date through its Southern Ontario At Risk Reptiles program, surpassing the previous record for incubated nests, set in 2025, by about 200.

In total, the nests represented seven species of turtles and one species of snake. By mid-September, the program expects to have released more than 16,000 hatchlings back into the wild, all successfully hatched in incubators.

“Every nest protected and every hatchling released represents another step toward recovery for reptiles that face increasing challenges across southern Ontario,” said Scott Gillingwater, a species at risk biologist with the conservation authority.

A record 458 spiny softshell nests were collected from the Thames River this year. The freshwater turtle was listed as endangered by the province in 2016.

The authority says the nests are expected to result in the release of up to 7,000 hatchlings, providing a significant boost to one of the country’s most endangered reptile species.

For more than 30 years, the program has focused on direct conservation action, including nest protection, incubation and hatchling release. The program has contributed to the first documented increase in Canada’s spiny softshell population in more than a century, the authority says.

Despite the program’s success, the authority says it has been unable to secure provincial funding for its species-at-risk research and recovery work, leaving much of the program reliant on support from municipalities, organizations, foundations, businesses and individual donors.

“These results demonstrate what is possible when communities come together to protect species at risk,” Gillingwater said.

stories.title: Canada promises trade ban on goods from 'illegal' Israeli settlements in new joint statement
stories.summary: Canada says it intends ban all trade of goods tied to Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada says it intends to ban all trade with goods tied to Israeli settlements in the West Bank, joining several European countries in a joint statement promising harsher measures against Israelis the governments say are undermining a two-state solution.

In the statement, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her counterparts in the U.K., France, and nine other countries called on Israel’s government to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank. The 12 foreign ministers also specifically criticized an apartment development, called E1, they said would essentially cut the West Bank territory in half.

“We firmly oppose actions tantamount to the annexation of Palestinian land and forcible displacement of the Palestinian people,” they said in Tuesday’s statement.

The territory, seen as a potential part of a future Palestinian state, is controlled by Israel, which refers to it as Judea and Samaria. It is inhabited by hundreds of thousands of Jews and millions of Arabs.

Anand’s statement said Canada intended to join the European countries in introducing a national trade ban on goods tied to “illegal” settlements in the West Bank, though it did not detail when or how that would happen. The United States ambassador to Israel has also recently criticized Israeli violence in the territory after meeting with Palestinian Americans living there.

“The Government of Israel must immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers, ensure accountability for settler violence, and investigate allegations against Israeli forces,” Anand said.

In a separate statement, Carney noted that “in taking this coordinated action, we reiterate our desire for a close and productive partnership with Israel, our enduring support for the Israeli people and our unwavering commitment to Israel’s security. We support a safe and secure Israel, living alongside a safe and secure Palestine.”

The promised trade ban is likely to be largely symbolic, though, with very little trade occurring between Israeli settlements and Canada. Now, Global Affairs Canada must figure out how to implement such a trade ban.

Raymond J. de Souza: The growing problem of settler violence in the West Bank

Mohamed Fahmy: Turkey's Islamist government sets itself up for a direct confrontation with Israel

The joint announcement was fiercely rebuked by the Israel’s ambassador to Canada Iddo Moed, who accused signatories of singling out his country and attempting to meddle in upcoming legislative elections.

“Every move of this nature only serves to push intervening nations out of any meaningful regional influence,” Moed said in a statement.

“Furthermore, these unilateral steps actively undermine prospects for peace, directly contribute to a surge in global antisemitism, and ignore the fundamental fact that the Jewish people have a documented historical connection and right to live across the Land of Israel.”

The announcement marks a worsening tone from Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government towards Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between longtime allies.

The British government went a step further than Canada on Tuesday, accusing Israel of carrying out “ethnic cleansing” in the Palestinian territories.

“What the Netanyahu government is doing is a stain on the conscience of the world,” U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a video.

Netanyahu has recently claimed some violence in the territory is instigated by Palestinians and that the Israeli attacks are being committed by just a handful of settlers.

On Tuesday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said the decision by Britain and other countries was a “grave miscalculation” that would “fall on the wrong side of history.” He also accused the countries of “gross interference” in Israel’s upcoming elections, where much of the ballot question is Netanyahu’s handling of the country’s safety before and since the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack by Hamas.

The CEO of Canada’s Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) accused the Liberal government of trying to appease the “most extreme elements” of society.

“They make diplomacy harder and do nothing to press the Palestinian Authority to fulfill the commitments it made to Prime Minister Carney, including to fundamentally reform its governance, to hold general elections in 2026 in which Hamas can play no part, and to demilitarize the Palestinian state,” CEO Noah Shack said.

There has been growing pressure from Israel’s diplomatic allies in Europe and Canada to halt growing violence in the West Bank in recent months. Late in August, Canada issued a warning to Canadian businesses about reputational damage if they traded with Israeli counterparts operating in the settlements Canada considers as illegal.

In recent months, media and NGO observers have alleged growing armed violence by Israeli settlers forcibly displacing entire Palestinian villages in the West Bank. Netanyahu’s government and the Israeli Defense Forces have been accused both internationally and domestically for turning a blind eye to the violence.

Canada and a dozen European countries including France and the U.K. also severely criticized Netanyahu’s government’s publication of tenders to build the E1 apartment project in the West Bank. The project would cut across land near Jerusalem and impede chances for a two-state solution between the Palestinians and Israel, the federal government says.

Israel’s embassy in Canada did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

stories.title: Iceland summons U.S. ambassador over Trump’s ‘unacceptable’ map post
stories.summary: On Monday, Trump posted an image with a map of North America, showing countries like Canada, Greenland and Iceland coloured in with the American flag.
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
Iceland’s foreign ministry said it has summoned the U.S. ambassador Billy Long to a meeting after U.S. President Donald Trump posted a map that showed the island covered with the U.S. flag, according to Icelandic public broadcaster RUV .

On Monday, Trump posted an image with a map of North America, showing countries like Canada, Greenland and Iceland coloured in with the American flag.

The map was labelled as “United States of America” and he shared the post without adding any further explanation.

“It is an insult to Icelanders, Canadians and Greenlanders,” Iceland’s prime minister Kristrun Frostadottir told reporters on Tuesday, referencing Trump’s Monday post on Truth Social.

“There is nothing funny or normal about making fun of the sovereignty of states, especially today, when sovereignty cannot be taken for granted,” Frostadottir added.

Frostadottir added that the reason to summon the ambassador for a meeting was to “make it absolutely clear that, from our perspective, this was completely unacceptable.”

“People within the U.S. administration have repeatedly told me that we should not take the current U.S. president literally, but we should take him seriously,” she added. “That is exactly what we are doing, and we are stressing that Iceland is a sovereign, independent state that is responsible for its own future.”

“No one else can decide or bargain over our independence or sovereignty. We do that on our own terms. We do it here at home, together,” Frostadottir said.

Frostadottir said that Iceland would continue to stand with the people of Greenland and would not soften its position on the matter, according to RUV.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the post “disturbing and, in many ways, completely inappropriate.”

“It’s obviously a sign that the U.S. president still harbors some kind of maximalist vision in his own mind. We need to rein that in,” Løkke Rasmussen told the national broadcaster DR on Tuesday.

The Arctic states have been on edge since Trump ramped up his rhetoric at the start of the year about U.S. control of Greenland.

His post came Monday as the European Union sought to reassure Greenland with the promise of a stronger partnership and hundreds of millions of euros in investment following Trump’s repeated threats.

This isn’t the first time the Trump administration has shared a map with Greenland covered with the American flag.

In January, Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, posted on X of the territory covered with the American flag, writing, “Soon.”

Soon pic.twitter.com/XU6VmZxph3 — Katie Miller (@KatieMiller) January 3, 2026

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen addressed the photo in a post at the time, writing, “First and foremost, let me say calmly and clearly, that there is neither reason for panic nor for insecurity.”

“The photo shared by Katie Miller of Greenland being produced wrapped in an American flag doesn’t change anything. Our country is not for sale and our future is not determined by social media posts,” he wrote.

“But the picture is disrespectful. The relations between countries and people are based on respect and on international law and not on symbolic markings that ignore our status and our rights.

“There’s no need to panic. But there’s good reason to speak up against the lack of respect.”

Trump has repeatedly called for U.S. jurisdiction over Greenland, and has pointedly not ruled out military force to take control of the mineral-rich, strategically located Arctic island that is an autonomous self-governing Danish territory.

Trump said in January that anything less than the Arctic island being in U.S. hands would be “unacceptable.”

During an unrelated event at the White House about rural health care, he recounted how he had threatened European allies with tariffs on pharmaceuticals.

“I May do that for Greenland too,” Trump said. “I May put a tariff on countries if they don’t go along with Greenland, because we need Greenland for national security. So I May do that.”

European leaders have insisted that it is only for Denmark and Greenland to decide on matters concerning the territory , and Denmark said it was increasing its military presence in Greenland in co-operation with allies.

By July, Trump revived his Greenland rhetoric and said that the United States should control the territory while threatening to “remove” U.S. troops in Europe.

“Greenland doesn’t help Denmark. Denmark doesn’t spend money to really help Greenland, but it’s an important part for the United States,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

The island was “surrounded by China ships and Russian ships,” Trump said, adding that Greenland “should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark.”

“We could remove all of our soldiers out of Europe,” he added.

—With files from Global News’ Uday Rana and The Associated Press

stories.title: The back-to-school rituals that help these families calm first-day jitters
stories.summary: From first-day rituals to annual traditions, here’s how these four families get ready for the new school year
stories.author: Ann Hui
stories.content:
This week, Libby Barnicke and her family will engage in what has become, for them, an important tradition. She’ll dress up her two boys in their crisp new school uniforms and line them up on the front porch for their annual back-to-school photo.

It’s a tradition that is replicated in households from coast to coast. For many families, these early weeks of September are a major occasion. The end of summer, and the start of a new year.

“I always view September as the new year. Not January first,” said Ms. Barnicke, who lives in Toronto. “It feels like the beginning. Like a renewal. It’s excitement, but also a lot of anxiousness.”

It’s a month that brings new milestones in many families. The start of a new routine, or adventure, or challenge. A new step toward independence. For many, it will be their first day in a new place.

The Globe and Mail spoke with four families experiencing “first days” this week. Here’s what they told us about how they feel, and how they’re preparing:

Aadhya is a chatty preschooler who lives in Toronto with her family. She knows how to spell her own name, and how to count to four fingers when asked her age. She likes rainbow-coloured tutus, chapatis with curried vegetables and reading books with her mom. When she grows up, she plans on being a doctor and also a princess.

What she’s most excited about

Aadhya’s older brother already attends the school where she’s headed, so he’s given her some ideas on what to expect.

“Kindergarten,” she said, “is where you help your teachers. Cleaning. Putting books away. Sitting in the circle.”

She’s most excited to see the school library, which her brother has described in great detail. She can’t wait to pick out her own books and bring them home.

What she’s worried about

Aadhya will miss the comforts of daycare. “The teachers love me a lot. I love my teachers a lot.”

She’ll miss her daycare friends, too. “I love my friends,” she said. “We hug with each other and hold each other’s hands.”

She’ll be parting ways with almost all of them. Most are heading off to a different school, so she’ll have to make new friends. When asked if this makes her nervous, she gives the tiniest nod.

“The new friends might hate me, and might not love me,” she said. “They might not want to be best friends with me.”

How the family is preparing

“She’s already been in the daycare setting, so the routine is kind of the same,” said her mom, Sonali. They’ve been working as a family to drill the importance of that morning routine in to their children: Of waking up by a specific time and leaving plenty of room each morning to get ready and out the door without feeling rushed.

Beyond that, Sonali said she’s been focused on preparing Aadhya for the practical challenges of kindergarten such as how to get through a full day without an afternoon nap, how to recognize her own name at her cubby and how to tell the difference between her stuff and all the other kids’, which often look similar.

Aadhya is also practicing how to open and close her own lunch bag and food containers. It’ll be her first time bringing lunch from home, and she’ll have to figure out how to navigate that. “It’s all about keeping things simple and accessible,” said Sonali.

Each year, Sonali asks family and friends to send in short video messages for the kids with their well-wishes for the new school year. She compiles all of them into a larger video that the family watches the night before school. They make popcorn, settle into the couch and make a night of it.

“It’s a tradition that we all look forward to,” Sonali said.

The transition from summer to a new school year is always an anxious, nerve-wracking time. “And, honestly not just for the kids,” she said.

“It’s emotional for the parents too – seeing your babies going out into the world.”

Until recently, Taylor attended a co-ed, public Catholic school in Toronto, where he lives with his family. But this week he is moving to an all-boys, private middle school that is connected to a high school. So he’ll be sharing the halls for the first time with kids who are much older, ranging from Grade 7 all the way up to Grade 12.

What he’s most excited about

Taylor is an athlete who plays soccer, football and hockey. “Any sport, basically.” So he’s looking forward to the new sports and activities available.

“It’s a lot bigger than my [former] school, so there’s lots of different types of activities and clubs,” he said. “It’s just a totally different environment.”

He’s also looking forward to the fact that he’ll be joined by many of his existing friends who are moving to the new school alongside him.

What he’s most worried about

“Probably the exams.” The curriculum in middle school, he expects, will be much more intense.

How they’re preparing

This week will represent a big step into independence for Taylor, said his mom Libby. Instead of getting dropped off and picked up by his parents each day, he’ll be responsible for getting himself to and from school.

For the first time, Taylor will have to navigate public transit on his own. He’ll also have to figure out where to buy his snacks after school, and how to pay for them. The family is having to discuss, for the first time, questions such as whether he’s ready for a debit card or a cellphone.

“It’s a change in tide,” said Libby. “We’re having meaningful conversations about what the new routine is going to look like – early adult conversations, I would say.”

Back to school rituals

This will be the seventh year that Libby has lined up her boys for their back-to-school photo (they missed one year because of the pandemic). “It’s just always been a marker for me to show the progress – to show just how big they’re getting.”

Still, beyond the anxiety and the nerves, she said, there’s a lot of excitement.

“I think there’s something very joyful about coming of age, and moving on,” she said. “I just can’t wait to see what he does with this next chapter.”

At first glance, Arshia seems like a typical Vancouver teenager. She likes sushi and swimming, music by Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter and books from the popular ‘ Powerless ’ YA series by Lauren Roberts.

But, if you spend just a minute talking to her, it’s clear that she’s no ordinary kid. Arshia was the valedictorian at her elementary school and runs her own small business online. She organizes fundraisers for the local children’s hospital and intends to be a lawyer one day – after graduating from Harvard Law School, of course.

She’s made the difficult decision to attend a different high school (which, in her Vancouver school district, is grades eight through 12) than all of her friends. She’s opting instead for a school with an International Baccalaureate program, which she considers more academically challenging.

Arshia is looking forward to the idea of a challenge. Of more intense classes, and the chance to join the basketball team, the debate club and the students’ council.

“I’m definitely feeling a little bit nervous, but I’m also just really excited for all the new opportunities and all the new people I’m going to meet.”

She’s excited, too, about having a bit more freedom.

“In elementary school, it’s a lot more structured. We were kind of taken to every class, things like that. But in high school, they’ll tell us to go to our different classes, and then it’s just entirely up to us.”

The family is big on organization and building good habits. Ever since they were little, Arshia’s mom Sophia Purohit Singh has taught her two kids how to balance their own schedules and make sure they’re staying on top of deadlines.

“The habits were developed way early on, where it was always about keeping yourself busy and organized. Having your own calendar and managing it,” said Sophia. “So there’s not time left over to go on their phone for hours.”

They’ve doubled down on this routine over the summer. Entirely of her own accord, Arshia has been working ahead on her math workbooks (“just to be ready for next year”), and has been talking through with her parents how she might juggle her many new assignments and responsibilities in high school.

Every year, the family spends at least one day combing through the house to see what school supplies they’ve left lying around.

“It’s stuff we’ve collected over the year, and figuring out how to reuse them,” said Arshia. And then they’ll go back-to-school shopping for everything else.

Back-to-school outfits, said Arshia, “are definitely still a thing.” For her first day of high school, she chose her outfit in advance: A new skirt she bought recently, with a t-shirt and hoodie, in case of cold. “I’m just going to wear what makes me comfortable,” she said.

She knows this is an important moment for her.

“This is kind of a big point of change in my life,” she said. “In a few years, my life is going to change a lot.”

Over the past few decades, Mr. Erickson has been a sawmill worker, a concrete labourer and a logging truck driver. But this week, the father of five from Lake Babine Nation in B.C. will take on a new career: A high-school teacher.

He’s a new graduate of Nitep, the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia, where, after going back to school in his late 30s, he recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in education. He’ll be teaching a small group of Indigenous students, grades eight through 12, at a high school in his community.

“My goal is to give Indigenous students the confidence to go on to bigger and better things. To show them they’re capable,” he said.

“If I can do it at the age of 41, there’s no reason why anybody else can’t do it.”

What he’s excited about

Mr. Erickson can only recall ever having one Indigenous teacher when he was growing up. “It was the only classroom where I felt like I wasn’t really being judged,” he said. Now, he’s excited to be that positive role model for his own students.

“I have a lot of life stories. I’ve had a lot of things happen in my life that I can relate with the kids.”

Plus, as the father of five daughters (who range in age from eight to 25), he has ample confidence and experience in dealing with teenagers.

As a teacher, he said, he won’t be “Mr. Erickson.” Just “Nick.”

“I want to help them and teach them,” he said. “But I also want to learn beside them.”

One more bonus? His wife, Marsha Erickson, completed the Nitep program alongside him. They’ll be sharing this experience as first-time teachers in the community together.

What he’s worried about

“I’m kind of nervous. I’m responsible for these kids. But if I’m my genuine, authentic self, I’m not going to have any problems. I’m just going to be the best person I can in front of them.”

Each year, the couple has taken back-to-school pictures of their five kids on the deck in front of the house. This year they’ll take photos again – only this time, with the addition of mom and dad.

“She’s already been in the daycare setting, so the routine is kind of the same,” said her mom, Sonali. They’ve been working as a family to drill the importance of that morning routine in to their children: Of waking up by a specific time and leaving plenty of room each morning to get ready and out the door without feeling rushed.

Beyond that, Sonali said she’s been focused on preparing Aadhya for the practical challenges of kindergarten such as how to get through a full day without an afternoon nap, how to recognize her own name at her cubby and how to tell the difference between her stuff and all the other kids’, which often look similar.

Aadhya is also practicing how to open and close her own lunch bag and food containers. It’ll be her first time bringing lunch from home, and she’ll have to figure out how to navigate that. “It’s all about keeping things simple and accessible,” said Sonali.

Each year, Sonali asks family and friends to send in short video messages for the kids with their well-wishes for the new school year. She compiles all of them into a larger video that the family watches the night before school. They make popcorn, settle into the couch and make a night of it.
“It’s a tradition that we all look forward to,” Sonali said.
The transition from summer to a new school year is always an anxious, nerve-wracking time. “And, honestly not just for the kids,” she said.
“It’s emotional for the parents too – seeing your babies going out into the world.”

Until recently, Taylor attended a co-ed, public Catholic school in Toronto, where he lives with his family. But this week he is moving to an all-boys, private middle school that is connected to a high school. So he’ll be sharing the halls for the first time with kids who are much older, ranging from Grade 7 all the way up to Grade 12.
What he’s most excited about
Taylor is an athlete who plays soccer, football and hockey. “Any sport, basically.” So he’s looking forward to the new sports and activities available.
“It’s a lot bigger than my [former] school, so there’s lots of different types of activities and clubs,” he said. “It’s just a totally different environment.”
He’s also looking forward to the fact that he’ll be joined by many of his existing friends who are moving to the new school alongside him.
What he’s most worried about
“Probably the exams.” The curriculum in middle school, he expects, will be much more intense.
How they’re preparing

This week will represent a big step into independence for Taylor, said his mom Libby. Instead of getting dropped off and picked up by his parents each day, he’ll be responsible for getting himself to and from school.

For the first time, Taylor will have to navigate public transit on his own. He’ll also have to figure out where to buy his snacks after school, and how to pay for them. The family is having to discuss, for the first time, questions such as whether he’s ready for a debit card or a cellphone.
“It’s a change in tide,” said Libby. “We’re having meaningful conversations about what the new routine is going to look like – early adult conversations, I would say.”
Back to school rituals

This will be the seventh year that Libby has lined up her boys for their back-to-school photo (they missed one year because of the pandemic). “It’s just always been a marker for me to show the progress – to show just how big they’re getting.”
Still, beyond the anxiety and the nerves, she said, there’s a lot of excitement.
“I think there’s something very joyful about coming of age, and moving on,” she said. “I just can’t wait to see what he does with this next chapter.”

At first glance, Arshia seems like a typical Vancouver teenager. She likes sushi and swimming, music by Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter and books from the popular ‘ Powerless ’ YA series by Lauren Roberts.

But, if you spend just a minute talking to her, it’s clear that she’s no ordinary kid. Arshia was the valedictorian at her elementary school and runs her own small business online. She organizes fundraisers for the local children’s hospital and intends to be a lawyer one day – after graduating from Harvard Law School, of course.

She’s made the difficult decision to attend a different high school (which, in her Vancouver school district, is grades eight through 12) than all of her friends. She’s opting instead for a school with an International Baccalaureate program, which she considers more academically challenging.
Arshia is looking forward to the idea of a challenge. Of more intense classes, and the chance to join the basketball team, the debate club and the students’ council.
“I’m definitely feeling a little bit nervous, but I’m also just really excited for all the new opportunities and all the new people I’m going to meet.”
She’s excited, too, about having a bit more freedom.

“In elementary school, it’s a lot more structured. We were kind of taken to every class, things like that. But in high school, they’ll tell us to go to our different classes, and then it’s just entirely up to us.”

The family is big on organization and building good habits. Ever since they were little, Arshia’s mom Sophia Purohit Singh has taught her two kids how to balance their own schedules and make sure they’re staying on top of deadlines.

“The habits were developed way early on, where it was always about keeping yourself busy and organized. Having your own calendar and managing it,” said Sophia. “So there’s not time left over to go on their phone for hours.”

They’ve doubled down on this routine over the summer. Entirely of her own accord, Arshia has been working ahead on her math workbooks (“just to be ready for next year”), and has been talking through with her parents how she might juggle her many new assignments and responsibilities in high school.
Every year, the family spends at least one day combing through the house to see what school supplies they’ve left lying around.
“It’s stuff we’ve collected over the year, and figuring out how to reuse them,” said Arshia. And then they’ll go back-to-school shopping for everything else.

Back-to-school outfits, said Arshia, “are definitely still a thing.” For her first day of high school, she chose her outfit in advance: A new skirt she bought recently, with a t-shirt and hoodie, in case of cold. “I’m just going to wear what makes me comfortable,” she said.
She knows this is an important moment for her.
“This is kind of a big point of change in my life,” she said. “In a few years, my life is going to change a lot.”

Over the past few decades, Mr. Erickson has been a sawmill worker, a concrete labourer and a logging truck driver. But this week, the father of five from Lake Babine Nation in B.C. will take on a new career: A high-school teacher.

He’s a new graduate of Nitep, the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia, where, after going back to school in his late 30s, he recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in education. He’ll be teaching a small group of Indigenous students, grades eight through 12, at a high school in his community.
“My goal is to give Indigenous students the confidence to go on to bigger and better things. To show them they’re capable,” he said.
“If I can do it at the age of 41, there’s no reason why anybody else can’t do it.”
What he’s excited about

Mr. Erickson can only recall ever having one Indigenous teacher when he was growing up. “It was the only classroom where I felt like I wasn’t really being judged,” he said. Now, he’s excited to be that positive role model for his own students.
“I have a lot of life stories. I’ve had a lot of things happen in my life that I can relate with the kids.”
Plus, as the father of five daughters (who range in age from eight to 25), he has ample confidence and experience in dealing with teenagers.
As a teacher, he said, he won’t be “Mr. Erickson.” Just “Nick.”
“I want to help them and teach them,” he said. “But I also want to learn beside them.”
One more bonus? His wife, Marsha Erickson, completed the Nitep program alongside him. They’ll be sharing this experience as first-time teachers in the community together.
What he’s worried about
“I’m kind of nervous. I’m responsible for these kids. But if I’m my genuine, authentic self, I’m not going to have any problems. I’m just going to be the best person I can in front of them.”
Each year, the couple has taken back-to-school pictures of their five kids on the deck in front of the house. This year they’ll take photos again – only this time, with the addition of mom and dad.

stories.title: 8 storeys a 'bridge too far' for some neighbours of Sarnia Road development
stories.summary: Some residents of a neighbourhood near Western University are opposing a developer's plan to increase the height of an already-approved building from six to eight storeys.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Some residents of a neighbourhood near Western University are opposing a developer's plan to increase the height of an already-approved building from six to eight storeys.
· Posted: Sep 08, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 8
Bill Tsioros describes himself as a “behind the scenes” kind of guy when it comes to stepping into the path of controversy.

But this week he’s walking door-to-door around his leafy-green neighbourhood west of Western University's campus. At each stop, he's asking neighbours to let him place one of the signs he purchased on their lawn.

The message on each sign urges London city councillors to vote 'no' on a developers’ application to expand their already-approved plans to build a 204-unit student residence on Sarnia Road — between Kininvie Drive and Stirrup Court — close to the Western University campus.
Tsioros and some of his neighbours are opposing an application by a numbered company to add two more storeys to a six-storey development council approved in June 2025.
The approved plan calls for 150 units on the Sarnia Road lots, which currently each have older single-family homes.

Now the developer is seeking approval to increase the building to eight storeys, for a total of 204 units.For Tsioros, it's too much density for a neighbourhood of single-family homes on larger lots. The added height, he argues, will lead to a building that towers over the backyards it surrounds.
“We’re not against development in London,” said Tsioros who lives on Kininvie Drive and works in the construction industry. “Eight storeys though, is a bridge too far.”

CBC News was unable to reach the owner of the property, which property records list as owned by an Ontario corporation with a mailing address in Markham headed up by David Ho. The developer is represented by planning firm Zelinka Priamo.

If approved, the amended application would deliver a building with a stepped-down design. The portion fronting Sarnia Road would be eight storeys high, with the section furthest from the road at four storeys high.

The combined footprint of the two lots at 299-307 Sarnia Rd. is almost three acres and borders about dozen backyards of homes on Kininvie Drive and Stirrup Court. The houses on Kininvie are on massive lots, some as large as football fields. It's a green space with more than 100 trees that Kininvie said was once largely unfenced and used as a shared space among neighbours.

A concept drawing shows the six-storey version of the application, which was approved by council in June 2025. The developer is now requesting approval to go to a total height of eight storeys. (Zelinka Priamo)

The developer's amended plan also calls for 188 underground parking spaces, a total Tsioros says is not enough to accommodate all residents and guests and prevent overflow parking onto surrounding streets.
Tsioros said on weekday mornings the traffic on Sarnia Road often backs up all the way to Wonderland Road. He said left turns from streets such as Kininvie Drive are already a "test of nerves."
He has hired a lawyer to speak in opposition of amended eight-storey plan, and raised his concerns about the development through the Orchard Park/Sherwood Forest Neighbourhood Association.

While city staff are recommending approval of adding the two storeys, the report coming to planning committee flags some issues. Among them, the building’s "institutional appearance" which the report says “should be modified to be more consistent with the residential character of the surrounding area.”

The staff report also points to limited sewage capacity in city wastewater pipes located downstream from the proposed development. Staff are calling for holding provision, which would essentially pause the development, until the sewage capacity issue is addressed.
The area's councillior Sam Trosow said while he voted in favour of the development at six storeys, he won’t support a height increase to eight, a request of council he calls “greedy."
“I could live with the six storeys, but eight storeys is just way out of balance,” said Trosow.

Councillor Trosow said the application highlights a problem he’s flagged often at council: that traffic studies submitted by developers often only account for the traffic their development would generate, without accounting for the traffic already there.

He will speak against the request to add two storeys when it is presented to council’s five-member planning committee on Wednesday. However, he’s not a member of that committee and won’t get a vote unless it comes to full council for ratification.
London planning committee rejects contentious Fanshawe Park Road proposal
Tsioros plans to be at city hall on Wednesday and hopes to get a more sympathetic ears from councillors, most of whom are seeking re-election in the Oct. 26 election.
He's more optimistic given that neighbours were successful in opposing a developer's plan to add two storeys to their already-approved development on Fanshawe Park Road near Adelaide.

"That's going to help," he said. "This isn't a northwest issue, this could be happening in any neighbourhood [off a main road] if you're on Commissioners, you're on Riverside, it could be happening there."

stories.title: Century-old statue returned to its base in Memramcook, N.B. after vandalism
stories.summary: A century-old bronze statue of a key Acadian figure in New Brunswick has been placed back on its base, after vandals somehow pushed it off last month.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
A bronze statue of a key Acadian figure in New Brunswick erected more than a century ago has been placed back on its base, after vandals apparently pushed it off last month.

The Village of Memramcook said in a statement in August that it was “horrified” to see the statue of Père Camille Lefebrve , which stands in the centre of the village, ON the ground.

“The people of Memramcook are very attached to Père Lefebvre,” Mayor Maxime O. Bourgeois said in a social media post.

“His statue is an important heritage symbol for us and l’Acadie would not be as we known it without his dedication to French-language education in the 1860s. We hope that light will be shed on this incident, which deeply upsets us.”

RCMP said it’s believed someone or a group of people pushed the monument between 7:35 p.m. on Aug. 25 and 8:10 a.m. on Aug. 26.

In an update on Sept. 1, Sackville RCMP said they were looking for information on a white 2019-2020 Dodge Ram as part of the investigation.

On Tuesday, the village said the statue has been restored, with the help of J.L. Breau Crane Rentals Ltd, BSM Services (1998) Ltd, and Maritime Hydraulics.

“Père Lefebvre is back! Just in time for the start of the school year,” the village posted on Facebook.

“We thank all those who took care of the restoration of the statue of this great believer of higher education in Acadie.”

The statue of Lefebvre was erected in 1914. According to the village, Lefebvre was a key figure in French-language education in Acadie and the founder of the Collège Saint-Joseph.

The RCMP investigation into the incident is ongoing.

stories.title: Quebec party leaders prepare for debates as campaign intensifies
stories.summary: The leaders of Quebec's five main political parties are preparing for debates that could shape the outcome of the October election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebecers can expect to see political parties starting to ramp up their activity in the provincial election campaign, according to a pollster.

There is less than one month to go before Quebec voters head to the polls on Oct. 5, to elect the next government.

Philip Fournier, who runs poll aggregator 338Canada, said fall election campaigns typically intensify after Labour Day as more citizens start tuning in.

“Generally, things really start to pick up,” he said in a recent interview. “It’s like the long weekend before the storm.”

With children going back to school, parents settling back into their routines, and a series of debates on the horizon, Fournier says the campaign is entering a critical period.

“It’s volatile,” he said. “All it would take is one slip-up for things to turn around … it could be much more damaging than making a gaffe in August when people are on vacation.”

Charles Milliard, the leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, says he is counting on the upcoming debates to boost his profile and popularity.

“There won’t be a middleman,” said Milliard at a press briefing in Sherbooke, Que., Tuesday morning. “There will be five people aspiring to lead Quebec who will engage in a debate of ideas — not a debate of spin, not a debate of polls, but a debate of ideas on the future of Quebec.”

According to Fournier, the five leaders will have to fight for the attention of voters who largely remain undecided.

Fournier said the Liberal leader will need to shift gears, as his party has consistently been lagging behind the Parti Québécois and the Coalition Avenir Québec in the polls.

Milliard acknowledged that he is “the least well-known leader” running in the election. He also claimed his opponents are “exploiting” the trade war with the United States for political gain.

Tariffs were the topic of the day on the campaign trail on Tuesday, after the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec government adopted an order-in-council on Monday requiring public contracts to be awarded to Quebec and Canadian companies.

Leader Christine Fréchette has been accused by her rivals of trying to capitalize on the trade war by stoking voters’ anxiety to gain their support, which she denies.

The five party leaders will give interviews and discuss their platforms on Radio-Canada’s airwaves on Wednesday evening.

The leaders are also scheduled to participate in their first debate, broadcast on TVA, ON Sept. 15. The following day, the leaders will face off in a second debate on Noovo. The final Radio-Canada debate will be held on Sept. 23.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.
paragraphs: Quebecers can expect to see political parties starting to ramp up their activity in the provincial election campaign, according to a pollster.
There is less than one month to go before Quebec voters head to the polls on Oct. 5, to elect the next government.
Philip Fournier, who runs poll aggregator 338Canada, said fall election campaigns typically intensify after Labour Day as more citizens start tuning in.
“Generally, things really start to pick up,” he said in a recent interview. “It’s like the long weekend before the storm.”
With children going back to school, parents settling back into their routines, and a series of debates on the horizon, Fournier says the campaign is entering a critical period.
“It’s volatile,” he said. “All it would take is one slip-up for things to turn around … it could be much more damaging than making a gaffe in August when people are on vacation.”
Charles Milliard, the leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, says he is counting on the upcoming debates to boost his profile and popularity.

“There won’t be a middleman,” said Milliard at a press briefing in Sherbooke, Que., Tuesday morning. “There will be five people aspiring to lead Quebec who will engage in a debate of ideas — not a debate of spin, not a debate of polls, but a debate of ideas on the future of Quebec.”
According to Fournier, the five leaders will have to fight for the attention of voters who largely remain undecided.
Fournier said the Liberal leader will need to shift gears, as his party has consistently been lagging behind the Parti Québécois and the Coalition Avenir Québec in the polls.
Milliard acknowledged that he is “the least well-known leader” running in the election. He also claimed his opponents are “exploiting” the trade war with the United States for political gain.

Tariffs were the topic of the day on the campaign trail on Tuesday, after the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec government adopted an order-in-council on Monday requiring public contracts to be awarded to Quebec and Canadian companies.
Leader Christine Fréchette has been accused by her rivals of trying to capitalize on the trade war by stoking voters’ anxiety to gain their support, which she denies.
The five party leaders will give interviews and discuss their platforms on Radio-Canada’s airwaves on Wednesday evening.

The leaders are also scheduled to participate in their first debate, broadcast on TVA, ON Sept. 15. The following day, the leaders will face off in a second debate on Noovo. The final Radio-Canada debate will be held on Sept. 23.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.
