stories.title: Some Cape Breton residents no longer stranded as flooding recovery continues
stories.summary: More than 200 millimetres of rain fell in less than two days across Cape Breton island, causing roads to be damaged or washed away and stranding some residents.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Some residents stranded due to washouts in one of Cape Breton’s counties May now travel, but people are still asked to take caution as recovery from this weekend’s severe flooding continues.

Trevor Boudreau, the MLA for Richmond, said on Facebook Tuesday that “significant headway” had been made on West Bay Road between St. George’s Channel and Roberta, N.S.

“All residents that have been stranded can now pass with caution in and out of the impacted area from St. George’s Channel side only through to as far as the major washout on the Roberta side,” Boudreau wrote. “There is still a major washout on the side coming from St. Peter’s and that fix will take some time.”

Nova Scotia’s Department of Public Works said in a post on X that they’ve reopened dozens of roads on the island, but more work is underway.

Public Works Minister Fred Tilley said hundreds of provincial employees and local contractors are working to restore the entirety of the island’s road network within the coming days.

“We are hoping to get all those folks that May be stranded access to the road network very soon,” Tilley said in an interview.

As that work continues, several schools in parts of Cape Breton are also closed on Tuesday.

Cape Breton-Victoria Regional Centre for Education said on Monday night that all schools in Victoria County would be closed Tuesday due to the ongoing local state of emergency.

The Strait Regional Centre for Education said schools in Richmond and Inverness counties would also be closed Tuesday due to local states of emergency in those counties. The centre also said classes at Tamarac Education Centre and Saerc were cancelled.

Nova Scotia Community College says its Strait Area Campus and Wagmatcook Learning Centre are also closed, though online classes and sessions will still continue as scheduled.

Parts of the island saw heavy rain this weekend after a slow-moving storm dumped more than 200 millimetres over less than two days. Areas of the northern mainland also received heavy rains.

The flooding has also been linked with one death after a 46-year-old woman from Richmond County was found dead on Saturday, several hours after her abandoned vehicle was discovered near a flooded bridge.

RCMP said the death was not believed to be suspicious. Premier Tim Houston on Sunday said the province was mourning the woman’s death following the flooding.

Lois Landry, warden of the hard-hit Richmond County, said a Zodiac rescue boat operated by a local fire department and a provincial helicopter were used to carry out daily wellness checks for any residents completely cut off by flooding.

At the peak of the flooding, according to a spokesperson for the province’s Department of Public Works, there were more than 120 closed or damaged roads on the island. Another 200 culverts were also washed away from driveways and major routes.

Twenty-five roads remained closed as of Tuesday afternoon, according to Public Works spokesperson Gary Andrea.

He said two damaged bridges will also need replacement, but further inspections are necessary to determine the scope of the work . A cost estimate is not yet known.

Officials say two damaged bridges will also need replacement.

More rain fell on the region on Monday, though Environment Canada reports amounts ranging from two to 20 mm, with the most amount in Cape Breton being seen in Ingonish Beach of about 20 mm reported.

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ikea Canada announces opening date for London location
stories.summary: The store, located at 1105 Wellington Rd., will span approximately 43,000 square feet, making it about one-fifth the size of the company’s Burlington, Ont., store.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Ikea Canada has announced the opening date of its first compact store format in the country at White Oaks Mall in London.

Opening Sept. 29, the new location is designed to offer customers a smaller-format shopping experience focused on everyday home furnishings and seasonal products while maintaining access to Ikea’s full product assortment through delivery and pickup options.

The store, located at 1105 Wellington Rd., will span approximately 43,000 square feet, making it about one-fifth the size of the company’s Burlington, Ont., store.

Ikea Canada CEO and Chief Sustainability Officer Selwyn Crittendon, said the new concept is intended to make the retailer’s products more accessible to customers in London and surrounding communities.

“We are excited to launch this new concept store as the first of its kind in Canada, making our affordable, functional and inspiring home furnishing solutions more accessible to those in London, Ontario and surrounding areas,” Crittendon said in a statement.

The store will carry more than 2,500 products, including everyday essentials and seasonal items. About 400 furniture products will be available for immediate purchase and pickup from a self-serve warehouse area.

Customers will also be able to order from Ikea’s full product lineup and choose from a range of delivery and collection options.

The company said its existing London-area locations will continue to operate. That includes the Ikea Plan and Order Point on Wonderland Road South, which offers consultations for projects such as kitchens and other complex home furnishing purchases, and the company’s pickup location on Wilton Grove Road.

By Devin Stevens The Canadian Press

The opposition Liberals and NDP were planning to table more than 2,000 new signatures as politicians returned to the legislature.

This is on top of more than 8,000 signatures already on record.

Premier Tim Houston’s government repealed the decades long ban in March 2025, but no new mining operation has started up in the meantime.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

Houston has said the element is mined safely in other places and that the province needs to develop its natural resources to improve its economy.

Petition organizers say the new signatures were collected by community members, grassroots organizations and local businesses.

Dr. Catherine Cervin, with the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment, said in a statement that uranium mining can release radioactive material into the water and air.

“The ban protected us because mining activities were required to cease if uranium was discovered at greater than 100 parts per million. We no longer have that protection,” Cervin said in a statement.

stories.title: University of Toronto staff agree to tentative deal after strike vote
stories.summary: Staff represented by the United Steelworkers had voted 96 per cent in favour of strike action as students returned to class and workers complained about growing demands on them.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Thousands of administrative and technical staff at the University of Toronto look set to avoid industrial action days after they voted to strike, with a tentative agreement now signed.

Staff represented by the United Steelworkers Local 1998 had voted 96 per cent in favour of strike action as students returned to class and workers complained about growing demands on them.

“UofT says it will find $20 million in savings next year by not replacing employees who leave the university,” said John Ankenman, president of Local 1998, after the strike vote.

“That will worsen the heavy workload burden that many of our members already face. The university has not responded in a significant way to the union’s contract proposals that would lead to increased job security, which is our members’ number one non-monetary priority.”

But by the start of the week, a tentative agreement was in place, pending approval from the 6,100 workers who were ready to strike.

A spokesperson for the United Steelworkers Local 1998 confirmed the deal to Global News, but said dates were yet to be set for it to be ratified.

The University of Toronto also confirmed the deal.

“I would like to thank both bargaining teams for their professionalism and hard work throughout negotiations,” Kenneth Corts, VP people, finance and digital services, said in a statement.

stories.title: A U.S. ban on Bombardier sales could ‘massively’ disrupt American aerospace: analyst
stories.summary: Montreal — Analysts say a threatened U.S. ban on Bombardier's business jet sales would damage the American aerospace industry as well as Canada's.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — A threatened U.S. ban on Bombardier Inc.’s business jet sales would damage the American aerospace industry as well as Canada’s, analysts say.

As part of a spate of social media posts deriding Canada on Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he would bar the Montreal-based plane maker’s business south of the border unless it moved its operations stateside.

“NO More Selling Bombardier IN THE United States!” he said. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.'”

Bombardier does the final assembly of its Challenger and Global business jets in Canada, while more than half of its revenue stems from American customers.

However, it also runs multiple plants in the United States and employs about 3,500 workers in Kansas, Texas, California and other states, with its defence division headquartered in Wichita, Kan., the company and analysts pointed out.

Bombardier said its pays more than US$2.5 billion to its 2,800 American suppliers across 47 states each year, indirectly supporting tens of thousands of jobs.

“The American aerospace industry is a clear winner on trade and exports,” Bombardier stated, adopting the language of the president and his fixation on triumph and trade surpluses.

America enjoys a US$109-billion aerospace and defence trade surplus, according to the U.S. Aerospace Industries Association.

Ross Aimer, CEO of California-based Aero Consulting Experts, highlighted the deeply entwined nature of aerospace manufacturing across the continent and beyond.

“A lot of these parts are made in the U.S. by U.S. workers. There’s really not an exclusively produced commercial jet or aircraft or even automobile these days,” he said in a phone interview.

Most Bombardier planes feature at least 40 per cent U.S. content, analysts say. Over half of the value of the ultra-long-range Global 7500 luxury jet derives from American parts.

The manufacturer constructs wings for the new Global 8000 on a production line south of Dallas. Its largest parts distribution hub sits a few blocks from Chicago’s O’Hare airport. Its plant in Los Angeles churns out components for its larger luxury planes.

Blocking a major manufacturer from the market would “undoubtedly” cause revenue and job losses at American parts producers, said National Bank analyst Cameron Doerksen.

“One would hope that large U.S. aerospace suppliers would lobby on behalf of one of their most important customers — both GE Aerospace and Honeywell Aerospace supply engines to Bombardier,” he said in a note to investors.

“Moving production to the U.S. would not be a practical option.”

Bombardier’s U.S. customer base also means a ban on sales would be “massively disruptive” to the many American jet fleet operators awaiting Bombardier deliveries, he said.

Trump’s threat came less than 11 hours before Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs on American goods took effect just after midnight on Tuesday, a response to the 50 per cent duties Washington imposed on Canada last month.

In retort, Trump signed several executive orders Tuesday evening completely banning the import of most Canadian alcoholic drinks, some dairy products and motorcycles starting Sept. 29. In a trade war ramp-up, he also slapped a 50 per cent levy on more items, ranging from mattresses to motorboats.

His Truth Social post Monday marked the second time this year Bombardier has come into the president’s crosshairs.

In January, Trump singled out Bombardier in a threat to ground all Canadian-made aircraft and slap them with a 50 per cent tariff unless Ottawa approved Gulfstream business jets — assembled in Savannah, Ga. — marking an earlier escalation of trade tensions between the two countries.

Whether Trump will follow through on his latest menacing statements remains up in the air, as does its legal legitimacy.

“It is not clear under what legal authority the U.S. could ban a single importer at a whim,” Doerksen said.

The White House had yet to issue an official policy change on business jet sales as of Tuesday afternoon.

The market also remains “structurally undersupplied,” with backlogs exceeding two years as demand for private planes soars, said Desjardins analyst Benoit Poirier.

Workers and politicians on both sides of the border spoke out strongly against the potential ban.

The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers said in a release it “firmly opposes” any U.S. prohibition on Bombardier sales, arguing it would undermine the aerospace industry and job growth in both countries.

Quebec incumbent premier Christine Fréchette said the province has to be prepared.

“Sometimes it’s the prelude to action. Sometimes it’s a threat that goes nowhere,” she said at a public gathering near Quebec City amid a provincial election campaign. The governing CAQ leader added: “The threat is real.”

Fréchette said she had spoken with Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and that the provincial government would be ready to support the company and its workers if necessary. Asked whether that could include financial assistance, she said that “nothing is off the table for the moment.”

Even some of the president’s fellow Republicans seemed to push back against his threat, albeit cautiously.

In Kansas, a state where Trump won by about 16 percentage points in 2024, U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran noted in a social media post that Bombardier supports a local workforce of more than 1,000 employees.

“I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the president is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” he wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:BBD.B)

— With files from Charlotte Glorieux

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

stories.title: 350 Dynacare workers strike in Manitoba due to ‘huge’ wage gap: union president
stories.summary: 350 Dynacare technologists and technicians are officially striking after talks between the company and the union representing those workers fell apart, the Mahcp president said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Hundreds of Dynacare workers are officially striking in Manitoba, according to their union president.

The strike, which saw 350 Dynacare technologists and technicians walk off the job at 6 a.m. Tuesday, began after negotiations stalled between the company and the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals (Mahcp), according to its union president, Jason Linklater.

Workers hit the picket lines at 8 a.m. Tuesday.

The union and company remain “significantly” far apart in contract talks, Linklater told 680 Cjob.

“The pressure that should have been there, at the bargaining table, wasn’t there. And it is because Dynacare fully expected the government to step in, like they did,” Linklater said, adding that “quite, frankly, Dynacare has done nothing to avoid this strike.”

At a Winnipeg picket line outside Dynacare’s Garden City clinic, passing cars honked to support striking workers – who rang bells, cheered and held signs. Speaking from the strike site, Linklater told reporters the Mahcp last spoke with Dynacare on Friday.

“They came to the table with additional money that was tantamount to telling us to ‘get lost.’ It was extremely offensive what they came (with). It was mocking, is what it was,” he said.

“This is very indicative of the state of health care right now. If people don’t start getting paid what they’re worth, they will simply leave.”

Bozena Turczynowicz retired earlier this year after working at Dynacare for 26 years. She said her former co-workers are striking for a “just cause.”

“Dynacare claims they don’t have the money to pay fair wages and hire full-time employees, which makes it so hard on the people who work right now because they’re permanently short staffed,” she told Global News.

Dynacare said it is aware of the Mahcp strike that began Tuesday morning.

“We remain hopeful that a resolution can be reached and continue to engage in efforts to find a path forward,” an email statement from a Dynacare spokesperson said, adding that the company “remains committed to reaching a fair and sustainable agreement.”

Its current wage offer remains on the table as the parties continue negotiations, according to the spokesperson. Dynacare also urged the union to accept interest arbitration.

“Every path to a resolution remains available, and we are committed to reaching an outcome that is fair for our employees and for the patients who depend on us,” they continued.

The company is awaiting the decision of a Manitoba Labour Board hearing held Tuesday about potentially making Dynacare employees essential service workers. After receiving that decision, Dynacare will “communicate the impacts to our employees, healthcare partners and customers.”

If deemed essential, the steps for workers to strike become more complex and, according to the Machp, current efforts could be derailed.

The lawyer representing the province before the labour board said that this strike May threaten the health of Manitobans who rely on Dynacare for blood sampling and lab testing.

Global News has reached out to the Manitoba government for comment.

Patients in need of laboratory services should contact their health care provider to discuss available options, the spokesperson noted. In response to the labour disruption, Shared Health is extending the hours at some of its labs to close at 8 p.m., it said in a news release.

stories.title: Melissa Auf der Maur excavates the past
stories.summary: In her new photo exhibition at the AGO, the Canadian musician captures a nostalgia for the style and energy of 1990s music culture
stories.author: Haley Steinberg, Photography by Carlyle Routh
stories.content:
Melissa Auf der Maur is, by her own admission, a little witchy. She has red hair. She believes in magic. As a teenager, she dreamed of mystical pyramids and three-dimensional sound. She received messages in her sleep, telling her to play music. In 1994, when she was 19, she met Smashing Pumpkins frontman Billy Corgan, who told her that she might be in his band one day; five years later, she was. She was hand-picked out of rock music obscurity by walking tornado Courtney Love to join Love’s band, Hole. She had visions of a winged demon that threatened to consume her if she didn’t redeem her creative freedom. She foresaw the advancing forces of corporatization and digitization on the alternative music scene, and she walked away.

She had the prescience to document all of this, in thousands upon thousands of photographs. These images, along with videos, tour ephemera and newly recorded music, are now on exhibition for the first time at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto. The show, My ’90s Rock Photographs, features a selection of Auf der Maur’s more than 15,000 pictures from the last analog decade. They span her five years as a bassist with Hole and one year with the Smashing Pumpkins.

The show is but one piece of a larger excavation project: Auf der Maur’s memoir, Even the Good Girls Will Cry, was released in March (on St. Patrick’s Day, her birthday); a photo book, published by DelMonico Books and the AGO, is out this month; and a feature documentary about Auf der Maur and her photo archive by Banger Films, The National Film Board and the CBC is in production.

“I tried to make it happen here,” Auf der Maur said when I met her at her apartment in Montreal in early June (she lives full-time in Hudson, New York, with her daughter and husband, filmmaker Tony Stone). She would have preferred to hand her archive over to a hometown institution, but it didn’t work out that way. The comment might sound like a snub to Toronto, but spending even a few minutes with Auf der Maur reveals a deep, almost cosmic, affinity for Montreal. “The city, she raised me,” is a recurring motif in her memoir and photo book.

Auf der Maur did not want to be a rock star. Despite her rabid music fandom (one hot summer in 1991, she went to a show practically every single night), she had been devoted to photography since age 13 and later studied self-portraiture at Concordia University. “I had always wanted and planned on being a photographer, but this music thing kept grabbing me,” Auf der Maur said. She was wary of big record labels and of America. “My mother left the U.S. in the ’60s, so I was raised being told the American people have the bum end of the stick.” When Love called her up to ask her to join Hole, at Corgan’s recommendation, Auf der Maur politely declined. It was August of 1994. “Will you just get on a plane,” Love said, “and tell me to my face that you don’t want to be in my band?” She got on the plane.

Auf der Maur joined Hole in the wake of death, destruction, demons and drugs. Kurt Cobain, Courtney Love’s husband and Nirvana’s enigmatic frontman, died by suicide the same week that Hole’s acclaimed album Live Through This was released. The group’s previous bassist, Kristen Pfaff, died of a heroin overdose months later. Nirvana fans and the media blamed Love for Cobain’s death, attacking her with the kind of misogynistic ruthlessness popular culture is only now reckoning with. Love was left with the couple’s toddler, Frances Bean, an eviscerated spirit, a broken band. In some of the most striking images in the book, a fresh-faced Auf der Maur documents her stay in Love’s Seattle guest room overlooking the garage, still encased in security tape, where Cobain took his life with a shotgun.

Ten days later, she’s playing in front of thousands of fans at the Reading Festival in the U.K., one of the oldest and largest music events in the world. It was Auf der Maur’s first show with Hole, her first outside of the tiny Montreal clubs she’d played with her hometown band, Tinker, where, as she writes in the memoir, she recognized every face in the crowd.

What follows are years of world tours, criss-crossing the globe performing in places as far as Tuktoyaktuk, Northwest Territories, and Fremantle, Australia.

Burning up road in tour buses, killing hours backstage and watching endless hotel room TV was often exhausting and lonely, but it could also be joyful and exhilarating. Auf der Maur, never without her camera, captured what it looked like, felt like: A frozen pink martini on a laminate table in Somewhere, USA, Love eating strawberry cake backstage at Lollapalooza 1995, a half-eaten room service tray in an anonymous hotel suite. There’s a sense in the images of happenstance, of accident. But this is a kind of deception, a photographic sleight of hand.

“It’s clear that the photographs, though they have this casual feeling about them, are very much not casual products,” says Sophie Hackett, the Ago’s curator of photography who co-curated the exhibition. “They are the products of someone who went to art school, who thought about being a visual artist, who developed her passion for the visual arts at the same time as she’s developing her passion for music.”

It was such a wonderful but overwhelmingly saturated decade of passion and pain, and obviously music, but addiction and death – a zeitgeist moment in our generation and the end of a millennium. — Melissa Auf der Maur

Auf der Maur’s self-portraits – particularly self-portraits in mirrors – are a throughline. They serve as both daily check-ins amid the chaos and instability of touring as well as opportunities to experiment with form. In one of the artist’s favourite images, Self-Portrait in House of Mirrors, USA, 1995 , Auf der Maur, wild red hair falling against her yellow T-shirt, is eerily spliced into multiples by intersecting mirrors. In another conceptual series, she captures herself in various stages of crawling across the turquoise carpet of a Copenhagen hotel room.

“It harkens back to an artist that was very formative for her, Francesca Woodman, who was an American woman working in the ’70s,” Hackett says. “I feel like she’s kind of crawling out of her skin in this moment, trying to crawl out of the situation, and also animate a pretty banal hotel room.”

Jim Shedden, the Ago’s curator of special projects and co-curator of the show, explains that Auf der Maur’s self-portraits are presented in the exhibition as a counterpoint to her series of audience images. “For her, that’s a kind of yin and yang,” he says. “They were both generative and regenerative for her. She had a really great relationship when she was onstage playing for the audience, but she also needed to be by herself and creating.”

As a grown woman, a mother to a teenage daughter, what does Auf der Maur see in these photographs? For years, that period of her life was so overwhelming that she couldn’t go near it. Now, diving back in, she wanted to “understand what I had left behind and what I had gone running from, because, in many ways, I did go running from the ’90s,” she said. “It was such a wonderful but overwhelmingly saturated decade of passion and pain, and obviously music, but addiction and death – a zeitgeist moment in our generation and the end of a millennium.”

Then and now, she understood she was living through a historic but fleeting moment, and that if she didn’t record it all, it would slip away into oblivion. This, Auf der Maur was saying with her camera, is what it was like to be a young woman in rock music at a time when the genre was dominated by the men of Nine Inch Nails, Nirvana and Soundgarden. This is being an artist. This is being alive.

“I’m utilizing my experience in that decade as an offering to anybody that cares as a study, an archaeological dig,” Auf der Maur said. She wants to understand how we got from that place of analog and DIY to this one, where a small number of tech oligarchs own all our time and creativity. “This is my question,” she said. “I owe it to the future. I owe it to my daughter.”

content_blocks.html: Melissa Auf der Maur is, by her own admission, a little witchy. She has red hair. She believes in magic. As a teenager, she dreamed of mystical pyramids and three-dimensional sound. She received messages in her sleep, telling her to play music. In 1994, when she was 19, she met Smashing Pumpkins frontman Billy Corgan, who told her that she might be in his band one day; five years later, she was. She was hand-picked out of rock music obscurity by walking tornado Courtney Love to join Love’s band, Hole. She had visions of a winged demon that threatened to consume her if she didn’t redeem her creative freedom. She foresaw the advancing forces of corporatization and digitization on the alternative music scene, and she walked away.

content_blocks.text: She had the prescience to document all of this, in thousands upon thousands of photographs. These images, along with videos, tour ephemera and newly recorded music, are now on exhibition for the first time at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto. The show, My ’90s Rock Photographs, features a selection of Auf der Maur’s more than 15,000 pictures from the last analog decade. They span her five years as a bassist with Hole and one year with the Smashing Pumpkins.

content_blocks.text: The show is but one piece of a larger excavation project: Auf der Maur’s memoir, Even the Good Girls Will Cry, was released in March (on St. Patrick’s Day, her birthday); a photo book, published by DelMonico Books and the AGO, is out this month; and a feature documentary about Auf der Maur and her photo archive by Banger Films, The National Film Board and the CBC is in production.

content_blocks.text: “I tried to make it happen here,” Auf der Maur said when I met her at her apartment in Montreal in early June (she lives full-time in Hudson, New York, with her daughter and husband, filmmaker Tony Stone). She would have preferred to hand her archive over to a hometown institution, but it didn’t work out that way. The comment might sound like a snub to Toronto, but spending even a few minutes with Auf der Maur reveals a deep, almost cosmic, affinity for Montreal. “The city, she raised me,” is a recurring motif in her memoir and photo book.

content_blocks.text: Auf der Maur did not want to be a rock star. Despite her rabid music fandom (one hot summer in 1991, she went to a show practically every single night), she had been devoted to photography since age 13 and later studied self-portraiture at Concordia University. “I had always wanted and planned on being a photographer, but this music thing kept grabbing me,” Auf der Maur said. She was wary of big record labels and of America. “My mother left the U.S. in the ’60s, so I was raised being told the American people have the bum end of the stick.” When Love called her up to ask her to join Hole, at Corgan’s recommendation, Auf der Maur politely declined. It was August of 1994. “Will you just get on a plane,” Love said, “and tell me to my face that you don’t want to be in my band?” She got on the plane.

content_blocks.text: Auf der Maur joined Hole in the wake of death, destruction, demons and drugs. Kurt Cobain, Courtney Love’s husband and Nirvana’s enigmatic frontman, died by suicide the same week that Hole’s acclaimed album Live Through This was released. The group’s previous bassist, Kristen Pfaff, died of a heroin overdose months later. Nirvana fans and the media blamed Love for Cobain’s death, attacking her with the kind of misogynistic ruthlessness popular culture is only now reckoning with. Love was left with the couple’s toddler, Frances Bean, an eviscerated spirit, a broken band. In some of the most striking images in the book, a fresh-faced Auf der Maur documents her stay in Love’s Seattle guest room overlooking the garage, still encased in security tape, where Cobain took his life with a shotgun.

content_blocks.text: Burning up road in tour buses, killing hours backstage and watching endless hotel room TV was often exhausting and lonely, but it could also be joyful and exhilarating. Auf der Maur, never without her camera, captured what it looked like, felt like: A frozen pink martini on a laminate table in Somewhere, USA, Love eating strawberry cake backstage at Lollapalooza 1995, a half-eaten room service tray in an anonymous hotel suite. There’s a sense in the images of happenstance, of accident. But this is a kind of deception, a photographic sleight of hand.

content_blocks.text: Auf der Maur’s self-portraits – particularly self-portraits in mirrors – are a throughline. They serve as both daily check-ins amid the chaos and instability of touring as well as opportunities to experiment with form. In one of the artist’s favourite images, Self-Portrait in House of Mirrors, USA, 1995 , Auf der Maur, wild red hair falling against her yellow T-shirt, is eerily spliced into multiples by intersecting mirrors. In another conceptual series, she captures herself in various stages of crawling across the turquoise carpet of a Copenhagen hotel room.

content_blocks.text: As a grown woman, a mother to a teenage daughter, what does Auf der Maur see in these photographs? For years, that period of her life was so overwhelming that she couldn’t go near it. Now, diving back in, she wanted to “understand what I had left behind and what I had gone running from, because, in many ways, I did go running from the ’90s,” she said. “It was such a wonderful but overwhelmingly saturated decade of passion and pain, and obviously music, but addiction and death – a zeitgeist moment in our generation and the end of a millennium.”

content_blocks.text: Then and now, she understood she was living through a historic but fleeting moment, and that if she didn’t record it all, it would slip away into oblivion. This, Auf der Maur was saying with her camera, is what it was like to be a young woman in rock music at a time when the genre was dominated by the men of Nine Inch Nails, Nirvana and Soundgarden. This is being an artist. This is being alive.

Quebec - The Quebec government has announced a series of measures to promote buying locally in response to the escalating trade war between Canada and the United States.

Premier Christine Fréchette says the measures will inject about $1.5 billion into the Quebec economy in the next four months.

Fréchette’s cabinet met as she took a break from the provincial election campaign to return to her role as premier and address the latest in the trade war.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs kicked in on Monday after the breakdown of talks with the United States.

stories.title: Only known woolly dog pelt returns to B.C. after more than 160 years
stories.summary: Vancouver - The only known pelt of an extinct woolly dog, a species raised for its thick coat by Coast Salish and Makah peoples, has returned to British Columbia for the first time.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - When Coast Salish artist Atheana Picha ran a gloved hand through the thick white pelt of an extinct woolly dog that has returned to British Columbia for the first time in more than 160 years, her thoughts turned to how her ancestors might have used the fur.

Perhaps they would have made a blanket or maybe a headband.

“And I thought, oh, it’s so amazing because this delicate material could make such beautiful blankets with the right hands,” said Picha. “As a weaver, that really resonated with me.”

The pelt belonged to Mutton, a canine companion of American naturalist George Gibbs, and had been in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., since Mutton died in 1859.

The only known pelt of an extinct woolly dog has returned to British Columbia for the first time. Woolly dogs were raised for their thick coat for thousands of years by Coast Salish and Makha peoples. Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and contemporary Indigenous art at the museum, says the pelt speaks to the species' extinction, one of many profound impacts of settler colonialism. (Sept. 8, 2026)

It’s now on display at the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver until next summer.

Known for their cloud-like coats, woolly dogs were bred by Coast Salish peoples for thousands of years, and were shorn like sheep for ceremonial blankets and textiles.

Debra Sparrow, a Musqueam weaver and artist, said her grandfather told her every village used to have them. The dogs were treated as though they were as valuable as gold because of their hair, which was spun after being mixed with mountain goat wool, she said in a statement.

It’s unclear how Gibbs obtained Mutton, but Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and Contemporary Indigenous Art at the museum, said Mutton is thought to have come from B.C.‘s Lower Mainland.

Gibbs had participated in the four-year-long northwest boundary survey expedition in late 1850s to map out the international land boundary between the American Pacific Northwest and B.C.

“We know that (Mutton) came from the Chilliwack area, and we know that is part of Sto:Lo First Nation Chilliwack peoples’ territories, and so it’s close to home,” said Wilson, who is a member of the Musqueam First Nation.

Weavers and members of local Coast Salish communities had a chance to spend time with Mutton’s pelt on Friday before the display was opened to the public.

Wilson said seeing the pelt for the first time left him emotional, especially when he noticed Mutton’s little paws and nose.

“We had a lot of community members from different nations that were here this morning to visit with this pelt, and you can feel the intensity in the room and the emotion of being able to reconnect with this species that was so important to our ancestors,” Wilson said. “People were sharing stories and sharing teachings.”

Wilson said early historical accounts from explorers and fur traders described woolly dogs being transported in canoes, sometimes 10 at a time.

“Just the fact of taking these dogs with them where they went, I think underscores their importance,” said Wilson.

Wilson said Mutton’s pelt reflects a species’ extinction, one of many profound impacts of settler colonialism.

“It also speaks to the lives of our ancestors, their relationship with the more-than-human world, and their teachings and knowledge that continue to be passed forward,” he said.

A number of factors contributed to the decline and eventual extinction of woolly dogs, Wilson said, including the dispossession of land from Indigenous Peoples and the potlatch ban, implemented by the Canadian government from 1885 to 1951, to force cultural assimilation. It had a major effect on the transmission of cultural practices and knowledge, said Wilson.

But he said even though woolly dogs no longer exist, the Indigenous cultures and values can still be carried on.

A statement from the University of B.C. said interest in woolly dogs is booming as Salish weaving experiences a resurgence, prompting researchers to study the textiles to understand the dogs’ role in Salish and Makah weaving traditions.

Picha said it was a beautiful experience to touch Mutton’s fur.

“Very honestly, the first thing I thought was, ‘Oh, it’s bigger than I imagined.’ But then I think about when it’s wrapped around the body of a dog, it would be a cute little thing,” said Picha.

She said the fur felt a little brittle, given its age, but even through a glove she could feel it was soft, “a little bit squishy … It was nice.”

Picha said she had heard stories from her parents and grandparents about the important role in their community played by woolly dogs, which were tended “very carefully.”

“We nourished them with a very specific diet (consisting of salmon and elk) so that their hair would get long and smooth and soft. And I think about how much care and love was put into these dogs, but how much they also gave to us,” she said.

paragraphs: Vancouver - When Coast Salish artist Atheana Picha ran a gloved hand through the thick white pelt of an extinct woolly dog that has returned to British Columbia for the first time in more than 160 years, her thoughts turned to how her ancestors might have used the fur.
Perhaps they would have made a blanket or maybe a headband.
“And I thought, oh, it’s so amazing because this delicate material could make such beautiful blankets with the right hands,” said Picha. “As a weaver, that really resonated with me.”
The pelt belonged to Mutton, a canine companion of American naturalist George Gibbs, and had been in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., since Mutton died in 1859.

The only known pelt of an extinct woolly dog has returned to British Columbia for the first time. Woolly dogs were raised for their thick coat for thousands of years by Coast Salish and Makha peoples. Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and contemporary Indigenous art at the museum, says the pelt speaks to the species' extinction, one of many profound impacts of settler colonialism. (Sept. 8, 2026)
It’s now on display at the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver until next summer.
Known for their cloud-like coats, woolly dogs were bred by Coast Salish peoples for thousands of years, and were shorn like sheep for ceremonial blankets and textiles.

Debra Sparrow, a Musqueam weaver and artist, said her grandfather told her every village used to have them. The dogs were treated as though they were as valuable as gold because of their hair, which was spun after being mixed with mountain goat wool, she said in a statement.
It’s unclear how Gibbs obtained Mutton, but Jordan Wilson, curator of Pacific Northwest and Contemporary Indigenous Art at the museum, said Mutton is thought to have come from B.C.‘s Lower Mainland.
Gibbs had participated in the four-year-long northwest boundary survey expedition in late 1850s to map out the international land boundary between the American Pacific Northwest and B.C.

“We know that (Mutton) came from the Chilliwack area, and we know that is part of Sto:Lo First Nation Chilliwack peoples’ territories, and so it’s close to home,” said Wilson, who is a member of the Musqueam First Nation.
Weavers and members of local Coast Salish communities had a chance to spend time with Mutton’s pelt on Friday before the display was opened to the public.
Wilson said seeing the pelt for the first time left him emotional, especially when he noticed Mutton’s little paws and nose.

“We had a lot of community members from different nations that were here this morning to visit with this pelt, and you can feel the intensity in the room and the emotion of being able to reconnect with this species that was so important to our ancestors,” Wilson said. “People were sharing stories and sharing teachings.”
Wilson said early historical accounts from explorers and fur traders described woolly dogs being transported in canoes, sometimes 10 at a time.
“Just the fact of taking these dogs with them where they went, I think underscores their importance,” said Wilson.
Wilson said Mutton’s pelt reflects a species’ extinction, one of many profound impacts of settler colonialism.
“It also speaks to the lives of our ancestors, their relationship with the more-than-human world, and their teachings and knowledge that continue to be passed forward,” he said.

A number of factors contributed to the decline and eventual extinction of woolly dogs, Wilson said, including the dispossession of land from Indigenous Peoples and the potlatch ban, implemented by the Canadian government from 1885 to 1951, to force cultural assimilation. It had a major effect on the transmission of cultural practices and knowledge, said Wilson.
But he said even though woolly dogs no longer exist, the Indigenous cultures and values can still be carried on.

A statement from the University of B.C. said interest in woolly dogs is booming as Salish weaving experiences a resurgence, prompting researchers to study the textiles to understand the dogs’ role in Salish and Makah weaving traditions.

“Very honestly, the first thing I thought was, ‘Oh, it’s bigger than I imagined.’ But then I think about when it’s wrapped around the body of a dog, it would be a cute little thing,” said Picha.
She said the fur felt a little brittle, given its age, but even through a glove she could feel it was soft, “a little bit squishy … It was nice.”
Picha said she had heard stories from her parents and grandparents about the important role in their community played by woolly dogs, which were tended “very carefully.”

“We nourished them with a very specific diet (consisting of salmon and elk) so that their hair would get long and smooth and soft. And I think about how much care and love was put into these dogs, but how much they also gave to us,” she said.

stories.title: Stocks with ties to the Canada Investment Summit that are seeing insider buying
stories.summary: A select group of Canadian firms will have an opportunity to convince investors that diversifying into Canada will pay off
stories.author: Ted Dixon
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney will host the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15, an event built around the message that Canada has what the world wants.

The Globe and Mail reported on Sept. 2 that the summit is expected to draw about 250 global financial executives, whose companies collectively oversee nearly $120-trillion in assets. Many of these foreign investors are likely sitting on portfolios weighted heavily toward the United States.

A select group of Canadian firms will have an opportunity to convince these investors that diversifying into Canada will pay off as the world undergoes generational geopolitical changes.

On that front, let’s first dispense with some thinking that we come across all too often here at home that Canada offers subpar opportunity compared with the U.S. This is demonstrably false, as evidenced by the performance of the INK Canadian Insider Index, which includes the top 50 TSX stocks preferred by insiders.

In the five years ended June 30, 2026, the index, including dividends, is up 23.03 per cent on an annualized basis, versus 13.41 per cent for the S&P 500 (both figures in local currency). Much of that outperformance has come since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, a moment we view as the starting point of the geopolitical realignment now at the forefront of this summit.

One factor that could help convince foreign investors is a company’s level of insider shareholdings as a demonstration of commitment toward the firm’s prospects. Several of the companies that are expected to attend the summit rank high in our insider screens. Linamar Corp. LNR-T is one of them.

When reporting second-quarter results, Linamar acknowledged that there is uncertainty about tariffs and how they might affect its cost competitiveness and market access. Nevertheless, it reported record Q2 sales of $3.14-billion, up 18.8 per cent from $2.64-billion in the same period last year. Non-Gaap normalized net earnings were $183-million ($3.08 per diluted share), up from $168.4-million ($2.81 per diluted share) in Q2 2025.

Over the same time period, normalized operating earnings in its Mobility segment, which makes powertrain and driveline components for a wide range of vehicles, grew 28.6 per cent to a record $194.0-million, more than offsetting a 23.8-per-cent decline in the industrial-segment normalized operating earnings, which fell to $78.7-million.

Importantly, recent trade friction with the U.S. has not fazed Linamar chief executive officer Jim Jarrell, who exercised 100,000 in-the-money options on June 9 and has not subsequently reported selling. Chief technology officer Mark Stoddart sold 18,932 shares in the public market on Aug. 18; however, he continues to hold 509,987 Linamar shares.

As of Sept. 3, Linamar has above-median ownership by officers and directors compared with other large-cap consumer cyclicals stocks. It is in the top 10 per cent of our INK Edge rankings, which are based on insider activity, holdings, stock valuations and price momentum.

Beyond tariffs, the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have disrupted global energy markets, offering Canada an opportunity to increase its market share as nations look to make their supply chains more resilient.

Suncor Energy Inc. SU-T will be in the summit spotlight. Suncor’s operations span everything from Alberta oil sands to Petro-Canada gas pumps, a scale that generated more than $5.6-billion in cash flow, provided by operating activities in the second quarter of 2026.

Suncor shares have gained more than 50 per cent this year, so it is not surprising to see some insider profit-taking at the firm. Over the past six months, insiders have been net sellers of $3.3-million worth of shares, net of option-exercise costs. For a $110-billion company, these are relatively small sales.

Moreover, insider holdings have increased slightly over that period to 2,036,771 shares. The uptick was in part thanks to one director taking $34,245 of retainer fees in shares in lieu of cash. On balance, Suncor remains in the top 30 per cent of our INK Edge rankings.

The development of mineral products provides Canada with its strongest trade advantage, according to a recent Export Development Canada report. The Northwest Territories will be at the summit to show the world that Canada’s North has vast untapped mining potential.

Honey Badger Silver Inc. TUF-X is working to restart the PC Silver Mine, a high-grade silver, zinc and lead deposit in the Mackenzie Mountains that already has five kilometres of underground workings and a mill left over from previous operations. The company, one of a small number of mining projects sponsored by the Government of the Northwest Territories, expects an updated economic assessment this year as it works toward bringing the mine back into production.

The stock has come under pressure recently as some private-placement investors have been taking profits after a statutory four-month hold was lifted on securities issued in an $11.5-million April 15, 2026, financing. However, we are more concerned with what senior management is doing, and CEO Chad Williams has spent $268,344 buying shares in the public market over the past six months. The buying helps Honey Badger make it into the top 30 per cent of the INK Edge rankings.

Disclosure: I hold shares of Honey Badger Silver.

Ted Dixon is CEO of INK Research, which provides insider news and knowledge to investors.

stories.title: Carney says he's not 'escalating the conflict' as Canada hits U.S. with retaliatory tariffs
stories.summary: Tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent come into effect Tuesday on $28 billion worth of U.S. imports
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — On the same day Canadian tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. imports came into effect, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he doesn’t believe in escalating the trade conflict.

“That’s not constructive,” said Carney, during a video address released on Tuesday. “But our tariffs are necessary protect our workers, protect our companies, and our communities.”

Carney said his government can’t allow American goods into Canada tariff-free, while the U.S. charges Canadian companies to export.

Canada’s latest round of tariffs against the U.S. is in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per-cent tariff on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. Trump slapped Canada with the new tariffs after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down on Aug. 21.

Carney announced a pause in negotiations last month and said several last-minute conditions in the draft text of an agreement made a deal with the U.S. untenable.

“We worked in good faith to reach a fair deal, but since a fair deal wasn’t on the table, we made the right choice to walk away from a bad one,” Carney said Tuesday.

Since trade talks were paused, there has been no communication between negotiators on both sides. The U.S. administration has vowed to respond to Canada’s latest round of tariffs. Over the weekend, Trump took to TruthSocial where he attacked aircraft maker Bombardier and posted a photo of the North American continent covered in an American flag.

Trump also took issue with the exchange rate and the value of the Canadian dollar. He called the loonie’s “imbalance” with the U.S. dollar “unacceptable.”

Trump’s Bombardier threat is an 'own goal' for Canada-U.S. defence ties, analysts say

Why Quebec is lagging behind on removing interprovincial barriers for alcohol sales

Carney in his address warned that the trade conflict with the U.S. will come at a cost.

“There’s always a cost to action, but it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still,” he said. “This is about who we are as Canadians. It’s about our livelihoods and the country we leave to our kids.”

stories.title: Person recovered from water after nearly six-hour search in Sarnia
stories.summary: A person has been recovered from the water in Sarnia following an extensive search operation near The Cove involving multiple emergency services and community partners.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A person has been recovered from the water in Sarnia following an extensive search operation near The Cove involving multiple emergency services and community partners.

Emergency crews were called to reports of a possible drowning shortly after 3 p.m. Monday.

Sarnia Fire Rescue said it immediately deployed three marine units while additional firefighters responded by land. Witnesses at the scene also assisted in the initial search.

The operation continued for nearly six hours, with crews using specialized equipment aboard the department’s marine vessels, including sonar and 3D imaging technology.

The individual was located and recovered from the water after several hours of searching.

Authorities have not released the person’s identity.

In a statement, Sarnia Fire Rescue extended its condolences to the individual’s family and friends and thanked the agencies, organizations and members of the public who assisted in the search.

stories.title: Live updates: Carney warns of cost to Canada as retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods take effect
stories.summary: In the 15-minute video, the Prime Minister outlines why his government walked away from trade negotiations and its current economic plan
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
– Adrian Morrow

After U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to ban Canadian airplane maker Bombardier from selling in his country, Kansas Senator Jerry Moran jumped to the company’s defence.

The Republican legislator was one of several people to point out that Bombardier doesn’t just export to the U.S. but actually operates in the country and employs Americans, including at a service centre in Wichita, Kan.

“I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” Moran wrote on X.

“I will continue working to see that Bombardier’s manufacturing operations not only remain in Kansas but continue to grow and create American jobs.”

While Moran’s language was relatively mild, it was still unusual to see a lawmaker from Mr. Trump’s party openly contradict the President on a priority file. Most traditional Republicans are free traders – and, during Trump’s first term, made known their disagreement with his protectionism – but have largely kept such opinions to themselves as his personality and policies have come to dominate the party.

In a message to Canadians on the day retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. took effect, Prime Minister Mark Carney reached back into the history of the late 19th century to draw two parallels with the present day.

The first is a story with which his audience is certainly intimately familiar: then-prime minister John A. Macdonald’s construction of the Canadian-Pacific Railway, connecting the Prairies and West Coast with the population centres of the east.

“Canada needed an economic and military corridor that could connect our peoples from east to west. And so, at an incredible human and financial cost, Canadians took what was a country on paper and made it real: They built an iron spine,” Carney said in the video.

The Prime Minister held up that project as a forerunner to the wide-ranging infrastructure-building program he is promising, which includes everything from oil pipelines to hydroelectricity to port improvements, as Ottawa seeks to expand economic ties to other countries and lessen dependence on the U.S. He also framed the railroad as a check on American expansionist designs on Canadian territory.

The second parallel Carney cited is likely more obscure to a Canadian audience: the U.S.’s McKinley Tariff of 1890. Authored by William McKinley, then an Ohio congressman and later a U.S. president, the policy built a 50-per-cent tariff wall around the American economy.

“Sound familiar?” Carney said. “McKinley’s 50-per-cent tariff was meant to pressure us into dependence and eventually annexation by the United States. In reality, it did just the opposite.”

The Prime Minister credited the tariff with pushing Canada to diversify trade. In the U.S., he blamed the levies for causing inflation and the Panic of 1893, a serious economic depression.

Carney isn’t the first to draw a parallel between McKinley and U.S. President Donald Trump, albeit for very different purposes. Trump himself lauded McKinley’s protectionist policies in his inaugural address last year. And the President restored McKinley’s name to Denali, the U.S.’s highest mountain, in an executive order.

– Laura Stone

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said Tuesday that Canada’s countertariffs are a necessary response to the U.S., but also called for a return to the negotiating table.

In a statement released by his office, Moe defended Canada’s retaliatory measures but cautioned that the country’s economy is bound to take a hit.

“These countertariffs are necessary to respond to the unjustified tariffs from the United States. However, we cannot lose sight of the fact that tariffs and countertariffs increase costs for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border,” he said.

“Our goal still needs to be getting back to the table to negotiate the best deal for Canadians.”

– Eric Reguly

A senior government source, who did not want to be identified, said that nothing specific will be announced during the event in Strasbourg.

“The two leaders will just expand on the importance of the Canada-EU relationship.”

The person said that any new initiatives are more likely to be unveiled at the Canada-EU summit at the end of October. The host city has yet to be determined. “More ambitious goals will be set then,” the person said.

Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, are expected to confirm that Canada and the EU will deepen their economic, security and strategic ties during her state-of-the-union address in Strasbourg on Sept. 16.

Carney will attend her speech. The next day, he will address the EU parliament.

Carney has made strengthening European ties at the expense of the United States a priority since becoming prime minister in March, 2025. Speaking to reporters two months later, Carney said 75 cents on every dollar in weapons spending go to U.S. products. “It will make sense to diversify on defence partnerships, particularly as we spend considerably more on defence.”

He added that “it‘s prudent to diversify your partnerships when there are questions of sovereignty at issue,” an apparent reference to Mr. Trump’s obsession with turning Canada into the “51st state.”

– Olivia Grandy

Most Canadians support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States and instead impose retaliatory countertariffs, even if it means paying more for goods, a new poll suggests.

A Nanos Research survey conducted for The Globe and Mail found that 85 per cent of more than 1,000 respondents said they support or somewhat support Mr. Carney’s rejection of the proposed trade deal with the Trump administration.

The survey also found that 80 per cent of respondents said they support or somewhat support Ottawa’s plan to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar countertariffs.

Nik Nanos, the chief data scientist for Nanos Research, said support for retaliatory tariffs is as high as the early days of the trade war at the beginning of last year, when American policies fuelled antipathy toward the United States and consumer boycotts of U.S. goods and travel.

“We’re back to a situation where the temperature is about as hot as it got when Donald Trump first said that Canada should be the 51st state,” Nanos said.

About seven in 10 survey respondents said they were willing or somewhat willing to pay higher prices for everyday goods as part of Canada’s response to U.S. tariffs.

Read the full story here.

– Arisa Valyear

A collection of radio stations across the country are playing only Canadian and non-American music today. Steve Jones, president of Stingray Radio, told The Globe that all of the Canadian broadcaster’s rock radio stations, including channels in Halifax (Q104), Moncton (Q103) and Kelowna (K96.3), are exclusively spinning tracks by homegrown artists and those from countries such as the U.K. and Australia.

“We’re putting a 100-per-cent tariff on American music and closing the musical border for one day,” Jones said. The special radio programming – featuring artists such as the Tragically Hip, Bryan Adams, Ozzy Osbourne and AC/DC – started at midnight and will end at 12:01 a.m. on Sept. 9.

– Mark Rendell

Canadian manufacturers across a range of industries are facing a “double shock” because of Washington and Ottawa’s tit-for-tat tariffs, according to Desjardins economist Florence Jean-Jacobs.

The new U.S. tariffs on around $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, imposed last month, will hit exporters’ revenues as they lose market share in the United States. At the same time, Ottawa’s “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory measures will push up production costs in Canada, Jean-Jacobs said in a note to clients.

“The most vulnerable include manufacturers of motor vehicles, chemicals, machinery, and electrical, computer and electronic products, as well as textile products and other miscellaneous manufacturing. However, the availability of Canadian substitutes will mitigate the effect of counter-tariffs in several cases,” she said.

Canadian officials have said they designed the tariff list – which included 629 items – with this cost shock in mind, and selected items that can be sourced domestically or from other countries.

In some cases, the switch will be relatively easy.

Jean-Jacobs noted that very few food products are on Ottawa’s tariff list, and for those that are, there are ready substitutes.

“Counter-tariffs are therefore unlikely to put significant pressure on food inflation and should help grocery retailers and food service operators avoid squeezed profit margins.”

The bigger pinch will be felt by manufacturers who cannot easily adjust their supply chains, she said.

“Consider breweries, wineries and distilleries. Their products now face prohibitive US tariffs of 50 per cent, which are drastically curbing their sales. At the same time, metal cans and glass containers used for beverage packaging are now subject to a 50 per cent tariff when imported from the United States. Producers that rely on these US-sourced inputs will need to quickly identify alternative suppliers or risk seeing their costs skyrocket. “

Close attention needs to be paid to construction industry costs, she said, given that Ottawa has targeted U.S. building materials, including heating, ventilation and air conditioning equipment, household appliances, electrical equipment and lighting.

“In some cases, these materials and equipment are sourced from highly specialized manufacturers, making substitutes difficult to find. Resulting disruptions could delay projects and increase costs,” Jean-Jacobs wrote.

– Jason Kirby and Dexter McMillan

Canada and the United States have enjoyed decades of free trade since 1989, with the signing of the initial Canada-United States free trade agreement – later expanded to become the North American free trade agreement, with Mexico, and then tweaked to become the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement during Trump’s first term.

The deals brought about extremely low effective tariff rates on U.S. goods coming into Canada of around 0.2 per cent.

Last year’s countertariffs, which Ottawa put in place in March, 2025, and largely reversed in September, 2025, pushed the rate to an estimated 1.2 per cent, according to an analysis by Trevor Tombe, an economics professor at the University of Calgary.

The Sept. 8 duties could push Canada’s effective tariff rate on U.S. imports to 3.8 per cent, he estimated, the highest level since the 1980s. That’s a significant departure from decades of free trade.

– Bill Curry

Gabriel Brunet, a spokesperson for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, told The Globe on Tuesday morning that there are currently no formal talks.

“Canadian and American officials have maintained ongoing discussions on a range of issues, although formal trade negotiations are not taking place at this time,” he said in a statement.

– The Canadian Press

The Quebec government has announced a series of measures to promote buying locally in response to the escalating trade war between Canada and the United States.

Premier Christine Fréchette says the measures will inject about $1.5-billion into the Quebec economy in the next four months.

Fréchette’s cabinet met as she took a break from the provincial election campaign to return to her role as Premier and address the latest in the trade war.

The ministers adopted an order-in-council requiring the government to take steps to favour local businesses when it comes to awarding contracts, such as reserving public bids for companies with a place of business in Quebec and Canada.

Those measures could also include requiring goods be produced and processed in the province, and granting a 15-per-cent preferential margin based on Quebec or Canadian value added.

She says Quebec is facing a bully and has the choice to either kneel down or to stand tall.

The Sept. 8 duties fall heaviest on swing states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while also targeting key industries in other Republican strongholds.

For instance, Harley-Davidson’s plant in Pennsylvania could feel the sting of tariffs on U.S.-made motorcycles. Over the past five years, the company sold an average of 7,400 motorcycles a year in Canada, according to its financial records, and generated average annual revenue of US$215-million for bikes, parts and services.

Ohio is hardest hit in dollar terms, since it shipped $3.3-billion worth of tariff-covered goods to Canada in 2025, with steel items high on the list. The state is home to Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., a steelmaker that has lobbied heavily for Mr. Trump’s steel tariffs – and which also happens to own Canadian steelmaker Stelco.

A 50-per-cent tariff is being applied to a variety of American dairy products. They include milk and cream, including concentrated and sweetened varieties and powders. It also applies to whey and several milk and whey protein products.

A 25-per-cent tariff applies to fresh cheese and curd, including grated, powdered and processed varieties. The list specifies the types of cheese: Camembert, brie, blue cheese, cheddar, mozzarella, Swiss, Gruyère, Havarti and Parmesan, to name a few.

Forestry and wood:

Canada is targeting U.S. wood products with 25-per-cent tariffs. The products include softwood such as pine, fir and spruce that have been sawed or sliced thicker than six millimetres.

Plywood and veneered panels made from a variety of different softwoods and hardwoods have been hit with a 50-per-cent levy.

Tariffs of either 25 or 50 per cent now apply to products like toilet paper, facial tissue, napkins and similar sanitary products (the rate depends on specific import sizes).

A 50-per-cent tariff applies to most types of paper and paperboard, envelopes and corrugated boxes and cases, with a lower 25-per-cent levy for some imports of kraft paper and bleached paper products under a certain weight.

Steel, aluminum and copper:

Multiple steel and aluminum products are being hit with a 50-per-cent tariff, up from the current 25-per-cent rate. They include steel rods, bars and sheets, along with prefabricated items such as bridges, towers, scaffolding, and door and window frames. Aluminum products such as wires, bars, rods and foil are all subject to the 50-per-cent tariff rate.

On Aug. 26, Ottawa added a 50-per-cent tariff to various sizes of copper wire.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s policy of imposing or raising tariffs on nearly every country in the world – and escalating his trade war against Canada – could cost him politically in November’s midterm elections.

That’s because U.S. voters are already anxious about the cost of living, and the opposition Democrats are doing everything they can to tie this to Trump’s signature policies, including the war in Iran, cuts to health care spending and tariffs.

In a campaign video released Tuesday morning, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a Senate seat in swing state Michigan, invites voters to play “The Price is Wrong.” In the two-minute spot, his mock game show highlights price increases to a range of goods, from dishwashing detergent to Tim Hortons coffee.

“Everything’s gotten more expensive over the last year because of Trump’s tariffs and his war in Iran,” El-Sayed says. “Americans are paying way more for everyday goods that they have to buy at the grocery store – all because of this insane war that’s spiking the price of gas … and now, a trade war that’s just expanded with Canada.”

El-Sayed’s messaging is emblematic of the “affordability” theme that Democrats are hoping will win them back control of the House of Representatives, possibly the Senate and several state governorships.

It is particularly significant in border states such as Michigan, whose economies are heavily reliant on Canada. And Trump may have just handed them a potent new weapon.

- Nicolas Van Praet

U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest attack on Bombardier Inc. BBD-B-T is spooking some investors as the Quebec plane maker gets dragged into Canada’s trade war with the United States with no talks in sight.

Bombardier shares were down 7 per cent to $293.49 in heavy trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange Tuesday morning. It’s the first trading day since the President floated a ban on Bombardier jets sales in the U.S. over the long weekend.

Analysts say it’s not clear what legal mechanism the White House would use to stop the company from exporting into the U.S., and Trump hasn’t explained what he intends to do. But his threat is not a welcome development for the company.

Saskatchewan’s government is set to slap its retaliatory tax on American booze today amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced last month his province would implement the 50-per-cent fee on American alcohol on the same day Canada’s reciprocal tariffs take effect.

Any U.S.-produced alcohol purchased through the Saskatchewan Liquor and Gaming Authority’s online ordering system, used by retailers across the province, is being hit by the levy.

Unlike other Canadian provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta do not have a ban on American alcohol products.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hasn’t followed Saskatchewan’s lead by implementing a reciprocal tax. Following Moe’s announcement, she said her cabinet would consider it.

Moe has said U.S. liquor would remain on store shelves, because the province doesn’t want to limit the public’s ability to choose.

“That is a very important core value for this government,” he said in late August.

- Bill Curry and Mark Rendell

Prime Minister Mark Carney released a video to Canadians Tuesday morning, outlining why Ottawa is moving ahead with retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of American goods.

In the 15-minute video, Carney summarized why his government walked away last month from trade negotiations.

“The most fundamental issue is that the cumulative U.S. demands revealed that they wanted us to become even more reliant on them, not less. In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership. Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us, so they can own us. And I promised, ‘that will never, ever happen,’” he said.

The video, the latest in a series that Carney has labelled “forward guidance,” does not announce any new measures. Instead, it outlines the government’s current economic plan and its rationale.

“First, we are matching the new U.S. measures dollar for dollar with new tariffs of our own. I don’t believe in escalating the conflict, that’s not constructive, but our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, companies and communities. We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff free while they charge our companies to export to them,” he said.

“Second, we’re supporting Canadians, because, up here, we take care of each other,” he said.

Later in the video, Carney said adversity will make the country stronger.

“There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still,” he said.

Carney does not have any scheduled public appearances Tuesday.

- Marieke Walsh and Sophia Bertuzzi

Instead of negotiations over the weekend, President Trump made a steady stream of insulting social media posts about Canada and floated a ban on Canadian luxury-jet maker Bombardier.

In one post on Truth Social, the President shared an illustration of himself in Team USA hockey gear towering over a wincing Mr. Carney clad in Team Canada colours and telling him to “Get up, governor.”

In another, Mr. Trump posted a map that showed the U.S. flag superimposed over Canada, Mexico, Greenland, Iceland, the entire Caribbean and most of Central America. The Prime Minister’s Office declined to comment on Mr. Trump’s posts.

On Monday, the President’s most substantive attack was on a Canadian company.

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” he wrote on his social-media platform. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a “piggy bank.”

The attack was made only on social media, with no formal policy announcement from the White House.

In a statement on Monday, Montreal-based Bombardier said that it was helping to drive trade surpluses in the U.S. – the single trade metric that most preoccupies Trump – by employing workers in the country and buying parts from American suppliers.

“The American aerospace industry is a clear winner on trade and exports. Bombardier is a strong contributor to the sector, creating tens of thousands of jobs across the United States. Aerospace is routinely one of the top export sectors for the United States and a continual trade surplus winner,” the company said.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette pledged to defend Bombardier in a statement on social media:

Canada’s countertariffs are designed to send a message that two can play the trade war game, and the federal government is hoping politicians in a number of states will be its messengers.

Canada’s tit-for-tat approach to the countertariffs means many of the items on Canada’s list of $27.6-billion worth of imports from the U.S. were on Mr. Trump’s $27.6-billion worth of Section 338 tariffs.

Those include products like honey, hair care products, metal furniture and cardboard boxes.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $28-billion worth of U.S. imports came into force at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday. They apply to 629 items – everything from clothing and home appliances to metals and electronics.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said Monday that there had been no eleventh-hour talks to prevent Canada from imposing the countertariffs.

The Canadian tariffs are in response to 50-per-cent tariffs that U.S. President Donald Trump levelled against Canada on Aug. 22. Ottawa’s levies are set mostly at 25 or 50 per cent, with a small number of goods subject to a lower 15-per-cent duty.

Canada walked away from negotiations late on Aug. 21, with Carney saying American negotiators had made unreasonable last-minute demands. No formal talks have taken place since.

Trump’s administration has promised to retaliate, meaning that Ottawa’s new countertariffs could widen the trade war, with ever-expanding economic pain for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border. And Trump has already said that he would double auto tariffs to 50 per cent from 25 per cent as of Jan. 1, 2027, and have them also apply to auto parts, which have so far been exempted.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $28-billion in U.S. imports took effect Tuesday, as Ottawa responded to President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war. Here's what's affected.

The Associated Press
