stories.title: Population growth drives school-building boom across London region
stories.summary: Both London-area school boards are opening new schools and planning more as enrolment pressures reshape where students learn.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The two major London-based school boards, serving the city and several surrounding communities, are opening and building new schools to accommodate the region’s growing population. Here are some things to know as students head back to class.

As students return to classes for the 2026-27 school year, some will be attending brand-new or newly renovated schools.

The newest addition to the London District Catholic school board – which operates 44 elementary schools and nine high schools – is the new $54.3-million replacement Regina Mundi Catholic Colleg e in the city’s southeast end. The original school opened in 1963 as a seminary, according to the Catholic board’s website.

“That’s a replacement build, but it is our newest building,” said the Catholic board’s education director, Vince Romeo, noting the school has capacity for about 700 students.

For the Thames Valley District school board, the $28.2-million Jackson Meadows public school, which opens its doors in southeast London for the first time on Tuesday, is its newest school. Thames Valley oversees 135 elementary schools and 27 high schools.

A second school, the $24.2-million Belmont Meadows public school in Belmont, with capacity for roughly 500 pupils, is “expected to be completed” in January 2027, Thames Valley officials said in an email statement.

“All students currently attending South Dorchester PS will switch schools to attend Belmont Meadows PS when it opens in January 2027,” the board’s website said, adding South Dorchester will close thereafter.

Thames Valley said a third school, the nearly $25-million Clover public school in Lucan, is expected to be completed in March. With capacity for about 530 pupils, the new school will serve junior kindergarten to Grade 3, while Wilberforce public school will be converted to a Grade 4-to-8 school.

$261M in funding for six new London-area schools: Province

New $100M high school part of $285M London-area school funding

Advertisement 1Story continues below

An anticipated 28,500 students are expected to attend classes Tuesday, Romeo said, pointing out the London District Catholic school board is the fastest-growing school board in Ontario.

“Of all 72 school boards in the province, we’re going into year six as the fastest growing at a rate of 30 per cent growth over the last five years,” he said.

Romeo said 1,900 positions have been filled, including board staff, classroom teachers and early childhood educators throughout the district to support growing enrolment. “And we’re looking at that hiring growth to continue into this school year.”

Romeo said the Catholic board is excited to welcome students as it receives substantial provincial investments for new schools and school renewals amid record growth.

While enrolment at the London District Catholic school board has reached record levels, enrolment at Thames Valley has dipped slightly: About 84,110 students were enrolled in Thames Valley schools during the 2024-25 school year, according to a July 2025 Free Press story. Figures on Thames Valley’s website indicate about 83,500 students were enrolled for the 2025-26 school year.

The board said enrolment data for the 2026-27 school year will not be finalized until later this fall.

The London District Catholic school board continues to experience growth hotspots across London, Romeo said. He described growth as “pretty well distributed” across the city, but identified northwest and southwest London as particularly active areas.

He also pointed to Middlesex and Elgin counties as communities where the Catholic board has been “seeing huge growth” recently.

“That’s being recognized by the ministry with the approval of a second St. Thomas secondary school that we are in the planning stages,” Romeo said. “We’re going to be replacing our elementary school in Lucan (too).”

Thames Valley directed The Free Press to its website, which indicates the board has planned several attendance-area reviews, including in southwest and northeast London, St. Thomas and Elgin County.

Earlier this year, the provincial government announced $1.6 billion in funding for schools across Ontario. Both Thames Valley and the London District Catholic school board received funding.

With enrolment numbers climbing, the Catholic board has several new schools in the works across the region.

Romeo named seven schools, including two scheduled to open within the next year.

“(In) Kilworth-Komoka, it is an elementary school that we are hoping to open next September . . . that is well into the planning stages, and we’re more than halfway through,” he said. “We are also, with the same timeline of September 2027, opening a northeast elementary school, sort of in the Highbury-Fanshawe Park Road area.”

Romeo said a new $100-million north London high school on Richmond Street north of Fanshawe Park Road will have capacity for roughly 2,000 students – one of the largest schools ever built by the Catholic board and one of its largest approvals from the Ministry of Education.

In London, Romeo said the southwest and southeast ends are being eyed for new elementary schools, along with a new high school in the south end. He also said construction on a new St. Thomas secondary school will begin shortly, while a replacement St. Patrick’s Catholic school in Lucan is in the planning stages to address growth there.

“We’re welcoming and needing more schools to complement the existing schools that we have now,” he said.

Thames Valley officials said that in addition to opening three new schools during the 2026-27 school year, the board is continuing work on “many other capital projects.”

Among them is a $43.6-million new high school for roughly 700 students in St. Thomas, for which the board is still seeking land, according to its website.

“It’s our first new high school in decades with the replacement of Arthur Voaden secondary school in St. Thomas,” Thames Valley said.

Thames Valley said it is also designing and building new schools in Talbotville, Thamesford and several locations across London. The board is also eyeing additions at Parkview public school in Komoka and Nissouri public school in Thorndale.

stories.title: In the age of artificial intelligence, professors try to make cheating hard again
stories.summary: Students at one Canadian university have assignments ranging from hand-written essays to generative AI free-for-alls
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
As the fall semester begins at universities across Canada, professors are grappling with a fundamental challenge of the artificial-intelligence era: How do you assess students when cheating has never been simpler?

Research essays and other take-home written assignments can be conjured from thin air with a prompt to Claude or ChatGPT.

And ferreting out such subterfuge is hard because many Canadian universities forbid or discourage professors from using AI-detection software, said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

“We ban the use of AI detectors as unethical because they’re not 100 per cent accurate,” Prof. Daley explained, referring to Western’s policy.

When cheating is easy and cheaters can’t easily be caught, instructors must get creative. Here is how four professors in different fields at one university are remaking their assignments for the new AI reality.

For the past few years, Western University philosophy professor David Bourget tried to assign essays that were AI-resistant. He asked narrow questions and picked obscure readings that, as far as he knows, stumped early versions of ChatGPT.

But as large language models (LLMs) improved, “all of these techniques stopped working,” Prof. Bourget said. “Then I had to turn around and, like everybody else, rethink how I do things.”

This year, he is running a pilot project where about 130 students enrolled in Introduction to the Philosophy of Mind, a second-year course, will research and write essays in an on-campus computer lab under the watchful eye of a teaching assistant.

Students will bring their own laptops. The supervisors, using QR codes on their phones, will sign the students in to external servers for Matcha , a software program that Prof. Bourget designed as a walled garden in which users can access word processors and online research materials but not AI tools.

The program, which stands for Modern Authoring Tool for Certified Human Authorship, has other features that record the work that goes into producing an essay, including research notes, early drafts and edits. Prof. Bourget co-founded a company to license the program.

The supervised nature of the lab keeps students from using AI on a secondary device, such as a phone, and typing the results into Matcha.

As a bonus, the lab will bring students and their teaching assistants together for what would otherwise be a virtual course. Prof. Bourget will be delivering his lectures online.

“My goal,” he said, “is to make cheating hard again.”

Selma Purac, the undergraduate program chair at Western’s Faculty of Information and Media Studies, realized the traditional essay was in peril in the fall of 2023, less than a year after the launch of ChatGPT.

She was marking a batch of 40 papers for a mass communication class she had taught for years. Thirty of the essays were remarkably similar. They read nothing like the student writing she was used to grading. Twenty-eight employed a word that Prof. Purac had never seen in a student essay, one she now recognizes as a favourite of ChatGPT’s. (She declined to reveal the word, saying she’d rather not give away the AI tell.)

Prof. Purac didn’t want to abandon essays. Writing them taught her students to read critically, develop strong arguments and find their voices. “But those skills were being degraded by the way in which my students were using LLMs,” she said.

Instead, Prof. Purac decided to reimagine the essay. Two years ago, she started breaking down her assignments into worksheets. She gave her students time outside of class to conduct research and outline their arguments, including pulling direct quotes from source material. Then, she had them write their essays in class with pen, paper, their worksheets and supervision.

For example, in her third-year course, Children, Advertising and Consumer Culture, she had for years assigned a close reading of an advertisement.

Before LLMs, students selected ads and composed their assignments at home. Now, Prof. Purac distributes a three-and-a-half page worksheet, which must be completed in point form, at least three weeks in advance of a two-hour, in-class writing period.

“I really like the way it demystifies the traditional essay,” she said.

Students studying at Western’s Ivey School of Business know they’ll be expected to use AI in the workplace. So Guneet Kaur Nagpal, who teaches marketing management and digital marketing analytics to undergraduates, had to find a way to teach students to master AI without losing the ability to think critically.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal developed a marketing strategy simulation tool called plAIbook that allowed her students to use generative AI as an assistant in solving business case studies. The program caps the number of prompts students can give AI and sets strict time limits.

The tool garnered positive feedback from faculty and students after it was piloted in 10 sections of a marketing class last spring. Prof. Kaur Nagpal built it as one of Western’s Generative AI teaching fellows. She and two other professors have been seconded to the university’s Centre for Teaching and Learning for two years to develop and assess new ways of teaching with AI.

On top of developing plAIbook, Prof. Kaur Nagpal and her colleagues overhauled some classic assignments. In the pre-ChatGPT era, she gave groups of students 48 hours to compare two legacy brands and develop a marketing plan for the weaker of the two. Now she asks groups to develop marketing plans in 24 hours, using AI, for newly minted brands from sources such as the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter or the start-up incubator Y Combinator.

She also traded a week-long take-home exam for a four-hour, in-class exam with the help of AI. Unfortunately, when she quizzed students orally on the material, she discovered that some who scored well on the written final with AI couldn’t even define simple terms.

“It’s telling and it’s troubling,” she said.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal plans to increase the weight of oral tests this fall.

Western history professor William Turkel was on sabbatical in the 2024-2025 academic year when he realized that generative artificial intelligence was improving at a clip that would force him and his colleagues to teach differently.

He changed the name of his third-year Digital Research Methods class to Digital Research Methods with Artificial Intelligence. He told his students to use AI as much as they liked, including as a virtual teammate for group projects.

But he warned that the standard fare spit out by an LLM would net only an average grade.

If students wanted higher marks, they would have to do something more ambitious. One example: Dispatch an LLM or multiple LLMs to comb through thousands of digitized texts at U.S. presidential libraries, and compare what American leaders said in real time about the Vietnam War to facts that emerged later in the Pentagon papers.

Prof. Turkel is also one of Western’s generative AI teaching fellows. He thinks students are better off embracing the inescapable new technology.

“How many undergrad students become professional historians? One in 100? One in 200?” he said. “The rest of them are going to workplaces where they can’t pretend AI doesn’t exist.”

stories.title: How Tiff helped Deepa Mehta find her place in Canada
stories.summary: Over the years, Mehta has kept up her association with Tiff as a filmmaker and industry leader
stories.author: Aparita Bhandari
stories.content:
As the 51st Toronto International Film Festival takes over the city Sept. 10-20, this series of articles examines some of the Canadian directors whose lives and careers have been impacted by Tiff.

As an emerging filmmaker living in Toronto in the late ’80s, Deepa Mehta didn’t feel very Canadian.

It was a time in her life when she was deeply unhappy. Her marriage had unravelled, and walking down the city streets, she sometimes heard racist abuse hurled in her direction. In fact, she missed India, the country of her birth, so much that at one point she rang up the Indian consulate wondering if she could get a job as a receptionist if she worked for free.

So when Piers Handling, former CEO of the Toronto International Film Festival, invited her to bring her debut feature film, Sam & Me to Tiff, Mehta says she felt Canadian for the first time.

“It was a very small film, but it was important to me,” she says. “For me, Canada was defined by Tiff… It meant the world to me for my first feature to be invited.”

Mehta had met Handling at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival, where Sam & Me screened and won an honourable mention for the Caméra d’Or prize. The film is about a young Indian immigrant Nikhil (Indian actor Ranjit Chowdhry, also the screenwriter of Sam & Me ), who becomes a caregiver to Sam (Peter Boretski), an eccentric, elderly Jewish man.

The warmth she received at Tiff was wonderful, says Mehta.

“I remember it was Cameron who introduced the film,” says Mehta, referencing Tiff’s current CEO Cameron Bailey, who was a programmer at the time. “And I got to meet so many wonderful filmmakers. I got to see an aspect of Canada and its growth. Especially [seeing] what’s happening now with South Asian cinema, I feel so happy.”

Born in Amritsar, Punjab, in 1950, Mehta was pursuing a master’s degree at Delhi University when she got involved in documentary filmmaking and met Canadian filmmaker Paul Saltzman, who she later married. She came to Canada in 1973 and started making TV series and short documentaries, moving to feature films with Sam & Me .

Tiff has championed Mehta’s work throughout her career. In 1996, former Tiff programmer David McIntosh invited her to bring Fire, the first in her elemental trilogy of films (along with Earth and Water ), to the festival. By then, Mehta had established other collaborators, including her current partner and film producer David Hamilton, with whom she founded Hamilton-Mehta Productions, as well as Hussain Amarshi, founder of Canada’s leading independent film distribution company Mongrel Media.

Starring celebrated Indian actresses Shabana Azmi and Nandita Das (who would go on to become a director and bring films such as Manto and Zwigato to Tiff), Fire sparked controversy for its depiction of same-sex desire.

For Anita Lee, Tiff’s chief programming officer, watching Fire at Tiff was a revelation.

“I remember at the time, even just the fact that it was a film that took place entirely in India, it was debated – is this a Canadian film? The fact that it was a romantic relationship between two women, within that Indian context, and the taboo of that subject matter; I recall the significant international discussion that happened around that film,” says Lee, who later went on to become a producer for Mehta’s film Heaven on Earth . “It was so groundbreaking for Canada.”

Over the years, Mehta has kept up her association with Tiff as a filmmaker and industry leader. She’s been an ambassador for its Share Her Journey initiative, set up in 2017 to champion women creators. She co-directed documentary I Am Sirat , about the life of a transgender woman in New Delhi, which screened at Tiff in 2023. This year, she’s acting as a jurist for the festival’s Canadian programming, which has been a source of delight, says Mehta.

“I want to see what’s happening in Canada today, with the young filmmakers. They have added something to Canada that was never there before. And they aren’t apologetic for who they are,” she says.

“It’s just so lovely. And I think Tiff has a lot to do with it.”

Tiff’s invitation to screen Sam & Me validated its place in the Canadian canon, says Malini Guha, associate professor of film studies at Carleton University. Mehta is one of the most prolific filmmakers to be working out of Canada, despite the significant challenges she faced as a racialized woman, she adds.

“A number of her films deal with the question of migration, the struggles of migration, particularly as they pertain to labour,” says Guha. She notes that films about migration usually deal with family conflicts or romantic relationships, but Sam & Me is unusual because of its focus on South Asian men living together in a Toronto rooming house, trying to make a go of it as immigrants.

In one scene, during a birthday party, a character named Xavier dresses up in a sari and dances to a popular Hindi movie song, says Guha.

“Nikhil brings Sam into this space, and he’s watching along with the nephew of the boarding house owner Keith, who is the most explicitly queer character in the film. They have a friend, Takahito, who is Japanese. And they’re all sitting there, watching this performance,” she says.

“It’s brilliant. It’s so joyful. And there are some non-normative gender and sexual ideas. It feels remarkable for a film of its time period.”

In fact, she missed India, the country of her birth, so much that at one point she rang up the Indian consulate wondering if she could get a job as a receptionist if she worked for free.
So when Piers Handling, former CEO of the Toronto International Film Festival, invited her to bring her debut feature film, Sam & Me to Tiff, Mehta says she felt Canadian for the first time.
“It was a very small film, but it was important to me,” she says. “For me, Canada was defined by Tiff… It meant the world to me for my first feature to be invited.”

Mehta had met Handling at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival, where Sam & Me screened and won an honourable mention for the Caméra d’Or prize. The film is about a young Indian immigrant Nikhil (Indian actor Ranjit Chowdhry, also the screenwriter of Sam & Me ), who becomes a caregiver to Sam (Peter Boretski), an eccentric, elderly Jewish man.
The warmth she received at Tiff was wonderful, says Mehta.

“I remember it was Cameron who introduced the film,” says Mehta, referencing Tiff’s current CEO Cameron Bailey, who was a programmer at the time. “And I got to meet so many wonderful filmmakers. I got to see an aspect of Canada and its growth. Especially [seeing] what’s happening now with South Asian cinema, I feel so happy.”

Born in Amritsar, Punjab, in 1950, Mehta was pursuing a master’s degree at Delhi University when she got involved in documentary filmmaking and met Canadian filmmaker Paul Saltzman, who she later married. She came to Canada in 1973 and started making TV series and short documentaries, moving to feature films with Sam & Me .

Tiff has championed Mehta’s work throughout her career. In 1996, former Tiff programmer David McIntosh invited her to bring Fire, the first in her elemental trilogy of films (along with Earth and Water ), to the festival. By then, Mehta had established other collaborators, including her current partner and film producer David Hamilton, with whom she founded Hamilton-Mehta Productions, as well as Hussain Amarshi, founder of Canada’s leading independent film distribution company Mongrel Media.

Starring celebrated Indian actresses Shabana Azmi and Nandita Das (who would go on to become a director and bring films such as Manto and Zwigato to Tiff), Fire sparked controversy for its depiction of same-sex desire.
For Anita Lee, Tiff’s chief programming officer, watching Fire at Tiff was a revelation.

“I remember at the time, even just the fact that it was a film that took place entirely in India, it was debated – is this a Canadian film? The fact that it was a romantic relationship between two women, within that Indian context, and the taboo of that subject matter; I recall the significant international discussion that happened around that film,” says Lee, who later went on to become a producer for Mehta’s film Heaven on Earth . “It was so groundbreaking for Canada.”

Over the years, Mehta has kept up her association with Tiff as a filmmaker and industry leader. She’s been an ambassador for its Share Her Journey initiative, set up in 2017 to champion women creators. She co-directed documentary I Am Sirat , about the life of a transgender woman in New Delhi, which screened at Tiff in 2023. This year, she’s acting as a jurist for the festival’s Canadian programming, which has been a source of delight, says Mehta.
“I want to see what’s happening in Canada today, with the young filmmakers. They have added something to Canada that was never there before. And they aren’t apologetic for who they are,” she says.
“It’s just so lovely. And I think Tiff has a lot to do with it.”

Tiff’s invitation to screen Sam & Me validated its place in the Canadian canon, says Malini Guha, associate professor of film studies at Carleton University. Mehta is one of the most prolific filmmakers to be working out of Canada, despite the significant challenges she faced as a racialized woman, she adds.

“A number of her films deal with the question of migration, the struggles of migration, particularly as they pertain to labour,” says Guha. She notes that films about migration usually deal with family conflicts or romantic relationships, but Sam & Me is unusual because of its focus on South Asian men living together in a Toronto rooming house, trying to make a go of it as immigrants.
In one scene, during a birthday party, a character named Xavier dresses up in a sari and dances to a popular Hindi movie song, says Guha.

“Nikhil brings Sam into this space, and he’s watching along with the nephew of the boarding house owner Keith, who is the most explicitly queer character in the film. They have a friend, Takahito, who is Japanese. And they’re all sitting there, watching this performance,” she says.
“It’s brilliant. It’s so joyful. And there are some non-normative gender and sexual ideas. It feels remarkable for a film of its time period.”

stories.title: Ground breaks on South Britannia in B.C., home to Canada's first surf park
stories.summary: Popular tourism corridor expands with new mixed-use development
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
Over a decade after the land was sold, shovels are now in the ground at South Britannia, a new mixed-use resort-like development along the Sea-to-Sky Highway just south of the Britannia Beach community in British Columbia, about a 45-minute drive north from Vancouver.

The project is being undertaken by Tiger Bay Development, formerly known as Taicheng Development, a company owned by Chinese real estate developer Peter Cheng and his son Long Cheng – just one example of the wave of Chinese developers that entered B.C. around the aughts and 2010s. The Chengs have been involved in numerous projects in China, but South Britannia is Tiger Bay’s one and only project.

Tiger Bay acquired the land, a large gravel pit and surrounding land that total to approximately 490 acres, in the early 2010s for $30.5 million after the previous owner became insolvent and the property went through a court-ordered sales process.

Originally envisioned for the site was a resort community with more than 4,000 homes, but the project was pared down after concerns from locals and the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District about the scale. The project was refined before a rezoning application was submitted in 2019 and then approved in 2025, with the revisions having won over some opponents. The project is an instance of a sprawling resort community sprouting from the ground up – and one that’s now being constructed.

The South Britannia development will now include 900 homes, 100 market rental units, 50 below-market rental units, retail space, tourist accommodations, outdoor sports amenities, 320 acres of green space and the crown jewel: A six-acre man-made surf park, the first of its kind in Canada.

“The resistance from the Regional District was regarding job opportunities,” said Tony Petricevic, Tiger Bay’s head of development. “They didn’t want it to be another commuting community. When I came along [around 2018], there was an opportunity to build more commercial [and places to work] to not only make the project more feasible, but also just capitalizing on the location.”

From there, Tiger Bay started exploring possibilities in addition to just residential, with an eye on sports tourism opportunities, as Mr. Petricevic notes that the Sea-to-Sky corridor is one that leans heavily into an outdoorsy lifestyle and culture – winter sports on Whistler Mountain, mountain-biking around Squamish, kitesurfing on Howe Sound.

They eventually settled on a surf park, a pool-like facility with artificially generated waves. And perhaps signalling how persuasive it has been to the community, the outdoor surf park will be delivered as part of Phase One of South Britannia, with the residential, retail and amenities coming in later phases.

The overall master plan for the project was designed by Whistler-based Ecosign Mountain Resort Planners and Vancouver-based Placemark Design .

Mr. Petricevic says the concept of a sports facility being integrated within a residential community was one that was fairly new at the time, so Tiger Bay’s focus was to get the integration aspect right while ensuring the project remained viable.

They ultimately concluded that not only was the surf park financially feasible, it made the overall project more feasible as well because it made way for other commercial components to be included to support the surf park and community.

The heart-shaped surf park will span six acres – around the middle of the overall South Britannia site – and include a beach house that’s home to a restaurant, bar, cafe, retail space, meeting space, wellness facilities, surf cabins and surf academy.

Mr. Petricevic says they wanted to respect the existing surf community, so they worked with groups such as Surf Canada and the Olympic training team to make sure they were on board. The hope is that the facility will also help grow the sport, with lessons provided on site and the controlled environment to make it easier for beginners to learn.

The surf park and beach house were designed by Vancouver’s Michael Green Architecture alongside engineering firm Stantec , with Spain’s Wavegarden as the artificial wave-generation systems provider.

The development permit for the surf park was submitted earlier this year, site work began in late August and the surf park is expected to open in 2029. The timing of the remaining phases will be in part determined by market conditions but are not expected to be advanced until after the surf park is complete.

“Rather than just peel the curtain and be like ‘Boom, here’s the surf park,’ we’re actually creating a series of steps people will have to take [within the development], through the design, to…discover the experience, instead of being bluntly shown it,” said Michael Green.

Mr. Green’s colleague, Chris Knight, added that other surf parks that have been built around the world were not integrated into the landscape, so that became something they strived for.

Mr. Knight added that the form of the beach house buildings were inspired by the look of pebbles on a beach.

Knowing the surf park would be the heart of South Britannia, not to mention the first phase, Green said it was important that they kick off the project on a high note and that “having ambition around it is really important.

“To take the unbelievable landscape of B.C., this unbelievable site, put it together with this [surf] culture and the Sea-to-Sky Highway, which is one of the single-most-visited tourism corridors in Canada, and you get the perfect story of how a project can go from being good to really great.”

stories.title: London municipal election: City council candidates in their own words
stories.summary: Londoners will elect their next city council on Oct. 26

stories.content: Londoners will elect their next city council on Oct. 26 and we’ve given those running for local office a chance to pitch their candidacy to LFP readers, in their own words. Answers were lightly edited for length and clarity.

stories.title: Carbon monoxide exposure at hockey arena provides ‘terrifying wake-up call’ for parents: report
stories.summary: A new report detailing a mass carbon monoxide exposure that sent dozens of young hockey players to hospital is renewing calls for mandatory detectors in Canadian arenas, where federal guidance recommends the devices, but does not require them.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Calgary – A new report detailing a mass carbon monoxide exposure that sent dozens of young hockey players to hospital is renewing calls for mandatory detectors in Canadian arenas, where federal guidance recommends the devices, but does not require them.

Players began reporting headaches, fatigue, dizziness, nausea and vomiting after spending much of the day inside the arena because of cold weather and back-to-back games.

At first, many parents thought a virus was spreading.

Marshall’s son, a goalie, had played his first game without issue. During the second, while sitting on the bench, he suddenly became violently ill and ran into the change room.

“He’s got his head in a bucket and he is puking and screaming, trying to get his hockey gear off of him,” Marshall said.

‘Something’s going on’

Moir, an off-duty firefighter whose son was also playing, initially thought the same thing.

“My son actually came off. Had a little bit of headache, wasn’t feeling good,” Moir said.

Then another player arrived with a headache, nausea and dizziness. A third soon followed.

“I was like, all right, something’s going on.”

Moir began to wonder whether carbon monoxide (CO) could be responsible.

While driving home, he called the local fire department, which sent a crew to the arena. Firefighters detected CO levels ranging from 90 to 150 parts per million and evacuated the building.

“There’s two different alarms for most detectors, like a low alarm and then a high alarm,” he said. “The detector went into high alarm right away.”

Moir was not initially informed of the test results. He contacted the arena manager himself and learned elevated CO levels had been detected and the arena had been evacuated. According to the Cmaj report, he was given no guidance about what players and family members who had already left should do.

Lee advised anyone who remained symptomatic to go to the emergency department for assessment.

“No way did I think I’d be calling the Children’s (Hospital) to say, ‘I’ve just sent 40-plus children in for assessment for a toxic carbon monoxide exposure,’” Lee said.

‘A terrifying wake-up call’

Marshall’s family had already left the arena believing her son might simply be sick. They were preparing to put him to bed when they learned he May have been exposed to carbon monoxide.

“If we had put him to bed, we don’t know what would have happened at that situation. And it’s a terrifying wake-up call as a parent.”

The Cmaj report states that at the Alberta Children’s Hospital, 23 children and two adults — by then more than three hours after the exposure — had CO levels requiring treatment and monitoring. No children were admitted to hospital, while both adults were transferred to an adult hospital.

The patients arrived during one of the hospital’s busiest times of year, amid the December surge in respiratory illnesses. The emergency department was already over capacity when staff learned dozens of children could be arriving with carbon monoxide exposure.

Paramedics screened exposed children and caregivers at the emergency department entrance using a non-invasive device to measure CO levels. Only those with readings above three per cent were brought into the department, where they were placed on oxygen and underwent blood testing to confirm their levels.

Lee said carbon monoxide interferes with the body’s ability to deliver oxygen to vital organs, which leads to symptoms such as headache, nausea, dizziness and vomiting.

“My priority was making sure that they all were seen by a medical professional and got whatever treatment needed,” Lee said, adding the treatment is high-concentration oxygen.

Marshall remembers the chaos as families descended on the children’s hospital.

“We were 40-plus kids coming in. All the parents could not come in at the same time,” she said.

In a statement to CTV News, the Village of Rockyford said permanent carbon monoxide monitors were installed during the off-season and additional safety measures were introduced, including portable CO monitors, upgrades to the heater exhaust system and air exchange fans, and new policies and procedures.

The village said it worked with the Rockyford Agricultural Society and Occupational Health and Safety on the changes, noting there were no safety codes requirements for CO monitors at the time of the incident.

Alarm guidance is voluntary

Health Canada recommends arenas install and maintain carbon monoxide alarms, but its guidance is voluntary.

Vittoria Vecchiarelli, an Ontario-based certified public-health inspector and author of a related Cmaj commentary, said a properly configured alarm could have provided an earlier warning.

“A carbon monoxide sensor with an alarm set at the right level would have alerted staff and players and parents,” she said, “and then action could have been taken sooner.”

The Rockyford incident was not an isolated one.

Vecchiarelli said at least 11 CO and one nitrogen dioxide (NO2) poisoning events were documented at Canadian ice arenas between 2016 and 2026, adding that the documented incidents May not capture the full extent of exposure in Canadian arenas.

“There’s no central catalogue where we can find a list of all the events, and we don’t know how often individuals are exposed to elevated levels that don’t prompt medical attention or intervention and/or emergency evacuation,” she said.

For Vecchiarelli, the incidents underscore the need to move beyond voluntary recommendations.

“We need to set enforceable limits for carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide, and require the installation of carbon monoxide sensors with alarms,” she said.

For families who spend much of the winter inside hockey arenas, the incident has also raised concerns about what repeated exposure could mean.

“We are 10 years into being a hockey family,” Marshall said. “We live at small rinks on the weekends. Never in my wildest dreams did I ever see this happening.”

Lee said while the most severe consequences of acute CO poisoning are well-known, there are also concerns about delayed symptoms and neurological problems associated with chronic exposure.

“Though we worry most about the sudden death of kids that are sleeping in an environment with high carbon monoxide, there are worries about delayed presentation and seizures and headache and confusion and memory and learning difficulties in kids that have chronic, ongoing exposures,” she said.

For children who spend significant amounts of time in arenas, including her own son, Lee said the possibility of repeated exposure is concerning.

CO is an odourless, colourless gas produced by incomplete fuel combustion. The blocked heater exhaust was identified as the source in Rockyford, but Vecchiarelli said there are other potential sources inside arenas, including fuel-powered ice resurfacing equipment and heaters, which can emit CO and (NO2).

“There are guidelines published by Health Canada and various provinces to improve air quality in ice arenas, which include the recommendation to install air monitoring equipment,” she said.

“However, they’re not enforceable.”

She pointed to Minnesota, where indoor air quality regulations include routine arena inspections, education and enforcement.

“They’ve had great success reducing carbon monoxide poisoning events and compliance among arena operators,” she said.

She added that arenas should also regularly maintain fuel-burning equipment, ensure sufficient ventilation and be encouraged to switch to electric ice resurfacing equipment to eliminate CO and (NO2) emissions from that source.

For Marshall’s family, the experience has already changed how they approach every rink they enter.

“It sits on my son’s hockey bag and it gives him peace of mind,” Marshall said.

Lee said the authors hope the report will have an impact beyond the Rockyford incident.

“We really wanted to publish this in a highly regarded medical journal, so that the story of what happened to these kids could be accessed by health-care professionals across the country,” she said, “and people that want to do research in the area of carbon monoxide exposure and prevention.”

For Marshall, the experience has left her wondering why monitors aren’t already required.

“You hear a couple different incidences that have happened and you wonder why they haven’t changed the regulations,” she said.

“It’s not hard. It’s an easy fix to do. They need to do something to fix it.”

CTV News reached out to Health Canada for comment but did not receive a response by deadline.

stories.title: Canadian rescued after yacht found partially submerged off Australian coast
stories.summary: Man was reported to be travelling from Darwin, ON the northern tip of Australia, to the Aussie territory of Christmas Island south of Jakarta, Indonesia
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
A Canadian tourist is reported to be in good health after his yacht was found by Australian rescuers partially submerged in a remote part of the Indian Ocean.

The Australian Maritime Safety Authority, or Amsa, says the man was reported to be travelling from Darwin, ON the northern tip of Australia, to the Aussie territory of Christmas Island south of Jakarta, Indonesia.

An Amsa news release says the yachtsman twice failed to check in with family in Canada on Sunday and his brother contacted authorities in Australia.

Officials say searchers found a partially submerged catamaran in ocean waters roughly 1,000 kilometres east-southeast of Christmas Island, and the man was found in the vessel’s dinghy, also known as a tender.

They say an air rescue helicopter dropped life-saving supplies, such as a life raft and emergency beacon, along with food and water, for the man who was later brought aboard a Royal Australian Navy helicopter.

Alex Barrell with the Amsa says boaters should be prepared before lifting anchor.

“This incident also highlights how quickly circumstances can change and deteriorate offshore and the importance of being prepared before heading to sea,” Barrell said in a news release Monday.

“Having reliable communications and a trusted person ashore who knows when to raise the alarm can make all the difference.”

Dan Gillis, manager of the Amsa Rescue Coordination Centre in Canberra, said in a video statement that there had been severe weather in the area where the vessel was last reported to be.

Gillis said the sailor was in good condition and was to be taken back to the Australian city of Darwin.

“Wonderful to be able to provide assistance to this Canadian sailor who got into trouble in a very remote part of the world,” he said in the video statement.

stories.title: Exclusive: Despite Mexican conviction, this B.C. man remains free in Canada
stories.summary: A W5 Exclusive investigation reveals the legal strategy that is allowing a B.C. man to maintain his freedom, despite being found guilty of murdering his girlfriend while on vacation in Mexico.
stories.author: Avery Haines
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content.

This is part one of a three-part series. On Wednesday, one of Ryan Friesen’s former girlfriends breaks her silence.

Ryan Friesen was convicted of killing his 23-year-old girlfriend, Kiara Agnew, at a Mexican resort in 2023. While he appeals that conviction, he lives as a free man in Canada.

It’s a legal reality that has infuriated many, pushing thousands of Canadians to sign a petition demanding he be sent back to prison.

‘We were screaming’

Friesen, from Dawson Creek, B.C., was initially found not guilty in Kiara’s death at his 2024 trial in Mexico. He returned to Canada, triggering a wave of protests from those who believed the verdict was wrong.

Then, in early 2026, in what legal observers call an exceedingly rare turn, a Mexican judge revoked that acquittal. The judge declared Friesen guilty of femicide.

For Kiara’s aunt, Tanya, who has spent years fighting for justice on her niece’s behalf, the ruling was a long-awaited vindication.

“We were so excited when we got that verdict,” Tanya said. “We were screaming in our homes.”

The case against him

According to court documents, the Mexican judge’s decision to overturn the acquittal and convict Friesen of femicide rested on several key findings:

There was no evidence of any other suspects at the scene of Kiara’s death

Injuries found on Friesen’s hands and knees were consistent with having inflicted the attack

A documented history of past abuse – outlined in Agnew’s own diary – established what the court characterized as a precedent of violence

According to the ruling, and diary entries featured in W5’s multiplatform investigative series “If I Am Ever Found Dead,” Kiara described a previous incident eerily specific to how she was found: Friesen passing out and falling asleep after beating her.

Friesen free for now

Despite the guilty finding, Friesen remains free in Canada while he appeals the Mexican conviction. Tanya says the family isn’t willing to wait quietly.

“He is free as a bird,” she said, “but the Canadian citizens are speaking up.”

A petition calling for Friesen’s imprisonment has drawn roughly 5,600 signatures.

There is no specific timeline for when the appeals court in Mexico will issue its decision, but it could come any day. For Tanya, the wait has taken its toll.

“It’s a very long road,” she said. “And we’re getting tired. We’ve had to fight for things that nobody should have to fight for. We shouldn’t have to be protesting for a convicted man to be put in prison.”

Friesen has not responded to repeated requests for comment. In his last communication with W5 in May, through his lawyer, Friesen maintained his innocence.

You can read parts 1 , 2 and 3 of W5’s investigative series on Kiara Agnew’s murder. You can also watch W5’s “If I’m Ever Found Dead” on CTV News’ YouTube channel .

W5 is the multiplatform investigative unit of CTV News, continuing its decades-long commitment to covering tough, relevant stories.

stories.title: Saskatchewan’s retaliatory tax on American alcohol to kick in for retailers
stories.summary: Unlike other Canadian provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta do not have a ban on American alcohol products
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s government is set to slap its retaliatory tax on American booze today amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced last month his province would implement the 50-per-cent fee on American alcohol on the same day Canada’s reciprocal tariffs take effect.

The move came after trade talks broke down between Canada and the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump implemented a 50-per-cent tariff on Canadian liquor and a range of other goods.

In return, Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to hit back with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs.

Any U.S.-produced alcohol purchased through the Saskatchewan Liquor and Gaming Authority’s online ordering system, used by retailers across the province, is being hit by the levy.

Unlike other Canadian provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta do not have a ban on American alcohol products.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hasn’t followed Saskatchewan’s lead by implementing a reciprocal tax. Following Moe’s announcement, she said her cabinet would consider it.

Moe has said U.S. liquor would remain on store shelves, because the province doesn’t want to limit the public’s ability to choose.

“That is a very important core value for this government,” he said in late August.

He added that residents have been showing support for Canadian products with their wallets, as American booze sales in Saskatchewan are down by about 40 per cent.

“I think that actually sends a much stronger message than any government-ordered ban,” Moe said. “The sale of Saskatchewan-made products has increased at the very same time.”

Opposition NDP Leader Carla Beck called the Saskatchewan Party government’s move a “weak and gutless response” to Trump’s attack on Canada’s sovereignty and economy.

stories.title: Rare hide from extinct wooly dog bred by B.C. First Nations is on display
stories.summary: While woolly dogs – like Mutton, whose pelt is on loan from the Smithsonian – largely disappeared, knowledge of their importance was kept alive in oral history, and traditional weaving
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
After more than 160 years in storage at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, the only known pelt of an extinct woolly dog is back on Canada’s West Coast.

Woolly dogs were once an abundant species, bred by Salish and Makah peoples along the Pacific coast for their soft, woolly fur, which was woven into clothing, blankets and robes, according to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia.

They had fluffy light-coloured coats, curled tails and pointy fox-like faces, similar to a Samoyed, only smaller. They were occasionally shorn for their coats, which were often combined with mountain goat hair and the fibres of plants to make a strong, warm wool. They were considered extinct by the late 1800s, according to UBC, though one was photographed in the 1930s .

Now, the only known pelt in existence is on display at the Museum of Anthropology at UBC until September, 2027, ON loan from the Smithsonian.

When Atheana Picha first laid eyes on it Friday morning during a special private event for the Indigenous community, emotion welled in her throat. She’d grown up hearing stories of woolly dogs passed down through generations.

“The woolly dogs were a big part of our family life,” Ms. Picha said. “Having met this relative now, who left us 200 years ago, is pretty powerful.”

For generations before European contact, textiles like robes and blankets that included woolly dog fur were considered prized possessions, and used sparingly to mark significant community milestones such as marriages and funerals.

While woolly dogs largely disappeared more than a century ago, knowledge of their importance was kept alive in Salish and Makah oral history, and traditional weaving. Ms. Picha herself learned those stories, and now helps keep the tradition alive.

“When we see a weaving ... it’s talking about whose territory we’re on, what history’s here,” she said.

Ms. Picha explained that Salish oral history describes how it was primarily women who cared for the woolly dogs, often keeping them isolated on small islands so they wouldn’t breed with other village dogs used for hunting. They were fed special diets to keep their coats healthy, and shorn about once a year for their fur.

After European contact, the practice of weaving remained an important trade tool for Salish people, but the introduction by settlers of industrially woven fabrics began to erode First Nations’ textile production.

It wasn’t long before colonial laws started banning many Indigenous cultural practices. Residential schools sought to erase Indigenous cultures altogether, said Jordan Wilson, the museum’s curator of Pacific Northwest and contemporary Indigenous art. The federal government’s decades-long potlatch ban, which barred First Nations from participating in traditional ceremonies, was particularly devastating, eroding a central hub for sharing cultural knowledge, he said.

In recent years, interest in woolly dogs and other traditional wool has grown as efforts to revive Salish weaving took off. Ms. Picha is a member of the Tsartlip First Nation on Vancouver Island, and learned traditional Salish weaving from master weaver Debra Sparrow of the Musqueam Nation. In the decades after European contact, the art of Salish weaving was nearly lost. Ms. Picha is part of a new generation of Salish women who are helping to bring it back, and having the chance to see a woolly dog’s fur up close, to feel its curl and texture, is invaluable, she said.

“Seeing the fibres on the pelt, they’re already twisting,” Ms. Picha said, tracing her finger over the pelt’s glass case. “They want to be spun. It’s just hungry to be turned into a blanket, turned into warmth.”

The pelt now on display in Vancouver is from a dog named Mutton, who was the companion of naturalist George Gibbs. Mr. Gibbs helped carry out land surveys establishing the Canada-U.S. border in the mid-19th century.

It’s not known exactly how Mr. Gibbs came to own Mutton, but Mutton is believed to have come from near present-day Chilliwack, B.C. Genetic research suggests Mutton lived to be about 18 months old. Mr. Gibbs sent the pelt to the Smithsonian along with other specimens from his time in Salish territory.

According to Mr. Wilson, the loan was made possible because of work by the Stó:lō House of Respect Caretaking Committee, a group of elders and knowledge-keepers from Stó:lō communities in the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon area. The group helped advocate for its temporary return.

Mr. Wilson is now part of the team responsible for caring for it. He first saw the pelt himself at the Smithsonian years ago, as part of his professional museum training. It’s one of the innumerable Indigenous cultural items removed from their homelands by settlers and sent to museums across the globe, separating the artifacts from their communities.

He said the opportunity to display the pelt close to its original home, even temporarily, is a major milestone.

“I think this is really important,” Mr. Wilson said.

It’s particularly special for the museum he works at. The Museum of Anthropology is usually focused on human creations and cultures, Mr. Wilson said. Western academia tends to view specimens like Mutton’s pelt as natural history artifacts, not anthropological ones.

But Mr. Wilson said that sort of stark division between the human and natural realms isn’t how Indigenous people view the world, or themselves.

From a genetic science perspective, Mutton’s pelt represents the extinction of a unique species, one of the many profound impacts of colonialism, he said. But from an anthropological perspective, it represents the generations-long sinew of Indigenous culture and history tying past to present.

“That really speaks to our ancestors’ connections to territory and place and the beyond-human world,” Mr. Wilson said.

Along with all that history, Ms. Picha sees a long-lost family member finally home for a visit.

“Looking at this pelt, I think of all the things that fed this dog to make it stronger,” Ms. Picha said. “I think of all the people that gave this dog a hug during its life, and all those people who fed it and petted it and saw so much joy.”

The pelt will be on display at the Museum of Anthropology on Ubc’s campus until the end of August, 2027.

stories.title: ‘The world was changing before my eyes’: Airline execs recall how they navigated 9/11
stories.summary: The attacks and the plunge in air travel that followed forced a frenzy of tough choices among aviation and government leaders in the days and weeks afterward, as Sept. 11 pushed some airlines to the brink and beyond, reshaping Canada’s aviation landscape.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calin Rovinescu was strolling through an art museum in Barcelona on a wedding anniversary getaway when he heard the news. In a pair of phone calls, his assistant told him planes had just struck the twin towers in New York City. “I was looking at Picasso’s unique, surrealistic art … as I was hearing a surrealistic story,” Air Canada’s then-executive vice-president recalled.

Rovinescu, who would go on to become CEO, remembers scrambling to find a quiet place to dial into an emergency meeting of Air Canada executives, rushing into the street and through the doors of a café. “The world was changing before my eyes, and the people around me had no clue what was about to happen,” he said.

The attacks and the plunge in air travel that followed forced a frenzy of tough choices among aviation and government leaders in the days and weeks afterward, as Sept. 11 pushed some airlines to the brink and beyond, reshaping Canada’s aviationfA landscape. Leading the call with Rovinescu was then-chief executive Robert Milton, who had just woken up from a nap in London after catching a redeye flight from Montreal.

Receiving special clearance from the Canadian, U.S. and U.K. governments, Milton managed to fly back to Canada the day after the tragedy alongside Rovinescu, who’d hopped over to London from Spain. European airspace remained open. “I remember being on the flight deck with the crew,” Milton said of the voyage, taken in a Bombardier Challenger business jet loaned last-minute by that company’s CEO.

Air Canada’s 300-plus planes were grounded. “It was truly eerie because there was no radio communication at all, whereas normally there’d be an armada of aircraft crossing the Atlantic in both directions. The chatter was non-existent.” Marie-Hélène Lévesque, special assistant to transport minister David Collenette at the time, drove back to Ottawa from Montreal the morning of Sept.

11 with her boss. They had ducked out of an airport conference, where his speech was interrupted by the jangle of cellphones in the audience as executives got word of the unfolding disaster. “In that minivan, all the major decisions were taken,” said Lévesque, now director general of the Public Health Agency of Canada.

Following the lead of American authorities, Collenette greenlit the closure of Canada’s airspace minutes after a Boeing 757 crashed into the U.S. Pentagon at 9:37 a.m. It marked the first time ever that either country had taken such a step. “This was the third plane, and we didn’t know how many more there were,” said then-deputy minister Margaret Bloodworth.

Before the battery died on his cell, Collenette instructed Nav Canada to order 270 planes over the Atlantic Ocean to turn around and fly back to Europe. He also oversaw the landing of 224 other diverted flights carrying 33,000 passengers to 17 Canadian airports in a matter of hours, the most extensive aircraft grounding in the country’s history.

In Gander, N.L., the airport took on 38 planes carrying 6,500 people. The hardiness and hospitality of the town’s 9,000-plus residents became known to the world via the Broadway hit musical “Come From Away,” which chronicled their experience hosting the stranded travellers. “Some of them sat for 24 hours because we weren’t ready to let them off the planes until we had enough customs and immigration people there to screen them.

We didn’t know who was on them,” said Bloodworth. “They didn’t know until they landed what had happened because it was not the days where you could have the internet from planes,” she added. “And the pilots by and large did not tell passengers until they landed, because there’s no point in panicking people.”

In the weeks and months that followed, politicians and bureaucrats allocated billions of dollars for new security measures and the creation of the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority, which took charge of passenger screening processes that until then had been in the hands of individual airlines.

An eventual gauntlet of checkpoints and protocols — shoes off, laptops out, liquids limited to 100 millilitres — signalled a permanent shift in how travellers fly. Meanwhile, airlines struggled to absorb the blow of plummeting demand. A majority of Air Canada revenues stemmed from flights to and from the United States, including routes where Canada was a layover point for overseas trips, Milton said.

The plunge in air travel demand in the post-9/11 months severely dented earnings. Air Canada cut 6,600 workers and posted a $1.25-billion loss in 2001 after losing hundreds of millions of dollars in sales in the fourth quarter alone. The US$15 billion in grants and loan guarantees that American rivals received didn’t help, as Canadian carriers received relatively little in financial aid — about C$160 million.

“When so much of your revenues are generated in the U.S market and your competition receives so much subsidization, you’re going to be destabilized. And we were destabilized,” Milton said. The country’s second-largest airline, discount carrier Canada 3000, soon folded. It was placed in bankruptcy in November 2001.

Numerous airlines across the globe met a similar fate, ranging from Ansett Australia to Swiss Air. Others restructured under bankruptcy protection in the decade that followed, including almost every U.S. legacy carrier and, in 2003, Air Canada. “It led to a big, big restructuring. It highlighted the fragility of the cost structure,” said Rovinescu.

“The events of 9/11 lasted a long time.” Though painful, Air Canada’s 18-month restructuring — brought on by the decline in travel sparked by the attacks and the Sars epidemic in 2002-03 — allowed it to wipe out $13 billion in debt, much of it incurred from its acquisition of Canadian Airlines in 2000.

It also reached aggressive cost-cutting deals with more than a half-dozen labour unions, pared down its regional jet fleet and focused on higher-margin international routes — a strategy that continues to this day. Air Canada’s bankruptcy protection process and the disappearance of Canadian Airlines and Canada 3000 paved the runway for Calgary-based WestJet to beef up its domestic network and grow into the country’s second-biggest carrier.

“It allowed WestJet to flourish ... without having to worry about a lot of competition pushing them around,” said John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University. “And 9/11 put carriers that were on the on the edge of financial performance out of business.” For all the vulnerability and financial brittleness that Sept.

11 revealed, it also showcased an underlying perseverance, said Rovinescu, who sees parallels with the COVID-19 pandemic’s hit to the travel industry. “COVID was in some respects worse because of the duration of it and the unpredictability as to when it would end. Whereas 9/11 was more of a controlled environment — we knew the ... closure was for a certain number of days,” he said.

“But the takeaway was, this is a resilient industry.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026. Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto condo developer launches $10M lawsuit against online critics, alleging a 'malicious campaign'
stories.summary: Claims pair are using social media to post damaging videos to hurt the company’s reputation and sales.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
A Canadian condo developer has launched a $10-million lawsuit against online critics whose videos complaining about two of the company’s newest projects have racked up hundreds of thousands of views on social media sites TikTok and RedNote.

In a statement of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court, Concord Adex alleges that the owners of the TikTok account @Sailor.of.Justice and a Chinese-language RedNote user known as Toronto Sailors Light the Lamp have conducted a “highly coordinated and malicious campaign to cause as much damage as possible” to the company’s reputation and sales.

Concord is separately suing more than 50 buyers for defaulting on agreements to purchase units in the two recently built condos in Toronto that feature in many of the online posts: the three-tower King’s Landing site on Esther Shiner Boulevard in North York and the twin-tower Canada House development on Concord Cityplace Way in downtown Toronto.

The developer’s lawsuit says that the social media users have intentionally interfered with Concord’s economic relations, alleging that their videos were posted “for the ulterior purpose of creating a false pretense” to get themselves and others out of their agreed deals.

The TikTok account’s most-watched video, which has been viewed close to 400,000 times, includes footage of floodwater gushing through a parking garage under Canada House, intercut with scenes of leaking ceilings, damaged flooring and bathroom clean-ups.

According to Concord’s legal filings, the video leaves viewers with the false impression that the company was responsible for the parking garage flood, when they say it was actually caused by a burst in the city’s water line. In addition, they say the video was filmed before any owners had moved into Canada House and that the damage was repaired before occupants arrived.

Other posts and comments by the TikTok and RedNote account holders falsely allege that Concord’s developments are poorly constructed, unsafe to live in and that the company was responsible for a gas explosion that interrupted construction of the King’s Landing project, Concord says.

According to reports at the time of the October 2025 explosion, seven people were taken to hospital. Ontario’s Ministry of Labour said in a statement to the Post that it could not provide any details as the investigation is ongoing.

The developer’s lawsuit takes issue with a total of 60 posts and comments made across the two accounts between July 2025 – soon after residents began occupying Canada House – and May 2026, a month after Concord received occupancy permits for the King’s Landing development. They include comments falsely implying that building inspectors had been bribed by Concord and a sarcastic reference wishing early death on a Concord representative with terminal cancer, the company alleges.

Alongside the unidentified TikTok user J. Doe 1, Concord’s claim names North York resident Yiwei Mao as the operator of the RedNote account, explaining that it was able to identify him through a Chinese court proceeding against the Shanghai-headquartered social media firm, whose users are predominantly based in China and southeast Asia.

Concord has launched a related action against TikTok’s Canadian subsidiary in the Ontario Superior Court, asking the social media giant to turn over user information for the Sailor of Justice account, including associated email addresses, phone numbers and IP addresses.

None of the allegations in Concord’s claim have been proven in court.

Neither Mao nor his lawyers replied to request for comment, but in a statement of defence filed in July, he denies the company’s allegations and asks the court to dismiss the claim.

Concord’s corporate entities cannot succeed with a defamation claim, Mao argues, for comments that refer solely to their individual officers, employees and lawyers – none of whom are named as plaintiffs. He also takes issue with Concord’s translation of his Chinese-language posts on RedNote, promising to provide his own versions before examinations for discovery.

In any case, Mao alleges that each of the posts are defensible, claiming that they are all either substantially true or were fair comment on matters of public interest.

“The words were published on the basis of an honest belief in the truth of the statements,” Mao’s defence continues.

Concord’s additional claims for intentional interference with economic relations and conspiracy are “dressed-up claims in defamation,” Mao says in his statement of defence, claiming they are “simply an attempt to stifle or muzzle the Defendant from exercising his right of free expression relating to matters of public interest.”

As part of its claim against Mao, Concord also seeks to retain $212,000 in deposits paid by Mao since he signed an agreement of purchase and sale (APS) for a $1.06-million unit in the King’s Landing development, back in December 2021.

Although Mao attended a pre-delivery inspection in April 2026, the company says he breached the agreement when he failed to close the deal as scheduled the following month. Concord’s claim demands damages to cover any loss in the unit’s value, as well as the marketing and carrying costs associated with the search for a fresh buyer.

In his statement of defence, Mao disputes the validity of the APS and says that the contract should be declared void. Mao alleges that he was rushed into signing the agreement and claims not to have received statutorily required disclosure documents at the time he signed.

He’s not the only one facing legal action over the failure to close a deal with Concord. Since February, Concord has filed more than 50 claims for breach of contract against buyers in its Canada House and King’s Landing projects, according to Ontario Superior Court records.

Like Mao, many of the buyers sued by Concord agreed to their purchases before the Toronto condo market crash. According to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, the average price of a unit in the city peaked in the first quarter of 2022, at around $810,000. Meanwhile, the most recent report – released in the spring of 2026 – pegged the average price at just below $650,000.

Probably driving the condo company crazy

In a statement, Concord lawyer Brian Kolenda said he was limited on what he could say due to the litigation, but added that the company had taken “appropriate steps to safeguard its business and reputation” and to ensure a safe work environment for its employees.

“Concord is always prepared to receive and address fair and legitimate concerns from its customers. However, if social media is used to spread defamatory material about our business and employees, we will respond appropriately,” said Kolenda, a partner at Toronto law firm Lenczner Slaght LLP. “The anonymous online activity at issue in our litigation goes well beyond any kind of legitimate online expression.”

Iain MacKinnon, a media and defamation lawyer who has no involvement in the case, says Concord could have a tough time when it comes to the non-contractual elements of their claim.

“It’s typically an uphill battle for corporations to sue for defamation,” he says, explaining that compensation for hurt feelings, mental anguish or humiliation is not a realistic prospect for businesses in the same way as individual plaintiffs.

“Corporate plaintiffs can only really get damages for provable financial losses,” adds MacKinnon, the principal at Toronto’s MacKinnon Law PC.

He says he will be watching the case to see if Mao or his co-defendant attempts to have the case dismissed under Ontario’s anti-Slapp law, which allows judges to screen out lawsuits that unduly chill expressions on matters of public interest.

“If there is a motion, a lot will turn on whether he has a valid defence,” MacKinnon says. “To me, the real question is whether this is intended to muzzle Mao and whether there is any validity to his claim that these condos are deficient in some way.

“I wouldn’t say it’s a terribly malicious campaign in the grand scheme of things, in terms of attacks on individuals. But it does appear to be somewhat relentless and that’s probably driving the condo company crazy.”

stories.title: Freedom of information? Here’s what Ontario’s government doesn’t want you to know
stories.summary: Tougher Freedom-of-Information (FOI) laws mean more requests for records are being rejected. We filed an FOI request to find out which ones
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
What was in his calendar between Feb. 5 and April 21, 2026?

And what briefings did he get for a June 2025 meeting with U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra?

These are just some of the many things that Ontario’s government won’t tell the public.

Between April 27 and June 19, records obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau show government’s cabinet office refused 48 freedom-of-information requests by citing new provincial legislation that allows the premier and his cabinet to keep their office records secret from public scrutiny. The change passed as part of omnibus legislation in April.

Freedom-of-information (FOI) legislation was originally meant as a tool the public could use to ask for specific government records, with a goal of making government more accountable and open. Federal, provincial and territorial governments each have their own versions of such laws.

Two of the refused Ontario FOI requests obtained by the IJB asked questions about the redevelopment of Ontario Place , where plans for a mega-spa have run up against opposition; two took interest in the 52-kilometre Highway 413 project northwest of Toronto; one request looked for calls Ford received about the private jet he was pressured to return.

Some of the requests were newly filed. One was from last year, and three were from 2023. (The legislated timeframe for a response to an FOI request is 30 days.) At least one, filed April 2, sought records that had already been released.

He calls himself a prophet. But some say this Toronto-area pastor exploited his flock for years

Not Criminally Responsible: The broken system behind the killers who don’t go to jail

All were turned down.

The list of refused freedom-of-information requests, which the IJB obtained through an FOI request of its own, is not exhaustive and is missing refused requests that were made to other ministries besides the cabinet office. But it provides a snapshot into what information the Ford government will no longer make public. Ford’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

At the time the legislative change was made, Ford said it was necessary to protect himself and his cabinet from “communist China,” to update what he characterized as an outdated framework and to protect the privacy of, for example, people he corresponds with. (Personal information was already exempted from Ontario’s freedom-of-information regime.)

Journalist and freedom-of-information expert Dean Beeby told the IJB the 48-denial tally is higher than he expected given that the legislation has only been in place for a brief time.

“The law would have put off a lot of people. People who might normally have filed (a request) would have sort of read the changes and decided not to bother,” he said.

“It sounds like a lot to me.”

And it shows what is lost through legislation like this, he said.

Two of the refused Ontario FOI requests obtained by the IJB asked questions about the redevelopment of Ontario Place , where plans for a mega-spa have run up against opposition; two took interest in the 52-kilometre Highway 413 project northwest of Toronto; one request looked for calls Ford received about the private jet he was pressured to return.

Some of the requests were newly filed. One was from last year, and three were from 2023. (The legislated timeframe for a response to an FOI request is 30 days.) At least one, filed April 2, sought records that had already been released.

stories.title: Cancer organizations urge national panel to review outdated testing advice for prostate cancer
stories.summary: Signatories say current guideline is out of step with clinical practice, and must be updated to advance detection and prevention
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Leading cancer organizations, in an open letter, are calling on a national panel on preventative health to immediately review its guidance for prostate cancer, which has not been updated for more than a decade.

The Canadian Cancer Society, Movember Canada, The Walnut Foundation, and the Canadian Urological Association are among 11 organizations, advocates and researchers in prostate cancer who released the letter Tuesday calling on the National Advisory Committee on Preventative Health Services to revise their recommendations.

The signatories said the current guideline, which is that prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is not recommended for any age, is out of step with clinical practice. They argue that it must be updated to advance cancer detection and prevention and to ultimately save lives.

“What we have now is a guideline that is frozen in time from over a decade ago,” the letter states. “We are asking that Canadians receive what they should reasonably expect from a national advisory body: a fair, transparent and timely review of the evidence as it exists today.”

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in Canada, with an estimated one in eight men expected to be diagnosed in their lifetime. The risk nearly doubles for Black men, who are often diagnosed at a younger age.

The national advisory committee, a new 14-person body, was announced by Ottawa in June. It is tasked with creating guidelines to support primary-care health professionals and teams in their delivery of preventive health services. An older version of the group was shut down more than a year earlier after it faced intense criticism for not lowering the screening age for breast cancer to 40 from 50.

The formal guidance for prostate cancer has not been updated since 2014, when the panel concluded that harms outweighed the benefits of PSA screening. The simple blood test can serve as an early warning signal of cancer in men with no symptoms.

Some of the concerns noted include overdiagnosis – the detection of cancers that would not progress to cause symptoms or death – and the prevalence of false-positive results.

The committee is an independent advisory body to the Public Health Agency of Canada.

Mark Johnson, a spokesperson with the national agency, said in a statement that the committee “will begin to identify and prioritize potential topics for future guideline development” in the coming months. He said both bodies are reviewing the open letter.

Brandon Purcell, an advocacy manager with the Canadian Cancer Society, said in an interview that the outdated recommendation continues to have real-world consequences, pointing to the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia who do not cover the cost of PSA testing for asymptomatic men with a physician referral.

He’s hopeful that new guidance would influence both provinces to update their policies, helping to ensure that the most at-risk groups can access testing.

“The truth with all cancers is that the earlier you find it, the more likely survival is,” said Mr. Purcell. “With prostate cancer, the difference really is staggering. When you’re able to find it at an earlier stage, the likelihood of survival is almost 100 per cent.”

Once the cancer spreads beyond the prostate, the survival rate drops significantly, “which is why it makes all the difference in the world to find it early.”

Since the 2014 recommendation , advancements have been made in the diagnosis and management of prostate cancer that help mitigate issues of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. For example, screening is shifting away from PSAs and rectal exams to targeted prebiopsy imaging and newer blood tests .

There is also greater emphasis now on the relationship between doctors and patients, who together make informed decisions about testing.

A study published in September, 2025, concluded that Canada’s screening approach should be reconsidered. The authors said the current strategy May amplify harms and disparities, especially among populations at highest risk.

Anthony Henry, president of The Walnut Foundation, a Canadian charity that provides support to Black men with prostate cancer and their families, said there must be greater awareness, especially in the Black community, ON the benefits of screening early.

The foundation, alongside the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, has recently started a free screening program in Toronto for Black men aged 40 and over. He said between 14 and 22 per cent of the people tested, depending on the population, require follow-up.

“It tells you there that there’s a problem,” said Mr. Henry, whose father died of prostate cancer, and who himself started screening at 40.

“My brother went on at age 57 to have prostate cancer. I went on to have prostate cancer at 53 and my uncle in his late 60s. What’s different between the three of us that survived from my dad is he wasn’t screened.”

Cancer organizations, in the open letter, highlighted that, since 2014, researchers have gained a better understanding of which men are at highest risk, including those with a family history and excess weight. The use of MRIs for diagnosing has also helped to reduce unnecessary biopsies, they noted.

Each year that passes without an update is a disservice to physicians and patients, said the group.

“Prioritizing prostate cancer would send a clear signal to patients, healthcare providers and health organizations across Canada that the era of woefully outdated guidance is coming to an end,” the letter states.
