stories.title: Canada’s counter-tariffs take effect today. Here’s what could cost you more
stories.summary: From furniture to dairy, hundreds of U.S. products are facing new or higher tariffs. Here is what buyers need to know.
stories.author: Anastasia Blosser
stories.content:
For Canadians already watching every dollar, Tuesday could bring another unwelcome addition to the household budget.

Canada’s latest round of counter-tariffs on U.S. imports took effect shortly after midnight Tuesday, covering $27.6 billion worth of American goods. The federal government says the measures apply to more than 700 U.S. product lines .

The measures target hundreds of products across sectors including steel and aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics. According to the federal government, tariffs will range from 15 to 50 per cent, depending on the product. Some existing tariffs will also increase to match the rate imposed by the United States .

Though some goods will be subject to high tariffs that will likely make them more expensive, that doesn’t necessarily mean prices will increase by the same amount. Economists and tariff experts told the Star the cost will depend on how much of the tariff businesses absorb and how much they pass on to consumers.

The Bank of Canada studied the effect of Canada’s previous round of counter-tariffs and found prices for affected products rose gradually after the tariffs took effect in March 2025. By mid-June, those products were about six per cent more expensive than comparable products that weren’t subject to tariffs — roughly one-quarter of the 25 per cent tariff.

The bank also found prices fell back toward their previous levels relatively quickly after most of those tariffs were removed. So while tariffs can push up prices, a 25 or 50 per cent tariff does not necessarily translate into the same increase at the cash register.

Here’s what consumers need to know:

Signal49 Research chief economist Pedro Antunes said tariffs on imported food products could add to costs, although domestic producers and other sources of supply could limit the impact.

Most grocery items have escaped the wrath of trade tensions as Canada's reciprocal tariffs took effect on Tuesday. But economists say some items, such as health and beauty products, could see prices rise in the short term. (Sept. 8, 2026)

Most food Canadians buy is produced domestically or imported from countries other than the United States, according to Statistics Canada. However, a University of British Columbia study found nearly half of the vegetables consumed in Canada, excluding potatoes, are imported, while roughly 75 per cent of fruit is imported.

Dairy is among the sectors targeted by the new counter-tariffs, including milk, cream and cheese. Antunes said there could be an adjustment cost, but Canada has lots of dairy manufacturing, and products could be imported from other trade partners.

Even when an American product is affected, retailers May be able to substitute products from Canadian or other suppliers. Antunes told the Star those alternatives could limit the effect on consumers, although reduced choice could also put upward pressure on prices. Consumers May therefore notice changes in particular products rather than an across-the-board jump in grocery costs.

Fish and seafood appeared on the initial list announced by the federal government, but the updated list for Tuesday’s measures is the one consumers and businesses should rely on. The government’s current list contains some fish-related products already subject to earlier measures, but does not impose the broad new seafood tariff that appeared in the original announcement.

Shampoo and conditioner could be among the personal-care products to see noticeable price increases. Joseph Steinberg, an economics professor at the University of Toronto, expects U.S.-made hair products to see “double-digit price increases” as retailers grapple with the added cost of retaliatory tariffs.

Counter-tariffs are expected to hit Sept. 8 — here’s how to shop smarter before and after the deadline.

Shampoo and conditioner are not named explicitly on Canada’s tariff list, but “preparations for use on the hair” are subject to a 50 per cent tariff.

Other beauty products are also facing the highest tariff rate, with products for the lips, eyes, manicures and pedicures subject to a 50 per cent tariff. The category also includes sunscreen and suntanning preparations.

Steinberg said he expects the higher costs to have an “interesting gender impact,” with women disproportionately affected by increases in personal-care and beauty products. Consumers looking to avoid the tariffs can look for Canadian-made products or alternatives sourced from Europe or Asia, where available.

For anyone planning a major appliance purchase, the new tariffs add another potential source of upward pressure.

The updated tariff list includes household appliances such as refrigerators, dishwashers and freezers, with many subject to a 25 per cent tariff. University of Toronto operations management professor Andre Cire told the Star those appliances could become more expensive as businesses adjust to higher costs.

The tariff is charged when a covered product enters Canada. Importers and retailers can then decide how much of that cost to absorb or pass on to consumers. Cire said it remains to be seen how much will ultimately be passed on.

The latest U.S. tariffs on more than 700 Canadian products took effect last month.

The increases also come with an important caveat: it’s the product’s origin that matters, not simply the brand name. A product made by an American company is not necessarily U.S.-origin, while a product made in the United States can be subject to the tariff even if its manufacturer is based elsewhere.

Furniture is another category that could hit household budgets, particularly for people planning a move, renovation or major purchase.

The tariff list covers a broad range of furniture, including wooden kitchen and bedroom furniture, domestic furniture and metal furniture. The Star’s previous reporting found furniture among the products that could become more expensive, with tariff experts warning that higher import costs could work their way through to consumers. Because furniture can be expensive, even a modest percentage increase can add up quickly.

Clothing and footwear are also among the consumer goods Canadians should watch, with specific U.S.-origin products appearing on the tariff list.

Some products facing tariffs May be less obvious. Golf clubs, for example, are among the U.S. consumer goods targeted by the measures, meaning golfers shopping for new equipment could face higher prices if they buy an affected U.S.-origin product.

With files from Lora Grady and Sadeen Mohsen.

stories.title: Canadian teens still rank among the world’s best in reading, math and science — but scores are slipping. Here’s why
stories.summary: Canada's decline in 2025 mirrors a global downward trend, according to findings from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
stories.author: Isabel Teotonio
stories.content:
Canadian students are still outpacing most of the developed world when it comes to math, reading and science, but their scores continue to slide, according to international test results released Tuesday.

Canada’s decline mirrors a global downward trend, according to the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd), which in 2025 tested 15-year-olds in those three subjects and surveyed them about habits, attitudes and home life.

But what stands out in the Canadian data is a rare combination of strong academic results with strong social-emotional outcomes, meaning most teens across the country are curious, persevering, goal-oriented and engaged in learning.

“Those kinds of things are actually also really important,” Andreas Schleicher, Oecd’s director for education and skills, told the Star in an interview. Canada, he said, is one of the few countries that manages to “reconcile” both, unlike some other countries such as Singapore that excel academically, but sometimes at the expense of student well-being.

The test was taken by more than 760,000 students worldwide, while in Canada about 24,600 teens in 897 schools took part. Canada’s scores are measured against the Oecd average — a benchmark drawn from 38 of the world’s wealthiest nations, including Canada — but the test included 91 countries and economies.

In 2025, four Chinese jurisdictions — Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang — competed as a single education system in Pisa, and along with Singapore topped the rankings across all three subjects. Also in the top 10 across all three subjects were Macao, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Estonia, and the United Kingdom. Canada scored ninth in science, eleventh in math and 12th in reading.

Oecd countries, however, recorded their worst results on record across all three subjects since the Pisa was first administered in 2000. Reading has slid since 2012, math has fallen sharply since 2018 and science has gradually declined over the past decade.

The Pisa report flags “steep declines” in reading as particularly alarming, calling it “the gateway through which most academic learning passes.”

“The decline in reading skills is really troubling, because (students) are losing the kind of reading skills that are particularly valuable in the AI world: the capacity of students to reflect, to contrast, critique, evaluate,” explained Schleicher.

By contrast, the report notes that instances of “hasty reading,” with students giving fast and incorrect responses, almost doubled in Oecd countries between 2018 and 2025. “In a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise,” it warns.

A change coming this fall for Grade 9s will make the provincewide test worth 20 per cent of the

Schleicher said skimming and scrolling through social media, and processing information quickly, May be making it tougher for kids to engage in deep reading with complex texts.

A separate concern is that the majority of young people in Oecd countries believe common sense should be relied on more than evidence and scientific study.

“I would have expected school is all about building an evidence-based world view and making you trust in science, research and data ... But at the end of the day, it doesn’t seem that we are that successful,” said Schleicher. Many schools, he added, May be teaching students about physics and chemistry, but they’re not teaching them to “think like a scientist.”

The most recent Pisa test, which is administered every three years, saw Canadian scores hit their lowest point, yet they remain above the Oecd average. Canadian teens achieved 510 points in science (Oecd average 482), 490 in reading (Oecd average 461), and 485 in mathematics (Oecd average 463). (For comparison purposes, the combined score of the four Chinese jurisdictions was 597 in science, 527 in reading, and 612 in math.)

For the first time, the 2025 test also measured computational problem solving, with Canadian teens scoring 525, versus an Oecd average of 500.

Another bright spot in the test is that the gap between Canada’s most and least socio-economically advantaged students remains below the Oecd average, suggesting Canada has a more equitable system than many of its peers.

Oecd Director for Education and Skills Andreas Schleicher says declining parental interest in education in Canada is worrisome.

However, Schleicher warned that Canada May be growing complacent.

“I do think Canada has become, perhaps, a bit complacent in levelling down the horizon of (its) learners,” he said, noting that score declines here have been steeper among students from advantaged backgrounds than disadvantaged, which is unusual. That, he said, suggests a lowering of ambitions and expectations.

Schleicher said when looking at the Canadian data he was struck by how parental interest in education has “deteriorated quite a lot,” noting parental involvement is an even stronger predictor of learning outcomes than family wealth.

For instance in 2025, only 69 per cent of students said their parents asked them at least once a week about school, down from 78 per cent in 2022. And weekly conversations about problems at school dropped to 40 per cent, down from 55 per cent.

“It’s not about parents doing three hours of homework with their kids. It’s more about parents showing students what you do in school matters to me,” he said. “That used to be the case in Canada: Parents were very interested. And now they seem to have become more like the client of schools.”

Tests from physics to phys-ed can help ensure students know the material. But should evaluations

When it comes to AI, Canadian students use chatbots for school work less than the Oecd average — 38 per cent reported using them at least once a week, compared with 46 per cent across Oecd countries. Pisa data show that students who don’t use AI tend to outperform those who do, but the report stops short of saying AI is the cause of lower scores.

Schleicher pointed to a broader concern, saying Canadian teens are increasingly using technology for passive consumption rather than creative or academic purposes.

“You do not become fit by watching sports — you become fit by doing sports. And we see the same: learning is always about cognitive effort. Technology makes things easier for you, but doesn’t make you stronger,” he said.

That digital distraction is showing up in Canadian classrooms, with 32 per cent of students saying their peers are often distracted by digital devices, compared with the Oecd average of 28 per cent.

And that’s concerning because Schleicher said cellphone use for leisure purposes in school “has probably done more damage than school closures during the pandemic.”

Improving outcomes in Canada isn’t a matter of increasing funding, said Schleicher, noting Canada already spends significantly on education. Rather, it’s about allocating resources more strategically.

Carleton University researchers urge the province to introduce universal early numeracy

High-performing education systems, he said, make deliberate choices about where to invest, and when forced to choose between hiring better teachers or reducing class sizes, they choose the former.

“They squarely put the emphasis on getting the best people to teach students, ensuring that the most talented teachers teach the most challenging students, get the best principals for the toughest schools. And they don’t care very much about the size of classes,” he said. “We don’t see much of a relationship between the size of classes and learning outcomes. We see a very robust relationship between the quality of teachers and the time teachers have for caring for students and outcomes.”

stories.title: Missing person
stories.summary: London, ON (September 8, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 37-year-old Devin Hamilton.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 8, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 37-year-old Devin Hamilton.

The missing person is described as male, White, approximately 5'10'', thin build, with brown hair. He was last seen on August 18, 2026, in the area of Wellington Road and Horton Street East.

While the investigation was initially led by the St. Thomas Police Service, investigators determined that the missing person was last seen in London. The London Police Service has since assumed carriage of the investigation in accordance with provincial best practices related to jurisdiction in missing person cases.

Family and police are concerned for his welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Replica firearms, drugs and identity documents seized
stories.summary: London, ON (September 8, 2026) – A suspect was arrested within minutes of a weapons complaint Monday evening after a witness reported seeing what appeared to be a firearm pointed at a passing vehicle in east London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (September 8, 2026) – A suspect was arrested within minutes of a weapons complaint Monday evening after a witness reported seeing what appeared to be a firearm pointed at a passing vehicle in east London.

On September 7, 2026, at approximately 5:45 p.m., a man was driving in the area of Belfield Street when he observed a suspect point what appeared to be a firearm toward the passenger side of his vehicle. The witness immediately contacted police.

Officers responded, located, and arrested a suspect a short distance away.

During a search following the arrest, officers located two replica firearms in the suspect's backpack.

One of the imitation firearms matched the description provided by the witness. As the investigation continued, officers also located several identification and banking documents belonging to other individuals, along with a quantity drugs and drug paraphernalia.

The following items were seized:

Two replica firearms

Multiple bank cards belonging to individuals other than the accused

Health cards belonging to individuals other than the accused

Membership cards belonging to individuals other than the accused

A driver's licence belonging to an individual other than the accused

Approximately 0.3 grams of suspected crystal methamphetamine

Drug paraphernalia

As a result of the investigation, Ryan John Wilson, 46, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Pointing a firearm;

Possession of an identity document;

Possession of imitation weapon;

Breach of probation; and

Possession of a Schedule I substance.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

The London Police Service would like to recognize the actions of the citizen in immediately reporting the incident, which led to the quick arrest of the accused by members of the LPS Uniformed Division.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Canada holds first defence co-ordination talks with China in more than eight years
stories.summary: Carney’s government, which has faced blowback from Trump over its relationship with Beijing, issued no statement to mark the event
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Canada has restarted military talks with China after a break of more than eight years that began with Beijing’s jailing of two Canadians in late 2018.

The two countries held a “defence coordination dialogue” on Sept. 4, according to a statement issued the day after the meeting by China’s Ministry of National Defense.

Beijing was the only side to publicly announce this new milestone in thawing relations between Canada and China under Prime Minister Mark Carney. Mr. Carney’s government, which has faced blowback from U.S. President Donald Trump over its new “strategic partnership” with China, issued no statement to mark the event.

In response to questions from The Globe and Mail, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence confirmed Monday that the meeting took place in Ottawa last week.

“As part of ongoing working-level dialogue, Canadian and Chinese defence officials met on September 4, in support of ongoing military-to-military communications at the functional level,” said department spokesperson Nick Drescher Brown in a statement.

“This meeting is consistent with Canada’s broader defence engagement with partners across the Indo-Pacific region and is anchored in our commitment to protecting the safety of Canadians and the strategic interests of Canada. As a matter of longstanding practice, the Government of Canada does not publicize working-level meetings by officials.”

Between 2013 and 2018, Canada conducted four “defence coordination dialogues” with China, with the last one in April, 2018.

A Canadian official said on background that fewer than 10 staff members from the Canadian Armed Forces , the Department of National Defence and the department of Global Affairs attended last week’s meeting with Chinese counterparts. The military ranks in attendance ranged between major general and the rank of colonel in the army and air force, which corresponds to captain in the navy, the same official said. The Globe is not naming the official because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

In a statement posted on China’s Ministry of Defense website, Beijing said the Canadian and Chinese sides “had a candid and in-depth exchange of views on international and regional issues of mutual interest, expressed willingness to strengthen practical exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries, and enhanced mutual understanding and trust.”

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and chief executive officer of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank, said the federal government owes Canadians a clear explanation as to why it is reopening this defence communication channel, noting that China has grown increasingly assertive in Asia since 2018.

In recent years, China’s armed forces have become far more assertive in contested zones throughout the Indo-Pacific, engaging in close encounters with foreign planes, sending maritime law enforcement ships to confront Philippine resupply craft in the South China Sea, and increasing pressure on Taiwan through frequent military manoeuvres close to the self-governing island. In earlier times, Beijing leaned heavily on negotiation and financial influence to press its sovereignty claims, but today it frequently underpins these with deployments of naval vessels, combat aircraft and civilian-crewed flotillas.

The Canadian official, speaking of the Sept. 4 meeting with China, played down the event, calling it a routine dialogue to exchange views on regional and global security matters, and to communicate respective priorities and concerns.

The official did not disclose the content of discussions, but China has vociferously complained about Canada sending warships through the Taiwan Strait separating the People’s Republic of China from the island Beijing considers a breakaway province. Canadian warships often traverse the Taiwan Strait with the United States and other Western countries, effectively challenging Beijing’s claims to what the West regards as an international waterway. The U.S. calls its transits “freedom of navigation” operations.

In late 2023, then-Canadian defence minister Bill Blair accused Beijing of unprofessional and unsafe conduct after a Chinese warplane fired flares in front of a Canadian helicopter flying over international waters in the South China Sea.

Ms. Nadjibulla said Canadians should hear about rekindled defence ties from Ottawa rather than having to rely on Beijing’s announcement.

“A lot has changed since Canada last conducted such dialogue with China in 2018,” she said. China’s increasingly aggressive conduct in the South China Sea and around Taiwan “remains a serious concern for Canada and its Indo-Pacific and European partners,” Ms. Nadjibulla noted.

Ottawa must explain if this channel is for risk management and crisis communication or whether it’s an expansion of the new strategic partnership Mr. Carney struck with China in January, she said.

In his statement, Mr. Drescher Brown said: “As the Prime Minister has consistently said, Canada’s renewed engagement with China will be guided by a series of guardrails. Under this framework, there are specific areas in which we will seek deeper cooperation with China and areas where we will not, which includes on defence.”

Retired general Wayne Eyre, formerly the chief of the defence staff, said the dialogue appears to be focused on communication, not co-operation, adding it’s important to sustain lines of communication with other countries, including rivals.

“Throughout history, maintaining communication with an adversary has been useful to deepen understanding and avoid unintended escalation,” he said. “Historical examples abound: Cold War hotline, Pakistan-India hotline, and US-Russia hotline during the Syrian conflict.” Mr. Eyre said even during his time in Korea “we had a line to the North Koreans.”

A senior U.S. military official also met with a Chinese counterpart in Victoria last week.

Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Pacific Command, met with General Yang Zhibin, commander of the People’s Liberation Army’s Eastern Theater Command, during the 28th Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defense Conference that took place Aug. 31 to Sept. 2.

The two countries held a “defence coordination dialogue” on Sept. 4, according to a statement issued the day after the meeting by China’s Ministry of National Defense.

Beijing was the only side to publicly announce this new milestone in thawing relations between Canada and China under Prime Minister Mark Carney. Mr. Carney’s government, which has faced blowback from U.S. President Donald Trump over its new “strategic partnership” with China, issued no statement to mark the event.
In response to questions from The Globe and Mail, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence confirmed Monday that the meeting took place in Ottawa last week.

“As part of ongoing working-level dialogue, Canadian and Chinese defence officials met on September 4, in support of ongoing military-to-military communications at the functional level,” said department spokesperson Nick Drescher Brown in a statement.

“This meeting is consistent with Canada’s broader defence engagement with partners across the Indo-Pacific region and is anchored in our commitment to protecting the safety of Canadians and the strategic interests of Canada. As a matter of longstanding practice, the Government of Canada does not publicize working-level meetings by officials.”
Between 2013 and 2018, Canada conducted four “defence coordination dialogues” with China, with the last one in April, 2018.

A Canadian official said on background that fewer than 10 staff members from the Canadian Armed Forces , the Department of National Defence and the department of Global Affairs attended last week’s meeting with Chinese counterparts. The military ranks in attendance ranged between major general and the rank of colonel in the army and air force, which corresponds to captain in the navy, the same official said. The Globe is not naming the official because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

In a statement posted on China’s Ministry of Defense website, Beijing said the Canadian and Chinese sides “had a candid and in-depth exchange of views on international and regional issues of mutual interest, expressed willingness to strengthen practical exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries, and enhanced mutual understanding and trust.”

stories.title: Federal program making it cheaper, more accessible for Canadians to go to national parks comes to an end
stories.summary: A federal program making it cheaper and more accessible for Canadians to go to national parks and sites from coast to coast is ending on Monday.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
ST. Andrews, Man. – A federal program making it cheaper and more accessible for Canadians to go to national parks and sites from coast to coast is ending on Monday.

The Canada Strong Pass was first introduced in 2025 and returned this summer.

The federal program provides free or discounted admission to national parks, historic sites, museums, and train travel across Canada.

No physical or digital pass is required to access the benefits. The temporary program – which started in June – will no longer exist, with regular admission prices returning Tuesday.

Teanna Dukart and her family were visiting Manitoba from Saskatchewan this Labour Day weekend, and decided to go to Lower Fort Garry, which is a national historic site in the rural municipality of St. Andrews, Man.

The Canada Strong Pass made their first visit to Lower Fort Garry a little easier on the wallet with free admission.

“It’s awesome that you don’t have to pay, with everything being so expensive nowadays,” Dukart told CTV News.

Atul Sharma and Celia Rodd have been actively taking advantage of the program, visiting national sites and parks across the country.

“I’m originally from Nova Scotia, so we go and visit my family every year. Last year we visited Evangeline, and now we are at Lower Fort Garry today,” Sharma, who is an active user of the program, told CTV News.

“I think it’s especially important for families with kids, because it makes those facilities accessible… and I think it’s even more important these days, where we’re trying to discourage tourism south of the border.”

Rodd says having the pass available makes it easier for them to plan trips within the country.

“When I start planning a trip, I could say this is available and I could easily afford to go there because it is free,” she said.

But as the program comes to an end, Sharma says he would like to see its temporary aspect changed into a permanent one.

“I would actually like to see the pass expanded to an all-year around option,” he said.

Dukart is of the same opinion, saying the savings could make it easier for families to get out and explore.

“It would definitely encourage me more to go out and do more things,” she said.

“I can imagine people with lots of kids and having to foot a bill for a lot of children to go out and explore… and it would kind of suck to not be able to enjoy things like this because you can’t afford it.”

Increased visitation in 2025

Parks Canada sites saw a 13 per cent increase in foot traffic last summer when the program was in place, reporting over 14 million visitors.

All provinces and territories saw increases in the number of visitors last year — except Saskatchewan.

Matthew Rothenberger says Manitoba’s Lower Fort Garry has seen an increase in visitors since the program was introduced.

“We’ve seen an influx of new Canadians coming to visit the site, people coming for their first time experiencing a national historic site, so it’s been very much appreciated in making it accessible to all Canadians,” said Rothenberger, who is an interpretation co-ordinator with Parks Canada.

He says having the program year-round would help Canadians experience national parks and museums during the winter months.

“I’d love to see it continue,” Rothenberger said.

“Most sites are a little bit seasonal in nature, but there are certainly some that have year-round operations, whether it be a national park or a national historic site or some of our marine conservation areas.”

There is no decision at this time from the federal government whether the program will return in 2027.

stories.title: London Mayor Josh Morgan launches re-election campaign with 4-part platform
stories.summary: has officially launched his re-election campaign, outlining a platform focused on housing, transit, economic growth and public safety. Morgan says he wants another four years to follow through on plans already underway at City Hall.
stories.author: Jack Sutton
paragraphs: London Mayor Josh Morgan has officially launched his re-election campaign, outlining a platform focused on housing, transit, economic growth and public safety. Morgan says he wants another four years to follow through on plans already underway at City Hall.
· Posted: Sep 07, 2026 8:30 PM EDT | Last Updated: 37 minutes ago
London Mayor Josh Morgan has officially launched his re-election campaign, unveiling a platform focused on housing, transit, economic growth and public safety.
Morgan launched his campaign Monday, at the Jet Aircraft Museum in east London, where he pitched what he says are his priorities for a second term.

"This platform is about taking advantage of the opportunities we have, meeting the challenges that we have faced head-on, and executing those really critical plans to make sure that we're a city prepared for the future and that we're a leader in Southwestern Ontario and Canada," Morgan said.
The platform is organized around four themes: community, connection, commerce and security.
Under community, Morgan is promising more housing initiatives, efforts to build on London's UNESCO City of Music designation, and the revitalization of downtown and neighbourhood parks.
He is also proposing a new downtown parking facility and an expansion of the micro-modular shelter in south London, with provincial support.

Under connection, Morgan says he would keep transit running past 11 p.m., complete the city's rapid transit corridors, expand connections along the Thames Valley Parkway and strengthen transportation links with neighbouring communities.

His commerce priorities include keeping property tax increases in the range of three per cent over the next four years, maintaining London's credit rating and seeking more funding from the provincial and federal governments.

And under security, Morgan is promising to expand the city's strategy for dealing with open drug use, improve traffic safety in school zones and increase the presence of special constables on transit and in public spaces.
Morgan described the platform as a high-level outline, with more details expected to be released during the campaign.
The mayor is seeking a second term after winning nearly 66 per cent of the vote in 2022.
Morgan had previously served two terms as the councillor for Ward 7 before winning the mayor's job, defeating Khalil Ramal and eight other candidates.
He now faces a larger field. Eleven candidates are currently running for mayor, including incumbent Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson.

Stevenson has said she plans to release her platform this week. Other candidates, including Kirsten Krose, Mustafa Zebuun, John Feher and Bronagh Joyce Morgan, have already outlined their priorities on their campaign websites. Tariq Khan has also said his platform will be released this week.
As nominations open for city council, Josh Morgan already has a challenger for mayor
Coun. Susan Stevenson enters race to become London's next mayor
London's youngest mayoral candidate aims to reach voters through viral videos and social media
Morgan is the first London mayor to seek re-election since Joe Fontana in 2010.
He is making continuity a central part of his case for another term, arguing that changing leadership every four years could interrupt long-term city plans.

"If we change direction every four years, if we start all of these plans and all of the progress we made over again and again, we will never tackle the challenges we have and we will never seize the opportunities that the city has," he said.
Morgan pointed to the city's mass mobility plan, climate emergency plan and economic development plan as examples of initiatives he says need more time to be fully implemented.
Without that follow-through, he said, they risk becoming "plans to sit on a shelf."
Morgan's platform does not yet include detailed costs or timelines for many of the commitments. He said more specific details will be released in the coming weeks.

Other mayoral candidates have released platforms—in varying levels of detail—on their campaign websites, including Kirsten Krose, Mustafa Zebuun, John Feher, and Bronagh Joyce Morgan. Susan Stevenson and Tariq Khan have both said their platforms will launch this week.

stories.title: Repair begins on damage from devastating storm, washing over Cape Breton
stories.summary: Holes on the road created by the washouts could be several feet deep and eight to 10 feet long, Inverness County councillor says
stories.author: Om Shanbhag
stories.content:
Heavy rain fell on parts of Nova Scotia on Monday as the province began to repair the damage left by a slow-moving storm that passed over Cape Breton Island, washing out roads, leaving thousands without power and one person dead.

Early Monday morning, Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a hazardous weather alert forecasting up to 25 to 40 millimetres of heavy rain, after 200 millimetres fell on the island and parts of the northern mainland over less than two days.

The ground could not absorb more rainfall and water would likely pool on roads and low-lying areas, the weather service warned. The alert ended in the afternoon on Monday.

“It just poured and poured, and then we had a lot of wind. It wasn’t a hurricane, but it wasn’t too far from it,” said Inverness County councillor John MacLennan. On Sunday, he left his home near Whycocomagh, N.S., to inspect the damage done by the storm.

Some roads nearby had two or three washouts, Mr. MacLennan said, ON gravel and paved roads alike. He said the holes created by the washouts could be several feet deep and eight to 10 feet long.

“The rain, when it started late in the evening, it never stopped, and we had a lot of flooded roads. Roads wiped out. Culverts wiped out,” Mr. MacLellan said.

He said some of his constituents faced severe damage to their homes owing to flooding from the storm. A neighbour visiting their daughter in Alberta asked him to check up on their home.

Mr. MacLennan said he was met with four feet of water inside the house, a toppled water heater and cupboards pulled away from the wall. The stove had a fine layer of silt on it, hinting that the water level had previously been higher.

In hard-hit Richmond County, Scott Touesnard, who owns a dock-building company, said the biggest change since the storm has been the loss of a train trestle he used to sit on as a child.

“The train had stopped going there years and years ago. But half of that is washed in the water, and then the water washed behind it as well, and took out a big part of the land,” he said.

Mr. Touesnard said there are some washouts near his business, but that it hasn’t stopped him from being able to get around.

A 46-year-old woman from Richmond County was found dead Saturday several hours after her abandoned vehicle was discovered near a flooded bridge. RCMP said Sunday the death is not believed to be suspicious and added they would not provide any more information.

On Saturday, Nova Scotia Power said in an online post that restoration of power May be delayed by washed-out roads. By Monday, all large-scale power outages in the area were resolved, though smaller outages persisted.

Lois Landry, warden of Richmond County, said a Zodiac rescue boat operated by a local fire department and a provincial helicopter were used to carry out daily wellness checks for any residents completely cut off by flooding.

Guests stranded at the Lakeside Luxury Domes camp in the Saint George’s Channel area created a makeshift, jerry-rigged exit route after the property was washed out, she said.

“We’re used to hurricanes on the East Coast, that’s not new to us. But there was wind coupled with rain we haven’t seen the likes of, really, ever,” she said.

Fred Tilley, Nova Scotia Minister of Public Works, said hundreds of provincial employees and local contractors are working to restore the entirety of Cape Breton Island’s road network within the coming days.

“It’s another one of these one-in-100-years storms that has wreaked havoc,” he said. “It’s always top of mind when we’re rebuilding to build for climate change where possible.”

While the province prepared for the storm, Mr. Tilley said, “there’s not much infrastructure that can handle that in Nova Scotia.”

At the peak of the flooding, according to a spokesperson for the province’s Department of Public Works, there were more than 120 closed or damaged roads on Cape Breton.

“Currently, about 44 are closed. The rest have either fully or partially reopened, including dozens overnight,” Toby Koffman, communications director for the department, said in a statement Monday.

Mr. Koffman said that two of eight bridges that were damaged will need to be replaced. As well, he said there are more than 200 culverts that were washed away, from driveways to major roads.

Ms. Landry said she’s lived on Cape Breton Island all of her 58 years, but she’s never seen so much flooding before.

A rainfall device in the area of Saint George’s Channel measured 230 millimetres of rain before it broke, she added.

“We really can’t even wrap our heads around that much rain … it compromised the ground beneath our infrastructure.”

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Love to see it continue’: Program making Parks Canada sites accessible, cheaper comes to an end
stories.summary: A federal program making it cheaper and more accessible for Canadians to go to national parks and sites from coast to coast is ending on Monday.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
ST. Andrews, Man. – A federal program making it cheaper and more accessible for Canadians to go to national parks and sites from coast to coast is ending on Monday.

The Canada Strong Pass was first introduced in 2025 and returned this summer.

The federal program provides free or discounted admission to national parks, historic sites, museums, and train travel across Canada.

No physical or digital pass is required to access the benefits. The temporary program – which started in June – will no longer exist, with regular admission prices returning Tuesday.

Teanna Dukart and her family were visiting Manitoba from Saskatchewan this Labour Day weekend, and decided to go to Lower Fort Garry, which is a national historic site in the rural municipality of St. Andrews, Man.

The Canada Strong Pass made their first visit to Lower Fort Garry a little easier on the wallet with free admission.

“It’s awesome that you don’t have to pay, with everything being so expensive nowadays,” Dukart told CTV News.

Atul Sharma and Celia Rodd have been actively taking advantage of the program, visiting national sites and parks across the country.

“I’m originally from Nova Scotia, so we go and visit my family every year. Last year we visited Evangeline, and now we are at Lower Fort Garry today,” Sharma, who is an active user of the program, told CTV News.

“I think it’s especially important for families with kids, because it makes those facilities accessible… and I think it’s even more important these days, where we’re trying to discourage tourism south of the border.”

“When I start planning a trip, I could say this is available and I could easily afford to go there because it is free,” she said.

“I would actually like to see the pass expanded to an all-year around option,” he said.

“It would definitely encourage me more to go out and do more things,” she said.

“I can imagine people with lots of kids and having to foot a bill for a lot of children to go out and explore… and it would kind of suck to not be able to enjoy things like this because you can’t afford it.”

“We’ve seen an influx of new Canadians coming to visit the site, people coming for their first time experiencing a national historic site, so it’s been very much appreciated in making it accessible to all Canadians,” said Rothenberger, who is an interpretation co-ordinator with Parks Canada.

He says having the program year-round would help Canadians experience national parks and museums during the winter months.

“I’d love to see it continue,” Rothenberger said.

“Most sites are a little bit seasonal in nature, but there are certainly some that have year-round operations, whether it be a national park or a national historic site or some of our marine conservation areas.”

There is no decision at this time from the federal government whether the program will return in 2027.

stories.title: Quebec courts restrict judges’ use AI guidelines
stories.summary: AI cannot replace judicial reasoning, court says following concerns about whether a Quebec judge used the technology to prepare a decision
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud
stories.content:
Quebec’s courts have issued new guidelines restricting judges’ use of generative artificial intelligence, stressing that judging must remain a fundamentally human responsibility.

The guidelines, jointly adopted by the Quebec Court of Appeal, Superior Court, Court of Quebec and the province’s municipal courts, say generative AI can be used for certain supporting tasks but cannot replace judicial reasoning, the assessment of evidence or deliberation.

Judging, they say, must remain the exclusive responsibility of judges.

“Generative AI, however sophisticated, possesses neither judgment nor conscience and is not subject to any form of accountability,” states the 10-page document. “It cannot understand the human, social and legal context specific to each case.”

The move comes months after questions were raised about whether a Quebec judge May have used generative AI in preparing a decision.

La Presse reported in March that a decision contained references to case law that did not exist, raising the possibility that generative AI had been used. The episode helped create a sense of urgency within the judiciary as it worked to establish rules for the technology.

The courts say there is currently no approved, secure institutional generative AI tool available to judges. They also warn that existing tools rely on algorithms whose workings remain largely opaque.

“Judging cannot be reduced to a technical exercise,” the guidelines say. “It is an intrinsically human function, based on deliberation, consideration of context, respect for dignity, the requirement of fairness and the exercise of moral responsibility.”

The courts acknowledge that generative AI can be useful, but say it cannot be used as a source of legal authority or reasoning, to assess evidence or to make decisions.

Judges May use it for limited tasks such as correcting, revising, rephrasing or translating text they have already written, certain administrative work, or locating information within specified sources.

Any such use must remain under human control, and AI-generated material must be independently verified.

The guidelines make clear that judges remain fully responsible for their legal reasoning, the contents of their decisions, and the accuracy of the facts, references, quotations and legal authorities they cite.

“No error can be attributed to the tool used,” the document says. “The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the judge’s obligation to verify or their full responsibility for the final result.”

The guidelines say AI cannot be used for substantive legal reasoning, analyzing or characterizing facts, assessing evidence or credibility, determining the outcome of a dispute, or drafting those parts of a decision.

“If the use of AI has the effect or purpose of determining the legal outcome, assessing credibility or interpreting disputed facts, interpreting the relevance of facts, or formulating the reasons for a decision, it must not be used,” the guidelines say.

The courts also warn judges about confidentiality risks.

Judges should not provide AI tools with draft judgments, notes about ongoing cases or information protected by law or a court order.

Until an authorized institutional system is available, judges using an AI tool for permitted purposes must also ensure its settings prevent information they enter from being used to train or improve the system.

When in doubt, the guidelines recommend judges refrain from using generative AI.

The guidelines are intended to protect principles including judicial independence, impartiality, fairness, human rights and access to justice, while ensuring confidentiality, security and data protection.

stories.title: B.C. mountaineer missing in Italy is seasoned survivalist, MLA says
stories.summary: A British Columbia legislature member who went to law school with missing mountaineer Kalie McCrystal says the woman’s family and friends are “sitting by the phone” as they await updates on the search in Italy.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A British Columbia legislature member who went to law school with missing mountaineer Kalie McCrystal says the woman’s family and friends are “sitting by the phone” as they await updates on the search in Italy.

Penticton-Summerland MLA Amelia Boultbee says she’s known McCrystal for a long time and says she’s “not just your average hiker,” and her disappearance while attempting to break a mountain-running record on the Matterhorn last week remains a mystery.

Boultbee says she’s been in touch with McCrystal’s sister and mother who are in Italy and they’ve been working mostly with Italian authorities.

She says the decision to suspend the search has been “very upsetting,” and the last time she was spotted via telescope before going missing showed no signs of any troubles.

Boultbee says McCrystal has done the Matterhorn several times before and it’s unusual that she went missing given her physical condition and extensive experience.

She says her friends and family are holding out hope that McCrystal is found alive.

“Nobody understands why there’s been zero trace of Kalie,” she said. “We also just want her family to get some answers.”

stories.title: Four teens dead, four sent to hospital after crash in Manitoba
stories.summary: RCMP responded just after 9 p.m. on Sunday to an intersection near the town of Winnipeg Beach
stories.content:
Mounties in Manitoba say four teens died and four other victims, including two children, were taken to hospital after two vehicles crashed and landed in a ditch near a resort town over the weekend.

RCMP say they responded just after 9 p.m. on Sunday to an intersection near the town of Winnipeg Beach, located about 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg.

Police say a car with four occupants was westbound on Highway 229, and was crossing Highway 8 when it was hit by a southbound van.

Both vehicles went into a ditch, with one of them rolling over on to its roof.

Police say the three 18-year-olds from Manitoba — including the female driver — and a 17-year-old from Ontario who were in the car died at the scene.

The four people from Winnipeg who were in the van, including the 49-year-old man who was driving, a woman and two children, were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

Mounties say in a news release that the intersection has stop signs, and a traffic reconstructionist is assisting in the investigation.

stories.title: Globe-trotting reporter draws on London childhood for new novel
stories.summary: After a long career as an international journalist, London native Russell Blinch is now writing novels.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us May earn us a commission, which supports our work.

After a long career as an international journalist, primarily with Thomson Reuters for 30 years, London native Russell Blinch is now writing novels. Raised in both London and Delaware, the 69-year-old is back with the second edition of his fifth book, a mystery novel titled A Grave Mistake, now available for purchase through Amazon. Blinch spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison about his career in journalism, his transition to novel writing and what his latest book is all about.

Q: What was your favourite story to write during your career as a journalist?

A: I’ve had a few intense stories over the years. I wasn’t a war correspondent or anything like that, but there’s been a lot of pretty fascinating stories. I was in San Francisco during the Rodney King riots when they broke out in L.A., and some rioting broke out in San Francisco, and that was a very . . . scary time. There was a moment there where everybody cleared out of San Francisco – our sales office and everything. But as a journalist, I had to stay in the bureau and cover it, and it was quite a fascinating period. I also covered one of the big earthquakes that was in L.A. I was sent on an airplane to L.A. when everybody else was leaving the city. In Canada, I covered Quebec separatism, which was always a very tough and fascinating story, especially if you’re telling it to a global audience. And in Singapore, I was the commodities editor for the continent, and the fascinating story there was watching China emerge as a major economic player. It was a never-ending story, and it still is, basically.

Q: How do you think your journalism background influences your writing as a novelist?

A: That’s a great question, because sometimes I’ve always wondered, maybe I’ve spent too much time in journalism. I think I’m more comfortable as a novelist, but then I think, I mean, I got a heck of a training. I sort of have a grasp of world events, or so I like to think, and so when I write, I just feel like I have a grasp of things. I have a knowledge of how things work, how energy works, how governments operate. It sort of just gives me this overall background, like it’s a PhD in real-world affairs kind of a thing. So it’s a big help.

Q: How did journalism change over the course of your career?

A: It’s night and day over the years. When I joined Reuters, we were a real-time agency when dailies and so forth were still existing, and we were sending out news as it happens. That’s what Reuters was all about. That’s what a wire agency is all about. But slowly, that’s all morphed into everything is real-time journalism now. So that’s how it’s changed. As well, I think people don’t understand traditional journalism anymore, and why we need it, and why we need those independent voices. People, especially in the U.S., are very divided, and they don’t understand why independent journalism is very important. We still need The New York Times, we still need The London Free Press, we still need The Globe and Mail because we just need these legitimate voices out there.

Q: Why did you decide to start writing novels? How did that come together?

A: I think that was always a side of me. There’s a lot of journalists who always think they have a book in them, and they probably do. I was a very big reader growing up in London and Delaware (he attended Saunders secondary school). Back then, you didn’t sit around and watch TV, because it was so boring. Everything was black and white and there was, like, one channel. So a lot of times you either are out there walking around and hiking and exploring things, or at home reading books, and definitely part of my life was reading books. So I really like people like le Carré. In Canada, I sometimes worry we don’t have these great Canadian authors anymore. I mean, where have these big names gone? Q: Tell me about A Grave Mistake. What inspired it?

There’s beef I have that I don’t think we’d write enough interesting, fun and intriguing stories about ourselves with historical touchstones here in Canada. I think we need more of it. I guess I was trying to write that fun and intriguing story with the historical touchstone of the War of 1812, which I think still fascinates many of us here. It’s something I drew out of my head, because my dad came over from England in 1956, and I was born a year later, and he built this house himself that’s still there in Delaware, Ontario. I think some writers might get in trouble and they pick a person they know and then they fictionalize them in a novel, and you can get sued for that, right? But I sort of mine people and change them, and they become their own people themselves, and they become real to me. Trey is one of the big heroes in the book, and he’s a teenager. And I got a lot of inspiration from my grandson, but Trey is his own person. It was the same with my grandfather; he’s based loosely on my father. So that’s the beauty of fiction: you get to steal people’s souls and elaborate on them.

After a long career as an international journalist, primarily with Thomson Reuters for 30 years, London native Russell Blinch is now writing novels. Raised in both London and Delaware, the 69-year-old is back with the second edition of his fifth book, a mystery novel titled A Grave Mistake, now available for purchase through Amazon. Blinch spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison about his career in journalism, his transition to novel writing and what his latest book is all about.

A: I’ve had a few intense stories over the years. I wasn’t a war correspondent or anything like that, but there’s been a lot of pretty fascinating stories. I was in San Francisco during the Rodney King riots when they broke out in L.A., and some rioting broke out in San Francisco, and that was a very . . . scary time. There was a moment there where everybody cleared out of San Francisco – our sales office and everything. But as a journalist, I had to stay in the bureau and cover it, and it was quite a fascinating period. I also covered one of the big earthquakes that was in L.A. I was sent on an airplane to L.A. when everybody else was leaving the city. In Canada, I covered Quebec separatism, which was always a very tough and fascinating story, especially if you’re telling it to a global audience. And in Singapore, I was the commodities editor for the continent, and the fascinating story there was watching China emerge as a major economic player. It was a never-ending story, and it still is, basically.

I think I’m more comfortable as a novelist, but then I think, I mean, I got a heck of a training. I sort of have a grasp of world events, or so I like to think, and so when I write, I just feel like I have a grasp of things. I have a knowledge of how things work, how energy works, how governments operate. It sort of just gives me this overall background, like it’s a PhD in real-world affairs kind of a thing. stories.title: Trump targets Bombardier, Canadian dollar in Truth Social blitz ahead of tariff deadline
stories.summary: 'No more selling Bombardier in the United States!' The president posted in a string of more than 60 posts.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump launched a string of complaints and threats targeting Canada, levelling an attack against aircraft maker Bombardier and posting a photo of the North American continent covered in an American flag.

“No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” the president posted on his Truth Social page Monday just hours before the looming midnight trade deadline. “Their products aren’t good enough! Over 50 per cent of their revenue comes from the United States — they live off American buyers, American companies, American airports, and American service — all while Canada blocks our Great American Banks, and companies, throughout the U.S.A.”

The comments were part of a social media blitz in which Trump intensified his attacks on both Canada and Mexico, heaping new uncertainty onto the ongoing trade disputes between the U.S. and its neighbours. The president made more than 60 posts on Monday, taunting “Governor Carney,” threatening to change the name of the state of New Mexico to “New America,” and complaining about the “imbalance” between the value of the Canadian and U.S. dollars.

At 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, Canada’s raft of sweeping counter-tariffs, ranging from 15 per cent to 50 per cent on $28 billion worth of goods, are to come into effect. As of late Monday afternoon, Canadian officials said they were not scheduled to continue talks with U.S. negotiators.

As part of his threat to block sales of Bombardier jets in the U.S., Trump claimed the move was in response to Canada blocking U.S.-based Gulfstream Aerospace and other companies from operating in Canada.

“That era is Over!” he said. “If they want our market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a “piggybank.” Buy American. Fly on American airliners. Enjoy American liquor and beverages. Sail on Lake America.”

Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, questioned whether Trump had the authority to block sales of Bombardier in the U.S. market.

“He can’t just ban their sale,” she said. “He can try to impose tariffs; he can impose other economic barriers; he can ask the FAA to decertify them. There are other things he can do, but he can’t just ban it like that.”

Kavanagh said Trump May be “frustrated” at Canada for not caving to his latest bout of trade threats and is expressing his willingness to deepen the conflict rather than level specific tariffs against specific products.

“The spirit of the post is kind of what to interpret, rather than the actual literal statement.”

The Federal Aviation Administration, not the White House, is the agency that certifies or decertifies aircraft in the U.S.

Bombardier models remain U.S. certified and the company is currently exempt from U.S. tariffs.

His Bombardier comments came just hours after the president had also voiced complaints about the value of the Canadian dollar, marking a new line of economic attack against Canada.

“Canada’s (currency) Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” he said. “It has been that way for years — but no longer!”

Those comments somewhat resemble complaints that Trump levelled against China for more than a decade, calling the country a “currency manipulator” for the way it artificially depressed the value of its Yuan.

Lower value currencies are viewed as advantageous for exporting nations, as it lets companies receive a higher-value currency in exchange for the goods they sell. Still, stronger currencies are generally viewed more favourably than weak ones for the buying power it affords consumers. Trump, whose bellicose trade policy has long sought to expand export capacity by attracting more manufacturers back inside U.S. borders, has long viewed the strong U.S. dollar as a detriment.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said Trump’s decision to target the Canadian dollar likely reflects the president’s desire to eliminate the U.S.’s trade deficit with Canada.

“The problem is that a stronger Canadian dollar would do next to nothing to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Canada, because most of that deficit is due to U.S. oil imports,” he said.

On Monday, the Canadian dollar was valued at $0.72 per US$1. The loonie was last valued higher than the U.S. in 2011, when high oil prices had rapidly inflated the value of the Canadian dollar.

“Canada’s (currency) Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” he said. “It has been that way for years — but no longer!”

Those comments somewhat resemble complaints that Trump levelled against China for more than a decade, calling the country a “currency manipulator” for the way it artificially depressed the value of its Yuan.

Lower value currencies are viewed as advantageous for exporting nations, as it lets companies receive a higher-value currency in exchange for the goods they sell. Still, stronger currencies are generally viewed more favourably than weak ones for the buying power it affords consumers. Trump, whose bellicose trade policy has long sought to expand export capacity by attracting more manufacturers back inside U.S. borders, has long viewed the strong U.S. dollar as a detriment.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said Trump’s decision to target the Canadian dollar likely reflects the president’s desire to eliminate the U.S.’s trade deficit with Canada.
“The problem is that a stronger Canadian dollar would do next to nothing to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Canada, because most of that deficit is due to U.S. oil imports,” he said.
On Monday, the Canadian dollar was valued at $0.72 per US$1. The loonie was last valued higher than the U.S. in 2011, when high oil prices had rapidly inflated the value of the Canadian dollar.

stories.title: Sapporo beer moving production to U.S. from Canada after tariffs
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump’s levies on beer made in Canada are the latest twist for the Japanese brewer
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Sapporo Breweries Ltd. is shifting some production to the US from Canada due to 50% tariffs imposed on beer exports from the country, seeking to reinvigorate its North American operations.

The Japanese brewer, which makes the top-selling Asian beer in the U.S., is also considering adding manufacturing capacity on the West Coast as it seeks to expand its flagship brand in one of its biggest overseas markets, Chief Strategy Officer Rieko Shofu said in an interview.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s levies on beer made in Canada are the latest twist for the Japanese brewer. The production shift plans are part of a broader revamp following years of acquisitions that failed to deliver sufficient returns. The company sold Stone Brewing in 2022 and liquidated Anchor Brewing in 2023.

“Tariffs are something out of our control,” Shofu said. “We’re going to move ahead with local production.”

Sapporo will move production of non-alcoholic beer currently made in Canada for the U.S. market by the first half of 2027. Sapporo is considering acquiring or building a brewery on the West Coast, or contracting with other manufacturers, the executive said.

“The U.S. is a huge market, and we have a lot of momentum right now in terms of how much we can expand our share of that market,” Shofu said.

The brewer is accelerating investments in its beer business after deciding last year to sell its real estate business. Sapporo plans to spend ¥300 billion to ¥400 billion (US$1.9 billion-$2.6 billion) on investments, including acquisitions, through 2030 as it seeks to grow operating profit to ¥40 billion from around ¥24 billion last year. Roughly 30% of that is targeted to come from overseas.

Asia is another focus. Sapporo announced a venture with Carlsberg A/S in July to expand in Southeast Asia. The company is also seeking investment opportunities in China and South Korea, according to Shofu.

At home, where Sapporo is the No. 4 beermaker, the company faces a different challenge as Japan’s shrinking population weighs on long-term alcohol consumption. Shofu said the company has a “considerable sense of urgency” about the domestic market and isn’t ruling out greater supply-chain cooperation with rivals over the longer term.
