stories.title: London municipal election: Mayor candidates, in their own words
stories.summary: Mayoral candidates answer a survey to help voters evaluate people running for the top job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked mayoral candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the top job. Here are their answers

Name: John Feher

Occupation: Retired

Family: I am married to Cathy (common law). Also I am a step-father to Kristen and her brother Kieren. And a very proud grandfather to two beautiful young ones, a boy and a girl. I am also the father of my son Connor who is 28 and we were lucky enough to adopt him at birth, with him being of Native heritage it was quite the process.

1. Do you live full time in the city?

2. Do you plan to utilize the strong mayor powers granted by the province? If so — how? If not — why?

Yes. Depending on the circumstances.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

1. Addressing homelessness

2. Affordable Housing

3. Job Implementation

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

No one. I am my own person with my own opinions and ideas.

5. What is your vision for London?

I have learned so much over the years, with my background and also being a member of the RCMI, I was taught by some of the wisest people I have ever met. I intend to make this city safe while cleaning up the downtown. My videos on social media will go more in-depth with that. I’m on all social media.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The homelessness crisis is London’s biggest challenge at this time. Mental health and drug addiction go along with this.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My background in the mental health field gives me a unique perspective on the crisis we have affecting London.

Name : Lawrence-Zachary

Occupation: Unemployed

Family : ??? Read lawrencezachary.ca/background

Yes, in an effort to reverse the decline of this city.

First is to ensure city hall bureaucrats accept oversight, meaning they don’t hide data from elected officials, and that they are working on behalf of London. Second, to build a municipal construction company – this would eliminate the rent-seeking that balloons the cost and duration of projects, ensuring that anything we decide to create is built in a cost-effective, timely manner. Finally completing the construction and integration of the Trimodal Port concept I came up with – many of the 27 positions in my platform’s blueprint to reverse the decline of this city reference it as their major revenue source.

The Trimodal Port plan is to take London’s existing infrastructure, its access to two major highways, two major rail lines that connect to ports on the east and west coasts of the country, and an international airport, and connect them with an inland port. This lowers the costs for businesses, reducing supply chain variables, reducing carbon footprint, and being able to deliver and be delivered to faster – consequently creating a massive incentive for manufacturers, and other businesses to migrate to London.

None, there’s no historical figure, certainly no city politician, with my qualities and values. Perhaps the closest politician would be Lee Kuan Yew, who built Singapore’s entire economic miracle by exploiting its geographic location and heavily utilized state-owned enterprises to generate massive revenue for the country while stamping out rent seeking and corruption – however we differ in important ways, such as the importance I put on personal liberty.

An aesthetic, culturally rich, prosperous city with low taxes, strong trustworthy institutions, and an engaged, demanding electorate that believes the value of this city is worth defending.

The decline of the city. We have 31.3% food insecurity, 33% downtown office vacancy, 8.2% unemployment (down from its 9.2% high only because fewer people are looking for work), over 80,000 residents without doctors, and a police service that takes too long to respond to Priority 2 calls while prioritizing closing cases instead of clearing them. This is unsustainable and demands structural solutions, and an injection of absolute accountability.

I am a systems architect and philosopher who can create solutions, not just point problems out or wait for one to be handed a solution to rubber stamp. My site currently has a 27-position blueprint I designed to reverse the managed decline of the city, divided into major and minor positions – all important, but the distinction represents the scope and urgency of that element of the plan.

Name: Kirsten Krose

Occupation: Founder and owner of a boutique public affairs firm

Family : I have one.

I plan to bring collaborative leadership to council, working to build consensus where possible, and pushing for outcomes that reflect the needs and preferences of Londoners. With a rapidly changing world, we are seeing politicians make decisions today on issues that we couldn’t have predicted four years ago.

I intend to be an accountable and transparent mayor, and I don’t think it’s responsible to speculate on what circumstances I would be willing to use this incredibly powerful tool at this time. What I can commit to is that I plan to work with – not against – council and the community to make sure every Londoner gets the services they need.

My top priorities are investing in services that work, traffic that moves, and communities that feel safe. And I intend to deliver on these priorities while respecting the taxpayer.

From the big issues like tackling homeless and housing, to the basic things like making sure the roads are plowed on time, Londoners deserve a city that works. We deserve to feel safe walking down the street, and shouldn’t be spending our time stuck in traffic.

I will work to lead council in making faster, thoughtful decisions, delivering good value for tax dollars, and holding ourselves accountable for keeping priorities moving forward.

Jane Bigelow, first female mayor of London – she was a disruptor.

My vision is for a city that works for everybody. When you ask people what they want from city hall, it’s about the fundamentals – the pothole that’s gone unfilled since winter, the permit that took four months to approve, the park bench that never got fixed.

When we get the basics right, everything else follows, and people can thrive. My vision is that every person, business, non-profit receives the services they need to thrive, and that by the end of my time as mayor, everybody feels that their quality of life has improved.

We are facing a growing need from the community for the supports and services needed to have a good quality of life. At the same time, the resources needed to do this work are becoming more constrained, and people no longer see that they are getting good value for their tax dollars.

Everybody sees the problems, but we don’t see accountability and transparency around budgeting, city contracts, and decision making. Londoners need to know that we are investing in the services that deliver real outcomes that address the barriers that are preventing London from reaching its potential.

I have strong professional and volunteer experience working with government, business, community organizations, and the public to deliver real results. While other candidates have been part of years of council decisions that have led to where we are today, I am an outsider and bring new perspectives, and extensive leadership experience bringing the right people together to find collaborative, meaningful solutions to problems. And while I have not been an elected politician, I have spent my professional career in politics: I’m not new to politics, government, stakeholder relations or just getting work done in complex environments.

Name: Dan Lenart

Occupation: Staff training (outreach/homeless), public education (stigma), advocacy, retired mental health worker

Family: Family buried in Toronto, some live here.

Full time last 36 years

Reluctantly, “strong mayor powers” sounds like a Trump-style dictator. The larger city council represents more of the city than one individual, “chief magistrate.” Even if the position is supposed to be “city wide”

#1 New city hall – Renting out or leasing 12 different sites for “city business” is too expensive, and needs to be carried out under ONE ROOF, if at all possible. $120 million has been set aside for a “new office/building.” Past attempts to finance a NEW site were unsuccessful. Broaden requests for proposals (RFP) to all of Canada, like our financial hub Toronto through a (PPP) “public private partnership.”

#2 Prevent homeless problem further increasing out of control – shift CIR bylaw (no special constables) from harassing/bullying our most vulnerable to inspecting substandard/”slumlord” housing.

#3 Improve traffic bottlenecks (+rush hour gridlock) with more river bridges/rail under/overpasses

George Wenige ran for mayor 21 times and won 19 (I believe), Mostly against Al Denis. Sometimes for a year or two, then the other would win.

My London – We have more dogs than any other city. Some homeowners place water dishes out for dog walkers, but will cheer the harassment and bullying of our most vulnerable.

“Them” – Houseless street folk are rounded up for jail/psychiatric hospital as eyesores and community pests bylaw enforcement + CIR as if they are not real people with full human rights. Many have given up, fallen off the work rolls and no longer look for or are interested in meaningful employment, possibly not even having a resume to hand out for job offers.

Many surveys have shown London is hurting. This is why bus ridership is low – they can’t afford cash fares. Was the BRT a bad decision? In a have-not city of inequality, car owners will not park them to ride the bus with the economically challenged.

Leadership at city hall should be for everyone, with full equal rights, regardless of present circumstances. Public safety? Citizens should NOT have to be afraid to call 911. Having worked here most of my life in various social service agencies, I believe I have insights towards these crucial lifestyle issues never mentioned in your newspaper.

Voter turnout has reflected this disconnection with lower and lower numbers showing up on election day. Will anyone show up October 26, 2026 to cast a ballot?

Name: Bronagh Joyce Morgan

Occupation: Legal editor and instructor; Business owner; London Arts Council roster artist and educator; AI evaluator

Family : My two living kids Rain and Holly, my partner Chris, and I live in northwest London. I have another daughter Violet who died at 3 days old in 2009. I don’t like her to be left out. She is an important part of our family and like my other family members, gives me strength and helps shape everything I do and think. I have a sister in Niagara (where I am from) and one in Colorado Springs. My parents aren’t alive anymore.

No I don’t. Collaboration on council is needed. I think we can get there on the big issues, every time, by having honest conversations in the open without resorting to personal attacks or needless politicking. And as leaders, we need to model collaborative behaviour.

1. One honest review of how bylaws, policies, and contracts are written to find opportunities to streamline and potential risks of uneven/unfair application . . . similar to what the provincial appointees for LHSC and TVDSB are being paid lots more than a mayor’s salary to do. Ensure everything we research, write, and communicate, and every meeting and report is clear, understandable, and accessible to the public. 2. Meet monthly in a public forum to hear Londoners’ views, no matter how angry the words they use to explain them (i.e. no tone policing). Behind anger is pain. There are many in London who are suffering. I want to hear from our most vulnerable citizens and people on the frontlines serving them to understand what we can do collectively as a city to ease their pain and improve their lives. 3. Look at multi-year funding cycles for service providers doing things that are municipal responsibilities.

I appreciated the measured approaches that Phil Squire took to issues. His voting always struck me as logic based, rather than left- or right-leaning. We both like running and the Majors. I also admired Mo Salih for many reasons, among them being his being the only person on a panel of “male allies” I attended at the London Club some years back (2018 I think, at the beginning of the MeToo movement) who explicitly stated men actually do need to cede some ground in a systemically sexist system. Currently my political hero on council is my longtime friend and former Green Party colleague Elizabeth Peloza. She is a smart, caring leader who I hope runs for mayor in 2030.

London has the money and the muscle to thrive economically while addressing social problems. What we need is to clear a path for people who know what they’re doing to move forward boldly. I have spent lots of my professional career making law make sense. I currently teach people in all levels of government how to write laws, policies, reports, etc. so they can be readily understood and implemented. There are problems with our bureaucracy that we all recognize, but it’s always easier to add more laws and policies than to re-think the ones we have. I want that one, not easy, job. I hope to leave council four years from now with a city that works for people at all levels. Streamlined, logical, easy to navigate, and aligned with our shared values as laid out in the many plans we’ve already written.

Fraught conversations about what we want and need. Promises of solutions that are either incomplete or not within the ability of one politician, one group, or one party to implement. Short-term, election-cycle politics and policy making. Listening to a select few people who engage because so many others are turned off politics because of these things, or are worn down by bureaucracy or administration, and simply give up.

I don’t know them all. I’m guessing I have one of the broadest skill sets and experience bases among them. Because I have worked so long with the public, as casual staff with the City of London for 17 years, and because I was a candidate in an election long before most of the other people running (2003 was the first provincial election I ran in), I have a deep understanding of what London needs and can be from the inside and outside of its systems. I may also be the only one who is still on friendly terms with every political opponent I have ever had, because I think civility is one of the most important qualities a leader can exhibit if we want people to stop turning away from politics, and instead start getting involved in the way our government functions.

Name: Josh Morgan

Occupation : Mayor, City of London

Family: 4 children and my partner.

Any candidate who understands the legislation will answer yes because a number of the duties are not optional.

The powers are new tools that happen to be vested in the mayor, but can be approached collaboratively and democratically. I have used them to directly involve council in the hiring of the city manager, create deeper council involvement in the budget process and get new ideas before council faster. Council has also unanimously asked me to use the powers to expedite areas of council priority.

I have never overridden or vetoed any democratic decision of council.

Improving affordability: Families and businesses have been impacted by tariffs and need to be supported while maintaining core services. We continue to find efficiencies, pursue innovative partnerships, and use federal and provincial funding to improve quality of life while keeping property taxes down and supporting a safe city for all.

Addressing homelessness: Push for more provincial recovery beds and supportive housing, work with other mayors to get state of emergency declared and support the province in developing a co-ordinated plan.

Grow the economy and create jobs by implementing the economic development, downtown, and master mobility plans.

Jane Bigelow

London is the key urban centre of Southwestern Ontario, providing leadership to the region. Its people are global leaders, innovators, entrepreneurs, who make our city stronger. London will be a safer, more affordable city with a thriving downtown, strong neighbourhoods, healthier businesses, and good-paying jobs. A city that faces and tackles challenges head on, without hesitation or fear of risk-taking. The job of the mayor is to be the biggest positive champion of our city, to empower its people to realize their potential, and improve their quality of life every day.

A broken taxation system and lack of resources to do what modern cities are asked and expected to do. Cities are often forced to cut services or raise taxes because of decisions beyond their control. Issues of homelessness and housing, transit and mobility, safety and vibrancy, and the revival of our downtown can no longer be supported by property taxes alone. We need a new deal for the fast-growing, mid-sized Canadian cites that allows them to access the resources necessary to meet our modern-day challenges and build thriving, vibrant communities.

I am a collaborator who brings people together. I am a champion for our city and believe in lifting it up, not tearing it down. I have been told that because of the partnerships we’ve created and the people we’ve empowered, that this has been one of the busiest and most effective terms for a London city council in decades. It involved effective advocacy when others doubted, innovative new programs, risk-taking, huge strides in public safety, historic philanthropy campaigns, whole of community action and billions of dollars of new investment in our city.

Name : Jeff Yam

Occupation: Real estate broker for 10 years+

Family: I have a beautiful 4-year-old daughter.

Yes, I live in the city full time.

Yes, I plan to utilize strong mayor powers to bring real, positive change to our community. Leadership requires standing up with common sense, acting with love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self control, and having the boldness to fight for our people. We need decisive action to ensure that the basic needs of everyone in our city are met, and these powers provide the tools necessary to make that vision a reality.

More priorities can be found on BGHCanada.com but these are the top 3.

1. Fair housing and affordability: Bringing basic living standards and attainable housing back to everyone in our community so that every resident has a stable place to call home.

2. Integrated support programs: Implementing comprehensive support to clean up our streets, assisting people in weaning off drugs, and empowering them to build better lives.

3. Roads of opportunity: Improving traffic flow and active transportation by introducing dedicated infrastructure like sidewalks and walking paths, alongside designating specific peak hours where select main corridors operate as one-way routes.

I identify most with Anne Marie DeCicco-Best because she embodied what it means to be a genuine, people-first leader. Throughout her 19 years on city council and a decade as mayor, her leadership was defined by an authentic connection to her community rather than political detachment. She earned the trust of her constituents from a young age by listening to their needs, championing initiatives that improved everyday life, and fiercely advocating for the city’s future. Her enduring dedication proved that true leadership isn’t just about holding office, it’s about consistently caring for the people you are elected to serve.

My vision for London, Ontario, centres on building economic resilience, protecting essential needs, and upholding true integrity in city leadership. We are heading into a challenging economic climate, and my top priority is protecting our local economy through prudent fiscal decisions that support local businesses without overburdening taxpayers. Community stability means making sure everyone’s basic needs, like housing support, public health, and basic social safety nets, are met. Navigating these times requires leadership built on strong ethics and accountability. I am committed to transparent governance that puts Londoners first and ensures city hall leads with integrity every single day.

London’s biggest challenge is that we have lost sight of our shared humanity. We have forgotten that at the end of the day, we all bleed red and share the same basic needs. A community cannot truly thrive or call itself great if it ignores its most vulnerable residents. Moving forward means going back to the basics: taking the time to understand the why, looking out for one another, restoring compassion to our local decision-making, and prioritizing real support for housing, mental health, and social care. My commitment is to lead with empathy and ensure that as London grows, no one in our city gets left behind.

What sets me apart from other candidates is that my leadership is guided by high emotional intelligence, deep wisdom, and a values-first approach. Leading with emotional intelligence means having the self awareness to listen carefully, understand the lived experiences of Londoners, and respond with empathy rather than reaction. True wisdom in governance comes from looking past short-term political wins to make thoughtful, long-term decisions that genuinely serve our community. While policy and strategy are essential, true leadership is about character and how you treat people. In challenging times, optics fall short. By grounding my work in actions of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self control, I bring the emotional maturity, integrity, and steady discipline our city needs.

Name : Mustafa Zeboon

Occupation: You can’t have an occupation when running for mayor.

Family : Not relevant

Yes I live full time in the city.

I believe strong mayor powers should be used responsibly, not routinely. My first approach will always be to work collaboratively with council, listen to residents, and build consensus. If using those powers is clearly in the best interest of London and helps deliver important priorities without unnecessary delays, I would consider them. Any decision to use them would be transparent and justified, so we can be focused on serving the people of London.

Homelessness, infrastructure, affordability.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

My vision is a safer, more affordable, and more accountable London. A city where families, businesses, and neighbourhoods can thrive, infrastructure keeps up with growth, and city hall delivers real results. I want to restore pride in our city and build a stronger future for every Londoner. I hope to make it one of the best cities in all of Ontario.

Apathy. Too many people feel their voices don’t matter and that nothing will change. When people lose faith in local government, it becomes harder to solve every other challenge. Rebuilding trust through transparency, accountability, and real action is the first step toward moving London forward. Let’s be hopeful.

I am a young candidate, and with that comes energy/determination, and a new perspective. I’m not tied to the status quo. I want to challenge old ways of thinking, engage directly with residents, and bring new ideas while staying focused on practical results. New problems require new solutions, not the same old solution for everything.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Christine Rosehart, Susan Stevenson.
paragraphs: We asked mayoral candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the top job. Here are their answers
Name: John Feher
Occupation: Retired

Family: I am married to Cathy (common law). Also I am a step-father to Kristen and her brother Kieren. And a very proud grandfather to two beautiful young ones, a boy and a girl. I am also the father of my son Connor who is 28 and we were lucky enough to adopt him at birth, with him being of Native heritage it was quite the process.
1. Do you live full time in the city?
2. Do you plan to utilize the strong mayor powers granted by the province? If so — how? If not — why?
Yes. Depending on the circumstances.
3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?
1. Addressing homelessness
2. Affordable Housing
3. Job Implementation
4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?
No one. I am my own person with my own opinions and ideas.
5. What is your vision for London?

I have learned so much over the years, with my background and also being a member of the RCMI, I was taught by some of the wisest people I have ever met. I intend to make this city safe while cleaning up the downtown. My videos on social media will go more in-depth with that. I’m on all social media.
6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?
The homelessness crisis is London’s biggest challenge at this time. Mental health and drug addiction go along with this.
7. What sets you apart from other candidates?
My background in the mental health field gives me a unique perspective on the crisis we have affecting London.
Name : Lawrence-Zachary
Occupation: Unemployed
Family : ??? Read lawrencezachary.ca/background
Yes, in an effort to reverse the decline of this city.

First is to ensure city hall bureaucrats accept oversight, meaning they don’t hide data from elected officials, and that they are working on behalf of London. Second, to build a municipal construction company – this would eliminate the rent-seeking that balloons the cost and duration of projects, ensuring that anything we decide to create is built in a cost-effective, timely manner. Finally completing the construction and integration of the Trimodal Port concept I came up with – many of the 27 positions in my platform’s blueprint to reverse the decline of this city reference it as their major revenue source.

The Trimodal Port plan is to take London’s existing infrastructure, its access to two major highways, two major rail lines that connect to ports on the east and west coasts of the country, and an international airport, and connect them with an inland port. This lowers the costs for businesses, reducing supply chain variables, reducing carbon footprint, and being able to deliver and be delivered to faster – consequently creating a massive incentive for manufacturers, and other businesses to migrate to London.

None, there’s no historical figure, certainly no city politician, with my qualities and values. Perhaps the closest politician would be Lee Kuan Yew, who built Singapore’s entire economic miracle by exploiting its geographic location and heavily utilized state-owned enterprises to generate massive revenue for the country while stamping out rent seeking and corruption – however we differ in important ways, such as the importance I put on personal liberty.
An aesthetic, culturally rich, prosperous city with low taxes, strong trustworthy institutions, and an engaged, demanding electorate that believes the value of this city is worth defending.

The decline of the city. We have 31.3% food insecurity, 33% downtown office vacancy, 8.2% unemployment (down from its 9.2% high only because fewer people are looking for work), over 80,000 residents without doctors, and a police service that takes too long to respond to Priority 2 calls while prioritizing closing cases instead of clearing them. This is unsustainable and demands structural solutions, and an injection of absolute accountability.

I am a systems architect and philosopher who can create solutions, not just point problems out or wait for one to be handed a solution to rubber stamp. My site currently has a 27-position blueprint I designed to reverse the managed decline of the city, divided into major and minor positions – all important, but the distinction represents the scope and urgency of that element of the plan.
Name: Kirsten Krose
Occupation: Founder and owner of a boutique public affairs firm
Family : I have one.

I plan to bring collaborative leadership to council, working to build consensus where possible, and pushing for outcomes that reflect the needs and preferences of Londoners. With a rapidly changing world, we are seeing politicians make decisions today on issues that we couldn’t have predicted four years ago.

I intend to be an accountable and transparent mayor, and I don’t think it’s responsible to speculate on what circumstances I would be willing to use this incredibly powerful tool at this time. What I can commit to is that I plan to work with – not against – council and the community to make sure every Londoner gets the services they need.
My top priorities are investing in services that work, traffic that moves, and communities that feel safe. And I intend to deliver on these priorities while respecting the taxpayer.

From the big issues like tackling homeless and housing, to the basic things like making sure the roads are plowed on time, Londoners deserve a city that works. We deserve to feel safe walking down the street, and shouldn’t be spending our time stuck in traffic.
I will work to lead council in making faster, thoughtful decisions, delivering good value for tax dollars, and holding ourselves accountable for keeping priorities moving forward.
Jane Bigelow, first female mayor of London – she was a disruptor.

My vision is for a city that works for everybody. When you ask people what they want from city hall, it’s about the fundamentals – the pothole that’s gone unfilled since winter, the permit that took four months to approve, the park bench that never got fixed.

When we get the basics right, everything else follows, and people can thrive. My vision is that every person, business, non-profit receives the services they need to thrive, and that by the end of my time as mayor, everybody feels that their quality of life has improved.

We are facing a growing need from the community for the supports and services needed to have a good quality of life. At the same time, the resources needed to do this work are becoming more constrained, and people no longer see that they are getting good value for their tax dollars.

Everybody sees the problems, but we don’t see accountability and transparency around budgeting, city contracts, and decision making. Londoners need to know that we are investing in the services that deliver real outcomes that address the barriers that are preventing London from reaching its potential.

I have strong professional and volunteer experience working with government, business, community organizations, and the public to deliver real results. While other candidates have been part of years of council decisions that have led to where we are today, I am an outsider and bring new perspectives, and extensive leadership experience bringing the right people together to find collaborative, meaningful solutions to problems. And while I have not been an elected politician, I have spent my professional career in politics: I’m not new to politics, government, stakeholder relations or just getting work done in complex environments.
Name: Dan Lenart
Occupation: Staff training (outreach/homeless), public education (stigma), advocacy, retired mental health worker
Family: Family buried in Toronto, some live here.
Full time last 36 years

Reluctantly, “strong mayor powers” sounds like a Trump-style dictator. The larger city council represents more of the city than one individual, “chief magistrate.” Even if the position is supposed to be “city wide”

#1 New city hall – Renting out or leasing 12 different sites for “city business” is too expensive, and needs to be carried out under ONE ROOF, if at all possible. $120 million has been set aside for a “new office/building.” Past attempts to finance a NEW site were unsuccessful. Broaden requests for proposals (RFP) to all of Canada, like our financial hub Toronto through a (PPP) “public private partnership.”
#2 Prevent homeless problem further increasing out of control – shift CIR bylaw (no special constables) from harassing/bullying our most vulnerable to inspecting substandard/”slumlord” housing.
#3 Improve traffic bottlenecks (+rush hour gridlock) with more river bridges/rail under/overpasses
George Wenige ran for mayor 21 times and won 19 (I believe), Mostly against Al Denis. Sometimes for a year or two, then the other would win.
My London – We have more dogs than any other city. Some homeowners place water dishes out for dog walkers, but will cheer the harassment and bullying of our most vulnerable.

“Them” – Houseless street folk are rounded up for jail/psychiatric hospital as eyesores and community pests bylaw enforcement + CIR as if they are not real people with full human rights. Many have given up, fallen off the work rolls and no longer look for or are interested in meaningful employment, possibly not even having a resume to hand out for job offers.

Many surveys have shown London is hurting. This is why bus ridership is low – they can’t afford cash fares. Was the BRT a bad decision? In a have-not city of inequality, car owners will not park them to ride the bus with the economically challenged.

Leadership at city hall should be for everyone, with full equal rights, regardless of present circumstances. Public safety? Citizens should NOT have to be afraid to call 911. Having worked here most of my life in various social service agencies, I believe I have insights towards these crucial lifestyle issues never mentioned in your newspaper.
Voter turnout has reflected this disconnection with lower and lower numbers showing up on election day. Will anyone show up October 26, 2026 to cast a ballot?
Name: Bronagh Joyce Morgan
Occupation: Legal editor and instructor; Business owner; London Arts Council roster artist and educator; AI evaluator

Family : My two living kids Rain and Holly, my partner Chris, and I live in northwest London. I have another daughter Violet who died at 3 days old in 2009. I don’t like her to be left out. She is an important part of our family and like my other family members, gives me strength and helps shape everything I do and think. I have a sister in Niagara (where I am from) and one in Colorado Springs. My parents aren’t alive anymore.

No I don’t. Collaboration on council is needed. I think we can get there on the big issues, every time, by having honest conversations in the open without resorting to personal attacks or needless politicking. And as leaders, we need to model collaborative behaviour.

1. One honest review of how bylaws, policies, and contracts are written to find opportunities to streamline and potential risks of uneven/unfair application . . . similar to what the provincial appointees for LHSC and TVDSB are being paid lots more than a mayor’s salary to do. There are many in London who are suffering. I want to hear from our most vulnerable citizens and people on the frontlines serving them to understand what we can do collectively as a city to ease their pain and improve their lives. 3. Look at multi-year funding cycles for service providers doing things that are municipal responsibilities.

I appreciated the measured approaches that Phil Squire took to issues. His voting always struck me as logic based, rather than left- or right-leaning. We both like running and the Majors. content_blocks.text: I identify most with Anne Marie DeCicco-Best because she embodied what it means to be a genuine, people-first leader. content_blocks.text: My vision for London, Ontario, centres on building economic resilience, protecting essential needs, and upholding true integrity in city leadership. content_blocks.text: London’s biggest challenge is that we have lost sight of our shared humanity. We have forgotten that at the end of the day, we all bleed red and share the same basic needs. stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 1 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 1 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 1 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Hadleigh McAlister

Occupation: Full-time city councillor

Family: My wife Samantha, our daughter Maeve and our dog Charlie.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

I live in Ward 1.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

I have and will continue to work full-time as a city councillor.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Housing and homelessness

Infrastructure

Improving city services

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I have the utmost respect for the Mathyssen family. Irene and Lindsay were compassionate and dedicated politicians who served their constituents well. I have had the pleasure of working with both and I endeavour to live up to the high standard of public service they set.

5. What is your vision for London?

I want everyone to be proud to call London their home. To achieve a higher quality of life that Londoners deserve, our city services need to meet the current and future needs of Londoners. It is important that we continue to invest in our recreational facilities, parks, infrastructure, libraries, transit, housing and homeless solutions. I want London to be a safe, accessible, inclusive, and prosperous city for current residents and future generations.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Londoners are faced with many socio-economic challenges right now. Our economy is still sluggish and adapting to volatile markets, housing and groceries have become unaffordable, and we’ve seen high numbers of people experiencing homelessness in our city. Over the last four years efforts have been made to address these important issues at the local level. London cannot solve all the challenges alone and to make real headway we need to have greater co-ordination between all levels of government.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I have recent experience dealing with the current challenges facing Ward 1 and London. When I took office in 2022, I saw what decades of neglect had done to Ward 1. I have worked tirelessly to ensure that the city invests in Ward 1. In four years, I have been able to secure historic investments in our aging recreational facilities and infrastructure. I have also been a vocal advocate for housing affordability, addressing homelessness and dealing with food security in London. I have a proven track record of working collaboratively with community organizations, city staff, my council colleagues, and provincial and federal representatives. I understand the current challenges that our city faces and will continue to be a strong and effective representative for Ward 1 and London.

Name: Roger Caranci

Occupation: Real estate agent

Family : Father of two and grandfather of five.

I will continue working as a real estate agent in a reduced capacity.

Safer streets through support for police, bylaw enforcement, and zero tolerance for tent cities and open drug use. Affordable housing that respects our neighbourhoods and fits the community. Getting back to basics by repairing potholes, plowing snow on time and protecting and maintaining our parks.

At this point, I identify most with my former colleague, the late Tom Gosnell. He built relationships, forged compromise and got things done. He returned to council after some time away and delivered a unique and invaluable perspective. Above all, he earned and maintained the trust of the people who elected him. That is the standard I set for myself when I served before and it is the standard I will bring back.

A well-run city. Currently listed as priority #8 of the City of London’s strategic plan. It should be #1. Cleaner streets and safer neighbourhoods. London should deliver the basics well and reject decline as inevitable. I want a city that supports families, businesses, and people who play by the rules.

Public safety and the condition of our streets and neighbourhoods. Too many people feel the city has lost control of parks, business areas, and open drug use. Basic services have slipped in favour of grandiose projects. It’s time for focus and accountability.

I have already done the job and I am proud of my record. As councillor from 2000 to 2010, I helped deliver the Hale-Trafalgar overpass, the HELP clean water initiative, and the renaming of Airport Road to Veterans Memorial Parkway. As president of Residenza Affordable Housing, our team has built and maintained 300 beautiful affordable homes for seniors, veterans, and low-income families. I bring experience, common sense and a record of results.

We asked Ward 2 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Shawn Lewis

Age: a full fledged GenX, 54

Occupation : City councillor & deputy mayor

Family : Single, 1 cat, and a hockey team worth of nephews and their friends.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Yes, I live in Ward 2 and have been proud to call the east end my home for over 25 years.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

Yes and I strongly believe it must be to properly do the job for a city of half a million people.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Every candidate will say homeless and addiction, but that must come alongside a recognition that the city cannot fix that alone, that there are provincial and federal changes needed. Some changes cannot be direct action via property taxes, but advocating with other levels of government and also has to include appropriate measures for community safety and policing.

Ensuring Ward 2 and the east end is getting necessary infrastructure renewal.

Enhancing customer service and efficiency at city hall for Londoners and providing good value for taxes in our services.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I learned a great deal from two women in our city, Cheryl Miller, who was a TVDSB trustee and then a member of council, and Irene Mathyssen, who served as a Member of Parliament who I had the privilege of working directly for. I also developed a great relationship and learned from Mayor Ed Holder in my first term on council.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision for London is for it to be a vibrant city that competes regionally and globally and offers a wide range of opportunities for work, housing, entertainment, and an excellent quality of life for the people who call it home, a city that is seen as the capital of Southwestern Ontario.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The biggest challenge facing London today is a problem not of our making, and shared by cities across the province and country, the issue of homelessness and addiction and the safety and economic problems that come from that.

It is a challenge created by the province closing mental health hospitals and providing rates of social assistance too low to help people and by a federal government that failed to match immigration policies to housing, education, health care, and infrastructure capacity to absorb newcomers appropriately. It is a problem that all 3 levels of government, as well as non-profits, charitable, faith organizations and civil society at large need to do their parts to address.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

The difference with me is I don’t tell people what I think they want to hear, I give them an honest answer even if I know they won’t like it. I don’t make grand promises to fix things or do things that a city simply cannot just do. At the same time my record speaks for itself, the promises I made in both my previous elections have been kept, I’ve brought those things forward and delivered results. I’m straightforward and my residents in Ward 2 know they can approach me in the grocery store or at the Malibu or wherever they run into me and chat, because I live, work, and play here, Ward 2 is my home too.

Name : Zack Ramsey

Occupation: Concrete construction worker

Family: I have a wife and two cats (Harvey and Booga)

I do not. I live just on the west side of Highbury Avenue. I chose to run in Ward 2 as it is where I spend a majority of my time and “living” in a ward should be defined as where you spend your awake time not where you sleep.

City council will be my sole occupation. I have worked 40- to 60-hour weeks all my life and I have no plans to slow down in such an important role.

Treat the crisis we face like crisis (homelessness, affordability, housing, etc.)

Organizing London tenants, workers, and communities so Londoners have more power to improve their lives.

Reforest the Forest City. (Expand our canopy coverage, grow more food in public, improve our parks, etc.)

I like a few city politicians but, none enough to say that I identify with them. While I love politics, I am running because I am disappointed in my elected officials. I am disappointed that instead of finding solutions that will improve the quality of Londoners’ lives they continue to make excuses at every opportunity.

I want London to be a place where you have a roof above your head, food in your belly, and the knowledge that your children will have a more prosperous future than yourself! I envision a London where people have free time to live their lives how they like and can be involved in their community!

Affordability: it affects all the other crisis London faces. If folks are paid too little and charged too much it forces them to work longer hours, which disconnects them from their community and their passions. When you have to work more hours you have to spend less time with your kids, less time with your friends, less time spent on your passions, and less time spent improving your city. Many Londoners are forced to make choices between food and rent or food and medication.

I do not believe that any of the problems we face can be solved solely by city council. To solve these large systemic issues it will require the collective effort of every Londoner. I believe the crisis we face are a feature of the system we live in not an accident or mistake. Every crisis that exists only exists because it is not profitable to solve.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Steve Reed, Alexandria Hames

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 3 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 3 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 3 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Peter Cuddy

Occupation : Ward 3 councillor, City of London

Family: Wife Lisa, 3 children

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

YES. City councillor has been my full-time job since being elected in 2022 and will continue to be my full-time occupation.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Serving the residents of Ward 3 and responding to their needs without delay.

Keep in property taxes in line with inflation or below inflation.

Cutting red tape at city hall.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Bernie MacDonald

5. What is your vision for London?

London has so much commercial and industrial opportunity due to our proximity to international trading partners, transportation infrastructure and our fast-growing economy. I want to build on that vision of economic growth. Revitalizing our downtown, encouraging residential development in our downtown by means of housing our homeless with the assistance of both federal and provincial governments. This will bring long-term sustainable growth to our core. All the while, we need to keep our property taxes in lockstep with inflation or below. Responsible fiscal management and keeping our city’s 4-star Moodys credit rating are critical to London’s growth.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Mental health / addiction, homelessness issues and the housing of our highest acuity are our greatest challenge. For this to succeed, we need to continue to partner with all levels of government to ensure long-term sustainable solutions are implemented.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My constituents will tell you that I am the hardest working councillor since Bernie MacDonald. That is high praise, as Bernie is a legend in Ward 3, and a role model to me personally. I respond to all residents as quickly as possible, often within the hour of their email or text. I call every resident personally for follow up calls to ensure their concerns have been resolved to their satisfaction. I am conciliatory, working with my colleagues to find solutions in committee and on council. My motions are often passed unanimously, as was the case of the renoviction motion passed in 2024. I speak to my colleagues to ask for their opinions, and ways to improve motions about to come to committee or council.

Name: Ben Durham

Occupation : Creative director, video producer, entrepreneur

Family: Happily married to the most amazing and supportive wife in London.

I live and own a home in Ward 3.

Yes, if elected as Ward 3 city councillor, this will be my sole full-time occupation.

In addition, if I had been at that table, I would have moved two amendments to the proposal:

1. Remove the part-time option entirely (because we are no longer a small city), and

2. Scale back the increase to a more modest, fiscally responsible number, rather than 35%

Smarter traffic, safer streets

Financial accountability

Tackle homelessness now

None. I’m my own person and I don’t pattern myself after other leaders.

My vision of London is one where:

London’s taken a leadership role by learning from successes around the world and adapting them for our city’s specific economic and geographic needs.

Transportation is modernized and allows more options for more people. Congestion is reduced, commutes are pleasant and predictable, and we’ve adapted well to our vibrant mid-sized city of London, Ontario.

The homelessness crisis is a thing of the past and the downtown is a bustling district with a strong pulse. Communities across London all have their own distinct personalities and draws but because of everyone tirelessly fighting for a better London together, we accomplish what many thought to be impossible: a brighter future for London.

Most people say “homelessness” is London’s biggest challenge (when asked).

However, after knocking on thousands of doors across Ward 3 and tallying residents’ concerns, it’s clear to me (with a sample size of thousands) that traffic-related issues such as road work co-ordination, traffic congestion, street safety (speeding), and road maintenance are cumulatively their most major concern.

That’s why, since day one, I’ve made “Smarter Traffic, Safer Streets” the NUMBER ONE PILLAR for my platform.

I’m the charismatic and strategic leader Ward 3 needs right now.

I’m firm but kind and determined to get things done.

No one else can outwork my dedication and time management skills.

I wake up at 7am, work until 3pm, and then tirelessly canvass 3-9pm, and then get the best sleeps of my life. And I have been doing this 6 days per week for the last few months and will continue to do so until October 26th (election day).

Name : Harkirat Kaur

Occupation : Disability support worker

Family: I come from a close-knit family and have built my life in London. My family has taught me the value of hard work, responsibility, perseverance and looking out for the people around me.

Yes. I live in Ward 3.

Yes. If elected, I will treat the role as a full-time responsibility. Being a councillor is more than attending council meetings. It means being accessible to residents, understanding what is happening in the ward, following up on concerns and being prepared to do the work between meetings. I would make serving Ward 3 my priority.

My three priorities are better-connected transportation, safer and stronger neighbourhoods, and more responsive city services. Ward 3 deserves reliable bus service, better cycling and active-transportation connections, and infrastructure that reflects how people actually move around our community. I also want to see safer neighbourhoods and more quality green space, including opportunities for a larger park where our community can gather and families can enjoy the outdoors. Finally, residents should be able to count on city services that are responsive, practical and accountable.

I respect many people who have served London, but I would not say that I model myself after one particular politician. I am running to bring my own perspective and to be an independent voice for Ward 3. I believe good representation starts with listening, asking difficult questions when necessary and making decisions based on what is best for residents – not simply following the way things have always been done.

I want London to be a city where people can build a good life and feel proud of the neighbourhood they call home. That means reliable public transportation, safer streets, accessible cycling and active-transportation routes, quality parks and green spaces, and city services that respond when residents need them. I also want London to grow thoughtfully, with infrastructure and services keeping pace with that growth. My vision is a city that is connected, safe, welcoming and practical – a city that works for families, seniors, students, workers and future generations.

One of our biggest challenges is ensuring that London’s growth keeps pace with the infrastructure and services residents depend on. We cannot measure success simply by how much the city grows. We also have to ask whether people can get where they need to go, whether neighbourhoods feel safe, whether there is enough quality green space and whether residents can get timely, responsive service from the city. Affordability and housing pressures add to that challenge. London needs thoughtful growth that improves quality of life rather than putting additional pressure on the people who already live here.

I am not a career politician, and I believe that gives me a different perspective. I am a working professional and someone who has spent my career working directly with people and understanding the challenges they face. I am not running for a title – I am running because I believe Ward 3 deserves a strong, independent and accessible voice at city hall. I will listen to residents, ask questions, do the work and be accountable for the decisions I make. I may be new to politics, but I am not new to responsibility, service or hard work.

Name : Leroy Osbourne

Age: respectfully decline. I wish for voters to look at my experience and community contributions than my birth year.

Occupation: university staffer

Family: respectfully decline given how divisive politics has been in recent years.

Yes, the council role will be my sole occupation and responsibility after family.

Cost of housing

Cost of living

Infrastructure

Tough to say just one. The personable, charismatic, commitment of Harold Usher. The thoughtfulness and straightforwardness of Jesse Helmer. The articulation and compassion of Sam Trosow and David Ferreira.

A place where people are proud of their city, has top-quality infrastructure, places that create an experience, addresses affordability and improves the quality of life of all of us.

Cost of living – addresses housing, poverty, quality of life.

Breadth of experience; I have seen issues up front for a long time. I have smart, innovative and pragmatic ideas for my ward and our city. From little homes communities, a community wealth fund idea and on-demand mini-buses for unserved areas. I want to look at successful initiatives of other municipalities, not reinventing the wheel or having endless staff and consultant reports. I wish to participate in decisive decisions that move us forward in positive ways.

Name: Zak Rahim

Occupation : I run a political consulting agency that has helped good people get elected to deliver positive results for our community. I believe that the political process is the true vehicle for positive change and I channel this belief into my small business. As a volunteer on the frontline of the homelessness crisis since 2017, I’ve dedicated my time to dealing with the worsening socioeconomic crisis in our community in real time.

Family : I’m unmarried with no kids. Like many young Londoners, the milestone of being married, finding your first home, and having kids is moving further and further away. We are all being impacted by the current socioeconomic crisis. However, the way that this crisis is impacting my generation is making me fearful for those that come after me.

No, I do not own property, and I chose to stay at home outside of the ward to lend my support to my family. My elderly grandfather is dependent on our collective efforts. In a housing crisis, our seniors are choosing between a nutritious meal and paying rent on a fixed income. I’m inspired to run so that seniors, like my grandfather, who’ve worked hard their whole lives don’t have to choose between the two basic necessities of food or shelter.

Yes. The role of a London city councillor should be full time regardless of the pay. It should also be full time considering that council voted themselves a 35% pay raise, which is beyond the rate of inflation. This is quite a lot to ask from Londoners given the economic context. It is council’s responsibility to deliver value for this money, including setting performance standards for committee.

Public accountability starting with who we appoint to our agencies. When council appoints political actors and rubber stamp their budget proposal the result is sky-high tax increases. Instead I’ll appoint experts to hold administration to account and lower taxes.

On taxpayer value, that means cutting wasteful spending across the city and making sure city contracts go towards supporting London jobs & businesses.

The cost of housing has far outpaced income growth, while London’s homelessness numbers have had similar growth. I want density done right, building up instead of endless sprawl, protecting the character of our neighbourhoods while cutting the red tape that slows down the housing, including supportive housing, that is needed yesterday.

Mayor Mike Bradley of Sarnia never shied away from holding Sarnia’s agencies to account by bringing scrutiny to administrations’ proposals, cutting spending to keep more money in the pocket of citizens.

Mayor Ed Holder of London’s leadership during COVID, and in response to the murder of the Afzaal family, embodied strong leadership that brought people together in a crisis to work together to deliver for our community.

Mayor Joe Preston who says “yes is the answer, now what is the question.” Has led to bold developments in alleviating the housing and homelessness crisis and growing the economy in St. Thomas. We need this quality of leadership in London to say yes to bold ideas.

A city that says yes. Yes to housing, Yes to helping the most vulnerable, Yes to fighting the socioeconomic causes of the crime and disorder, and yes to keeping London affordable & vibrant.

London is facing a homelessness crisis that is made worse by our lack of institutional capacity. Yes, we started building more homes, but we remain behind the overall demand. The cost of living remains high, which pushes people to the streets. On the frontlines, I witnessed several people freeze to death in the winter. I spent my nights during the coldest point of winter at the city’s Boyle Memorial Community Centre warming shelter. I saw the city scrambling to effectively stand up its winter response services. Coupled with constantly hearing from Londoners that folks are struggling on our streets, I realized that we are lacking the proper means to give people some level of dignity in their lives.

I attended council throughout this term as an observer and advocated for policy decisions meant to improve the situation on our streets. I understand the cost of living crisis firsthand. I’ve seen the interrelated effects of homelessness. All of this prompts me to work tirelessly on the frontline. I bring a humanitarian perspective and business leadership that will translate into respecting the taxpayer, doing more with less and delivering results for Londoners.

I want to deliver results with compassion for our community in mind to ensure a better London for the next generation.

Name: Peter Cuddy
Occupation : Ward 3 councillor, City of London
Family: Wife Lisa, 3 children
1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?
YES. City councillor has been my full-time job since being elected in 2022 and will continue to be my full-time occupation.
3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?
Serving the residents of Ward 3 and responding to their needs without delay.
Keep in property taxes in line with inflation or below inflation.
Cutting red tape at city hall.
4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?
Bernie MacDonald
5. What is your vision for London?

London has so much commercial and industrial opportunity due to our proximity to international trading partners, transportation infrastructure and our fast-growing economy. I want to build on that vision of economic growth. Revitalizing our downtown, encouraging residential development in our downtown by means of housing our homeless with the assistance of both federal and provincial governments. This will bring long-term sustainable growth to our core. All the while, we need to keep our property taxes in lockstep with inflation or below. Responsible fiscal management and keeping our city’s 4-star Moodys credit rating are critical to London’s growth.
6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Mental health / addiction, homelessness issues and the housing of our highest acuity are our greatest challenge. For this to succeed, we need to continue to partner with all levels of government to ensure long-term sustainable solutions are implemented.
7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My constituents will tell you that I am the hardest working councillor since Bernie MacDonald. That is high praise, as Bernie is a legend in Ward 3, and a role model to me personally. I respond to all residents as quickly as possible, often within the hour of their email or text. I call every resident personally for follow up calls to ensure their concerns have been resolved to their satisfaction. I am conciliatory, working with my colleagues to find solutions in committee and on council. My motions are often passed unanimously, as was the case of the renoviction motion passed in 2024. I speak to my colleagues to ask for their opinions, and ways to improve motions about to come to committee or council.
Name: Ben Durham
Occupation : Creative director, video producer, entrepreneur
Family: Happily married to the most amazing and supportive wife in London.
I live and own a home in Ward 3.
Yes, if elected as Ward 3 city councillor, this will be my sole full-time occupation.

1. Remove the part-time option entirely (because we are no longer a small city), and
2. Scale back the increase to a more modest, fiscally responsible number, rather than 35%
Smarter traffic, safer streets
Financial accountability
Tackle homelessness now
None. I’m my own person and I don’t pattern myself after other leaders.
My vision of London is one where:
London’s taken a leadership role by learning from successes around the world and adapting them for our city’s specific economic and geographic needs.

Transportation is modernized and allows more options for more people. Congestion is reduced, commutes are pleasant and predictable, and we’ve adapted well to our vibrant mid-sized city of London, Ontario.

The homelessness crisis is a thing of the past and the downtown is a bustling district with a strong pulse. Communities across London all have their own distinct personalities and draws but because of everyone tirelessly fighting for a better London together, we accomplish what many thought to be impossible: a brighter future for London.
Most people say “homelessness” is London’s biggest challenge (when asked).

However, after knocking on thousands of doors across Ward 3 and tallying residents’ concerns, it’s clear to me (with a sample size of thousands) that traffic-related issues such as road work co-ordination, traffic congestion, street safety (speeding), and road maintenance are cumulatively their most major concern.
That’s why, since day one, I’ve made “Smarter Traffic, Safer Streets” the NUMBER ONE PILLAR for my platform.
I’m the charismatic and strategic leader Ward 3 needs right now.
I’m firm but kind and determined to get things done.
No one else can outwork my dedication and time management skills.

I wake up at 7am, work until 3pm, and then tirelessly canvass 3-9pm, and then get the best sleeps of my life. And I have been doing this 6 days per week for the last few months and will continue to do so until October 26th (election day).
Name : Harkirat Kaur
Occupation : Disability support worker
Family: I come from a close-knit family and have built my life in London. My family has taught me the value of hard work, responsibility, perseverance and looking out for the people around me.
Yes. I live in Ward 3.

Yes. If elected, I will treat the role as a full-time responsibility. Being a councillor is more than attending council meetings. It means being accessible to residents, understanding what is happening in the ward, following up on concerns and being prepared to do the work between meetings. I would make serving Ward 3 my priority.

My three priorities are better-connected transportation, safer and stronger neighbourhoods, and more responsive city services. Ward 3 deserves reliable bus service, better cycling and active-transportation connections, and infrastructure that reflects how people actually move around our community. I also want to see safer neighbourhoods and more quality green space, including opportunities for a larger park where our community can gather and families can enjoy the outdoors. Finally, residents should be able to count on city services that are responsive, practical and accountable.

I respect many people who have served London, but I would not say that I model myself after one particular politician. I am running to bring my own perspective and to be an independent voice for Ward 3. I believe good representation starts with listening, asking difficult questions when necessary and making decisions based on what is best for residents – not simply following the way things have always been done.

I want London to be a city where people can build a good life and feel proud of the neighbourhood they call home. That means reliable public transportation, safer streets, accessible cycling and active-transportation routes, quality parks and green spaces, and city services that respond when residents need them. I also want London to grow thoughtfully, with infrastructure and services keeping pace with that growth. My vision is a city that is connected, safe, welcoming and practical – a city that works for families, seniors, students, workers and future generations.

One of our biggest challenges is ensuring that London’s growth keeps pace with the infrastructure and services residents depend on. We cannot measure success simply by how much the city grows. We also have to ask whether people can get where they need to go, whether neighbourhoods feel safe, whether there is enough quality green space and whether residents can get timely, responsive service from the city. Affordability and housing pressures add to that challenge. London needs thoughtful growth that improves quality of life rather than putting additional pressure on the people who already live here.

I am not a career politician, and I believe that gives me a different perspective. I am a working professional and someone who has spent my career working directly with people and understanding the challenges they face. I am not running for a title – I am running because I believe Ward 3 deserves a strong, independent and accessible voice at city hall. I will listen to residents, ask questions, do the work and be accountable for the decisions I make. I may be new to politics, but I am not new to responsibility, service or hard work.

Yes, the council role will be my sole occupation and responsibility after family.

I wish to participate in decisive decisions that move us forward in positive ways.
