So-called “working royals” are members of the royal family who carry out official duties on behalf of the monarch. They receive administrative and other support from the Royal Household to do so.
A letter issued by the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the Royal Household, said that following the couple’s relocation there had been “a number of requests for guidance”.
The letter was issued “to help avoid doubt or confusion.”

“It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the sovereign, and are no longer working members of the royal family,” it said.

“This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”

Current senior working royals are: Charles, his wife Queen Camilla, son and heir Prince William and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales, as well as Charles’s sister Princess Anne and brother Edward and his wife Sophie, known as the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh.
Others include several of the late Queen Elizabeth II’s cousins.

Harry and Meghan, formally known as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are reportedly living in central England’s Cotswolds region and are said to have enrolled their children at private schools there for the coming academic year.
Harry’s grandmother Queen Elizabeth stripped them of their “Royal Highness” titles, police protection and public funding when they quit royal duties in 2020.
“Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness… are not used,” the letter added.

“The charitable work of the duke and duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
The clarification comes amid uncertainty over what, if any, security the Sussexes will have paid for by the state.
Britain’s Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec) — an independent body overseen by the interior ministry — decides which politicians, royals and others get police protection.
Harry battled the ministry in the courts after Ravec downgraded his security following his 2020 move.
He lost his bid to reverse the decision but with his permanent return, Ravec’s risk management board will likely be re-evaluating the threat level he faces.

stories.title: Oil climbs on Hormuz risks and rising Chinese buying
stories.summary: As a result, oil now finds itself on the precipice of US$100 a barrel for the third time this year
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Oil moved higher on a thin day of holiday trading as risks to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz continued to support prices, alongside the return of Chinese crude purchasing.

Brent briefly topped US$98 a barrel, before easing slightly. Iran said that a deal with Oman to manage shipping through Hormuz is imminent, raising questions over how the US would respond after it struck Iranian vessels over the weekend. Tehran also warned that ships face the risk of attack near the Oman coastline.

Separately, Saudi Aramco’s oil facilities in Jazan came under fresh attack on Monday, according to people familiar with the matter. It was the latest in a series of strikes that have already forced a major refinery in the area to shut operations.

The continued price risks stemming from the Middle East conflict are being amplified by a return of Chinese buying. A rebound in Beijing’s purchases has driven up the price of barrels from West Africa to Canada in recent days. Earlier in the war, China’s oil-buying hiatus was one of the key factors quelling prices.

As a result, oil now finds itself on the precipice of $100 a barrel for the third time this year, with Brent crude up about 60% so far in 2026. Refined products such as diesel have posted even steeper gains amid the six-month conflict and separate supply disruptions caused by the Russia-Ukraine war.

“The pace at which inventories are drawing down has accelerated so much in crude just over the last couple of weeks,” Amrita Sen, co-founder and director of research at Energy Aspects, said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “I really think crude is poised to take a significant leg higher.”

Monday’s trading session was relatively subdued because of the US Labor Day holiday. The start of a major conference in Singapore also drew traders away from their desks. The Iran war, tightening global inventories and China’s demand outlook are expected to dominate the agenda at the Asia-Pacific Petroleum Conference.

Hedge funds have turned the most bullish on Brent since May after the recent flare-up between the US and Iran, increasing their net-bullish positions in the week ended Sept. 1. Net-long wagers on US crude rose to the highest since June.

“In an upside price scenario, where shipping attacks broaden and intensify, we see Brent potentially reaching $120,” Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “The events of the last few days do suggest that the risk of shipping disruptions broadening and intensifying is an important one.”

stories.title: Monday Sports Notes: Mustangs crush York, Majors lead series 2-1, Knights split Western trip, Benati scores miracle winner
stories.summary: The Michael Faulds era at Western University began in dramatic fashion with a 78-7 win over York Sunday night.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Michael Faulds era at Western University began in dramatic fashion with a 78-7 win over York Sunday night.

Quarterback Jerome Rancourt threw for two touchdowns and ran in three more as Western scored 10 majors en route to the blowout victory.

“We had eight months of kind of bottled up, wanting to play, right?” Faulds told media after the game.

Faulds gave credit to more than 10 first-time starting players. Rancourt finished his evening 24-28 passing for 339 yards while adding 49 more on the ground.

“I did tell pros that I was coming back prior to the draft to be doing this,” said Rancourt.

“To run the QB1 spot and I’ve been waiting for so long and I’ve worked hard to get to get to, and then I think it’s been paying off I can do more than run a ball.”

Western will now head west to Windsor to face the Lancers Saturday. Windsor split its first two games including a win over Laurier this weekend.

London Majors lead playoff series 2-1

The London Majors nearly completed a miracle ninth-inning comeback.

Trailing the Welland Jackfish 6-0 going into the bottom of the ninth in game three at Labatt Park, the Majors started to rally.

The first seven batters of the inning reached base, but the Jackfish got three straight outs to survive and cut the series deficit to 2-1 heading back to Welland Wednesday night.

With the tying run at third, Deivy Mendez struck out Ryder Hancock to end the game.

Cristian Inoa doubled home a pair of runs in London’s five-run ninth. Maikol Escotto, Starling Joseph, and David Draayers drove in the Majors’ other runs.

After Wednesday’s game, the Majors and Jackfish will return to Labatt Park Friday for Game five.

Knights split west coast exhibition series

Coves evens the score!🚨 pic.twitter.com/abHD6pOufB — London Knights (@LondonKnights) September 5, 2026

Coves evens the score!🚨 pic.twitter.com/abHD6pOufB

The London Knights are home from an historic west coast exhibition series after splitting the two games in Victoria, B.C.

One night after being blown out 7-1, the Knights bounced back with a 5-3 victory in game two of ‘Clash of the Kingdoms.’

London scored three times in under four minutes during the second period to pull ahead and go onto victory.

Jaxon Cover lead the Knights with two goals and an assist including the game winner. Thomas Zocco scored his third goal of the preaseason while Caleb Mitchell and Cohen Bidgood also scored.This was the first time a game was played between these two leagues outside of the Memorial Cup since 2010.

London will wrap up its exhibition schedule with a home-and-home series with the Sarnia Sting Thursday and Friday.

Julia Benati scores from half to win NSL game

Julia Benati wins it with a shot from Half 😱 @hfxtidesfc pic.twitter.com/H9Q7LsAAcQ — Northern Super League (@NorthernSuperLg) September 6, 2026

With just seconds remaining in a 0-0 game, Julia Benati from Dorchester, Ont. scored a miracle game winner for the Halifax Tides of the Northern Soccer League.

The Vancouver Rise had keeper Jessica Wulf pushed up as they pressed forward for a winner, but when the ball was turned over in the Halifax end, Benati made a few moves toward half and drilled a 50-metre strike into the empty goal to give Halifax a 1-0 win in the 95th minute.

It was a massive goal as the Tides now take over the fourth and final playoff spot from the Rise with 24 points

stories.title: Brain injury patient advocates for donations to help Parkwood Institute purchase therapy system
stories.summary: Hassan Abdul-Wahed is still navigating the long road back from a serious accident in May 2025.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Hassan Abdul-Wahed is still navigating the long road back from a serious accident in May 2025.

“I had a traumatic brain injury, like an accident relating with a vehicle,” said Abdul-Wahed.

“I remember I had to get a bunch of surgeries, and spent time at Victoria [Hospital], University [Hospital], and then around the three-month mark I was at Parkwood [Institute] and stayed there for the rest of the time.”

To help people like Abdul-Wahed, the Canadian Cedars of Hope hosted a 5-kilometre run and walk to support the Acquired Brain Injury Program at Parkwood Institute.

The event was called Miles for Minds and came after Abdul-Wahed made a near-miraculous recovery at St. Joseph’s Hospital.

“There’s no way I can pay the hospital back no matter what I do,” said Abdul-Wahed.

“I just have to try my best and hopefully we’ll have more events in the future to spread more awareness.”

The event raised about $7,000 toward the goal of $55,000 to purchase the XCite Therapy system. It’s an innovative technology that uses electrical stimulation to help patients regain strength, movement and independence.

“The way it works is you apply electrical current with this device and the Xcite then specifies these different electrodes to be turned on in a certain pattern that mimics real functional activities like reaching, grasping, walking and standing,” said Jeff Weiler, coordinator of The Gray Centre for Mobility and Activity at St. Joseph’s Health Care London.

“This would be really beneficial for patients as they’re going along the rehabilitation journey.”

The technology can be used for patients with a brain injury, but also with a stroke or spinal cord injury.

Weiler says Abdul-Wahed would have benefited during treatment from the XCite.

“He would have applied these to his legs and the XCite would excite these muscles in a pattern that would help him learn to stand again,” said Weiler.

“This type of machine will really speed up therapy for certain patients.”

With the current healthcare landscape, Weiler believes these devices are tough to purchase. Community events really help augment the tools therapists can provide to patients.

Abdul-Wahed doesn’t remember anything from his accident.He May still never be the same as he once was, but he’s grateful to be alive and raise awareness for brain injuries.

“We know with the hospital there’s still things they need more funding, so we can’t just say it and want someone else to do it,” said Abdul-Wahed.

“We have to take initiative and try our best to spread awareness and help others push the word to raise money.”

content_blocks.text: Hassan Abdul-Wahed is still navigating the long road back from a serious accident in May 2025.
“I had a traumatic brain injury, like an accident relating with a vehicle,” said Abdul-Wahed.

“I remember I had to get a bunch of surgeries, and spent time at Victoria [Hospital], University [Hospital], and then around the three-month mark I was at Parkwood [Institute] and stayed there for the rest of the time.”
To help people like Abdul-Wahed, the Canadian Cedars of Hope hosted a 5-kilometre run and walk to support the Acquired Brain Injury Program at Parkwood Institute.

“This would be really beneficial for patients as they’re going along the rehabilitation journey.”

stories.title: Trump’s trade war with Canada becoming U.S. midterms ballot box issue
stories.summary: Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties on Tuesday. Many are aimed at key industries in states where there are competitive midterm races.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
As the United States braces for pivotal midterm elections this November, there’s a new and unexpected issue on voters’ minds in many states: President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada.

“Canada is our friend, our closest ally and our biggest trading partner,” Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins told Politico in an interview published last week.

“This is not China that we are talking about. This is not an adversarial country. And … our economies are so linked, if you try to hurt one you end up hurting Maine.”

Collins has long been a political force in her border state but Trump’s unpopular policies — including his tariff campaign against Canada — have put her seat in jeopardy.

7:25 Ottawa’s counter-tariffs kick in Tuesday: Economist breaks down what Canadians can expect

Canada is Maine’s largest trading partner and many of the state’s critical industries, like seafood and lumber, are integrated with Canadian sectors. Collins has acknowledged that the tariffs on Canada are “terrible for Maine” and are making the job of re-election a lot harder.

While Collins’ seat in Maine could be the most vulnerable, it’s not the only one being rattled by Trump’s attacks on Canada as Republicans look to hold power in Congress.

Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont., said long-term historical trends show that, in general, midterm elections are usually bad for the party of the president in power.

He said while many political observers have been predicting for some time the House will flip to the Democrats, the Senate could also be in play now.

“Some of the key states that have become battleground states are ones with really close trading relationships with Canada,” Lebo said, pointing to Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio.

“You’ve got Republican candidates who have to be confronted with trade policies against Canada that are making it harder to export stuff to Canada and are making some things really expensive for people in those states to import.”

2:08 ‘Canada? Really?’: Americans react to Trump’s tariffs on Canada

The relationship between Canada and the United States was upended by Trump’s return to the White House. Suddenly, Canada found itself the target of tariffs and threats of annexation from a president who sees it less as a close ally and more as an adversary.

While Canadians have been laser-focused on the upheaval, many Americans have been oblivious to the downturn in the relationship. That changed last month when tensions escalated after trade talks between the two countries broke down.

Trump subsequently imposed 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks and cement to honey. Trump also ramped up his anti-Canada rhetoric and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties on Tuesday. Many are aimed at key industries in states where there are competitive midterm races.

Both countries have accused each other of adding last-minute changes to negotiations. Trump’s team has spread out on American news stations in an attempt to place the blame at Ottawa’s feet and to accuse Prime Minister Mark Carney of tanking a deal for domestic political reasons.

Carney, pushing back on those claims, said last week that he doesn’t think “appointed, unelected cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics.”

It’s not clear whether the Trump administration’s claims about the trade war are breaking through. Both the tariffs and the order to rename Lake Ontario are proving to be very unpopular with Americans.

2:00 Trump calls Canada’s exchange rate with the U.S. ‘unacceptable’

An Ipsos/Reuters poll published last week suggested two-in-three Americans disapproved of the lake’s name change. It also found only 20 per cent of Americans supported higher tariffs on Canada.

A source with who was not authorized to speak publicly said Republicans from border states approached United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during an event at the White House on Sept. 2. They told Trump’s trade czar to find an off-ramp from the trade war because it was becoming politically toxic, the source said.

Democrats have been quick to jump on the weaknesses the trade war with Canada has exposed. Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said last week “this vanity war is not a war with Canada.”

“It’s a war on Michigan because we have to pay the price,” he said. “And we pay it every single day for goods that should not cost as much as they do.”

Lebo said some Republican candidates are already trying to distance themselves from Trump and his tariffs on Canada.

5:20 The potential cost of Canada’s counter-tariffs

While New York’s Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul has been vocal in her criticism of the trade war with Canada, her Trump-backed opponent Bruce Blakeman has been harder to pin down.

“I’m not going to talk about federal issues,” Blakeman said when asked by Spectrum News about the trade tensions in late August.

Other Republicans are doubling down. Anthony Constantino, a Republican running for a House seat in New York State, said renaming Lake Ontario was an act of “marketing genius” and claimed “Trump showed strength in negotiations with Canada by playing a card he had available to play.”

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said the bigger picture is that the United States economy is in a state of flux, which is causing a lot of uncertainty ahead of the November election.

The war with Iran, rising gas prices and tariffs have affected domestic investment and employment at a time when the top issue on the ballot box is affordability.

Sands said while neither party can expect a “cake walk” in November, Trump has handed Democrats an opening with his attack on Canada.

Democrats have long been looking for something to unite centrist party members with more left-wing factions like the Democratic Socialists of America. Sands said the trade war with Canada could do just that.

“They feel that they can make the case that this is a senseless trade war,” he said.

“I think most Americans don’t even understand why it’s happening.”

stories.title: More heavy rain forecast for Cape Breton as it recovers from weekend storm
stories.summary: People are asked to check conditions before leaving, follow all road closures, don’t drive through floodwater, and turn around if drivers encounter flooding or a damaged road.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Parts of Cape Breton are being warned of more rain even as residents recover from this weekend’s storm that caused severe flooding and left one woman dead.

Environment Canada issued yellow rainfall warnings early Monday for Sydney Metro and Cape Breton County, and Victoria County.

Between 25 and 40 millimetres of rain are expected, with locally high amounts possible in thunderstorms, the national weather service said.

The rain is expected to last until this afternoon.

“Due to the impacts of the previous storm, it is advised to listen to local officials regarding road and safety conditions,” Environment Canada said.

That storm swept much of the province Saturday, but Cape Breton was hardest hit, with some parts of the island seeing more than 120 mm of rain in a single day. There were even reports of more than 200 mm in Richmond County.

Inverness, Victoria and Richmond counties all declared local states of emergencies Saturday due to severe flooding and widespread damage. All three had been dropped by Monday.

Premier Tim Houston also said Sunday that the province was mourning the loss of a woman who died during the flooding.

Nova Scotia RCMP said Sunday they had located the body of a Cleveland, N.S., woman after she went missing the previous morning. Police said they had found her vehicle parked near her residence on the far side of a flooded bridge. Her death was not believed to be suspicious, RCMP said.

“My thoughts are with her loved ones and everyone who is grieving this tragic loss,” said Premier Tim Houston on X.

Emergency Management Minister Kim Masland also gave her condolences to the family of the woman who died, calling it a “heartbreaking loss.”

“I want her loved ones to know that all Nova Scotians are standing with them,” Masland wrote in a statement.

Masland’s department said she was on the ground in Port Hawkesbury Monday, seeing the damage caused on West Bay Road and speaking with emergency officials.

The minister went on to say that the immediate priority of the government was public safety and every decision was focused on protecting people and allowing emergency responders and crews to do their work safely.

She said local, municipal, provincial and emergency management partners are providing a “unified response.”

Residents are again advised to follow local authorities’ advice, avoid non-essential travel and take care of themselves.

People are asked to check conditions before leaving, follow all road closures and barricades, don’t drive through floodwater, and turn around if they encounter flooding or a damaged road.

Emergency Management Minister Kim Masland also gave her condolences to the family of the woman who died, calling it a “heartbreaking loss.”
“I want her loved ones to know that all Nova Scotians are standing with them,” Masland wrote in a statement.
Masland’s department said she was on the ground in Port Hawkesbury Monday, seeing the damage caused on West Bay Road and speaking with emergency officials.

The minister went on to say that the immediate priority of the government was public safety and every decision was focused on protecting people and allowing emergency responders and crews to do their work safely.
She said local, municipal, provincial and emergency management partners are providing a “unified response.”
Residents are again advised to follow local authorities’ advice, avoid non-essential travel and take care of themselves.
People are asked to check conditions before leaving, follow all road closures and barricades, don’t drive through floodwater, and turn around if they encounter flooding or a damaged road.

stories.title: Environment Canada forecasts more heavy rainfall for parts of Cape Breton Island
stories.summary: It’s forecasting 25 to 40 millimetres of total rainfall, with higher amounts possible in certain areas
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Environment and Climate Change Canada has issued a heavy rainfall warning for northern parts of Cape Breton Island.

The national weather service says the area has a reduced ability to absorb rain.

It’s forecasting 25 to 40 millimetres of total rainfall, with higher amounts possible in certain areas.

Torrential rain over the weekend destroyed some roads, barriers and bridges across Cape Breton Island and the northern mainland.

A 46-year-old woman from Richmond County was found dead Saturday several hours after her abandoned vehicle was discovered near a flooded bridge.

The province’s Department of Emergency Management says drivers should listen to local officials regarding road safety conditions.

stories.title: Could GLP-1s spell relief for opioid addiction?
stories.summary: Researchers test whether drugs to reduce food cravings can help people with substance-use disorders, but urge a cautious approach
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Adam Scioli gets excited when he speaks about GLP-1 medications.

Not because they’re known globally for revolutionizing weight-loss management, but because he thinks this class of drugs is the next frontier of addictions treatment.

Dr. Scioli helped to transform care at Caron Treatment Centers in the United States during his recent tenure at the elite non-profit as an addictions psychiatrist and chief medical officer. Caron is believed to be the first of very few rehabilitation facilities in the world that prescribe GLP-1s off-label to treat substance-use disorders.

Caron added GLP-1s to its arsenal of addiction medications in 2024 and has since prescribed them to more than 500 residential clients. Dr. Scioli said researchers warned him and his colleagues that they were “putting the cart before the horse,” but it’s a decision they stand by.

“It’s no doubt groundbreaking. It’s no doubt transformative,” he said.

GLP-1 medications, such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, are only approved by the U.S. Federal Drug Administration and Health Canada for diabetes and chronic weight management. Early research, however, has shown that this class of drugs May help dampen drug cravings, similarly to how they quiet intrusive thoughts about food.

GLP-1s, developed initially for blood glucose and weight control, work by mimicking natural hormones that bind to receptors in the brain that process hunger and satiety. They also alter the brain’s dopamine pathway – the circuit for reward, motivation and desire – which helps to mute the mental preoccupation with eating.

That pathway is also central to addiction. The use of addictive substances triggers massive dopamine surges. So, a natural question has emerged: Could GLP-1s be the next big treatment for substance-use disorders?

Dr. Scioli said he has seen evidence to support this idea.

“What we’ve observed is that these GLP-1 receptor agonists seem to provide a cognitive buffer,” he said. “They allow our patients to recognize their triggers without being compelled to act on them.”

Canadian researchers are part of a growing network of scientists who are putting such early findings to the test. Results have varied, but studies so far have shown that GLP-1s have the potential to lower the risk of developing a substance-use disorder and reduce negative outcomes and cravings associated with drug use, including for nicotine, alcohol and opioids.

Experts who spoke to The Globe and Mail are optimistic about the prospects of GLP-1s, especially as opioid deaths continue to mount across the country. But, above all else, they are urging prudence.

These drugs are not yet an established treatment and robust trials are still needed to confirm their safety and efficacy with greater certainty. Such trials would need to look, for example, at the longer-term effects, dosing and who stands to benefit the most.

“There is a sense that these May be miracle drugs,” said James MacKillop, director of the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research at McMaster University. “But there always has to be quite a lot of caution when something doesn’t have the gold-standard evidence that we look for.”

GLP-1s have shown tremendous success in treating weight loss and diabetes and have been praised for their potential to address a slew of other medical issues, such as heart disease and neurodegenerative disorders.

There is also an undeniable excitement about the prospect of GLP-1s being able to blunt cravings broadly. Researchers are even looking at their potential for behavioural addictions including sports betting, compulsive shopping and pornography.

To date, addiction-related research has largely focused on the relationship between GLP-1s and alcohol use disorder, but it is increasing for other substances. Most studies have been performed on rats and mice rather than on humans.

The gold standard, as Dr. MacKillop put it, requires randomized control trials where people are split into two groups. One cluster receives the new treatment while the other does not, removing bias and reliably proving true cause-and-effect results. So far, these are limited, especially for opioid addiction.

But on the horizon in Canada is a randomized trial run by Eli Lilly, a leader in the GLP-1 medication market, which makes Mounjaro and Zepbound. This trial, expected to end in 2028, aims to investigate whether brenipatide, an experimental GLP-1 drug, enhances the recovery of people with opioid use disorder who are already taking a proven treatment called buprenorphine.

Eli Lilly is looking to enroll 465 participants, ages 18 to 75, across Canada, the U.S. and Britain. The Canadian trial sites are located in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.

Alberta-based addiction physician Monty Ghosh, Calgary’s site investigator, said this is the first study of its kind in Canada. If brenipatide proves successful, he said it could lead to the expansion of treatment options for opioid use disorder.

“This is hugely exciting as we have such limited options. This would provide us with a whole new class of medications to manage this severe disorder,” he said.

The most common treatments for opioid use disorder in Canada are buprenorphine and methadone, long-acting prescribed medications used to manage drug withdrawal and cravings.

Other options include naltrexone, slow-release oral morphine or an injectable opioid agonist treatment, which is typically reserved for cases where oral treatments have not been successful.

There is no single medication currently available that can blunt cravings across all drug classes, which could make GLP-1s a novel solution.

The first randomized controlled trial to test GLP-1s against opioid addiction was conducted by researchers at Pennsylvania State University at a Caron treatment centre.

The trial involved 20 participants and found that those who received the GLP-1 drug liraglutide had a 40-per-cent reduction in opioid cravings compared with those who received the placebo.

Those findings, released in 2024, set the foundation for a larger clinical trial currently in progress with an anticipated 200 participants across four U.S. sites. It will test whether patients who receive semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, reduce their illicit opioid use over 12 weeks.

One of the principal investigators, Jennifer Nyland, an associate professor of neuroscience and experimental therapeutics at Penn State, said the study is targeting patients who are struggling with illicit opioid use despite being on standard medications.

She said they are using a subtherapeutic dose, meaning it is lower than what is needed to produce weight loss. This has so far proved effective for silencing drug appetite in animal studies. But Dr. Nyland added that researchers are still determining what the baseline dose should be for humans.

Her team will evaluate whether the GLP-1 is reducing urges by examining urine tests and participant-logged data. Dosing can be increased depending on how a participant responds.

“That’s why it’s important that we are testing a variety of different GLP-1 agonists for reducing the use of various drugs in both clinical trials and animal models – to give people options,” she said.

Observational studies have also been crucial to understanding GLP-1 potential. Take, for example, research published in March that analyzed the medical records of more than 600,000 U.S. veterans who were prescribed either a GLP-1 or SGLT2 inhibitor, which is a common treatment for Type 2 diabetes.

Senior author Ziyad Al-Aly, a Washington University clinical epidemiologist, said they sought to answer two questions: Can GLP-1s prevent addiction? And can they reduce harm for those already struggling with it? The answer to both was yes.

Among veterans living with addiction who were taking a GLP-1, the study found there were 50 per cent fewer substance-related deaths and 39 per cent fewer drug overdoses compared with those taking an inhibitor. Additionally, the group taking GLP-1s had a significantly lower risk of developing a new addiction to a number of substances the researchers tested for, including nicotine, alcohol, cocaine and opioids.

“I’m excited about this because finally we have a drug that seems to be working on addiction,” said Dr. Al-Aly, adding he’s never seen anything like it before. “At the same time, I see the uncertainties that need to be resolved, the side effects that people don’t talk about enough.”

GLP-1 drug makers have been busy converting their wares into new, more easily administered forms, like these Wegovy tablets at Novo Nordisk’s production line in Malov, Denmark. Canada is reviewing several generic GLP-1 drugs for use here. Tom Little/Reuters

The most common side effects of GLP-1s are gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. There are also less common but more serious side effects, such as inflammation of the pancreas, bowel obstruction and gallbladder disease.

Much less is known about the effects on those with addiction.

Alexander Caudarella, chief executive of the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction, has a list of questions he said need to be answered before this treatment method should be widely prescribed.

He wants to know how long the medication stays active in the body, what happens to individuals when they stop using it and whether discontinuation will heighten the risk of relapse or overdose.

“We don’t want to deprive people of having access to something that could be a game changer, but you want to make sure that we’re doing all the research that’s necessary,” said Dr. Caudarella, who is worried that off-label prescriptions will take off before there are conclusive answers.

Researchers in this field also want to know whether the body will adapt to GLP-1s and respond less over time, if efficacy will be comparable across drug classes and how the use of multiple substances could interact with the medication.

It is also still unclear who the best candidates are for the proposed treatment. The illicit-drug-using population is vulnerable, and many have concurrent mental illnesses. Additionally, there could be a risk of malnourishment.

In the long term, Dr. MacKillop, from McMaster, said he is concerned about the possibility of anhedonia, which is the reduced or total inability to feel pleasure. Such symptoms have been anecdotally reported by some GLP-1 users.

“If these drugs effectively abolish our capacity for pleasure, are we giving up that core part of who we are as people?” he said. “They May be lifesavers in some cases … but they May be more selectively relevant for really severe cases as opposed to a very large proportion of the population.”

Although Canada is likely years away from designating GLP-1s for addiction treatment, there are also concerns about who will be able to access this class of drugs. Coverage gaps related to the cost of the treatment already exist across the country.

Last year’s installation of the Blue Hat Memorial Project in Campbell River, B.C., underscored the human cost of addiction. Its 50,000 flags – blue for men and boys, purple for women and girls – each represented a life lost to overdoses. Nationally, that toll has kept growing, though annual rates have been declining. Chad Hipolito/The Globe and Mail

There is also a broader ethical question to ponder, said Dr. Al-Aly, the Washington researcher.

In Canada, more than 56,000 people have died from opioid-related poisonings since 2016, driven by the rise of illicit fentanyl. In the U.S., that figure stretches beyond 400,000. Add in other substances, such as cocaine and alcohol, and the numbers in both countries increase substantially.

So, Dr. Al-Aly asks: Is it fair to withhold a possible treatment option when studies, like his, have demonstrated that GLP-1s can reduce the risk of harm?

He concedes that the answer isn’t so simple. Though GLP-1s could help people with addiction, he said, they May also lead to harms not yet fully investigated or understood.

“I would hate to see someone start on a GLP-1 and, for one reason or the other, stop it and experience a roar of addiction coming back again where all of a sudden they’re feeling the magnetic pull to cocaine or opioids,” he said.

This, too, is a road that could lead to overdose and, potentially, death.

At Caron, patients must undergo a comprehensive medical evaluation by the non-profit’s addictions medicine team to determine if they are a suitable candidate for GLP-1 therapy. Patients prescribed the medication off-label are then carefully monitored.

Dr. Scioli, who recently left Caron and is stepping into the role of president of the American Osteopathic Academy of Addiction Medicine, said his former patients have so far not reported any negative outcomes.

He said GLP-1s helped bring a spark back to many of their lives, allowing patients to reconnect with themselves and their loved ones.

But he stressed that GLP-1s are not a stand-alone treatment option and must be coupled with other supports, such as psychiatric services and other substance-use disorder medications.

“It certainly sets patients up for long-term success, but it’s not a magic bullet,” Dr. Scioli said. “I’d reserve the word miracle for a cure.”

To get ready for generic Ozempic’s debut in Canada, The Globe’ limited-series podcast Skinny Inc. took a deeper look at the GLP-1 revolution. Learn more about the science and big business behind the drugs, and the effect they’ve had on the body positivity movement and mental health.

He concedes that the answer isn’t so simple. Though GLP-1s could help people with addiction, he said, they May also lead to harms not yet fully investigated or understood.

“I would hate to see someone start on a GLP-1 and, for one reason or the other, stop it and experience a roar of addiction coming back again where all of a sudden they’re feeling the magnetic pull to cocaine or opioids,” he said.
This, too, is a road that could lead to overdose and, potentially, death.

At Caron, patients must undergo a comprehensive medical evaluation by the non-profit’s addictions medicine team to determine if they are a suitable candidate for GLP-1 therapy. Patients prescribed the medication off-label are then carefully monitored.

Dr. Scioli, who recently left Caron and is stepping into the role of president of the American Osteopathic Academy of Addiction Medicine, said his former patients have so far not reported any negative outcomes.
He said GLP-1s helped bring a spark back to many of their lives, allowing patients to reconnect with themselves and their loved ones.
But he stressed that GLP-1s are not a stand-alone treatment option and must be coupled with other supports, such as psychiatric services and other substance-use disorder medications.
“It certainly sets patients up for long-term success, but it’s not a magic bullet,” Dr. Scioli said. “I’d reserve the word miracle for a cure.”

stories.title: Food allergy education a must as kids head back to school, doctors say
stories.summary: More than three million adults in Canada self-report they have a food allergy and among children under 18, there's more than 600,000 with food allergies.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
As Canadian students return to the classroom, some have to plan how to deal not just with school work but allergies.

More than 600,000 children under 18 have a food allergy, according to Food Allergy Canada.

That means many enter or return to school having to take precautions to ensure they stay healthy while learning.

Dr. Samira Jeimy, an allergist in London, Ont., said for a child with allergies, entering the classroom can add to an already stressful time.

“That increased stress from the flux and the transition can definitely impact allergic and immunologic disease,” she said. “And then there’s the new or changing exposures that happen in September.”

A food allergy occurs when a person’s immune system, which normally protects from germs and diseases, mistakenly treats a food substance as dangerous. According to Food Allergy Canada, the body then reacts to the food by having an allergic reaction.

When first exposed to the allergen, which is often the protein found in the food, the immune system creates antibodies called immunoglobulin. When the person is exposed again to the protein, antibodies and chemicals such as histamine are released.

Histamine can cause a reaction in a person’s respiratory system, gastrointestinal tract, skin or cardiovascular system, Health Canada says.

In some cases, the allergy can cause anaphylaxis that starts rapidly and can be fatal. People who are at risk of anaphylaxis are advised to carry an epinephrine device such as an EpiPen, which can treat an allergic reaction.

That’s why Jeimy said as kids go back to school, parents should discuss how to deal with allergies with students and their teachers.

This includes reviewing inhaler usage, which helps with allergic asthma, a condition that can arise during a reaction.

“We always anticipate a lot of asthma exacerbations when school starts,” Jeimy said. “Really knowing when to use your inhaler, how to use the inhaler, when to escalate therapy and when to seek extra help is super important because colds and flus are huge, maybe the number one trigger for asthma exacerbations.”

It’s important to also remind children and teens how to properly use their EpiPen should a reaction occur.

“These life-threatening outcomes are totally preventable if people are educated, the students have the EpiPen on them, they know what symptoms to look out for, it’s administered properly,” said Dr. Allan Grill, chief of family medicine at Markham-Stouffville Hospital.

Most allergic reactions can happen within minutes, but some can take longer. They can also start with mild symptoms but get worse quickly.

The symptoms can involve the heart, lungs, throat, stomach, skin and other parts of the body. They can range from feeling faint or dizzy, a weak pulse, shortness of breath, wheezing, widespread hives, severe itching, severe abdominal pain, or severe swelling of the face or eyes. In some cases, a severe allergic reaction or anaphylaxis can also cause confusion, agitation and decreased activity.

Grill said people should know the warning signs and parents should remind their children to get back in the habit of safe routines.

Even a small amount of an allergen that makes it onto a fork or knife through cross-contamination can cause an allergic reaction, Food Allergy Canada says, which is why more education is always helpful.

“It is about being familiar with food allergy being a serious medical condition,” said Jennifer Gerdts, executive director of Food Allergy Canada. “What we do know when we hear from the community is when a plan is in place, it’s been discussed, and people are aware of the food allergy, the kids feel confident.”

— with files from Global News’ Katherine Ward

stories.title: Environment Canada warns of more heavy rain for Cape Breton Island, N.S.
stories.summary: Halifax - Environment and Climate Change Canada has issued a heavy rainfall warning for northern parts of Cape Breton Island.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rebuilding efforts in northern Nova Scotia ramped up on Monday after days of torrential rain triggered floods that destroyed roads, washed out bridges and are believed to have caused one death.

Public Works Minister Fred Tilley said hundreds of provincial employees and local contactors are working to restore the entirety of Cape Breton Island’s road network within the coming days.

“We are hoping to get all those folks that May be stranded access to the road network very soon,” Tilley said in an interview.

A slow-moving storm dumped more than 200 millimetres of rain on the island and parts of the northern mainland over less than two days.

While the province prepared for the storm, Tilley said, “there’s not much infrastructure that can handle that in Nova Scotia.”

“It’s another one of these one in 100 year storms that has wreaked havoc,” he said. “It’s always top of mind when we’re rebuilding to build for climate change where possible.”

Gary Chandler, a resident of Inverness County, said he couldn’t leave the area where he lives in rural Cape Breton on Saturday because a culvert on his dirt road washed out.

The 57-year-old and his partner soon discovered they were essentially stuck between two broken culverts on one side and a broken bridge on the other, and unable to drive out of the area until they were fixed.

For about three days, Chandler and his family had to walk through the nearby woods and cross a small brook to transfer groceries, clothes and supplies between vehicles left on the opposite sides of the washouts.

“If any emergency vehicles had to get in, they would not be able to,” Chandler said on Monday.

“They would’ve had to have a helicopter to get to ... anybody that would get sick or hurt.”

Chandler said when he checked on Monday afternoon, one of the culverts was restored and he was able to drive into Whycocomagh, ending days of blocked access.

Environment Canada had forecast up to 25 to 40 millimetres of heavy rain Monday morning for most of northern Cape Breton Island, with higher amounts possible in thunderstorms.

The weather service said that water would likely pool on roads and low-lying areas, as the ground couldn’t absorb more rainfall.

The rain let up enough later in the afternoon and Environment Canada pulled its rainfall warnings, with forecasts showing lighter rain in some areas of Cape Breton.

But it advised travellers to listen to local officials about road safety conditions while avoiding low-lying areas and watching for washouts near rivers and culverts.

The flooding has been linked with one death after a 46-year-old woman from Richmond County was found dead on Saturday, several hours after her abandoned vehicle was discovered near a flooded bridge.

RCMP said on Sunday the death is not believed to be suspicious and added they would not provide any more information.

The province’s Emergency Minister Kim Masland said on Monday her condolences are with the woman’s loved ones and community as they mourn.

“When tragedy takes the life of a fellow Nova Scotian, it is felt across our province. I want her loved ones to know that all Nova Scotians are standing with them,” Masland said in a statement.

“My thoughts are also with everyone affected by these devastating floods. This is an incredibly difficult time for many families and communities, and I want people to know that we are here.”

Lois Landry, warden of the hard-hit Richmond County, said a Zodiac rescue boat operated by a local fire department and a provincial helicopter were used to carry out daily wellness checks for any residents completely cut off by flooding.

Guests stranded at the Lakeside Luxury Domes camp in the Saint George’s Channel area created a makeshift, “jerry-rigged” exit route after the property was washed out, she said.

“We’re used to hurricanes on the East Coast, that’s not new to us. But there was wind coupled with rain we haven’t seen the likes of, really, ever,” she said in a phone interview.

At the peak of the flooding, according to a spokesperson for the province’s Department of Public Works, there were more than 120 closed or damaged roads on the Island.

“Currently, about 44 are closed. The rest have either fully or partially reopened, including dozens overnight,” Toby Koffman, communications director for the department, said in a statement Monday.

Koffman said two of eight bridges that were damaged will need to be replaced, while more than 200 culverts were washed away, from driveways to major roads.

He said it would take some time before the province can estimate the total cost of the damage caused by the flooding.

Landry said she’s lived on Cape Breton Island all of her 58 years, and she’s never seen so much flooding before.

A rainfall device in the Saint George’s Channel area measured 230 millimetres of rain before it broke, she added.

“We really can’t even wrap our heads around that much rain ... it compromised the ground beneath our infrastructure.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Ninth-inning comeback falls just short as London Majors drop Game 3 to Welland
stories.summary: The London Majors now lead their best-of-seven Canadian Baseball League playoff series 2-1 after losing Game 3 Sunday to the Welland Jackfish.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
London Majors starting pitcher Victor Payano throws a pitch during the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series against the Welland Jackfish in London on Friday, September 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

The London Majors now lead their best-of-seven Canadian Baseball League playoff series 2-1 after losing Game 3 Sunday to the Welland Jackfish.

The final score at Labatt Park was 6-5, but an explosive ninth inning from the home side resulted in a near-comeback that would have put the Jackfish in a stranglehold.

Welland held a 6-0 lead heading into the bottom of the ninth. The Jackfish had scored four runs in the top of the inning to pad their lead. But London racked up five runs in their final time at the plate to make it a one-run game, though the output fell just shy of tying things up.

Cristian Inoa doubled home a pair of runs in London’s five-run ninth, with Maikol Escotto, Starling Joseph and David Draayers driving in the Majors’ other runs.

With two outs and the tying Majors run on third, Welland pitcher Deivy Mendez struck out Ryder Hancock to finish off London’s near-comeback.

So far, the series has been a close affair, with every game being decided by just a single run.

In Game 2, the Majors headed into the ninth inning with a two-run lead, with Welland’s Justin Gideon hitting a solo home run to bring it within one. London then made quick work of the next three batters to finish the game with a 5-4 victory.

The first game of the series saw a tight battle that stretched into the 11th inning, with London’s Jarrett Burney hitting a walk-off RBI single for Hancock to score from second base, winning the game 6-5.

The series, now sitting at 2-1 for the Majors, will head back to Welland on Wednesday for the all-important Game 4. Whatever the outcome, the series will then shift back to London on Friday night for Game 5.

stories.title: New ambassadorship program leads to ‘calm’ environment, following recent violent incidents
stories.summary: A well-known Indigenous advocate in Winnipeg is working as an ambassador alongside security staff at a downtown Dollarama store.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – A well-known Indigenous advocate in Winnipeg is working as an ambassador alongside security staff at a downtown Dollarama store.

Vivian Ketchum is working with Impact Security Group (ISG), helping prevent conflicts between security guards and shoppers. The program comes months after the store was the site of a serious assault involving a security guard.

Police allege a 46-year-old man tried to leave the Dollarama with stolen items, and allegedly assaulted and threatened to kill a security guard. The security guard then restrained the man.

A video recorded in February went viral on social media after it appeared to show a security guard holding a man on the ground before punching and stomping on him.

The security guard, who worked for ISG, was removed from active duty and arrested by Winnipeg police.

Ketchum was among dozens of people who rallied outside the store following the incident, calling for changes to how security and safety are handled. Months later, she’s now become part of that change.

“I go into the store, and I prevent any situation from escalating with the security guards and alleged shoplifters,” she said. “I also notify the shoppers when there’s a situation that’s occurring.”

She also greets customers as they enter the store, connects with people outside the store and works to build relationships with the surrounding community.

Her goal, she said, is to bring empathy into an environment where tensions can quickly escalate.

“I want the kids and parents to be feel safe shopping in the store,” she said. “What I try to do is connect with the community I love.”

Different approach to security

Ketchum says she was contacted by Ron D’Errico from ISG for this new ambassadorship program. She said she was a little leery at first, but decided it would be a good role to help create change.

The program is designed to address concerns around racial profiling and stereotyping, while providing education and support to both security guards and the retailer.

D’Errico, who is Isg’s president and CEO, said Ketchum can also help navigate situations involving law enforcement, including when an individual is arrested or removed from the store.

He believes the approach is already making a difference. D’Errico says the store has experienced an 80 per cent decrease in shoplifting and other crime-related issues since Ketchum began working there.

“We’ve had no incidents with violence since we put this program in place. Guards are reporting that the environment is very calm, it’s relaxed, and as a matter of fact, it’s very vibrant,” he said.

“More people are coming in, and more people shopping.”

D’Errico says retailers across the country have reached out to him about this ambassadorship program and he says the hope is to expand Ketchum’s role to other retailers across the country.

“We’re in discussions and working out the parameters of putting this program in place. It actually is a program that has proven amazing results,” he said.

“We’re coming at it with empathy and understanding, transparency and communication. Those are keys to building any relationship and maintaining that relationship is key to solving this problem.”

Experts call approach a ‘welcome turn’

University of Winnipeg criminologist Kelly Gorkoff says the idea of bringing in an Indigenous advocate to act as a liaison in the store is a good step.

“This is for two main reasons – first, it provides some help to those who act as security guards – who are hired by private companies and have little to no training or labour support; second, it recognizes that individuals who commit crime have needs that if addressed, can reduce crime – in other words, crime prevention,” she said.

“An advocate or a community safety ambassador can deal directly with people who might be thinking about stealing something, who need food, who need supports and those people will listen to someone advocating for their wellbeing opposed to wanting to arrest them, or punch them, or fight them,” she added.

Michael Weinrath agrees with Gorkoff.

The University of Winnipeg criminology professor says the introduction of this program serves a number of important functions, including the importance of cultural communication. He says it also provides a potential mediator in situations where shoplifting May occur.

“It’s a certainly a much softer and more socially acceptable way to try to deal with those sorts of problems,” he said.

“It’s good to see an Indigenous person in a position such as this, trying to do some good and trying to help people get along, cooperate and resolve conflicts in a good way.”

As for Ketchum, she just wants to make a difference and make downtown a safe place for everybody.

“I’m hoping my small role helps,” she said.

stories.title: Western Mustangs score 10 touchdowns, romp to 78-7 win in head coach's debut
stories.summary: “This is just Game 1. They’re only going to get better.”
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Everyone braced for some growing pains in Michael Faulds’ inaugural season as Western football coach.

But at first glance, the Mustangs already look like a well-oiled machine.

The new boss rolled out plenty of first-time starters and impressive fresh faces in a 78-7 clobbering of the York Lions Sunday night at Western Alumni Stadium. His charges racked up 10 touchdowns, pulled down three interceptions and dominated in all three phases of the game.

“We had eight months of bottled-up wanting to play,” Faulds, the former Wilfrid Laurier coach and legendary Mustangs quarterback, said. “We had a three-week training camp (because of a first-week bye). It was really eight months of work. (On) January 5, we told the guys we’re going to be the hardest-working team in the country.”

They’re off to a dream start. Quarterback Jerome Rancourt and, later, Ben Casselman were nearly flawless under centre and receivers like Nik Shewchuk and Banting grad Emmett Charles have emerged as explosive playmakers.

“We had some great receivers that graduated (in Seth Robertson and Brayden Misseri),” Faulds said. “The rest of the league and, I think, our own supporters were naming who left, but they weren’t naming who’s here. We have multiple weapons. They weren’t naming the work Jerome and Ben have put in the eight months I’ve been here.

“This is just Game 1. They’re only going to get better.”

He is still getting to know his players, but it’s clear they believe in him.

Season preview: What to expect from Michael Faulds' Western Mustangs

PHOTOS: Western Mustangs football training camp

Advertisement 1Story continues below

“It’s been great,” Rancourt said. “He set the tone very early. The body of work we’ve been putting in, it’s been unreal. York was going to pay for it – and it showed.”

NEW PIVOT: Rancourt’s efficiency was off the charts. The engineering student from Quebec City finished his three quarters of work 24-for-28 with 339 yards and two touchdown passes for a ridiculous 211.0 quarterback rating. He also rushed for three majors.

“It feels great,” he said. “It’s been a long time coming and I just told guys to trust the process. That’s what I did through my first year not dressing, then special teams and receiver and some tight end last year. I knew what I was capable of and I think now I display it.”

The 6-foot-5, 270-pounder carved up York early with his arm while the Lions defence was on its heels waiting for him to tuck and run. They were forced to respect the pass and that opened up some rushing gaps.

“I’ll show what they allow me to show,” he said. “That’s why I came back here to Western. I did tell the pros I was coming back to be doing this – run the QB1 spot I’ve been waiting for. I think it’s been paying off. We executed well on offence.

“Everybody got a piece of it.”

YOUNG DEFENCE: Paul Gleason has been the Western defensive co-ordinator for decades.

This is his youngest defence – and it’s not even close.

“I thought starting one freshman some years was going out there,” he said. “We had five freshmen start and eight back there. We have two transfers so everyone’s trying to figure each other out. Having that extra week was a blessing.

“The young kids get more reps.”

One of them, CCH grad Nathan Summers, stopped York’s momentum cold. The Lions, who scored 35 points last week against Carleton, were starting to move down the field with precision before the linebacker made the first of Western’s three interceptions.

The Mustangs immediately scored a touchdown after that turnover and never looked back.

“The Summers kid, his football IQ is through the roof,” Gleason said. “He jumped that, made a great play and changed the momentum. We trusted him (and started him). We figured we’ll play him now and come playoffs, he won’t be a rookie anymore.

“This was the proving ground. We’re going to stick with these kids. We’re going to play them and see what happens.”

The Mustangs decimated York’s running game and, other than one third-quarter drive, were largely perfect.

ON THE SIDELINES: Former Mustangs coach Greg Marshall was in attendance for the opener and couldn’t have been happier about the blowout . . . Western pounded York 83-0 in its opener on the road three years ago and hasn’t lost to the Lions since 1980 back when they were called the Yeomen . . . In last year’s opener, the Mustangs won a four-overtime barnburner against Queen’s in Kingston, so this was a contrast . . . Western kicker Mateo Pasquini has big boots to fill after taking over from OUA all-time leading scorer Brian Garrity. He converted 10 extra points and booted two field goals. Veteran Oliver Griffiths is handling punt duties, kickoffs and holding for Pasquini, a 6-foot, 170-pounder from Etobicoke . . . Former Western linebacker Fraser Sopik is the special teams co-ordinator for York . . . One of the biggest roars from the crowd came with the game no longer in doubt. Londoner Geoff Clubine, a 5-foot-9, 207-pound running back and former Beefeater, took his first OUA carry for 28 yards and a touchdown after walking on to the team last year. He is the first member of his family to go to university. “We have a thing called ‘My Why’ and people get to say a little about their life,” Faulds said. “Geoff did it this week and people got a little glimpse of his life and why he runs so hard.” . . . There was really just one moment when it was clear that Faulds hadn’t been in Western’s locker room after a win for a long time. That was during the team’s Victory Song. “It was amazing to sing it,” he said. “I’ll admit I knew maybe 75 per cent of it. I kind of mouthed some of it.” At this rate, he’ll memorize it quickly. . . . Faulds launched his coaching career as York’s offensive co-ordinator from 2010-12 and thought it was cool the Lions were his first Mustangs opponent. “It was a little bit nostalgic,” he said. “I’m such a competitor during the game. I thought about it a little bit more this morning. Fantastic support (at Western). We sent the fans home happy.”

paragraphs: Everyone braced for some growing pains in Michael Faulds’ inaugural season as Western football coach.
But at first glance, the Mustangs already look like a well-oiled machine.

The new boss rolled out plenty of first-time starters and impressive fresh faces in a 78-7 clobbering of the York Lions Sunday night at Western Alumni Stadium. His charges racked up 10 touchdowns, pulled down three interceptions and dominated in all three phases of the game.

“We had eight months of bottled-up wanting to play,” Faulds, the former Wilfrid Laurier coach and legendary Mustangs quarterback, said. “We had a three-week training camp (because of a first-week bye). It was really eight months of work. (On) January 5, we told the guys we’re going to be the hardest-working team in the country.”

They’re off to a dream start. Quarterback Jerome Rancourt and, later, Ben Casselman were nearly flawless under centre and receivers like Nik Shewchuk and Banting grad Emmett Charles have emerged as explosive playmakers.

“We had some great receivers that graduated (in Seth Robertson and Brayden Misseri),” Faulds said. “The rest of the league and, I think, our own supporters were naming who left, but they weren’t naming who’s here. We have multiple weapons. They weren’t naming the work Jerome and Ben have put in the eight months I’ve been here.
“This is just Game 1. They’re only going to get better.”
He is still getting to know his players, but it’s clear they believe in him.
Season preview: What to expect from Michael Faulds' Western Mustangs
PHOTOS: Western Mustangs football training camp

“It’s been great,” Rancourt said. “He set the tone very early. The body of work we’ve been putting in, it’s been unreal. York was going to pay for it – and it showed.”

NEW PIVOT: Rancourt’s efficiency was off the charts. The engineering student from Quebec City finished his three quarters of work 24-for-28 with 339 yards and two touchdown passes for a ridiculous 211.0 quarterback rating. He also rushed for three majors.

“It feels great,” he said. “It’s been a long time coming and I just told guys to trust the process. That’s what I did through my first year not dressing, then special teams and receiver and some tight end last year. I knew what I was capable of and I think now I display it.”

The 6-foot-5, 270-pounder carved up York early with his arm while the Lions defence was on its heels waiting for him to tuck and run. They were forced to respect the pass and that opened up some rushing gaps.

“I’ll show what they allow me to show,” he said. “That’s why I came back here to Western. I did tell the pros I was coming back to be doing this – run the QB1 spot I’ve been waiting for. I think it’s been paying off. We executed well on offence.
“Everybody got a piece of it.”
YOUNG DEFENCE: Paul Gleason has been the Western defensive co-ordinator for decades.
This is his youngest defence – and it’s not even close.

“I thought starting one freshman some years was going out there,” he said. “We had five freshmen start and eight back there. We have two transfers so everyone’s trying to figure each other out. Having that extra week was a blessing.
“The young kids get more reps.”

One of them, CCH grad Nathan Summers, stopped York’s momentum cold. The Lions, who scored 35 points last week against Carleton, were starting to move down the field with precision before the linebacker made the first of Western’s three interceptions.
The Mustangs immediately scored a touchdown after that turnover and never looked back.

“The Summers kid, his football IQ is through the roof,” Gleason said. “He jumped that, made a great play and changed the momentum. We trusted him (and started him). We figured we’ll play him now and come playoffs, he won’t be a rookie anymore.
“This was the proving ground. We’re going to stick with these kids. We’re going to play them and see what happens.”
The Mustangs decimated York’s running game and, other than one third-quarter drive, were largely perfect.

ON THE SIDELINES: Former Mustangs coach Greg Marshall was in attendance for the opener and couldn’t have been happier about the blowout . . . Western pounded York 83-0 in its opener on the road three years ago and hasn’t lost to the Lions since 1980 back when they were called the Yeomen . . . In last year’s opener, the Mustangs won a four-overtime barnburner against Queen’s in Kingston, so this was a contrast . . . Western kicker Mateo Pasquini has big boots to fill after taking over from OUA all-time leading scorer Brian Garrity. He converted 10 extra points and booted two field goals. Veteran Oliver Griffiths is handling punt duties, kickoffs and holding for Pasquini, a 6-foot, 170-pounder from Etobicoke . . . Former Western linebacker Fraser Sopik is the special teams co-ordinator for York . . . One of the biggest roars from the crowd came with the game no longer in doubt. Londoner Geoff Clubine, a 5-foot-9, 207-pound running back and former Beefeater, took his first OUA carry for 28 yards and a touchdown after walking on to the team last year. He is the first member of his family to go to university. “We have a thing called ‘My Why’ and people get to say a little about their life,” Faulds said. “Geoff did it this week and people got a little glimpse of his life and why he runs so hard.” . . . There was really just one moment when it was clear that Faulds hadn’t been in Western’s locker room after a win for a long time. That was during the team’s Victory Song. “It was amazing to sing it,” he said. “I’ll admit I knew maybe 75 per cent of it. I kind of mouthed some of it.” At this rate, he’ll memorize it quickly. . . . Faulds launched his coaching career as York’s offensive co-ordinator from 2010-12 and thought it was cool the Lions were his first Mustangs opponent. “It was a little bit nostalgic,” he said. “I’m such a competitor during the game. I thought about it a little bit more this morning. Fantastic support (at Western). We sent the fans home happy.”

stories.title: These are the happiest provinces in Canada, according to a new poll
stories.summary: Are things looking up for Canadians? According to a new survey, many of us across the country are feeling happier than we were a year ago.
stories.author: Elianna Lev
stories.content:
Are things looking up for Canadians? According to a new survey, many across the country are feeling happier than they were a year ago. Canadians’ happiness is up slightly from 2025, according to Leger’s Happiness Index 2026, with the national average sitting at 70.5 out of 100, compared to 68.7 in the previous year.

Out of all provinces, Quebec ranked the happiest at 74.5. Newfoundland and Labrador ranked second at 71.0, followed by New Brunswick at 70.3. Meanwhile, Ontario landed in the middle with a 69.3 index while Prince Edward Island came in last, with a 67.7 index – up slightly from 66.5 a year earlier.

Amongst the country’s largest cities, Montreal came first with an index of 72.7 out of 100, with Brampton in second place, with 71.7 – up five points from 66.7 in 2025 – and Toronto in third, with a 69.4 index, up a few points from 65.8 a year earlier.

Quebec also ranked higher when it came to optimism, with a 72.2 index, compared to 66.6 in the rest of the country. Fewer Quebecers also said they were unhappy – 22 per cent – compared to 33 per cent for the rest of the country.

Andrew Enns, Leger’s executive vice-president for central Canada, told CTVNews.CA that the spike in happiness index from this year to last could have something to do with the time of year the survey was conducted. The 2025 survey was done in March and April, while this year’s was conducted in June.

“One of the factors that might be bumping things a little bit was the fact that March, April, in Canada is a certain time of year where we’re starting in some parts of the country to get out and feel a little more free from winter,” he said.

“But for most of us, it’s still not so great. June is definitely a better time, that’s what makes us happy.” American index almost identical to Canada The survey also took the temperature on happiness south of the border, with surprising results.

Overall, Americans ranked 70.5 out of 100 on the happiness Index, which was the exact same number as Canada. However, Enns said U.S. states showed a bit more extreme results compared to Canada. “They had a few states that were higher than most provinces in Canada,” he said.

“But then they also have some states that are quite at the lower end.” The happiest states were Florida with a 75.3 index, followed by Kansas at 74.5, then New Jersey with a 74.4 index. On the bottom of the list was West Virginia with a happiness index of 62.5.

Enns said that overall, there wasn’t a great deal of differences between the two countries when it came to level of happiness and what’s driving those sentiments. What contributes to happiness? Enns said the things that contributed to happiness strongly related to our community, access to outdoor spaces, our neighbours and family.

stories.title: Citing ‘evolving global context,’ this school board is cancelling all international trips
stories.summary: School boards across Canada are taking different approaches to international field trips amid heightened geopolitical tensions and travel uncertainty, with some cancelling or restricting trips while many others continue to send students abroad.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Calgary - School boards across Canada are taking different approaches to international field trips amid heightened geopolitical tensions and travel uncertainty, with some cancelling or restricting trips while many others continue to send students abroad.

Edmonton Public Schools took one of the broadest approaches, announcing in June it would cancel all international excursions for the 2026-27 school year, citing an “ongoing political, economic and public health challenges around the world,” that includes military conflicts, civil unrest and other risks. The decision affects planned trips to destinations including Thailand, France, the United Kingdom, Costa Rica and Portugal.

Joe Pavelka, a professor of ecotourism and outdoor leadership at Mount Royal University who has run international field schools for 25 years, questions the blanket approach.

“I’m a little surprised and a little disappointed that Edmonton would cancel their international offerings,” Pavelka said.

He said there are circumstances where cancelling an international trip clearly makes sense.

“If there was a war going on in Europe, then there’s a good chance you wouldn’t send your student,” he said.

But Pavelka said the current environment is more difficult to assess.

“People certainly feel less safe, but there’s no real way to pinpoint: Is this place unsafe or more unsafe compared to any others?”

‘Given the political climate’

Wayne Smith, a professor and director at the Institute for Hospitality and Tourism Research at Toronto Metropolitan University, sees the decision differently.

“It’s unsurprising, to be honest with you, given the political climate that we’re seeing right now,” Smith said.

“The fact is that we are in a trade war at the moment. You know, there’s all kinds of security concerns.”

But Edmonton’s approach is far from universal.

CTV News contacted more than a dozen school boards and districts across Canada and found most continue to allow international student travel, although policies and approval processes vary.

The Toronto District School Board and Regina Public Schools said there has been no change and international trips continue. The Ottawa-Carleton District School Board continues to facilitate trips, while the Vancouver School Board does not have a policy prohibiting international field trips.

Edmonton Catholic Schools also said international trips are proceeding as planned.

In Calgary, international travel is returning to some public schools after the Calgary Board of Education paused trips during the 2025-26 school year while it reviewed its processes. Some schools are now planning international trips for 2026-27 under updated staff guidelines and trip procedures.

“The Calgary Board of Education believes in the enhanced educational value of international travel,” the board said in a statement.

It added that student and staff safety remains its top priority.

“We continually monitor travel advisories for all destinations and respond to any change which May include trip cancellation at any time.”

At Western Canada High School in Calgary, Grade 12 student Matthew Wang said students have heard about a potential trip to Spain.

Wang said he sees value in having those opportunities available to students.

“I feel like these trips are a great learning opportunity for students, and they’re also just really fun to go on.”

Other school boards have opted for more targeted restrictions.

Several Winnipeg school divisions continue to suspend trips to the United States, rather than international travel altogether.

Pavelka said managing the risks associated with student travel requires preparation and people who understand the destination.

“It’s important to go in advance. It’s important to have people who understand how to deal with risk on the ground,” he said.

Smith said international travel can also present complications depending on a student’s citizenship or immigration status.

“Not every student is a Canadian citizen,” he said. “What do you do with students who are permanent residents or here on visas?”

“So there’s a lot of complications that go with international travel, but the school boards are just deciding this is not worth a bite at the apple.”

Other boards continue to make those decisions individually.

‘Field trips are very beneficial’

The Calgary Catholic School District said student trips are proceeding in 2026-27 and are considered on a case-by-case basis. The English Montreal School Board leaves decisions about trip destinations to individual schools.

The Toronto Catholic District School Board said it does not have an official policy prohibiting trips to specific destinations, with curriculum-related trips to Europe and other locations proceeding in 2026-27.

Greater Saskatoon Catholic Schools, however, stopped approving out-of-country excursions in 2011.

For students, the debate over safety also raises questions about what could be lost when international travel is taken off the table.

“You can see why they did it, but I do think it is a kind of big loss for hands-on learning in the actual environment,” said Ethan Liu, a Grade 12 student at Western Canada High School.

Ariel Lyon, another student at Western Canada High School, said travelling can provide students with an experience that can’t be replicated in a classroom.

“I think international school field trips are very beneficial. It lets students go and see other cultures,” Lyon said.

“There’s a great difference between just hearing what’s in a textbook, watching a video, and actually getting to live through that experience.”

Pavelka said individual trips May sometimes need to be cancelled as conditions change, but he cautions against abandoning international student travel over the long term.

“Whatever the reason, that’s fine. But don’t take it off the table in a long-term sense, because I think that these programs are far too valuable and far too important in terms of shaping young people as they go forward.”
