stories.title: Lessons from the birth of Labour Day
stories.summary: A bitter labour dispute at The Globe and Mail in 1872 was the spark for a decades-long balancing act between employers and workers
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The fact that Labour Day originated in Toronto has been lost over time. Indeed, the holiday’s genesis stems from a bitter labour dispute at this very newspaper. It’s a story that provides insights into the delicate balance between labour and employers in Canada through the decades.

In 1872, a group of Toronto printers went on strike, fighting for a nine-hour work day. (The standard work day was 10 to 12 hours at the time.) The workers’ demand to reduce their hours had been refused by print shop owners, and in particular, George Brown, a respected father of Confederation and founder of The Globe, a predecessor to The Globe and Mail.

Ten thousand people marched in support of the workers to Queen’s Park. After, Brown launched legal action for “conspiracy” and, given that union activity was a criminal act at the time, 24 members of the strike committee were jailed. Brown’s fierce editorials in The Globe, claiming that employees ruled their bosses with a “rod of iron” and that employees are healthier and happier without “idle time,” angered those Ontario workers.

Many of the printers lost their jobs, but the incident led then prime minister Sir John A. Macdonald, a rival of Brown’s who was keen to gain worker support, to legalize union activities. In the years that followed, unions across North America pushed for shorter work days, and the eight-hour day eventually became standard.

Annual parades held to show support for the strikes and the “Nine-Hour Movement” spread across the country, and were eventually formalized as the Labour Day holiday in 1894. There’s some dispute around the origins of America’s Labor Day, but some historians believe U.S. labour leader Peter J. McGuire, inspired after visiting a Toronto labour gathering, organized the first American Labor Day parade in 1882. It also became a U.S. federal holiday in 1894.

Macdonald’s legalization of unions helped to balance the power of employers and employees. Unions have played an important role in reducing work hours, boosting wages and benefits, and improving safety. By establishing norms, these efforts have also benefited workers who are not unionized.

At times, however, the relationship between organized labour and employer interests has fallen out of balance. A 2015 Supreme Court ruling that declared the right to strike is fundamental and protected by the Constitution tipped the scales in labour’s favour. As a result, governments have limited ability to legislate workers back to the job.

A 2024 law on replacement workers, brought forward by Justin Trudeau’s Liberals with the support of the NDP, created an even bigger imbalance by limiting employers’ options during labour disputes. The law bans temporary replacement workers during a strike or lockout in federally regulated sectors. Research shows that jurisdictions with bans on replacement workers have more frequent strikes that last longer, prolonging the economic harm.

At the provincial level, the 2022 attempt from Doug Ford’s Ontario government to use the notwithstanding clause to impose a contract on education support workers and ban their right to strike went too far. The pushback from other unions, who saw the right to strike threatened, caused Mr. Ford to roll back his plan. That didn’t stop the Alberta government from invoking the notwithstanding clause last year in legislation regarding striking teachers.

Canada has seen an upsurge in labour disruptions, with the loss of 4.3 million person-days last year, a record high . Many have caused widespread disruption in critical industries such as aviation, railways and ports.

These types of disruptions could make it harder for the government to achieve its aim of boosting the economy through large infrastructure projects. In response, the federal government has created a new tripartite advisory council made up of union, business and government leaders. Rather than create another layer of bureaucracy, the government should repeal the 2024 replacement-worker law.

Canada has come a long way since the labour strife of George Brown’s era. (A dispute with a worker actually lead to his untimely death, after a disgruntled former staffer shot him in 1880 and the wound became infected.)

Collective bargaining and unions are essential in Canada, and their positive contributions ensure that workers have meaningful participation in workplace decisions. Like Sir John A. Macdonald, today’s policymakers need to ensure that the interests of labour and employers are kept in balance.

stories.title: Trump's trade war with Canada is becoming a ballot box issue ahead of U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Washington - As the United States braces for pivotal midterm elections this November, there's a new and unexpected issue on voters' minds in many states: President Donald Trump's escalating trade war with Canada.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - As the United States braces for pivotal midterm elections this November, there’s a new and unexpected issue on voters’ minds in many states: President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada.

“Canada is our friend, our closest ally and our biggest trading partner,” Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins told Politico in an interview published last week.

“This is not China that we are talking about. This is not an adversarial country. And … our economies are so linked, if you try to hurt one you end up hurting Maine.”

Collins has long been a political force in her border state but Trump’s unpopular policies — including his tariff campaign against Canada — have put her seat in jeopardy.

Canada is Maine’s largest trading partner and many of the state’s critical industries, like seafood and lumber, are integrated with Canadian sectors. Collins has acknowledged that the tariffs on Canada are “terrible for Maine” and are making the job of re-election a lot harder.

While Collins’ seat in Maine could be the most vulnerable, it’s not the only one being rattled by Trump’s attacks on Canada as Republicans look to hold power in Congress.

Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont., said long-term historical trends show that, in general, midterm elections are usually bad for the party of the president in power.

He said while many political observers have been predicting for some time the House will flip to the Democrats, the Senate could also be in play now.

“Some of the key states that have become battleground states are ones with really close trading relationships with Canada,” Lebo said, pointing to Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio.

“You’ve got Republican candidates who have to be confronted with trade policies against Canada that are making it harder to export stuff to Canada and are making some things really expensive for people in those states to import.”

The relationship between Canada and the United States was upended by Trump’s return to the White House. Suddenly, Canada found itself the target of tariffs and threats of annexation from a president who sees it less as a close ally and more as an adversary.

While Canadians have been laser-focused on the upheaval, many Americans have been oblivious to the downturn in the relationship. That changed last month when tensions escalated after trade talks between the two countries broke down.

Trump subsequently imposed 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks and cement to honey. Trump also ramped up his anti-Canada rhetoric and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties on Tuesday. Many are aimed at key industries in states where there are competitive midterm races.

Both countries have accused each other of adding last-minute changes to negotiations. Trump’s team has spread out on American news stations in an attempt to place the blame at Ottawa’s feet and to accuse Prime Minister Mark Carney of tanking a deal for domestic political reasons.

Carney, pushing back on those claims, said last week that he doesn’t think “appointed, unelected cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics.”

It’s not clear whether the Trump administration’s claims about the trade war are breaking through. Both the tariffs and the order to rename Lake Ontario are proving to be very unpopular with Americans.

An Ipsos/Reuters poll published last week suggested two-in-three Americans disapproved of the lake’s name change. It also found only 20 per cent of Americans supported higher tariffs on Canada.

A source with who was not authorized to speak publicly said Republicans from border states approached United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during an event at the White House on Sept. 2. They told Trump’s trade czar to find an off-ramp from the trade war because it was becoming politically toxic, the source said.

Democrats have been quick to jump on the weaknesses the trade war with Canada has exposed. Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said last week “this vanity war is not a war with Canada.”

“It’s a war on Michigan because we have to pay the price,” he said. “And we pay it every single day for goods that should not cost as much as they do.”

Lebo said some Republican candidates are already trying to distance themselves from Trump and his tariffs on Canada.

While New York’s Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul has been vocal in her criticism of the trade war with Canada, her Trump-backed opponent Bruce Blakeman has been harder to pin down.

“I’m not going to talk about federal issues,” Blakeman said when asked by Spectrum News about the trade tensions in late August.

Other Republicans are doubling down. Anthony Constantino, a Republican running for a House seat in New York State, said renaming Lake Ontario was an act of “marketing genius” and claimed “Trump showed strength in negotiations with Canada by playing a card he had available to play.”

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said the bigger picture is that the United States economy is in a state of flux, which is causing a lot of uncertainty ahead of the November election.

The war with Iran, rising gas prices and tariffs have affected domestic investment and employment at a time when the top issue on the ballot box is affordability.

Sands said while neither party can expect a “cake walk” in November, Trump has handed Democrats an opening with his attack on Canada.

Democrats have long been looking for something to unite centrist party members with more left-wing factions like the Democratic Socialists of America. Sands said the trade war with Canada could do just that.

“They feel that they can make the case that this is a senseless trade war,” he said.

“I think most Americans don’t even understand why it’s happening.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Mounties no longer required to wear name tags while on duty
stories.summary: Previous RCMP policy allowed name tag removal only while working at protests
stories.author: Matthew Frank
stories.content:
The RCMP has quietly changed its uniform policy to no longer require officers to wear name tags while on duty, a move that has drawn criticism from advocates and experts who say it will limit police transparency, complicate the complaints process and fuel distrust in Indigenous communities.

The national police force made the change in a uniform policy amendment that has been in place since March 30, according to a briefing note obtained by The Globe and Mail through access-to-information legislation. The updated policy allows officers to instead display their regimental number, a change from the previous policy, which only permitted officers to remove their name tags when they were working at protests.

The briefing note, signed by RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme, is dated April 26 and addressed to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree. It states the change was made to tackle officer safety concerns and deter doxxing, which is the act of publicly sharing someone’s personal information, while “maintaining accountability.”

However, the RCMP also acknowledged the change carries potential consequences.

“There is a risk that stakeholders May perceive numeric identifiers as reducing transparency and therefore there are potential impacts on community and Indigenous relations, particularly in small communities,” the document stated.

The RCMP is the latest Canadian police force to no longer require name tags, as law enforcement agencies try to adapt to the changing threat of doxxing and internet harassment against officers.

Last year, the Calgary Police Service changed its policy to allow officers the choice of either name tags or badge numbers for their uniforms. Vancouver’s municipal police force also has a similar policy. In Winnipeg, the city’s police officers only display their badge numbers.

While Toronto police officers have been required to wear name tags since 2006, Toronto Police Service spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said the force is examining the policy.

“We recognize the increasing concerns around the online identification and targeting of police officers, including the potential impact on members and their families,” she said in an e-mail.

Mr. Anandasangaree was not available for an interview, according to spokesperson David Taylor, who said in an e-mail that questions about the policy change are “best addressed by the RCMP.”

The policy change does not impact the RCMP’s ability to identify members or hold them accountable, and the public complaints process has not been changed, the force’s spokesperson Jessica Kingsbury said.

“The RCMP is committed to accountability, transparency, and building strong and trusting, respectful relationships with the communities we serve -- from large urban centres to rural, remote, and Indigenous communities across Canada,” she said in an e-mail.

But Gordon Bluesky, acting Grand Chief of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs, said trust can’t be assumed between First Nations and the RCMP.

“A number May identify an officer within an RCMP system, but policing in our Nations should be about more than identifying someone in a database,” he said in a statement.

“Our citizens should know the officers serving their communities, and those officers should know the communities they serve.”

The uniform change is a disproportionate response to a “handful of doxxing situations” related to protest policing and undermines public trust in law enforcement, said Shakir Rahim, a director at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

When a number is the only marker to identify an officer, Mr. Rahim said it can make tracking police misconduct more difficult, noting that court documents involving a police officer don’t always include their badge number.

“That raises an inherent conflict where you’re trying to hold an officer or an institution accountable, and you need information from them for that purpose. But now they are the ones deciding whether you will actually receive that information,” Mr. Rahim said.

Tandeep Sidhu, a criminologist at the University of Manitoba, said removing officers’ name tags can deter members of the public from filing complaints because it’s harder to memorize a number under stress than a name.

He said the move to apply a protest policing measure this widely could further isolate officers from the public when doing community police work, particularly in smaller towns.

“For those who already had a mistrust of the police, this is only going to further solidify their mistrust of the police,” Prof. Sidhu said.

But Chris Voller, vice-president for the National Police Federation, which represents RCMP officers, said he supports the shift away from name tags because the internet and artificial intelligence have raised the risk of threats against officers’ families.

Regimental numbers are also more precise when identifying an officer in the complaints process, he said, because it is a unique identifier and some members might share the same surname.

“If any of those [oversight] agencies actually need a police officer to be accountable, they have a Rolodex to find out exactly who that is,” Mr. Voller said in an interview.

RCMP officers have previously been criticized for removing their name tags.

The Civilian Review and Complaints Commission for the RCMP investigated officer conduct during the Fairy Creek protests on Vancouver Island that blocked a logging company from accessing an old-growth forest.

While enforcing a 2021 civil injunction barring protesters from blocking a road, RCMP officers removed their name tags and didn’t have an alternative identifying marker on their uniform, which a 2024 report from the commission determined was “unreasonable.”

The report recommended the RCMP ensure its officers are always easily identifiable, and noted that regimental numbers are permanently linked to officers and available on public documents, meaning “RCMP members could still fear being ‘doxed’ as a result of those numbers.”

In February, 2022, RCMP officers refused to release their badge numbers while clearing protesters during the convoy protest on the Ambassador Bridge, fearing doxxing and harassment, The Canadian Press reported.

Toronto police have also faced backlash for removing name tags.

After the June, 2010, G20 summit protests in Toronto, nearly 100 police officers faced disciplinary action for removing their name tags. One officer who was later convicted of assault for beating a protester didn’t have a name tag visible during the incident and, according to the Special Investigations Unit, the badge number he provided on an arrest document didn’t correlate with any police records.

The Toronto Police Service Board said in a 2012 name badge policy document it views the markers as a matter of “significant interest” because the public should be able to easily identify officers.

With a report from Canadian Press

stories.title: Burnout isn't new: How 18th-century farming set the stage for modern worker exhaustion - CBC.CA
stories.summary: Mental Health Research Canada reports that nearly 40 per cent of workers currently feel burnt out. Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography at Western University, spoke with Afternoon Drive host Chris Ensing about how early capitalism and agricultural advances laid the groundwork for today's burnout.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Mental Health Research Canada reports that nearly 40 per cent of workers currently feel burnt out. Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography at Western University, spoke with Afternoon Drive host Chris Ensing about how early capitalism and agricultural advances laid the groundwork for today's burnout.
· Posted: Sep 07, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago

The latest data from Mental Health Research Canada shows that 39 per cent of Canadian workers currently feel burnt out, up from 35 per cent in 2023. While hustle culture and the grind mindset feel like modern phenomena, worker exhaustion actually dates back hundreds of years.

Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography at Western University, spoke with Afternoon Drive host Chris Ensing about how early capitalism and agricultural advances laid the groundwork for today's burnout.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Chris Ensing: This idea of burnout, people have heard of it before, but let's get a definition. What is burnout?

Nathan TeBokkel: The World Health Organization defines it as a state of vital exhaustion. It's a kind of detachment from your current surroundings, a feeling of a lack of accomplishment, a feeling of exhaustion in general.
CE: How long has this been around?

NT: It's really climbed into the mainstream more recently, especially after the pandemic, when everyone had to work a little more or differently. But it's been around a long time. The Oxford English Dictionary puts burnout at around 1937 in this exact way that we're using it now. But I think the metaphorical history of the word is a lot older, up to 250 years old.
CE: Why are you so interested in this?

NT: I'm a beekeeper, and I live and work on a fruit and vegetable farm. I'm also a scholar of English literature, and I study the Romantic era around 1800, right when the agricultural revolution is taking off in England. They were developing techniques for increasing productivity, and capitalism was taking off. I connect those two things: Romantic literature and the beginning of capitalism through agriculture.
CE: What have you found in your research that connects burnout to farming?

NT: One of the earliest instances I found is in the travel diary of an agriculturalist named Arthur Young. In his early tours, he writes about a subtenant farmer named William White who is burnt out. White was working really hard to master new techniques like irrigation to lift himself out of poverty. Despite his barn burning down twice, he kept farming while rebuilding it with his own hands, working to the point where he lost a lot of weight. In Young's account, this idea of being burnt out, like the barn physically burning down, corresponds directly to vital exhaustion.
LISTEN | Feeling burnt out? Turns out that's nothing new:
Afternoon Drive 10:14 Feeling burnt out? Turns out, that's nothing new
Worker exhaustion and burnout date back hundreds of years. Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in english and geography at Western University, explains more to guest host Chris Ensing.
CE: Are there other moments in your research that connect burnout to that period?

NT: There are a lot of stories like this. That era saw a proliferation of print media—journals and travel accounts—that spread these new agricultural techniques around and standardized them. Part of that literature was creating certain characters as models for people to follow.
CE: So people were seeing others who could do more, leaving the impression that they should do more as well?

NT: It becomes standardized and normativized. You have the idea that people could work this much, and that they should. Little narratives come into play, like working your way up in society: if you work hard enough, you can do anything.
CE: How do you see the similarities between what you're researching and the technology advances today?

NT: Every time a new technology comes online, everyone says, "Finally, this will let us work a little bit less." AI will let us work a little less; the swing plow will let us work a little less. And it never does. It frees up time that we then fill with more work.
CE: So efficiency means doing more with the time you have out of necessity?

NT: These myths around labour correspond to a project of getting workers to work more for less. They used schemes like allotment gardens—giving workers a plot of land to grow food because they weren't being paid enough cash to feed their family. You had guys going home after a long day in the field, working all night in the moonlight to survive. That's where we get the idea of moonlighting, or today's side hustle.
CE: Did you come across any historical versions of self-care to beat burnout?

NT: No. The people writing these accounts were managing the labourers. They wrote about making sure workers had just enough food and sleep to have energy, but they don't talk about self-care in the same way we do now.
CE: What has this research done for you in your own life?

NT: It's a little bit hard not to feel hopeless, because every labour-saving device can paradoxically be used to create more labour. But there is a strange sense of long historical solidarity with people who have been subject to these same conditions and survived—and actually thrived anyway. There's something nice in that.
With files from Chris Ensing.

Worker exhaustion and burnout date back hundreds of years. Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in english and geography at Western University, explains more to guest host Chris Ensing.
CE: Are there other moments in your research that connect burnout to that period?

NT: There are a lot of stories like this. That era saw a proliferation of print media—journals and travel accounts—that spread these new agricultural techniques around and standardized them. Part of that literature was creating certain characters as models for people to follow.
CE: So people were seeing others who could do more, leaving the impression that they should do more as well?

NT: It becomes standardized and normativized. You have the idea that people could work this much, and that they should. Little narratives come into play, like working your way up in society: if you work hard enough, you can do anything.
CE: How do you see the similarities between what you're researching and the technology advances today?

NT: Every time a new technology comes online, everyone says, "Finally, this will let us work a little bit less." AI will let us work a little less; the swing plow will let us work a little less. And it never does. It frees up time that we then fill with more work.
CE: So efficiency means doing more with the time you have out of necessity?

NT: These myths around labour correspond to a project of getting workers to work more for less. They used schemes like allotment gardens—giving workers a plot of land to grow food because they weren't being paid enough cash to feed their family. You had guys going home after a long day in the field, working all night in the moonlight to survive. That's where we get the idea of moonlighting, or today's side hustle.
CE: Did you come across any historical versions of self-care to beat burnout?

NT: No. The people writing these accounts were managing the labourers. They wrote about making sure workers had just enough food and sleep to have energy, but they don't talk about self-care in the same way we do now.
CE: What has this research done for you in your own life?

NT: It's a little bit hard not to feel hopeless, because every labour-saving device can paradoxically be used to create more labour. But there is a strange sense of long historical solidarity with people who have been subject to these same conditions and survived—and actually thrived anyway. There's something nice in that.
With files from Chris Ensing.

Mental Health Research Canada reports that nearly 40 per cent of workers currently feel burnt out. Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography at Western University, spoke with Afternoon Drive host Chris Ensing about how early capitalism and agricultural advances laid the groundwork for today's burnout.

· Posted: Sep 07, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago

The latest data from Mental Health Research Canada shows that 39 per cent of Canadian workers currently feel burnt out, up from 35 per cent in 2023. While hustle culture and the grind mindset feel like modern phenomena, worker exhaustion actually dates back hundreds of years.

Nathan TeBokkel, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography at Western University, spoke with Afternoon Drive host Chris Ensing about how early capitalism and agricultural advances laid the groundwork for today's burnout.

The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Chris Ensing: This idea of burnout, people have heard of it before, but let's get a definition. What is burnout?

Nathan TeBokkel: The World Health Organization defines it as a state of vital exhaustion. It's a kind of detachment from your current surroundings, a feeling of a lack of accomplishment, a feeling of exhaustion in general.

CE: How long has this been around?

NT: It's really climbed into the mainstream more recently, especially after the pandemic, when everyone had to work a little more or differently. But it's been around a long time. The Oxford English Dictionary puts burnout at around 1937 in this exact way that we're using it now. But I think the metaphorical history of the word is a lot older, up to 250 years old.

CE: Why are you so interested in this?

NT: I'm a beekeeper, and I live and work on a fruit and vegetable farm. I'm also a scholar of English literature, and I study the Romantic era around 1800, right when the agricultural revolution is taking off in England. stories.title: Two years after Ontario repealed wage-cap law, 23,000 Opseu workers still waiting for back pay
stories.summary: Compensation issue is behind labour stoppage of roughly 4,000 community service workers who have been locked out or on strike since May
stories.author: Alice Boyle
stories.content:
More than two years ago, Ontario repealed Bill 124, a law capping wages for public-service workers that had been widely criticized and subjected to legal challenges since Queen’s Park enacted it in 2019.

But even as swaths of the public sector have been awarded retroactive pay to the tune of billions of dollars, others are still fighting for compensation.

Around 23,000 members of the Ontario Public Service Employees Union have yet to receive back pay, according to estimates from Opseu. Most are front-line social services workers in such areas as child protection, developmental services, and addictions and mental health. These jobs tend to be filled by women, many of whom have waited years for thousands of dollars in back pay.

The compensation issue is at the heart of a labour stoppage of roughly 4,000 community service workers, who have been locked out or on strike since May. Their back pay demands are in line with other public-sector workers. In the interim, many key services, including support for children and adults with disabilities, have been reduced.

But front-line service workers say they have little choice but to fight for pay that they’re entitled to.

“People do this because they care, but they should still be fairly compensated because the work is skilled work,” said Alex Dunsmuir, a developmental services worker at the Norfolk Association for Community Living and the president of Opseu Local 204.

The Ontario government enacted Bill 124 to cap pay increases for public-sector workers at 1 per cent annually, citing the province’s fiscal challenges. Labour groups derided the legislation on grounds that it impeded their ability to bargain.

Early in 2024, the Ontario Court of Appeal upheld a Superior Court ruling that the act was unconstitutional. The province then repealed the act in its entirety.

Large bargaining units – such as those for nurses and teachers – benefited from centralized bargaining and wage reopener clauses that allowed them to negotiate and secure back pay on a quicker timeline.

But community support workers rely on decentralized bargaining units that negotiate with their workplaces on an individual basis.

The province has left it up to the respective workplaces that community and social services workers bargain with to provide back pay , but these organizations claim they have not received adequate funding to do so.

Ontario’s 2025 budget projected over the next three years that spending for the Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services would decrease at an average of 0.5 per cent annually. A report from the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario said that if the Mccss spending plan is followed, it will be the smallest three-year change in more than 30 years. To maintain the ministry’s services with the current standard of quality and accessibility, spending would need to increase by 4.2 per cent annually for the next three years, the FAO estimates.

In an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, the ministry stated that the government “has made historic investments in the development services sector, including nearly $4-billion this year, an increase of $1.6-billion since we took office. In this year’s budget alone, we announced $407-million over three years to address operational needs at agencies that deliver ministry-funded services, which builds on the $310-million investment that organizations received through Budget 2024.”

But front-line service workers tell a different story. They are, for one, among the lowest-paid in the public sector.

The government of Ontario lists the median salary for social services workers at $55,100 a year. The left-leaning Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives found that between 2018 and 2025, Ontario ranked third lowest out of all provinces on wage increases for social assistance workers.

A 6.5-per-cent pay increase for a social and community services worker – the goal of current bargaining efforts, and in line with increases across the public sector – earning a median salary would amount to roughly $3,600 a year.

Beyond salaries, underfunding is having wider effects, according to front-line services workers. Ms. Dunsmuir supports people with disabilities and helps integrate them into their communities. Her workplace has been understaffed because of underfunding, she says, which has limited her staff’s ability to help those seeking their services. Many former staff members who have quit have cited the intense physical and emotional stress they experienced at work.

“There’s no relief,” she said. “There’s no more staff coming.”

Because of labour action, multiple community and social service centres across Ontario have had to temporarily halt programs that assist children and adults with disabilities.

The delays in back pay are falling hard on women, who tend to be overrepresented in these roles. Opseu reports that women make up 78 per cent of social and community workers, 87 per cent of social workers and 82 per cent of direct support professionals in developmental services.

Ms. Dunsmuir said the public perception of these strikes reflects how society undervalues care work, which is typically done by women. She’s seen comments on social media urging the workers to get back on the job because of whom they support, rather than respecting their right to bargain for back pay.

“This sector is definitely dominated by women,” said Patricia Crooks, a community support worker at Sistering, a 24/7 drop-in centre in Toronto that provides low-barrier practical and emotional support for women and gender-diverse people. “We feel like we’re being punished just for being women.”

Despite chronic staffing shortages and employee burnout, Ms. Dunsmuir said she still loves her job. She believes that even a one-time pay raise would make a difference for her and her colleagues, many of whom work multiple jobs. But she said the province needs to increase its funding in the long term for workplaces like hers to function sustainably.

The job, she said, still has “real joys.” With increased provincial funding, “those joys could offset the struggles and the hardships.”

stories.title: 'It’s going to be painful': Trade watchers warn of tit-for-tat escalation between U.S. and Canada
stories.summary: N/A
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect on Tuesday and with an American response almost inevitable, trade watchers are warning Canada should prepare itself for economic pain.

“We May be in an escalating war, and the question is who’s going to have the greater threshold for pain in this, and are Canadians ready for it because it’s going to be painful,” said Fen Osler Hampson, professor of International Affairs at Carleton University.

“I think it May be too early to go back to the table because the Americans will simply throw the same demands at us, and you know if they were unacceptable first-time around, are they going to be more the second time around?” said Hampson.

Negotiations between Canadian and American officials have remained stalled since Aug. 21, after Prime Minister Mark Carney paused trade talks with the U.S.

As a result, a 50 per-cent U.S. tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods has come into effect, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. In response, Carney intends to impose retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the U.S. has drawn up potential options to respond to Canada’s tariffs. He told Fox News last Thursday that negotiations remain stalled, but he has exchanged a few texts with the Canadian side.

Carney and Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc have both expressed a willingness to return to the table, but only with a change in “attitude” on the American side.

“I don’t see in the language from Carney and LeBlanc that would lead me to think that they have left themselves room to back down, and I also think there’s too much political advantage to them within Canada to keep the line that they’re taking,” said Mark Warner, trade lawyer at Maaw Law.

Still, Carney holds significant political capital, and polling suggests Canadians support the prime minister walking away from a bad deal.

Warner said polled Canadians believe they can withstand the pain from tariff escalation with the U.S., but he wonders how long that could last.

“So the question is, what does that mean as it (trade war) starts to bite more?” he said.

stories.title: Can Canada stop the U.S. trade war from escalating? Or should it lean in even harder?
stories.summary: Ottawa is preparing to strike back against the latest round of Trump tariffs on almost $28 billion worth of Canadian imports, and some say it should go even further.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa — Before Donald Trump ‘s second term in the White House, there was a rough sequence to Canada’s trade wars with the United States. Things got bad. Things got tense. Then, through an agreement that each country believed was mutually beneficial, things cooled down.

This was the case when trade tensions preceded the signing of 1965’s Canada-United States Automotive Products Agreement — also known as the “Auto Pact” — which helped establish an integrated car manufacturing industry across the border. It happened again when protectionism gave way to free trade after the hard-fought federal election campaign of 1988.

“You kind of see a pattern here,” explained Dimitry Anastakis, the L.R. Wilson and R.J. Currie Chair in Canadian Business History at the University of Toronto.

“The way to avoid escalation is by cutting a new deal.”

That’s exactly what Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to do. But last month he abruptly suspended negotiations, declaring Canada was “attacked” by American trade demands that would sacrifice the country’s independence.

Now Ottawa is preparing to strike back against the latest round of Trump tariffs on almost $28 billion worth of Canadian imports. At one minute past midnight on Tuesday morning, Canada’s response is set to kick in. Tariffs on American steel and aluminum will double to 50 per cent. Other tariffs will hit U.S. cheese, molasses, makeup, copper, smartphones and more. The U.S. government has already signalled it will respond to this retaliation, as Trump threatens to increase tariffs on Canadian autos on Jan. 1 in what experts warn could be ” cataclysmic ” for the Ontario-based sector.

This is what the road to trade war escalation looks like. And it’s not clear how, if or when the two countries will change course.

“You’ve got an administration here that is completely detached from reality,” said Anastakis of the U.S. government, noting that Trump has shown an ideological commitment to high tariffs and given no sign he’s going to budge.

“We’re in the unfortunate situation of having a target on our back because of an irrational administration that really wants to prove a point, which is ultimately self-destructive for their economy, for their consumers, and for the global economy,” he added.

“We are in a kind of Never Never Land.”

Right now, Carney and several of his cabinet ministers have insisted that Canada can weather the storm. Ottawa and provincial governments have pledged to support workers and businesses impacted by the trade war, including through a $7.5-billion aid package that bolsters Employment Insurance and provides favourable loans to impacted businesses. The government is also orienting Ottawa’s spending power towards a multibillion-dollar rearmament plan for the Canadian military, which it wants to use to boost domestic industries, while striving to double the amount of annual exports to countries other than the U.S. within the next decade.

But with Trump’s latest round of tariffs, and the Canadian retaliation, the trade war could be entering a new and more damaging phase — especially if it keeps escalating.

“A war of attrition is not going to go well for either side, but it’s going to go particularly poorly for the Canadian side,” said Matthew Holmes, chief of public policy at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

“From the messages we had from the prime minister and the negotiating team recently, there are serious questions about whether they’re negotiating in good faith.”

After focusing largely on specific sectors like steel, autos, aluminum and lumber, ON Aug. 22 the Trump administration slapped 50 per cent import taxes on a range of Canadian-made consumer goods and manufactured products. The new tariff list included honey, hockey sticks and cement, and had an impact on many more small- and medium-sized businesses across the country, Holmes said.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce estimates these newly tariffed exports represent about five per cent of the total volume of trade sold into the U.S. from businesses that employ about 90,000 people.

In its response that comes into effect Tuesday, the federal government said it tried to send a message to the U.S. while doing a minimal amount of damage to Canadian businesses, including by trying to avoid increasing costs of material that Canadian manufacturers need to make their products, and ensuring the tariffs hit in areas where non-U.S. alternatives exist.

Holmes said the chamber is still analyzing the impacts, but that the balancing act of minimizing the effects of the trade war on Canadians will get harder the more things escalate.

So far, the economic hit — at least at the national level — is “nominal,” Holmes added, even if it is more pronounced in sectors that have been targeted. The Canadian economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.3 per cent in the second quarter of this year, according to Statistics Canada , while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe predicts the new American tariffs could shave 0.4 per cent off the country’s gross domestic product (GDP).

But further escalation will increase the damage. In a report last week, Deloitte estimated that a total collapse of free trade between Canada and the U.S. — in the form of a withdrawal from the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma) that Trump signed in 2018 — would result in $402 billion of lost GDP growth by 2036. About 163,000 jobs per year would also be lost, the report predicted, with sectors like automaking, electronics and machinery manufacturing taking a much steeper hit.

Overall, such a scenario would be “bad” but “not devastating,” said Matthew Stewart, a partner in the economic and financial advisory group at Deloitte.

To Brian Clow, who served as deputy chief of staff to prime minister Justin Trudeau, the federal government seems to be changing tack after the collapse of trade talks by using a strategy that Ottawa used with Trump during his first term. Under Trudeau, the government imposed retaliatory tariffs in 2018, before the two sides — along with Mexico — replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement inked in the 1990s with Cusma.

“Will it work this time? We’ll see — but clearly, the government and the Canadian people broadly are behind the strategy,” Clow told the Star.

“The goal is to create economic and political pressure within the United States so that there is influence on Trump to back down.”

That May require more pressure, and some Canadian leaders argue the country should be ready to ramp it up. Premier Doug Ford, after proclaiming that Trump should “kiss my ass,” said Canada must consider slapping export taxes on electricity to make it more expensive in the U.S. Others, like former Alberta premier and federal Conservative cabinet minister Jason Kenney, say Canada should be ready to tax exports of potash, critical minerals and oil — the latter a major export to the U.S. that was worth $126.1 billion in 2025 alone .

Kenney is aware this puts him offside with Alberta’s current government, as well as the provincial administration in Saskatchewan. But it would be a mistake to take those measures off the table, Kenney argued, describing the export taxes as “very powerful economic levers to pull” in a trade conflict against a country with an economy that is more than 10 times larger than Canada’s.

“We’re talking here about a president who has said explicitly that he will use ‘economic force’ to annex or acquire Canada — an idea with which he seems to be nearly obsessed, and which he has backed up with prejudicial tariffs,” Kenney said.

“I think the best way of avoiding escalation is that they know that we have a very powerful tool to further increase energy prices in the United States, when that’s the number-one issue for Americans in a product that they cannot substitute.”

He added that he believes Canada has time on its side, in part because of a sense of public solidarity and the approach of midterm elections in the U.S. that could see opponents of his tariffs voted into the national legislature.

Such swings in power have helped end trade wars in the past, said Anastakis, the historian at the University of Toronto. In the 1930s, a protectionist Republican agenda was thwarted in the U.S. when Franklin D. Roosevelt became president and a law was passed that paved the way to lower tariffs.

The difference now, however, is that social media makes it difficult to tone down hostile rhetoric, he argued.

And then there’s Trump’s devotion to tariffs, which he describes as the “most beautiful” word in the English language.

“It’s not going to get resolved until cooler heads are actually in spots where they can prevail,” he said. “Right now there are no cooler heads on the American side.”

stories.title: Bob Aaron: A B.C. court just sent a loud message to anyone who’s ever eyeballed a neighbour’s tree
stories.summary: Never assume that because a neighbour has said go ahead and "trim the trees," everyone agrees on what those words mean.
stories.author: Bob Aaron
stories.content:
A British Columbia homeowner has learned the hard way that lopping off a neighbour’s trees without permission can be a costly mistake.

Jacalyn Hays and five members of the Fenton family own adjacent cottage properties in Sicamous, B.C., overlooking Shuswap Lake.

In July 2021, Alan Fenton asked Hays for permission to trim or top her trees to improve his view of the lake. Hays claimed she gave him limited approval to trim just small saplings provided they were no more than three inches in diameter and six or seven feet in height.

The problem was that the parties had very different ideas about exactly what had been authorized. Unfortunately some much larger trees were cut and topped, and one 50-foot tree was completely felled.

That turned a neighbourhood tree-trimming exercise into a lawsuit for trespass. Judge George Leven of the B.C. Provincial Court issued his decision last month, following hearings in May.

As is so often the case in property disputes, the problem was not simply what somebody said. It was proving what had actually been said.

Hays told the court that her property had once been a “shaded oasis” and was now “unbearable” since it was exposed to direct sunlight for much of the day.

Fortunately for Hays, she had recorded an important conversation in which Fenton admitted, “I have to take responsibility.”

The judge used the recording to conclude that Hays had not consented to the cutting of the larger trees.

The defendants, including the unlicensed and uninsured tree cutter, were held liable in trespass.

The judge noted that the defendants had ample opportunity to phone or email Hays to confirm exactly what could be cut. Instead, the defendants proceeded without obtaining first-hand confirmation.

All of the defendants were found liable.

The next question was damages. For Hays, the loss of the trees meant loss of shade. She sought compensation for expenses resulting from her losses, including replacement trees, installation of a shade structure, new air conditioning, professional reports and a shelter for a propane tank.

The judge considered what expenses reasonably flowed from the trespass and tried to arrive at an award that was fair to both sides, but he refused to award the full cost of replacing the trees themselves.

The damages, however, did not end with out-of-pocket expenses.

The court also recognized something homeowners instinctively understand: trees can be part of the enjoyment of a property. Their removal can affect privacy, appearance, shade and comfort.

Hays complained about the increased heat caused by the lost shade, the appearance of the property and concern over the stability of the slope where the trees had stood.

The judge awarded $35,000 damages as compensation for the trees and diminished enjoyment of the property. That amount is the maximum permitted monetary jurisdiction of the provincial court.

Although this was a British Columbia decision and does not bind Ontario courts, the warning for Toronto homeowners is clear. Never assume that because a neighbour has said go ahead and “trim the trees,” everyone agrees on what those words mean.

Is permission being given to remove one branch? To prune everything extending over the property line? To reduce the height of a tree? Or to cut it down? Those are all very different things.

In Ontario, the issue can be even more complicated when a tree trunk grows on the boundary between two properties.

Under Ontario law, every tree whose trunk grows on the boundary between adjoining properties is the common property of the two owners. Injuring or destroying a boundary tree without both owners’ consent is an offence.

Toronto has another layer of protection. Under the city’s tree bylaw, trees on private property with a diameter of 30 centimetres (12 inches) or more are generally protected against injury or removal without a permit. The city also cautions homeowners dealing with a neighbour’s overhanging branches that they cannot trespass onto the neighbour’s property to remove them, and cannot damage the neighbour’s tree.

The practical lesson from Hays is simple. If neighbours agree that tree work can be done, put the agreement in writing. Identify the tree. Take photographs. Mark the branches that can be removed. Specify whether the work involves pruning, topping or removal.

And make sure an arborist sees the written agreement before the chainsaw starts.

A five-minute email or call between neighbours could have prevented the B.C. litigation.

Trees can survive for a century. Unfortunately, a neighbour’s oral permission May have a much shorter life expectancy.

stories.title: Ontario’s new school year starts with major curriculum changes and one big labour question. Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: Ontario teachers and school support staff start the year without a contract, leaving uncertainty around labour peace.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
The province’s new family support offices are opening in every school board. Kindergarten students will learn a revamped curriculum, there are new history lessons in Grade 7, 8 and 10 — a grade where teens will also have mandatory financial literacy lessons, with a must-pass test . High schoolers will be marked on attendance and participation, and have to write exams in almost all courses.

But there’s one big question no one has the answer to as this school year begins: Will there be labour peace?

The answer is: for now. But with talks in limbo as everyone awaits a labour board ruling, the year begins with many unknowns.

“The first few days are really exciting, and that’s the first thing on their minds, and they then have (bargaining issues) in the back of their minds,” said René Jansen in de Wal, president of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, referring to the teachers.

René Jansen in de Wal President of Oecta with the union’s new ad campaign at Union Station.

The unions have appealed to the board after an early disagreement with the government, which is seeking to add items for provincial negotiations that they feel are better suited for local units and boards to hammer out under Ontario’s two-tier bargaining system.

While waiting for that decision, the five big education unions — representing 275,000 public, Catholic and French elementary and secondary teachers, as well as support staff — have planned an in-school day of solidarity and rallies while watching and waiting for the labour board decision.

No strike votes have been planned as yet and no possible job action can happen until there have been meaningful negotiations.

“This could drag on for a few months before we get much indication which way it’s going to go,” said Rob Kristofferson, a labour studies expert at Wilfrid Laurier University.

Education union leaders at the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario headquarters in downtown Toronto.

Education Minister Paul Calandra is optimistic a deal can be reached without labour strife, saying “everything that we’re doing is about putting student achievement first. Every teacher I talk to, every educator I talk to, has the exact same mission.”

He said the changes coming this fall “aren’t revolutionary changes. Some of these things bring us back to a time when we were having better student achievement, better outcomes, and teachers have better control of their classroom, and I am confident that our educators can deal with the changes.”

On the labour front, he said he was “heartened” to hear David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, say there will be no job action early on.

David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, and Martha Hradowy, president of Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, at a union press conference in June.

“I fully expect that there is an opportunity for the government and the unions to come to an agreement,” Calandra said. “We’ll be working hard on that. I don’t expect any labour challenges; I think students will be in school for a number of months going ahead ... It behooves us to work together to come to an agreement so students stay in the classroom. And I still remain optimistic.”

But for Stephanie Ross, a labour studies expert at McMaster University, “the fact that we have not gotten to some meaningful discussions yet, and that we’re still dealing with process, that means people should be paying close attention.”

She believes “the likelihood of disruption is greater than the last time because of the strategies of the unions to be more united,” adding that doesn’t necessarily mean a strike down the road, but “there could be various kinds of pressure techniques that are used.”

Indeed, in a recent memo to members obtained by the Star, the Catholic teachers’ union advised it “is actively planning and preparing for the next steps, should they become necessary.”

Martha Hradowy, president of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, said “families have dealt with alot of uncertainty in public education over the last several years, and nobody wants another school year to be dominated by labour negotiations — I would say our members don’t want that either.

“But the best way to create stability is to bargain, to sit down, to deal seriously with the issues, find compromises where we can, and to get agreements.”

She said her union is “asking the government to work with us on three fundamental things: better supports for students, meaningful investment in public education, and respect for teachers and education workers. I think if we start there, I think that there’s a path forward.”

Among the other changes this year are $750 spending cards for teachers, who began ordering in an online Staples portal Sept. 1, with a list of 200-plus items to start. A number of teachers reported finding lower prices at the retail site, leading Staples to say it will price match.

The province is also spending $16.8 million over three years for experienced teachers who help mentor younger educators.

Meanwhile, the new policy that ties attendance to marks for high school students — 15 per cent of final marks in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent in grades 11 and 12 — has led to some confusion, with Ontario principals seeking clarification. They are hoping to meet with Calandra soon.

stories.title: Stevens scores 3 TDs as Riders beat Bombers in OT
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan Roughriders earned some breathing room in the CFL's West Division standings with a thrilling 32-26 overtime victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sunday.
stories.author: Jeff DeDekker
stories.content:
Regina – The Saskatchewan Roughriders earned some breathing room in the CFL’s West Division standings with a thrilling 32-26 overtime victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sunday.

The victory improves the Roughriders’ record to 8-4, good for second place in the West Division behind the Edmonton Elks who have an 8-3 record heading into Monday’s game in Calgary against the Stampeders. The Bombers slipped to 6-6 after Sunday’s loss.

The Riders had the first possession in overtime and scored on a one-yard run by quarterback Tommy Stevens. It was the third touchdown of the game for Stevens, who now has 15 rushing touchdowns on the year. The ensuing two-point conversion attempt failed, opening the door for the Bombers.

The Riders, however, sealed the victory by stopping the Bombers on a third-and-six attempt from the Saskatchewan 31-yard line.

Trailing 16-13 heading into the fourth quarter, the Riders took a 20-16 lead on a one-yard touchdown run by Stevens at the 11:21 mark.

The Bombers pulled to within one point on Sergio Castillo’s fourth field goal of the game, coming with 5:44 remaining.

The Riders replied on their next possession, going 70 yards on five plays, culminating with a three-yard touchdown run by Stevens.

The Bombers forced overtime when quarterback Zach Collaros hit Dorian Singer on a five-yard touchdown pass on the final play of regulation.

First downs were hard to come by early with Saskatchewan getting the first of the game with five minutes left in the first quarter on its fourth possession. Winnipeg got its opening first down three minutes into the second quarter on its sixth possession of the game.

With Saskatchewan holding a 5-3 lead after the first quarter, the Riders got into the end zone at the 12:20 mark of the second quarter when quarterback Trevor Harris connected with Quali Conley on a seven-yard scoring pass.

After Castillo cut the deficit to 12-6 with his second field goal of the game, the Bombers took a 13-12 lead when Collaros hit Kevens Clercius on a 12-yard touchdown pass with 38 seconds left in the half.

Harris passed Doug Flutie for 10th spot on the CFL’s all-time passing list with a 72-yard completion to Daniel Wiebe early in the second quarter. Harris entered the game with 41,228 passing yards, 127 yards behind Flutie, who had 41,355 passing yards.

After passing for 341 yards on Sunday, Harris now has 41,590 passing yards and trails Matt Dunigan who occupies ninth place with 43,857 yards. Anthony Calvillo is the all-time passing yardage leader with 79,816 yards.

Blue Bombers: Host the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Saturday, Sept. 12.

Roughriders: Visit the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Saturday, Sept. 12.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Indigenous actor and filmmaker Georgina Lightning dies at 63
stories.summary: Lightning was the first Indigenous woman in North America to direct a major feature film with her 2008 debut, Older Than America
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Georgina Lightning, the Cree actor, director and screenwriter who broke barriers for Indigenous women in the film industry, died Saturday after an incident at an Indigenous equestrian championship west of Edmonton. She was 63.

Ms. Lightning was shooting a documentary about the three-day Indian Relay event at the Enoch Rodeo Grounds when the incident occurred, according to friends and family.

Police responded at 6:40 p.m. after a horse veered off track and struck a woman standing in a designated media area, said Alberta RCMP public information officer Corporal Mathew Howell. Emergency medical services attended and declared the woman deceased on the scene, Cpl. Howell said. Occupational Health and Safety, Alberta’s workplace-safety regulator, will be taking over the investigation.

“She was doing what she loved, where she loved, and with who she loved,” Edmonton-Rutherford MLA Jodi Calahoo Stonehouse, a close friend of Ms. Lightning’s, said in an interview.

Born in Edmonton and a member of the Samson Cree Nation, Ms. Lightning moved to Los Angeles in the 1990s with her three young children to attend the American Academy of Dramatic Arts and pursue a career in film. Her acting credits included Blackstone , The West Wing and DreamKeeper .

She eventually expanded into producing, directing and screenwriting, becoming an advocate for Indigenous peoples to have a greater role not only in front of the camera but in deciding which stories are told.

Ms. Lightning became the first Indigenous woman in North America to direct a major feature film with her 2008 directorial debut, Older Than America , about the intergenerational effects of U.S. residential schools, which went on to win more than two dozen festival awards. The film was dedicated to her father, George De Jong, who died by suicide after years of struggling with the effects of his experience in the Canadian residential school system.

Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse said Ms. Lightning had spent years working on the film about the Indian Relay, which was in its final stages of shooting.

“Georgina wanted to show not just the excitement of the race, and the joy it brings to the nations as it travels around, but also the healing of the horse spirit, the effect that it has on the families and the riders,” she said.

Indian Relay is a traditional horse race in which participants race bareback around a track at high speed, switching horses after each lap. The sport grew out of centuries-old Indigenous horse cultures after the animals were reintroduced to North America in the late 15th and early 16th centuries.

Presented with the option of shutting down the event after Saturday’s incident, Ms. Lightning’s family said both the race and her work should continue. Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse was at the racetrack on Sunday, finishing Ms. Lightning’s final interviews.

Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse described her friend as a firecracker who held those in power to account, but also had “a tremendous amount of love for people.” She was deeply spiritual, grounded by her faith and connection to ceremony, and devoted to mentoring young people across North America. She was also fiercely proud of her three children and grandchildren.

“Last night when her children and I sat down, we said we have to finish what she started because she was just so determined to tell these stories that no one was telling,” Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse said. “She’s been so determined to take up space where there are no First Nations peoples’ voices being heard.”

Danielle Paradis, a Métis freelance journalist who was working with Ms. Lightning on a documentary about climate change in the Prairies, said the filmmaker was always fighting to show the “bigger picture” in her work.

“She wanted to make sure that whoever was working on [the documentary] understood the complexities of resource extraction in Indigenous communities, because that’s often presented as one of the only ways out of poverty for these communities,” Ms. Paradis said.

“And so, what’s the real conversation about that? Because you’ve got to have money and jobs to feed your family, but you also have to have water and land. It was brave. We’re in an age when so many people are cowardly to talk about that sort of stuff.”

Ms. Paradis said Ms. Lightning was most passionate about fighting for Indigenous women, ensuring that there is a clear path for them and that they are recognized for the work that they do.

She added that she was moved by Ms. Lightning’s humility, despite her many accolades.

“Her answer was always, ‘Teach me,’” she said. “It was such a rare and humble way of approaching things.”

The Enoch Cree Nation said it is mourning the loss of a community member and that the chief and council extend their condolences to the family.

“Our community is grieving, and we are holding them in our thoughts and prayers,” the nation said in a statement issued Saturday.

stories.title: One dead after Cape Breton floods prompt state of emergency, cut power for thousands
stories.summary: Body of 46-year-old woman found on Saturday afternoon after she was reported missing, RCMP say
stories.author: Sophia Bertuzzi
stories.content:
Torrential rains and high-speed winds hammered Cape Breton Island and parts of the northeastern mainland of Nova Scotia over the weekend, flooding and damaging roads, cutting off power to tens of thousands of residents, and leaving one person dead.

Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a severe weather warning for all of Cape Breton on Saturday morning while 200 millimetres of rain poured over the region. A state of emergency was declared for the counties of Inverness, Richmond and Victoria.

In Richmond County, first responders recovered the body of a missing 46-year-old Cape Breton woman, the RCMP said. Crews started searching for her after she was reported missing earlier that morning when her vehicle was found parked near her home on a flooded bridge in the community of Cleveland, N.S. In a news release, the RCMP said the death was not considered suspicious.

On Sunday, Environment Canada ended its weather alerts, but Nova Scotia’s Department of Emergency Management said roads across the region continued to be affected by flooding.

Jacqueline Cassel-Cramer and Arthur Cramer, who have been road-tripping around Nova Scotia for the past week in a rented camper van, said the rain and windy conditions picked up around Friday evening.

The Winnipeg-based couple in their 60s pulled into a campground near Baddeck, N.S., ON Cape Breton’s Bras d’Or Lake on Friday night unaware of any weather advisories. Ms. Cassel-Cramer said they had told the campground owners of their plan to visit the Fortress of Louisbourg National Historic Site on the southeastern coast of the island the next day.

“They said, ‘There’s a massive storm. You’re not going to be able to go anywhere.’ They really tried to talk us out of it,” Ms. Cassel-Cramer said.

Throughout the night, the weather turned inclement, she said, recalling the camper van rocking back and forth from the wind, and heavy rain seeping into parts of the van.

“That was pretty intense, and it got rather scary. I was starting to feel a little bit afraid,” Ms. Cassel-Cramer said.

These conditions continued Saturday throughout the day and evening, before ameliorating Sunday morning.

“We could see a little bit of blue sky trying to break through the clouds,” she said on Sunday.

The couple has since made their way west along Highway 105, which was clear despite washouts on the shoulders toward the Canso Causeway, the crossing that connects Cape Breton Island to the mainland of Nova Scotia.

On the other side of Bras d’Or Lake, near Dundee, N.S., Sophie Symonds woke up around 4 a.m. on Saturday morning when her downstairs neighbours called her because their apartment had flooded.

In a hurry, Ms. Symonds and her neighbours scrambled to salvage what they could from the ground-floor apartment while losing power in the process. Outside, the water on the street reached their knees. If they ventured out, the strong current would have swept them away, she said.

“The whole road kind of looked like we were on a river. We had no road left.”

Ms. Symonds’ apartment is about a 15-minute walk away from Dundee Resort and Golf Club, where she and her neighbours work. In truckloads, Ms. Symonds and about 10 other employees managed to make it to the resort that morning – where they have been hunkered down since.

Despite the storm, guests and employees of the resort made the most of being stranded.

“Everybody was gathering and laughing and talking, and just trying to make the best of the situation. It was nice to have everybody in one spot,” she said.

On the Western coast of Cape Breton, the village of Inverness was also battered with high-speed winds and buckets of rain.

“It was unbelievable. I thought the roof was going to come off my house, seriously,” Ruth Skinner, an Inverness local, said.

Earlier this morning, Ms. Skinner and her friend of 50 years, Ray Walker, the owner of Dusky Diamonds Bed & Breakfast, drove down to the beach to get some fresh, salty air.

Ms. Skinner’s house and Mr. Walker’s bed and breakfast had suffered power outages beginning in the early hours of Saturday morning – among the 40,000 homes and businesses that lost power, according to Nova Scotia Power.

“We wanted to have a look at the waves, and because there’s no power, hard to get any work done at the Dusky,” Ms. Skinner said.

Since then, the power has returned to Mr. Walker’s bed and breakfast. They have a full house this evening.

On their evening plans: “Turn the heat up, get it nice and warm, and relax,” Ms. Skinner said.

stories.title: Trade talks remain frozen as Canadian countertariffs set for Tuesday
stories.summary: Ottawa has pledged to impose levies on $28-billion worth of U.S. imports
stories.author: Marieke Walsh
stories.content:
Talks between Canadian and American officials remained at an impasse Sunday, with Ottawa saying that there have been no formal meetings to avert the imposition of fresh retaliatory tariffs .

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has pledged to impose levies on $28-billion worth of U.S. imports effective 12:01 a.m. Tuesday. The policy will hit a range of products from steel and aluminum to textiles, stoves and hundreds of other goods.

The planned tariffs are a response to new 50-per-cent levies that President Donald Trump imposed on Canada after Mr. Carney withdrew from trade talks on Aug. 21.

In the lead-up to those U.S. tariffs, Canadian and U.S. officials held near-daily meetings as they tried to strike a deal to avert the levies and reduce others that the White House had previously imposed. This time though, there has been no last-minute rush to avoid additional economic pain from the new Canadian tariffs.

Instead, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is spending the Labour Day weekend back in his home province of New Brunswick, a federal official said. Mr. LeBlanc, the official said, has had no formal talks with his U.S. counterparts this weekend and none are scheduled.

The official said that the last time any formal talks took place was Aug. 21 – the day the negotiations in Washington fell apart.

Similarly, Canada’s top trade negotiator, Janice Charette, has had no formal talks with her American counterparts and none are planned, a second official said.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the officials, who were not authorized to release the information.

Mr. Carney’s office said the Prime Minister has not spoken with the President since the week formal trade talks ended.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s office said Canada’s plan for countertariffs remains whole and they will come into effect as planned on Tuesday.

The new tariffs are aimed at shoring up the domestic market for Canadian companies hit by U.S. tariffs while also ramping up political pressure south of the border.

But the tariffs can also hurt Canadian businesses that rely on imported material and products from the U.S.

Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters, an industry group representing manufacturers of all sizes, has repeatedly warned that countertariffs will increase costs for businesses reliant on American inputs, particularly smaller manufacturers with little ability to quickly change their supply chains.

The association has called for the federal government to continue providing tariff remission for companies that cannot competitively source other input alternatives.

“The ultimate objective must remain the removal of U.S. tariffs and a durable agreement that restores certainty for manufacturers and workers on both sides of the border,” said Dennis Darby, president and CEO of CME, last week.

The Trump administration has already pledged to retaliate if Canada goes ahead with its countertariff response.

On Friday, The Globe reported that White House officials are hoping to hit back against Canada’s retaliation no later than Wednesday. The Trump administration is considering banning imports of Canadian alcohol, dairy products, and possibly steel, The Globe reported based on a source.

Debate continues within the Trump administration on how tough the measures should be, with some in the President’s orbit calling for even more punitive actions. What those would consist of remained unclear.

Late last week, Mr. Trump suggested in a social-media post that the trade war between the two countries would lead to Canada’s economic collapse. The ramifications will be “worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian Politician. Just watch!” he threatened.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump and his officials continued to attack and deride Canada. The President’s social-media page again posted about the renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent compared Canada to a “yippy dog.”

He argued that Canada’s countertariffs will have a negligible effect on U.S. prices.

“It is not much of a hit to us, if any,” he told Fox News.

In the past few weeks, the Prime Minister has repeatedly said Canada will only return to the negotiating table when the U.S. changes its attitude.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Mr. Carney said on Sept. 1.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters last week that he was confident the trade war would ultimately end with a negotiated deal.

“That’s where this is going to wind up – the sooner, the better,” Mr. Johnson said.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are increasing political pressure on Republicans by targeting industries in states that are vulnerable in this fall’s midterm elections.

For example, the state likely to suffer the single biggest hit from Canada’s tariffs is Republican-run Ohio , where Democratic candidates are mounting competitive gubernatorial and senate campaigns.

Canadian unions, in particular, have been vocal supporters of Mr. Carney’s tariff countermeasures, saying that Canada should fight back against Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which are designed to target Canada’s industrial base, and force concessions.

“The Canadian countertariffs are a good first response, but we need to take action at home to keep workers on the job by fast-tracking procurement dollars, implementing national industrial strategies, and calling on corporate Canada to step up and Buy Canadian,” said Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, in a statement on Aug. 25.

With reports from Vanmala Subramaniam, Adrian Morrow and Mark Rendell

stories.title: Sikh community targeted with death and hate messages amid holy procession
stories.summary: The Sikh community is disappointed after seeing death threats spray painted on several signs along their procession route in downtown Winnipeg ahead of the event on Sunday.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Winnipeg’s Sikh community is disappointed after seeing death threats spray-painted on several signs along their procession route downtown ahead of the event on Sunday.

Nagar Kirtan is an annual event celebrating Sikhism’s holy scripture. It features a procession carrying the Guru Granth Sahib, the religion’s holy book, along with songs of faith.

An image of the graffiti circulating on social media shows a death threat against Indians and a swastika on a transit sign advising of road closures for the event. Winnipeg police confirmed several signs were tagged with hate messages.

“I don’t know why people hate, or something like that, because nowadays the racism has gone beyond the lines,” said Jagmeet Brar, an attendee.

The president of the Sikh Society of Manitoba said the community is staying strong and keeping a positive attitude.

“It’s (hate) everywhere in the world,” said Harbans Singh Brar, the society’s president. “Don’t worry. Come here and enjoy yourself. We will pray for the whole community.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew condemned the hateful graffiti.

“There is no place for racism against Sikhs. There’s no place for hate for Punjabi people, and there’s no place for hate in that sort of activity in this province,” he said.

Const. Claude Chancy said police increased their presence at the event. The graffiti is being investigated as a hate crime.

Hate-motivated crimes more than doubled, rising from 44 in 2024 to 112 in 2025, according to the Winnipeg Police Service’s 2025 statistical report.

Const. Claude Chancy said police increased their presence at the event. The graffiti is being investigated as a hate crime.
Hate-motivated crimes more than doubled, rising from 44 in 2024 to 112 in 2025, according to the Winnipeg Police Service’s 2025 statistical report.
