stories.title: Food influencer gets to know B.C. by eating flora and fauna
stories.summary: From starfish gonads to Dungeness crab, West Coast foraging has become a hit on social media
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
After a purple starfish is barbecued, its yellow gonads look a bit like scrambled eggs and they taste a little like them too, except with a bit of a bitter “pop.”

That’s one of the many revelations social media influencer Justin Park relayed during his quest to fish and forage for dozens of different species of flora and fauna from across British Columbia.

Some of the tapas the amateur chef has profiled for his tens of thousands of online followers include globally renowned favourites such as spot prawns and Dungeness crab. But his creations often skew more obscure and eye-popping, such as making crostini with acorn and oak weevils, fashioning fruit roll-ups out of salal berries and pickling bull kelp.

The 30-year-old from Honolulu said he gave himself just under a year to see how much of B.C. he could find and eat after free-diving for fish and shellfish around Victoria, where the U.S. naval veteran recently completed a two-and-a-half-year contract working on submarines for the Royal Canadian Navy. The challenge is now over, but he said he is still editing videos chronicling the up to 70 different species he ate during that period.

Anecdotally, it appears more and more North Americans are finding and fixing their own meals from the wild as an antidote to a variety of modern ills: Inflating grocery store prices, the ecological and health harms of industrial agricultural systems and the tiny screens monopolizing our free time.

Data are scarce on people who are using snorkels or shovels in order to secure their next meal. Results from the last census, in 2021, show only three per cent of Canadian households reported hunting close to home, with that number reaching as high as seven per cent for those living outside larger cities. In B.C., the province has issued 13-per-cent more fishing licences to residents over the past decade ending in 2023, the last year for which data is available.

Tom Cervenka, a Vancouver computer programmer who sells field guides to berry and mushroom picking in various provinces, said he believes the COVID-19 pandemic and our increasing dependence on social media created an uptick in Canadians becoming more interested in self-sufficiency.

“How can I look after myself without relying on food distribution chains that could fail conceivably?” said Mr. Cervenka, who also leads mushroom tours of Pacific Spirit Regional Park, which surrounds the University of British Columbia’s sprawling campus.

Mr. Park said he took to social media to share his exhilaration with the province’s natural bounty, as well as to challenge people to get outside their comfort zones and consider trying to catch and prepare their own meals – as long as they obey the rules and avoid species in peril.

“I was just so excited to discover these things: I didn’t know you could just dig in the sand and catch a Dungeness crab and go home with a $30 crab,” Mr. Park said during a recent phone interview from Ecuador, where he travelled this summer.

“I was just like blown away by how much food there was, not only in the sea, but on land as well.”

Still, he is keen to get people to pivot from the popular meats of crab, salmon and halibut and embrace lesser-known foods that Indigenous people have consumed for millennia.

Dr. Jennifer Grenz, a member of the Lytton First Nation and a food systems scientist with Ubc’s Department of Forest Resources Management, said it is great that Mr. Park is sharing how to access the abundance Western Canada has to offer.

She added that an increasing number of Indigenous influencers are posting their own videos online to share traditional knowledge, referencing chef and educator Jared Qwustenuxun Williams, who also refers to himself as the Indigenous Forest Punk.

Among the traditional practices seeing a resurgence are “sea gardens,” which First Nations often built by piling rock walls along intertidal zones to trap sediment and make a healthy habitat for shellfish, Dr. Grenz said.

“Humans are inherently lazy, right?” she added of the common misconception that Indigenous peoples were constantly hunting and gathering to survive, explaining that this method of sustainable aquaculture offered minimal effort and maximum returns.

Dr. Grenz, author of Medicine Wheel for the Planet: A Journey Toward Personal and Ecological Healing , said the erasure of traditional knowledge was rammed home when she was called into the principal’s office after her twin daughters got in trouble during a class hike. The pair were showing their classmates how to pick and eat salmon berries when their teacher found out and “flipped out.”

The school explained that teaching people to eat wild berries was against its rules.

“I’m like, ‘well, they know their plant identification, they’re teaching them: This is food. They’re just teaching their friends to find food out in the places they go all the time,’ ” she said. “And then that’s when I was like, ‘do you want this to be a news story or do you want to apologize to them?’”

“They apologized to them.”

stories.title: More than half of Canadians support rejecting proposed trade deal and countertariff measures, poll finds
stories.summary: About two-thirds also said they were worried or somewhat worried about the impact that tariffs will have on them and their families
stories.author: Olivia Grandy
stories.content:
Most Canadians support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States and instead impose retaliatory countertariffs, even if it means paying more for goods, a new poll suggests.

A Nanos Research survey conducted for The Globe and Mail found that 85 per cent of more than 1,000 respondents said they support or somewhat support Mr. Carney’s rejection of the proposed trade deal with the Trump administration.

The survey also found that 80 per cent of respondents said they support or somewhat support Ottawa’s plan to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar countertariffs on a range of U.S. products, scheduled to take effect on Tuesday.

Negotiations to avoid additional U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods fell apart last month when Mr. Carney ordered his officials to withdraw from talks and return home. He later said the Americans introduced unreasonable demands on a range of issues, from French-language requirements to tariffs on trucks .

Nik Nanos, the chief data scientist for Nanos Research, said support for retaliatory tariffs is as high as the early days of the trade war at the beginning of last year, when American policies fuelled antipathy toward the United States and consumer boycotts of U.S. goods and travel.

“We’re back to a situation where the temperature is about as hot as it got when Donald Trump first said that Canada should be the 51st state,” Mr. Nanos said.

About seven in 10 survey respondents said they were willing or somewhat willing to pay higher prices for everyday goods as part of Canada’s response to U.S. tariffs.

Yet, only time will tell how many Canadians will hold on to these views when “economic causalities start piling in” from the trade war, Mr. Nanos said. He added the near-consensus could be short-lived, mirroring the common trend of public opinion during wars.

“That’s the risk for the Carney administration,” he said.

The online random survey sampled 1,037 Canadians from Aug. 30 to Sept. 2 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The margin of error for regional results is higher.

Respondents from the Prairies were comparatively less likely to support Canada rejecting the possible trade deal, at about 17 per cent. Similarly, about 19 per cent of respondents from the region opposed Canada implementing countertariffs.

“Albertans and folks in the Prairies, specifically, are more likely to have an affinity with the United States in terms of the importance of the bi-national relationship and the importance of the trade talks,” Mr. Nanos said. Still, he flagged that even in this region, nearly 77 per cent somewhat rejected the potential U.S.-Canada deal.

Overall, respondents expressed high levels of support for the country’s elbows-up posture: More than three in four said they had both sought out purchasing Canadian goods and avoided purchasing American goods or services in response to Mr. Trump’s comments.

Six in 10 Canadians are either confident or somewhat confident that Canada can protect its economic interests if a new agreement with the U.S. is reached, the poll found.

Meanwhile, about two-thirds also said they were worried or somewhat worried about the impact that tariffs will have on them and their families.

These coinciding views seem to reflect the “clear-headed” understanding Canadians have about the effects of a trade war, Mr. Nanos said.

“They know that you’re not going to enter into a tariff war with the United States without suffering.”

Three-quarters of Canadians disagreed in some way that the U.S. is a trustworthy ally of Canada. The lowest level of agreement (4.7 per cent) came from Quebeckers. Mr. Carney has said that the U.S. tried to influence Canada’s language protections during the August trade talks.

Despite the lack of trust, polling did suggest that some Canadians still believe there is a chance the relationship between the two countries could rebound. More than three in five expected Canada’s relationship with the U.S. to be better (22 per cent) or somewhat better (39 per cent) five years from now.

Put another way, Mr. Nanos pointed out that only one in five respondents firmly said the relationship would improve after this time period.

“Even the hope that Canadians have that things will get better to one extent or another in the next five years is tepid,” he said.

stories.title: In B.C.’s busy waters, coast pilots guide ships into safe harbour
stories.summary: Skilled mariners, dispatchers, and Talon Helicopter crews work together to cover the largest pilotage district in the world
stories.author: James MacDonald
stories.content:
Spend enough time on Dallas Road in Victoria, B.C., and you’ll see it: A small yellow vessel sailing out to meet the hulking bulk carriers, container ships, cruise ships and car carriers that ply the Salish Sea.

Whether during the calm, warm days of a B.C. summer, or the cold, rain-whipped nights of a coastal winter storm, the Pacific Guardian makes the trip. It has a crucial mission: to deliver ship pilots to the vessels that transit in and out from the Pacific.

The ship pilot’s job is to board vessels travelling the immense coast of the province, helping them to safely navigate unfamiliar waters and busy ports.

Ship pilots are professional mariners with decades of experience on the water. While ship captains and crew know their own vessel, they are less familiar with local waterways, tides, coastlines, and ports.

At more than 25,000 kilometres, the BC coastline is the largest pilotage district in the world. The BC Coast Pilots and PPA are responsible for territory from the southern tip of Vancouver Island to the southern tip of Alaska, as well as the length of the Fraser River.

In 2025, more than 140 pilots – along with launch captains, deckhands, dispatchers, and Talon Helicopter crews – responded to 15,200 ship assignments.

Talon Helicopter crews transfer ships pilots on and off of vessels in the pilotage district along the coast.

Ship pilots are some of the most skilled and knowledgeable mariners on the water.

“They need between 700 and 1,000 days at sea on the BC coast [as] the prerequisites to entry,” explained John Wilson, CEO of the PPA.

“Then they do a very comprehensive examination on navigation chart knowledge of the coast. That normally takes them a year or two of ... almost full-time preparation. If they’re successful on the exam, then they have an oral board [exam] that’s between four and five hours in length.”

It takes another seven years to become an unrestricted pilot, able to navigate the largest of vessels.

Joe McDonugh, small vessel machinery operator and deckhand on the PPA pilot vessel the Pacific Guardian, stands watch on deck after the crew dropped off a ships pilot for the cruise ship Anthem of the Seas' final approach and docking at the Port of Victoria.

Pilot Michel Drouin speaks to the challenges of the job.

“No two [ship] bridges are alike. You must not let things bother you too much, just go along with it.”

Mr. Drouin is among the most experienced BC Coast pilots, and the only BC Coast pilot to navigate a submarine, the Hmas Collins, through Seymour Narrows, a notoriously challenging and treacherous stretch of water between Vancouver Island and the mainland.

Mr. Drouin’s deep knowledge of the ports, tides, and corners of the coast are the hallmark of the skill set these ship pilots bring to shipping traffic around British Columbia.

stories.title: Canada must move to better protect wild salmon populations
stories.summary: The end of open-net pens must lead to a safer ecosystem
stories.author: Tony Allard
stories.content:
Tony Allard is the chair of Wild Salmon Forever/Wild First.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has long argued that market prices fail to capture what societies most value : healthy ecosystems, natural abundance and the interests of future generations. British Columbia’s transition away from open-net-pen Atlantic salmon farms is an early test of whether his government will govern by that principle.

Open-net pens place farmed Atlantic salmon in the same coastal waters used by migrating wild Pacific salmon. They can create pathways for sea lice and pathogens, while releasing feed and waste into the marine environment.

While industry has argued that sea lice levels, for example, have not changed with salmon farm closures, the result is an unequal allocation of risk: operators receive commercial benefits, while wild salmon, Indigenous peoples, coastal communities and the public bear environmental costs.

Wild Pacific salmon are more than a commodity. They nourish ecosystems, sustain fisheries and tourism and remain central to Indigenous cultures, laws and economies. Their worth cannot be reduced to a dollar figure and set against one industry’s contribution to British Columbia’s economy. Not everything of value is fungible. There is a difference between what can be counted and what truly counts.

In 2019, Ottawa committed to develop a plan to transition B.C.’s salmon farms away from open-net pens. In June, 2024 , the federal government made the essential commitment: open-net-pen salmon aquaculture in B.C.’s coastal waters would be prohibited by June 30, 2029. Existing operators seeking renewed licences could receive five-year terms to facilitate that transition.

The transition is not theoretical. In February, 2023 , the federal fisheries minister refused to reissue licences for open-net salmon farms in the Discovery Islands, an important migration corridor for wild Pacific salmon.

In January, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld that decision, affirming the minister’s authority to take a precautionary, conservation-based approach where scientific uncertainty remains.

Now the Carney government must ensure that 2029 becomes an enforceable regulatory outcome, rather than a date softened or deferred as it approaches.

Mr. Carney has warned of the “ tragedy of the horizon ”: the temptation to delay action because the greatest consequences fall outside today’s political and economic time frames. This transition is precisely such a test.

The costs of change are immediate. Workers, farm operators and coastal communities face disruption and deserve a credible plan. But that is an argument for early planning, retraining and investment – not for prolonging a system that shifts risks onto wild salmon, Indigenous peoples and future generations.

Ottawa’s 2024 transition plan established the right direction. After July 1, 2024 , new applicants for salmon aquaculture in coastal B.C. would be considered only for marine or land-based closed-containment systems.

The government also identified waste removal and the treatment or filtration of discharged water as core features of the new model. Those commitments must now become binding rules.

Any post-2029 finfish-aquaculture system in B.C. should meet three tests in order to ameliorate any environmental risks:

Farmed fish must be physically separated from wild salmon and their migration routes.

Solid waste must be captured and removed, not discharged into the marine environment.

Discharged water must be filtered or treated to prevent the transfer of viruses, bacteria and parasites to the marine environment, with transparent monitoring, public reporting and meaningful enforcement.

Without these standards, “closed containment” will become a label rather than a safeguard. If waste, sea lice or escaped fish can still meaningfully interact with wild salmon, the policy will have changed its terminology without adequately changing the risk.

A sound transition must also support people. Ottawa and Victoria should invest in worker retraining, economic diversification and Indigenous-led opportunities in coastal communities. Shellfish and seaweed aquaculture, alongside genuinely closed-containment finfish operations, can attract investment and sustain employment without recreating the central flaw of open-net pens.

The choice is not between the environment and the economy. It is whether commercial benefits remain concentrated among operators and shareholders while ecological risks are borne by wild salmon, Indigenous peoples, coastal communities and future generations.

If a business model depends on transferring its environmental costs to others, its owners and managers should expect that model to change. If the natural systems on which business and society depend are harmed, industry is behaving in an ethically irresponsible and economically irrational way: It transfers unpriced costs while eroding the basis for durable value creation.

Transition planning takes time. Endless dithering carries a cost, too. Each delayed deadline extends the status quo while wild salmon and the public bear risks that May be difficult – or impossible – to reverse.

Mr. Carney has argued that public policy must recognize values beyond price. Wild Pacific salmon are a test of whether that principle will be applied.

June 30, 2029, must be a deadline – not an opening bid for another delay.
paragraphs: Tony Allard is the chair of Wild Salmon Forever/Wild First.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has long argued that market prices fail to capture what societies most value : healthy ecosystems, natural abundance and the interests of future generations. British Columbia’s transition away from open-net-pen Atlantic salmon farms is an early test of whether his government will govern by that principle.

Open-net pens place farmed Atlantic salmon in the same coastal waters used by migrating wild Pacific salmon. They can create pathways for sea lice and pathogens, while releasing feed and waste into the marine environment.

While industry has argued that sea lice levels, for example, have not changed with salmon farm closures, the result is an unequal allocation of risk: operators receive commercial benefits, while wild salmon, Indigenous peoples, coastal communities and the public bear environmental costs.

Wild Pacific salmon are more than a commodity. They nourish ecosystems, sustain fisheries and tourism and remain central to Indigenous cultures, laws and economies. Their worth cannot be reduced to a dollar figure and set against one industry’s contribution to British Columbia’s economy. Not everything of value is fungible. There is a difference between what can be counted and what truly counts.

In 2019, Ottawa committed to develop a plan to transition B.C.’s salmon farms away from open-net pens. In June, 2024 , the federal government made the essential commitment: open-net-pen salmon aquaculture in B.C.’s coastal waters would be prohibited by June 30, 2029. Existing operators seeking renewed licences could receive five-year terms to facilitate that transition.

The transition is not theoretical. In February, 2023 , the federal fisheries minister refused to reissue licences for open-net salmon farms in the Discovery Islands, an important migration corridor for wild Pacific salmon.
In January, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld that decision, affirming the minister’s authority to take a precautionary, conservation-based approach where scientific uncertainty remains.
Now the Carney government must ensure that 2029 becomes an enforceable regulatory outcome, rather than a date softened or deferred as it approaches.

Mr. Carney has warned of the “ tragedy of the horizon ”: the temptation to delay action because the greatest consequences fall outside today’s political and economic time frames. This transition is precisely such a test.

The costs of change are immediate. Workers, farm operators and coastal communities face disruption and deserve a credible plan. But that is an argument for early planning, retraining and investment – not for prolonging a system that shifts risks onto wild salmon, Indigenous peoples and future generations.

Ottawa’s 2024 transition plan established the right direction. After July 1, 2024 , new applicants for salmon aquaculture in coastal B.C. would be considered only for marine or land-based closed-containment systems.
The government also identified waste removal and the treatment or filtration of discharged water as core features of the new model. Those commitments must now become binding rules.
Any post-2029 finfish-aquaculture system in B.C. should meet three tests in order to ameliorate any environmental risks:
Farmed fish must be physically separated from wild salmon and their migration routes.
Solid waste must be captured and removed, not discharged into the marine environment.

Discharged water must be filtered or treated to prevent the transfer of viruses, bacteria and parasites to the marine environment, with transparent monitoring, public reporting and meaningful enforcement.

Without these standards, “closed containment” will become a label rather than a safeguard. If waste, sea lice or escaped fish can still meaningfully interact with wild salmon, the policy will have changed its terminology without adequately changing the risk.

A sound transition must also support people. Ottawa and Victoria should invest in worker retraining, economic diversification and Indigenous-led opportunities in coastal communities. Shellfish and seaweed aquaculture, alongside genuinely closed-containment finfish operations, can attract investment and sustain employment without recreating the central flaw of open-net pens.

The choice is not between the environment and the economy. It is whether commercial benefits remain concentrated among operators and shareholders while ecological risks are borne by wild salmon, Indigenous peoples, coastal communities and future generations.

If a business model depends on transferring its environmental costs to others, its owners and managers should expect that model to change. If the natural systems on which business and society depend are harmed, industry is behaving in an ethically irresponsible and economically irrational way: It transfers unpriced costs while eroding the basis for durable value creation.

Transition planning takes time. Endless dithering carries a cost, too. Each delayed deadline extends the status quo while wild salmon and the public bear risks that May be difficult – or impossible – to reverse.
Mr. Carney has argued that public policy must recognize values beyond price. Wild Pacific salmon are a test of whether that principle will be applied.
June 30, 2029, must be a deadline – not an opening bid for another delay.

stories.title: Employers, job seekers increasingly using AI in the hiring process
stories.summary: As artificial intelligence becomes more common in recruiting, employers and job seekers are increasingly relying on the technology to gain an edge in the hiring process.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Jacqueline Hansen
stories.content:
Landing a job interview increasingly means navigating artificial intelligence, whether it’s helping write a resume, screening an application or even conducting an initial interview.

The growing use of AI in hiring comes as Canada’s job market remains challenging for many job seekers, prompting both employers and applicants to adopt new technology in an effort to gain an advantage.

Companies are using a range of AI-powered tools to sort through applications, evaluate candidates and streamline recruitment.

“Employers are using it to be able to help them manage their time. To help them rank, to help them sort, to help them summarize,” said Jason Murray, president and managing partner at executive recruitment firm BES Executive Search in Toronto.

Some technologies are even replacing traditional first-round interviews.

Toronto-based Ribbon has developed an AI-powered interviewing platform in which candidates interact with a conversational bot rather than a human recruiter.

Other platforms, such as Ottawa-based Knockri, rely on recorded interview questions and artificial intelligence to analyze candidate responses.

Knockri chief executive and co-founder Jahanzaib Ansari said the system is designed to identify aspects that predict success in a particular role.

“We’re looking for certain behaviors and skills that correlate to success predictors in that job role,” he said.

Ontario introduced new rules this year requiring employers to disclose when AI is being used to recruit or screen job candidates.

The requirement comes as references to AI in job postings have risen sharply across a wide range of occupations.

Supporters of AI hiring tools argue they can help reduce some forms of human bias by focusing on job-related competencies rather than subjective impressions.

Ansari said the technology is designed to avoid penalizing candidates for characteristics unrelated to job performance.

“I grew up with a terrible stutter. So that is not penalized,” he said.

But critics and some job seekers remain skeptical.

Complaints are common on professional networking sites such as LinkedIn, where candidates often speculate that automated systems rejected their applications before a human reviewed them.

Murray said the technology must be used carefully.

“Here we have technologies that can actually make us go backwards if we’re not using them correctly,” he said.

At the same time, job seekers are increasingly turning to AI tools of their own.

Some applications promise to help users prepare resumes, tailor cover letters and even generate interview answers in real time during virtual interviews.

Murray said new tools are emerging that could allow applicants to automate large portions of the job application process.

“There are a lot of AI technologies that are starting to pop up that will allow individuals to not be a part of their application process at all,” he said.

However, employers May view some uses of AI differently than others.

Ansari compared certain AI-assisted interview tools to using a calculator when independent thinking is expected.

“It’s like there is a particular time in an interview or an assessment, you want them to just use their brain and not the calculator,” he said.

As AI becomes more deeply embedded in recruitment, employers and candidates alike are weighing where to draw the line between embracing technology and relying on it too heavily.

Both sides appear to agree on one thing: AI is becoming an increasingly influential presence in the hiring process, and its role is likely to continue expanding.

stories.title: What is Regina-style pizza? Winnipeg Blue Bombers diss Saskatchewan dish ahead of Labour Day Classic
stories.summary: Playful trash talk ahead of the annual Labour Day Classic that will pit Winnipeg against Saskatchewan has left a bad taste in the mouths of some Roughriders fans.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Regina - Playful trash talk ahead of the annual Labour Day Classic that will pit Winnipeg against Saskatchewan has left a bad taste in the mouths of some Roughriders fans.

“It’s awful and our opinion will never change,” the post read.

Regina-style pizza is generally defined by its thickness and generous amounts of meat and cheese.

The Blue Bombers first went on record saying “Regina-style pizza is terrible,” back in 2023.

This week’s statement doubled down on the comments, comparing a slice of the pizza to three-week old lasagna that someone slapped onto a piece of dough.

“Finally, after three long years of reflection, we’d like to say it didn’t change anything. It’s still terrible,” the post read.

The words did not sit well with Jim Kolitsas, whose father and uncles invented the iconic dish for their restaurant more than 50 years ago.

“Winnipeg must be saying that because they are nervous about the game and going to lose on Sunday,” Kolitsas said.

There are four key elements to their Regina-style pizza, Kolitsas said.

It starts with fresh dough lathered with tangy tomato sauce then layered with a generous amount of meat. It ends with a mound of mozzarella cheese covering all the toppings and then baked until the dough is crispy on the outside and soft on the inside.

The thickness of each slice is a defining characteristic.

But Kolitsas believes the most distinctive innovation is placing the cheese on top to allow the mozzarella to caramelize.

“It just tastes good and that is why it became so popular,” Kolitsas said.

“We have seen it copied all across the province.”

The Kolitsas brothers originally from Greece first cooked up the idea of Regina-style pizza in 1970 when they opened up Houston Pizza in the city.

Before that, Kolitsas said pizza in the city was largely thin, light on flavour and lacked character.

“Pizza was not very popular then and if it was around, it was a different style,” he said.

These days, Regina-style pizza is synonymous with the Labour Day Classic, resulting in a surge of orders for Houston Pizza on game day.

Several other restaurants in the city have adopted the pizza style.

Western Pizza has been serving up the Regina dish since 1976.

The restaurant has four booths inside Mosaic Stadium – home of the Saskatchewan Roughriders – that sell Regina-style pizza by the slice at every game.

“We know we have the best pizza in Regina,” Western Pizza manager Mike Maroudis said.

“It is Saskatchewan pizza. Alberta and Manitoba do not have our style.”

Each restaurant in the city has its own variation of the Regina-style pizza. >> Each restaurant where? Chains of Houston pizza? Or in the prairies? (I’m talking about any pizza restaurant in Regina that serves this kind of pizza)

At Western Pizza, Maroudis says “lots of meats and lots of cheese” define the hearty pizza.

“It is almost like a deep dish,” he said.

Fans from both sides of the football feud seem to enjoy it, according to Maroudis.

Not only do their restaurants feed an influx of Winnipeg fans over the long weekend, Maroudis says Western Pizza typically gets a pizza order from the Blue Bombers after every Labour Day Classic.

“They love our pizza,” Maroudis said. “We know that for a fact.”

“Finally, after three long years of reflection, we’d like to say it didn’t change anything. It’s still terrible,” the post read.
The words did not sit well with Jim Kolitsas, whose father and uncles invented the iconic dish for their restaurant more than 50 years ago.
“Winnipeg must be saying that because they are nervous about the game and going to lose on Sunday,” Kolitsas said.
There are four key elements to their Regina-style pizza, Kolitsas said.

It starts with fresh dough lathered with tangy tomato sauce then layered with a generous amount of meat. It ends with a mound of mozzarella cheese covering all the toppings and then baked until the dough is crispy on the outside and soft on the inside.
The thickness of each slice is a defining characteristic.
But Kolitsas believes the most distinctive innovation is placing the cheese on top to allow the mozzarella to caramelize.
“It just tastes good and that is why it became so popular,” Kolitsas said.
“We have seen it copied all across the province.”
The Kolitsas brothers originally from Greece first cooked up the idea of Regina-style pizza in 1970 when they opened up Houston Pizza in the city.
Before that, Kolitsas said pizza in the city was largely thin, light on flavour and lacked character.
“Pizza was not very popular then and if it was around, it was a different style,” he said.
These days, Regina-style pizza is synonymous with the Labour Day Classic, resulting in a surge of orders for Houston Pizza on game day.
Several other restaurants in the city have adopted the pizza style.
Western Pizza has been serving up the Regina dish since 1976.
The restaurant has four booths inside Mosaic Stadium – home of the Saskatchewan Roughriders – that sell Regina-style pizza by the slice at every game.
“We know we have the best pizza in Regina,” Western Pizza manager Mike Maroudis said.
“It is Saskatchewan pizza. Alberta and Manitoba do not have our style.”

Each restaurant in the city has its own variation of the Regina-style pizza. >> Each restaurant where? Chains of Houston pizza? Or in the prairies? (I’m talking about any pizza restaurant in Regina that serves this kind of pizza)
At Western Pizza, Maroudis says “lots of meats and lots of cheese” define the hearty pizza.
“It is almost like a deep dish,” he said.
Fans from both sides of the football feud seem to enjoy it, according to Maroudis.
Not only do their restaurants feed an influx of Winnipeg fans over the long weekend, Maroudis says Western Pizza typically gets a pizza order from the Blue Bombers after every Labour Day Classic.
“They love our pizza,” Maroudis said. “We know that for a fact.”

stories.title: Canada’s tariffs are coming for Michigan — and it's not just auto plants that will feel the pain
stories.summary: Trade talks remain stalled, and Canada’s new duties on U.S. goods could squeeze Michigan suppliers and wholesalers first, before consumers.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Unless Washington and Ottawa change course, Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on more than 700 U.S. products entering Canada — covering CA$27.6 billion in annual imports — are scheduled to take effect Tuesday.

The duties, ranging from 15 to 50 per cent, come as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that “there are no negotiations happening on trade right now.” A source close to the Canadian side said on Friday that no talks were underway.

The Canadian duties would cover a broad range of vehicle-related goods, including a 25 per cent tariff on trailers and semi-trailers, as well as higher duties on steel, aluminum and industrial inputs used in automotive and equipment manufacturing. The U.S. measures raise costs for Canadian goods entering the United States; Canada’s retaliation does the same for selected U.S. goods entering Canada.

Analysts say the Canadian package is broader in scope than the U.S. measures it answers.

“The actual tariffs imposed by the United States were really a list of annoyances,” said Patrick Anderson, CEO of Lansing-based Anderson Economic Group. “The Canadian tariffs appear to be much more pervasive… Canada’s reaction here has been both rhetorically and substantively significantly larger than what the U.S. actually imposed.”

Several U.S. states will feel the impact, including Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Texas, and Maine, but Michigan could take the hardest hit, analysts say. The mitten-shaped state is most exposed because it ships about $1.5 billion in tariff-listed products to Canada each year. Canada was the destination for 36 per cent of Michigan’s goods exports in 2025, according to U.S. trade data, and motor vehicles and auto parts accounted for a large share of that.

“Michigan is the single largest auto parts exporter to Canada,” said Jason Miller, a supply chain management expert and professor at Michigan State University, noting that “the auto parts suppliers in Michigan who are exporting to those plants are going to be hurt.”

A Republican senator could be one of the first political victims of Trump's tariff war

Harley-Davidson becomes unlikely flashpoint in Canada-U.S. trade war

“The Detroit metro area writ large is about the most export-dense manufacturing area to Canada of anywhere in the country,” he added.

“The worst affected province would be Ontario, and the worst affected states would be Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Texas,” Anderson predicted.

Analysts and industry groups say the earliest pain May show up not on factory payrolls but in wholesale margins and inventory decisions.

“Everybody’s focusing on manufacturing, but there are so many jobs in the wholesaling side of imported products,” Miller said, noting that he’s curious about “Michigan wholesalers getting caught up in this and being negatively affected.”

Drew Beardslee, the vice president of government affairs at the Michigan Retailers Association, says the earliest impacts will be on wholesale margins and inventory decisions, with consumers seeing effects within a quarter.

“Like when you grab a rope and sort of lift up on it, you can watch it travel down the rope. And so I think it sort of travels through the supply chain that way in terms of where the cost is,” Beardslee explained, using the rope imagery to liken how the duty is paid at entry and then moves through the importer, wholesaler, retailer, and then, often, to the consumer.

Canadian importers would pay the duty when covered U.S. goods enter Canada. They could absorb the cost, pass it along to wholesalers, retailers, and consumers, demand price concessions from U.S. suppliers, or replace those suppliers, depending on contracts and market dynamics.

Businesses were already grappling with thin margins and uncertainty caused by shifting U.S. trade policy. Tariff changes have caused a whiplash effect for everyone involved in trade this past year — from importers and retailers to consumers and customs officials. It’s been hard to keep up, but not knowing the tariff levels from one week to the next makes business planning incredibly difficult.

“The cost associated with tariffs was bad enough, but the inconsistency with which they were applied made it so hard to guess what to do,” said Beardslee. “What they’re looking for more than anything is some more consistency and certainty.”

Beardslee pointed out that grocery margins are already just two to three per cent and that 73 per cent of respondents to a Michigan Retailers Association member survey reported that tariffs have already “had a negative or strong negative impact” on them since April 2025.

Further duties mean wholesalers could be “squeezed dramatically,” Anderson said, ON contracts already signed. Smaller distributors, meanwhile, have “much less room to manoeuvre” and less influence to seek exemptions.

The uncertainty also makes it hard for businesses to react to everything that’s happening, stymying both positive and negative planning decisions.

“Expansion plans get put on hold when uncertainty is high,” said Miller. “But believe it or not, layoff plans also get put on hold when uncertainty is high.

“I think especially for companies in Maine, in Michigan, in Wisconsin, northern Minnesota, where there’s a lot of cross-border business involved, what you’re going to have right now is a freezing of decisions.”

Believe it or not, layoff plans also get put on hold when uncertainty is high

Given the time of year, Beardslee pointed to tariff volatility impacting retailers and distributors of back-to-school products as an example. Prices are already up on common school items, such as shoes, pencils, crayons, binders, and folders, he said, comparing tariff collections and effective tariff rates from March through June of this year to 2025.

“Those kinds of products are one area where you’d expect to see more (price increases),” he said. “Our retailers are trying to source things months in advance, so when that effective tariff rate is changing constantly, it could very well be that when an order is placed that there was no effective tariff rate on it, but by the time it arrives, there is.”

Anderson agreed and noted that there is a bigger risk to long-term trade between Michigan and Canada.

Some retailers, he said, “May just decide it’s too much trouble to stock them when they can get cheaper goods from China and Vietnam.”

Owing to the negative tenor of trade politics between the two countries, not to mention the unhelpful renaming of Lake Ontario, distributors and retailers May already be looking for new suppliers, he said.

“Unfortunately, raising the rhetorical temperature… makes business people start thinking really hard about finding other places to get their goods,” said Anderson.

“So unfortunately, some of the damage here is already done.”

stories.title: SuperDogs lap up the love, 50 years after being unleashed on adoring fans
stories.summary: Vancouver - Lisa Sun recalls watching the SuperDogs at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver as many times as she could as a kid, delighting in the performers' speed, skill and comic relief.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Lisa Sun recalls watching the SuperDogs at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver as many times as she could as a kid, delighting in the performers’ speed, skill and comic relief.

Now it’s Sun and her three pugs, Mario, Luigi and Yoshi, who are entertaining crowds at the fair, 50 years after it hosted the first SuperDogs show.

Their role? “Definitely comedy,” Sun said.

“When they come out onstage, people know they’re not going to be the fastest.... But you know what? They have personality, they have character.”

The crowd-favourite SuperDogs bring generations together in a brief break from everyday life at Vancouver’s Pacific National Exhibition, where the show began 50 years ago in 1976. (Sept. 5, 2026)

Sun’s pugs wear sparkly pink bandanas as they perform their tricks. They twirl left and right in unison, and stand on their hind legs to give each other what she calls a “pug hug.”

The pugs are among hundreds of canines from across Canada, many of them rescues from humane societies and animal shelters, that have been part of the SuperDogs shows, which are also held at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto.

While some trainers and their dogs travel for shows, most are local and return to their family homes each night after delighting crowds that can number in the thousands.

David Acer, a writer and host for the show in Vancouver, describes SuperDogs as “pure joy from beginning to end,” helping fans let their troubles go for a moment.

“It’s really among the only entertainment I’ve been a part of where I can look in the stands and see a five-year-old, a 20-year-old and a 70-year-old all laughing at the same thing,” he said following a SuperDogs performance on Thursday.

“I think every generation is feeling the pressure and the stress of the current climate, and this is an opportunity for them to come and not feel that together.”

SuperDogs lore tells of the show’s beginnings at the PNE in August 1976, when Herb Williams, a former teacher and advertising executive-turned entertainer, recruited a handful of dogs to perform tricks for fairgoers in a parking lot.

Fifty years later, SuperDogs holds three shows a day for audiences at the PNE and the CNE. The two fairs close on Monday.

The shows feature dogs small and large racing, catching Frisbees, leaping over hurdles, and weaving in and out of obstacles. Afterwards, the audience is invited to “pat and chat,” an opportunity to meet the dogs and their trainers.

Acer said the canine performers are all “super” in different ways.

“Some of them are super athletic, some of them are super smart, some of them are super cute, some of them are super fast,” he said.

“We actually think every dog is a super dog, so if you have a dog at time, (there’s) something that makes them super too.”

Still, certain dogs have exuded stand-out star power, landing them in the inaugural “Paws of Fame” class to mark the 50th anniversary of SuperDogs.

They include the “slowest SuperDog ever,” an English bulldog named Pot Roast who performed between 1992 and 1998, and Demolition Derby, an old English sheepdog described as “a big, lovable buffoon who introduced true comedy” to the show.

Sun’s first-generation trio of pugs, Snap, Crackle and Pop, were also among the 20 honourees, along with Flint, a collie who also served as a search-and-rescue dog with the Calgary Fire Department.

It’s gratifying “knowing how many hearts melt when they see these pug faces and how much joy they bring,” said Sun, who has worked with SuperDogs for 15 years.

Sun said the show offers a lighthearted distraction and a break from everyday worries, inspiring cheers and laughs from generations of fans.

“For that half hour you’re sitting in the audience, you’re not thinking about anything else but watching the dogs do their comedy, do their athleticism, do their Frisbee playing, do their dancing onstage, their racing relays,” she said.

“It’s such a blessing to be on the other side now,” Sun added. “Running with the dogs, ON the stage, doing the thing that I used to love to watch as a kid.”

Sun said dog owners shouldn’t underestimate their own canine companions.

“Always look at the dog in front of you,” she said. “They’re each individuals that can learn so many things.”

The website for the group Suite Melody Care, which brings young musicians into hospitals and care homes, lists Williams, who is in his 90s and lives in Ontario, as one of its directors. He made his final SuperDogs appearance in 2012.

The site says Williams and his SuperDogs entertained audiences that have included British royals and celebrities such as Joan Rivers and Luciano Pavarotti.

After the PNE and CNE close, the SuperDogs will be at fall fairs in Burns Lake, B.C.; Rock Creek, B.C.; Uxbridge, Ont.; and at a dog-focused event in Newmarket, Ont.

Ultimately, Acer said SuperDogs encourages people to love their dogs.

“If people go home after seeing a SuperDogs show and give their dog one more hug, one more treat, throw a Frisbee for them, it’s a win for everybody.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Reader to Reader: September 5, 2026
stories.summary: A Free Press reader who now lives in Germany, sends thanks to the Londoner who helped their son during an incident in 2024.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
A Free Press reader who now lives in Germany, sends thanks to the Londoner who helped their son during an incident in 2024.

Were you walking your dog, possibly a German shepherd, ON Friday, Sept. 20, 2024 around 10 a.m. or 11 a.m. near the Dollarama in Pond Mills, close to Sir Wilfrid Laurier secondary school? Did you happen upon a swarm of about eight to 10 youth beating a hapless teen on the ground while holding his friend back and had the incredible courage to disrupt them? If this is you, or you know who this might be, we want to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Our son suffered a concussion, but it could have been much worse without your intervention, since at least one of the perpetrators continued stomping on his head while he already was lying on the ground.

Unfortunately, it has taken this long for us to come to terms with the incident and to write this letter. We don’t know who you are and will never be able to thank you enough, but please know your brave intervention saved his life. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

K. Sugar-Holder, Germany

Vining Cemetery, at 22157 Purple Hill Rd., will have its annual decoration day on Sunday. Donations to assist with the upkeep of the cemetery are always welcomed. Send a cheque made payable to Vining Cemetery to L.D. Monteith, trustee and treasurer at 34542 Granton Line, Granton ON N0M 1V0

L.D. Monteith, Granton

London Sweet Adeline Chorus invites women of all ages to guest night Wednesday from 6:45 to 9 p.m. at the Church of Ascension, 2060 Dundas St. E.

Email to register: londonchorussa@gmail.com , but walk-ins are welcome. Perhaps you are not available to attend Sept. 9, but wish to join on another Wednesday evening. No problem, just email us in advance.

Cathy Pickering, London

Free bridge lessons for seniors start Thursday. Call Jim at 519-657-6264 for details.

Frank Pontarelli, London

Indoor yard and bake sale, Saturday, Sept. 12, 9 a.m. to noon at Rowntree Memorial United Church, 156 Elliott St. (at Cheapside). Participating in Carling Neighbourhood Yard Sale.

Maryjane Jolliffe, Rowntree ­Memorial United Church fundraising committee

Do you have photos tucked away in bags or boxes throughout your house? Let’s change that. Whether you want to create a scrapbook for a family vacation, a new baby, a wedding, or your child’s school memories, this free beginner-friendly class will help you create lasting memories to share with loved ones. Two class times available: Saturday, Sept. 12 or Sunday, Sept. 13, both at 1 p.m. Reserve your spot and free scrapbook kit by emailing rjguillemette24@gmail.com .

Robin Guillemette, London

An introductory session for people considering learning to play bridge Saturday, Sept. 19, 9:30 to 11:30 a.m. at London Bridge Centre, at 1206 Dearness Dr., unit 9. No experience necessary. There is no fee, but registration is required.

Graeme Tindale, g_tindale@hotmail.com

The Rotary Club of London-Hyde Park will host two all-candidates meetings on Sept. 22 at 7 p.m. for wards 7 and 8 and Sept. 29 at 7 p.m. for mayoral candidates at West Haven Golf and Country Club, 7038 Egremont Dr.

Free, but please register at hydeparkrotary.org

Barbara Robins, Rotary Club of London-Hyde Park

Barbecue chicken dinner, Wednesday, Sept. 16, at St. George’s Anglican Church, 172 King St., Thorndale.

Drive-thru takeout between 4:30 and 6:30 p.m. Adult meals include half chicken, coleslaw, baked potato with sour cream, dinner roll with butter and ­dessert.

Tickets: adults $25, children younger than 12 $15, by calling Laurie at 519-461-1901 or Ed at 519-461-1936.

Jeffrey McDonald, Thorndale

The London Singers Community Choir is looking for new members for our 27th concert season. Our first rehearsal is Sept. 23 at 7 p.m. at St. Aidan’s Church, 1246 Oxford St. W. Come early to register. If you can read music, love a challenge and want to meet some great singers and wonderful people, please call 519-852-0916 and/or email TheLondonSingers@gmail.com and we will send you more information.

Darien Fraher, chairperson, board of directors, The London Singers and Orchestra

Reader to Reader runs every second week in The London Free Press. Reader to Reader helps readers connect with one another. You can pay tribute, give thanks, look for an out-of-print book, search for a long-lost friend or family member.

E-mail your letter to: lfp.letters@sunmedia.CA (no attachments please) and include “Reader” in the subject line. Or go to lfpress.com/letters and choose Letters to the Editor topic.

The next Reader to Reader runs September 19. The deadline is September 14.

content_blocks.text: A Free Press reader who now lives in Germany, sends thanks to the Londoner who helped their son during an incident in 2024.
Gratitude endures

Were you walking your dog, possibly a German shepherd, ON Friday, Sept. 20, 2024 around 10 a.m. or 11 a.m. near the Dollarama in Pond Mills, close to Sir Wilfrid Laurier secondary school? Did you happen upon a swarm of about eight to 10 youth beating a hapless teen on the ground while holding his friend back and had the incredible courage to disrupt them? If this is you, or you know who this might be, we want to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Our son suffered a concussion, but it could have been much worse without your intervention, since at least one of the perpetrators continued stomping on his head while he already was lying on the ground.

Unfortunately, it has taken this long for us to come to terms with the incident and to write this letter. We don’t know who you are and will never be able to thank you enough, but please know your brave intervention saved his life. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
K. Sugar-Holder, Germany

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: September 5, 2026
stories.summary: Free Press readers sound off on the topics of the day, including former London councillors, Donald Trump and Canadian Parliament.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced his intention to address the European Parliament.

Carney recently implied Canada walked away from trade talks with the U.S. because of demands impinged on our sovereignty.

However, Carney has to decide if he is prime minister of Canada or of Europe.

If Carney is prime minister of Canada, his first parliamentary talk should be in Ottawa, to the people of Canada.

Canadians need full transparency regarding recent events such as the rewriting of the original Gordie Howe Bridge agreement and the collapse of the recent trade talks. Only then can the government be held accountable. We cannot be blindly playing follow the leader.

Press conferences and social media posts should not be replacing the scrutiny of Parliament.

Gordon Smith, London

According to Statistics Canada, this city has seen its per-household income drop from near best in the country to near worst during two generations. This is not happenstance. It was the result of ineptitude. And some of it happened on their watch. Past councils, including those of Joe Fontana, thought money grows on trees. It doesn’t. It grows on the type of productive industries that these councils refused to bring into the city. One wonders if these candidates have learned their lessons and plan on making London a thriving industrial centre.

David Nielsen, London

LFP Letters to the Editor: September 4, 2026

LFP Letters to the Editor: September 3, 2026

The London and Middlesex Local Immigration Partnership asked 387 newcomers to rate their own lives and jobs. The answers point in different directions.

On life satisfaction and belonging, men and women rated themselves within half a point of each other, ON a seven-point scale. That gap is there, but small.

On employment, the same people answered differently. Men were far more likely to work full-time (67.5 per cent), while women were more likely to work part-time or be unemployed and looking for work. Among women, 37.4 per cent held jobs needing no formal education, above the survey-wide average of 26.8 per cent, even though more than 60 per cent of respondents hold a university degree.

A job that wastes someone’s training is a number worth ­noticing.

Tristan Johnson, London and Middlesex Local Immigration Partnership

The U.S. national debt has now topped $40.1 trillion. It would take $117,000 from every living American to rid themselves of their national debt. If the U.S. Treasury was a business, would you invest?

What makes the current U.S. administration believe any responsible Canadian would willingly tie their horse to that wagon? It defies logic that a country paying $1 trillion a year in interest payments on their debt, would knowingly alienate themselves from their largest trading partner, ally and closest neighbour.

Although there are clearly economic implications for Canadians (at least in the short term), the position taken by Canada to reject the negotiating tactics deployed by the current U.S. administration was, unfortunately, the only plausible outcome.

Lake America? Please. Let’s treat the most recent executive order as if it has the same force and effect as it would over my signature, and give it zero airtime.

Chris Symons, London

The Mouse That Roared, by Leonard Wibberly, 1955, is the first in a series of comedic novels which chronicles the defeat of America by the Duchy of Fenwick, a tiny, fictional European nation with an “army of 20 men armed with longbows and chain mail.”

The sequel being written today will be The Sweet Guy Who Spoke Quietly, by Mark Carney, 2026, armed with nothing but his word.

The failure of the Americans to negotiate a deal with Canada, Canada of all peoples, has to be embarrassing, even for U.S. President Donald Trump.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

stories.title: Her son was 'caged' for 5 years. Video of his life in isolation at this Ontario hospital left her 'absolutely, completely horrified'
stories.summary: Jake Gordon now slowly being released from seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. His mom credits the Star's ongoing investigation for the change.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
Jake Gordon walks around his tiny room in circles.

The room is about twice the length of the six-foot-three man. He’s locked inside.

There’s a mat on the floor and a toilet. Dressed in his pyjamas, he paces, tries to lie down, crouches in a corner, and occasionally looks out the window. At one point, his door is opened slightly, and a plate of food is delivered; he eats it sitting on his mat.

The surveillance footage goes on for six-and-a-half hours, offering a rare glimpse into the life of a seriously mentally ill patient being held in seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, Ont.

Gordon, a 30-year-old Toronto man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, lived in isolation at Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital for five years. His mother, who is also his substitute decision-maker, shared the surveillance footage with the Star, believing the public needs to see what is happening inside the walls of the facility.

Diane Worden received the footage at the end of last month, the first time she had been able to see for herself her son’s living conditions. She wasn’t sure she could get through watching all of it.

“I was absolutely, completely horrified,” Worden said.

“He’s been in that teeny, tiny room, caged like an animal. And to think that’s been happening for five years. It’s sickening.”

The video is from August 2025, about a year before significant changes were made to Gordon’s care at Waypoint, leading to his release from seclusion just last month.

The hospital has always refused to divulge the number of people in long-term seclusion, but it’s understood to be at least a dozen. Aside from Gordon, it was revealed during an unrelated Ontario Review Board hearing last month that there are another 11 secluded patients in a different unit.

During his time in isolation, Gordon didn’t shower regularly, his teeth rotted, he gained weight and developed trouble walking. And he seriously injured his eye in an incident for which Worden is still seeking details.

In her opinion, her son ended up sicker than ever.

But on the heels of the Star’s coverage, Gordon started spending an increasing amount of time out of seclusion and out of restraints; he was being taken to the canteen and into the courtyard; he was seen by a dentist and an optometrist; he was being given access to music more often; and he was showering again.

And then last month, the hospital told Worden that her son was getting a new psychiatrist and they were ending his time in seclusion altogether.

“These sudden, sweeping changes are no coincidence. It is a direct result of your reporting and the pressure from advocates,” Worden said.

“Every week that goes by, something has changed; they’re just more involved with him than they’ve ever been.”

When she went to visit her son last month, he was not only now walking again, but dancing.

“He’s smiling; he tells me how beautiful I am,” Worden said. “He’s not the person he was, but he’s getting closer.”

The other patient whose seclusion is set to come to an end after five years is Andrew Azevedo, a 39-year-old man who also has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and was profiled in the Star in April . His Waypoint psychiatrist, Dr. Achal Mishra, revealed at Azevedo’s Ontario Review Board hearing on Aug. 20 that he was within days or a few weeks of being released from seclusion. The hospital has since told Azevedo’s family that the plan is to de-seclude him in mid-September.

Mishra denied that the Star’s investigation was the “impetus” for changes to his patient’s care, while acknowledging that “of course it impacted Waypoint, it was not something we would ignore.”

Waypoint’s CEO, Dr. Nadiya Sunderji, declined to comment on Gordon’s case as she said the hospital is bound by patient confidentiality requirements. She said no directive has been issued to release more patients from seclusion.

“The discontinuation of seclusion for an individual patient is a clinical decision made by health care professionals based on that patient’s individual circumstances,” Sunderji said. “Waypoint follows a least-restraint philosophy and is committed to ending the use of seclusion and restraint whenever it is safe and clinically appropriate.”

Waypoint has said that patients in seclusion continue to receive mental health treatment and are escorted out of their rooms for periods of time “when clinically appropriate and safe.” Depending on their care and safety plan, patients May have access in their rooms to items including a TV, reading materials and puzzles, as well as the ability to make phone and video calls.

Reached by the Star, the chair of the hospital’s board, Steve Parry, backed the hospital’s leadership in response to questions about the damning assessment in the Azevedo case prepared by Andrea Monteiro, who previously held senior roles in the correctional system. Sunderji had previously said the facility “categorically” disagrees with Monteiro’s opinion regarding torture.

Parry said he was “fully aligned” with Sunderji’s comments.

‘I knew nothing about Waypoint’

Jake Gordon was a quiet but happy child growing up in the West Hill neighbourhood of Scarborough. He had a “wonderful circle of friends,” his mother recalled, and loved playing hockey.

His family started noticing changes in his behaviour toward the end of high school, around 2013. He had trouble sleeping, fell out with some of his friends and couldn’t get out of bed to do his exams. He was diagnosed with social anxiety and depression, and ultimately bipolar disorder.

What followed after high school graduation was a series of hospitalizations, including at St. Michael’s Hospital following a car accident in 2015, where he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. His aggression became worse: he would have confrontations with hospital security and was frequently placed in restraints. Improvement from medication was never long-lasting, leading to a recognition that Gordon’s illness was treatment-resistant.

In between hospitalizations, he was living at home with his parents and brother. Sometimes he wouldn’t leave the house for weeks. But one night in the winter of 2018, he went outside with no coat or shoes and ended up getting into a tow truck to keep warm. He then drove away with it to get cigarettes.

His mother recalled he was apprehended by the police and taken to court, where, she said, it was recognized he was “very ill.” The case ended there without going any further; Gordon was released into his mother’s care, and she took him straight to the hospital.

Despite his challenges, Gordon kept up with his hockey practice.

“The one thing he lived for was his hockey,” Worden said. “He would take his equipment and get on the bus and go on his own. He absolutely loved it.

“When manic, he would literally be in the driveway for eight hours shooting pucks.”

After his condition deteriorated at a local hospital, the decision was made to send Gordon to Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby in 2020.

Gordon had a “phenomenal team” at Ontario Shores, Worden said, but he ended up assaulting another patient and a nurse, and was charged in relation to the latter. He received a conditional discharge — meaning probation and no criminal record.

In the wake of the assaults, Gordon was sent to Waypoint in January 2021. He’s been there ever since.

She said that the team at Ontario Shores had assured her the transfer would be temporary — “That Waypoint would have the ability to change Jake’s behaviour and to manage him better.”

His life in seclusion — ‘He worsened’

Unlike other patients in prolonged seclusion at Waypoint, Gordon is not there because of involvement in the criminal justice system. He’s not been found unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible, and he has no charges hanging over him.

He’s being held at Waypoint involuntarily under the Mental Health Act; his involuntary admission is renewed by a doctor every three months after concluding that he poses a serious risk of bodily harm to himself and others.

Involuntary admission can be indefinite. Lawyer Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who is not representing Gordon and his family, said that once involuntary admission is renewed, a patient can challenge it before the Consent and Capacity Board, whose three-member panels are made up of a medical professional, lawyer and layperson.

The board must also hold a mandatory review of the patient’s case every year, where the patient can ask for orders such as a transfer to another facility, but the board tends to be quite conservative — “Rarely is substantial relief granted in favour of the patient,” Szigeti said.

Worden said she plans to start attending her son’s board hearings. She said he’s been held in seclusion since his arrival at Waypoint in 2021, with the hospital saying it’s due to a mix of aggressive behaviour, self-harming and psychotic episodes, but she said his 83,000-page clinical file shows he sometimes went weeks with no concerns being noted.

“He didn’t transition well; it was very traumatic for him to be plucked out of Ontario Shores and put into Waypoint,” Worden said. “He worsened.”

She told the Star she understands that her son has been placed in different rooms during his time in seclusion at Waypoint, and it’s not clear if the one seen on video from 2025 is typical.

The room looks somewhat like segregation cells in prisons, said former federal correctional investigator Howard Sapers.

“But in many ways, it is more spartan,” he said in an email.

A segregation cell would usually have a raised bunk, not a mat on the floor, as well as something to sit on, like a fixed bench, Sapers said.

Around the time he arrived at Waypoint, Gordon began experiencing extrapyramidal symptoms — violent involuntary movements commonly caused by antipsychotic medications.

His mother describes them as seizures, causing Gordon’s eyes to roll to the back of his head and his throat to close, making it difficult to breathe — “It’s very painful.”

She became concerned about Gordon’s well-being at Waypoint: If he was locked in seclusion, how would staff know he was having a seizure in order to quickly administer medication to bring the symptoms under control, as well as to stop Gordon from sticking his fingers in his eyes, as he was prone to do?

Staff assured her that the room was being recorded on video and that Gordon, like all patients in seclusion, was being checked on by a staff member every 15 minutes.

“Well, in 15 minutes, the seizure could be horrific,” Worden said.

In her independent assessment filed in the Azevedo case, Monteiro concluded that these 15-minute check-ins are conducted like “security rounds” in prisons, where a staff member looks into the room and May or May not engage with the patient.

Worden’s worst fear came true in August of last year when her son caused what doctors would later describe as “extensive trauma” to his eye with his fingers. Although she initially believed it was due to the seizures, Worden said it appears to have been the result of a psychotic episode, based on her review of Waypoint’s medical notes.

“There are several notes stating he was screaming throughout the day, which is entirely uncharacteristic of him,” she said.

He was taken to Georgian Bay General Hopsital that evening; Worden said she first found out about the incident the next morning from Georgian Bay, not Waypoint.

The prognosis for his eye is “guarded,” Worden said; she said Gordon could have double vision for the rest of his life.

She asked Waypoint for footage from Aug. 21, 2025, capturing the incident, as well as the 24 hours leading up to it. The hospital responded that due to the passage of time, only a portion of the footage from Aug. 21 — totalling six-and-a-half hours — had been retained, and parts of it were redacted before being given to Worden.

The incident is not captured in the footage provided. Worden is continuing to push the facility for answers.

“I am determined to find out how this horrific self-harm could have happened when staff were supposed to be monitoring him every 15 minutes,” she said.

A mom’s search for accountability

Much like the family of Andrew Azevedo, Worden was worried that the hospital might be moving too quickly when they informed her last month that her son’s seclusion was being terminated. She asked them to go slowly.

“They agreed to start with just a few hours out a day, and so far, everything seems to be going well,” she said.

She said she doesn’t believe the improvement can solely be attributed to any medication changes, given Gordon’s poor response to many different drugs in the past; she believes the effort the hospital is now putting into his care plan has made a major difference. She also believes the staff truly care for her son and May have been advocating for change from within.

He’s not the person he was, but he’s getting closer.

But there’s more work to be done. Her goal now is for her son to become well enough that he can be transferred to a facility closer to home, like going back to Ontario Shores.

“There’s no question Jake is too sick to come home,” Worden said.

And she wants to see some accountability from the hospital’s leadership and Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“It feels like they have become so desensitized to this,” Worden said. “Thank goodness there has been all this public outcry.”

“This is undeniably a systemic crisis,” she said. “How is it that the CEO can allow this to happen at her facility? She makes like $700,000 a year.” (According to the Sunshine List, Sunderji, who has served as CEO since 2022, saw her salary increase last year from just under $400,000 to $658,000.)

Jones’s office has never responded to questions from the Star regarding seclusion at Waypoint. Under provincial law, Jones has the power to impose directives on the hospital’s board or order that inspectors conduct a review of Waypoint’s operations.

“I think she needs to answer your questions, I think she needs to be accountable to the people who have family there and tell us what’s going to happen in the future,” Worden said.

“Sylvia’s my age. What if it was one of hers? Would she allow this to happen?”
paragraphs: Jake Gordon walks around his tiny room in circles.
The room is about twice the length of the six-foot-three man. He’s locked inside.

There’s a mat on the floor and a toilet. Dressed in his pyjamas, he paces, tries to lie down, crouches in a corner, and occasionally looks out the window. At one point, his door is opened slightly, and a plate of food is delivered; he eats it sitting on his mat.

The surveillance footage goes on for six-and-a-half hours, offering a rare glimpse into the life of a seriously mentally ill patient being held in seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, Ont.

Gordon, a 30-year-old Toronto man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, lived in isolation at Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital for five years. His mother, who is also his substitute decision-maker, shared the surveillance footage with the Star, believing the public needs to see what is happening inside the walls of the facility.
Diane Worden received the footage at the end of last month, the first time she had been able to see for herself her son’s living conditions. She wasn’t sure she could get through watching all of it.
“I was absolutely, completely horrified,” Worden said.
“He’s been in that teeny, tiny room, caged like an animal. And to think that’s been happening for five years. It’s sickening.”
The video is from August 2025, about a year before significant changes were made to Gordon’s care at Waypoint, leading to his release from seclusion just last month.

The hospital has always refused to divulge the number of people in long-term seclusion, but it’s understood to be at least a dozen. Aside from Gordon, it was revealed during an unrelated Ontario Review Board hearing last month that there are another 11 secluded patients in a different unit.

During his time in isolation, Gordon didn’t shower regularly, his teeth rotted, he gained weight and developed trouble walking. And he seriously injured his eye in an incident for which Worden is still seeking details.
In her opinion, her son ended up sicker than ever.

But on the heels of the Star’s coverage, Gordon started spending an increasing amount of time out of seclusion and out of restraints; he was being taken to the canteen and into the courtyard; he was seen by a dentist and an optometrist; he was being given access to music more often; and he was showering again.
And then last month, the hospital told Worden that her son was getting a new psychiatrist and they were ending his time in seclusion altogether.
“These sudden, sweeping changes are no coincidence. It is a direct result of your reporting and the pressure from advocates,” Worden said.
“Every week that goes by, something has changed; they’re just more involved with him than they’ve ever been.”
When she went to visit her son last month, he was not only now walking again, but dancing.
“He’s smiling; he tells me how beautiful I am,” Worden said. “He’s not the person he was, but he’s getting closer.”

The other patient whose seclusion is set to come to an end after five years is Andrew Azevedo, a 39-year-old man who also has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and was profiled in the Star in April . His Waypoint psychiatrist, Dr. Achal Mishra, revealed at Azevedo’s Ontario Review Board hearing on Aug. 20 that he was within days or a few weeks of being released from seclusion. The hospital has since told Azevedo’s family that the plan is to de-seclude him in mid-September.
Mishra denied that the Star’s investigation was the “impetus” for changes to his patient’s care, while acknowledging that “of course it impacted Waypoint, it was not something we would ignore.”

Waypoint’s CEO, Dr. Nadiya Sunderji, declined to comment on Gordon’s case as she said the hospital is bound by patient confidentiality requirements. She said no directive has been issued to release more patients from seclusion.

“The discontinuation of seclusion for an individual patient is a clinical decision made by health care professionals based on that patient’s individual circumstances,” Sunderji said. “Waypoint follows a least-restraint philosophy and is committed to ending the use of seclusion and restraint whenever it is safe and clinically appropriate.”

Waypoint has said that patients in seclusion continue to receive mental health treatment and are escorted out of their rooms for periods of time “when clinically appropriate and safe.” Depending on their care and safety plan, patients May have access in their rooms to items including a TV, reading materials and puzzles, as well as the ability to make phone and video calls.

Reached by the Star, the chair of the hospital’s board, Steve Parry, backed the hospital’s leadership in response to questions about the damning assessment in the Azevedo case prepared by Andrea Monteiro, who previously held senior roles in the correctional system. Sunderji had previously said the facility “categorically” disagrees with Monteiro’s opinion regarding torture.
Parry said he was “fully aligned” with Sunderji’s comments.
‘I knew nothing about Waypoint’
Jake Gordon was a quiet but happy child growing up in the West Hill neighbourhood of Scarborough. He had a “wonderful circle of friends,” his mother recalled, and loved playing hockey.

His family started noticing changes in his behaviour toward the end of high school, around 2013. He had trouble sleeping, fell out with some of his friends and couldn’t get out of bed to do his exams. He was diagnosed with social anxiety and depression, and ultimately bipolar disorder.

What followed after high school graduation was a series of hospitalizations, including at St. Michael’s Hospital following a car accident in 2015, where he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. His aggression became worse: he would have confrontations with hospital security and was frequently placed in restraints. Improvement from medication was never long-lasting, leading to a recognition that Gordon’s illness was treatment-resistant.

In between hospitalizations, he was living at home with his parents and brother. Sometimes he wouldn’t leave the house for weeks. But one night in the winter of 2018, he went outside with no coat or shoes and ended up getting into a tow truck to keep warm. He then drove away with it to get cigarettes.

His mother recalled he was apprehended by the police and taken to court, where, she said, it was recognized he was “very ill.” The case ended there without going any further; Gordon was released into his mother’s care, and she took him straight to the hospital.
Despite his challenges, Gordon kept up with his hockey practice.
“The one thing he lived for was his hockey,” Worden said. “He would take his equipment and get on the bus and go on his own. He absolutely loved it.
“When manic, he would literally be in the driveway for eight hours shooting pucks.”
After his condition deteriorated at a local hospital, the decision was made to send Gordon to Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby in 2020.

Gordon had a “phenomenal team” at Ontario Shores, Worden said, but he ended up assaulting another patient and a nurse, and was charged in relation to the latter. He received a conditional discharge — meaning probation and no criminal record.
In the wake of the assaults, Gordon was sent to Waypoint in January 2021. He’s been there ever since.
She said that the team at Ontario Shores had assured her the transfer would be temporary — “That Waypoint would have the ability to change Jake’s behaviour and to manage him better.”

Involuntary admission can be indefinite.
