stories.title: As Donald Trump’s trade war rages, Mark Carney looks to the European Union — and it’s looking back
stories.summary: While the U.S. president makes angry social media posts and changes the name of Lake Ontario, Ottawa is trying to shift the historical southward focus of Canada’s economy.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
Canada and Europe are having a moment. The timing could not be better.

With the Canada-U.S. trading relationship moving from aggression to open hostility, Foreign Minister Anita Anand was huddling in Ireland this week with her European counterparts.

While U.S. President Donald Trump drafts angry social media posts, Prime Minister Mark Carney is drafting a speech he’ll deliver this month to the European Parliament.

And while Washington changes the name of Lake Ontario, Ottawa is trying to shift the historical southward focus of Canada’s economy, with a key moment in that effort coming this fall.

All of this is part of carefully calibrated dance with the European Union as it and Canada move from transatlantic BFFs to something … considerably better.

“We’re sort of building this plane as we’re flying it,” said Mark Camilleri, the Brussels-based president and chief executive of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association.

“I don’t think anybody actually has a set understanding of where we’re going to land here.”

Some have championed Canada as the eventual 28th member of the European Union. But joining a bureaucratic behemoth would be a strange choice indeed for a government trying to do big things quickly and assert its sovereignty on the global stage.

Stéphane Dion, Canada’s former ambassador to the EU and France, has suggested formally joining a looser collective known as the European Political Community. He told a Senate committee in June that membership could strengthen political ties, serve as a one-stop venue for consulting fellow leaders and “consolidate our status as ‘the most European of non-European countries.’”

Both those options also risk the wrath of a United States, which has been critical of Europe and sought greater influence and control over its geographical neighbours .

But if Canada is going to emerge from the U.S. trade war economically intact and fundamentally transformed, something more tangible than symbolism or geopolitical poetry is required.

With the North American border dispute escalating and Trump’s tariff damage looming, pressure is on to reach a new depth in the relationship with Europe in time for an annual Canada-EU meeting planned for October.

“We cannot have another summit … that just confirms that we love each other,” Joost Korte, the EU’s special envoy for Canada, told a committee of the European Parliament in the spring.

“It needs to go a bit deeper … and we need to come up with concrete things. Otherwise, we’ve failed, yes, absolutely.”

Expectations are building, and Carney stoked the fire last month when he promised “intense discussions” to deepen economic and security ties with Europe.

“We can build such unparalleled access because we’re trusted, because we’re reliable, and because we have what the world needs,” he said.

This fall, the two sides hope to finalize a digital trade agreement that could touch on everything from online commerce, consumer protections and cybersecurity to the regulation of artificial intelligence.

After Canada was accepted into Europe’s defence procurement plan , there’s the possibility of deeper integration of the Canadian and European defence industries and having the Canadian Armed Forces participate more systematically in joint training missions with their European counterparts.

Officials could also announce Canada’s full participation in Erasmus Plus , a European travel-and-study program for university students.

But the whole of the emerging Canada-EU partnership is shaping up to be bigger than the sum of its parts, said Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s ambassador to Canada.

In an interview, she said there is no precedent for the new relationship that Ottawa and Brussels are forging — not in the partnership the 27-member bloc has with the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland or other non-member states.

“What is going to happen is quite unique. By that, I mean there is no existing integration model that we could simply mirror,” she said.

“We’re going to be creative and imaginative. There needs to be a name that best illustrates the depth of our relationship. I don’t think the word exists yet.”

Whatever it ends up being called, it looks set to respond to the calls of veteran Canada-EU observers.

“What I talk about is the need to stop looking at Europe as a transactional partner, but really look at it as a long-term partner, as a strategic partner,” said Camilleri.

“The relationship has, for a long time, been nice to have, but not a must-have. I think it’s definitely moved into that must-have territory in order to reach the objectives and the ambitions that the current government has expressed, and which seems to be what the Canadian population wants as well.”

It’s not just Canada that needs Europe as an alternative for goods normally sold south of the border.

The Russia-Ukraine war and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed Europe’s reliance on oil and gas from uncertain parts of the world and the need to accelerate the transition to lower-emission energy sources.

Javier Moreno Sanchez, a Spanish member of the European Parliament and chair of its committee on Canada-EU relations, likened Canada on the global stage to “a good student who behaves well and, because of that, has often been overlooked.

“You forget them because they’re not a problem,” he said.

But in a more turbulent, chaotic and unpredictable world, that stability and reliability is cherished, as are Canada’s vast natural riches.

“Canada has a wealth of energy resources and of critical minerals,” Korte told European parliamentarians, explaining how he had toured the country, met with officials and determined what aspects of the Canada-EU relationship hold the most promise.

“They have the stuff that we need, and so that would be a no-brainer to co-operate much more, particularly on the critical minerals,” he said. “But of course it needs to be taken out of the ground, and then it needs to come to Europe.”

Korte noted that the Carney government, with the creation of its Major Projects Office to fast-track key infrastructure construction, was serious about doubling down on Europe. But he warned, “We need to give the guarantee that these investments will pay off.”

A key indicator of Europe’s interest in developing and securing Canada’s critical minerals will come at an investment summit in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15. Carney has set a goal of securing $1 trillion of foreign investment.

Achim Hurrelmann, a Carleton University politics professor and co-director of the school’s Centre for European Studies, said the Canada-U.S. trade war might scare off those who would invest in Canada to secure access to U.S. markets.

“The hope that setting up a base in Canada to supply the United States has become much less realistic,” said Hurrelmann. “But that’s why there’s a much of a focus on strategic raw materials, where it’s really the European interest to secure these materials to be less dependent on China.”

Already, the European Investment Bank has shown an interest in expanding into Canada with the signing last spring of a letter of intent to explore future co-operation.

But the interest expressed by larger institutional investors is having a trickle-down effect, said Yvonne Denz, head of the Toronto-based Canadian German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

“For a lot of these medium-sized companies in Germany that are family-owned, where there’s a family office that’s taking care of the investments, Canada is … somewhat of a safe haven,” she said.

“If you look at it from a European perspective, as a country like Germany with very few resources and neighbours close by that are not always your friendly … Canada seems very, very stable.”

The forging of closer ties between Canada and Europe is a rush toward certainty.

It is, said Denz, “a signal that even though it feels like the world is breaking up and splitting apart, you have these two blocs that are forging even closer relationships.”

One person is dead following a single-vehicle collision in Southwold Township.

Elgin County OPP and Middlesex-London Paramedic Service were called to John Wise Line shortly after 7:25 p.m. Friday for a report of a single-vehicle collision.

The driver was pronounced dead at the scene.

John Wise Line is closed between Begg Road and Middle River Road while the investigation continues.

stories.title: Mark Carney runs into backlash over push to build Canadian data centres
stories.summary: Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster Canada’s digital sovereignty.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
The data centre backlash that has gripped U.S. politics is spreading north, complicating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to attract investment in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In many respects, Canada is an alluring alternative for Silicon Valley firms: it has a cooler climate, abundant energy resources and plenty of open land. But a growing number of Canadian communities are looking to slam the brakes on server farm projects.

Two municipalities — Oakville, Ontario and Rocky View County, Alberta — have implemented one-year moratoriums on data centre developments. In the sparsely-populated province of Manitoba, Premier Wab Kinew vetoed a project that would have been built outside of Winnipeg, saying the drawbacks outweighed the benefits.

A huge 7.5 gigawatt proposal by Canadian entrepreneur and Shark Tank personality Kevin O’Leary has also sparked pushback, while protestors have marched against data centres proposed in Vancouver which have been championed by all levels of government.

The Canadian hesitancy mirrors the skepticism toward data centres that has led to hundreds of local bans in the U.S., as well as a statewide moratorium in New York. Supersized data centres are loud and energy-hungry, and many people are still not convinced about the benefits of AI the facilities are meant to support.

Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster the country’s digital sovereignty. But tech policy critics warn that efforts to store Canadians’ data domestically aren’t always a protection against U.S. influence, while the economic benefits of these projects May be more modest than some claim.

Although the number of local bans in Canada is limited for now, public polling suggests the hesitancy is more widespread. An Angus Reid Institute poll found 68% of respondents would oppose a large AI data centre near their home, while a survey by Leger found four in five respondents said they’re concerned about potential increases to electricity bills and environmental impacts.

Two of the three petitions with the most signatures gathered to submit to Canada’s House of Commons are calling for a stop to data centres. The left-wing New Democratic Party is calling for a nationwide pause.

“I don’t think their concerns are groundless, but I don’t think we can put the brakes on progress,” said Jim Balsillie, the former head of BlackBerry Ltd., who has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian technological sovereignty.

Canadian Advantage

Canada’s AI data centre expansion is still in its early stages, but it’s poised to ramp up fast. Recent research from Toronto’s York University shows there are only five operational hyperscale data centres, defined as 50 megawatts or above, but 159 more are announced or under construction. That push is also showing up in trade data: Canadian imports of U.S. goods hit a record high in June driven by a surge in the computer parts used for data centres.

The federal government argued in its AI strategy that Canada is “uniquely positioned to lead in building this infrastructure responsibly and sustainably.”

“As demand for AI compute grows, Canada’s approach will be to link new data centre development with clean energy expansion, robust environmental standards, and tangible benefits for local communities,” the document said.

Balsillie said the challenge with data centres is that, unlike other forms of capital investment, they don’t necessarily spur the same kind of economic benefits to people, while the negative spillovers can be material for communities.

“It’s a fine line between being strip-mined for low value-add, metaphorically, and capturing high value-added sovereign participation in this era of AI,” Balsillie said.

Carney’s government unveiled a framework on Thursday to help guide communities’ decisions on data centre development. It said such projects must create lasting local benefits, limit environmental impacts and ensure electricity costs are not pushed onto residents. Tech giants including Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Anthropic PBC signed on to the principles.

BCE Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mirko Bibic applauded the framework, which he said acknowledged the critical nature of AI infrastructure and the need for more domestic compute capacity.

“On the other hand, there’s an acknowledgement that while we do that, we need to engender trust amongst all stakeholders in the country — citizens, communities, investors,” Bibic said in an interview Friday on BNN Bloomberg.

Provincial governments are also trying to address concerns surrounding energy costs. British Columbia is restricting electric grid use for data centres and forcing operators to compete for access.

Energy-rich Alberta’s government has been particularly bullish about data centres and attracted the bulk of Canada’s proposals. Nonetheless, it’s stipulated operators must supply their own power. The province will be home to a $13-billion Meta data centre, set to be the largest in the country.

Even so, an analysis by the Pembina Institute suggested Albertans could see their electricity bills rise by as much as $460 per year, because the centres would be allowed to connect to the grid before their own generation comes online. The Brookings Institute found data centres create a modest amount of jobs and workers see no wage gain, while home prices tend to rise by 2-5% in communities that harbor the infrastructure.

“Canada has always been seduced by this promise of jobs, and we’ve given away a lot historically in the past in order to get jobs here. And data centres don’t really have that promise,” said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think tank.

Federal and provincial officials have also pitched data centres as a necessity to bolster Canada’s sovereignty at a time when tensions are high with the U.S.

“Ontario has a choice: we can build the economy of the future and ensure Canadians’ data stays in Canada and out of President Trump’s hands, or we can get left behind and risk Canadians’ data being sent down to the U.S.,” Premier Doug Ford said in August.

But Balsillie said holding Canadians’ data domestically doesn’t necessarily protect it from the Trump administration. Under the Cloud Act, U.S. law enforcement can compel American tech companies to hand over electronic data, regardless of where it is stored.

“It’s not sovereign if you haven’t got sovereign governance,” he said.

The Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, signed in 2020, also blocks some restrictions on cross-border information transfers.

That complication applies to the supply chain, too. Balsillie argued that CoreWeave Inc., a New Jersey-based company, is in line to receive a portion of federal funding for “sovereign” computing infrastructure, awarded to Cohere Inc., a Canadian AI company. The government declined to comment and CoreWeave didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Cohere spokeswoman Amanda Taggart said: “Training frontier models requires highly specialized infrastructure, and at the time no Canadian vendor had the experience, timelines or chipsets required to train large language models from scratch at this scale. Those capabilities are still developing in Canada, and we want to help build them. That effort is already underway, and we look forward to sharing more soon. In the meantime, we are working with partners from across the world in order to continue our growth and build a generational AI company from Canada.”

Patrick Searle, the head of the Council of Canadian Innovators, which represents tech CEOs in the country, said in a statement that there are “active conversations ongoing between government and industry exploring how to build digital infrastructure in a way that responds to public concerns.”

“At the same time, this is increasingly an issue of economic sovereignty,” he added. “As compute becomes increasingly important to our economy, national security and competitiveness, Canada needs sufficient infrastructure and technological capacity here at home.”

content_blocks.text: The data centre backlash that has gripped U.S. politics is spreading north, complicating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to attract investment in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In many respects, Canada is an alluring alternative for Silicon Valley firms: it has a cooler climate, abundant energy resources and plenty of open land. But a growing number of Canadian communities are looking to slam the brakes on server farm projects.

Two municipalities — Oakville, Ontario and Rocky View County, Alberta — have implemented one-year moratoriums on data centre developments. In the sparsely-populated province of Manitoba, Premier Wab Kinew vetoed a project that would have been built outside of Winnipeg, saying the drawbacks outweighed the benefits.

A huge 7.5 gigawatt proposal by Canadian entrepreneur and Shark Tank personality Kevin O’Leary has also sparked pushback, while protestors have marched against data centres proposed in Vancouver which have been championed by all levels of government.

The Canadian hesitancy mirrors the skepticism toward data centres that has led to hundreds of local bans in the U.S., as well as a statewide moratorium in New York. Supersized data centres are loud and energy-hungry, and many people are still not convinced about the benefits of AI the facilities are meant to support.

Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster the country’s digital sovereignty. But tech policy critics warn that efforts to store Canadians’ data domestically aren’t always a protection against U.S. influence, while the economic benefits of these projects May be more modest than some claim.

Although the number of local bans in Canada is limited for now, public polling suggests the hesitancy is more widespread. An Angus Reid Institute poll found 68% of respondents would oppose a large AI data centre near their home, while a survey by Leger found four in five respondents said they’re concerned about potential increases to electricity bills and environmental impacts.

Two of the three petitions with the most signatures gathered to submit to Canada’s House of Commons are calling for a stop to data centres. The left-wing New Democratic Party is calling for a nationwide pause.

“I don’t think their concerns are groundless, but I don’t think we can put the brakes on progress,” said Jim Balsillie, the former head of BlackBerry Ltd., who has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian technological sovereignty.

content_blocks.text: Canada’s AI data centre expansion is still in its early stages, but it’s poised to ramp up fast. Recent research from Toronto’s York University shows there are only five operational hyperscale data centres, defined as 50 megawatts or above, but 159 more are announced or under construction. That push is also showing up in trade data: Canadian imports of U.S. goods hit a record high in June driven by a surge in the computer parts used for data centres.
The federal government argued in its AI strategy that Canada is “uniquely positioned to lead in building this infrastructure responsibly and sustainably.”

“As demand for AI compute grows, Canada’s approach will be to link new data centre development with clean energy expansion, robust environmental standards, and tangible benefits for local communities,” the document said.

Balsillie said the challenge with data centres is that, unlike other forms of capital investment, they don’t necessarily spur the same kind of economic benefits to people, while the negative spillovers can be material for communities.
“It’s a fine line between being strip-mined for low value-add, metaphorically, and capturing high value-added sovereign participation in this era of AI,” Balsillie said.

Carney’s government unveiled a framework on Thursday to help guide communities’ decisions on data centre development. It said such projects must create lasting local benefits, limit environmental impacts and ensure electricity costs are not pushed onto residents. Tech giants including Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Anthropic PBC signed on to the principles.
BCE Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mirko Bibic applauded the framework, which he said acknowledged the critical nature of AI infrastructure and the need for more domestic compute capacity.

“On the other hand, there’s an acknowledgement that while we do that, we need to engender trust amongst all stakeholders in the country — citizens, communities, investors,” Bibic said in an interview Friday on BNN Bloomberg.
Provincial governments are also trying to address concerns surrounding energy costs. British Columbia is restricting electric grid use for data centres and forcing operators to compete for access.

stories.title: Hiker Stanislav Volo, missing for five days in B.C., is found alive
stories.summary: Sea to Sky RCMP said Volo was taken to hospital with minor injuries
stories.content:
A hiker missing for five days in mountainous terrain near Squamish, B.C., has been found alive, walking himself to safety after a massive search.

Squamish Search and Rescue shared a photo of Stanislav Volo, 43, smiling broadly and giving a thumbs-up with two overjoyed rescuers.

“After several long days of searching, we are incredibly relieved to share that Stanislav has been found alive and is safe,” the organization said in a social media post late Friday.

It said Volo walked out himself and was found on the Indian Arm forest service road.

Sea to Sky RCMP said Volo was taken to hospital with minor injuries.

The Mounties said partners in the search included RCMP Integrated Police Dog Services, Squamish Search and Rescue, RCMP Lower Mainland Emergency Response Team, RCMP Air Services and the Sea to Sky Gondola team.

Volo had last been seen getting off the Sea to Sky Gondola at 11:33 a.m. on Sunday, aiming to hike to the challenging Mount Habrich Loop.

But he had been missing since failing to catch the gondola back down that day.

The search narrowed on Tuesday after a 911 call was made from Volo’s cellphone.

While Sue Nicholson with the Squamish Search and Rescue said the call was garbled and dropped out, it led rescuers to believe that he was still in the Mount Habrich Loop area.

Volo’s sister Ola pleaded on social media this week for help from other hikers who might have crossed paths with him.

But Squamish Search and Rescue warned the public on Thursday not to enter the Habrich area on their own after noticing messages about the search were being widely shared.

On Friday, it had better news to share.

“We know so many people across Squamish, the Sea to Sky, and beyond have been following his story, sharing our posts, sending messages and hoping alongside his family,” the organization said on social media. “Today, we get to share the news we’ve all been waiting for.”

stories.title: Toronto police announce arrest in arson that damaged MP’s vehicle
stories.summary: Threatening behaviour toward politicians in general has been on the rise in recent years
stories.author: Matthew Frank
stories.content:
Toronto police have arrested and charged one suspect and are searching for another for allegedly setting multiple cars on fire outside an east Toronto MP’s home.

In the early morning on Aug. 27, a suspect allegedly poured gas on vehicles parked outside the home of Liberal MP Salma Zahid in the Scarborough area of Toronto and set two on fire, damaging a third car, police said in a Friday news release.

The level of threats and abuse faced by MPs across all parties has spiked in recent years.

Police and firefighters responded to a 1:21 a.m. call about the fires, they said. No injuries were reported.

Roshvin Crofton, 24, was arrested on Aug. 30 and faces five charges, including arson causing to property and mischief over $5,000, Toronto police said in a news release. Investigators are still searching for another suspect in the alleged arson and are looking for any information involving a black 2025 Hyundai Sonata between Aug. 23 and Aug. 27, police said.

Ms. Zahid said in a statement that she welcomes both the arrest and news that police are seeking another person connected to the case. The investigation is ongoing and there’s no information on a motive, she said.

“With the support of my colleagues and with the guidance of security professionals, I will continue my work representing the people of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East and I look forward to returning to Ottawa when the House of Commons resumes sitting later this month,” she said.

Ms. Zahid, who represents the riding of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East, was first elected in 2015.

It’s the second time in nearly two years that a vehicle was allegedly set ablaze in front of a home on Ms. Zahid’s street. The 2024 case, which occurred outside an address a few houses away from the MP’s, is still being investigated, police said.

Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre previously condemned the alleged arson in August.

Sergeant-at-Arms Patrick McDonell previously told a House of Commons standing committee that the number of security files his office opened on threatening behaviour towards MPs climbed from eight in 2019 to 530 in 2023. Threats and harassment against federal politicians also increased by 700 per cent in the same time frame, he said in 2024.

Female MPs in particular have been targeted with abuse and death threats .

In 2022, a man approached and aggressively harassed former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland in rural Alberta, and called her a traitor who should leave the province.

Liberal MP Iqra Khalid, who represents Mississauga-Erin Mills, said in 2024 that people have spat at her and made threats against her life. Members of a right-wing extremist organization had stalked her office and shared her address, she said, as well as videotaped her as she walked around her community.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna spoke out when she was in office about the threats and harassment she received, which led her to request additional security.

RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme has suggested the federal government draft new laws that make it easier to charge people who threaten elected officials.

Internal RCMP documents from 2024 warned protecting parliamentarians and other public figures put a “significant strain” on personnel.

RCMP estimates from 2025 said the number of threats against public officials across the country increased from approximately 1,300 in 2022 to 2,600 in 2023 and was projected to exceed 3,500 in 2024.

stories.title: ‘Targeting’ and ‘intimidation’: Council candidates undeterred by razor-slashed campaign signs
stories.summary: A pair of candidates running for seats on London City Council independently contacted CTV News about threatening tactics used to destroy some of their campaign signs.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A pair of candidates running for seats on London City Council independently contacted CTV News about threatening tactics used to destroy some of their campaign signs.

Ward 13 candidate Andrew Crook kept some of his signs that were slashed to pieces using a razor blade or knife.

“Actually bringing a weapon to damage them, and especially when it’s a long chain of signs, not just one sign, but multiple signs in a row, it’s clearly somebody who’s targeting,” Crook said.

He had a total of 15 signs damaged last weekend, including several with a blade.

Although Crook’s signs humorously read “A name that demands honesty”, he says the impact to his campaign is no laughing matter.

“Fifty bucks a sign is typically what it runs, so it adds up pretty quickly,” he explained. “And that’s not to mention the stress and having to go out and (replace) it.”

Ward 12 candidate Ribal Zebian also had some of his signs slashed since the nomination period closed. “One small one was cut up, and two large signs were cut up. We have a total of 13 lost signs,” he said.

He believes the use of a blade goes beyond vandalism, and was intended to be a threat.

“It’s a form of intimidation,” he said. “The individuals who are doing this are trying to intimidate my campaign, trying to make us get (off) the ballot.”

Undeterred, both candidates remain committed to campaigning for a seat on council.

“It hurts. It hurts because these are things that in a democratic country, you would assume these things wouldn’t be happening,” Zebian added.

“This is our democracy, and ultimately, I think it’s important that we respect the people putting their names out there,” Crook said. “You don’t have to agree with me, you don’t have to support me, but don’t devastate (my) signs.”

According to Deputy City Clerk Sarah Corman, “The City of London addresses concerns and complaints related to election sign placement, size, timing, and other requirements under the Election Sign By-law. Any concerns about theft or destruction of election signs should be forwarded to the London Police Service, as vandalism or mischief falls under the Criminal Code.”

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Town of Gander urges calm as Pete Hoekstra’s planned visit for 9/11 anniversary angers locals
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador says he is returning on Sept. 11 to honour enduring bond with the place that famously welcomed and sheltered American passengers
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
A week before U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra is set to give remarks in Gander to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the Newfoundland town that became famous for its kindness on that day addressed growing community anger about his attendance.

“We understand why people feel strongly about this,” said a statement from the town released Friday afternoon. “We are proud Canadians, and we understand the frustration and disappointment many Canadians are feeling about the current state of the relationship between Canada and the United States.”

As the terrorist attacks were unfolding on Sept. 11, 2001, 38 planes carrying thousands of passengers were diverted to Gander. The town famously stepped up, with locals opening up their homes, setting up shelters and providing meals and medication to the stranded passengers, many of whom were American. They formed lifelong bonds and connections that are emotionally depicted in the immensely popular Broadway musical Come From Away . Gander’s kindness, a symbol of co-operation between the Canada and the U.S., has also been immortalized in a new Heritage Minute , released this week.

But anti-American tension has ratcheted up in recent weeks with U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, his order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America and the slew of trolling memes coming out of the White House. This week, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted on social media a screenshot of a young Canadian cadet and her instructor at the end of summer training camp, mocking them with the words “this is real,” raising the ire of people across the country.

Mr. Hoekstra himself has faced fierce backlash for months, after saying earlier in the year that annexing Canada as the 51st state would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mr. Trump. A House of Commons petition signed by more than 260,000 Canadians calling for his removal remains active.

Mr. Hoekstra’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Earlier this week Mr. Hoekstra said in a statement that he is returning to Gander on the 9/11 anniversary to say thank you and to honour the enduring bond.

Mr. Hoekstra is hosting a breakfast for volunteers and attending a commemoration service in Gander where he’s speaking on friendship and connection.

Plans for his attendance have triggered controversy and emotion in the community and on social media, said Mayor Percy Farwell in an interview with The Globe and Mail prior to the town’s statement.

“There is a certain delicacy to the timing this year,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump’s trade war. “This story does transcend that.”

“Administrations come and go and ambassadors come and go but at the end of the day we have a lasting relationship.”

The town explained in its statement that it followed the appropriate protocol when planning the commemoration by extending invitations to government and diplomatic representatives, adding that this doesn’t mean the town endorses “any individual, their comments or their political views.”

In his interview, Mr. Farwell asked that the focus of the commemoration be about people, the close to 3,000 people who lost their lives on 9/11 and the acts of humanity in Gander, not politics.

Meanwhile, the popular national satire publication The Beaverton had already re-written the script with a post titled “Come from Away sequel will see Newfoundlanders put the friggin’ boots to Pete Hoekstra.”

stories.title: As glaciers melt near mountains, risks multiply and Canada isn’t prepared, scientists warn
stories.summary: The Himalayan disaster that led to flooding in Nepal is a cautionary tale about the climate crisis
stories.author: Om Shanbhag
stories.content:
Six years ago, a rapidly retreating glacier in the southern Coast Mountains of British Columbia shrunk away from the base of the nearby mountainside causing millions of tonnes of rock to fall.

The Elliot Creek landslide , with a mass similar to that of all Canadian automobiles combined, landed in an alpine lake, creating a tsunami and draining the lake. The displaced water flooded a nearby fjord, destroying kilometres of salmon habitat and scouring nearby forest.

According to a 2022 study , despite detecting the resulting seismic event, its location remained unknown until forestry workers found the site two weeks later.

In the remote valleys of the Coast Mountains, the tsunami and flooding caused no structural damage or fatalities. But its root cause appears to be similar to the landslide behind the Aug. 26 floods in Nepal , which have claimed the lives of more than 1,250 people.

As the Himalayan glacier thinned and retreated, geologists believe the removal of ice could have caused the high-altitude landslide.

But in both the Himalayas and Canada, scientists don’t know where the next such event will happen.

The effects of climate change are creating evolving risks in high mountain regions, Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, said.

“With glaciers, they’re changing so quickly that the hazard – and therefore the risk – is not the same now as it was five years ago or in five years’ time from now,” Prof. Shugar said.

Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilize high-mountain rock and ice, strengthening prospects for disasters such as the Himalayan flood along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet, scientists say, while warning climate change May not be sole trigger.

Glaciers are receding and thinning at an unprecedented rate, with glaciers in Western Canada expected to largely disappear by the end of the century, according to a report released by Environment and Climate Change Canada this week.

The report expects the number and severity of floods and landslides to increase as glacier ice melts, even if carbon dioxide emissions reach net-zero. The Paris Agreement established a global goal to reach net zero by 2050.

“Even if we did turn off the taps today, we have a lot of global warming that’s already built into the system, baked in, and so we are going to see these impacts,” Prof. Shugar said.

Between 2021 and 2024, glaciers in Western Canada lost 12 per cent of their volume, melting twice as fast as they did in the last decade, according to a study co-authored by Prof. Shugar, Brian Menounos, Hakai affiliate and geography professor at the University of Northern British Columbia and others.

“It’s clear that our high mountains are changing rapidly, and it really does call for a combined systematic effort to monitor these high elevations,” Prof. Menounos said. However, risk mapping and management is often only completed after a disaster happens.

“Sadly, in many cases, we use a whack-a-mole approach,” he said.

Jeffrey Crompton, a researcher at the Geological Survey of Canada, is in the early stages of creating a monitoring system which would identify the greatest hazards and the risks they pose to people and infrastructure.

“It’s a huge problem, and we need a lot more resources than we currently have to be able to get at it,” he said.

Luck has saved many Canadians from alpine disaster, Dr. Crompton said. Despite Canada not having the same densely populated river valleys as in the Himalayas, several large landslide events in North America could have led to tragedies.

Last year in Tracy Arm, an Alaskan fjord, a landslide event , similar to the Elliot Creek event occurred. As the South Sawyer glacier lost ice, it exposed a cliff face that soon gave way, displacing enough water to cause a tsunami. Tracy Arm sees a lot of marine traffic, with tour boats and cruise ships frequently operating in the fjord. Happenstance meant few boaters were near the landslide when it happened.

Other events have also come close to tourist areas and mining communities, such as northern B.C.’s Canoe Glacier landslide in 2021, and have posed threats to infrastructure, such as highways, pipelines and power lines.

“Back to back to back, all of these very large events [are] happening, and they all kind of follow this common theme of happening in these mountainous regions where there’s rapid deglaciation,” Dr. Crompton said.

Glaciers in the Arctic are also melting at a rapid pace, increasing the threat of disaster in the region. As shipping increases through the north, the area could be the next frontier for these hazardous events, Prof. Shugar said.

“We’re starting to see really, really big [landslides], and that’s a concern, and that’s something that I think we as a scientific community, but also we as a society, need to be paying attention to as we consider development in mountain environments,” Prof. Shugar said.

Switzerland and Norway both have risk mitigation systems, which allow the two countries to monitor for hazards and keep communities safe in alpine locations and fjords, Prof. Shugar said.

“We in Canada have nothing like that,” Prof. Shugar said. “We don’t even know where the unstable slopes are, let alone knowing which ones might collapse.”

stories.title: The Globe and Mail wins two Online Journalism Awards
stories.summary: Journalists honoured for stories about the first professional football player to come out as transgender and an experimental brain surgery
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail has won two Online Journalism Awards, one for a feature about the first professional football player to come out as transgender, and the other for a personal story about an experimental brain surgery.

Jana G. Pruden’s piece, titled Her turn to play , won in the category of Topical Reporting: Gender and Identity, Large Newsroom.

The piece profiled Maven Maurer, who as Mike Maurer was a Grey Cup winner and MMA fighter. The story gave readers an intimate view into Maven’s journey – her fears, her vulnerabilities and, ultimately, her courage.

Anna Mehler Paperny’s essay, titled Holes in my head, wires in my brain , won in the Personal Narrative category. The piece used illustration, animation and video to bring readers inside Ms. Paperny’s experience with deep brain stimulation to treat her chronic depression.

Digital storytelling editor Laura Blenkinsop and a team including Timothy Moore, Mark Medley, John Sopinski and Bryan Gee contributed to the piece.

The Globe and Mail was also named a finalist in three other categories.

The Globe’s coverage of the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., in February was nominated for Breaking News, Large Newsroom. The Globe mobilized a large team of reporters to Tumbler Ridge and in bureaus across the country after an 18-year-old shot and killed eight people, including five children at the town’s school, before killing herself. It was one of the country’s deadliest mass shootings.

Jennifer Yang, Melissa Tait and Timothy Moore were named finalists in two categories – Excellence in Science Reporting, Large Newsroom, and Feature, Large Newsroom – for The two halves of Maryam .

The piece told the story of Maryam Fatima, a baby who developed catastrophic seizures and whose doctors proposed a treatment that would destroy half her brain to save her life. The piece offered both an intimate portrait of a family’s agonizing decision and also a deeply reported look at the science behind the procedure.

The awards are run by the Online News Association and recognize excellence in digital journalism around the world. The winners will be honoured at a ceremony in New York on Oct. 1.

stories.title: Randolph College for the Performing Arts ordered to cease operations
stories.summary: A restraining order was issued against the school by the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, ordering it to cease operations
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
a postsecondary theatre school that lost its accreditation in February, has been issued a restraining order by the provincial government requiring the school to cease operations as a career college.

Last week, the school told The Globe and Mail that it had filed an application with the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to reinstate its status as a college. But on Aug. 31, the ministry issued its restraining order against Randolph for contravening the Ontario Career Colleges Act. A notice on the ministry’s website said the school can no longer advertise itself as a career college, offer vocational programs or charge fees for such programming.

Randolph, which until February had 86 students enrolled, operated as an unregistered career college after its accreditation expired on Feb. 1, according to the restraining order . When asked why the school’s accreditation had lapsed, founder George Randolph told The Globe it had switched auditing companies, “which took longer than anticipated.” (Randolph, who in 2017 formally resigned from the school after an independent investigator found that he had engaged in “unwelcome comments and physical gestures,” has served as vice-chair of the school’s board since 2019.)

The ministry said in its restraining order that the college offered and advertised unapproved vocational programs between Feb. 1 and Aug. 28, and collected tuition fees from students enrolled in the unapproved courses.

Randolph’s tuition was $13,710 per academic year for a program that condensed three academic years into two calendar years of study, for a total program cost of $41,130 per student.

Failure to comply with the actions of the restraining order could result in fines of up to $250,000.

In an e-mailed statement to The Globe on Sept. 1, Randolph, the founder, said the college is reviewing the matters raised by the ministry with legal counsel. He declined to answer specific questions about the college’s finances and personnel, citing the “ongoing regulatory process.”

Former students affected by the closing of the school have been provided two options by the ministry: They can either work with the province to find a new program to finish their studies, or they can receive a partial refund for fees paid to Randolph.

In e-mails sent to faculty and students on Aug. 31, Randolph’s board said the school would begin winding down the remaining administrative, student, employment and regulatory obligations for its diploma program.

Randolph Kids, a popular program for students aged three to 17 that included dance, acting and singing classes, has also closed. However, the children’s program will resume operations this fall under the umbrella of the Canadian Centre for Arts Education and Innovation, a new not-for-profit business incorporated in April.

On Tuesday evening, O’neil Edwards, listed on Randolph’s website as its executive director until Aug. 20, told parents at an informational Zoom meeting that the new centre’s programming will continue in the former Randolph space at 730 Bathurst Street.

In a June 12 e-mail to a parent of a Randolph College student, viewed by The Globe, ministry investigator Eric Joly said the college had not been allowed to charge or collect fees since its registration had expired on Feb. 1.

However, e-mails and bank records shared with The Globe this week show that in March, the school solicited and accepted thousands of dollars in tuition payments from students for college courses that had not yet been taught. In an Aug. 26 e-mailed statement to The Globe, the school’s founder said tuition received after Feb. 1 was related to instruction that had already been provided prior to the college’s loss of accreditation.

Lily Burden, who was scheduled to start her fourth term of Randolph instruction this fall, said her experience at the college was “wonderful” until February’s accreditation issue came to light. “The workload was a lot, but it was amazing,” she said. “I know I got at least some of an amazing education.”

Lily’s parents, Steve and Sarah Burden, who paid for their daughter’s tuition, similarly praised the program – especially for its industry connections. (Randolph alumni include Saturday Night Live cast member Veronika Slowikowska as well as actors Matt Raffy, Amaka Umeh and Paul Nolan.)

But the Burden family became concerned when the June 12 e-mail from Joly informed them they shouldn’t be paying tuition to the school. A Feb. 26 e-mail to the Burdens from Randolph’s finance administrator said it was “perfectly fine” to proceed with payment for Lily’s second year.

“That was the first notification we got from any government ministry,” Steve said about the June e-mail. Students had been informed by the school of the accreditation issue in February, Lily said, and were told that as a result, the school would pivot its course offerings to nongraded workshops.

“It’s a huge loss,” Sarah said, pointing out that between Randolph’s two unaccredited terms and its cancelled fall term, her daughter has lost a full calendar year of education. “She should be graduating next year. Now we don’t know when she’ll graduate.”

stories.title: Quebec will not administer free flu shots this fall
stories.summary: Quebec was the second province after Alberta to stop providing free COVID-19 vaccines to its population last year
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha, Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Quebec will no longer administer free flu shots for its entire population this fall, a year after it stopped providing COVID-19 vaccinations at no cost.

Other provinces, when reached by The Globe and Mail, said they are still maintaining their flu shot coverage, typically offering the vaccine for free to everyone six months of age and older.

The Quebec Health Department said its decision relied on the guidance of the province’s immunization committee, an independent advisory panel also known by its French abbreviation, CIQ.

“In recent years, particularly during the pandemic, the decision was made to offer free vaccination to everyone. This year marks a change so that the vaccination program reflects the recommendations of the CIQ,” department spokesman Émile Giard said in an e-mail.

In an 11-page interim scientific opinion released in April, CIQ recommended that Quebec harmonize the criteria for its flu and COVID-19 vaccination programs.

“There is an interest in synchronizing the vaccination campaigns against COVID-19 and against influenza during the fall to increase coverage, facilitate planning and reduce costs.”

The CIQ opinion noted that the benefits of vaccination against COVID-19 “for healthy people aged 65 to 74 are more limited.”

As a result, it suggested maintaining the previous year’s policy on offering COVID-19 shots for Quebeckers 75 and older, immunocompromised people and those living in remote locations, seniors’ homes and long-term care facilities.

Marilie Beaulieu-Gravel, a spokeswoman for an association representing pharmacy owners in Quebec, also known by its French acronym Aqpp, said it is too early to know how much its members would charge for a flu shot.

Quebec was the second province after Alberta to stop providing free COVID-19 vaccines to its population last year. Alberta limited coverage to specific high-risk and vulnerable populations, in addition to health care workers after union bargaining and widespread pushback.

The two provinces scaled back after the federal government decided in January, 2025, to stop funding provinces for the purchase of COVID-19 shots.

Alberta has since defended its approach to COVID-19 coverage as a way to reduce vaccine waste, but has also cited Quebec’s analysis as part of its reasoning. Roughly eight per cent of Alberta’s population was vaccinated against COVID-19 last season. Coverage was 14 per cent in 2024-25 when it was universally available.

The Western province has been tight-lipped on its 2026-27 vaccine campaign, but further details are expected to be released in the coming weeks.

However, ON Friday, Alberta’s Ministry of Primary and Preventative Health Services confirmed it has no plan to change its flu immunization program, meaning residents will still be able to access flu shots free of charge this season.

The ministry declined to answer questions from The Globe and Mail about COVID-19 coverage.

Canada’s National Advisory Committee on Immunization recommends that the seasonal flu vaccine should be offered annually to everyone six months of age and older who does not have a medical reason to avoid it. The committee said vaccination is “particularly important” for people at high risk of flu-related complications or hospitalization, including seniors and pregnant individuals.

For COVID-19 shots, Naci strongly recommends the vaccine be offered to high-risk individuals and that adults older than 80, long-term care home residents, moderate or severely immunocompromised individuals and adults 65 to 79 with underlying medical conditions receive a second dose per year. Everyone else May receive an annual vaccine.

In Saskatchewan, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines will continue to be provided free of charge to all residents six months and older. The same is true in Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba.

The British Columbia Ministry of Health said free flu shots will be available to all residents six months and older, but it’s unclear who will be covered for COVID-19 shots. While COVID-19 vaccines will be available this fall, eligibility and immunization locations have yet to be announced.

The government website states: “If a COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for you, you will receive a notification.”

Similarly, Nova Scotia said that details of the full respiratory vaccine program, including COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, shots, will be announced in coming weeks.

stories.title: Bombers, Riders fans clash over ‘Regina-style’ pizza in Labour Day Classic trash talk
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan Roughriders will meet the Winnipeg Blue Bombers at Mosaic Stadium on Sunday. Ahead of the game, Riders and Bombers fans are duking it out over Regina-style pizza.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Annual trash talk between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders, among the teams and their fandoms, is building ahead of Sunday’s Labour Day Classic.

This year, it’s all about the pizza.

In a social media post Tuesday, the Bombers reiterated its three-year-old statement that, “honestly, Regina-style pizza is terrible.”

After three years “reflecting” on the various “not kind” responses the team received from Riders fans, it said its opinion remains unchanged.

“It’s still terrible. Honestly, it’s worse than we ever thought. It’s like someone took a three-week old lasagna and slapped it on a piece of dough. It’s awful, and our opinion will never change,” the team posted.

Regina-style pizza is characterized by its square slices and gratuitous servings of toppings, including vegetables and meat, that are covered by cheese and are served atop a thick layer of crust.

Marina Rubina, a Regina resident, Riders fan and content creator, said when she saw the Blue Bombers’ post, she was angry and shocked. She took the trash talk as an opportunity to post a video showing what she thought was worth showcasing in Winnipeg.

In it, after extensively researching for 14 minutes, she concluded she “still couldn’t find a reason to go” to the Manitoban city. Upon that realization, she helped herself to a slice of pizza.

“You can come to Regina just to try the pizza. (Then,) it’s already worth it to make the trip,” she said, adding she loves the city’s pizza pie.

More than 570 kilometres west of Regina, in Winnipeg, Cassie Liebrecht, a lifelong Bombers fan, told Global News she found the Blue Bombers’ pizza post “hilarious.”

“I loved seeing that. There’s always such good humour attached to it, and I love seeing the rivalries. I love amping up the rivalries especially before big games like this. It just adds to the excitement,” Liebrecht said.

She said she had never heard of Regina-style pizza before the Bombers’ post, but Liebrecht is now following the topic ahead of Sunday’s game, which she will be watching from her cabin.

Scott Charney has supported the Blue since he was a child. He said he is also a fan of any, and all, pizza – including Regina-style.

“I’m a pizza guy so I like all pizza. I’m going to eat it regardless,” Charney said.

The Labour Day Classic is set to kick off at Mosaic Stadium on Sunday at 5 p.m. local time.

The Roughriders are currently second in the CFL’s West Division, with a 7-4 record. Winnipeg is trailing with its 6-5 record, but the team is coming off a huge win against the league-leading Montreal Alouettes.

stories.title: Timeline of turmoil for B.C. Conservatives, with nine defections in three weeks
stories.summary: The B.C. Conservatives have been in a state of upheaval since former finance critic Peter Milobar quit the official Opposition caucus three weeks ago. The party has since suffered a parade of defections from legislators citing differences with Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay of strategy and ideology.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservatives have been in a state of upheaval since former finance critic Peter Milobar quit the official Opposition caucus three weeks ago. The party has since suffered a parade of defections from legislators citing differences with Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay of strategy and ideology.

Here’s a timeline of the turmoil.

Aug. 14: Milobar (Kamloops Centre) quits the caucus, citing a lack of “ideological alignment” with Findlay. Milobar, a former leadership contender and finance critic for the Opposition, had clashed with Findlay in a debate when she accused him of having a conflict of interest because Milobar’s Indigenous wife once held paid positions with the local Indigenous band.

Aug. 22: Reann Gasper (Abbotsford-Mission) resigns her seat so Findlay can run in a byelection. Gasper is appointed Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.

Aug. 24: Ian Paton (Delta South) quits the party, saying the Conservatives’ direction under Findlay no longer aligns with his beliefs and he intends to form a new party with Milobar. Milobar says at the announcement that he and Paton could be a party of two, but suggests there could be more defections.

Aug. 25: Rosalyn Bird (Prince George-Valemount) quits the Conservatives to sit as an Independent, issuing a statement warning about divisive leadership. She says legislators “should be able to firmly reject racism, antisemitism, homophobia and hatred while still having difficult and necessary conversations about immigration, Indigenous reconciliation, addiction, crime, gender, religion and the many other issues on which reasonable people sometimes disagree.”

Aug. 26: Teresa Wat (Richmond-Bridgeport) resigns to sit as an Independent on Aug. 26. She accuses Findlay of reneging on a promise to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” reportedly made by Findlay about Wat, calling her “CCP,” a reference to the Chinese Communist Party. Findlay calls Wat’s departure is a “betrayal of the hardworking volunteers, campaign workers and voters who helped get her elected.”

The same day, Brennan Day (Courtenay-Comox) quits the caucus, saying he no longer supports the direction of the party under Findlay. Day says he has lost confidence in the judgment, conduct and ethical standards of Findlay’s leadership and the people she surrounds herself with.

Aug. 27: Bruce Banman (Abbotsford South) quits and rallies other Conservatives to join him “regardless of political affiliation.” He says many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP is becoming increasingly likely.

Aug. 28: Findlay says suggestions that a recording shows she illegally offered jobs to legislators, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection, are “preposterous.” Police say they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators that was released on social media on Thursday. Findlay later announces a caucus meeting to be followed by a news conference on Aug. 31.

Aug. 29: Premier David Eby calls a byelection in Abbotsford-Mission, with voting day set for Saturday, Sept. 26.

Aug. 30: Findlay cancels the caucus meeting and news conference.

Aug. 31: A’a: Liya Warbus (Chilliwack-Cultus Lake) quits the caucus, saying she has lost faith in Findlay’s leadership, citing the sudden cancellation of the caucus meeting and the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Sept. 1: Paton says he has been asked to speak to the RCMP. He says he expects to be asked about his allegation that Findlay’s chief of staff, Chris Delaney, had said that if he stepped down as an MLA so Findlay could run in a byelection, he could be given a position as an adviser at the same salary.

Sept. 2: Legislators Donegal Wilson (Boundary-Similkameen) and Scott McInnis (Columbia River-Revelstoke) quit caucus, both citing Findlay’s reported connections to Alberta separatists as part of a series of concerns. Their departures reduce the Conservative caucus to 28; it had had 44 members after the 2024 election.

Findlay announces that Delaney has resigned as her chief of staff, and she has appointed Gasper to replace him. Findlay says she is the victim of a “co-ordinated political attack.”

Sept. 4: Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and A’a:liya Warbus say in a joint statement that they’re joining the yet-to-be-named party being formed by Milobar and Paton.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 04, 2026.

stories.title: As volunteers decline, Elgin County clubs look online for recruits
stories.summary: The new directory brings 32 service clubs into one place as organizations grapple with falling volunteer participation.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
Two organizations have collaborated to establish an online directory aimed at boosting volunteerism in Elgin County service clubs as participation declines.

Service clubs across Elgin County have partnered with Volunteer Elgin, a non-profit initiative that connects people with volunteer opportunities, and the Elgin St. Thomas Community Foundation – which connects donors to charitable community campaigns – on a centralized online service club directory that “will highlight the many clubs contributing to community life and provide a simple starting point for residents who want to learn more,” a Volunteer Elgin news release said.

“We want to create a visible online presence for people who are seeking opportunities, and a place where all of the service clubs can be accessed in one spot,” said Tracy Robinson, executive director of the Elgin St. Thomas Community Foundation.

The impetus for launching the online portal came from listening to the community and hearing from service clubs struggling to recruit and retain volunteers, Robinson said.

The initiative grew out of challenges identified at an annual breakfast hosted at the Rotary Club of St. Thomas, according to the release.

Formal volunteering has declined sharply, with national data showing a 40 per cent decrease in volunteer hours between 2013 and 2023, the release said.

Robinson said service clubs are an indicator of the health of a community.

“There’s countless volunteer hours that service club members give, and if they’re struggling, then you know there’s a real problem,” she said.

The hope is that the directory will bolster service club membership so they can “continue to serve our communities,” said Carolyn Johnson, chair of Volunteer Elgin.

A member of the Talbot Trail Optimist Club in St. Thomas, Johnson welcomed the opportunity for the group to gain more exposure through the directory.

St. Thomas mentors changing young lives one match at a time

London agencies ask: Where have all the volunteers gone?

“Our club is quite thrilled to have a little more exposure, so we can get some new volunteers,” she said.

The Kinsmen Club of St. Thomas, which has donated to multiple community causes, including $50,000 toward the city’s affordable housing development Project Tiny Hope, is listed in the directory, said deputy director Rico Mena.

Contrary to the broader decline in volunteering, Mena said the club has recently seen a surge in members, underscoring the importance of online exposure.

“One of our members put a post on Facebook, and we doubled our numbers this year, which is fantastic,” he said, adding he hopes the directory will lead to even more recruits.

Mena said the group now has 24 active members.

“A lot of people didn’t realize that there is a Kinsmen (Club) in town, or didn’t realize what we do in town. So, it’s just a matter of getting out there.”

While the initial phase focuses on building the directory, the larger goal is to help service clubs promote membership opportunities, increase public awareness and help residents find ways to get involved, the Volunteer Elgin release said.

So far, 32 service clubs are listed in the directory.

“Volunteers are really the basis of any special events and things within our community,” Johnson said. “They make for stronger communities. They make for bigger and better events. They provide better services.”

Visitors to Volunteer Elgin’s website can also search for “member agencies,” including organizations such as Big Brothers Big Sisters Elgin, which Johnson, who also serves as executive director, said needs more volunteers.

“We’re struggling for volunteers,” she said. “Not only are volunteers down, our numbers of children seeking our service are increasing. So, (that’s) creating quite a gap.”

For people looking to learn more about Elgin County service clubs or groups seeking to join the directory, visit Volunteer Elgin’s website .

“A lot of people didn’t realize that there is a Kinsmen (Club) in town, or didn’t realize what we do in town. So, it’s just a matter of getting out there.”

While the initial phase focuses on building the directory, the larger goal is to help service clubs promote membership opportunities, increase public awareness and help residents find ways to get involved, the Volunteer Elgin release said.
So far, 32 service clubs are listed in the directory.

“Volunteers are really the basis of any special events and things within our community,” Johnson said. “They make for stronger communities. They make for bigger and better events. They provide better services.”

Visitors to Volunteer Elgin’s website can also search for “member agencies,” including organizations such as Big Brothers Big Sisters Elgin, which Johnson, who also serves as executive director, said needs more volunteers.
“We’re struggling for volunteers,” she said. “Not only are volunteers down, our numbers of children seeking our service are increasing. So, (that’s) creating quite a gap.”
For people looking to learn more about Elgin County service clubs or groups seeking to join the directory, visit Volunteer Elgin’s website .

stories.title: ‘It’s no prank’: Residents in Middlesex County fear injury as wheel nut loosening continues
stories.summary: It is a potentially dangerous act that hasn’t let up, according to residents of a community north-west of London, Ont.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
It is a potentially dangerous act that hasn’t let up, according to residents of a community north-west of London, Ont.

Wheel nuts continue to be loosened from vehicles in Ailsa Craig, Ont.

“I’ve known four people, actually, who had their lug nuts loosened. The tires hadn’t fallen off, they heard the noise first. Thank God,” said resident Wayne Higman.

But in one case, a tire flew off while a vehicle was moving.

Tonya Nichol told CTV News London she was almost back to town after running errands when it happened last month.

“Just as I turned the corner to come into town, the tires vacated my vehicle, crossed the road and into the ditch.”

The aftermath left her truck damaged and her heart in her throat. She can’t get the thought out of her head about what might have happened if she’d been going faster.

“I had my daughter and her friend from dance in the truck at the time. It could have been three of us injured if we had been going highway speeds and it fell off then.”

Her anger took her to social media, where she discovered she wasn’t alone.

“Since then, we’ve heard at least 8 other people have been affected by it.”

CTV News also spoke to a volunteer firefighter who nearly lost her tire.

All the stories are enough to warrant concern from police and residents.

“I’m worried, it doesn’t sound safe, it puts the whole community at risk,” said Kevin Peterson.

The level of concern amplified once people began to suspect that this could potentially be related to an online challenge.”

A social media challenge has circulated online for several years, encouraging the dangerous prank.

Police forces across the province have tried to alert people to the danger.

In Ailsa Craig, O.P.P. have confirmed that two people were caught on video surveillance tampering with wheel nuts. They have not been apprehended.

Meanwhile, residents here report checking their tires before they drive until the perpetrators are caught or at least learn there is nothing funny about their actions.

“That’s no prank to pull because there’s a lot of danger, people taking lug nuts off tires,” said Higman.

“It could cost somebody their life,” added Nichol solemnly, as she reflected again on her good fortune that her tire came off at a slow speed.

stories.title: Lunenburg water conservation continues after Dares Lake dam breach
stories.summary: Water conservation efforts continued for a second day in Lunenburg, N.S., along with school and business closures, as crews worked on repairs to the Dares Lake dam.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
Water conservation efforts continued for a second day in Lunenburg , N.S., along with school and business closures, as crews worked to repair the Dares Lake dam.

The recently-constructed dam was breached Wednesday around 1 p.m. after a crack formed, sending water into the pump building.

Since the dam is the Town of Lunenburg’s main water supply, many businesses, industries, and restaurants were forced to close in an effort to conserve water.

Mayor Jamie Myra says the breach overflowed the lake and submerged the pump building. That meant no water was being pumped into the town’s water treatment facility.

“So eventually if that wasn’t rectified, we’d run out of water,” he said.

Closures in the town range from cafes to daycares, and larger companies like High Liner Foods, which is headquartered in Lunenburg.

“If it doesn’t get back up and running within the next 12 to 24 hours, you’re talking hundreds of thousands of dollars (in revenue) lost (in the town) over Labour Day weekend,” said Myra.

For tourists who stopped by the popular waterfront community, it was a disappointment.

“We were going to go and have lunch at the Salt Shaker. I feel bad for the businesses, they’re losing a lot of money,” said one visitor.

Myra says the dam was installed within the last year and cost the town about $1 million.

“I never ever envisioned the new dam just collapsing or giving way. That, to me, is a shocker,” he said.

As of Friday, two out of the three pumps in the building are working but not at 100 per cent, according to the mayor.

“People have been listening to the directive, people have been using less water, and the two pumps that are out working are somewhat being able to catch up to the water capacity,” he said.

“So if things keep going in the right direction, we’re hoping sooner rather than later our water utility is back up to the standards it needs to be to start delivering safe drinking water to everybody.”

Myra says the breach has now been secured and the focus remains on getting all three pumps fully operational.

He applauds the town’s efforts to fix the problem and apologizes to the businesses and students at Bluenose Academy who haven’t been able to return to class for the new school year.

“I really learned in the last 48 hours how close this community is. We haven’t had any pushback from residents (or) business owners. We all want the same end result and we’re all working together to get there,” he said.

Myra adds that anyone with property damage caused by the breach should contact his office.

Property owner Connor Veinot is keeping a close eye on the water.

What was once a small stream on his property has risen four feet and is threatening to flood his yard.

“I didn’t think it would rise that fast,” he said.

Now that the breach has been secured, he’s hopeful the water will recede. However, heavy rain in the forecast has him fearing the worst.

“Damage, erosion, undermining and stuff. Hopefully we don’t get a lot of downpour on top of it because it is a lot of force and I’m scared that it might take the bridge out behind me,” he said.

As for the cause of the damage, Myra says it’s still unclear but he’s in touch with provincial officials as they work to figure that out.

“(The dam) was a partnership between other levels of government as well. So it’ll be more than just us that are wondering what happened,” he said.

stories.title: London-area unemployment climbs to 8.5% amid tariff uncertainty
stories.summary: The region lost about 1,600 jobs in August as economists pointed to trade uncertainty and weaker hiring.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The London region’s unemployment rate rose to 8.5 per cent in August from 8.2 per cent in July, according to Statistics Canada figures released Friday.

The London census metropolitan area includes London, St. Thomas, Strathroy and parts of Elgin and Middlesex counties.

The region’s labour force shrank by about 800 people, to 341,800 in August from 342,600 in July. Of those, 312,900 were employed in August, compared with 314,500 in July.

The rise in unemployment may be due to uncertainty surrounding trade negotiations with the United States, said David Ristovski, an economist with Signal49 Research, an economic forecasting agency formerly known as the Conference Board of Canada.

“The recent weakness that we’ve been seeing over the last six to eight months really stems from the uncertainty surrounding the ongoing trade situation with the United States, and so, that’s significantly impacting multiple sectors,” he said.

The latest jobs report comes after U.S. President Donald Trump implemented Section 338 tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between American and Canadian negotiators fell apart.

Canadian dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of comparable U.S. goods will come into effect Tuesday.

Additional tariff threats could be causing Canadian businesses to take a more cautious approach to hiring in the near term, reducing demand for labour, Ristovski said.

“That’s what we think has sort of played out in London over the last six to eight months,” he said.

Other factors, such as job seekers becoming discouraged and leaving the labour force, people leaving the city to pursue work elsewhere, or leaving the job market to pursue schooling, might also be contributing to the higher unemployment rate, Ristovski said.

“There’s also a bit of weakness in the education sector, given that there have been minimal population gains in recent months, particularly among international students,” he said.

Statistics Canada reported the London region’s population grew slightly in one month, to 541,000 from 540,500.

Ristovski expects a trade deal between Canada and the United States by Jan. 1, 2027, which he said would help London’s economy and labour market bounce back.

But there is still uncertainty on that front, he said, and if a deal isn’t reached, conditions could potentially worsen.

“That will have many negative repercussions, not only in the London region, but especially other cities and metropolitan areas in and around Southwestern Ontario,” he said.

Canada’s overall unemployment rate held steady at 6.4 per cent, while Ontario’s rose one-tenth of a percentage point to 6.9 per cent.

Other factors, such as job seekers becoming discouraged and leaving the labour force, people leaving the city to pursue work elsewhere, or leaving the job market to pursue schooling, might also be contributing to the higher unemployment rate, Ristovski said.
“There’s also a bit of weakness in the education sector, given that there have been minimal population gains in recent months, particularly among international students,” he said.
Statistics Canada reported the London region’s population grew slightly in one month, to 541,000 from 540,500.
Ristovski expects a trade deal between Canada and the United States by Jan. 1, 2027, which he said would help London’s economy and labour market bounce back.
But there is still uncertainty on that front, he said, and if a deal isn’t reached, conditions could potentially worsen.

stories.title: Another golf push cart company is threatened by Canada's tariffs on Chinese EVs
stories.summary: An Ontario company being threatened by a massive retroactive tax bill isn't alone.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — An Ontario company that is being threatened by a massive retroactive tax bill because its golf carts were categorized by Ottawa as electric vehicles (EVs) isn’t alone.

At least one other Canadian company that also has its motorized push carts manufactured in China says it has also received a tax bill from Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) that is large enough to threaten its business.

Hanson Xie, director of operations of Markham, Ont.-based Axglo Inc., says the federal government has told his company to pay about $500,000 in back taxes for the importation of its carts. The three and four-wheeled buggies are just large enough to carry a golf bag, but have never been confused with an electric-powered sedan or sport utility vehicle.

Xie said his six-person company, which has been in the golf cart business since 2009, is profitable but doesn’t have the money to cover an unexpected bill of that size. “What type of small business has $500,000 to pay Cbsa?”

As National Post reported late last month , Xie’s tax tale is similar to JPSMGolf of Pickering, Ont., a competitor that had been hit earlier this year with a tax bill of $178,000. In both cases, the companies are facing hefty interest charges as they look for solutions.

The government has an appeal process for such matters, but companies say they must first either pay their tax bill or post a bond that is lost if they lose the appeal.

It’s unclear how many other Canadian companies that make small motorized products have also been hit with retroactive tax bills because they’ve been categorized as EVs. The domestic golf cart business has only a handful or so players, but small businesses that import and sell mobility scooters, power wheelchairs and other electric or battery-powered gadgets May also fall under the same automotive classification.

In a letter to JPSMGolf earlier this year, Cbsa confirmed its ruling that his golf carts are “undoubtedly” considered EVs because they “are conveyances used by the golfer to get their bag and associated accessories across the golf course during play.”

The government says this golf push cart is a Chinese EV. The tariffs are crippling a Canadian company

Ottawa needs to be more transparent about major projects, think tank says

Finance Canada, which categorizes importers’ goods, was unavailable for comment. When contacted about the JPSMGolf case, a Cbsa spokesperson said that the department couldn’t comment on specific company cases, nor does it have the authority to deviate from the wording of surtax rulings.

But an Ottawa customs broker said he regularly deals with categorization problems. Olexiy Tyshchenko, of Ambassador Customs Brokerage, said not every product fits neatly into one of the government’s specific categories, especially when it comes to new technologies and products.

“This happens quite often,” said Tyshchenko. “I’m not surprised.”

The two Ontario golf cart companies’ retroactive tax bills stem from a 17-month window in 2024-25 where Chinese-made EVs were taxed by Ottawa at a rate of 100 per cent, following a brief trade war between the two countries. The Trudeau government applied the tariff to protect the Canadian auto industry and to stay on side with similar policies by the United States and some other Western countries.

That trade war and the surtax ended earlier this year after the Carney government reached a deal with Beijing to allow 49,000 Chinese EVs (about 3 per cent of the Canadian market) into the Canadian market at a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent. In exchange, China agreed to drop its tariffs on Canadian seafood and some key agricultural products.
