stories.title: Welcome home, Mustangs and Falcons!
stories.summary: Tips for living, learning, and exploring the cityAs post-secondary students settle in, the Ci
stories.content:
As post-secondary students settle in, the City of London welcomes new and returning students to London for the upcoming school year.

Moving to a new city and starting school at the same time can be challenging, but there are lots of tips and resources to help students feel right at home.

Make the most of your time here! There are plenty of ways to get involved and be a part of the community.

The City of London’s website london.ca is a great tool to learn about services and programs, including information about your City Councillor , your neighbourhood , or even your water bill.

We offer many different recreation and sport opportunities at community centres, pools, and arenas. View our programs and courses online to see what’s being offered this fall and winter. Looking for activities on Labour Day? The City is offering free recreation activities across London on September 7, including recreational swimming, Zumba, badminton, yoga, and pickleball.Enjoy the last few days of summer with us!

Looking to gain work experience? We post several internships and student opportunities throughout the year. All current employment opportunities are available online – check back frequently for updates!

Get Involved is our online engagement platform for residents to participate in City projects and initiatives. Your feedback helps us develop new plans and programs for London.

In between studying and classes, be sure to make time to explore all that London has to offer. Visit Tourism London for a guide to things to do and places to see.

In a band and looking to get into the music scene in London? Or just looking to enjoy some live local music? Check out the London Music Office for events, networking opportunities and programming to help make your mark on London’s music scene.

Do you love nature? London has designated Environmentally Significant Areas , which offer many different trails and paths to help you explore local forests, wetlands, and meadows.

With concerts, pop-up markets, cultural events, food and art festivals, there's something for everyone on Dundas Place. Check out the events calendar and join in on the fun!

Looking to hit your step goal or go for a bike ride?

Our bike and walk map can help you discover more than 350 km of pathways, bike lanes and cycle tracks in London, including London’s primary multi-use recreational trail, the Thames Valley Parkway .

Bike lockers are available downtown where you can securely store and lock your bike. Download the Movatic app to begin to use this bike parking.

If you’re using a personal e-scooter, learn more on our website about where they can be used in London.

If you’re taking public transit:

Review your schedule ahead of time and familiarize yourself with LTC routes and service updates that help us ride safely together.

The Transit app can help you plan your trip, check transit routes and get real-time information. As part of a one-year pilot, London Transit riders can access enhanced features at no additional cost, including more trip-planning options and customizable settings such as personalized walking times.

If you’re driving:

If a school bus is displaying flashing red lights, traffic in both directions must stop. You are also required to stop at pedestrian crossovers where people are crossing the street. London also has red light cameras at a number of intersections to make streets safer.

Bus-only lanes separate buses from mixed traffic to help reduce congestion. Do not drive in these bus-only lanes, and watch for signs, red paint, diamonds and arrows to recognize them.

Slow down, follow road and parking signage, and be mindful of others traveling. Help us keep our roads safe .

Construction is underway on Western Road and Philip Aziz Avenue, including road, watermain, sewer, sidewalk and cycling improvements.

Philip Aziz Avenue is currently closed at Western Road and will remain closed until the end of July 2027. Traffic is reduced through the construction area.

Students are invited to a drop-in session on September 9 from noon to 2 p.m. at the UCC to learn about the project, upcoming work and impacts to travel around campus.

The East London Link is a Rapid Transit project connecting Downtown to Fanshawe College, with new transit lanes, road improvements and upgraded infrastructure along the corridor.

As students return to campus in September, construction and lane restrictions on Oxford Street and Highbury Avenue may affect travel to and from Fanshawe. Plan ahead, allow extra time and follow posted detours and signs.

London Transit service will return to London Lane at the Fanshawe College terminal on September 6, following completion of the remaining work at the location.

Check london.ca/roadconstruction for current road construction and closures that may affect your trip to campus, and to see the City’s top 10 construction projects.

Get settled in London by reviewing this important information for your new home.

Service London is the City’s customer service portal. You can report different issues and book a furniture pick-up online at service.london.ca

To report a missed recycling collection or ask a recycling-related question, please contact Miller Waste . Recycling collection is no longer managed by the City.

Put waste in the right place and find your home’s garbage and Green Bin collection dates if you’re living off-campus this year. The Recycle Coach app can also provide you with a personalized collection schedule and reminders about collection dates.

Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are your landlord’s responsibility to install and maintain. Your responsibility is to flag it if they are not working properly. Take the Saved by the Beep pledge and receive a monthly reminder to check your alarms.

The City’s by-laws are in place to keep your new home safe and make sure you’re protected as a tenant. Review some of these common City of London by-laws that can help you and your new home:

The Property Standards By-law addresses property maintenance, pests such as cockroaches, and access to vital services such as heat, hydro or water.

The Yard and Lot Maintenance By-law helps ensure that refuse is not being hoarded, dumped, or poorly contained on properties.

The Sound By-law addresses noise complaints.

The Municipal Waste & Resource Materials Collection By-law requires owners and occupants to keep the boulevard (the grassy portion between the sidewalk and curb) next to their property free of garbage and recyclables.

The Open Air Burning By-law regulates when, where and how you can have outdoor fires. Following these regulations ensures you do not create a nuisance for neighbours.

Have questions about a particular by-law or looking to register a complaint? Connect with our Enforcement team at 519-661-4660 or by email at enforcement@london.ca .

content_blocks.html: Tips for living, learning, and exploring the city

content_blocks.text: As post-secondary students settle in, the City of London welcomes new and returning students to London for the upcoming school year.
content_blocks.html: As post-secondary students settle in, the City of London welcomes new and returning students to London for the upcoming school year.

content_blocks.text: Moving to a new city and starting school at the same time can be challenging, but there are lots of tips and resources to help students feel right at home.
content_blocks.html: Moving to a new city and starting school at the same time can be challenging, but there are lots of tips and resources to help students feel right at home.

content_blocks.text: Londoner starter pack – fun and free things to do
content_blocks.html: Londoner starter pack – fun and free things to do

content_blocks.text: Make the most of your time here! There are plenty of ways to get involved and be a part of the community.
content_blocks.html: Make the most of your time here! There are plenty of ways to get involved and be a part of the community.

items.text: The City of London’s website london.ca is a great tool to learn about services and programs, including information about your City Councillor , your neighbourhood , or even your water bill.
items.html: The City of London’s website london.ca is a great tool to learn about services and programs, including information about your City Councillor, your neighbourhood, or even your water bill.

items.text: We offer many different recreation and sport opportunities at community centres, pools, and arenas. View our programs and courses online to see what’s being offered this fall and winter. Looking for activities on Labour Day? The City is offering free recreation activities across London on September 7, including recreational swimming, Zumba, badminton, yoga, and pickleball.Enjoy the last few days of summer with us!
items.html: We offer many different recreation and sport opportunities at community centres, pools, and arenas. View our programs and courses online to see what’s being offered this fall and winter. Looking for activities on Labour Day? The City is offering free recreation activities across London on September 7, including recreational swimming, Zumba, badminton, yoga, and pickleball.Enjoy the last few days of summer with us!

items.text: Looking to gain work experience? We post several internships and student opportunities throughout the year. All current employment opportunities are available online – check back frequently for updates!
items.html: Looking to gain work experience? We post several internships and student opportunities throughout the year. All current employment opportunities are available online – check back frequently for updates!

items.text: Get Involved is our online engagement platform for residents to participate in City projects and initiatives. Your feedback helps us develop new plans and programs for London.
items.html: Get Involved is our online engagement platform for residents to participate in City projects and initiatives. Your feedback helps us develop new plans and programs for London.

items.text: In between studying and classes, be sure to make time to explore all that London has to offer. Visit Tourism London for a guide to things to do and places to see.
items.html: In between studying and classes, be sure to make time to explore all that London has to offer. Visit Tourism London for a guide to things to do and places to see.

items.text: In a band and looking to get into the music scene in London? Or just looking to enjoy some live local music? Check out the London Music Office for events, networking opportunities and programming to help make your mark on London’s music scene.
items.html: In a band and looking to get into the music scene in London? Or just looking to enjoy some live local music? Check out the London Music Office for events, networking opportunities and programming to help make your mark on London’s music scene.

items.text: Do you love nature? London has designated Environmentally Significant Areas , which offer many different trails and paths to help you explore local forests, wetlands, and meadows.
items.html: Do you love nature? London has designated Environmentally Significant Areas, which offer many different trails and paths to help you explore local forests, wetlands, and meadows.

items.text: With concerts, pop-up markets, cultural events, food and art festivals, there's something for everyone on Dundas Place. Check out the events calendar and join in on the fun!

content_blocks.text: Looking to hit your step goal or go for a bike ride?
content_blocks.html: Looking to hit your step goal or go for a bike ride?

items.text: Our bike and walk map can help you discover more than 350 km of pathways, bike lanes and cycle tracks in London, including London’s primary multi-use recreational trail, the Thames Valley Parkway .
items.html: Our bike and walk map can help you discover more than 350 km of pathways, bike lanes and cycle tracks in London, including London’s primary multi-use recreational trail, the Thames Valley Parkway.

items.text: Bike lockers are available downtown where you can securely store and lock your bike. Download the Movatic app to begin to use this bike parking.
items.html: Bike lockers are available downtown where you can securely store and lock your bike. Download the Movatic app to begin to use this bike parking.

items.text: If you’re using a personal e-scooter, learn more on our website about where they can be used in London.
items.html: If you’re using a personal e-scooter, learn more on our website about where they can be used in London.

content_blocks.text: If you’re taking public transit:
content_blocks.html: If you’re taking public transit:

items.text: Review your schedule ahead of time and familiarize yourself with LTC routes and service updates that help us ride safely together.
items.html: Review your schedule ahead of time and familiarize yourself with LTC routes and service updates that help us ride safely together.

items.text: The Transit app can help you plan your trip, check transit routes and get real-time information. As part of a one-year pilot, London Transit riders can access enhanced features at no additional cost, including more trip-planning options and customizable settings such as personalized walking times.
items.html: The Transit app can help you plan your trip, check transit routes and get real-time information. As part of a one-year pilot, London Transit riders can access enhanced features at no additional cost, including more trip-planning options and customizable settings such as personalized walking times.

content_blocks.text: If you’re driving:
content_blocks.html: If you’re driving:

items.text: If a school bus is displaying flashing red lights, traffic in both directions must stop. You are also required to stop at pedestrian crossovers where people are crossing the street. London also has red light cameras at a number of intersections to make streets safer.
items.html: If a school bus is displaying flashing red lights, traffic in both directions must stop. You are also required to stop at pedestrian crossovers where people are crossing the street. London also has red light cameras at a number of intersections to make streets safer.

items.text: Bus-only lanes separate buses from mixed traffic to help reduce congestion. Do not drive in these bus-only lanes, and watch for signs, red paint, diamonds and arrows to recognize them.
items.html: Bus-only lanes separate buses from mixed traffic to help reduce congestion. Do not drive in these bus-only lanes, and watch for signs, red paint, diamonds and arrows to recognize them.

items.text: Slow down, follow road and parking signage, and be mindful of others traveling. Help us keep our roads safe .
items.html: Slow down, follow road and parking signage, and be mindful of others traveling. Help us keep our roads safe.

content_blocks.html: Construction starter pack – Projects affecting campus

content_blocks.text: Western University:
content_blocks.html: Western University:

items.text: Construction is underway on Western Road and Philip Aziz Avenue, including road, watermain, sewer, sidewalk and cycling improvements.
items.html: Construction is underway on Western Road and Philip Aziz Avenue, including road, watermain, sewer, sidewalk and cycling improvements.

items.text: Philip Aziz Avenue is currently closed at Western Road and will remain closed until the end of July 2027. Traffic is reduced through the construction area.
items.html: Philip Aziz Avenue is currently closed at Western Road and will remain closed until the end of July 2027. Traffic is reduced through the construction area.

items.text: Students are invited to a drop-in session on September 9 from noon to 2 p.m. at the UCC to learn about the project, upcoming work and impacts to travel around campus.
items.html: Students are invited to a drop-in session on September 9 from noon to 2 p.m. at the UCC to learn about the project, upcoming work and impacts to travel around campus.

content_blocks.text: Fanshawe College:
content_blocks.html: Fanshawe College:

items.text: The East London Link is a Rapid Transit project connecting Downtown to Fanshawe College, with new transit lanes, road improvements and upgraded infrastructure along the corridor.
items.html: The East London Link is a Rapid Transit project connecting Downtown to Fanshawe College, with new transit lanes, road improvements and upgraded infrastructure along the corridor.

items.text: As students return to campus in September, construction and lane restrictions on Oxford Street and Highbury Avenue may affect travel to and from Fanshawe. Plan ahead, allow extra time and follow posted detours and signs.
items.html: As students return to campus in September, construction and lane restrictions on Oxford Street and Highbury Avenue may affect travel to and from Fanshawe. Plan ahead, allow extra time and follow posted detours and signs.

items.text: London Transit service will return to London Lane at the Fanshawe College terminal on September 6, following completion of the remaining work at the location.
items.html: London Transit service will return to London Lane at the Fanshawe College terminal on September 6, following completion of the remaining work at the location.

content_blocks.text: Check london.ca/roadconstruction for current road construction and closures that may affect your trip to campus, and to see the City’s top 10 construction projects.
content_blocks.html: Check london.ca/roadconstruction for current road construction and closures that may affect your trip to campus, and to see the City’s top 10 construction projects.

content_blocks.text: Home life starter pack – Waste collection schedule and by-law information
content_blocks.html: Home life starter pack – Waste collection schedule and by-law information

content_blocks.text: Get settled in London by reviewing this important information for your new home.
content_blocks.html: Get settled in London by reviewing this important information for your new home.

items.text: Service London is the City’s customer service portal. You can report different issues and book a furniture pick-up online at service.london.ca
items.html: Service London is the City’s customer service portal. You can report different issues and book a furniture pick-up online at service.london.ca

items.text: To report a missed recycling collection or ask a recycling-related question, please contact Miller Waste . Recycling collection is no longer managed by the City.
items.html: To report a missed recycling collection or ask a recycling-related question, please contact Miller Waste. Recycling collection is no longer managed by the City.

items.text: Put waste in the right place and find your home’s garbage and Green Bin collection dates if you’re living off-campus this year. The Recycle Coach app can also provide you with a personalized collection schedule and reminders about collection dates.
items.html: Put waste in the right place and find your home’s garbage and Green Bin collection dates if you’re living off-campus this year. The Recycle Coach app can also provide you with a personalized collection schedule and reminders about collection dates.

items.text: Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are your landlord’s responsibility to install and maintain. Your responsibility is to flag it if they are not working properly. Take the Saved by the Beep pledge and receive a monthly reminder to check your alarms.
items.html: Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are your landlord’s responsibility to install and maintain. Your responsibility is to flag it if they are not working properly. Take the Saved by the Beep pledge and receive a monthly reminder to check your alarms.

items.text: The City’s by-laws are in place to keep your new home safe and make sure you’re protected as a tenant. Review some of these common City of London by-laws that can help you and your new home:
items.html: The City’s by-laws are in place to keep your new home safe and make sure you’re protected as a tenant. Review some of these common City of London by-laws that can help you and your new home:

items.text: The Property Standards By-law addresses property maintenance, pests such as cockroaches, and access to vital services such as heat, hydro or water.
items.html: The Property Standards By-law addresses property maintenance, pests such as cockroaches, and access to vital services such as heat, hydro or water.

items.text: The Yard and Lot Maintenance By-law helps ensure that refuse is not being hoarded, dumped, or poorly contained on properties.
items.html: The Yard and Lot Maintenance By-law helps ensure that refuse is not being hoarded, dumped, or poorly contained on properties.

items.text: The Sound By-law addresses noise complaints.
items.html: The Sound By-law addresses noise complaints.

items.text: The Municipal Waste & Resource Materials Collection By-law requires owners and occupants to keep the boulevard (the grassy portion between the sidewalk and curb) next to their property free of garbage and recyclables.
items.html: The Municipal Waste & Resource Materials Collection By-law requires owners and occupants to keep the boulevard (the grassy portion between the sidewalk and curb) next to their property free of garbage and recyclables.

items.text: The Open Air Burning By-law regulates when, where and how you can have outdoor fires. Following these regulations ensures you do not create a nuisance for neighbours.
items.html: The Open Air Burning By-law regulates when, where and how you can have outdoor fires. Following these regulations ensures you do not create a nuisance for neighbours.

stories.title: Fanshawe prepares to welcome students back to residence
stories.summary: Media are invited to join Fanshawe as the College prepares to welcome students back to residence
stories.content:
Media are invited to join Fanshawe as the College prepares to welcome students back to residence this weekend in time for the start of the fall semester.

More than 1,600 students will live in one of the College's residence buildings at the London Campus. Just over 1,300 of these students are beginning their first year of post-secondary education.

"For many students, moving into residence is their first big step into college life and, for many of our first-year students, their first time living away from home," says Erica Robertson, general manager of Fanshawe's Residence and Conference Centre. "There’s always a lot of excitement on move-in weekend, along with some nerves for both students and parents. Our goal is to make the experience feel organized, welcoming and supportive from the moment they arrive."

Move-in takes place on Saturday, September 5 and Sunday, September 6. Students will be greeted by a large group of volunteers along with residence staff and residence advisors who will help students get settled in their new home away from home.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.ca

stories.title: Jason Kenney calls for investigation into Alberta separatist party after a mysterious $190,000 surge in donations
stories.summary: Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney urges elections watchdog to investigate a mysterious $190,000 surge flowing into a provincial separatist party.
stories.author: Emma McIntosh
stories.content:
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney is calling on police and the province’s election regulator to investigate the finances of a separatist political party.

Kenney’s comments follow a Star investigation into a mysterious surge in donations into the coffers of the Republican Party of Alberta (RPA), a provincial group that advocates for the province to separate from Canada.

The Star’s analysis found the party received a sudden influx of $190,000 in 2025 despite having reported no donations the year before. The cash came from fewer than 50 people, with more than half of them giving $5,000, the maximum amount allowed under Alberta rules.

The RPA’s donations soon dried up after that initial flood: the party reported just $6,000 in donations in the second half of 2025, and $1,000 in the first quarter of this year.

In an interview with the Star, Kenney said it’s highly unusual for that percentage of donors to give the max amount — especially to a young, populist party, which would typically be fuelled by larger numbers of ordinary people giving smaller amounts of money. Very few people can afford to give thousands of dollars to a political party, he said.

“It just doesn’t add up,” said Kenney, whose call for an investigation was first posted to the social media site X last week. “At the very best, something highly unusual is going on here.”

The RPA and its leader, Cameron Davies, did not answer questions from the Star for this story.

In a statement, Elections Alberta said it cannot publicly comment on what it may or may not be investigating. The agency also pointed to a 2025 change to its governing legislation, which Elections Alberta says raised its threshold for launching a probe. Now, it can only do so if it has “reasonable grounds to believe an offence has occurred.”

“This is a very high threshold, much higher than the threshold imposed on other administrative regulators,” Elections Alberta said. “This is the threshold required by police to arrest someone following an investigation.”

Alberta RCMP spokesperson Fraser Logan said the law enforcement agency can’t comment on whether it has received a complaint or started an investigation. “Further to that, the Alberta RCMP are unable to take these complaints either online or via email,” Logan said. “We encourage anyone with concerns regarding this matter to reach out to their nearest RCMP detachment or their local police.”

The Star also found $18,000 of the donations appear to have been made by four interconnected people based in British Columbia, a violation of Alberta election rules that require donors to legally reside in the province at the time they contribute.

Apollo Chung

One of the four was Apollo Chung, a longtime political operative who has worked for three political parties in B.C., and in 2025 served as executive director of the Alberta Republican Party.

Public records viewed by the Star connected Chung to a Vancouver address. He has not answered questions from the Star, but this week he told the online media outlet PressProgress that he recently lived in Alberta. He did not specify exactly when or how long he lived there.

Most recently, Chung had been director of operations for the B.C. Conservative party, but leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay announced last week that he had been fired. Findlay did not give a reason for the move, but Chung’s departure came after audio recordings were posted online of an unidentified Findlay staffer talking about monetizing their work in politics.

The Star cannot independently verify the authenticity of the audio. Chung told PressProgress that he was speaking in the audio, but that it was “doctored,” presented without context and part of an exaggerated conversation about fundraising. Findlay’s office has not responded to questions from the Star.

In his post, Kenney expressed concern about one of the alleged recordings, pointing out that Chung had also recently held a top role at the RPA. The combination of the alleged audio recording and the unusual fundraising patterns at the RPA raises questions, Kenney said.

“I just, connecting the dots, think that there’s a lot of smoke,” Kenney told the Star. “It all looks to me like something that demands an investigation.”

The RPA’s Davies has previously said that to his knowledge, the party did not accept out-of-province donations.

Kenney was Alberta’s premier from 2019 until he resigned in 2022, under siege from far-right and populist forces within the United Conservative Party he helped create. Over the last year, he has been an outspoken critic of Alberta separatism, which remains a minority opinion on the province as it heads to a referendum on the issue this fall.

The Alberta Republican Party leader previously had an ownership stake in the same polling company that reported support for his new party was surging.

That stance has, at times, appeared to make him a target. Earlier this year, his home address was allegedly revealed to a group of separatist volunteers as part of a massive voter data breach that is now under investigation by Elections Alberta, the RCMP and the province’s privacy commissioner.

The voter data involved in the breach was publicly posted by a separatist group called the Centurion Project, but Elections Alberta said it had originated with the RPA. Neither Davies nor the RPA responded to questions from the Star about the breach.

Kenney, who has repeatedly alleged there are “dodgy” characters in the separatist movement, has history with some of those involved, especially Davies, a longtime conservative political operative in Alberta.

Davies was previously fined by Elections Alberta after the watchdog investigated purported irregularities in the 2017 leadership race that made Kenney the leader of the provincial United Conservative Party. Among them were allegations that senior members of Kenney’s campaign had co-ordinated with another candidate to sling mud at a key rival.

Davies worked on that alleged ‘kamikaze’ campaign, and Elections Alberta later concluded he helped fuel it with illegal donations. The watchdog never accused Kenney of any wrongdoing in the scandal, and Kenney has said he did not know how the ‘kamikaze’ campaign was funded.

Speaking to the Star for this story, Kenney said he attended a meeting with the political operative in 2017 “against my better judgment.”

“I’ve never trusted the guy,” Kenney said.

— with files from Alex Boyd

stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

Dear Parents and Caregivers,

We are excited to welcome you back to Thames Valley for the 2026-2027 school year!

My name is Kevin Auckland, and it is both a privilege and an honour to serve you, and every student throughout Thames Valley, in the role of Chief Executive Officer.

In this role, I am motivated by the opportunity to help guide the system forward with clarity, purpose and an unwavering focus on equity, student achievement and well-being. As we begin another exciting school year, my commitment as your CEO is to listen deeply, communicate transparently and lead alongside you, in service of students. I look forward to sharing monthly updates with you throughout this school year.

We have prepared helpful resources below and on our website to support your family during the transition back to school. You will also receive further information from your child’s school before classes begin, to ensure every student has a great first day.

Thames Valley welcomes and values parents and caregivers as partners in your student’s education. I encourage you to explore the many ways you can be involved in your school community this year, and to reach out to the school directly for support.

Whether you are new to Thames Valley or back for another fulfilling year, I wish your family a strong start this September!

Kevin Auckland Chief Executive Officer Thames Valley District School Board

Elementary and Secondary 2026-2027 School Year Calendars are available on our website. Classes begin on Tuesday, September 8. We look forward to welcoming you back!

View the School Year Calendars

Everyone has a role to play in creating positive school and work environments that are safe, caring and inclusive. The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) Code of Conduct ensures that the rights and responsibilities of all members of the school and Thames Valley community are clearly communicated and understood.

Read the TVDSB Code of Conduct

The beginning of a new school year can be both an exciting and challenging time for many students and will impact their well-being in different ways. Thames Valley has resources available for parents and caregivers to support student mental health and well-being.

Family Well-being Community Workshop Series – Watch pre-recorded webinars presented by local community service providers on a wide variety of topics, including school anxieties and back-to-school worries.

"By Your Side" Parent/Caregiver Resources – Check out School Mental Health Ontario's free online resource hub for parents and caregivers, designed to support mental health learning and well-being for every family.

As part of our ongoing commitment to student account security, the TVDSB student password guidelines require students to reset their passwords at least once a year. Beginning September 1, 2026, all students will be prompted to change their password when they log in to board systems.

Students in Kindergarten to Grade 2 will enter their default password first, then the new password with support from the classroom teachers.

Students in Grades 3 to 12, Continuing Education, and Remote Learning programs will enter their current password, then the new password.

To assist families and students, information about the password reset process, password requirements, and student password guidelines will be available through the TVDSB Parent Portal before school resumes. School staff will also be available to assist students with password resets. Students are encouraged to complete their password change as soon as possible after returning to school. Thank you for supporting safe and secure use of digital learning tools at TVDSB.

stories.title: Conservative MP launches ‘stay’ campaign in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Dane Lloyd, the Conservative MP for the Edmonton-area riding of Parkland, is spearheading the initiative to convince Albertans that the province can do better within Canada.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — With a little more than six weeks before Albertans decide on a question of independence, a new campaign has emerged on the “stay” side targeting the province’s largest voting bloc: Conservatives.

More specifically, the 1.4 million Albertans who cast ballots for Conservative candidates in last year’s federal election.

Dane Lloyd, the party’s MP for the Edmonton-area riding of Parkland, is spearheading the initiative. He says the reason for that focus is “self-evident” in a province historically awash in Conservative blue.

“We are the largest political demographic in Alberta,” he told the Star on Friday. “We have a critical voice that needs to be heard and needs to be engaged.”

Lloyd says the campaign will involve Conservatives from Alberta and beyond, with the focus on getting people engaged ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum through social media, lawn signs, canvassing and phone calls.

It is launching as champions of independence argue that the referendum is less about secession than it is about Alberta’s place within Canada.

“We’re trying to get as many people to understand that Alberta can do better,” said constitutional lawyer and independence advocate Keith Wilson.

Albertans who vote in next month’s referendum will have their choice of two options: “Alberta should remain a province of Canada,” or “The government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

Lloyd was tapped by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre earlier this summer to lead their party’s response to the referendum. He told the Star he has spent the past two months hosting round tables and speaking with Albertans in both the “pro-Canada” and separatist camps.

“What was universal was that every single one of those people viewed themselves as a patriotic Canadian,” Lloyd said.

“What that made clear to me is that this needs to be a campaign that’s focused on reminding people of our love for our country, that it’s fundamental and that, yes, there needs to be change to the status quo,” he said.

“Ottawa does need to change, but that doesn’t mean leaving Canada.”

While Lloyd notes that there are campaigns similar to his, he says they aren’t speaking specifically to Conservative voters.

“It’s a campaign that recognizes that the status quo is not all right. We don’t support the status quo, but fundamentally it’s not a problem with Canada. It’s a problem with Ottawa and that’s where we need to see the change,” he said.

“There’s many campaigns out there talking to many different audiences and our campaign’s focused on reaching that audience — but not just that audience, all Albertans — to try and get them out to vote for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.”

Wilson, who is among the leaders of the independence group “Let Alberta Decide” and helped write a 214-page report outlining a separatist vision for what an independent Alberta could look like, argues the federalist side has “no plan” to deal with what he and others say are the structural issues that constrain Alberta.

While Wilson says “many” supporters of Alberta independence are also support the federal Conservatives, including those who live in Poilievre’s own deep-blue riding of Battle River—Crowfoot, the issue runs deeper than frustrations over seeing the party shut out of power in Ottawa for more than a decade.

He says past attempts to remedy those grievances — from the rise of the populist Reform Party to the election of Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, who famously declared after his first victory that the “West is in” — have failed.

“Many have come to the conclusion that Canada is structurally broken,” Wilson said.

For whatever frustrations exist, Lloyd argues that change is possible, pointing to past battles Alberta has won and ways the province and Conservatives have “been moving the needle” in Ottawa.

“We’re talking about pipelines again as a country,” he said, “and it’s not a conversation about whether or not to have pipelines — it’s about when and how fast we can get pipelines built.”

stories.title: Former Metrolinx CEO Phil Verster joins federal government’s Alto high-speed rail project
stories.summary: Once-embattled Metrolinx CEO Phil Verster is joining the federal government’s $90 billion Alto high-speed rail project. Read about his new role.
stories.author: Andy Takagi
stories.content:
Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Nick Lachance Toronto Star File Photo[](http://www.thestar.com/news/gta/former-metrolinx-CEO-phil-verster-joins-federal-government-s-alto-high-speed-rail-project/article_19bf830c-b844-4ff1-b40d-50ceb7ffe71e.html)

ByAndy Takagi Transportation Reporter

Phil Verster, the once-embattled CEO of provincial transit agency Metrolinx, is making his return to Canadian transit.

Verster will be joining the federal government’s Alto high-speed rail project as a consultant, the Crown corporation confirmed to the Star.

“His work mainly focuses on helping us better understand GTA intermodal and regional transit dynamics, and how to integrate Alto’s HSR service with the existing local transit network,” said Alto spokesperson Caroline Des Rosiers.

Article continues below

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

“His experience also helps us draw lessons from past transit projects in the region as we advance the planning and development of Alto.”

Alto would not say how much Verster would be paid. In his final year at Metrolinx, he was paid $837,097.

Verster did not respond to the Star’s request for comment.

During his seven years at the helm of Metrolinx, Verster oversaw the construction of the Eglinton Crosstown and Finch West LRTs, both of which missed several opening dates promised by Verster and Metrolinx, and ended up costing billions more than initially budgeted.

Originally appointed to the role under then-premier Kathleen Wynne in 2017, Verster — as previously reported by the Star — maintained a contentious relationship with the private contractors that worked on the Eglinton Crosstown.

Verster left the agency in December 2024 and was replaced by current Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay.

According to his LinkedIn, Verster worked as an executive adviser for the Royal Commission of Riyadh City from January to November of 2025.

Now, Verster is set to consult on the largest Canadian transportation project in decades. The Alto high-speed rail line, which is expected to cost as much as $90 billion and open in the 2040s, promises to connect Toronto to Montreal in three hours, with speeds of up to 300 km/h.

With files from Ryan Tumilty and Robert Benzie.

Andy Takagi is the transportation reporter for the Star.Reach him via email: atakagi@thestar.CA

During his seven years at the helm of Metrolinx, Verster oversaw the construction of the Eglinton Crosstown and Finch West LRTs, both of which missed several opening dates promised by Verster and Metrolinx, and ended up costing billions more than initially budgeted.

Originally appointed to the role under then-premier Kathleen Wynne in 2017, Verster — as previously reported by the Star — maintained a contentious relationship with the private contractors that worked on the Eglinton Crosstown.
Verster left the agency in December 2024 and was replaced by current Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay.
According to his LinkedIn, Verster worked as an executive adviser for the Royal Commission of Riyadh City from January to November of 2025.

Now, Verster is set to consult on the largest Canadian transportation project in decades. The Alto high-speed rail line, which is expected to cost as much as $90 billion and open in the 2040s, promises to connect Toronto to Montreal in three hours, with speeds of up to 300 km/h.

stories.title: Leaders of B.C.’s centre-right movements struggling to come together
stories.summary: A void is growing in the province with nine MLAs recently leaving the provincial Conservative party
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Two efforts to build a more centrist alternative to the B.C. Conservatives are emerging from the party’s turmoil, but their leaders are unable to agree on which one should unite voters disillusioned with both the governing NDP and the embattled opposition.

CentreBC Leader Mike Bernier and Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar, who quit the Conservative caucus last month and announced his intention to start a new party, are friends who share many of the same values and much of the same policy agenda. CentreBC was founded in March, 2025, as an option for voters dissatisfied with the Conservatives.

But after several discussions, the two remain at an impasse on forging a united centre-right alternative, raising the prospect of a fractured vote in the future. The next provincial election is scheduled for October, 2028, but could be called much sooner.

“We’re in that weird spot that we’ve got to figure out how to work together, otherwise we’re splitting the vote,” Mr. Bernier said.

Mr. Bernier, a former BC Liberal cabinet minister and MLA for Peace River South, became leader of CentreBC in July, feeling a Conservative party under Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay didn’t represent most British Columbians. CentreBC, founded by former BC United MLA Karin Kirkpatrick in 2025, presents itself as a “socially progressive, fiscally responsible choice.”

Mr. Milobar left the Conservative caucus on Aug. 14, saying his values don’t align with Ms. Findlay’s. Delta South MLA Ian Paton followed suit 10 days later, and the two announced their intention to form a new party with Mr. Milobar as interim leader.

Since Mr. Milobar’s departure, a total of nine sitting MLAs have quit the Conservative caucus, all citing issues with leadership, communication and differences over the party’s direction. The Conservative exodus has fuelled a growing push for a more centrist political option, with defectors and other politicos largely agreeing on the need but not the vehicle.

Ms. Findlay, meanwhile, is doubling down on her leadership, attributing her party’s challenges and disagreements to its rapid growth, while vowing to bring positive change.

The B.C. Conservatives went from having less than 2 per cent of the vote in 2020 to coming within three seats of forming government four years later. Ms. Findlay became the party’s leader in late May.

“I was elected to lead this party, and I intend to lead it with determination, with humility and with the experience to know that strong leaders listen, learn and make changes when changes are needed,” she said in a statement to media on Thursday.

Ms. Findlay has not responded to interview requests from The Globe and Mail.

Mr. Bernier said CentreBC has spent 18 months building the infrastructure of an established party, including its constitution, databases and website. At least 20 candidates have said they want to run for the party, he said.

Lakhwinder Jhaj will be CentreBC’s first candidate in the Sept. 26 Abbotsford-Mission by-election, where Ms. Findlay is vying for a seat. The Conservative leader will face off against Ms. Jhaj, a community advocate and businessperson, and NDP candidate Pam Alexis, a former cabinet minister who represented the riding from 2020 to 2024.

Ms. Jhaj previously ran for the BC Liberals and the NDP, as well as the Liberal Party of Canada.

Mr. Bernier said he made the case to Mr. Milobar that he could build on the organization CentreBC had already put in place.

“I’ve had sit-down meetings with Peter and said, ‘Why would you start up something new and compete against something we’ve already started doing when we should all just be working together on a path to keep that centre, centre-right all in one tent?’ ” he said.

Mr. Bernier added that he has “no ego” in the venture and no attachment to being the one at the helm.

“If we’re able to work together and Peter or somebody else wanted to be the leader of the party, by all means, let’s do that,” he said.

For Mr. Milobar, the question came down to which vehicle could attract enough sitting MLAs to give a new party a foothold in the legislature.

“There just wasn’t traction within the MLAs I was talking to, and others that were contemplating leaving, around CentreBC,” he said. “Some have felt that some of their policy, or where they were headed, is a little left of centre for their liking.”

Having sitting MLAs was important to establish the new party as a viable political force from day one, Mr. Milobar said.

“That revolves around having as many sitting MLAs as possible within a new upstart party so that you can generate the news, you can be recognized inside the legislature and you can get that extra credibility and attention that comes with being an official party with seats inside of the legislature,” he said.

Mr Milobar said he is working with lawyers on the party’s constitution and expects the new organization to be up and running when the legislature’s fall session begins Oct. 5.

Randy Hawes, the former Conservative riding association president for Abbotsford-Mission, is among those trying to get the parties to work together, arguing that anything else is “just handing the NDP the government again.”

Mr. Hawes resigned from his position on Aug. 24 after learning through media reports that MLA Reann Gasper had given up her seat to give Ms. Findlay a chance to run.

“I don’t see this going anywhere unless they unite,” he said. “That’s an absolute must.”

stories.title: Ottawa issues comprehensive climate report that reflects country’s physical transformation
stories.summary: From retreating glaciers to wildfires and marine heat waves, climate change will likely become even more pronounced, assessment finds
stories.author: Jenn Thornhill Verma, Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Canadians are feeling the effects of climate change to a greater degree and facing more serious consequences than federal scientists projected less than a decade ago.

That’s the message in a comprehensive federal report released on Thursday. It details how climate change is physically transforming the country and how those trends are likely to become more pronounced in the future, from floods, wildfires and heat waves to vanishing glaciers and permafrost.

A striking feature of the report is the high degree of certainty that ties so many diverse effects to fossil-fuel emissions as the primary driver of climate change.

“Warming temperatures have driven wide-ranging, interconnected, and sustained changes across Canada,” the report notes unequivocally in one of its headline statements .

Running nearly 1,500 pages, Canada’s Changing Climate Report 2026 is the country’s definitive statement on the physical state of the climate. Only the second such document ever issued by the federal government, it is the product of more than 100 experts working over a three-year period.

But unlike its predecessor, whose release in 2019 was widely publicized and accompanied by minister-led press conferences and technical briefings to help the public grasp its implications, the second edition was quietly posted online ahead of a late-summer holiday weekend.

The report arrives at a sharply different political moment. In late June, Prime Minister Mark Carney conceded Canada will not meet its 2030 greenhouse-gas emissions targets.

A statement from Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin’s office did not address the report’s findings. It said the government is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 through “a pragmatic and durable approach,” citing clean-energy investments, $2.1-billion committed to the National Adaptation Strategy and a new goal of $13-billion in international climate finance over five years.

The minister was not available for an interview.

Even so, the report requires little interpretation: Much of what was anticipated in 2019 has now come to pass, plus more that was not yet on climate scientists’ radar then.

Canada has warmed about two degrees since 1948 and Northern Canada about 2.6 degrees. Since 1970, the country has warmed nearly twice as fast as the global average, and the Canadian Arctic three times as fast. Precipitation is up 9.7 per cent nationally since 1949, and 18.9 per cent in the North. Human influence, the report finds, is the only explanation for the collective changes observed.

“We have fundamentally altered our climate system, and even if we do succeed at limiting warming to a certain threshold, there are parts of our environment that will continue to change,” said Chris Derksen, director of the Climate Modelling Research Division at Environment and Climate Change Canada.

A hotter and wetter North

Average annual temperature and precipitation increased measurably in Canada from the late 1940s to 2023, with the trend growing more pronounced after 1970. The Arctic has experienced the most rapid change and is now 2.6°C warmer on average than it was less than a century ago, especially in the northwest during winter months. The averages do not capture weather extremes, which have also increased in severity during the same time period.

Change in annual temperature (1948–2023)

Dotted areas indicate statistically insignificant changes

Change in annual precipitation (1949–2023)

The globe and mail, source:

Environment and climate change Canada

Some of the changes are fixed: Sea level rise, glacier melt and permafrost thaw will continue even if temperatures stabilize. Western Canada’s glaciers will largely disappear by the end of this century. Other changes are a choice. Under current global policies, Canada warms five degrees above preindustrial levels by century’s end. Under a scenario with no climate policies, warming reaches 6.9 degrees and the area burned by wildfire climbs 287 per cent. Under net zero, warming stabilizes after 2050 and reaches 3.5 degrees.

Extremes are where warming is already being felt, and the rarer the event, the more it changes: A once-in-50-years heat extreme occurs nearly four times as often at two degrees of global warming. Droughts and flash floods will become more frequent and severe. Fire seasons are already longer.

“Every increment of warming will cost us more in damages,” Dr. Derksen said. “It will cost us more to adapt to those changes.”

And on comparable scenarios, the warming now projected for Canada is greater than the last assessment estimated.

This week, a United Nations Environment Programme report concluded the world will cross 1.5 degrees of warming within the next few years – the tougher of the two limits nearly 200 countries, including Canada, set in Paris a decade ago.

If the 2019 edition made the predictions, then the 2026 report provides the receipts. The inaugural report warned of more intense heat, heavier rain, deeper drought and worsening fire risk. Canada then experienced the 2021 B.C. heat dome, the floods that levelled the province’s highways that November, years of drought on the Prairies and the record 2023 fire season. The current edition puts those risks in plainer language – heat extremes, flooding, drought, fire weather – and adds marine heat waves.

Summer sea surface temperatures have risen everywhere in Canada, but most sharply in Atlantic Canada and Hudson Bay, by as much as 2.5 degrees. Off Nova Scotia, marine heat wave conditions have persisted more than 100 days annually on the Scotian Shelf almost every year since 2012. The ocean is also acidifying and losing oxygen below the surface.

The report is clear that Canadians are stuck with some of these changes, said Sabine Dietz, executive director of CLIMAtlantic, one of five regional climate service providers. However, she said, “every point of a degree that we can bring the temperature back down or we can reduce the increase, we will benefit from it.”

Christina Caron and Glen Hodgson: Not addressing climate change costs the economy more. When will we finally get this?

That Canada can see these changes coming at all is a function of its own capacity. Dr. Derksen said his department runs one of roughly 15 Earth system models in the world.

And while much of what Canadians can expect from the climate over the next 10 to 20 years is largely a given because of past choices, the scenarios diverge more widely when projected further into the future.

“We made a lot of effort to show that end-of-century climate changes are still very much dependent on political decisions that are made now,” said Damon Matthews, a professor and climate scientist at Concordia University in Montreal who was co-lead author on the chapter of the report that deals with future projections.

Similar to the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change physical science volume, the report describes the changes under way and what the models project, but stops short of prescribing what to do about them.

“The big question is, so what? So what do we do with this?” said Alain Bourque, head of Ouranos, the Quebec climate services consortium whose scientists contributed to the assessment.

That question is also the agenda of Adaptation Canada 2026, a national conference in Toronto later this month where the report’s authors will meet practitioners.

For Mr. Bourque, the answer must involve policies that drive toward carbon neutrality. Short of that, the report lays a foundation for those seeking to understand the effects on individuals and communities.

“Canadians and Ontarians must prepare for a hotter future and act now to avoid the worst impacts,” said Ewa Jackson, director of the Ontario Resource Centre for Climate Adaptation.

“Ultimately, warming in Canada will stop only when global emissions reach net zero,” said Sherilee Harper, a professor and Canada Research Chair in climate change and health at the University of Alberta. “Until then, every fraction of a degree we avoid will quite literally save lives.”

It said the government is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 through “a pragmatic and durable approach,” citing clean-energy investments, $2.1-billion committed to the National Adaptation Strategy and a new goal of $13-billion in international climate finance over five years.
The minister was not available for an interview.
Even so, the report requires little interpretation: Much of what was anticipated in 2019 has now come to pass, plus more that was not yet on climate scientists’ radar then.

Canada has warmed about two degrees since 1948 and Northern Canada about 2.6 degrees. Since 1970, the country has warmed nearly twice as fast as the global average, and the Canadian Arctic three times as fast. Precipitation is up 9.7 per cent nationally since 1949, and 18.9 per cent in the North. Human influence, the report finds, is the only explanation for the collective changes observed.

“We have fundamentally altered our climate system, and even if we do succeed at limiting warming to a certain threshold, there are parts of our environment that will continue to change,” said Chris Derksen, director of the Climate Modelling Research Division at Environment and Climate Change Canada.
A hotter and wetter North

Average annual temperature and precipitation increased measurably in Canada from the late 1940s to 2023, with the trend growing more pronounced after 1970. The Arctic has experienced the most rapid change and is now 2.6°C warmer on average than it was less than a century ago, especially in the northwest during winter months. The averages do not capture weather extremes, which have also increased in severity during the same time period.
Change in annual temperature (1948–2023)
Dotted areas indicate statistically insignificant changes
Change in annual precipitation (1949–2023)
The globe and mail, source:
Environment and climate change Canada

Some of the changes are fixed: Sea level rise, glacier melt and permafrost thaw will continue even if temperatures stabilize. Western Canada’s glaciers will largely disappear by the end of this century. Other changes are a choice. Under current global policies, Canada warms five degrees above preindustrial levels by century’s end. Under a scenario with no climate policies, warming reaches 6.9 degrees and the area burned by wildfire climbs 287 per cent. Under net zero, warming stabilizes after 2050 and reaches 3.5 degrees.

Extremes are where warming is already being felt, and the rarer the event, the more it changes: A once-in-50-years heat extreme occurs nearly four times as often at two degrees of global warming. Droughts and flash floods will become more frequent and severe. Fire seasons are already longer.
“Every increment of warming will cost us more in damages,” Dr. Derksen said. “It will cost us more to adapt to those changes.”
And on comparable scenarios, the warming now projected for Canada is greater than the last assessment estimated.

This week, a United Nations Environment Programme report concluded the world will cross 1.5 degrees of warming within the next few years – the tougher of the two limits nearly 200 countries, including Canada, set in Paris a decade ago.

If the 2019 edition made the predictions, then the 2026 report provides the receipts. The inaugural report warned of more intense heat, heavier rain, deeper drought and worsening fire risk. Canada then experienced the 2021 B.C. heat dome, the floods that levelled the province’s highways that November, years of drought on the Prairies and the record 2023 fire season. The current edition puts those risks in plainer language – heat extremes, flooding, drought, fire weather – and adds marine heat waves.

Summer sea surface temperatures have risen everywhere in Canada, but most sharply in Atlantic Canada and Hudson Bay, by as much as 2.5 degrees. Off Nova Scotia, marine heat wave conditions have persisted more than 100 days annually on the Scotian Shelf almost every year since 2012. The ocean is also acidifying and losing oxygen below the surface.

The report is clear that Canadians are stuck with some of these changes, said Sabine Dietz, executive director of CLIMAtlantic, one of five regional climate service providers. However, she said, “every point of a degree that we can bring the temperature back down or we can reduce the increase, we will benefit from it.”
Christina Caron and Glen Hodgson: Not addressing climate change costs the economy more. When will we finally get this?
That Canada can see these changes coming at all is a function of its own capacity. Dr. Derksen said his department runs one of roughly 15 Earth system models in the world.

And while much of what Canadians can expect from the climate over the next 10 to 20 years is largely a given because of past choices, the scenarios diverge more widely when projected further into the future.

“We made a lot of effort to show that end-of-century climate changes are still very much dependent on political decisions that are made now,” said Damon Matthews, a professor and climate scientist at Concordia University in Montreal who was co-lead author on the chapter of the report that deals with future projections.

Similar to the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change physical science volume, the report describes the changes under way and what the models project, but stops short of prescribing what to do about them.
“The big question is, so what? So what do we do with this?” said Alain Bourque, head of Ouranos, the Quebec climate services consortium whose scientists contributed to the assessment.
That question is also the agenda of Adaptation Canada 2026, a national conference in Toronto later this month where the report’s authors will meet practitioners.

For Mr. Bourque, the answer must involve policies that drive toward carbon neutrality. Short of that, the report lays a foundation for those seeking to understand the effects on individuals and communities.
“Canadians and Ontarians must prepare for a hotter future and act now to avoid the worst impacts,” said Ewa Jackson, director of the Ontario Resource Centre for Climate Adaptation.

“Ultimately, warming in Canada will stop only when global emissions reach net zero,” said Sherilee Harper, a professor and Canada Research Chair in climate change and health at the University of Alberta. “Until then, every fraction of a degree we avoid will quite literally save lives.”

stories.title: “It just picked the shed up and put it in the neighbour’s field”: Shocked residents picking up pieces following massive storm
stories.summary: A large shed used to cover the Eedy family’s farm machinery, but now that shed is a rolled up ball of metal and wood.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A large shed used to cover the Eedy family’s farm machinery, but now that shed is a rolled up ball of metal and wood.

“It was a tornado. A tornado came through late yesterday afternoon,” said Sandra Eedy, who lives and farms near Winthrop.

While the Eedy’s themselves walked away unscathed, a mechanic working on their combine in the shed, held onto that combine for dear life, as the storm rolled through Huron and Perth counties, around 5:30 p.m. Wednesday.

“He did come out unscathed, but not without a lot of bad memories. The walls just fell out. But, I assume that’s after the roof came off. So ,that’s the mess. The steel is everywhere. It went right across the county road. How nobody was in the path of that when it was coming through, is amazing, It’s probably best, because there could have been actually more people hurt from it, as it was going through the air,” said Eedy.

A few concessions away, Kevin Murray’s family got hit with a double whammy, damage to their home, and the entire loss of their family’s century old barn.

“The grain bin, it moved from it’s foundation, and our barn next door, it’s down, and a bunch of the neighbors sheds and barns are down, too. It’s pretty bad,” said the Winthrop area farmer.

On Sawmill Road near Winthrop, more than six sheds or barns were flattened by the violent storm. Further east, towards Monkton, a 5 storey high steel grain bin bent in half, by Wednesday’s strong winds.

In Seaforth, the local golf course lost more than 50 trees, and is closed indefinitely. All told, damage stretches from as far west as Bayfield, and as far east as Cambridge. The hardest hit areas of Midwestern Ontario, appear to be concentrated on an area from Seaforth, Egmondville, and Clinton, through Kinburn, Winthrop, Brodhagen, Bornholm, and south of Monkton.

Hydro remains out for thousands of residents in Huron and Perth Counties.

“I was just moving my truck from underneath those trees there, and I put it in the back yard, and then the wind came up, and I couldn’t even see the highway for the rain. Some lady pulled in my laneway because she couldn’t see. And so I sat there till it let up a bit, and my neighbor ran across the road to me and said, your tree fell down on your house. I never even seen it. I never heard it. So, I come out here, and there it is,” said Tony McDonald, cleaning up a tree leaning on his house in Kinburn.

Tornado investigators with the Northern Tornadoes Project are in the region, combing through the damage. With no visible funnel clouds caught on camera, they’re not yet able to say the damage in Huron and Perth Counties is from a tornado, but whatever it was, it left a swath of field and property damage across a vast area.

“Scott, it’s just like it picked it up, picked the shed up, and put it in the neighbor’s field. That’s essentially what happened,” said Eedy.

“The trampoline took out our hydro wire to the house. I have never seen anything like that. We had hail come in ‘91, but nothing like this at all. The fields are flat, the corn’s flat. It’s not nice, at all,” said Murray.
